perModule.summary: This module is the foundation everything else in the engine stands on, and it is the weakest part of the codebase I looked at. There is one live gameplay bug (RectangleF::get_edges returns a non-cyclic edge order that StructurePaintable indexes as clockwise, so levels marking their right face paintable get the left face painted) and one live collision bug the reviewers only stumbled on sideways (triangles_intersect checks 4 of the 9 edge pairs, so two triangles can genuinely cross and be reported disjoint). Beyond those, the striking pattern is how much of the surface is dead and wrong at the same time: Vector2F::cross is not a cross product, MattMath::sign is not a sign function, rotate_vector_by_ref clobbers its own input, Colour::desaturate is a verbatim copy of saturate, and MatrixF never allocates its storage so every matrix factory writes out of bounds — none of it has a single caller, all of it is shipped in the public engine header. Structurally, the two decisions that most block the reusable-engine goal are making RectangleF (the universal AABB and value type) inherit a polymorphic Shape, and welding d3d11.h and SimpleMath into the math header for the sake of four Viewport members. The reviewers were broadly accurate on facts and consistently overstated consequences: several NaN-propagation stories die on inspection because the setters validate and throw, the 'crashes level loading' claim is unreachable because every ramp-gradient consumer is commented out, and the Colour.h cost figures ('58 of 81 TUs', '30,000 hex parses') are unsupported. I confirmed 49 distinct issues after merging, rejected 3 escalations outright, and downgraded roughly a dozen severities; I also found two defects the reviewers missed — the triangles_intersect loop bounds and the Segment-based RectangleRotated constructor that never normalises its axes and therefore throws for essentially every input.
themes: Dead-and-wrong public API: cross, sign, rotate_vector_by_ref, desaturate and the entire MatrixF/Matrix3x3F subsystem are all defective and all uncalled — shipped in the engine header waiting for a first caller

Value types fused with polymorphic behaviour: RectangleF/Circle/Triangle/Quad inherit Shape, costing a vptr, constexpr-ability, safe assignment and trivial copyability on the engine's most-copied type

Duplication instead of abstraction: four unitisation functions with two contradictory zero-length contracts, five copies of the camera transform, six retypings of the convex-vs-convex intersection algorithm — and the copies have already diverged into real bugs

Silent failure on external data: colour_from_name returns WHITE for unknown names, set_from_hex returns black for anything not 6 or 8 chars, from_top_left_bottom_right accepts inverted rectangles, RectangleF::intersection encodes 'no overlap' as a rectangle at the origin

No language-level guardrails: zero explicit, zero nodiscard, exact float == on every type under /fp:fast, an absolute 1e-4 epsilon at world coordinates of 6000, and no <LanguageStandard> set at all so the project silently builds as C++14
Game concerns leaking into engine headers: Splatoon team colours in colour_consts, a paintable-face convention encoded as Segment equality, and Camera/Viewport living inside the math library

perModule.summary: I read every cited line range in MattMath.h (all 1139 lines), the Circle/Triangle/Quad/Segment/Camera/RectangleRotated regions of MattMath.cpp, shape_type.h, rotation_origin.h, the relevant EricsonMath routines, and the first-party callers (StructurePaintable, LevelObjectBuilder, Structure, Level, Player, CollisionTools, Visual, DrawObject) plus both vcxproj files. Of 104 candidates I confirmed all of them after merging ~50 duplicate pairs and triples down to 66 distinct findings; I rejected none outright, but I downgraded four graded "critical" (nothing here crashes, corrupts memory or loses data in a live path) and corrected three factual overstatements: TriangleRightAxisAligned slicing does not read past the object (the subclass adds no data members, so only the dynamic type is lost); the unchecked dynamic_cast in Shape::intersects cannot currently produce a null dereference because every subclass's shape_type tag matches its dynamic type; and the uninitialised `t` in the segments_intersect wrapper is never read back. The genuinely dangerous cluster is the shape-interface contracts: get_edges() has no defined ordering and RectangleF's differs from every other shape's, which is a live gameplay bug in StructurePaintable (a level declaring its bottom face paintable paints the right face); inflate() means three different things across five implementations with three different failure policies; and triangles_intersect only tests 4 of the 9 edge pairs, silently missing real collisions throughout the quad and OBB paths. RectangleRotated, the newest code, is better structured than its neighbours but is not yet correct: its Segment constructor throws for every input, its edges_valid() is provably vacuous, its axis setters can never actually rotate it, and its point-in-OBB query allocates three vectors and runs a full Quad validation to answer a two-dot-product question. Two additional real bugs outside the candidate set that I noticed while verifying: Vector2F::cross (MattMath.cpp:1720-1723) returns (x*oy, y*ox) instead of the scalar x*oy - y*ox, and Vector2F::rotate_vector_by_ref (1800-1806) uses the already-overwritten vec.x when computing vec.y. Also worth a look: RectangleRotated::operator== / operator!= are declared (MattMath.h:1110-1111) but never defined anywhere in MattMath.cpp, so any use is a link error, and StructurePaintable stores `const std::vector<Segment>&` (StructurePaintable.h:56) bound to a stack local created in LevelObjectBuilder.cpp:107.
themes: Undefined interface contracts on Shape: get_edges() ordering, inflate() semantics, and the missing contains()/transform() are unspecified, so polymorphic callers get different geometry depending on the concrete type behind the pointer - the biggest blocker to MattMath being a reusable engine core, and it has already produced a live face-painting bug in StructurePaintable.

Validation theatre in Quad and RectangleRotated: constructors and setters throw aggressively, but the checks run before the state they validate exists (edges_valid), use absolute epsilons on size-dependent quantities, mutate before validating so a throw leaves the object corrupt, and are bypassed entirely by `= default` default constructors that produce objects failing the class's own is_valid().

Allocation-heavy hot paths: get_edges/get_points/get_triangles all return std::vector by value, RectangleRotated caches four fixed corners in a heap vector rebuilt on nine mutators, point-in-OBB round-trips through a validating Quad, and the OBB 'cheap AABB early-out' is more expensive than the test it guards - all inside an O(n^2) per-frame loop that CollisionTools reruns dozens of times per contact.

Copy-paste divergence: two calculate_gradient bodies, two calculate_points overloads, four calculate_view_rectangle spellings, two normalize implementations with different zero-guard policies, three EPSILON constants, and three parallel intersection APIs - each pair free to drift, and several already have.

Missing or wrong maths in the newest code: unnormalised axes in the Segment constructor, exterior instead of interior triangle angles, a vertex index used as an edge index, an unsigned get_angle(), an unclamped acos, and a Camera 'inverse' that is the reciprocal of the correct transform and works only because its sole caller passes the arguments in the wrong slots.

The project builds as C++14 (no LanguageStandard in either vcxproj), which forces hand-rolled clamp/lerp/PI, blocks std::optional and constexpr constants, and leaves the shape constants as dynamically-initialised statics with cross-TU ordering hazards.

perModule.summary: This module group is where the engine ambition and the actual code diverge most sharply. Collision response is a 40-iteration bisection search that mutates geometry in place rather than computing a contact manifold; there is no normal, no penetration depth, and no minimum-translation vector anywhere, so "collision direction" ends up being a centre-to-centre unit vector that callers quantise to eight compass points and throw an uncaught exception on when it doesn't match. That single missing abstraction (`Contact { normal, penetration }`) accounts for the majority of the real bugs here: the sign-inverted push-out for the up-left quadrant, the swapped band cases in the edge classifier, the inverted containment axis, the depth query that heap-clones a shape and re-runs the whole resolver to answer one boolean, and the silent failure to separate anything penetrating deeper than its own bounding box while unconditionally returning true. EricsonMath is a partly-adapted transcription of a 3D textbook: roughly 40% of both files is commented-out dead code, four exported functions have zero callers, three divisions are unguarded against degenerate geometry reachable from level JSON, and `closest_pt_point_OBB` still loops over three axes of a two-axis type so it throws on every possible call. `Partitioner` is misnamed — it splits index ranges for thread scheduling, while the spatial partitioning its name promises does not exist at all, leaving `Level::update_level_logic` testing every pair twice per frame with no broad phase. `collision_object_type` is the sharpest engine-reuse violation: a 23-value cross-product of object kind, team and weapon returned by the engine's own `ICollisionGameObject`, with seven hand-maintained predicates of which five are dead and one is duplicated verbatim in `Level::count_projectiles`. `Mh.h` is a whole UI toolkit in a two-letter file with raw non-owning children, containers declared before the widgets they point at, and one `is_visible_in_viewport` that calls itself. Of the 105 candidates, I confirmed the substance of nearly all of them but merged them down to 48 and corrected several overstated consequences — most notably that the `std::max` sign bug is currently unobservable, that the `ThreadPool` `-1` default is unreachable, and that the `MTexture` recursion is latent rather than a live crash.
themes: No contact manifold: resolution is a 40-iteration bisection over mutated geometry instead of an analytic MTV, which is the root cause of the sign-inversion, band-swap, containment-axis, depth-by-simulation and silent-failure-to-separate bugs

3D textbook code ported to 2D without adapting it: a 3-axis loop on a 2-axis type that throws unconditionally, hand-unrolled axis blocks with a zero-velocity hole, ~40% commented-out dead code, and four exported functions with zero callers

Game rules welded into engine types: collision identity is a class x team x weapon cross-product enum on the engine's own collision interface, ramp facing is a collision category, and DirectX::SpriteBatch is baked into the root game-object interface

Missing and misnamed abstractions: 'Partitioner' splits thread work while no spatial broad phase exists, both call sites hand-roll the same parallel_for, and the quadratic collision loop runs every pair twice per frame single-threaded

Contracts encoded in comments rather than types: documented zero-vector returns that never happen, ZERO overloaded as both sentinel and legal direction, out-params unwritten on failure paths, discarded bool results, and raw mutable Shape* with no null or aliasing guards

Ownership left undefined: raw non-owning children in MContainer with containers declared before the widgets they alias, a base-class pointer into a derived-owned unique_ptr, and a stateless class heap-allocated and threaded through four layers as a bare pointer

Build configuration is not doing its job: no LanguageStandard (so C++14, forcing hand-rolled clamp and out-param APIs), no TreatWarningAsError despite /W4, and /fp:fast under exact float equality comparisons

perModule.summary: This module group is the sharpest illustration of the engine-vs-game problem in the codebase: Player.cpp is 1263 lines and Player.h declares ~90 members, fusing kinematics, an eight-direction collision responder, two sprite hierarchies, audio cues, camera and viewport state, input, weapon ownership and Splatoon rules (teams, respawn timers, a per-weapon damage table) into a single `final` class that inherits `DrawObject` twice through a non-virtual diamond — so it can never even be converted to a drawable. There is one genuine critical defect: `Player::draw` mutates animation and sprite-sheet state (including two `std::string` members) and `Level::draw_active_level` submits one thread-pool task per player, each of which draws every player, so the same object's `draw` runs concurrently on N threads with no synchronisation. Below that sit several real correctness bugs — the input vector is positionally compacted so a controller drop-out shifts every player's controls and reads past the end of the vector in `Level`; spawn points are chosen with the global player index into per-team arrays; dead players keep firing invisible projectiles; the `STRUCTURE_RAMP_LEFT` collision branch is an empty `// TODO` that the level loader will happily feed; and `on_no_collision` forgets `ON_CEILING`. Two whole subsystems are dead weight: `ProjectileDetails::player_damage` has zero call sites while `player_consts` maintains a second, wildly divergent damage table, and sixteen private `Player` accessors plus `_score` and `_secondary_type` are never called by anything. Of the 100 candidates, I rejected two substantive claims that did not survive checking — the "tunnelling through 25 px platforms" scenario is geometrically impossible for a 120 px-tall AABB moving 31.7 px per fixed frame, and the "free jump after respawn" scenario cannot occur because `on_no_collision` runs on every dead frame — and I downgraded several others whose consequences were overstated.
themes: Player is a god class with a non-virtual DrawObject diamond — no part of it is reusable without the Splatoon rules attached
Rendering mutates simulation state, and the parallel draw path makes that an unsynchronised data race on std::string members
Index-by-position contracts with unchecked operator[]: compacted input vectors and global-index-into-per-team spawn arrays
Game rules welded into the entity — a hardcoded per-weapon damage ladder, a hardcoded sound bank name, and team hostility as ten enum comparisons
Duplicate sources of truth everywhere: two damage tables, three team-colour copies, two dt pointers, two COUNTDOWN constant blocks, two identical input setters
Large volumes of dead code the compiler cannot see — 16 unused accessors, two unreferenced headers, unreachable throw branches, and /W4 warnings (C4189, C4062) that nobody reads
Caller-owned invariants: Level must drive a precise seven-call-per-frame sequence, and const is meaningless because unique_ptr launders mutation

perModule.summary: The weapons module carries two verified showstoppers on normal code paths: `Weapon::stop_sounds()` throws for Sniper and Bucket, and it is called for every player at the end of every round with no catch anywhere on the tick path, so any match containing either weapon terminates the process; and `Weapon::draw` mutates its own `std::string`/origin/effects/rotation state while being entered concurrently by up to 16 Win32 thread-pool threads, because each split-screen draw task iterates all players. Beyond those, the module is structurally the opposite of the reusable-engine goal it is supposed to demonstrate: `Weapon` inherits `TextureObject` (so the whole module compiles against DirectX), owns rendering, input parsing, ammo economy, fire timing, audio and projectile spawning in one class, hardcodes Splatoon's two-team/four-player model into its constructor and into a struct's field names, and its base class switches on `wep_type` to name sounds - so the base knows the complete list of its own subclasses. Tuning is a compile-time C++ table of internal-linkage aggregates duplicated into every translation unit, while levels and sound banks already load from JSON. There is a second tier of real but latent defects clustered around the same seams: `add_player_velocity::NONE` falls into the `Y_ONLY` branch, `RelativeVelocityWeapon`'s `shoot`/`calculate_projectile_launch_velocity` hide rather than override the base virtuals (which is why the update loop had to be duplicated), and fire rate is quantised to the tick with `shoot_interval` values of 0.0f and 0.0001f feeding an uncapped projectile list into an O(n^2) collision sweep. I rejected three candidate findings outright - the "redundant includes" claim (direct includes of directly-used types are correct), the claimed static-initialisation-order fiasco between the two consts headers (same TU, defined first), and the claimed ill-formed duplicate `case MAX_PRIM_WEP` (no switch in the repo lists it) - and downgraded several enum/hiding issues from high to medium because they are traps rather than live bugs.
themes: Throwing from teardown and lookup paths: get_sound_effect_instance_name(), get_sound_name() and WeaponBuilder all throw std::exception on a default case, and none of those paths has a catch - a missing sound becomes a terminated process

Mutable draw state on shared objects: the whole draw path is 'set members, then draw' rather than 'pass parameters', which is both the source of the multi-threaded data race and the reason draw cannot be const

Type tags standing in for polymorphism: wep_type is simultaneously the factory discriminator, a stored member, a menu option and an array bound, and the base class switches on it - so adding a weapon means editing the base

Game rules welded into what should be engine code: player_team, player_num, team_colour, PlayerInputData and the 2x4 sound-name matrix are all baked into the base Weapon and into WeaponDetails' field names

Hierarchy used to carry data: RelativeVelocityWeapon exists for two floats, Sniper/Bucket exist for one-shot vs looping audio, and each split costs a duplicated update loop, a duplicated shoot, a duplicated draw, or two identical overrides

Non-owning raw pointers cached with no contract: _dt, _resource_manager (duplicated with the base's copy) and _sound_bank (from a lookup that silently returns nullptr) are stored for the object's lifetime and propagated into every projectile

Dead surface area: five never-called accessors, two never-set flags gating unreachable draw branches, five constructor parameters no caller ever passes, and three parameters no body reads - carried identically across ten files

Toolchain drift: no <LanguageStandard> in the vcxproj means C++14, which blocks inline constexpr, string_view, std::clamp and [[nodiscard]]; no TreatWarningAsError means the /W4 C4100 warnings this module generates are invisible

perModule.summary: The projectile module has four live correctness bugs, three of which I could trace all the way to a process kill or a broken weapon: `get_delete_timer()` returns `_timer` so the lifetime check is a self-comparison and no projectile ever expires (which then meets `Level`'s unconditional `throw` on out-of-bounds objects, with no handler anywhere on the update path); `ProjectileMist` tags itself `SPRAY`, making two collision-type enumerators unreachable; `ProjectileRolling::update()` never applies its computed displacement or advances its animation, so the roller weapon does not work at all; and the hand-rolled structure filter omits both ramp types even though `is_structure()` in the same codebase covers them and the shipped level contains a ramp. Every one of these is a symptom of the same structural problem rather than an isolated slip — state that should be derived is instead hand-copied into five near-identical leaf classes, and predicates that exist once are re-typed by hand in six places. Against the stated goal of a reusable engine, the module's biggest liability is not the bugs but the layering: `player_team`, two-team Splatoon rules and a `weapon x team` cross-product enum are compile-time dependencies of the base `Projectile` class, so free-for-all, 3+ teams and neutral projectiles are literally unrepresentable, and a projectile cannot express any effect beyond "delete me" because the effect is implemented by whatever it hits. The data layer is half-dead: four of nine `ProjectileDetails`/`DiffusionDetails` fields are never read, damage lives in a second table in `player_consts.h` with the opposite sign convention, and the render-size/collision-size split the struct promises is unimplemented. Of the 82 candidates I received, all described real code — I found no outright fabrication — but they collapsed to 35 distinct findings after merging, and I downgraded several consequences that were overstated (the `std::map` draw-path race is latent rather than live corruption; the rolling hitboxes are deleted on structure contact rather than immortal; the interior-pointer and default-constructor hazards are API traps with no current caller). One sub-claim was simply wrong and I corrected it in place: `Weapon::get_projectile_builder()` does have a caller, at Weapon.cpp:565.
themes: Hand-copied state that should be derived: the projectile_type tag, the structure-type list, the update() prologue and the centring offset are each duplicated across five leaf classes, and each has already drifted at least once (mist tagged SPRAY, ramps missing from both copies of the structure filter, Rolling missing its offset and animation tick)

Game rules welded into what should be engine code: player_team, a two-team switch with a throwing default, and a weapon-x-team cross-product collision_object_type enum are all compile-time dependencies of the base Projectile class, and the enum is re-expanded by hand in six files

Accessors that return the wrong member: get_delete_timer() returns _timer, get_col_rect_size() and get_base_size() return `size` instead of `col_rect_size` — all three hidden by identically-shaped names and by tuning data where the two fields happen to be equal

Half-dead data layer: rotat_origin, diffusion_type, player_damage and delete_timer are written by every constant and read by nothing, while the damage that is actually applied lives in a second table with the opposite sign convention and magnitudes differing by five orders of magnitude

Five subclasses that exist only to re-declare the same RectangleF, forcing ~150 lines of identical boilerplate (is_colliding, get_shape, is_visible_in_viewport, both draws) into the leaves and making every fix a five-site edit

Pre-C++17 defaults compounding the design: no <LanguageStandard> in the vcxproj means per-TU dynamically-initialised const aggregates with std::string members, hand-rolled clamp ladders, no [[nodiscard]], and a static-init-order dependency between projectile_consts.h and weapon_consts.h

Per-frame work that should be construction-time: string-keyed map lookups for the sprite sheet on every update and every draw per viewport, a nested switch recomputing a constant collision type inside an O(n^2) loop, and ~16 non-inlinable virtual calls to move two floats

perModule.summary: The level module works, but it works by coincidence in several places, and it is the part of the codebase furthest from the stated reusable-engine goal. There is one live, shipped gameplay bug — `StructurePaintable::generate_paint_tiles` maps `Shape::get_edges()` indices 0-3 to top/right/bottom/left while `RectangleF::get_edges()` returns top/bottom/left/right, so three of four paintable faces are generated on the wrong side of the structure in every level; I confirmed this against the actual JSON (the castle ceiling in king_of_the_hill is unpaintable, both castle walls paint on their outside faces). There is one memory-corruption bug — `LevelLoadedInfo::load_from_json` passes `sizeof(unique_ptr)` as the length of a one-byte buffer, so every level load performs thousands of small heap overflows, and the same idiom is copy-pasted into three other asset loaders. Structurally, `Level` is a god class whose public API is three raw pointers to vectors of D3D11 objects: it owns the world, ticks the simulation, runs an O(n²) collision loop with no broad phase, drives the camera and HUD, plays audio, enforces the match rules, and records deferred-context command lists — none of which can be reused or tested apart from any other. The engine/game boundary has been crossed in both directions: `IPaintableGameObject` bakes Splatoon paint scoring and a fixed two-team model into a core interface, `collision_object_type` cross-multiplies class × team × weapon into 23 flat enumerators that four hand-written predicate chains then re-derive, and the match length, countdown font and sound cue names are compile-time constants inside `Level.h`. Concurrency is the least safe area: the multithreaded draw calls non-const `draw()` on shared `PaintTile` objects from several threads at once, the zoom-out path touches the immediate D3D context and the main thread's SpriteBatch from a worker, and any exception thrown inside a task escapes a Win32 thread-pool callback and terminates the process. I rejected two candidate findings whose stated mechanisms do not hold: collision responses are not fired 2-4 times per pair (the filters make the dispatch asymmetric but single), and holding Start during level load cannot crash on the null countdown text (pause is release-edge triggered).
themes: Data smuggled through geometry: four JSON booleans are encoded as Segments and decoded back via an undocumented edge ordering and exact float equality, producing the module's one live shipped gameplay bug

Enum tags used as a substitute for the type system: collision_object_type cross-multiplies class × team × weapon into 23 values, is re-derived by four duplicated predicate chains, and is recovered with a dynamic_cast behind a catch that can never fire
Engine and game welded together: paint scoring, a two-team model, match length, countdown assets and D3D11 deferred contexts all appear in what should be reusable engine types

Thread-safety treated as an afterthought: non-const draw() mutating shared objects across worker threads, the immediate context driven from a task, and exceptions escaping Win32 thread-pool callbacks into std::terminate
Exceptions used for ordinary gameplay conditions with no handler anywhere in the process, plus MSVC-only throw std::exception("literal") at 54 sites

Ownership and lifetime stated nowhere: a dangling reference member, raw back-pointers invalidated by device loss, a raw const Shape* silently cloned, and unique_ptr<vector<unique_ptr<T>>> that defeats const rather than expressing ownership
No input validation between level JSON and the objects built from it — unchecked rapidjson accessors, no parse-error check, no range checks, and a divide by a tile count that can be zero

Dead and half-finished surface left in place: five write-only Level members on a 23-parameter constructor, six fully commented-out ramp files still in the build, an unimplemented game-mode enum, and ~170 lines of commented-out draft implementations

perModule.summary: The menus module is the weakest layer I have read in this repo, and the damage is concentrated in three places. First, the input layer is structurally wrong: `MenuInput::update_and_get_menu_inputs()` returns a vector compacted to connected pads only, while every consumer indexes it as if it were a 4-slot array keyed by player number — this yields controller cross-wiring when a pad slot is empty, an unchecked out-of-bounds read in both pause-menu `update()` bodies, and a forward path through team/weapon select that cannot be completed if fewer pads are connected than players were chosen, with no on-screen explanation. The `connection_state` field that exists precisely to fix this is unconditionally set to CONNECTED and never read. Second, `MenuPage` — the base class for all UI — is a D3D11 command-list orchestrator: it owns deferred contexts, sprite batches, sampler states, the thread pool and the partitioner, so no UI type in this engine can exist without DirectX, and every one of the twelve concrete pages carries a byte-identical `draw()` plus a duplicated container pair. Third, navigation is stringly typed: roughly ninety `highlighted_element == "play"`-style comparisons stand in for a focus model, the compared name is snapshotted before the input loop and goes stale after the first `change_highlight`, and there is no navigation stack, so eight page classes hardcode each other as predecessors. Underneath all of it sits `StateContext::transition_to`, which destroys the running state from inside its own `update()` and relies on an unwritten "never touch `this` afterwards" rule that two pause-menu call sites already break. The lifetime story is uniformly latent rather than currently exploding — member declaration order in `GameStates.h` puts pages after the data they borrow, `MContainer` holds raw pointers into members declared after it, and every `*MenuData` is a frozen copy of the whole `GameData` service locator that goes stale on device restore — all of which survive only because the relevant destructors happen to be trivial today. Of the 101 candidates I read and merged into 62 findings; I rejected none outright but corrected three overstatements (the pause-menu "quit branch evaluated on a destroyed object" claim, the "team select soft-locks with no escape" claim, and a non-existent `end_menu_consts::DETAIL_FONT`) and downgraded several severities where the defect is real but unreachable on any current code path.
themes: Input indexing: a compacted pad vector indexed as if it were a stable player-slot array, producing an unchecked OOB read in PauseMenu and an uncompletable team/weapon select

UI base class is a renderer: MenuPage owns D3D11 deferred contexts, command lists, sprite batches, thread pool and partitioner, so no UI can exist without DirectX — the single biggest blocker to the engine-reuse goal
Stringly-typed navigation: ~90 widget-name comparisons instead of a focus model, with the compared name snapshotted before the input loop and going stale after the first move
Self-destroying state machine: transition_to deletes the running state from inside its own update(), safe only by an unwritten and already-violated 'return immediately' convention

Massive duplication with no shared abstraction: twelve identical draw() bodies, twelve container pairs, four copies of the same theme constants, three copies of the enum-cycling routine, two copies of all_players_confirmed/unconfirmed
Game content welded into engine code: weapon, stage and mode catalogues hardcoded in switch statements and header string constants, plus raw Win32 window management inside a menu page

Resolution handling has no single source of truth: geometry destructively baked in init(), fullscreen apply discards the chosen resolution, window rect used where client rect is meant, and ResultsMenu writes design-space pixels into already-scaled rectangles every frame

Silent failure everywhere: worker-thread exceptions call std::terminate, ResourceManager/SpriteSheet operator[] inserts on a missing key instead of erroring, save failures print to a console that does not exist, and rand() is never seeded
Latent lifetime hazards held together by trivial destructors: member declaration order inversions, MContainer's raw child pointers, and per-page frozen copies of the GameData service locator

perModule.summary: This module is where the engine ambition and the actual code diverge most sharply. Two defects are genuinely critical and both are verified in source: `SpriteSheet::load_from_json` (duplicated verbatim in `SoundBank.cpp`) passes `sizeof(std::unique_ptr<char>)` as the size of a one-byte allocation to RapidJSON's `FileReadStream`, which I confirmed against the vendored `filereadstream.h` does `fread(buffer_, 1, bufferSize_, fp_)` — a heap overflow on every asset load, followed by a `release()` leak and an unchecked `fopen`; and `Game::create_device_dependent_resources` destroys and recreates both the `ResourceManager` and the dt float on device-restore while the entire object graph survives holding raw pointers to them. Beyond those, the dominant structural problem is that `draw()` is a mutating, non-const operation throughout the hierarchy while `Level::draw_active_level` genuinely fans the same objects out to N thread-pool workers: `Player::draw`, `TextDropShadow::draw`, `PaintTile::draw` and `Weapon::draw` all write `std::string` and animation state that other threads are concurrently reading, and `ThreadPool::work_callback` has no exception guard, so a thrown `frame_index out of range` terminates the process. The resource layer compounds everything — all four `ResourceManager` getters use `map::operator[]` wrapped in a `catch(std::out_of_range)` that can never fire, so a missing asset silently returns `nullptr` into a render-path dereference. On the engine-reuse goal specifically, `InterfaceGameplay` is a Splatoon HUD (team colours, respawn timers, hardcoded atlas and font names) sitting in the rendering layer, `DebugText` includes `Player.h` and knows eighteen of its fields, `DrawObject.h` transitively drags RapidJSON and XAudio2 into every renderable, and `Player` carries two complete copies of all render state because `TextureObject` and `AnimationObject` are inherited rather than composed. I rejected or downgraded several sub-claims: the `map::operator[]` race is latent rather than active (every runtime frame name exists in the atlas JSON), `SpriteFrame::get_source_rectangle`'s interior pointer is safe because SpriteBatch copies the rect, the `FLT_MIN` frame-time sentinel has no live trigger, `AnimatedSprite`'s frame-index bug is unreachable because the class is entirely dead code, and the DirectXTK UTF-8 conversion-buffer race could not be verified since only the header is vendored.
themes: Unsafe C-idiom carryover in the asset loaders: sizeof on a smart pointer as a buffer size, unchecked fopen, release() instead of reset(), and zero JSON validation — a heap overflow on every sprite sheet and sound bank load

draw() mutates shared object state while the renderer runs it on N thread-pool workers over the same objects; nothing below IGameObject is const, and the const markers that do exist are laundered through unique_ptr members and a const getter returning a mutable ResourceManager*

Lookup failure is silent everywhere: map::operator[] in all four ResourceManager getters and in SpriteSheet::draw, each wrapped in unreachable error handling, so a typo'd asset name yields nullptr or an invisible zero-size sprite instead of a diagnosable load error

Game content welded into engine classes — InterfaceGameplay's team/health/respawn HUD, DebugText's Player dependency, hardcoded atlas and font names in engine headers, and DrawObject.h pulling RapidJSON and XAudio2 into every renderable

Inheritance used where composition belongs: a five-deep render hierarchy of pure state bags, Player holding two non-virtual copies of DrawObject, Drawer as a base class for two dead helper functions, Text existing only to widen four setters' access, and AnimatedSprite as a dead better-designed fork of AnimationObject

Non-owning raw pointers with undocumented lifetime contracts: cached ResourceManager*/dt across device restore, a non-AddRef'd ID3D11ShaderResourceView in SpriteSheet, and defaulted constructors that produce objects with no way back to a valid state

Parsed-then-discarded and declared-then-unused code: SpriteFrame's origin and rotated flags, SpriteFrame::_source_rectangle2, ProjectileDetails::rotat_origin, InterfaceDraw, set_draw_rotation_by_rectangle_rotated's empty stub, and Drawer's entire helper API

Build configuration left at defaults — no LanguageStandard element means a silent C++14 build, which is why std::clamp, std::optional, inline variables and string_view are unavailable for the fixes this module needs; 54 MSVC-only throw std::exception("literal") sites pin the engine to one compiler

perModule.summary: The platform layer is a thin, mostly-unmodified Microsoft DirectX template with a multithreaded deferred-context renderer and a split-screen viewport system bolted onto it, and nearly every serious defect sits precisely at that seam. The author's additions to `DeviceResources` (a pool of 16 raw `ID3D11DeviceContext*` in a `unique_ptr<vector<>>`) violate the ownership discipline the surrounding vendor code follows everywhere else: the contexts are never released, are never recreated on device loss, and are handed out through a `noexcept` accessor that throws. The device-lost path is comprehensively broken in a second, independent way — `Game::create_device_dependent_resources()` is misnamed and rebuilds the ThreadPool, ResourceManager, ViewportManager, Partitioner and the shared frame-delta float, so a single TDR turns every live `Level`, `Player` and `Weapon` into a bag of dangling raw pointers. Even on the happy path, member declaration order in `Game.h` destroys the AudioEngine before the ResourceManager that owns its WaveBanks, which is undefined behaviour on every clean shutdown. Beyond lifetimes, there are three concrete logic bugs I could reproduce on paper: the nested switch in `calculate_viewport` falls through between layouts (so `get_all_viewports` silently returns a fullscreen viewport for the missing 3-player quadrant), and `calculate_camera_scroll_border` clamps its minimum above its maximum at the shipped 1280x720 default, inverting the camera dead zone in every multiplayer layout. Structurally, `Game` is a god object that is simultaneously the window host, the device-lost sink, the root state machine (by inheritance) and the owner of twelve subsystems, all published through a `GameData` pointer bag; the viewport service owns a D3D context and a SpriteBatch and mutates the immediate context from a worker thread; and display-mode management lives in a menu screen. Nothing in this layer is currently extractable as an engine without taking the Splatoon clone with it.
themes: Device-lost recovery is comprehensively broken: subsystems are reconstructed instead of GPU resources, deferred contexts are never recreated, and every cached raw pointer dangles afterwards

Ownership by raw pointer with no contract — deferred contexts, the parallel SpriteBatch* mirror, the heap frame-delta float, and the whole GameData service locator — makes lifetimes unanalysable and is the root of most findings here

Destruction order is load-bearing and undocumented: AudioEngine dies before its WaveBanks, the State tree dies after every service it borrows, and the Main.cpp globals are declared in reverse dependency order

Two conflicting sources of truth for screen size: the saved resolution enum drives every viewport and camera calculation while the swap chain is sized from a discarded client rect, so AdjustWindowRect, GetClientRect and the entire resize path are no-ops

Game-specific vocabulary welded into the platform layer — screen_layout is defined in terms of players, viewport_consts names a sprite sheet, Main.cpp hardcodes GameMenu, and window/display-mode control lives inside a menu screen
Hand-written switch tables instead of data: calculate_viewport falls through between cases, and the four-row resolution table is written five times in ResolutionManager and twice more in Save

Build configuration undermines the code: no <LanguageStandard> (so C++14), no TreatWarningAsError, /fp:fast with float equality comparisons, and a PCH that forces the entire DirectXTK 3D surface into all 81 TUs of a 2D game

perModule.summary: This module group is where the project's youth shows most sharply: a single copy-pasted JSON-reading idiom, replicated verbatim into four classes, writes 8 bytes into a 1-byte heap allocation on every asset load and then leaks it — real heap corruption executed at every startup, hidden only by CRT allocation granularity. The same four copies also pass an unchecked FILE* into rapidjson and never inspect the parse result, so in Release (NDEBUG is set) a missing or truncated file is undefined behaviour rather than an error. A second systemic defect runs through ResourceManager: four of five getters use `std::map::operator[]` wrapped in a `catch(std::out_of_range)` that the standard guarantees can never fire, so every missing-asset diagnostic in the engine is dead code, every miss silently inserts a null entry, and the lookup mutates a container that up to 16 thread-pool workers read concurrently during draw — a genuine data race. The correct idiom (`.at()`, const) sits ten lines away in `get_level_info`, which makes this an oversight rather than a misunderstanding. Structurally, the engine-reuse goal is blocked in three concrete places: `ResourceLoader` hardcodes this one game's twelve assets and three level names as string literals, `ResourceManager` keys its level cache on the game's `level_stage` enum, and `GameData` is a 13-pointer service locator that game-specific menu payloads inherit from. Lifetime management is the other weak axis — `OnDeviceRestored` replaces every service object while the live scene keeps the old addresses, `Game`'s members are freed before its `StateContext` base destroys the state tree that points at them, and `ThreadPool` owns raw Win32 handles with a user-declared destructor and an implicitly-generated copy constructor. The good news is that the fixes are mostly mechanical and highly leveraged: one shared JSON loader, one `.at()` sweep, one manifest file, and deleting `= default` from three constructors would eliminate roughly half the findings here.
themes: Copy-paste propagation of defects: the broken 1-byte JSON reader exists in 4 files, the operator[]-in-dead-catch getter in 4 places, and the resolution conversion table in 4 functions across 2 classes — every one of them a candidate for a single shared helper that does not exist

Error handling that looks present but is provably inert: catch blocks for exceptions the called code cannot throw (map::operator[], WaveBank::Play, WaveBank::CreateInstance), rapidjson asserts compiled out by NDEBUG, and bool failure returns consumed only to pick a std::cout message in a GUI app with no console

Silent nullptr instead of a loud failure: operator[] inserting nulls, reset_all_* keeping keys with null values, CreateInstance returning nullptr unchecked, and default constructors that leave dependencies null with no setter to repair them — every one converts a diagnosable lookup error into an access violation somewhere unrelated

Non-owning raw pointers cached at construction with no lifetime contract: Level::_sound_bank, SpriteSheet::_texture, SoundBankObject::_resource_manager, the float* dt threaded through the codebase, and the whole GameData bag — all invalidated by OnDeviceRestored, by reset_all_*, or by Game's member-before-base destruction order

Game-specific knowledge welded into engine subsystems: asset names and level-to-enum mappings compiled into ResourceLoader, the level_stage enum used as a key type in ResourceManager, and per-team/per-player-slot voice names hardcoded into the sound bank schema — a second game cannot call load_all_resources() at all

Build configuration undermining the code: no <LanguageStandard> pins the project to C++14 (hence hand-rolled clamp, no filesystem, no string_view, no nodiscard, no try_emplace), and /W4 with no TreatWarningAsError produces output nobody reads — proven by a committed unreachable duplicated return statement

Inheritance used for implementation reuse and pointer bags: SoundBankObject as a public non-virtual mixin on four UI hierarchies, MenuData deriving from the service locator, and menu constructors whose correctness depends silently on base-clause ordering

const as decoration rather than information: every playback method on SoundBank and SoundBankObject is const while mutating audio state, ResourceLoader's five loaders split const/non-const at random, and a const getter hands out a mutable pointer to owned state

perModule.summary: This module group is the load-bearing spine of the whole program — `StateContext`/`State` drive every frame, and `IGameObject`/`ICollisionGameObject` are the root interfaces of every object in the engine — and it is the part of the codebase least ready to be called an engine. Three defects stand out: `StateContext::transition_to` is effectively `delete this` executed from inside the outgoing state's own `update()` at roughly thirty call sites, surviving today only because no site happens to touch a member afterwards; `GameLevel::update` hands `Level` a gamepad-input vector that has been compacted by connection state and is then indexed by player number, which is a real out-of-bounds read the moment a controller is unplugged mid-match; and `Game` inherits `StateContext`, so the entire live level graph is destroyed after every subsystem it borrows raw pointers from, with the audio-engine-before-sound-banks half of that ordering already violated on every clean exit. Structurally, the engine/game line has not been drawn anywhere here: `collision_object_type` puts Splatoon's weapons and teams into the core collision interface, `IGameObject` puts `DirectX::SpriteBatch` into the identity of every drawable, and `GameStates.h` makes the state machine and the concrete screens mutually dependent, with `GameMenu` and `GameLevel` constructing each other by concrete type. A recurring pattern across the group is code that is correct only by coincidence — member declaration orders, reassignment orders, and the absence of a single statement after a transition are all load-bearing and undocumented. On the positive side, the reviewers' most alarming claims did not all survive: the command-list leak-on-throw is impossible because those throws occur on thread-pool workers that terminate rather than unwind, the NaN-producing unit-velocity accessors have no callers at all, and two of the three `MAX` enum sentinels are actually correct — only `team_colour_enum`'s is wrong.
themes: Lifetime and destruction order are correct only by coincidence — transition_to destroys the running state, Game destroys subsystems before the state tree that borrows them, and four menu member groups are declared in reverse dependency order

Game rules are welded into what should be engine interfaces: collision_object_type enumerates weapons×teams on ICollisionGameObject, IGameObject hardwires SpriteBatch and Camera, and TeamColour bakes exactly-two-teams into member names
Input identity is broken at the source: connection-compacted vectors are indexed by player number, producing an out-of-bounds read on controller disconnect and mis-attributed pause menus
Two-phase construction everywhere — init() as a peer of update()/draw() with no enforcement, no exit hook, and no null guards on the members it creates

Ownership expressed with raw pointers and hand-written release: heap-allocated scalars used as signalling channels, manual ID3D11CommandList Release, a 13-pointer service-locator bag copied into every menu
No error handling exists on any path — 58 MSVC-only throw std::exception sites, zero try/catch, and thread-pool callbacks that terminate the process on any throw
Virtualisation and inheritance used by reflex: 27 protected virtual accessors on a 20-byte mixin with one no-op override, and a non-virtual diamond giving Player two complete DrawObject subobjects

Build configuration stuck at C++14 with no LanguageStandard set, blocking [[fallthrough]], std::optional, [[nodiscard]] and inline constexpr — several of which are the correct fix for defects in this group

findings.title: RectangleF::get_edges() returns {top, bottom, left, right} while its only consumer indexes it as clockwise
findings.detail: Verified. MattMath.cpp:808-818 returns `{get_top_edge(), get_bottom_edge(), get_left_edge(), get_right_edge()}`. Every other shape is cyclic: Triangle::get_edges (3502-3511) is p0->p1, p1->p2, p2->p0; RectangleRotated::get_edges (4284-4293) is edge_0..edge_3 built from _points[i],_points[i+1]; RectangleRotated::edges_valid (4539-4555) does `edges[(i+1)%4]`, which only makes sense for a cyclic list. The sole consumer, StructurePaintable.cpp:188-212, maps i==0->top, i==1->right, i==2->bottom, i==3->left. Only index 0 agrees. LevelObjectBuilder.cpp:104-124 builds _paintable_edges from rectangle.get_left_edge()/get_top_edge()/get_right_edge()/get_bottom_edge() driven by the `paintable_faces` JSON block, and the match at StructurePaintable.cpp:193 is Segment==Segment. So a level marking `"right": true` matches edges[3] (the right edge) and sets left_edge=true, painting the LEFT face. Mapping is bottom->right, left->bottom, right->left. All three shipped levels use paintable_faces (close_quarters.json:258,280; king_of_the_hill.json:242+; turbulence.json:242+).
findings.suggestion: Return cyclic order {top, right, bottom, left} and document on Shape::get_edges() that edge i joins point i to point i+1. Then re-verify StructurePaintable.cpp:195-210 against the new order. Better: delete the Segment-equality index matching entirely and pass the paintable faces as the PaintableFaces flags struct that is already commented out at LevelObjectBuilder.cpp:100-105 and StructurePaintable.cpp:216-280.
findings.verify_note: Read MattMath.cpp:808-818, 3502-3511, 4284-4293, 4539-4555; StructurePaintable.cpp:182-290; LevelObjectBuilder.cpp:100-135; grepped paintable_faces in ArtAttack/levels/*.json. Downgraded from 'critical' — this is a wrong-behaviour bug, not a crash or memory error.

findings.title: triangles_intersect only tests 4 of the 9 edge pairs — two triangles can cross and be reported as disjoint
findings.detail:
Verified, and this is the most serious live defect the reviewers surfaced (it was buried inside a design candidate about copy-pasted algorithms). MattMath.cpp:393-404:
```cpp
std::vector<Segment> a_edges = a.get_edges();  // 3 edges
std::vector<Segment> b_edges = b.get_edges();  // 3 edges
for (int i = 0; i < 2; i++)
{
    if (segments_intersect(a_edges[i], b_edges[0]) ||
        segments_intersect(a_edges[i], b_edges[1]))
```
`i < 2` skips a_edges[2], and b_edges[2] is never tested at all. Only 4 of the 9 pairs are checked. Two triangles that overlap edge-on with no vertex of either inside the other (the vertex checks at 384-390 fail) and whose only crossings involve edge 2 return false. This is not dead code: Triangle::intersects(Triangle) forwards here, and triangle_quad_intersect (409-424), quads_intersect (492-511) and quad_rectangle_rotated_intersect (545-561) are all built on it. The function also has no AABB early-out, unlike its siblings at 196 and 264.
findings.suggestion: Replace the double loop with a full `for (i in 0..2) for (j in 0..2)` over both edge lists, or — better — write one convex-vs-convex separating-axis test against get_points()/get_edges() and delete the six near-identical hand-written copies at 193-229, 260-298, 381-407, 426-445, 453-490 and 619-661.
findings.verify_note: Read MattMath.cpp:381-407 and the four call sites at 409-424, 492-511, 545-561, plus Triangle::intersects. The loop bounds are exactly as quoted.

findings.title: RectangleF — the engine's universal value type and AABB — inherits polymorphic Shape
findings.detail:
Verified. `struct RectangleF : public Shape` (MattMath.h:184); Shape (68-89) has a virtual destructor plus 11 pure virtuals. `typedef MattMath::RectangleF AABB;` (301). Consequences I checked in the source rather than assumed:
- Not a literal type, so `const RectangleF RectangleF::ZERO` (MattMath.cpp:1134) must be dynamically initialised, and RectangleF can never be constexpr.
- `get_bounding_box()` returns RectangleF **by value** (MattMath.h:71; RectangleF's own is `return *this;` at MattMath.cpp:719-722), so every AABB query materialises a vptr-carrying object. Shape::AABB_intersects (143-146) constructs two per call.
- Shape declares a destructor but no copy control, so its copy-assignment is implicitly public: `Shape& a = circle; Shape& b = rect; a = b;` compiles and silently does nothing.
- 24 bytes instead of 16 on x64, not trivially copyable, arrays of rects cannot be memcpy'd or packed.
Six reviewers raised versions of this; merged here. For a project whose stated goal is a reusable 2D engine, fusing 'is a rectangle' with 'participates in a collision double-dispatch hierarchy' is the single biggest structural problem in this module.
findings.suggestion: Split the roles: a plain literal `RectangleF`/`AABB` (public floats, constexpr ctors, no base) as the math primitive, and a separate polymorphic or variant-based collision layer. As a zero-cost stopgap today, give Shape `protected: Shape(const Shape&) = default; Shape& operator=(const Shape&) = default;` to close the slicing-assignment hole (Core Guidelines C.67).
findings.verify_note: Read MattMath.h:68-89, 184-301; MattMath.cpp:719-722, 143-151, 1134. Shape has no declared copy ctor/assignment, so both are implicitly generated and public.

findings.title: MattMath.h is a god header spanning pure math, collision, colour, D3D11 and camera — and hard-depends on d3d11.h
findings.detail:
Verified by reading the whole header. 1139 lines backed by a 4568-line .cpp declaring: `direction` enum (12-23), Shape (68-89), ~30 free intersection functions (91-182), RectangleF (184-299), Vector2I (354-392), Vector2F (402-498), RectangleI (508-565), Vector4F (567-584), Colour (586-645), Vector3F (655-674), MatrixF with Gaussian elimination and determinant (684-748), Matrix3x3F (750-765), Viewport wrapping D3D11_VIEWPORT (767-806), Circle/Triangle/TriangleRightAxisAligned/Quad/Segment (808-1006), Camera (1007-1045), RectangleRotated (1047-1134).

`#include <d3d11.h>` (line 6) exists for exactly four members of `Viewport` (786, 789-790, 799). `#include "SimpleMath.h"` (line 4) leaks through every type: Vector2F(SimpleMath::Vector2) at 411, RectangleF(SimpleMath::Rectangle)/(RECT) at 198-199, Colour(SimpleMath::Color) at 598, plus matching operator= and get_sm_*/get_xm_* on all of them. So the engine's vocabulary types cannot compile without the DirectX SDK — which is exactly why MattMathTests can only test them by `#include`-ing MattMath.cpp directly (MathTests.cpp:5).
findings.suggestion: Split with a clear dependency direction: MattMath/Vector.h + Rectangle.h (zero dependencies), MattMath/Colour.h, MattMath/Shapes.h + Intersect.h, and a presentation-layer Viewport.h + Camera2D.h. Move every get_sm_*/get_xm_*/RECT/D3D11_VIEWPORT conversion into a MattMath_DirectXInterop.h of free functions that only the renderer includes.
findings.verify_note: Read the full MattMath.h; confirmed line ranges and that d3d11.h is used only by Viewport. Confirmed MathTests.cpp:5 includes MattMath.cpp, not MattMath.h.

findings.title: 302 internal-linkage objects defined in a header, every Colour constructed by parsing a hex string at static-init time
findings.detail:
Verified by count: 149 `const std::string` in `colour_consts::html` (lines 10-157) and 153 `const MattMath::Colour` (160-313), all at namespace scope in a header. Namespace-scope `const` has internal linkage, so each including TU gets its own copy and its own dynamic initialisers. Each Colour runs `Colour(const std::string&)` -> `set_from_hex` (MattMath.cpp:2359-2384), which does three or four `hex.substr()` allocations plus `std::stoi(..., 16)` calls — thousands of runtime hex parses before `main` to reproduce compile-time constants.

Correction to the reviewers: they claimed 58 of 81 TUs. I measured 14 files that reference Colour.h directly (DrawObject.h, Level.h, LevelBuilder.h, LevelEndInfo.h, MenuHighlight.h, PaintTile.h, PlayerBuilder.h, player_consts.h, ResultsMenu.h, SpriteSheet.h, StructurePaintable.h, TeamColour.cpp, ViewportManager.h, Weapon.h). The transitive fan-out through DrawObject.h/SpriteSheet.h is large but I did not verify 58, so treat the multiplier as 'most of the drawable hierarchy', not a measured 58.

Real secondary hazard, verified: `std::stoi` throws `std::invalid_argument` on a non-hex digit, and `set_from_hex` has no digit validation. A typo in any of the 149 literals throws out of a namespace-scope dynamic initialiser, which calls std::terminate before main with no attributable diagnostic.
findings.suggestion: Give Colour a constexpr constructor and define the palette as `inline constexpr Colour ALICE_BLUE{0.941f, 0.973f, 1.0f, 1.0f};` (C++17). That removes the duplication, the pre-main parsing and the terminate risk in one change, and deletes the parallel `html::` string table whose only purpose is to be parsed back into the same numbers. Requires setting <LanguageStandard> in the vcxproj, which is currently unset.
findings.verify_note: grep -c on Colour.h: 149 'const std::string', 153 'const MattMath::Colour'. Read set_from_hex at MattMath.cpp:2359-2384. Counted 14 direct includers, correcting the reviewers' unverified '58 of 81'.

findings.title: Splatoon team colours are baked into the engine's colour palette header
findings.detail:
Verified. `const MattMath::Colour TEAM_BLUE = { 6, 52, 204, 255 };` plus TEAM_YELLOW, TEAM_ORANGE, TEAM_PINK, TEAM_GREEN sit in `colour_consts` immediately after the 149 HTML colours, and are consumed by TeamColour.h to build the team pairings. Any project reusing this engine inherits ArtAttack's team palette in its core colour header — a direct hit on the stated engine-first goal.

Also verified: these five are the only constants in the file that use the `Colour(int,int,int,int)` 0-255 path; every other one goes through the hex-string constructor. Two construction paths in one file, differing only by literal type (see the Colour-constructor-overlap finding).
findings.suggestion: Move TEAM_* into the game layer next to TeamColour.h (e.g. game/team_palette.h), leaving colour_consts with only standard named colours. The engine should have no concept of 'teams'.
findings.verify_note: Read Colour.h:305-320. Confirmed the five TEAM_* constants and that they use the int constructor while all 153 others use the hex-string one.

findings.title: MatrixF(int, int) never sizes _elements, so every matrix factory writes out of bounds on an empty vector
findings.suggestion: Delete MatrixF, Matrix3x3F and the free add/subtract/multiply/divide/gaussian_elimination/transpose/identity/zero/determinant functions (MattMath.h:684-765, MattMath.cpp:2476-3050). A 2D engine has no use for a dynamically-sized dense matrix class with a recursive determinant. If it must stay, `_elements.assign(size_t(rows)*columns, 0.0f)` in the constructor and validate against _elements.size().
findings.verify_note: Read MattMath.cpp:2478-2513, 2701-2712, 2733-2975, 2987-3048 and MattMath.h:684-765. Grepped MatrixF/Matrix3x3F repo-wide: zero hits outside MattMath.{h,cpp}. Downgraded from 'critical' because it is unreachable.

findings.title: TriangleRightAxisAligned does not override clone(), so every level ramp is stored as a sliced Triangle
findings.detail:
Verified. `Triangle::clone()` (MattMath.cpp:3453-3456) hard-codes `std::make_unique<Triangle>(*this)`, and TriangleRightAxisAligned (MattMath.h:895-914) adds get_hypotenuse/get_hypotenuse_gradient/find_hypotenuse but no clone() override. LevelObjectBuilder.cpp:161-176 builds a TriangleRightAxisAligned for every ramp and passes `&triangle` to Structure, whose constructor stores `_collision_shape(collision_shape->clone())` (Structure.cpp:22). So every ramp's stored shape is a plain Triangle.

Severity tempered from the reviewers' 'high': the derived class adds no data members, and every consumer of the derived interface is currently commented out — StructureRamp.cpp is entirely commented (lines 1-27), including the `static_cast<const TriangleRightAxisAligned*>(get_shape())` at line 25 that would be UB against a sliced object. So this is a latent trap that fires the moment ramp gradients are re-enabled, not a live bug today.

Also verified in the same type: `TriangleRightAxisAligned::calculate_gradient(int)` (MattMath.h:913) is declared *private* and *hides* rather than overrides the public non-virtual `Triangle::calculate_gradient` (893).
findings.suggestion: Add `std::unique_ptr<Shape> clone() const override { return std::make_unique<TriangleRightAxisAligned>(*this); }`, and adopt the rule for every Shape leaf. Enforce it structurally with a CRTP ShapeClonable<Derived> mixin so a new leaf cannot forget. Rename or virtualise calculate_gradient so it stops shadowing.
findings.verify_note: Read MattMath.h:842-914, MattMath.cpp:3453-3456 and 3633-3694, Structure.cpp:7-25, LevelObjectBuilder.cpp:155-178, StructureRamp.cpp (fully commented out). Grepped TriangleRightAxisAligned repo-wide: only LevelObjectBuilder.cpp:161 is live.

findings.title: rotate_vector_by_ref clobbers vec.x before using it to compute vec.y
findings.suggestion: Delete it. `vec.rotate(angle)` already covers the in-place case, and three spellings of one 4-multiply operation is why one of them rotted. If it must stay, compute both components into locals first.
findings.verify_note: Read MattMath.cpp:1757-1767, 1792-1807. Grepped rotate_vector_by_ref repo-wide: zero call sites. Grepped rotate_vector: 5 call sites, all the correct overload.

findings.title: Vector2F::cross returns (x*b.y, y*b.x) — the two unsubtracted terms, not a cross product
findings.suggestion: Change to `float cross(const Vector2F& other) const { return x*other.y - y*other.x; }` plus a static overload mirroring `dot`, and fold MattMath::sign into it. Add a unit test in MattMathTests/MathTests.cpp, which already covers dot/length.
findings.verify_note: Read MattMath.cpp:1716-1723 and MattMath.h:442-443. Grepped '.cross(' repo-wide: zero call sites.

findings.title: MattMath::sign truncates a float determinant to int, returning 0 for any |cross| < 1
findings.suggestion: Delete it, or rename to `float orient2d(...)` returning the raw determinant (the standard name and contract) and add a separate `int sign_of(float)` with an epsilon band. Express it in terms of a fixed Vector2F::cross so the operation exists once.
findings.verify_note: Read MattMath.cpp:86-91 and MattMath.h:56-57. Grepped for callers: none.

findings.title: Colour::desaturate is a byte-identical copy of Colour::saturate
findings.suggestion: Implement one primitive (`adjust_saturation(float factor)`) and express both in terms of it, so desaturate(1.0f) yields pure luminance and desaturate(0.0f) is a no-op. Hoist the luma weights to named constants.
findings.verify_note: Read MattMath.cpp:2385-2400 side by side; bodies are identical. Grepped saturate/desaturate for callers: none outside MattMath.

findings.title: normalized()/normalize() divide by zero while the identical to_unit_vector()/unit_vector() guard against it
findings.detail:
Verified. `normalized()` (1724-1728) and `normalize()` (1729-1734) divide by `length()` with no zero check; `to_unit_vector()` (1774-1787) and `static unit_vector()` (1852-1863) perform the same computation but test `length == 0.0f` and return (1,0). Four functions, two mutually incompatible zero-length contracts, no documentation of which is which.

I have to correct the reviewers on the consequences, which were overstated across several candidates:
- MovingObject::get_unit_velocity()/get_unit_dx() (MovingObject.cpp:52-55, 100-103) do call the unguarded `normalized()` on members that are zero at rest — but both have **zero callers**, so no NaN reaches gameplay today.
- RectangleRotated::set_x_axis/set_y_axis (4359-4380) normalise then call axes_valid(), which does are_equal(length, 1.0f) — false for NaN — and throws. NaN does not get stored. Same for the OBB constructor at 4186-4200. The claim that these 'silently store NaN and stop colliding' is wrong.
- What *is* genuinely unguarded: Triangle::inflate (3464-3466) and Quad::inflate (3821-3824) normalise centre-to-vertex vectors with no degenerate check, producing NaN points for a degenerate shape.
A separate real bug I found next door: `RectangleRotated(const Segment& center_line, float thickness)` (4201-4215) assigns `_x_axis = center_line.get_direction()` **without normalising** (unlike the other constructor at 4191-4192), so axes_valid() rejects any centre line whose length isn't 1 and the constructor always throws.
findings.suggestion: Collapse to two functions — `Vector2F normalized() const` and `void normalize()` — both with one documented zero-length policy, and delete to_unit_vector/unit_vector. Returning (1,0) is the worst option: it invents a direction the caller cannot distinguish from a real one. Separately, normalise the axes in the Segment-based RectangleRotated constructor.
findings.verify_note: Read MattMath.cpp:1724-1734, 1774-1787, 1852-1863, 3457-3472, 3813-3830, 4186-4215, 4353-4380, 4522-4538; MovingObject.cpp:52-55, 100-103. Grepped get_unit_velocity/get_unit_dx: declaration and definition only, no callers.

findings.title: angle_between feeds an unclamped quotient to std::acos and has no zero-length guard
findings.detail:
Verified: `return std::acos(Vector2F::dot(a, b) / (a.length() * b.length()));`. Two unguarded failures: (1) no clamp to [-1,1], so rounding on nearly parallel/antiparallel inputs yields 1.0000001 and acos returns NaN — and the project builds with FloatingPointModel=Fast in all four configurations (ArtAttack.vcxproj:94,116,139,165), which licenses reassociation of the dot product; (2) zero-length input divides by zero.

Downstream, verified: Triangle::get_angle_0/1/2 (3512-3527) are built on it, and TriangleRightAxisAligned::find_hypotenuse (3665-3684) tests `are_equal(angle, PI_OVER_2)` for each. Every comparison against NaN is false, so it returns -1 and get_hypotenuse()/get_hypotenuse_gradient() (3633-3652) throw 'Triangle is not a right triangle' about a triangle that is one.

I reject the escalation that this 'crashes level loading': LevelObjectBuilder.cpp:161-176 only calls `triangle.get_bounding_box()` on the TriangleRightAxisAligned, never get_hypotenuse, and every consumer of the hypotenuse API (StructureRamp.cpp) is commented out. RectangleRotated::get_angle() (4460-4463) has the same exposure and also has no callers.
findings.suggestion: Guard both ends: `const float denom = a.length()*b.length(); if (denom == 0.0f) return 0.0f; return std::acos(MattMath::clamp(dot(a,b)/denom, -1.0f, 1.0f));`. For find_hypotenuse specifically, test `are_equal(dot(e0, e2), 0.0f)` — far better conditioned near 90 degrees than an acos round-trip — and return bool+out-param instead of a magic -1 the caller turns into a throw.
findings.verify_note: Read MattMath.cpp:1808-1811, 3512-3537, 3633-3694, 4460-4463; confirmed FloatingPointModel=Fast at ArtAttack.vcxproj:94,116,139,165. Checked LevelObjectBuilder.cpp:155-178 — get_hypotenuse is not called during level load.

findings.title: MatrixF::operator== iterates rows over the column count and columns over the row count
findings.detail:
Verified. `get_dimensions()` (2523-2526) returns `Vector2I(this->_columns, this->_rows)` and is documented at MattMath.h:697 as '// x = columns, y = rows'. But operator== does:
```cpp
for (int i = 0; i < dimensions.x; i++)      // i ranges over COLUMN count
    for (int j = 0; j < dimensions.y; j++)  // j ranges over ROW count
        if (this->get_element(i, j) != ...) // get_element(row, column)
```
So the row index ranges over the column count and vice versa. Square matrices work by accident; for a 2x3, `get_element(2, 0)` fails row_valid and throws std::invalid_argument out of an equality operator. Dead code (no MatrixF users), hence medium not high.
findings.suggestion: Compare `_rows`, `_columns` and `_elements` directly and delete get_dimensions(), whose x=columns/y=rows convention needs a comment to explain it and is a trap for exactly this reason. Or delete the whole matrix subsystem.
findings.verify_note: Read MattMath.cpp:2523-2526, 2647-2670, 2701-2712 and the comment at MattMath.h:697.

findings.title: Vector3F's seven free operators are declared `static` in the header, giving them internal linkage
findings.detail:
Verified. MattMath.h:676-682 declares all seven arithmetic operators `static`, at namespace scope in a header. The definitions at MattMath.cpp:3110-3137 are written without `static`, but per [dcl.stc] the earlier declaration wins and they retain internal linkage. Every TU other than MattMath.cpp sees seven declared-but-never-defined internal functions, so the first TU to write `v3a + v3b` outside MattMath.cpp fails to build.

Confirmed as a copy-paste slip: the structurally identical operator sets for Vector2I (394-400), Vector2F (500-506), Colour (647-653) and MatrixF (729-732) are all correctly non-static. It has not bitten yet because Vector3F's only external use is Drawer, which reads `.x/.y/.z` members directly (Drawer.cpp:34,43) and never uses the operators.
findings.suggestion: Drop `static` from all seven. Better: once Drawer takes a real Camera instead of abusing Vector3F as {translation.x, translation.y, scale}, delete Vector3F entirely — those four member accesses are its only external use.
findings.verify_note: Read MattMath.h:655-682 and MattMath.cpp:3110-3137. Compared with the non-static operator sets at MattMath.h:394-400, 500-506, 647-653, 729-732. Read Drawer.cpp:33-53 to confirm no operator use.

findings.title: Colour's int and float constructors overlap: Colour(1, 1, 1) is near-black, Colour(1.0f, 1.0f, 1.0f) is white
findings.detail:
Verified. `Colour(float,float,float)` / `(float,float,float,float)` take 0..1 (MattMath.cpp:2187-2196); `Colour(int r, int g, int b, int a = 255)` takes 0..255 and divides by 255 (set_from_int_rgba, 2351-2358). With integer literals the int overload is an exact match and wins outright, so `Colour(1,1,1)` gives (0.0039, 0.0039, 0.0039) — visually black — where white was almost certainly meant. `Colour(0,0,0)` happens to be right, which hides the bug. A mixed call like `Colour(1.0f, 0, 0)` is genuinely ambiguous (float->int and int->float are both conversion rank), so the overload set is a compile-error trap too. /W4 issues no diagnostic for the silent case.

Same struct, verified separately: `Colour() = default` leaves `a = 0.0f` (MattMath.h:591) — a default-constructed Colour is fully transparent — while `Colour(r,g,b)` sets a = 1.0f (MattMath.cpp:2188). Two different notions of default alpha in one type; a Colour member left default-initialised draws nothing, which reads as a missing texture rather than an unset colour. Neither the int constructor nor `Colour(const std::string&)` is explicit.
findings.suggestion: Replace the int constructor with `static Colour from_rgba8(std::uint8_t r, g, b, a = 255)`, update Colour.h:309-313, make the string constructor explicit (or a named try_parse), and change the default member initialiser to `float a = 1.0f`.
findings.verify_note: Read MattMath.h:586-600 and MattMath.cpp:2187-2214, 2351-2358. Confirmed the a=0.0f NSDMI at MattMath.h:591 against a=1.0f at MattMath.cpp:2188.

findings.title: Not one constructor in MattMath.h is explicit, creating a lossy implicit conversion cycle between the vector types
findings.detail:
Verified by count: `grep -c explicit ArtAttack/MattMath.h` returns 0. The consequences that compile silently at /W4:
- `Vector2I(const Vector2F&)` (h:362, truncating via static_cast<int> at MattMath.cpp:1375-1379) and `Vector2F(const Vector2I&)` (h:413) are both implicit, so `v2i == v2f` compiles by truncating the float side: `Vector2I(1,1) == Vector2F(1.9f, 1.9f)` is true.
- `Vector2F(float f)` (h:409) broadcasts a scalar into both components (MattMath.cpp:1529-1533). Combined with `typedef Vector2F Point2F` (h:33) and `virtual bool intersects(const Point2F&)` (h:78), `rect.intersects(0.5f)` and `shape->offset(3.0f)` compile and mean the point/vector (0.5,0.5) and (3,3).
- `RectangleI(MattMath::RectangleF rectangle)` (h:524) is not only implicit but takes its polymorphic argument **by value**, unlike every sibling constructor at 515-526 which takes const&. The body (MattMath.cpp:1982-1988) only reads four floats. It also duplicates the existing `RectangleF::get_rectangle_i()` (h:229).
- `RectangleF(const RECT&)` / `(SimpleMath::Rectangle)` (h:198-199) and `Colour(const std::string&)` (h:600) likewise convert implicitly.
Nothing in the type system distinguishes a position from a size from a direction either — all three are Vector2F.
findings.suggestion: Mark every cross-type converting constructor explicit, and take RectangleI(const RectangleF&) by const reference (or delete it in favour of get_rectangle_i()). Where truncation is intended, replace the constructor with a named conversion so the loss is visible at the call site. Consider making Point2F a distinct type rather than a typedef of Vector2F.
findings.verify_note: grep -c explicit ArtAttack/MattMath.h = 0. Read MattMath.h:354-413, 508-526; MattMath.cpp:1375-1384, 1529-1553, 1982-1988.

findings.title: RectangleF::intersection returns a zero rect at the origin as its no-overlap sentinel, and the collision resolver uses it unchecked
findings.suggestion: Split query from computation: keep `bool intersects()` for the test and change intersection to `bool intersection(const RectangleF&, RectangleF& out) const`, or std::optional<RectangleF> once the project is on C++17. At minimum make the sentinel obviously invalid (negative width) and document it.
findings.verify_note: Read MattMath.cpp:920-923, 1099-1121 and CollisionTools.cpp:209-229. The intersection result is consumed without any emptiness check.

findings.title: RectangleF has no width/height >= 0 invariant, and from_top_left_bottom_right builds inverted rects straight from level JSON
findings.suggestion: Normalise the two corners in from_top_left_bottom_right (std::minmax), add `bool RectangleF::is_valid() const { return width >= 0.0f && height >= 0.0f; }`, and have LevelObjectBuilder reject invalid rectangles at load with a message naming the offending object — rather than the current bare `throw std::exception("Invalid rectangle type")`.
findings.verify_note: Read MattMath.cpp:252-258, 760-775, 881-887, 1099-1133 and LevelObjectBuilder.cpp:36-56, 79-96.

findings.title: from_top_left_bottom_right's float overload takes (top, left, bottom, right) while its sibling takes (top-left, bottom-right)
findings.detail: Verified. The Vector2F overload takes a top-left *point* then a bottom-right *point*, i.e. (x,y) then (x,y). The float overload takes (top, left, bottom, right) — y, x, y, x, the opposite pairing. The definition at MattMath.cpp:1129-1133 is internally consistent with its parameter names (`return RectangleF(left, top, right - left, bottom - top);`), but a caller mirroring the sibling will write `from_top_left_bottom_right(left, top, right, bottom)` and get x and y transposed with width/height swapped — no diagnostic possible, all four parameters are float. Zero callers; both live uses (LevelObjectBuilder.cpp:51, 94) take the Vector2F form. A landmine, not a live bug.
findings.suggestion: Delete the float overload. If a scalar form is wanted, name it so the signature and the name agree: `from_ltrb(float left, float top, float right, float bottom)`.
findings.verify_note: Read MattMath.h:293-296 and MattMath.cpp:1122-1133; grepped from_top_left_bottom_right — only the Vector2F overload is called.

findings.title: colour_from_name silently returns WHITE for unknown names, omits the TEAM_* colours, and is `static` in a header
findings.detail:
Verified. A 150-line if-chain of `if (name == "ALICE_BLUE") return colour_consts::ALICE_BLUE;` ending in `return colour_consts::WHITE;` at line 465.

1. Silent fallback on external data. This is the sole colour path for level content — LevelObjectBuilder.cpp:65, 142, 176, 196 all pass `json["colour"].GetString()` straight in, and none of them checks HasMember/IsString first. A typo produces a white object with no exception and no log, while every other JSON field in that file throws (`"Invalid collision type"` at :34, `"Invalid rectangle type"` at :55, `"Invalid paintable edges"` at :128). Colour is the one field that fails silently.
2. Incomplete table, verified: the five TEAM_* colours defined immediately above at Colour.h:309-313 have no entries in the ladder. A level author writing `"colour": "TEAM_BLUE"` — the obvious guess — gets white.
3. `static` at namespace scope in a header means every including TU compiles its own copy of the ~150-branch function and discards it in all but the one TU that calls it.
findings.suggestion: Return `bool try_colour_from_name(std::string_view, Colour& out)` or std::optional so the caller must handle the miss, add the TEAM_* entries, back it with one function-local `static const std::unordered_map`, and move the definition into a .cpp. Have LevelObjectBuilder throw with the offending file, object and colour string.
findings.verify_note: Read Colour.h:305-469 (start, TEAM_* block, ladder tail and WHITE fallback) and LevelObjectBuilder.cpp:60-70, 138-146, 170-200. Confirmed no TEAM_* branch exists in the ladder.

findings.title: Every value type compares floats with exact ==, and two live code paths depend on bit-exactness under /fp:fast
findings.detail:
Verified. Bit-exact operator== on Vector2F (1574-1577), RectangleF (863-869), Colour (2242-2248), Vector4F (2166-2172), Vector3F (3058-3063), Segment (4045-4049), Viewport (3287-3295), RectangleI (2053-2059). Meanwhile `MattMath::are_equal` (93-100) exists for exactly this and is used at only three sites outside MattMath.cpp (Player.cpp:767, 802, 811). FloatingPointModel=Fast is set in all four configurations.

Two live dependencies I verified:
- Player::on_structure_ramp_collision (Player.cpp:254-261) does `direction == Vector2F::DIRECTION_UP`, `== DIRECTION_UP_LEFT`, etc. This works only because direction_to_8_cardinal_direction (MattMath.cpp:1870-1904) returns copies of those exact global constants. Any refactor that recomputes the direction instead of returning the constant silently breaks ramp collision.
- StructurePaintable.cpp:193 does `edges[i] == this->_paintable_edges[j]`, comparing Segments whose endpoints were computed by get_left_edge()/get_top_edge()/etc. in two different translation units (LevelObjectBuilder.cpp:112-124 vs StructurePaintable.cpp:188). Both recompute `x + width`; under /fp:fast nothing guarantees identical contraction in both TUs.
findings.suggestion: Keep operator== exact (correct for a value type) but stop using it for geometric predicates. Have direction_to_8_cardinal_direction return the existing `MattMath::direction` enum (MattMath.h:12-23), and replace the Segment matching in StructurePaintable with the face-flags struct noted in the get_edges finding. Add are_equal overloads for RectangleF/Segment for cases that genuinely want tolerance.
findings.verify_note: Read the listed operator== bodies; grepped are_equal outside MattMath.cpp (3 hits, all Player.cpp); read Player.cpp:245-268 and StructurePaintable.cpp:186-212; confirmed FloatingPointModel=Fast in all four vcxproj configs.

findings.title: EPSILON is an absolute 1e-4, smaller than one float ULP at the coordinate magnitudes the levels use — and a second EPSILON 100x tighter is visible in the same TU
findings.detail:
Verified. `constexpr float EPSILON = 0.0001f;` (MattMath.h:46) is the default for `are_equal(float, float, float epsilon = EPSILON)` (h:59), the codebase's only tolerance primitive (MattMath.cpp:93-96, `fabs(a-b) < epsilon`).

The levels are not unit-scale: close_quarters.json out_of_bounds is {x:-100, y:-100, width:6200, height:6200}.
