One ULP of a float at magnitude 6000 is about 4.9e-4 — five times larger than EPSILON — so at world scale are_equal is *harsher* than 'equal after one rounding step'. Consumers that rely on it structurally: RectangleRotated::axes_valid (4522-4538), edges_valid (4539-4565, which compares edge *lengths* in world units with the same absolute 1e-4), TriangleRightAxisAligned::find_hypotenuse (3665-3684), Vector2F::get_direction (1662-1714, which applies the absolute epsilon to raw components).

Two smaller defects verified in the same three lines: the Vector2F overload spells its default as the literal `0.0001f` (h:61) instead of naming EPSILON, so the two can drift apart silently; and EricsonMath.h:75 declares a second `constexpr float EPSILON = 0.000001f`, visible in MattMath.cpp because it includes EricsonMath.h at line 3. Unqualified EPSILON inside namespace MattMath resolves to MattMath::EPSILON by inner-scope lookup, which is what each site wants — but the resolution is invisible at the point of use.
findings.suggestion: Provide a relative-plus-absolute comparison and reserve the absolute form for comparisons against zero. Change h:61's default to `= EPSILON`. Rename the two constants (MattMath::DEFAULT_EPSILON, EricsonMath::INTERSECTION_EPSILON) and qualify every unqualified use in MattMath.cpp. Use std::fabs (float overload) rather than fabs, which forces a float->double->float round trip.
findings.verify_note: Read MattMath.h:44-61, MattMath.cpp:93-100, 3665-3684, 4522-4565; EricsonMath.h:75; ArtAttack/levels/close_quarters.json:52-58 for the coordinate range.

findings.title: Viewport::get_d3d_viewport_ptr reinterpret_casts `this` to an unrelated D3D11_VIEWPORT
findings.suggestion: Delete it. Callers needing a pointer for RSSetViewports should hold the value: `const D3D11_VIEWPORT vp = v.get_d3d_viewport(); ctx->RSSetViewports(1, &vp);`. If a zero-copy path is ever needed, make Viewport *contain* a D3D11_VIEWPORT and return &_vp rather than punning.
findings.verify_note: Read MattMath.cpp:3201-3216 and MattMath.h:767-806. Grepped get_d3d_viewport_ptr repo-wide: declaration and definition only.

findings.title: RectangleRotated mutators modify state, then validate, then throw — leaving the cached points inconsistent with the extents
findings.detail:
Verified at six sites. inflate (4295-4305):
```cpp
this->_hw_extents += Vector2F(amount, amount);   // committed
if (!this->half_widths_valid()) { throw std::invalid_argument(...); }
this->_points = this->calculate_points();
```
On the throw path _hw_extents already holds the invalid value while _points still describes the previous extents — the object's cached corners no longer correspond to its stored state. Any later get_bounding_box() (4217-4232), contains() or intersects() silently reports geometry from the stale cache. No exception guarantee at all, not even basic. Same shape at set_x_axis (4359-4369), set_y_axis (4370-4380), set_half_extents (4381-4391), set_half_x_width (4392-4402), set_half_y_width (4403-4413).

This matters because Shape::inflate is invoked polymorphically from the collision path and nothing in CollisionTools catches std::invalid_argument — the object survives the unwind corrupted and keeps colliding.
findings.suggestion: Validate first, commit second: compute the candidate into a local, check it, then assign and recompute _points. That gives the strong guarantee for free. Make half_widths_valid/axes_valid take the value to check rather than reading members.
findings.verify_note: Read MattMath.cpp:4269-4305, 4353-4413, 4482-4538; confirmed no try/catch around Shape::inflate in CollisionTools.cpp.

findings.title: RectangleRotated stores exactly 4 points in a heap std::vector and reallocates it on every mutation
findings.detail:
Verified. `std::vector<Point2F> _points = { Point2F::ZERO, ... }` (MattMath.h:1119-1120) with a count fixed at 4 forever — get_point_0..3 (MattMath.cpp:4414-4429) and get_edge_0..3 (4434-4449) index _points[0..3] unconditionally. One heap allocation per RectangleRotated construction, plus one per mutation: every mutator re-runs `calculate_points()`, which itself allocates a fresh `std::vector<Point2F> points(4)` and returns it by value (4487-4499). Sites: offset (4273), set_center (4357), set_x_axis (4368), set_y_axis (4379), set_half_extents (4390), set_half_x_width (4401), set_half_y_width (4412), inflate (4304), both constructors (4199, 4214). `offset()` is what CollisionTools::bracket_object_collision_generic (CollisionTools.cpp:55-68) drives once per iteration.

Separately verified: `get_quad()` (4450-4455) calls `calculate_points()` again — allocating a second vector — instead of using the cache it just maintained.
findings.suggestion: Change _points to std::array<Point2F,4> and have calculate_points fill it in place (void recalculate_points()), eliminating all allocation and the copy-return. get_points() (MattMath.h:1091) then returns const std::array<Point2F,4>&. Fix get_quad() to use the cache.
findings.verify_note: Read MattMath.h:1113-1133 and MattMath.cpp:4269-4310, 4353-4455, 4482-4510; CollisionTools.cpp:53-70.

findings.title: Shape::get_edges() returns std::vector<Segment> by value, forcing a heap allocation per edge query in the narrow phase
findings.detail:
Verified. `virtual std::vector<Segment> get_edges() const = 0;` (MattMath.h:87) forces every implementation to allocate for a count that is always 0, 3 or 4 and known at compile time: RectangleF (MattMath.cpp:808-818), Triangle (3502-3511), Quad (3943-3953), RectangleRotated (4284-4293), and Circle returns an empty vector (3340-3344). `std::vector<Triangle> get_triangles()` (MattMath.h:961) and `std::vector<Vector2F> get_points()` (865, 946) have the same shape.

Call sites inside the intersection functions, all verified: 219, 288, 369, 393-394 (two allocations for one triangle-pair test), 435, 480, 599, 646-647 (two per OBB pair). quads_intersect (492-511) allocates two vector<Triangle> then calls triangles_intersect up to 4 times, each allocating two vector<Segment> — up to 10 allocations for one quad-vs-quad test. CollisionTools::bracket_object_collision_generic (CollisionTools.cpp:55-68) then repeats `collider->intersects(collidee)` for `iterations` passes.

Note: the reviewers' claim of an O(n^2) all-pairs loop in Level::update_level_logic is outside this module and I did not verify it; the allocation counts above are verified independently of it.

Also verified: `RectangleF collider_aabb = collider->get_bounding_box();` at CollisionTools.cpp:35 and again at :57 is computed and never read — dead in both functions.
findings.suggestion: Return a fixed-capacity type: `virtual int get_edges(Segment (&out)[4]) const` returning the count, or std::array from the concrete types with a fill-a-span form on the virtual interface. Note RectangleRotated::get_points() already returns const& while Triangle/Quad return by value — that inconsistency is itself a bug magnet. Delete the dead collider_aabb locals.
findings.verify_note: Read MattMath.h:87, 865, 946, 961; MattMath.cpp:808-818, 3340-3344, 3485-3511, 3943-3953, 4284-4293 and the eight call sites; CollisionTools.cpp:32-70.

findings.title: Shape::intersects dynamic_casts after already switching on the shape_type tag, and dereferences both results unchecked
findings.detail:
Verified:
```cpp
switch (other->get_shape_type())
{
case shape_type::RECTANGLE:
    return this->intersects(*dynamic_cast<const RectangleF*>(other));
...
default: throw std::invalid_argument("Shape type not recognized");
```
Three issues, in descending order of how much I believe them:
1. The switch has already established the dynamic type, so the dynamic_cast buys nothing and costs an out-of-line MSVC RTTI walk on the innermost call of the collision system. static_cast is correct here.
2. Hand-rolled double dispatch: Shape declares seven intersects overloads (MattMath.h:73-79) but shape_type enumerates five, because Segment and Point2F are not Shapes — so two of the seven pure virtuals every shape must implement can never be reached through the dispatcher. Adding a shape means editing a shape_type value, a pure virtual, five overrides, a switch case and ~6 free functions.
3. `other` is dereferenced with no null check and the dynamic_cast result is dereferenced with no null check. Not reachable today (all get_shape() implementations return member addresses or unique_ptr::get()), but the author clearly intended defensiveness here — the default case throws — and only half-implemented it. This part is speculative rather than a live defect.
findings.suggestion: Replace the dynamic_casts with static_cast immediately. Longer term, replace the hierarchy with a closed sum type (std::variant over the concrete shapes) and a single `intersects(const Shape&, const Shape&)` via std::visit over a symmetric overload set, so the compiler enforces exhaustiveness. Also fix the misleading free-function name at MattMath.h:117: rectangle_rotated_rectangle_intersect(const RectangleF&, const RectangleRotated&) reads as (rotated, rect) but takes the opposite order.
findings.verify_note: Read MattMath.cpp:119-141, MattMath.h:68-89, 96-182, shape_type.h. Confirmed shape_type has 5 shape values while Shape has 7 intersects overloads.

findings.title: The convex-vs-convex intersection algorithm is retyped once per shape pair, and the copies have diverged
findings.detail:
Verified. The same three-phase algorithm (AABB reject -> does A contain any vertex of B -> does B contain any vertex of A -> do any edges cross) appears with only the accessors changed at rectangle_triangle_intersect (193-229), rectangle_rotated_rectangle_intersect (260-298), triangle_rectangle_rotated_intersect (453-490), triangles_intersect (381-407), rectangles_rotated_intersect (619-661) and triangle_segment_intersect (426-445). A second family — 'split the quad into triangles and loop' — is typed six times at rectangle_quad_intersect (231-245), circle_quad_intersect (319-331), triangle_quad_intersect (409-424), quads_intersect (492-511), quad_segment_intersect (513-528), quad_point_intersect (530-543) and quad_rectangle_rotated_intersect (545-561).

The copies have already diverged in two verified ways: triangles_intersect is missing the AABB early-out its siblings have, and its edge loop is wrong (see the separate high finding). This is the concrete cost of the duplication, not a hypothetical one.
findings.suggestion: Every one of these shapes exposes get_points() and get_edges(). Write the convex-vs-convex test once against those two accessors — ideally as a separating-axis test over the union of both shapes' edge normals, an O(n+m) function correct for all convex pairs — and keep only the genuinely special cases (circle-vs-X) separate.
findings.verify_note: Read MattMath.cpp:193-661 in full. Confirmed the structural repetition and the two divergences in triangles_intersect.

findings.title: Colour clamps inside every arithmetic operator, destroying linearity, while its [0,1] invariant is unenforceable through public fields
findings.detail:
Verified. Colour has public `float r,g,b,a` (588-591) *and* a full getter/setter pair per channel (616-624), and calls clamp_colours() from every constructor (MattMath.cpp:2190, 2195, 2200, 2205), every operator= (2221, 2230, 2239), every compound operator (2253-2306), every setter (2326-2349), set_from_int_rgba, set_from_hex, saturate, desaturate, brighten, darken, invert. Every free operator constructs through the clamping constructor (2445-2472). That is roughly 25 defensive calls guarding an invariant that `c.r = 5.0f;` destroys, which makes the 8 accessor methods pure ceremony.

The consequence that actually matters for an engine: clamping inside arithmetic breaks linearity. `(a - b) + b != a`, and `c *= 2.0f; c /= 2.0f;` is not the identity. So the type cannot be used for additive paint/light accumulation, difference or tint computation, or any multi-step blend — which is exactly what a Splatoon-like paint engine needs colour arithmetic for.
findings.suggestion: Make Colour a plain unclamped linear 4-float value type with constexpr aggregate construction, no clamping in operators, and no getter/setter pairs over public fields. Provide an explicit `Colour saturated() const` and clamp at the single point of conversion to the render target (get_xm_vector/get_sm_colour).
findings.verify_note: Read MattMath.h:586-645 and MattMath.cpp:2187-2472; counted the clamp_colours() call sites.

findings.title: MattMath.h declares std::unique_ptr and std::string without including <memory> or <string>
findings.detail:
Verified. The header's entire include list is SimpleMath.h, shape_type.h, <d3d11.h>, <cmath>, <vector>. It then declares the engine's ownership primitive at line 85 — `virtual std::unique_ptr<Shape> clone() const = 0;` — plus unique_ptr at 206, 822, 859, 937, 1067, and std::string at 600 and 628. Colour.h includes only MattMath.h yet declares 149 const std::string objects.

It compiles by two separate accidents, both verified: in the game project, pch.h includes <algorithm> (42), <memory> (49) and <stdexcept> (50) and is force-included ahead of everything; in MattMathTests, pch.h is an empty stub (I read it — it contains only the include guard) and MathTests.cpp:5 `#include "..\ArtAttack\MattMath.cpp"` works only because CppUnitTest.h on line 2 drags in <string> and <memory> first. MattMath.cpp itself uses std::min/std::max, std::invalid_argument and std::make_unique with none of <algorithm>, <stdexcept> or <memory> included directly.

For a header meant to be a reusable engine's public interface, a consumer who includes MattMath.h first — the normal thing — gets an error pointing at the header, not at their code.
findings.suggestion: Add <memory>, <string> and <cstdint> to MattMath.h, <string> to Colour.h, and <algorithm>/<stdexcept>/<memory> to MattMath.cpp. Apply include-what-you-use to every engine header rather than relying on the consumer's PCH ordering.
findings.verify_note: Read MattMath.h:1-10 and the cited use sites; read MattMathTests/pch.h (empty stub) and MathTests.cpp:1-10; grepped ArtAttack/pch.h for <memory>/<string>/<algorithm>/<stdexcept>.

findings.title: Every named constant is dynamically initialised, and DebugText.h reads one across TUs during static init
findings.detail:
Verified. None of the constants is constant-initialised, because no constructor involved is constexpr: `RectangleF::ZERO` (1134), `Vector2I::ZERO` (1495), `Vector2F::ZERO/ONE/DIRECTION_RIGHT/DOWN/LEFT/UP` (1907-1912), `RectangleI::ZERO` (2138), `Camera::DEFAULT_CAMERA` (4180). The four diagonal directions (1913-1916) each run `unit_vector()` — a sqrtf and two divides — before main.

The cross-TU dependency is real and verified: DebugText.h:14 has, at namespace scope in a header, `const static MattMath::Vector2F DEBUG_POSITION = MattMath::Vector2F::ZERO;`. That object is dynamically initialised in every including TU from an object dynamically initialised in MattMath.obj, and the relative order across TUs is unspecified. It is benign today only because the correct value is bitwise zero, which zero-initialised static storage already holds. The same line written with Vector2F::ONE, DIRECTION_UP or Camera::DEFAULT_CAMERA (scale = 1.0f) would silently read zeros in a link order the author never tested. The same hazard spreads through ~20 default arguments (DrawObject.h:15, AnimatedSprite.h:17/25, MovingObject.h:14, Mh.h:86/125/154) and through the default member initialisers at MattMath.h:810, 844, 978-979, 984-985, 1114-1120.

One correction to the reviewers: they claimed all these constructors are written as body assignments. RectangleF(float,float,float,float) (MattMath.cpp:667-670) and all four Colour value constructors (2187-2206) do use member-init lists. The non-constexpr point stands regardless — they are out-of-line and RectangleF cannot be a literal type while it inherits Shape.
findings.suggestion: Make the constructors constexpr and inline in the header, and declare the constants `static constexpr` — under C++17 they become implicitly inline and the ordering question disappears. This depends on detaching RectangleF from Shape and on setting <LanguageStandard>. Failing that, use the Meyers-singleton accessor form. Compute the diagonal directions from literals rather than a runtime unit_vector() call.

findings.title: set_from_hex validates only the string length; a leading '#' silently yields black and a bad digit throws during static init
findings.detail:
Verified. Three defects in one function:
1. Any length other than 6 or 8 falls to the else branch and becomes opaque black with no diagnostic. `"#ff0000"` is 7 characters, so the near-universal way of writing a hex colour silently produces black.
2. No digit validation. `std::stoi` throws std::invalid_argument on a non-hex character (e.g. "gg0000" passes the length check). Colour.h constructs 153 of these at namespace scope, so a single bad literal there propagates out of a dynamic initialiser and calls std::terminate before main, with no attributable diagnostic.
3. Cost: three or four substr temporaries plus three or four std::stoi calls (each doing strtol with locale handling) per colour, to decode 8 hex nibbles — multiplied by every Colour constant in every including TU.
findings.suggestion: Add `bool try_set_from_hex(std::string_view)` that strips an optional leading '#', validates every character with std::isxdigit and returns false on failure. Decode nibbles with a small lookup rather than substr+stoi. Once the palette is constexpr this function leaves the startup path entirely.
findings.verify_note: Read MattMath.cpp:2359-2384 and Colour.h:160-313 (153 Colour constants, all constructed from html:: hex strings).

findings.title: Camera lives in the math header, writes its transform five times, and is bypassed by Drawer, which reinvents it as a Vector3F
findings.detail:
Verified. Camera (translation + scale) is a presentation concept in the maths library, and its core transform `(x - t.x) * scale` is written out five times: calculate_view_rectangle() const (MattMath.cpp:4116-4123), calculate_view_rectangle(RectangleF&) const (4124-4131), static calculate_view_rectangle(rect, camera) (4132-4140), static calculate_view_rectangle(rect, camera, out) (4141-4150), and calculate_view_position (4170-4175).

Meanwhile Drawer does not use Camera at all. Drawer.cpp:42-53:
```cpp
RectangleI Drawer::calculate_draw_rectangle(const Vector2F& position, const Vector2F& size, const Vector3F& camera)
{
    Vector2F draw_pos = (position - Vector2F(camera.x, camera.y)) * camera.z;
```
— a Vector3F whose .x/.y are treated as translation and .z as scale, i.e. Camera with the type information thrown away. That is Vector3F's only external use in the codebase. And Matrix3x3F, which has rotation/scale/translation factories and would have unified all of it, has zero callers.
findings.suggestion: Move Camera out of MattMath into the presentation layer as Camera2D backed by a single transform. Expose one `Vector2F world_to_view(Vector2F) const` and derive the rectangle overloads from it; delete the other four. Change Drawer::calculate_draw_rectangle to take `const Camera&`, then delete Vector3F.
findings.verify_note: Read MattMath.cpp:4092-4180 and MattMath.h:1007-1045; Drawer.cpp:33-53; grepped Vector3F outside MattMath — only Drawer.

findings.title: Vector2I division has no zero guard, and Vector2I::scale(SimpleMath::Vector2) truncates the scale factor to int
findings.detail:
Two verified defects in the same block, merged.

1. `operator/=(const Vector2I&)` (1439-1444), `operator/=(int)` (1451-1456) and the free forms (1512-1519) do raw integer division. Unlike the float equivalents, integer division by zero is UB and raises #DE on x86 — an instant process kill, not a quiet NaN. No guard, no documented precondition. Zero callers today, which is the only reason no crash has been seen; graded medium not high for that reason.

2. Worse and more concrete — `void Vector2I::scale(const DirectX::SimpleMath::Vector2& amount)` (1475-1479):
```cpp
this->x *= static_cast<int>(amount.x);
this->y *= static_cast<int>(amount.y);
```
The *scale factor* is truncated to int before multiplying, so `scale({1.5f, 1.5f})` multiplies by 1 (no-op) and `scale({0.5f, 0.5f})` multiplies by 0 (zeroes the vector). This is the one overload whose entire purpose is fractional scaling, and it cannot do it.
findings.suggestion: Delete the component-wise integer division operators — nothing calls them and the operation has no obvious meaning for a 2D point. Fix scale(const Vector2&) to multiply in float and round: `x = static_cast<int>(std::lround(x * amount.x))`, or delete it too.
findings.verify_note: Read MattMath.cpp:1439-1456, 1465-1494, 1512-1523. Grepped Vector2I division operators and scale(Vector2) for callers: none.

findings.title: `X(const X&) = default;` on every type suppresses the implicit move constructor and move assignment
findings.detail:
Verified on 17 types: RectangleF (h:192), Vector2I (360), Vector2F (408), RectangleI (516), Vector4F (575), Colour (594), Vector3F (662), MatrixF (687), Matrix3x3F (753), Viewport (778), Circle (814), Triangle (847), TriangleRightAxisAligned (898), Quad (923), Segment (988), Camera (1013), RectangleRotated (1050). A user-declared copy constructor — `= default` still counts — suppresses both implicit move operations, so all 17 are copy-only.

For the plain-float types this is harmless noise. It costs real work on the only two that own heap memory: RectangleRotated holds `std::vector<Point2F> _points` (h:1119-1120) and MatrixF holds `std::vector<float> _elements` (h:723). Every apparent move of those — vector reallocation, NRVO failures, `*this = MattMath::add(*this, other)` in MatrixF::operator+= (MattMath.cpp:2673) — is a deep copy plus a fresh allocation. Graded low because RectangleRotated should not have a heap vector at all (separate finding) and MatrixF should be deleted.
findings.suggestion: Delete every `X(const X&) = default;` line. They add nothing — the implicit copy constructor already exists and does the same thing — and they are the sole reason move operations are missing. Rule of zero.
findings.verify_note: Read all 17 declarations in MattMath.h and the vector members at h:723 and 1119-1120.

findings.title: Matrix3x3F publicly inherits MatrixF, which has no virtual destructor and value-semantic operators
findings.detail:
Verified. `struct Matrix3x3F : MatrixF` (h:750) where MatrixF (684-727) declares no destructor and no virtual member at all. Three hazards: deleting through a MatrixF* is UB with no protection (no virtual dtor, no protected dtor); MatrixF::operator= is public and implicit, so `MatrixF& r = m3x3; r = MatrixF(5,7);` turns a '3x3' into one claiming 5 rows and 7 columns while still statically typed Matrix3x3F; and the free operators (h:729-732) return MatrixF, so composing two Matrix3x3F transforms yields a MatrixF that cannot be fed back without re-validation.

Graded low rather than medium only because the whole subsystem is unreachable dead code — but combined with the uninitialised _elements defect, Matrix3x3F is not usable as written under any circumstances.
findings.suggestion: Delete both types. If a 3x3 transform is ever wanted, make it a distinct type over std::array<float,9> — constexpr-friendly, allocation-free, with its own operators returning Matrix3x3F.
findings.verify_note: Read MattMath.h:684-765. MatrixF has no destructor declaration and no virtual functions; Matrix3x3F inherits publicly.

findings.title: Matrix3x3F's element-count check is unreachable — the base constructor already threw
findings.detail:
Verified. `Matrix3x3F::Matrix3x3F(const std::vector<float>& elements) : MatrixF(3, 3, elements)` then checks `if (elements.size() != 9) throw`. The mem-initialiser runs first, and MatrixF(int, int, const std::vector<float>&) (2483-2493) already does `if (rows * columns != elements.size()) throw std::invalid_argument("Number of elements does not match the dimensions of the matrix")`. With rows=columns=3 that is the identical condition, so the derived check can never fire and the caller always sees the less specific base message.

Verified in the same lines: that base check compares `int` (rows * columns) against `size_t` (elements.size()) — a signed/unsigned mismatch at /W4 (C4018/C4389), and TreatWarningAsError is set nowhere in either vcxproj, so it accumulates silently.
findings.suggestion: Delete the dead derived check; cast both sides of the base comparison after validating rows >= 0 && columns >= 0, or take dimensions as an unsigned type so the invalid state is unrepresentable. Or delete the whole subsystem.
findings.verify_note: Read MattMath.cpp:2483-2493 and 2987-2994; grepped TreatWarningAsError in both vcxproj files — absent, with WarningLevel Level4 on the engine and Level3 on the tests.

findings.title: direction_to_8_cardinal_direction maps the zero vector to DIRECTION_RIGHT with no way for the caller to tell
findings.detail:
Verified. `angle()` is `std::atan2(y, x)` (1749-1752) and atan2(0,0) is 0, so a zero-length input falls into the first branch (`angle >= -PI/8 && angle < PI/8`) and is reported as pointing right. I checked all eight sector boundaries against the y-down convention (DIRECTION_UP = {0,-1}) and they are correct and exhaustive; the degenerate input is the only hole.

Live path: Player::on_structure_ramp_collision (Player.cpp:247-250) feeds it the output of CollisionTools::calculate_object_collision_direction, a centre-to-centre vector that is zero when two shapes are exactly concentric. That resolves as a rightward collision.

Secondary, verified: the eight-way sibling `Vector2F::get_direction()` (1662-1714) uses are_equal(x, 0.0f) with the default absolute epsilon and returns MattMath::direction::NONE for the degenerate case. Two functions answering 'which of eight directions is this', one returning Vector2F and one returning the enum, with different degenerate behaviour.
findings.suggestion: Return direction::NONE (or the enum generally, which would also fix the exact-float comparisons in Player.cpp) and take an explicit minimum-magnitude threshold so a degenerate input must be handled. Then delete one of the two eight-way classifiers.
findings.verify_note: Read MattMath.cpp:1662-1714, 1749-1752, 1870-1905; Player.cpp:245-268. Checked each of the eight angular branches for coverage.

findings.title: RectangleI's Rectangle and RECT constructors narrow long to int implicitly, unlike every sibling
findings.detail:
Verified:
```cpp
RectangleI::RectangleI(const SimpleMath::Rectangle& rectangle)
{ this->x = rectangle.x; ... }          // long -> int, no cast
RectangleI::RectangleI(const RECT& rectangle)
{ this->x = rectangle.left; ... this->width = rectangle.right - rectangle.left; }
```
SimpleMath::Rectangle stores long and RECT stores LONG; both assigned to int members with no cast. Every other narrowing in these files is explicit: RectangleI(const Vector2F&, const Vector2F&) at 1967-1973, RectangleI(RectangleF) at 1982-1988, RectangleF::get_rectangle_i() at 823-829, RectangleI::get_sm_rectangle() at 2036-2042 all use static_cast. These eight assignments are the odd ones out and produce C4244 at /W4 with nothing failing the build.

No data is currently lost — long and int are both 32-bit on Windows — so this is about consistency and about not training yourself to ignore C4244.
findings.suggestion: Add static_cast<int> to all eight assignments, and turn on TreatWarningAsError for the engine project so the next one gets caught.
findings.verify_note: Read MattMath.cpp:1959-2002 and compared with the explicit casts at 823-829, 1967-1988, 2036-2052.

findings.title: Float-to-int rectangle conversions truncate toward zero with no rounding, NaN check or range check
findings.detail:
Verified. get_rectangle_i (823-829), get_sm_rectangle (830-836) and get_win_rect (837-846) all use bare static_cast on x, y, width, height. static_cast truncates toward zero, not toward negative infinity, so the mapping is discontinuous at 0: both -0.5f and 0.5f become 0. For rectangles at negative coordinates — and the levels do use them, close_quarters.json out_of_bounds starts at (-100, -100) — this is a systematic off-by-one on the left and top edges. The same pattern repeats in RectangleI's float constructors (1967-1981) and Vector2I's (1375-1384).

The NaN part of the reviewers' claim is technically correct (converting NaN or an out-of-int-range float to an integer type is UB) but I am grading it low rather than higher because the NaN sources in this module are all in unreachable code paths (see the normalize and angle_between findings).
findings.suggestion: Introduce one `int to_pixel(float)` helper using std::lround with a debug assert on std::isfinite and a clamp to int range, and route all of these through it. Pick and document a single convention (floor for positions, ceil for sizes is usual for rectangles) instead of letting truncation choose implicitly.
findings.verify_note: Read MattMath.cpp:823-846, 1375-1384, 1959-2002, 2036-2052; checked coordinate ranges in ArtAttack/levels/close_quarters.json.

findings.title: Three separate hand-rolled clamp implementations, and clamp passes NaN straight through
findings.detail:
Verified. MattMath.h:51-54 declares clamp(float), clamp_ref(float&), clamp(int), clamp_ref(int&); the bodies (MattMath.cpp:34-85) are four 12-line if/else ladders that C++17's std::clamp replaces exactly. `Vector2F::clamp`/`clamped` (1739-1748) do not call them — they hand-roll `std::min(std::max(...))` — so one operation exists three ways in one file.

Also verified: `MattMath::clamp` returns NaN unchanged, because `value < min` and `value > max` are both false for NaN. Colour::clamp_colours (2438-2444) is built entirely on it and is the Colour type's only invariant enforcement, so a NaN channel passes through to get_xm_vector() and the sprite batch. The NaN sources (Colour::operator/=(0.0f) at 2298-2306, operator/ at 2465-2468) have no callers, which is why I am grading this low rather than the 'high' one reviewer assigned. There is also no assert that min <= max: clamp(v, 10.0f, 0.0f) returns 10 for every input.
findings.suggestion: Set <LanguageStandard> and delete MattMath::clamp/clamp_ref in favour of std::clamp; rewrite Vector2F::clamp/clamped in terms of it. Until then, make clamp_colours NaN-safe (`if (!(v >= 0.0f)) v = 0.0f; else if (v > 1.0f) v = 1.0f;`) and guard Colour's division operators against a zero divisor.
findings.verify_note: Read MattMath.cpp:34-85, 1739-1748, 2289-2306, 2438-2444, 2461-2468. NaN behaviour follows directly from the branch structure.

findings.title: Four names for unitisation and a `normal()` one character from `normalize()` that means something entirely different
findings.detail:
Verified. Unitisation exists four times: normalized() (1724-1728), normalize() (1729-1734), to_unit_vector() (1774-1787), static unit_vector() (1852-1863) — with two incompatible zero-length contracts (see the separate robustness finding). Independently, `void Vector2F::normal()` (1768-1773) rotates the vector 90 degrees in place:
```cpp
float temp = x; x = -y; y = temp;
```
It is one character from normalize() and means a completely different thing. There is also a static `normal(vec)` (1865-1868).

Usage confirms the API is untended: to_unit_vector 0 callers, normalize 0 outside MattMath, normalized 2 (both in MovingObject, itself uncalled), unit_vector 3 in ArtAttack plus the tests. The same member/static/by-value/by-ref duplication runs through the whole type: angle() + static angle(vec); dot(other) + static dot(a,b); clamp() + clamped(); rotate() + rotate_vector() + rotate_vector_by_ref(); and RectangleF::intersection has both a member and a static form, Camera::calculate_view_rectangle has four.
findings.suggestion: Keep exactly two unitisation functions with one documented contract; rename normal()/normal(vec) to perpendicular(). Pick one form per operation (value-returning free functions for pure maths) and implement any second form by calling the first, so the maths exists once.
findings.verify_note: Read MattMath.cpp:1716-1748, 1757-1799, 1830-1868 and MattMath.h:438-486; grepped each name for external callers.

findings.title: RectangleF exposes ~70 members over four public floats, including a 20-strong hand-enumerated anchor cross-product
findings.detail:
Verified. Between h:256 and h:291: inflate x3, inflate_to_size x2, scale_at_center x3, offset x2, scale x2, scale_size_and_position x2, set_position x2, set_position_at_center x2, set_position_x, set_position_x_from_right, set_position_y, set_position_y_from_bottom, set_position_from_top_right x2, set_position_from_bottom_left x2, set_position_from_bottom_right x2, set_size x2, set_width, set_height. That is {which anchor} x {Vector2F or two floats} enumerated by hand — and incompletely: there is set_position_x_from_right but no set_position_from_top_left. h:208-211 also duplicates the public fields with get_x/get_y/get_width/get_height.

I spot-checked the reviewers' zero-caller claims and they hold for union_of, set_position_from_bottom_left/right, set_position_x_from_right, Vector2F::is_contained_within, min_vec, max_vec, angle_between, vec_from_angle_magnitude, cross, sign, rotate_vector_by_ref, Vector4F, MatrixF, Matrix3x3F and Viewport::get_d3d_viewport_ptr.
findings.suggestion: Delete the zero-caller members. Replace the positioning family with one anchor-based call — `void set_position(Vector2F, anchor = anchor::top_left)` — using a small enum (direction.h already contains a TOP_LEFT..BOTTOM_RIGHT enum that could be repurposed and namespaced). Drop get_x/get_y/get_width/get_height.
findings.verify_note: Read MattMath.h:184-301 and MattMath.cpp:932-1098; grepped the named members repo-wide for callers.

findings.title: Include guard is a bare BORDER_THICKNESS macro that will eat any future constant of that name
findings.detail:
Verified — the file is 12 lines:
```cpp
#ifndef BORDER_THICKNESS
#define BORDER_THICKNESS
```
Unlike every sibling (MATTMATH_H, COLOUR_H, DIMENSION_H), this defines an object-like macro named exactly BORDER_THICKNESS expanding to nothing. Any TU that includes it — CameraTools.h:4, and transitively anything using the camera — then cannot declare `constexpr float BORDER_THICKNESS = 8.0f;`, which preprocesses to `constexpr float = 8.0f;` and errors at the declaration rather than at the macro. Not hypothetical for this codebase: the adjacent constants are PaintTile.h `THICKNESS` and ViewportManager.h `DIVIDER_THICKNESS`.

Also verified: line 7 is `float top = 0.0f;;` (stray second semicolon); the struct sits in the global namespace while every comparable primitive lives in MattMath; and it is aggregate-initialised positionally from four same-typed floats at CameraTools.cpp:77-83, where transposing two is invisible to the compiler. RectangleF meanwhile only offers symmetric inflate (MattMath.cpp:932-949) — there is no way to inset a rectangle by four independent amounts, which is exactly what a scroll border, a UI margin or a nine-slice needs.
findings.suggestion: Rename the guard BORDER_THICKNESS_H (or switch the project to #pragma once), drop the stray semicolon, move the struct into namespace MattMath as `Thickness`, and add `RectangleF deflated(const Thickness&) const` / `inflated(...)`. CameraTools then becomes `rect.deflated(scroll_border)` instead of four hand-written edge computations.
findings.verify_note: Read BorderThickness.h in full; grepped BorderThickness — CameraTools.h:4, CameraTools.cpp:14/74/77 only; read CameraTools.cpp:70-92.

findings.title: dimension.h and direction.h are dead headers declaring maximally generic names at global scope, one of which collides with MattMath::direction
findings.detail:
Verified. dimension.h declares `enum class dimension { X, Y }` at global scope. It is included by nothing: grep for `dimension.h` and for `dimension::` across ArtAttack and MattMathTests returns zero hits. It exists only as ArtAttack.vcxproj:194. Same for direction.h (vcxproj:195): zero includers, and it declares a global `enum class direction` (anchor positions TOP_LEFT..BOTTOM_RIGHT) that collides by name with `MattMath::direction` (MattMath.h:12-23, the eight compass points returned by Vector2F::get_direction()).

That collision is a live hazard, not a stylistic one: Player.cpp writes unqualified `direction` under `using namespace MattMath;`, so the moment anyone includes direction.h in that TU the name becomes ambiguous or silently resolves to the wrong enum. For an engine that is meant to be reusable, leaking `dimension` and `direction` into the global namespace is a problem in its own right.
findings.suggestion: Delete dimension.h and its vcxproj entry. Either delete direction.h or rename its enum to `anchor` and move it into MattMath. Rename MattMath::direction to something that says what it is (cardinal_direction / direction_8), since Segment::get_direction() already returns a Vector2F under the same word. Also convert the three typedefs (Point2F h:33, AABB h:301, OBB h:1136) to `using`.
findings.verify_note: Read dimension.h and confirmed its guard is DIMENSION_H (correcting one reviewer who implied otherwise). Grepped 'dimension.h', 'direction.h', 'dimension::' — zero includers. Confirmed vcxproj entries at lines 194-195 and the two `direction` enums.

findings.title: Six pairs of out-parameter / discard intersect overloads where a single optional-returning function belongs
findings.detail:
Verified. The free API duplicates itself purely to make the contact point optional: rectangle_circle_intersect with and without `Point2F&` (h:99-103), circle_triangle_intersect (123-127), circle_segment_intersect (132-136), segments_intersect with `float& t, Point2F& p` and without (170-173). The discard overloads declare a dummy and throw it away (MattMath.cpp:314, 344, 578-579).

I reject the reviewers' sub-claim that these pass *uninitialised* dummies: Point2F is Vector2F, whose members have default initialisers (`float x = 0.0f;` at MattMath.h:404-405), so `Point2F point;` is value-correct. The `float t;` at 578 genuinely is uninitialised but is never read. So this is API duplication, not a correctness bug — graded low accordingly.
findings.suggestion: With C++17, collapse each pair into one function returning std::optional<Point2F> (or an optional Contact{point, t}). That removes the parallel overload set and the throwaway dummies in one change.
findings.verify_note: Read MattMath.h:96-182 and MattMath.cpp:306-346, 563-581. Checked MattMath.h:404-405 for Vector2F's default member initialisers, which refutes the uninitialised-dummy claim.

findings.title: No [[nodiscard]] anywhere, on an API built from confusable const/mutating name pairs
findings.detail: Verified: `grep -c nodiscard ArtAttack/MattMath.h` returns 0. This API is the textbook case for it, because it deliberately pairs a const version and a mutating version under near-identical names: `Vector2F normalized() const` vs `void normalize()` (h:445-446), `Vector2F clamped(...) const` vs `void clamp(...)` (h:450-451), and `RectangleF intersection(const RectangleF&) const` (h:249) sitting inside a block of mutators (inflate, scale_at_center, offset, h:256-267). Writing `rect.intersection(other);` or `v.clamped(a,b);` as a statement compiles silently and does nothing. Same for every factory: intersection(a,b), union_of, from_top_left_bottom_right, Vector2F::lerp/min_vec/max_vec/unit_vector/rotate_vector, Camera::calculate_*, and Shape::clone (h:85) — discarding a clone leaks nothing thanks to unique_ptr, but silently drops the object.
findings.suggestion: After moving to C++17, add [[nodiscard]] to every const accessor and static factory in MattMath.h, starting with the const/mutator pairs where the diagnostic maps directly onto a real class of bug.
findings.verify_note: grep -c nodiscard ArtAttack/MattMath.h = 0; read the cited declaration pairs.

findings.title: No <LanguageStandard> is set, so the whole project silently builds as C++14 — which blocks most of the fixes above
findings.detail:
Verified: `grep LanguageStandard` over both vcxproj files returns nothing, while WarningLevel (Level4 on the engine, Level3 on the tests), FloatingPointModel (Fast, all four configs) and ConformanceMode (true) are all set explicitly. With MSVC v145 and no explicit standard, the project defaults to an old standard rather than anything current.

I am promoting this from the several candidates that mentioned it in passing because it is the blocking dependency for a large share of the other findings: inline constexpr variables (the Colour.h palette and every MattMath constant, which would eliminate the static-initialisation-order hazard), std::optional (the intersection sentinel and the six out-param overload pairs), std::clamp, std::string_view, std::variant (the Shape dispatch), and [[nodiscard]]. Also verified: TreatWarningAsError is set nowhere, so the C4244/C4018/C4505 warnings the other findings mention accumulate silently at /W4.
findings.suggestion: Set <LanguageStandard>stdcpp17</LanguageStandard> (or stdcpp20) in all four configurations of both projects, and enable TreatWarningAsError at least for the engine project so new narrowing and unreferenced-function warnings are caught.
findings.verify_note: grepped LanguageStandard/FloatingPointModel/TreatWarningAsError/WarningLevel/ConformanceMode across ArtAttack.vcxproj and MattMathTests.vcxproj; LanguageStandard and TreatWarningAsError are absent from both.

findings.title: REJECTED AS WRITTEN, but a real adjacent bug: the Segment-based RectangleRotated constructor never normalises its axes
findings.suggestion: Normalise both axes in the Segment constructor exactly as the four-argument one does, and add a MattMathTests case constructing an OBB from a centre line of realistic length — the existing RectangleRotated tests evidently do not cover this path.
findings.verify_note: Read MattMath.cpp:4186-4215, 4063-4070, 4522-4538. The cited lines 4191-4192 are in the four-arg constructor; the Segment constructor at 4201 performs no normalisation at all.

findings.title: RectangleRotated(Segment, thickness) never normalises its axes, so it throws for every segment whose length != 1
findings.detail: Merges 5 duplicate candidates (all four "segment ctor" reports plus the "three divergent construction paths" report). Verified verbatim: line 4205 `this->_x_axis = center_line.get_direction();` and 4206 `this->_y_axis = Vector2F::normal(this->_x_axis);`. `Segment::get_direction()` (4063-4066) returns `point_1 - point_0` raw; `Vector2F::normal` (1865-1868) returns `(-y, x)` and does not normalise. `axes_valid()` (4522-4529) requires `are_equal(_x_axis.length(), 1.0f, EPSILON)` with EPSILON=1e-4 (MattMath.h:46). So the ctor at 4209-4212 throws unless the centre line is 1.0 +/- 1e-4 long. The sibling ctor at 4191-4192 does call `normalize()` on both axes -- a straight copy-paste omission. Two further defects hide behind the throw: (a) `_hw_extents = (length/2 + thickness, thickness)` makes the box 2*thickness LONGER than the centre line while `thickness` doubles as a half-width -- an undocumented asymmetry; (b) `normal((1,0)) = (0,1)` = DIRECTION_DOWN, whereas the other ctor's default `_y_axis` is DIRECTION_UP (MattMath.h:1116), so the two constructors wind opposite ways. Severity downgraded from the reported "critical": nothing crashes or corrupts, and there is no first-party caller, so this is a dead-on-arrival public API rather than a live crash.
findings.suggestion: Delegate: `RectangleRotated(const Segment& l, float t) : RectangleRotated(l.get_center(), l.get_direction(), Vector2F::normal(l.get_direction()), Vector2F(l.get_length()/2.0f, t)) {}` -- the 4-arg ctor already normalises. Decide and document whether the box should overhang the endpoints. Pick one y-axis convention for both ctors. Add a MathTests case; MathTests.cpp only ever calls the 4-arg form (lines 359, 376, 493, 631, 738, 785, 801, 833-866).
findings.verify_note: Read MattMath.cpp:4186-4215, 4063-4070, 1865-1868, 4522-4538; MattMath.h:46, 1115-1116; grepped MathTests.cpp for RectangleRotated construction sites.

findings.title: is_valid() runs before _points is populated, so edges_valid() is vacuously true for every input
findings.detail: Merges 3 duplicate candidates. Both ctors do `if (!is_valid()) throw; this->_points = this->calculate_points();` -- validation first, cache second. `is_valid()` (4464-4480) calls `edges_valid()` (4539-4565), which builds its edges from `get_edges()` (4284-4294) -> `get_edge_0..3()` (4434-4449) -> `_points`. At that moment `_points` is still the NSDMI `{ZERO, ZERO, ZERO, ZERO}` (MattMath.h:1119-1120). All four edges are `Segment(ZERO, ZERO)`: every `get_direction()` is (0,0) so every perpendicularity dot is exactly 0 and passes; every `get_length()` is 0 so both opposite-length checks pass. `edges_valid()` therefore returns true unconditionally during construction and has never rejected anything. The `if (edges.size() != 4) throw` at 4542-4545 is likewise unreachable -- `get_edges()` always builds exactly four. Severity downgraded from the reported "high": the consequence is a dead validator, not a wrong result, and no first-party code calls `is_valid()` (grep found zero callers outside MattMath.cpp).
findings.suggestion: Validate the primary state (`_center`, `_x_axis`, `_y_axis`, `_hw_extents`) directly and delete `edges_valid()` entirely -- for an OBB, orthonormal axes plus positive extents already imply perpendicular, pairwise-equal edges, so re-deriving the corners to check them is circular. Delete the unreachable size check.
findings.verify_note: Read MattMath.cpp:4186-4215, 4284-4294, 4434-4449, 4464-4480, 4482-4499, 4539-4565 and MattMath.h:1119-1120; traced that _points is not written until after the throw site.

findings.title: edges_valid() dots un-normalised edge vectors against an absolute epsilon, so validity depends on rectangle size
findings.detail: `Vector2F::dot(edges[i].get_direction(), edges[(i+1)%4].get_direction())` uses `Segment::get_direction()` (4063-4066), which is un-normalised, so the residual for two exactly-perpendicular edges scales with the product of the edge lengths while the tolerance is a fixed `EPSILON = 0.0001f` (MattMath.h:46). Same for `are_equal(edges[0].get_length(), edges[2].get_length(), EPSILON)` -- float carries ~7 significant digits, so two ~2000-unit lengths cannot be compared to 1e-4 (one ULP at 2048 is ~1.2e-4). `<FloatingPointModel>Fast</FloatingPointModel>` is set in all four ArtAttack configurations (ArtAttack.vcxproj:94, 116, 139, 165), which permits reassociation and enlarges the residual. This is latent today only because of the ordering bug above; fix that and large OBBs start throwing from a valid constructor.
findings.suggestion: Normalise the directions before dotting, or use a relative test: `std::abs(dot) <= EPSILON * len_a * len_b` and `std::abs(l0 - l2) <= EPSILON * std::max(l0, l2)`. Compare squared lengths to drop four sqrt calls. Better: delete the function per the previous finding.
findings.verify_note: Read MattMath.cpp:4539-4565 and 4063-4070; confirmed EPSILON=1e-4 at MattMath.h:46 and /fp:fast in ArtAttack.vcxproj.

findings.title: find_hypotenuse returns a VERTEX index that both callers use as an EDGE index, so get_hypotenuse() returns a leg
findings.detail: `find_hypotenuse` (3665-3684) tests `get_angle_0/1/2` -- the angles at vertices 0, 1, 2 -- and returns 0/1/2 accordingly. `get_hypotenuse()` (3641) then does `return this->get_edges()[hypotenuse];` and `get_hypotenuse_gradient()` (3651) does `return this->calculate_gradient(hypotenuse);`. Edge indices are edge_0 = p0->p1, edge_1 = p1->p2, edge_2 = p2->p0 (3490-3501). The hypotenuse is the edge OPPOSITE the right angle: a right angle at vertex i means hypotenuse index (i+1) % 3. With the right angle at p0 the code returns edge p0->p1, a leg. Wrong for every right triangle. Only reachable from commented-out code (StructureRamp.cpp:24-26), but that is the ramp feature actively being worked on.
findings.suggestion: Return `(i + 1) % 3` from `find_hypotenuse`, or rename it `find_right_angle_vertex` and adjust both call sites. Replace the angle search with three `length_squared` comparisons (no acos, no sqrt) and add a test asserting `get_hypotenuse()` on TriangleRightAxisAligned((0,0),(1,0),(0,1)) is the segment (1,0)-(0,1).
findings.verify_note: Read MattMath.cpp:3490-3511 (edge definitions), 3512-3537 (angles), 3633-3652, 3665-3684; confirmed StructureRamp.cpp is fully commented out.

findings.title: Triangle::get_angle_N returns the supplement of the interior angle
findings.detail: `get_angle_0()` is `angle_between(get_edge_0().get_direction(), get_edge_2().get_direction())`. edge_0 direction is `p1 - p0`; edge_2 direction is `p0 - p2` -- head-to-tail, not both emanating from p0. The interior angle at p0 is between `(p1 - p0)` and `(p2 - p0)`, so the code computes pi minus that. `get_angle_1` and `get_angle_2` have the same defect, so `get_angles()` (3528-3537) sums to 2*pi instead of pi. Worked example: p0=(0,0), p1=(4,0), p2=(1,1) -> interior 45 deg, code returns acos(-4 / (4*sqrt(2))) = 135 deg. Masked at the only consumer (`find_hypotenuse`) purely because 90 degrees is its own supplement; every other use is wrong.
findings.suggestion: `get_angle_0 = angle_between(points[1] - points[0], points[2] - points[0])` and equivalently for vertices 1 and 2. Add a test asserting the three angles sum to pi.
findings.verify_note: Read MattMath.cpp:3490-3537 and worked the numeric example by hand against the actual edge-direction definitions.

findings.title: triangles_intersect tests only 4 of the 9 edge pairs and is asymmetric in its arguments
findings.detail: Verified verbatim at 397-404: `for (int i = 0; i < 2; i++) { if (segments_intersect(a_edges[i], b_edges[0]) || segments_intersect(a_edges[i], b_edges[1])) return true; }`. Outer bound is 2 instead of 3 and `b_edges[2]` is never tested, so pairs (a0,b2), (a1,b2), (a2,b0), (a2,b1), (a2,b2) are skipped -- `triangles_intersect(a,b)` can disagree with `triangles_intersect(b,a)`. This is the workhorse behind `triangle_quad_intersect` (409-424), `quads_intersect` (492-511), `quad_segment_intersect`, `quad_point_intersect` and `quad_rectangle_rotated_intersect`, so the miss propagates through the entire quad/OBB path -- a projectile can pass through a structure with no diagnostic. The vertex-containment pre-pass at 384-390 hides most cases but not a hexagram configuration, and not a degenerate triangle: `test_point_triangle` -> `barycentric` (EricsonMath.cpp:729-743) divides by `denom = d00*d11 - d01*d01`, which is 0 for collinear points, giving NaN and all-false comparisons. `Triangle` has no validity check, so degenerate triangles are constructible. The function also has no AABB early-out, unlike every neighbouring routine.
findings.suggestion: `for (int i=0;i<3;i++) for (int j=0;j<3;j++) if (segments_intersect(a_edges[i], b_edges[j])) return true;` -- or replace the whole point-in/edge-cross approach with SAT over the six edge normals, which is correct and allocation-free. Add an `a.get_bounding_box().intersects(b.get_bounding_box())` early-out.
findings.verify_note: Read MattMath.cpp:381-407 and traced the callers at 409-424, 453-490, 492-511, 513-561; read EricsonMath.cpp:729-752.

findings.title: calculate_camera_from_view_rectangle is not the inverse of calculate_view_rectangle; its parameters are named backwards and its divisor is unguarded
findings.detail: Merges 3 candidates (correctness / design / robustness). Body verified at 4165-4167: `Camera(view_rectangle.x - world_rectangle.x, view_rectangle.y - world_rectangle.y, world_rectangle.width / view_rectangle.width)`. The forward transform (4116-4123) is `view = (world - t) * s`; the true inverse is `s = view.w / world.w`, `t = world.x - view.x / s`. The code returns the RECIPROCAL scale and a translation that drops the `/s` and flips the sign. It only works at its sole call site because Level.cpp:150-156 passes the arguments swapped relative to their names: `_zoom_out_start_bounds` (a world-space level rect, Level.h:133, loaded from JSON at LevelLoadedInfo.cpp:46-52) goes into the `view_rectangle` slot and `RectangleF(Vector2F::ZERO, resolution)` (the screen rect) into `world_rectangle` -- so `s = screen.w / level.w` and `t = level.pos - 0`, which happens to be right only because the screen rect's origin is (0,0). Anyone calling it per its parameter names gets a garbage camera. There is also no guard on `view_rectangle.width == 0`, and that width comes straight from `_json_doc["level_bounds"]["zoom_out_start_bounds"]["width"].GetFloat()` with no validation, so a data typo yields an infinite scale and a blank frame with no diagnostic. A stale commented-out alternative sits at 4160-4162, evidence the semantics were never pinned down.
findings.suggestion: Rename the parameters to match reality, or fix the body to be the true inverse and fix Level.cpp. Guard the zero divisor and validate the rectangle at load time with a message naming the level file. Delete the commented-out alternative. Add a round-trip test: `calculate_view_rectangle(w, calculate_camera_from_view_rectangle(v, w)) == v`.
findings.verify_note: Read MattMath.cpp:4116-4169, Level.cpp:140-160, Level.h:133-134, LevelLoadedInfo.cpp:46-52.

findings.title: Quad() and RectangleRotated() = default bypass every invariant, and a default-constructed OBB makes contains() throw from inside the collision loop
findings.detail: Merges 3 candidates. Both classes throw `std::invalid_argument` from every user-written constructor and setter (Quad: MattMath.cpp:3710, 3728, 3741, 3756, 3772, 3887, 3897, 3907, 3917; RectangleRotated: 4194, 4209, 4299, 4363, 4374, 4385, 4396, 4407) and then declare `= default` default constructors that check nothing. Traced the failure: a default-constructed `RectangleRotated` has `_hw_extents = ZERO` (so `half_widths_valid()` at 4512-4521 is false -- permanently invalid by the class's own definition) and `_points` = four ZEROs. `contains(point)` (4265-4268) -> `point_rectangle_rotated_intersect` (611-617) -> `get_quad()` (4450-4455) -> `calculate_points()` with zero extents produces four identical points -> `Quad(vector)` (3716-3732) -> `is_valid()` (3832-3849) tests `edges[0].intersects(edges[1])`, both `Segment(ZERO,ZERO)`, and `segments_intersect` short-circuits `if (a == b) return true` (565-570) -> `is_valid()` false -> the Quad ctor throws. So a const query named `contains()` throws out of the middle of `Player::is_colliding` / `CollisionTools::bracket_object_collision_generic`. `Quad(RectangleF(0,0,0,0))` (3734-3745) throws for exactly the same reason. A default `Quad` is likewise invalid by its own `is_valid()`.
findings.suggestion: Delete the defaulted default constructors, or give them genuinely valid states (unit square / unit extents with `_points` computed). Independently, `contains()` must not be able to throw: implement it as `|dot(p - _center, _x_axis)| <= _hw_extents.x && |dot(p - _center, _y_axis)| <= _hw_extents.y` instead of round-tripping through a validating `Quad`.

findings.title: Every RectangleRotated and Quad mutator writes the member first and validates second, so a throw leaves the object corrupt
findings.detail: Merges 4 candidates. Pattern verified at all six RectangleRotated sites -- `inflate` (4295-4305), `set_x_axis` (4359-4369), `set_y_axis` (4370-4380), `set_half_extents` (4381-4391), `set_half_x_width` (4392-4402), `set_half_y_width` (4403-4413) -- and all four `Quad::set_point_N` (3883-3921). After the throw the primary field holds the rejected value while `_points` still describes the previous geometry, so `get_half_extents()` and `get_point_0()`/`get_bounding_box()`/`get_edges()` describe different rectangles. `set_x_axis`/`set_y_axis` are worse: `x_axis.normalized()` (1724-1728) has no zero guard, so `set_x_axis(Vector2F::ZERO)` writes NaN into `_x_axis` and then throws, leaving NaN axes forever. `Shape::inflate` is virtual and called through `Shape*`, so a caller that catches the exception has no way to know its shape is now garbage.
findings.suggestion: Compute the candidate value into a local, validate the local, throw before committing anything, then assign and recompute `_points`. That restores the strong exception guarantee for all ten setters. Guard `normalized()` against zero length.
findings.verify_note: Read all ten mutator bodies at MattMath.cpp:3883-3921 and 4295-4413, plus Vector2F::normalized at 1724-1728.

findings.title: Shape::inflate(float) is one virtual with three mutually incompatible geometric meanings and three different failure policies
findings.detail: Merges 4 candidates. `virtual void inflate(float amount) = 0;` has no documented contract. Verified implementations: `RectangleF::inflate(float)` (946-949) -> `inflate(a,a)` moves each side out by `a`; `RectangleRotated::inflate` (4295-4305) `_hw_extents += (a,a)` -- same perpendicular growth; `Circle::inflate` (3346-3349) `radius += a` -- same; but `Triangle::inflate` (3457-3472) and `Quad::inflate` (3813-3830) do `points[i] = center + dir_i * len_i + dir_i * amount`, pushing each VERTEX radially from the centroid, so the perpendicular edge offset is `amount * cos(theta)` and varies per edge -- for a square, `amount/sqrt(2)`; for a sliver triangle, arbitrarily small. So `shape->inflate(2.0f)` grows a rectangle's boundary by 2 and a triangle's by 1.41 or less. Negative amounts diverge too: RectangleRotated throws, Circle silently produces a negative radius, Triangle/Quad silently invert through the centroid and produce NaN when a vertex sits on the centroid (`edge.normalize()` at 3464-3466 / 3821-3824 divides by zero). StructurePaintable.cpp:118-119 has `//shape->inflate(-THICKNESS);` commented out -- a real caller that wanted the polymorphic negative case and presumably found it didn't work. Graded high rather than medium: this is exactly the kind of undefined interface contract that blocks the engine-reuse goal.
findings.suggestion: Define the contract as "offset every boundary outward by `amount` along its normal" (Minkowski dilation) and implement Triangle/Quad by offsetting each edge line and re-intersecting adjacent edges -- not by scaling from the centroid. Pick one negative-amount policy for all five. Or drop the virtual and expose shape-specific `expand` free functions with defined semantics.

findings.title: Shape::get_edges() has no documented ordering and RectangleF's differs from every other shape's; StructurePaintable indexes it as if it didn't
findings.detail: Merges 2 candidates. `RectangleF::get_edges()` returns `{ top, bottom, left, right }` (808-818). `Quad::get_edges()` (3943-3953) and `RectangleRotated::get_edges()` (4284-4294) return perimeter order p0->p1, p1->p2, p2->p3, p3->p0. `Triangle::get_edges()` (3502-3511) returns three. `Circle::get_edges()` (3340-3344) returns an empty vector. StructurePaintable.cpp:188-212 consumes the polymorphic result and hard-codes `i==0 -> top, i==1 -> right, i==2 -> bottom, i==3 -> left`. I confirmed the shape really is a `RectangleF`: LevelObjectBuilder.cpp:80-141 builds a `RectangleF rectangle` and passes `&rectangle` as the collision shape, and builds `_paintable_edges` from `rectangle.get_left_edge()/get_top_edge()/get_right_edge()/get_bottom_edge()`. So three of four mappings are wrong: a level whose JSON declares only `paintable_faces.bottom` matches `edges[1]` (the bottom edge) and sets `right_edge = true`, painting the right face instead. Only index 0 (top) is correct.
findings.suggestion: Document `Shape::get_edges()` as perimeter order starting at `get_points()[0]` and reorder `RectangleF::get_edges()` to `{ top, right, bottom, left }`. Better: key paintable edges by geometry (they are already compared with `operator==` at StructurePaintable.cpp:193) rather than re-deriving a face name from a positional index.
findings.verify_note: Read MattMath.cpp:792-818, 3340-3344, 3502-3511, 3943-3953, 4284-4294; StructurePaintable.cpp:180-215; LevelObjectBuilder.cpp:80-141 to confirm the concrete shape type.

findings.title: Circle::get_edges() returns an empty vector -- a null-object hole in the Shape interface that silently no-ops callers
findings.detail: Merges 2 candidates. `get_edges()` is pure virtual on `Shape` (MattMath.h:87) because several intersection routines are written as "test my edges against yours" (MattMath.cpp:288-295, 369-376, 599-606, 646-657). A circle cannot honour that, so it returns nothing and every edge-driven algorithm silently reports "nothing to do" instead of failing. The real consumer is StructurePaintable.cpp:188 `std::vector<Segment> edges = this->get_shape()->get_edges();` followed by `for (int i = 0; i < edges.size(); i++)` -- a circular paintable structure would generate zero paint tiles and no diagnostic. This is interface segregation violated: `get_edges` belongs to polygons, not to all shapes.
findings.suggestion: Introduce a `ConvexPolygon` interface (`get_points()`/`get_edges()`/vertex count) implemented by RectangleF, Triangle, Quad and RectangleRotated but not Circle, and have edge-driven algorithms take `const ConvexPolygon&` so the type system rejects a circle at compile time.
findings.verify_note: Read MattMath.cpp:3340-3344, MattMath.h:87, StructurePaintable.cpp:186-213.

findings.title: normalize()/normalized() have no zero-length guard while the sibling to_unit_vector()/unit_vector() do, and the shape code uses the unguarded pair
findings.detail: Merges 2 candidates. `normalized()` (1724-1728) and `normalize()` (1729-1734) divide by `length()` unconditionally; `to_unit_vector()` (1774-1787) and `unit_vector()` (1852-1863) both check `length == 0.0f` and fall back to (1,0). Four functions, one job, two degenerate-input policies, and no naming hint which is which. The shape code consistently picks the unguarded pair: `Triangle::inflate` (3464-3466) and `Quad::inflate` (3821-3824) normalise centre-to-vertex vectors, so a vertex coincident with the centroid writes NaN straight into `points[i]` -- and NaN comparisons are all false, so the shape silently stops colliding rather than throwing. `RectangleRotated` ctor (4191-4192) and `set_x_axis`/`set_y_axis` (4361, 4372) take the same path. `/fp:fast` is on in all four configurations, so the compiler may assume no NaNs and the downstream behaviour is unpredictable rather than merely wrong.
findings.suggestion: Give `normalize()`/`normalized()` the same zero guard (or an assert) and collapse the four near-duplicates into one. In Triangle/Quad::inflate, skip vertices whose offset from the centre is below EPSILON, and hoist the `(p - center).length()` that is recomputed after the normalise.

findings.title: angle_between has no acos domain clamp and no zero-length guard
findings.detail: Merges 2 candidates. `return std::acos(Vector2F::dot(a, b) / (a.length() * b.length()));` -- the quotient is not clamped to [-1,1], so for nearly-parallel vectors float rounding gives 1.0000001 and acos returns NaN; and a zero-length input makes the denominator 0. Both are reachable from the shape API: `Triangle::get_angle_0/1/2` (3512-3527) feed it edge directions, and a degenerate triangle gives a zero direction. The NaN then propagates: `find_hypotenuse` (3665-3684) compares NaN against PI_OVER_2 with `are_equal` (93-96, `fabs(NaN - x) < eps` is false), so all three branches fail, it returns -1, and `get_hypotenuse()` throws "Triangle is not a right triangle" for a triangle that is one. `/fp:fast` in all four configurations makes the domain overshoot more likely, not less.
findings.suggestion: `float d = a.length() * b.length(); if (d <= 0.0f) return 0.0f; return std::acos(MattMath::clamp(Vector2F::dot(a,b) / d, -1.0f, 1.0f));` -- `MattMath::clamp` already exists at line 34. Prefer `atan2(cross, dot)`: signed, numerically stable, no epsilon.

findings.title: RectangleRotated::get_angle() is acos-based and therefore unsigned, so +theta and -theta are indistinguishable
findings.detail: Merges 3 candidates. `return Vector2F::angle_between(this->_x_axis, Vector2F::DIRECTION_RIGHT);` -- `angle_between` (1808-1811) returns [0, pi], so an OBB rotated -30 degrees and one rotated +30 degrees both report 0.5236, and no orientation in the lower half plane is representable. The intended consumer is `DrawObject::set_draw_rotation_by_rectangle_rotated` (DrawObject.cpp:66-69), currently an empty `// TODO: Implement this function` stub, which would mirror half of all rotations. The class already stores the full basis and `Vector2F::angle()` (1749-1752) is already `std::atan2(y, x)`, so the signed angle is free. There is also no matching `set_angle`/`rotate` -- see the set_x_axis finding.
findings.suggestion: `return std::atan2(this->_x_axis.y, this->_x_axis.x);` -- signed, exact, cheaper, no epsilon. Document the sign convention for y-down screen space.
findings.verify_note: Read MattMath.cpp:1749-1752, 1808-1811, 4460-4463; DrawObject.cpp:66-69 (confirmed empty stub); Visual.cpp:34.

findings.title: set_x_axis / set_y_axis can never actually rotate a RectangleRotated -- they validate the new axis against the unchanged other axis
findings.detail: `set_x_axis` (MattMath.cpp:4359-4369) assigns `_x_axis = x_axis.normalized()` and then calls `axes_valid()` (4522-4538), which tests `are_equal(Vector2F::dot(_x_axis, _y_axis), 0.0f, EPSILON)` against the OLD, unchanged `_y_axis`. Any new x-axis not already perpendicular to the current y-axis throws, so the only values that succeed are the axis it already had (or its negation). `set_y_axis` (4370-4380) is identical. There is no `set_angle`, no `rotate`, no combined `set_axes` (checked the full public interface at MattMath.h:1056-1111), so an OBB is effectively un-rotatable after construction -- in the one shape whose entire reason for existing is that it rotates.
findings.suggestion: Replace both setters with `set_rotation(float radians)` deriving both axes from the angle, and/or `set_axes(x, y)` that validates the pair together. Storing a single angle and deriving the axes on demand makes the perpendicularity invariant unrepresentable-as-broken and deletes `axes_valid()`.
findings.verify_note: Read MattMath.cpp:4359-4380 and 4522-4538; scanned MattMath.h:1056-1111 for any rotation setter.

findings.title: Point-in-OBB does 3 heap allocations, a full Quad validity check and 2 barycentric solves instead of 2 dot products
findings.detail: Merges 3 candidates. `RectangleRotated::contains(p)` (4265-4268) forwards to `point_rectangle_rotated_intersect` (611-617), which is `Quad quad = rect_rotated.get_quad(); return quad_point_intersect(quad, point);`. `get_quad()` (4450-4455) calls `calculate_points()` -- allocation #1 -- even though the identical corners are already cached in `_points`. `Quad(const std::vector<Point2F>&)` (3716-3732) then runs `is_valid()` (3832-3849), which calls `get_edges()` -- allocation #2 -- and does 6 pairwise `segments_intersect`. Then `quad_point_intersect` (530-543) calls `get_triangles()` (3965-3973) -- allocation #3 -- and runs up to 2 barycentric solves (EricsonMath.cpp:729-752). The correct test is two dots and two compares. This is not cold: `rectangles_rotated_intersect` (619-661) calls `contains()` 8 times before it even looks at edges, `triangle_rectangle_rotated_intersect` 3 times (463-474), `rectangle_rotated_rectangle_intersect` 4 times (270-273), `segment_rectangle_rotated_intersect` twice (593), and `CollisionTools::bracket_object_collision_generic` (CollisionTools.cpp:53-68) re-runs the whole narrow phase `BRACKET_ITERATIONS` times per resolved contact. As a bonus, because `Quad`'s ctor throws on invalid input, this read-only query can throw.
findings.suggestion: Implement `RectangleRotated::contains` directly in the OBB local frame (`Vector2F d = point - _center; return std::abs(Vector2F::dot(d,_x_axis)) <= _hw_extents.x && std::abs(Vector2F::dot(d,_y_axis)) <= _hw_extents.y;`) and have `point_rectangle_rotated_intersect` forward to it. Make `get_quad()` build from the cached `_points`.

findings.title: RectangleRotated exposes a full OBB interface (axes, half-extents, indexed accessors) that no intersection routine uses; the OBB path is brute-force point/edge enumeration instead of SAT
findings.detail: `get_axis(int)` (4315-4327), `get_half_width(int)` (4340-4352), `get_half_extents()` and `get_center()` are exactly the interface Ericson's OBB SAT consumes, and `EricsonMath.h:141` already declares `closest_pt_point_OBB(const Point2F&, const OBB&, Point2F&)`. Yet `rectangles_rotated_intersect` (619-661) does an AABB pre-check, then 8 `contains()` calls (each the 3-allocation path above), then a 4x4 = 16 segment-segment loop -- where 2D OBB-vs-OBB SAT is 4 axis projections and no allocation. `circle_rectangle_rotated_intersect` (353-379) likewise enumerates edges rather than using `closest_pt_point_OBB`. The class stores exactly the right data and then never uses it.
findings.suggestion: Implement `rectangles_rotated_intersect` as 4-axis SAT over `get_axis(0/1)` of both boxes, `contains` as the two-dot-product test, and `circle_rectangle_rotated_intersect` as `distance_squared(circle.center, closest_pt_point_OBB(...)) <= r*r`. This is also the general answer to the fat-interface finding: convex shapes should expose projection/support and one SAT routine should serve them all.
findings.verify_note: Read MattMath.cpp:353-379, 619-661, 4307-4352; EricsonMath.h:141 and EricsonMath.cpp:769-786.

findings.title: The "cheap AABB early-out" in the OBB and triangle paths is more expensive than the test it guards
findings.detail: `rectangles_rotated_intersect` opens with `if (!a.intersects(b.get_bounding_box())) return false;` (623). `a.intersects(const RectangleF&)` (4237-4240) dispatches to `rectangle_rotated_rectangle_intersect` (260-298), which is a FULL OBB-vs-AABB test: its own bounding-box check, 4 `rotated_rect.contains()` calls, 4 `rect.contains()` calls, a `get_edges()` allocation and 4 segment-AABB tests -- roughly 15 heap allocations, strictly more work than the loop it is guarding. Same mistake at 457: `if (!triangle.intersects(rect_rotated.get_bounding_box()))` routes to the full `rectangle_triangle_intersect` (193-229). By contrast the guards at 264 and 587 do reduce to cheap tests, so the pattern is inconsistent as well as slow.
findings.suggestion: Use `a.get_bounding_box().intersects(b.get_bounding_box())` (which reaches `EricsonMath::test_AABB_AABB`, EricsonMath.cpp:283-296) at both sites.

findings.title: Shape::get_edges/get_points/get_triangles return std::vector by value, forcing a heap allocation per narrow-phase call
findings.detail: Merges 4 candidates (the "narrow phase heap-allocates dozens" report and three get_edges/std::array reports). `virtual std::vector<Segment> get_edges() const = 0;` forces an allocation for a container that is always 0, 3 or 4 elements. Implementations: RectangleF 808-818, Circle 3340-3344, Triangle 3502-3511, Quad 3943-3953, RectangleRotated 4284-4294. Same for `Triangle::get_points` (3485-3489), `Triangle::get_angles` (3528-3537), `Quad::get_points` (3871-3881) and `Quad::get_triangles` (3965-3973). Verified call sites inside the intersection routines: 219, 234, 288, 321, 369, 393-394 (two per call), 412, 435, 480, 495-496, 516, 533, 549, 599, 646-647 (two per call), plus `Quad::is_valid` at 3835 and `RectangleRotated::edges_valid` at 4541. One quad-vs-OBB query fans out to dozens of malloc/free pairs, and `CollisionTools::bracket_object_collision_generic` (CollisionTools.cpp:53-68) reruns the narrow phase `BRACKET_ITERATIONS` times per contact while `calculate_object_collision_depth` (CollisionTools.cpp:270-281) additionally `clone()`s the whole collider per query. Every shape has a compile-time-known vertex count; nothing here needs dynamic allocation.
findings.suggestion: Return `std::array<Segment,4>` / `std::array<Point2F,4>` per concrete type, or expose `int edge_count()` + `Segment edge(int)` and index. For the polymorphic path, fill a caller-supplied buffer -- that works under the current (default) C++ standard. Drop `get_triangles()` in favour of two direct calls.
findings.verify_note: Read every listed implementation and call site in MattMath.cpp; read CollisionTools.cpp:25-69 and 265-281.

findings.title: RectangleRotated caches four fixed corners in a heap std::vector, reallocating on construction, copy, clone and every one of nine mutations
findings.detail: Merges 4 candidates. `std::vector<Point2F> _points = { ZERO, ZERO, ZERO, ZERO };` -- four 8-byte points in a heap container. Every `RectangleRotated`, including a default-constructed one, allocates; `clone()` (4276-4279) allocates twice; and `calculate_points()` (4482-4499) builds a fresh `std::vector<Point2F> points(4)` that is then move-assigned over `_points` at every one of nine sites: 4199, 4214, 4273 (`offset`), 4304 (`inflate`), 4357, 4368, 4379, 4390, 4401, 4412, plus 4452 in `get_quad()`. `offset()` in particular is called via `CollisionTools::move_object_by_direction_relative_to_size` (CollisionTools.cpp:29) once per bracket iteration per contact per frame. `get_quad()` ignores the cache and recomputes, so the class has two sources of truth for the same four points. Because the copy ctor is user-declared (`= default`, MattMath.h:1050) moves are suppressed, so vector growth and push_back copy rather than move -- see the rule-of-zero finding.
findings.suggestion: `std::array<Point2F, 4> _points;` and have `calculate_points` return it by value (trivially copyable, no allocation). Build `get_quad()` from `_points`. Then reconsider whether the cache earns its keep at all -- four multiply-adds is likely cheaper than keeping nine mutators coherent.
findings.verify_note: Read MattMath.h:1113-1130 and every `_points = calculate_points()` site found by grep in MattMath.cpp; read CollisionTools.cpp:15-33.

findings.title: Circle intersection tests take a square root where a squared comparison is exact and free
findings.detail: `circles_intersect` (300-304) is `Vector2F::distance(a.center, b.center) <= a.radius + b.radius`, and `Vector2F::distance` (1820-1824) calls `sqrtf`. Same at `circle_segment_intersect` (339) and `circle_point_intersect` (348-351). `Vector2F::distance_squared` (1825-1829) already exists and is used by none of them, and `EricsonMath::test_circle_circle` (EricsonMath.cpp:298-306) already does the squared form correctly -- so the file contains both the right and the wrong implementation of the same test. Circles are the projectile shape, so these are among the highest-frequency calls in the engine, and the bracket search reruns them per iteration.
findings.suggestion: `float r = a.radius + b.radius; return Vector2F::distance_squared(a.center, b.center) <= r * r;` and the equivalent in the other two. No behaviour change for non-negative radii, one transcendental removed from the hottest path.
findings.verify_note: Read MattMath.cpp:300-351, 1820-1829; EricsonMath.cpp:298-306.

findings.title: get_quad() recomputes cached corners and pays full Quad validation; Quad(RectangleRotated) then validates a second time, and 4 of the 6 validation tests are provably dead
findings.detail: `get_quad()` (4450-4455) calls `calculate_points()` although `_points` already holds exactly those corners, then constructs a `Quad` which runs `is_valid()` -- another allocation plus 6 segment-segment tests. `Quad::Quad(const RectangleRotated&)` (3747-3760) calls `get_quad()` (paying all of that), copies the four points out, and calls `is_valid()` AGAIN. I verified the dead-test claim: `is_valid()` loops i<j over four edges, so it tests pairs (0,1),(0,2),(0,3),(1,2),(1,3),(2,3). The four adjacent pairs share a vertex, and `EricsonMath::test_2D_segment_segment` (EricsonMath.cpp:697-725) requires `a1 * a2 < 0.0f` strictly -- for a shared endpoint one signed area is exactly 0, so the product is 0 and the test can never fire. Only the two diagonal pairs (0,2) and (1,3) can ever detect self-intersection; two-thirds of the work is provably useless.
findings.suggestion: Build the quad from the cached `_points`, give `Quad` a private non-validating constructor for input already known to be a rectangle, and reduce `is_valid()` to the two diagonal pairs.
findings.verify_note: Read MattMath.cpp:3747-3760, 3832-3849, 3923-3953, 4450-4455, 4482-4499; EricsonMath.cpp:697-725 and worked the shared-endpoint signed-area case.

findings.title: Quad fan-triangulates on the fixed 0-2 diagonal and is_valid() never rejects concave quads, so every quad query is wrong for concave input
findings.detail: Merges 2 candidates. `get_triangle_0()` = (p0,p1,p2) and `get_triangle_1()` = (p0,p2,p3) always split on the p0-p2 diagonal. For a simple but concave quadrilateral whose reflex vertex is p1 or p3, that diagonal lies outside the shape and the two triangles cover area the quad does not occupy. `is_valid()` (3832-3849) only rejects self-intersection -- it says nothing about convexity -- so such quads construct successfully. Since `quad_point_intersect` (530-543), `quad_segment_intersect` (513-528), `quads_intersect` (492-511), `circle_quad_intersect` (319-331), `rectangle_quad_intersect` (231-245) and `quad_rectangle_rotated_intersect` (545-561) are all defined purely in terms of `get_triangles()`, every one reports false positives inside the concave notch. The header comment (MattMath.h:916-919) promises only clockwise-from-top-left ordering, never convexity -- an unchecked precondition.
findings.suggestion: Decide what `Quad` is. If it is the collider type (which is what every algorithm assumes), rename it `ConvexQuad`, enforce convexity in `is_valid()` via consistent cross-product sign across the four vertices, and replace the triangulation-based routines with SAT over the four edge normals -- faster and correct.

findings.title: segments_intersect reports collinear overlapping segments as disjoint; the a == b patch only covers identically-ordered duplicates
findings.detail: `segments_intersect(a, b, t, p)` special-cases `if (a == b)` and otherwise delegates to `EricsonMath::test_2D_segment_segment` (EricsonMath.cpp:697-725), which requires `a1 * a2 < 0.0f` AND `a3 * a4 < 0.0f` -- strictly opposite signed areas. Collinear segments give zero areas and fall through to `// Segments not intersecting (or collinear) return 0`. Two segments lying on the same line and fully overlapping are reported disjoint. The `a == b` patch is narrow: `Segment::operator==` (4045-4049) compares componentwise, so `Segment((0,0),(10,0))` and `Segment((10,0),(0,0))` -- the same geometry reversed -- are not equal and the collinear miss stands; partial overlap is never handled. This is the primitive under `Quad::is_valid`, `triangles_intersect`, `triangle_segment_intersect`, `segment_rectangle_rotated_intersect` and `rectangles_rotated_intersect`, so two OBBs sharing a collinear face edge are reported as not colliding. Note the strict signs also mean endpoint-touching never counts, whereas `rectangle_point_intersect` (252-258) and `circle_point_intersect` (348-351) use `<=` so touching DOES count -- the codebase has no single convention.
findings.suggestion: Handle collinearity explicitly: when all four signed areas are ~0, project both segments onto the dominant axis and test 1D interval overlap. Then decide once whether touching counts and apply it uniformly across all primitives.

findings.title: Circle::inflate allows a negative radius, after which the circle tests disagree with each other and its AABB is inside out
