findings.detail: `void Circle::inflate(float amount) { this->radius += amount; }` -- no clamp, no validation, unlike `RectangleRotated::inflate` (4295-4305) which throws for non-positive extents. With radius -5: `EricsonMath::test_circle_AABB` (EricsonMath.cpp:368-375) and `test_circle_triangle` (483-492) compare against `radius * radius`, so -5 behaves exactly like +5 and the circle still collides; `circle_point_intersect` (348-351) and `circle_segment_intersect` (339) compare `distance <= radius` with the raw value, so nothing ever intersects; `circles_intersect` (300-304) compares against `a.radius + b.radius`, so a negative radius shrinks the other circle's reach; and `get_bounding_box()` (3318-3324) returns width/height of -10, which `test_AABB_AABB` (EricsonMath.cpp:283-296) turns into min > max, inverting the broad phase. One object, four mutually inconsistent answers.
findings.suggestion: Clamp (`radius = std::max(0.0f, radius + amount)`) or throw as RectangleRotated does -- and pick one policy across the hierarchy. Independently, make every circle test use `radius * radius` so the sign cannot leak into the result.

findings.title: calculate_gradient divides by delta-x with no zero check, returning +/-inf for vertical edges
findings.detail: The index is validated (`if (edge < 0 || edge > 2) throw`) but the divisor is not: `(points[(edge+1)%3].y - points[edge].y) / (points[(edge+1)%3].x - points[edge].x)`. A vertical edge yields +/-inf; a zero-length edge yields NaN. No guard, no documented sentinel. Reachable from `get_hypotenuse_gradient()` (3643-3652), which is the value the ramp movement code is meant to consume -- a level author drawing a ramp with a vertical hypotenuse gets an infinite slope rather than an error. `/fp:fast` permits the compiler to assume this never happens.
findings.suggestion: Return the gradient through an out-param plus a bool, or return the edge direction vector and let callers handle the vertical case. Either way, do not hand an infinity to gameplay code.
findings.verify_note: Read MattMath.cpp:3594-3603, 3643-3652; confirmed /fp:fast in ArtAttack.vcxproj.

findings.title: TriangleRightAxisAligned::calculate_gradient is a byte-for-byte copy of the base version, declared private so it hides an accessible public base member
findings.detail: Merges 3 candidates. `Triangle::calculate_gradient` (3594-3603) is public (MattMath.h:893) and non-virtual; `TriangleRightAxisAligned::calculate_gradient` (3685-3694) has an identical body and is private (MattMath.h:913). Because neither is virtual this is name hiding, not overriding: `TriangleRightAxisAligned t; t.calculate_gradient(0);` fails to compile because the derived private name hides the accessible base one, so the derived class publicly LOSES an operation its base offers. Two copies of the same three lines free to drift apart. In the same class, `int find_hypotenuse(const Triangle& tri) const` (MattMath.h:912) takes a parameter that is only ever `*this` (call sites 3635, 3645) -- a const member function taking itself as an argument.
findings.suggestion: Delete `TriangleRightAxisAligned::calculate_gradient` outright. Make `find_hypotenuse` a no-argument private const member (or a free function on `const Triangle&`) and share one guard between `get_hypotenuse` and `get_hypotenuse_gradient`.
findings.verify_note: Diffed MattMath.cpp:3594-3603 against 3685-3694; read MattMath.h:893 and 910-913 for access specifiers.

findings.title: RectangleRotated's corners come out counter-clockwise from bottom-left, contradicting the Quad contract they are fed into
findings.detail: With the class defaults `_x_axis = DIRECTION_RIGHT (1,0)` and `_y_axis = DIRECTION_UP (0,-1)` (MattMath.h:1115-1116) in y-down screen space, I evaluated `calculate_points` for center (0,0), extents (1,1): p0 = (-1, 1) bottom-left, p1 = (1, 1) bottom-right, p2 = (1, -1) top-right, p3 = (-1, -1) top-left -- counter-clockwise on screen, starting at the bottom-left. `Quad`'s header contract (MattMath.h:916-919) says "ordered in a clockwise direction, starting from the top left", and `Quad(const RectangleF&)` (3734-3739) does produce TL, TR, BR, BL. `get_quad()` (4450-4455) feeds the RectangleRotated corners straight into `Quad`, so `get_point_0()` is the bottom-left and the winding is opposite to every other quad in the system. The Segment constructor produces yet a third convention (its `normal()` y-axis points DOWN for a rightward segment). Nothing breaks today because triangulation and barycentric containment are winding-agnostic, but anything that assumes point 0 is the top-left -- sprite drawing, the positional edge mapping in StructurePaintable.cpp:189-212 -- will be wrong.
findings.suggestion: Pick one convention (clockwise from top-left in screen space), state it on `Shape`, and make `calculate_points`, `Quad(RectangleF)` and the Segment ctor all honour it. Add a test asserting `get_points()[0]` is the top-left for an axis-aligned RectangleRotated.
findings.verify_note: Read MattMath.cpp:3734-3745, 4487-4499, 4450-4455 and MattMath.h:916-919, 1115-1116; evaluated the corner formulas numerically.

findings.title: closest_pt_point_OBB loops over three axes of a 2D OBB, so get_axis(2) throws on every call
findings.detail: Merges 2 candidates. `for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) { float dist = Vector2F::dot(d, b.get_axis(i)); ... }` -- `OBB` is a typedef for `MattMath::RectangleRotated` (MattMath.h:1136), which is 2D. `RectangleRotated::get_axis` (MattMath.cpp:4315-4327) and `get_half_width` (4340-4352) accept only 0 and 1 and otherwise `throw std::invalid_argument("Axis must be 0 or 1")`. The third iteration therefore always throws; the function cannot complete for any input. A straight port of Ericson's 3D routine with the loop bound left at 3. Grep confirms it has no callers (only the declaration at EricsonMath.h:141), so this is a landmine rather than a live bug -- but it is the natural building block for the OBB collision response the recent work is heading towards.
findings.suggestion: Change the bound to `i < 2`. Better, unroll the two axes using `get_x_axis`/`get_y_axis` and `get_half_x_width`/`get_half_y_width` and delete the throwing integer-indexed accessors. Add a test -- MathTests.cpp covers neither.
findings.verify_note: Read EricsonMath.cpp:769-786, EricsonMath.h:141, MattMath.cpp:4315-4352, MattMath.h:1136; grepped for callers.

findings.title: MattMath::sign truncates a float cross product to int, so it returns 0 ("collinear") for any triangle of area < 1
findings.detail: `return static_cast<int>((p1.x - p3.x) * (p2.y - p3.y) - (p2.x - p3.x) * (p1.y - p3.y));` -- the name and the `int` return say -1/0/+1, but it actually returns the truncated signed area. For any three points whose signed area is in (-1, 1) it returns 0 regardless of which side the point is on, and truncation toward zero also destroys any magnitude ordering. It is declared in the public header next to the other geometry helpers (MattMath.h:56-57) and is a near-duplicate of `EricsonMath::signed_2D_tri_area` (EricsonMath.cpp:688-692) except for the cast. Severity kept low: grep confirms zero callers anywhere in the tree, so this is currently only a trap for whoever next writes a point-in-polygon test.
findings.suggestion: Delete it and use `EricsonMath::signed_2D_tri_area`. If a true sign is wanted: `float a = signed_2D_tri_area(...); return (a > EPSILON) - (a < -EPSILON);`
findings.verify_note: Read MattMath.cpp:86-91, MattMath.h:56-57, EricsonMath.cpp:686-692; grepped the whole tree for callers of MattMath::sign.

findings.title: circle_segment_intersect silently returns false for a zero-length segment because the projection yields NaN
findings.detail: `closest_pt_point_segment` (EricsonMath.cpp:756-767) computes `t = dot(c - a, ab) / dot(ab, ab)`. For a degenerate segment the divisor is 0, `t` becomes NaN, both clamps (`if (t < 0)`, `if (t > 1)`) are false for NaN so it stays NaN, and `d = a + NaN * ab` is NaN. `Vector2F::distance(...) <= circle.radius` is then false: a circle sitting exactly on a degenerate segment is reported as not intersecting. Degenerate segments are reachable -- a default-constructed RectangleRotated produces four, and `RectangleF::get_edges()` on a zero-height rect produces two. The no-out-param overload (342-346) also declares an uninitialised `Point2F point` purely to discard it, so nothing signals that the query was meaningless.
findings.suggestion: Guard in `closest_pt_point_segment`: if `dot(ab, ab) < EPSILON` set `t = 0` and `d = a`. Circle-vs-point then falls out correctly.
findings.verify_note: Read MattMath.cpp:333-351 and EricsonMath.cpp:756-767.

findings.title: Shape::intersects switches on a hand-maintained type tag and then dynamic_casts anyway, dereferencing the result unchecked
findings.detail: Merges 4 candidates. The switch at 121-135 has already established the concrete type from `get_shape_type()`, so each `*dynamic_cast<const RectangleF*>(other)` pays an MSVC RTTI walk for nothing -- on the hottest path in the engine (`Level::update_level_logic` runs pairwise `is_colliding`, and `CollisionTools::bracket_object_collision_generic` reruns the narrow phase `BRACKET_ITERATIONS` times per contact). The result is dereferenced immediately with no null test. Two consequences reported by reviewers are OVERSTATED and I am correcting them: (a) no current subclass can produce a null cast -- `TriangleRightAxisAligned` reports `shape_type::TRIANGLE` and `dynamic_cast<const Triangle*>` succeeds on it; (b) `other` itself is never null-checked and `Structure() = default` (Structure.h:10) leaves `_collision_shape = nullptr` (Structure.h:40), but I found no code path that actually default-constructs a `Structure`, so that is latent, not live. What is real today is the wasted RTTI plus a `default: throw std::invalid_argument` arm reachable only via `shape_type::NONE`, thrown from inside a query.
findings.suggestion: Pick one mechanism: trust the tag and use `static_cast` (with a debug assert on the dynamic_cast), or drop the tag and do proper double dispatch (`virtual bool intersects_with(const Shape&) const`). Take `const Shape&` rather than `const Shape*` throughout so null is not representable, and delete the pointer overloads and the free `shapes_*` wrappers.
findings.verify_note: Read MattMath.cpp:119-175; Structure.h:10, 40; Player.cpp:155-183; CollisionTools.cpp:53-69, 240-250; confirmed no first-party default-constructed Structure.

findings.title: TriangleRightAxisAligned does not override clone(), so every ramp's stored collision shape loses its derived type
findings.detail: Merges 2 candidates, with a correction. `TriangleRightAxisAligned` declares no `clone()` override, so it inherits `Triangle::clone()` (3453-3456) = `std::make_unique<Triangle>(*this)`. LevelObjectBuilder.cpp:161-176 creates a stack-local `TriangleRightAxisAligned`, passes `&triangle`, and `Structure`'s ctor stores `collision_shape->clone()` (Structure.cpp:22). The `unique_ptr<Shape>` a ramp owns for its whole life is therefore a plain `Triangle`, and `get_shape_type()` reports `TRIANGLE`, so nothing downstream can recover the right-triangle identity that is the subclass's entire reason to exist. CORRECTION to the reviewers: this is NOT a memory-safety issue and the "reads past the object" claim is wrong -- `TriangleRightAxisAligned` adds no data members, only member functions, so the slice is value-preserving and the commented-out `static_cast` at StructureRamp.cpp:25-26 would in practice work (formally UB, practically benign). Downgraded from high/memory-safety to medium/design accordingly.
findings.suggestion: Add `std::unique_ptr<Shape> clone() const override { return std::make_unique<TriangleRightAxisAligned>(*this); }`, and enforce clone-per-leaf with a CRTP mixin so a new subclass cannot forget. Better: delete the subclass -- it is two free functions in a trench coat -- and provide `bool is_right_triangle(const Triangle&)`, `int hypotenuse_index(const Triangle&)`, `Segment hypotenuse(const Triangle&)`. Also have `Structure` take `unique_ptr<Shape>` by value so the ownership transfer is visible at the call site.
findings.verify_note: Read MattMath.h:842-914 (confirmed the derived class declares no data members), MattMath.cpp:3453-3456, 3609-3694; LevelObjectBuilder.cpp:161-176; Structure.cpp:7-25; StructureRamp.cpp:1-26.

findings.title: TriangleRightAxisAligned enforces neither of the two invariants its name promises
findings.detail: All three constructors (MattMath.cpp:3609-3631) simply forward to `Triangle` and validate nothing. Axis-alignment is never checked at all -- the parameter names `top`, `left`, `right` are the only documentation. Right-angledness is discovered only at USE time, when `get_hypotenuse()` (3633-3642) calls `find_hypotenuse` and throws `std::invalid_argument("Triangle is not a right triangle")` from a const accessor. Since `Triangle` has public data (`Vector2F points[3]`, MattMath.h:844), no virtuals of its own and no invariant, a caller can also break the promise after construction. Inheriting to add two helper functions buys nothing the type system enforces.
findings.suggestion: Delete the class in favour of free functions, or make it a distinct value type with a factory that returns failure (`static bool try_make(...)`) rather than a subclass that throws on use. Cache the hypotenuse index at construction using squared lengths -- no acos, no sqrt.
findings.verify_note: Read MattMath.h:842-914 and MattMath.cpp:3609-3652.

findings.title: get_hypotenuse and get_hypotenuse_gradient each re-run find_hypotenuse -- up to 6 sqrt and 3 acos plus a heap allocation to identify one edge
findings.detail: `find_hypotenuse` (3665-3684) calls `get_angle_0/1/2` until one matches PI_OVER_2. Each `get_angle_N` (3512-3527) builds two `Segment`s, takes two directions and calls `angle_between` = 2 sqrt + 1 acos, so the worst case is 6 sqrt and 3 acos. A right triangle's hypotenuse is the longest edge -- three `length_squared` comparisons, no transcendentals. The result is not cached, so calling both accessors pays for it twice, and `get_hypotenuse()` does `this->get_edges()[hypotenuse]` (3641), allocating a three-element vector to read one element when `get_edge_0/1/2()` are right there.
findings.suggestion: Determine and cache the hypotenuse index once at construction (which is also where right-angled-ness should be validated), using squared lengths. Replace `get_edges()[i]` with a switch over `get_edge_0/1/2()`.

findings.title: Shape is an O(N^2) fat interface: adding a primitive forces edits to every existing shape
findings.detail: Merges 2 candidates; severity downgraded from the reported "critical" (nothing crashes -- this is a design cost, not a defect). `Shape` declares seven pure-virtual `intersects` overloads (lines 73-79). Adding an eighth primitive (capsule, ray, convex polygon) requires: a new `shape_type` value, a new pure virtual on `Shape`, an implementation in all five existing concrete shapes, a new `case` in `Shape::intersects(const Shape*)` (MattMath.cpp:119-136), and roughly seven new free functions. That is the classic binary-dispatch explosion and it is the single biggest structural obstacle to MattMath being a reusable collision library. It already shows: `shape_type::NONE` (shape_type.h:11) is a value no shape ever returns, existing only so the `default:` arm can throw.
findings.suggestion: Collapse the pairwise matrix. Give every convex primitive `Vector2F support(const Vector2F& dir) const` and write one generic SAT/GJK `intersects(const Shape&, const Shape&)` -- N implementations instead of N^2 -- keeping specialised fast paths (AABB-AABB, circle-circle) as an optimisation table rather than as the interface. `Shape` should then carry only `get_bounding_box`, `get_center`, `contains`, `clone` and `support`.
findings.verify_note: Read MattMath.h:68-182 and MattMath.cpp:119-136; counted the seven virtuals and the five concrete implementers.

findings.title: Three parallel public APIs for the same operation, and get_shape_type() leaks so eight call sites bypass all of them
findings.detail: The same intersection is reachable three ways: ~30 free `*_intersect` functions (MattMath.h:96-182), the member `intersects` overloads that merely forward to them (e.g. `Circle::intersects(const Triangle&)` at MattMath.cpp:3372-3375 is `return circle_triangle_intersect(*this, other);`), and `shapes_intersect(a,b)` (157-165) which forwards to the member which forwards to the free function. Argument order is not guessable from the name: `rectangle_rotated_rectangle_intersect(const RectangleF&, const RectangleRotated&)` (MattMath.h:117) takes the axis-aligned rect FIRST. Worse, `Shape::get_shape_type()` is public, so callers route around the polymorphism entirely -- I verified the identical `if (other_shape_type == shape_type::RECTANGLE) return true;` short-circuit in Player.cpp:172, PaintTile.cpp:96, ProjectileBall.cpp:73, ProjectileJet.cpp:72, ProjectileMist.cpp:74, ProjectileRolling.cpp:66, ProjectileSpray.cpp:74, plus CollisionTools.cpp:244-245. The ~30 free functions have zero first-party callers outside MattMath.cpp and the tests.
findings.suggestion: Publish one entry point -- `bool intersects(const Shape&, const Shape&)` -- and move the pairwise routines into a `detail` namespace or an anonymous namespace in the .cpp. Demote `get_shape_type()` to a dispatcher-only tag; eight call sites using it to skip the narrow phase means the interface is not giving callers what they need.
findings.verify_note: Read MattMath.h:80-182, MattMath.cpp:157-175, 3364-3391; grepped shape_type::RECTANGLE across ArtAttack/ and confirmed all eight sites.

findings.title: The geometry library #includes d3d11.h and DirectXTK, hard-binding a renderer-agnostic module to D3D11
findings.detail: Merges 2 candidates. `MattMath.h` opens with `#include "SimpleMath.h"` and `#include <d3d11.h>`, so every gameplay/AI/physics file that wants a `Vector2F` compiles all of `d3d11.h` and `Windows.h`. The coupling is not incidental: `struct Viewport` (767-806) exists solely to convert to/from `D3D11_VIEWPORT` and `SimpleMath::Viewport`, including `const D3D11_VIEWPORT* get_d3d_viewport_ptr()`; `RectangleF` has `RectangleF(const RECT&)`, `get_win_rect()` and `get_sm_rectangle()` (198-199, 230-231); and `Circle` (816), `Triangle` (851-853) and `Quad` (929-932) each carry duplicate constructor sets taking `SimpleMath::Vector2` purely to skip a conversion. For a module whose stated purpose is to be the reusable core of a 2D engine, the geometry primitives must not know the graphics API exists.
findings.suggestion: Split into a pure-C++ `MattMath/` (Vector2F, RectangleF, Circle, Triangle, Quad, Segment, RectangleRotated) and a `MattMathD3DInterop.h` in the rendering layer providing free `to_d3d(const Viewport&)`, `to_rect(const RectangleF&)`, `from_sm(const SimpleMath::Vector2&)`. Move `Viewport` out of the math namespace -- it is a rendering concept. Delete the `SimpleMath::Vector2` constructor overloads from the shapes.

findings.title: MattMath is a god module: shapes, colour, a general dynamic matrix, viewport and camera in one 1139-line header / 4568-line TU
findings.detail: Verified contents of the single header: scalar helpers (44-66), a `direction` enum (12-23), the `Shape` hierarchy plus ~30 free intersection functions (68-182), `Vector2I`/`Vector2F`/`Vector3F`/`Vector4F`, `RectangleI`/`RectangleF`, `Colour` with hex parsing and `saturate`/`desaturate`/`brighten`/`darken` (586-645), a dynamically-sized `MatrixF` with `gaussian_elimination`/`determinant`/`is_upper_triangular` (684-748), `Matrix3x3F` (750-765), a D3D `Viewport` (767-806), `Camera` (1007-1045) and the six shape primitives. `Colour` and `MatrixF` have no relationship whatsoever to 2D collision geometry. This is also why MattMathTests cannot test the shapes without `#include "..\ArtAttack\MattMath.cpp"` wholesale (MathTests.cpp:5-6) -- there is no smaller unit to link against.
findings.suggestion: Break into focused headers behind an umbrella (`Vector2.h`, `Rectangle.h`, `Shapes.h`, `Intersection.h`, `Matrix.h`), move `Colour` into a render module and `Viewport`/`Camera` into a view module, one class per header/source pair. That is also the precondition for making the engine a static library that the test project links against instead of #including .cpp files.
findings.verify_note: Read all 1139 lines of MattMath.h; read MathTests.cpp:1-20.

findings.title: MattMath.h uses std::unique_ptr and std::string without including <memory> or <string>
findings.detail: Merges 2 candidates. The header includes only `SimpleMath.h`, `shape_type.h`, `<d3d11.h>`, `<cmath>` and `<vector>`, yet declares `virtual std::unique_ptr<Shape> clone() const = 0;` at line 85 (plus five overrides at 206, 822, 859, 937, 1067) and `Colour(const std::string& hex);` at line 600. It compiles only because DirectXTK's `SimpleMath.h` transitively drags in the MSVC STL's memory and string machinery -- an accident of one vendor's header layout, in the most widely included header in the project. A DirectXTK update or a different standard library breaks it, and the failure will look like hundreds of unrelated errors. `<cmath>` is not used by anything in the header and belongs in the .cpp.
findings.suggestion: Add `#include <memory>` and `#include <string>`; move `<cmath>` to MattMath.cpp. Combine with the D3D split above.
findings.verify_note: Read MattMath.h:1-8 and confirmed std::unique_ptr at 85/206/822/859/937/1067 and std::string at 600, with no <memory>/<string> include.

findings.title: Shape supports only offset() and inflate() -- no rotate, scale or transform -- which is why RectangleRotated had to be bolted on as a whole new type
findings.detail: Severity downgraded from the reported "high": this is an absence rather than a defect, and a separate OBB type is a defensible (if costly) design. Still real: `Shape` has exactly two mutations, `offset(Vector2F)` (84) and `inflate(float)` (88). There is no `rotate(float)`, no `scale`, no `transform`. So a rotated box could not be expressed as "a RectangleF plus a rotation" and instead needed an 88-line class (1047-1134) plus six new free intersection functions plus a new `shape_type` value plus five new `intersects` overrides in every existing shape. The header already contains `Matrix3x3F::rotation/scale/translation` factories (759-764) that would express this directly and are used by nothing in the tree.
findings.suggestion: Introduce `struct Transform2D { Vector2F position; float rotation; Vector2F scale; }` with `Matrix3x3F to_matrix()` and `inverse()`, and give `Shape` one `virtual void transform(const Transform2D&)` -- or keep shapes in local space and put the transform on the collider, as most 2D engines do. `RectangleRotated` then becomes `RectangleF` + `Transform2D`, and `Camera` becomes a `Transform2D`.
findings.verify_note: Read MattMath.h:68-89, 750-765, 1047-1134; grepped for Matrix3x3F usage (none outside MattMath).

findings.title: Camera exposes four spellings of the same forward transform, three of them dead, with no inverse and no rotation
findings.detail: Merges 2 candidates. `calculate_view_rectangle` exists as a const value-returning member (1021), a const in-place member (1023), a static (1025) and a static with an out-param (1028); all four bodies (MattMath.cpp:4116-4150) are the same four lines of arithmetic copy-pasted. Grepping ArtAttack/ shows only the first is ever called (AnimationObject.cpp:69, TextureObject.cpp:59). The in-place overload is also a genuine overload-resolution trap: for a non-const lvalue argument, binding to `RectangleF&` is a better match than binding to `const RectangleF&` (less cv-qualified reference wins), so `camera.calculate_view_rectangle(my_rect)` silently picks the MUTATING overload while the reader expects a value. There is no `view_to_world` inverse anywhere -- which any reusable 2D engine needs for mouse picking -- no rotation, and no zoom-about-a-point, all while a fully-built `Matrix3x3F` sits unused in the same header.
findings.suggestion: Keep only `[[nodiscard]] RectangleF calculate_view_rectangle(const RectangleF&) const` and delete the other three. Replace the class with `struct Camera2D { Transform2D view; }` exposing `world_to_view` / `view_to_world` derived from one matrix and its inverse, and move it into the rendering module (`CameraTools.h` already lives outside, so the split is half done).
findings.verify_note: Read MattMath.h:1007-1045 and MattMath.cpp:4092-4180; grepped calculate_view_rectangle across ArtAttack/ (only AnimationObject.cpp:69 and TextureObject.cpp:59).

findings.title: get_rectangle_rotated_to_axis() is a renderer workaround welded onto a geometry primitive, and it silently discards the rotation
findings.detail: `RectangleF RectangleRotated::get_rectangle_rotated_to_axis() const { return RectangleF(this->_center, this->_hw_extents.x, this->_hw_extents.y); }` -- the OBB with its rotation thrown away. Its only caller is `Visual::Visual(..., const RectangleRotated&, ...)` (Visual.cpp:34), which needs an axis-aligned destination rect for `SpriteBatch`; the rotation was supposed to be recovered by `DrawObject::set_draw_rotation_by_rectangle_rotated`, which is an empty `// TODO: Implement this function` (DrawObject.cpp:66-69). So a sprite-batching detail lives in the math layer and currently drops rotation on the floor.
findings.suggestion: Delete the method from the shape. The renderer's job is to take a `RectangleRotated` and produce (destination rect, rotation, origin); put that adapter in the drawing layer, and implement it using `atan2(_x_axis.y, _x_axis.x)` rather than the unsigned `get_angle()`.
findings.verify_note: Read MattMath.cpp:4456-4463, Visual.cpp:20-40, DrawObject.cpp:60-69.

findings.title: Sibling shapes disagree on encapsulation and invariants, and the free algorithms reach past the accessors into Triangle's raw array
findings.detail: Merges 2 candidates. Within one family: `Circle` has public `center`/`radius` and no invariant (negative radius constructible); `Triangle` has public `Vector2F points[3]` (844) plus accessors on top, and no invariant (degenerate triangles fine); `Quad` has private `points[4]` (978-979) and throws from every ctor and setter; `RectangleRotated` has private members with orthonormality and positive-extent enforcement and throws from setters; `Segment` has public members and no interface. A caller holding a `Shape*` cannot know whether a mutation returns, throws or corrupts. The inconsistency is load-bearing: `triangles_intersect` reads `a.points[i]` directly (386), `triangle_point_intersect` reads `triangle.points[0..2]` (449-450), `triangle_rectangle_rotated_intersect` reads `triangle.points[0..2]` (472-474) -- so `Triangle`'s representation is baked into three free functions and cannot be changed. Both `Triangle` and `Quad` use raw C arrays rather than `std::array`, so there is no `size()`, no `begin()/end()`, and the file uses zero standard algorithms.
findings.suggestion: Pick one policy family-wide. For value-type geometry the pragmatic choice is public data, no throwing constructors, and opt-in free predicates (`is_valid`/`is_degenerate`/`is_convex`) -- that keeps the shapes trivially copyable and constexpr-able. If enforced invariants are wanted instead, close `Circle`, `Triangle` and `Segment` too and return failure rather than throwing. Use `std::array` in both `Triangle` and `Quad`.

findings.title: Segment and Point2F participate in the Shape intersects interface but are not Shapes, so two of the seven pure virtuals are unreachable through the polymorphic entry point
findings.detail: Merges 2 candidates. `Shape` declares `virtual bool intersects(const Segment&)` and `virtual bool intersects(const Point2F&)` (77-78), yet `Segment` (982-1006) does not derive from `Shape` and `Point2F` is a typedef of `Vector2F` (33). `Shape::intersects(const Shape*)` (MattMath.cpp:119-136) switches on `shape_type`, which has no `SEGMENT` or `POINT` value (shape_type.h:4-12), so those two overrides can never be reached polymorphically. `Segment` has only two ad-hoc `intersects` members (`Segment`, `RectangleF`, MattMath.cpp:4054-4062) -- so `circle.intersects(segment)` compiles but `segment.intersects(circle)` does not, and the stubs for exactly those cases sit commented out at 4079-4086. `Segment` also has no `get_bounding_box`, `offset` or `clone`, so it cannot be stored in the `unique_ptr<Shape>` the whole collision system is built on -- even though a segment is the natural shape for a raycast, a paintable edge or a thin projectile.
findings.suggestion: Make `Segment` (and a distinct `Point` type) first-class `Shape` implementations with their own `shape_type` values so one dispatch path covers everything, or delete `Segment`'s two lopsided members so the asymmetry is at least not advertised.
findings.verify_note: Read MattMath.h:33, 68-89, 982-1006; MattMath.cpp:119-136, 4054-4086; shape_type.h.

findings.title: contains(Point2F) is duplicated non-virtually on five shapes instead of being on Shape, so nothing holding a Shape* can ask the most basic 2D query
findings.detail: `RectangleF::contains` (248), `Circle::contains` (838), `Triangle::contains` (889), `Quad::contains` (973) and `RectangleRotated::contains` (1065) are each declared separately and none is virtual. Four of the five bodies are the identical one-liner `return this->intersects(point);` (MattMath.cpp:912-915, 3392-3395, 3584-3587, 4023-4026); `RectangleRotated::contains` (4265-4268) forwards to the free function instead, for no reason. Because none is on `Shape`, code holding a `Shape*` -- which is how every collider is stored (`Structure.h:40`, `ICollisionGameObject::get_shape()`) -- cannot ask whether a collider contains a point. Point containment is the most basic query a 2D engine needs: mouse picking, spawn validity, trigger volumes.
findings.suggestion: Add `virtual bool contains(const Point2F&) const = 0;` to `Shape` and delete the five duplicates. `Shape` is also missing `get_area()` (only `RectangleF` has one, MattMath.h:228) despite paint scoring summing shape areas.

findings.title: Every derived shape redeclares intersects and none adds `using Shape::intersects;`, so Shape's own convenience overloads are hidden on all of them
findings.detail: `Shape` declares non-virtual `intersects(const Shape*)` and `intersects(const Shape&)` (80-81). Every derived class then declares its own `intersects` overload set -- RectangleF (241-247), Circle (831-837), Triangle (882-888), Quad (966-972), RectangleRotated (1058-1064) -- and none contains `using Shape::intersects;`. C++ name lookup stops at the first scope with a match, and no `const Shape&` converts to any of the seven parameter types, so `circle.intersects(some_shape_ref)` does not compile even though `Circle` IS a `Shape` with that operation; callers must write `static_cast<const Shape&>(circle).intersects(other)`. It only goes unnoticed because every real call site already holds a `Shape*` (Player.cpp:163/179, PaintTile.cpp:87/103, CollisionTools.cpp:62/235, and the five projectiles). `AABB_intersects` is not redeclared and so is NOT hidden -- two sibling APIs behaving differently for no visible reason.
findings.suggestion: Add `using Shape::intersects;` to each derived class, or delete the pointer/reference convenience overloads from `Shape` and let callers use the free functions.
findings.verify_note: Read MattMath.h:80-83, 241-247, 831-837, 882-888, 966-972, 1058-1064 and confirmed no `using` declaration in any derived class.

findings.title: Every Quad constructor runs an O(n^2) self-intersection check and throws, including for input that is unconditionally valid, while accepting the genuinely broken cases
findings.detail: Merges 2 candidates. All five ctors end with `if (!this->is_valid()) throw std::invalid_argument("Quad is not valid");` (3710, 3728, 3741, 3756, 3772), and `is_valid()` (3832-3849) allocates a `vector<Segment>` and runs six segment-segment tests. `Quad(const RectangleF&)` (3734-3745) pays all of that to discover a rectangle is not self-intersecting. Meanwhile the documented invariant -- "ordered in a clockwise direction, starting from the top left" (MattMath.h:916-919) -- is never checked, nor is convexity, nor degeneracy: four identical points pass only because of the `a == b` short-circuit, and three collinear points pass because `test_2D_segment_segment` uses strict `< 0.0f` sign tests (EricsonMath.cpp:705, 712) and reports collinear as non-intersecting. So the class throws on the cheap-to-avoid case and accepts the genuinely broken ones -- and because `Quad`s are constructed inside const query paths (`get_quad()` -> `contains()`), the throw escapes into the per-frame collision loop where nothing catches `std::invalid_argument`. The exception message contains none of the offending coordinates.
findings.suggestion: Make constructors trivial and total. Expose `is_simple()`/`is_convex()` as opt-in queries or a `static bool try_make(points, Quad& out)` factory, and give `RectangleF`->`Quad` a direct path that skips validation. Include the four coordinates in any message that does survive.

findings.title: Shape is a polymorphic base with public implicit copy construction and copy assignment, so slicing is silent and base-to-base assignment is a no-op
findings.detail: `struct Shape` (68-89) correctly declares `virtual ~Shape() = default;` but constrains nothing else. It has an implicitly generated public copy constructor and copy assignment, and being a `struct` everything is public. So `Shape& a = *shape_a; a = *shape_b;` compiles cleanly and does literally nothing (`Shape` has no data members and the vptr is not copied), leaving the caller believing one shape was assigned to another. Slicing on construction is equally unguarded and is the supported code path today -- see the `TriangleRightAxisAligned::clone()` finding. For a base used exclusively through `Shape*` / `unique_ptr<Shape>` (`Structure.h:40`, all of `CollisionTools`), leaving value semantics wide open is a standing invitation.
findings.suggestion: Make the copy operations `protected` (or delete copy assignment) on `Shape` so only derived classes invoke them, force polymorphic copying through `clone()`, and add `protected: Shape() = default;`. That one change would have made the ramp slicing a compile error.
findings.verify_note: Read MattMath.h:68-89 and confirmed no declared copy/move operations and no protected section.

findings.title: Redundant `X(const X&) = default;` on every shape suppresses the implicit move operations
findings.detail: Merges 2 candidates. Verified declarations: RectangleF:192, Circle:814, Triangle:847, TriangleRightAxisAligned:898, Quad:923, Segment:988, Camera:1013, RectangleRotated:1050. A user-declared copy constructor suppresses the implicit move constructor AND move assignment. The compiler would have generated an identical copy constructor anyway, so these lines buy nothing and cost the moves. For the POD-ish shapes it is only noise, but `RectangleRotated` holds a `std::vector<Point2F> _points` (1119-1120), so every return-by-value where NRVO does not apply, every `std::vector<RectangleRotated>` growth and every `push_back(std::move(obb))` performs a heap allocation and deep copy a move would have made free.
findings.suggestion: Delete all eight `X(const X&) = default;` lines and let the rule of zero apply -- the compiler then generates copy AND move correctly. If the intent was to document copyability, use a comment.
findings.verify_note: Read each cited header line; confirmed RectangleRotated's vector member at MattMath.h:1119-1120.

findings.title: Missing `explicit` on converting constructors lets nonsense like circle.intersects(5.0f) compile
findings.detail: `Vector2F(float f);` (409, defined MattMath.cpp:1529-1533 as `x = f; y = f;`) is a non-explicit single-argument converting constructor, and `Point2F` is a typedef of `Vector2F` (33). Every shape has `bool intersects(const Point2F&) const`. So `circle.intersects(5.0f)` compiles and silently means "the point (5,5)" -- no other overload is viable, so there is not even an ambiguity error. Also non-explicit: `Quad(const std::vector<Point2F>&)` (926), `Quad(const RectangleF&)` (927) and `Quad(const RectangleRotated&)` (928), so a `RectangleF` implicitly becomes a `Quad` via a conversion that THROWS for a degenerate rectangle; and `Camera(const Viewport&, float scale = 1.0f)` (1016), callable with one argument, so any `Viewport` implicitly becomes a `Camera`.
findings.suggestion: Mark every single-argument (or defaulted-to-single-argument) constructor `explicit`. For `Vector2F(float)`, prefer deleting it and adding a named `Vector2F::splat(float)`.
findings.verify_note: Read MattMath.h:33, 409, 926-932, 1016 and MattMath.cpp:1529-1533.

findings.title: No LanguageStandard is set in either vcxproj, so the project builds as C++14 and reimplements clamp/lerp/PI by hand
findings.detail: Verified: grepping `LanguageStandard` across ArtAttack.vcxproj and MattMathTests.vcxproj returns nothing, so MSVC v145 defaults to /std:c++14 and none of `std::clamp`, `std::optional`, `std::string_view`, `if constexpr`, inline `constexpr` statics or `<numbers>` is available. Consequently: `MattMath::clamp` (declared 51/53, defined MattMath.cpp:34-48 and 60-74) is a 15-line if/else reimplementation of `std::clamp`, written twice instead of as a template; `lerp` (66, defined 110-113) is `std::lerp`; `PI` (44) is `std::numbers::pi_v<float>`; `are_equal` (MattMath.cpp:93-96) calls the C global `fabs` rather than `std::fabs`; and `to_radians`/`to_degrees` (101-108) are not `constexpr` despite being pure arithmetic on a `constexpr` constant. Bumping the standard is the single change that unlocks most of the other fixes in this review.
findings.suggestion: Add `<LanguageStandard>stdcpp20</LanguageStandard>` to all four configurations of both vcxproj files (better: factor the four near-identical ItemDefinitionGroups into a shared .props). Then delete `clamp`/`clamp_ref`/`lerp` and make `to_radians`/`to_degrees`/`are_equal` constexpr.
findings.verify_note: Grepped both vcxproj files for LanguageStandard (no matches); read MattMath.h:44-66 and MattMath.cpp:34-113.

findings.title: Namespace-scope shape/camera constants are dynamically initialised, creating cross-TU initialisation-order dependencies
findings.detail: Merges 2 candidates. `Camera::DEFAULT_CAMERA` (declared 1044, defined MattMath.cpp:4180 as `{ Vector2F::ZERO, 1.0f }`) is byte-identical to a default-constructed `Camera` (NSDMIs at 1009-1010 already give ZERO and 1.0f); it exists only because no constructor is `constexpr`. Same for `Vector2F::ZERO`/`DIRECTION_*` (MattMath.cpp:1907-1916, where 1913-1916 even call `unit_vector()` at dynamic-init time), `RectangleF::ZERO` (1134), `Vector2I::ZERO` (1495), `RectangleI::ZERO` (2138). These are dynamically initialised statics whose cross-TU ordering is unspecified, and other TUs already read them at namespace scope: `DebugText.h:14` is `const static MattMath::Vector2F DEBUG_POSITION = MattMath::Vector2F::ZERO;`, copied from a static defined in a different TU. Harmless today only because the pre-dynamic zero value happens to be correct. `RectangleRotated`'s NSDMIs (1115-1116) read `DIRECTION_RIGHT`/`DIRECTION_UP`, so any future namespace-scope OBB inherits the hazard.
findings.suggestion: Give the simple value types `constexpr` constructors and declare the constants `static constexpr` in-class (C++17 makes them implicitly inline). Delete `DEFAULT_CAMERA` in favour of `Camera{}`. Requires the standard bump above.

findings.title: RectangleRotated::get_points() hands out a reference into a member vector that every mutator replaces wholesale
findings.detail: It is the only shape accessor in the file returning a container by reference -- `Triangle::get_points()` (3485-3489) and `Quad::get_points()` (3871-3881) both return by value. All nine mutators do `this->_points = this->calculate_points();`, which move-assigns a fresh vector and frees the old buffer, so any caller that takes a `const Point2F*` or an iterator out of the returned reference -- the natural thing to do with a returned container -- is holding a dangling pointer the moment the shape is offset, and `Shape::offset` is called once per bracket iteration per contact. Grep confirms there are currently no callers of `RectangleRotated::get_points()` anywhere in the tree, so this is a live trap rather than a live bug.
findings.suggestion: Return `std::array<Point2F, 4>` by value (consistent with the array recommendation and with Triangle/Quad). There is no reason to hand out a reference to 32 bytes.
findings.verify_note: Read MattMath.cpp:3485-3489, 3871-3881, 4269-4433; grepped get_points() across ArtAttack/ and MattMathTests/ (no external callers).

findings.title: Inconsistent return conventions across the shape accessors: by-value, by-const-ref and fresh-vector all coexist for the same operation
findings.detail: For the same conceptual operation the three shapes each pick differently. Element accessors: `Triangle::get_point_0..2()` return `const Vector2F&` (862-864); `Quad::get_point_0..3()` return `const Point2F&` (942-945); `RectangleRotated::get_point_0..3()` return `Point2F` BY VALUE (1087-1090) despite `_points` being a stable member. Plural accessors: `Triangle::get_points()` returns a freshly built `std::vector` (MattMath.cpp:3485-3489); `Quad::get_points()` likewise (3871-3881); `RectangleRotated::get_points()` returns `const std::vector<Point2F>&` (1091). A consumer cannot form any expectation about whether a getter costs an allocation, and two of the three silently do.
findings.suggestion: Standardise: element accessors return `const T&`, plural accessors return `const std::array<T,N>&` over storage the shape already holds. That also removes all three fresh-vector allocations.
findings.verify_note: Read MattMath.h:862-865, 942-946, 1087-1091 and the corresponding definitions in MattMath.cpp.

findings.title: Untyped int axis/edge selectors validated with a runtime throw, and a -1 sentinel where an optional belongs
findings.detail: `RectangleRotated::get_axis(int)` (MattMath.cpp:4315-4327) and `get_half_width(int)` (4340-4352) accept only 0 and 1 and otherwise throw from a const accessor; `Triangle::calculate_gradient(int edge)` (3594-3603) throws for anything outside 0..2. A two- or three-valued selector passed as `int` and checked at runtime is a compile-time check thrown away -- `get_axis(2)` should not compile, and today it throws from deep inside collision code (that is exactly how `closest_pt_point_OBB` fails). `TriangleRightAxisAligned::find_hypotenuse` (3665-3684) compounds it by returning `-1` for "not a right triangle", which both callers then re-check with two copies of the same three-line guard (3636-3639, 3646-3649).
findings.suggestion: Introduce `enum class axis { x, y };` and store the axes in a `std::array<Vector2F,2>` so the accessor is total and cannot throw. Return `std::optional<int>` (or an `enum class edge`) from `find_hypotenuse` and share one guard.

findings.title: typedef instead of using, and Point2F is a weak alias that lets directions and extents masquerade as points
findings.detail: `typedef Vector2F Point2F;` (33), `typedef MattMath::RectangleF AABB;` (301), `typedef RectangleRotated OBB;` (1136). Besides being `typedef` rather than `using`, `Point2F` is a WEAK alias -- the same type as `Vector2F` -- so the distinction it draws carries no meaning and the compiler will never enforce it. The confusion has already leaked into the newest code: `RectangleRotated` uses `Point2F` for things that are unambiguously directions and sizes -- `get_x_axis()`/`get_y_axis()`/`get_axis(int)` (1072-1074), `get_half_extents()` (1075), `set_x_axis`/`set_y_axis` (1081-1082), `set_half_extents` (1083) -- while the corresponding private members are correctly typed `Vector2F` (1115-1117).
findings.suggestion: Switch all three to `using`. Correct the RectangleRotated axis/extent signatures to `Vector2F` today. Longer term, make `Point2F` a real distinct type so `point + point` does not compile but `point + vector` does.

findings.title: No [[nodiscard]] anywhere, including on clone() and the pure-query predicates
findings.detail: Not one function in the 1139-line header carries the attribute. The places it would actually catch bugs: `virtual std::unique_ptr<Shape> clone() const = 0;` (85) -- discarding it constructs and destroys a shape for nothing; the seven `intersects` predicates per shape plus `contains` and `is_valid` (940, 1108) -- `quad.is_valid();` as a statement is a plausible typo for a check and compiles silently; `RectangleF intersection(const RectangleF&) const` (249), which sits among a pile of mutating `void` members (`inflate`, `scale`, `offset`, `set_*`) so `rect.intersection(other);` reads like an in-place operation and does nothing; `Vector2F normalized() const` (445) next to `void normalize()` (446) -- the same trap; and all the `Camera` factories (1033-1038) and `RectangleF::intersection`/`union_of`/`from_top_left_bottom_right` (290-296).
findings.suggestion: Mark every const accessor, predicate and factory `[[nodiscard]]`. Mechanical, and the cheapest bug-catching change available in this file.
findings.verify_note: Read the whole of MattMath.h; confirmed zero occurrences of nodiscard.

findings.title: Out-parameters where a return value belongs, each needing a hand-written discarding twin
findings.detail: `rectangle_circle_intersect(..., Point2F& point)` (100), `circle_triangle_intersect(..., Point2F& point)` (124), `circle_segment_intersect(..., Point2F& point)` (133) and `segments_intersect(..., float& t, Point2F& p)` (170-171) each require a manually written "I don't care" overload that declares a dummy local purely to throw it away -- MattMath.cpp:312-317, 342-346, 576-581. `MattMath::clamp_ref(float&, ...)` / `clamp_ref(int&, ...)` (52, 54) and `Camera::calculate_view_rectangle(RectangleF&)` (1023) are the same anti-pattern for pure functions. CORRECTION to the candidate: it claims `t` is "read uninitialised" in the wrapper at 576-581 -- it is not. `t` is declared uninitialised and passed by reference, but the wrapper never reads it back, so there is no UB, only a pointless local.
findings.suggestion: Define `struct SegmentHit { float t; Point2F point; };` and return `std::optional<SegmentHit>` (needs the standard bump). That collapses each pair of overloads into one and makes "no hit means no point" unrepresentable. Delete `clamp_ref` in favour of `value = std::clamp(value, lo, hi)`.
findings.verify_note: Read MattMath.h:52-54, 96-176, 1023; MattMath.cpp:306-346, 563-581; traced that `t` is never read after the call in the wrapper.

findings.title: Dead private calculate_points(Segment, float) overload, and neither parameterised overload touches `this`
findings.detail: `std::vector<Point2F> calculate_points(const Segment& center_line, float thickness) const;` (1128-1129, defined MattMath.cpp:4501-4510) is never called from anywhere -- grep across the whole tree finds only its own definition. The constructor it was clearly written for (4201-4215) inlines the same four lines instead, which is exactly how the two copies drifted apart (both carry the same missing-normalisation bug). Both parameterised overloads (4487-4499 and 4501-4510) are `const` non-static member functions that never read a single member; they are pure functions of their arguments.
findings.suggestion: Delete the Segment/thickness overload and have the constructor delegate to the 4-argument primary constructor. Make the remaining parameterised overload `static` (or a free function in an anonymous namespace in the .cpp).
findings.verify_note: Read MattMath.h:1122-1129 and MattMath.cpp:4482-4510; grepped calculate_points across the tree.

findings.title: Members assigned in constructor bodies instead of member initialiser lists, so they are initialised twice
findings.detail: Every member of these types has a default member initialiser, and several constructors then assign over it in the body: `Circle::Circle(float,float,float)` (3313-3317), all three `Triangle` constructors (3405-3426), all five `Quad` constructors (3700-3776), `Camera::Camera(const Viewport&, float)` (4100-4105) and `RectangleRotated::RectangleRotated(const Segment&, float)` (4201-4207). The two-argument `Circle` (3305-3312), the `Segment` constructors (4037-4044), `RectangleF(float,float,float,float)` (667-670) and the 4-arg `RectangleRotated` (4186-4189) right next door do it correctly, so the file is inconsistent with itself. For `Quad`, body-assignment is also what forces the validity check to be a post-hoc `if (!is_valid()) throw` on a half-built object rather than part of construction.
findings.suggestion: Use member initialiser lists throughout and have the multi-argument constructors delegate to one primary constructor rather than repeating the assignments five times.

findings.title: Bounding boxes are recomputed from scratch on every call and never cached, plus two dead-store AABB locals in the bracket search
findings.detail: `Triangle::get_bounding_box` (3427-3441) runs four nested min/max chains over three points; `Quad::get_bounding_box` (3778-3792) and `RectangleRotated::get_bounding_box` (4217-4231) do four chains over four points. None caches. `Shape::AABB_intersects` (143-146) calls `get_bounding_box()` on both operands every invocation, and every concrete `is_colliding` does AABB-then-narrow, so in `Level::update_level_logic`'s pairwise loop each object's AABB is rebuilt O(n) times per frame. I also confirmed both dead stores the candidate reported: `CollisionTools.cpp:35` and `CollisionTools.cpp:58` each do `RectangleF collider_aabb = collider->get_bounding_box();` and never use the variable -- a wasted virtual call plus min/max chain per bracket iteration, and a /W4 C4189 nobody sees because `TreatWarningAsError` is not set in either vcxproj. For `RectangleRotated` the AABB is a pure function of `_points`, which is already recomputed and cached on every mutation, so caching it there is free.
findings.suggestion: Cache the AABB alongside `_points` in `RectangleRotated` and invalidate it in the same setters. For Triangle/Quad, cache with a dirty flag, or have `Level` build a per-frame AABB array once and do broad phase against that. Delete the two unused `collider_aabb` locals.
findings.verify_note: Read MattMath.cpp:143-151, 3427-3441, 3778-3792, 4217-4231; CollisionTools.cpp:33-70 (confirmed both locals unused); grepped vcxproj for TreatWarningAsError (absent).

findings.title: Two different unqualified EPSILON constants 100x apart, and the tests define a third set
findings.detail: `MattMath::EPSILON = 0.0001f` (MattMath.h:46) and `EricsonMath::EPSILON = 0.000001f` (EricsonMath.h:75) -- both `constexpr float EPSILON` at namespace scope, two orders of magnitude apart, with no comment on what either is a tolerance for. MathTests.cpp:9-10 does `using namespace MattMath; using namespace EricsonMath;` in the same file, so an unqualified `EPSILON` there would be ambiguous; the test file works around it by defining a third set -- `MathTestConstants::EPSILON_F` (1e-6), `EPSILON_F_2` (2e-6), `EPSILON_F_100` (1e-4) at MathTests.cpp:14-16 -- which is itself the signal that the tolerance story is unclear. Compounding it, `MattMath::EPSILON` is used as an ABSOLUTE tolerance by `are_equal` (MattMath.cpp:93-99) and applied to unnormalised dot products and world-space lengths (see the edges_valid finding).
findings.suggestion: Name the constants for what they measure (`ANGLE_EPSILON`, `POSITION_EPSILON`, `UNIT_EPSILON`), add a relative-tolerance overload of `are_equal`, and have the tests use the production constants rather than a private third set.
findings.verify_note: Read MattMath.h:46, EricsonMath.h:75, MathTests.cpp:1-20, MattMath.cpp:93-100.

findings.title: shape_type::NONE is produced by no shape but is the only way to reach the dispatcher's throwing default branch
findings.detail: Grepping `shape_type::NONE` across ArtAttack/ and MattMathTests/ returns zero hits -- no `get_shape_type()` override ever returns it (RectangleF:725, Circle:3327, Triangle:3445, Quad:3797, RectangleRotated:4235 all return their concrete tags). Meanwhile `Shape::intersects(const Shape*)` (MattMath.cpp:133-134) handles it only via `default: throw std::invalid_argument("Shape type not recognized")`, thrown from inside the per-frame collision loop. So the enum advertises a "no shape" state that the dispatcher treats as fatal, reachable only through a programming mistake the type system could have prevented. `Segment` has no `shape_type` value at all despite being one of the seven `intersects` overloads.
findings.suggestion: Delete `shape_type::NONE`. If a null-shape concept is needed, model it as a null `Shape*`. Decide whether `Segment` is a `Shape` and make the enum consistent either way.
findings.verify_note: Grepped shape_type::NONE across ArtAttack/ and MattMathTests/ (zero hits); read shape_type.h and MattMath.cpp:119-136.

findings.title: Zoom-out start and finish cameras are rebuilt every frame from frame-invariant inputs
findings.detail: `_zoom_out_start_bounds` and `_zoom_out_finish_bounds` are set once in the constructor (Level.cpp:45-46) from the level JSON and never change, and the screen resolution does not change mid-zoom. Only `zoom_out_camera_ratio()` (Level.cpp:176-179) varies per frame. Yet both endpoint cameras -- including two `RectangleF` constructions, two `get_resolution_vec()` calls through a raw pointer, and two divisions -- are recomputed every frame to produce identical values. Small in absolute cost, but it is the only per-frame use of the Camera API and it illustrates the wider pattern of recomputing derived values at the point of use rather than caching them where their inputs change.
findings.suggestion: Compute `start_camera` and `finish_camera` once when the level enters `level_state::ZOOM_OUT` (or in the constructor) and store them; the per-frame work then reduces to the single `calculate_intermediate_camera` lerp.
findings.verify_note: Read Level.cpp:40-50, 140-180 and Level.h:126-134.

findings.title: Band cases in calculate_object_collision_direction_by_edge resolve on the wrong axis
findings.detail:
Reaching line 176 requires `left_edge && right_edge && !top_edge && !bottom_edge` (I traced all five preceding branches: 152, 156, 161, 166, 171 — none fire in that state). That state means the collidee's AABB crosses both *vertical* edges of the collider but neither horizontal edge, i.e. a horizontal slab strictly inside the collider's y-range. It spans the collider completely in x, so no horizontal displacement can ever separate them — the only meaningful axis is vertical. The code returns `compare_point_collision_depth_horizontal(...)` → LEFT/RIGHT. Line 182 is the exact mirror (vertical slab, must resolve horizontally) and returns UP/DOWN.

Reachable when a platform is thinner than the player and the player has penetrated far enough that its bottom edge is below the platform's bottom — the thin-platform / fast-fall case. Player::on_structure_collision (Player.cpp:488ff) then dispatches on_left/on_right, zeroing velocity_x and shoving the player sideways instead of landing it.
findings.suggestion: Swap the two helper calls: `left_edge && right_edge` must use `compare_point_collision_depth_vertical`, `top_edge && bottom_edge` must use `compare_point_collision_depth_horizontal`. Add unit tests for both band cases — MattMathTests/CollisionToolsTests.cpp has none.
findings.verify_note: Read CollisionTools.cpp:136-207 and hand-traced the branch ladder for the slab configuration; confirmed no earlier branch catches l&&r&&!t&&!b. Confirmed the dispatch consumer at Player.cpp:488-526.

findings.title: Bisection push-out can silently fail to separate, and resolve_object_collision reports success unconditionally
findings.detail:
Three interlocking defects verified in the source:

1. Total reachable displacement is bounded. `move_object_by_direction_relative_to_size` (lines 12-30) offsets by `bounding_box_size * relative_amount` where `relative_amount = 1/1.5^i`, i = 1..40. Sum of (2/3)^i over i≥1 = 2, so the collider can never be pushed further than ~2x its own bounding box, and less in practice because the search alternates direction. Anything penetrating deeper than that stays welded inside the geometry, every frame.

2. Failure is undetectable. `bracket_object_collision`'s only `false` return is `else if (i == 1)` (line 42), which is dead: `resolve_object_collision` already verified `collider->intersects(collidee)` at line 235 and nothing has moved yet, so at i==1 `colliding` is always true. The loop never reports the shapes still overlapping after the last iteration.

3. Even that return value is discarded — line 251 calls `bracket_object_collision_generic(...)` as a statement, and line 260 does `return true;` regardless. Every Player call site ignores the bool anyway (Player.cpp:282-339, 548-573), so a stuck player is indistinguishable from a working one.
findings.suggestion: Derive the push distance from the actual penetration (MTV), not from the mover's own size. As an interim fix: propagate the bracket's result out of `resolve_object_collision`, and make the bracket return false when the shapes still intersect after the final iteration rather than only at i==1.
findings.verify_note: Read CollisionTools.cpp:12-69 and 231-261 in full; computed the geometric-series bound; confirmed line 251 discards the return and 260 is unconditional; confirmed the i==1 branch is unreachable given the guard at 235.

findings.title: Collision response is an iterative bisection that mutates geometry; there is no contact/manifold concept anywhere
findings.detail:
The entire narrow-phase resolution strategy is a numerical search. `bracket_object_collision_generic` runs BRACKET_ITERATIONS = 40 fixed iterations (CollisionTools.h:7); each iteration performs a full `Shape::intersects` (a switch + `dynamic_cast` double dispatch, MattMath.cpp:119-136, which for the triangle path allocates `std::vector<Segment> edges = triangle.get_edges()` at MattMath.cpp:339), a `pow(ITERATION_POWER, i)` call, and a virtual `get_bounding_box()`. It converges only approximately and never produces an exact contact.

Algorithm selection is a shape_type switch (lines 244-254) with the comment "one or both of the sprites are using pixel collision" — pixel collision does not exist anywhere in this codebase. RECTANGLE_ROTATED, which was added to shape_type and to Shape, silently falls into the 40-iteration branch and nobody had to notice.

Measuring penetration depth reuses the same machinery plus a heap allocation: `calculate_object_collision_depth` (270-281) clones the shape via the virtual `Shape::clone()` and runs the whole search on the clone just to read back `amount`. Player.cpp:576-638 calls that on every diagonal contact and then calls the resolver again, inside Level::update_level_logic's quadratic pair loops.

For a project whose stated goal is a reusable engine, the missing abstraction is the important part: there is no `Contact { normal, penetration, point }` anywhere.
findings.suggestion: Have the narrow phase return a contact manifold computed analytically (SAT/MTV for convex polygons, centre-distance for circles, closest-point for circle-vs-polygon — EricsonMath already has the closest-point building blocks). Resolution becomes `position += normal * penetration`: O(1), allocation-free, exact. BRACKET_ITERATIONS, ITERATION_POWER, both bracket functions, move_object_by_direction_relative_to_size and calculate_object_collision_depth all disappear.
findings.verify_note: Read the whole of CollisionTools.cpp, plus Shape::intersects (MattMath.cpp:119-136) and rectangle_triangle_intersect (MattMath.cpp:330-348) to confirm the per-iteration cost and the allocation. Confirmed shape_type::RECTANGLE_ROTATED exists in the dispatch but not in the resolver's switch.

findings.title: "Collision direction" is a centre-to-centre unit vector, not a surface normal, and callers snap it to eight compass points
findings.detail:
`shape_shape_collision_direction` is literally `Vector2F::unit_vector(collidee_center - collider_center)` (lines 109-123); `calculate_object_collision_direction` just gates it on `intersects`. Centre-to-centre is the correct contact normal only for two circles. A player standing on a wide platform gets a direction pointing at the platform's centre, potentially far off to one side, not straight down.

Every consumer compensates by quantising. Player::on_structure_ramp_collision does `direction = Vector2F::direction_to_8_cardinal_direction(direction)` (Player.cpp:250) and Player::on_structure_collision is an eight-way if/else ladder over DIRECTION_UP … DIRECTION_DOWN_RIGHT ending in `throw std::exception("Invalid collision direction.")` (Player.cpp:490-526). The real geometry is discarded and replaced by a compass rose, with "not a compass point" made a fatal error thrown from inside the per-frame update loop.

This is why ramps need dedicated enum tags and a bespoke handler instead of falling out of the normal.
findings.suggestion: Produce a real contact normal from the narrow phase. Game code then classifies with a dot product against its own up-vector and a tunable slope threshold. That removes direction_to_8_cardinal_direction, the eight-branch ladder, the eight on_*_collision methods, and makes arbitrary slopes work by construction.
findings.verify_note: Read CollisionTools.cpp:109-134 and Player.cpp:245-358 and 470-525; confirmed the quantisation call and the throwing else-branch.

findings.title: Collision identity is a cross-product of game class x team x weapon, welded into the engine's collision interface
findings.detail:
The enum's 23 enumerators multiply three orthogonal concepts: object kind, team, and weapon — PROJECTILE_SPRAY_TEAM_A/B, PROJECTILE_JET_TEAM_A/B, PROJECTILE_ROLLING_TEAM_A/B, PROJECTILE_BALL_TEAM_A/B, PROJECTILE_MIST_TEAM_A/B, PLAYER_TEAM_A/B, PLAYER_TEAM_A_DEAD/B_DEAD, PAINT_TILE, POWER_UP. This is returned by `ICollisionGameObject::get_collision_object_type()`, so the Splatoon team model and weapon roster live inside the engine's collision interface.

Cost is combinatorial and confirmed at the call sites: a third team or a sixth weapon means editing the enum, all seven predicates in this file, and every consuming ladder — Player::on_collision (Player.cpp:186-244), Player::on_projectile_collision (Player.cpp:645+), Level::count_projectiles (Level.cpp:658-682), PaintTile::on_collision, StructurePaintable::on_collision. None of that is engine work; all of it is forced by an engine-level type.

Given the stated goal (reusable engine, game as proof), this is the clearest instance of the anti-goal.
findings.suggestion: Engine side: a `CollisionFilter { uint32_t layer; uint32_t mask; }` on ICollisionGameObject plus an opaque game-defined type id. Broad phase rejects by `(a.layer & b.mask) && (b.layer & a.mask)`. Team and weapon become game data on the game's own object types, so "is this an enemy projectile" is one expression evaluated in game code with no engine enum to edit.
findings.verify_note: Read collision_object_type.h in full and the consuming ladders at Level.cpp:658-682 and Player.cpp:186-244, 245-358, 470-525.

findings.title: MTexture::is_visible_in_viewport calls itself — unconditional infinite recursion
findings.suggestion: `return this->_rectangle.intersects(view);` — the class already stores the rectangle, and Structure::is_visible_in_viewport (Structure.cpp:39-42) does exactly this. Add a unit test asserting an off-screen widget returns false.
findings.verify_note: Read Mh.cpp:162-165 and Mh.h:74-110; grepped every is_visible_in_viewport declaration/definition in the repo and confirmed no base implementation on the TextureObject side and no external caller of MContainer::is_visible_in_viewport.

findings.title: closest_pt_point_OBB loops over 3 axes of a 2D OBB — throws std::invalid_argument on every call
findings.suggestion: `i < 2`, or unroll it explicitly like closest_pt_point_AABB does and drop the throwing integer-indexed accessors in favour of the existing get_x_axis()/get_y_axis()/get_half_x_width()/get_half_y_width(). MattMathTests already compiles EricsonMath.cpp directly, so one assertion would have caught this.
findings.verify_note: Read EricsonMath.cpp:769-786, MattMath.cpp:4315-4352 (both throw sites), MattMath.h:1136 (typedef), and grepped the whole repo for callers — none.

findings.title: MContainer stores raw non-owning children with no ownership contract, and every menu declares containers before the widgets they point at
findings.detail:
`std::vector<std::pair<std::string, MObject*>> _children;` (Mh.h:54) with `add_child(MObject* child)` doing `_children.push_back(std::make_pair(child->get_name(), child))` (Mh.cpp:40-43) — no null check, no ownership, no delete. The API is equally consistent with `add_child(new MTexture(...))`, which would leak silently.

The real owners are unique_ptr members of the page classes, and the containers are declared *before* the widgets. EndMenu.h:64-72 verified: `_texture_container`, `_text_container`, then `_box`, `_heading`, `_change_teams`, … Reverse-order member destruction means the containers spend the tail of their lifetime holding pointers to already-destroyed widgets. Same inversion in MainMenu.h, ResultsMenu.h, PauseMenu.h. It does not crash today only because MContainer has no user destructor and nothing touches children during teardown — correctness rests on an undocumented ordering assumption.

The construction side has the mirror hazard: every widget member defaults to nullptr, so calling add_child before make_unique (EndMenu.cpp:214 vs EndMenu.cpp:137) is an immediate null dereference inside add_child.

Secondary defects in the same class: the name is stored twice (in MObject::_name and as the pair key) with no sync mechanism; `remove_child(name)` erases only the first match even though MObject's default name is the shared literal "error_name" (Mh.h:27); `get_children()` (Mh.cpp:74-77) returns the whole vector by value, deep-copying a std::string per child, and is not const.
findings.suggestion: Make the container own its children: `std::vector<std::unique_ptr<MObject>> _children;` with `MObject* add_child(std::unique_ptr<MObject>)` returning a borrowed pointer. That deletes ~16 unique_ptr members from MainMenu.h, makes destruction order well-defined, and gives remove_child an unambiguous meaning. Drop the duplicated name key and search on `child->get_name()`.
findings.verify_note: Read Mh.h:31-55 and Mh.cpp:40-77; read EndMenu.h:55-77 to confirm the container-before-widget declaration order and EndMenu.cpp:214-223 for the .get() call sites.

findings.title: Two incompatible public "collision direction" algorithms with no rule for choosing between them
findings.detail:
The public API exposes `calculate_object_collision_direction` (centre-to-centre, CollisionTools.cpp:125-134) and `calculate_object_collision_direction_by_edge` (AABB edge-overlap classification, CollisionTools.cpp:136-207). They return different answers for the same input, carry near-identical doc comments, and nothing states which is correct when. Player uses the edge version for generic structures (Player.cpp:488) and the centre version for ramps (Player.cpp:247) — the caller is expected to have internalised which heuristic fits which case.

`..._by_edge` takes `const Shape*` but immediately reduces both arguments to `get_bounding_box()` (lines 139-140), so the polymorphic parameter type is a lie; the doc comment even admits "This function is less accurate with non-rectangle shapes". Its body is a 72-line ladder of twelve hand-written boolean combinations plus two helpers plus a fallthrough.
findings.suggestion: One narrow-phase query returning a Contact. If an AABB-only fast path is genuinely wanted, express it in the type system (`contact(const RectangleF&, const RectangleF&)`) so it cannot be handed a triangle. An MTV subsumes ..._by_edge, calculate_containing_collision_direction and both compare_point_collision_depth_* helpers.
findings.verify_note: Read CollisionTools.h:24-41 and CollisionTools.cpp:125-207; confirmed the two Player call sites use different functions for different object categories.

findings.title: std::max over signed direction components inverts the push-out for the up-left quadrant only
findings.suggestion: `float larger = std::max(std::abs(d.x), std::abs(d.y));` with an epsilon guard rather than `!= 0.0f` (exact float comparison under /fp:fast). Better: replace the whole routine with an MTV that picks the axis of smaller overlap and displaces only on it, which makes both defects unrepresentable.
findings.verify_note: Read CollisionTools.cpp:209-229 and the direction constants at MattMath.cpp:1911-1916; hand-evaluated all four diagonals and all four cardinals; traced the only diagonal-passing call path through calculate_object_collision_depth (line 275, clone) to Player.cpp:576-638 (abs comparison).

findings.title: calculate_containing_collision_direction picks the axis opposite to the one its own comment describes
findings.suggestion: Invert the comparison to `>` (or swap the two returns), rename to x_delta/y_delta, and add a CollisionToolsTests case for the containment path — the existing tests only cover partial overlaps.
findings.verify_note: Read CollisionTools.cpp:71-107 and the two call sites at 154 and 206; confirmed the direction semantic ("points from collider toward collidee") from shape_shape_collision_direction at 109-123.

findings.title: calculate_object_collision_direction_by_edge never tests intersection, contradicting its documented contract
findings.detail:
CollisionTools.h:32-33 states "If the objects are not colliding, a zero vector is returned." The implementation never calls `intersects` and has no path returning `Vector2F::ZERO`: for two disjoint shapes all four edge flags are false, every branch falls through, and line 206 returns `calculate_containing_collision_direction(...)`, which always yields one of UP/DOWN/LEFT/RIGHT. A non-collision is reported as a confident direction.

The sibling `calculate_object_collision_direction` (125-134) *does* guard with `if (!collider->intersects(collidee)) return Vector2F::ZERO;`, so two functions documented identically behave differently.

Note the trap for whoever fixes this: Player::on_structure_collision's dispatcher ends with `throw std::exception("Invalid collision direction.")` (Player.cpp:523-526), so making the function honour its own docs would turn a silent phantom resolution into an uncaught exception from the update loop. Both sides need fixing together.

Also: the comment at line 152, "collidee is equal size of collider", is wrong — all four collider edges intersecting means the collidee *contains* the collider.
findings.suggestion: Add the intersection precondition, and simultaneously change Player's dispatcher to treat ZERO as "no collision, do nothing" rather than throwing. Throwing from a per-frame collision handler is not a recoverable design.
findings.verify_note: Read CollisionTools.cpp:136-207 line by line (no intersects call, no ZERO return) and Player.cpp:488-526 for the throwing else-branch.

findings.title: Vector2F::ZERO is overloaded as both "no collision" and a legal direction, and exactly-concentric shapes throw
findings.detail:
`shape_shape_collision_direction` returns ZERO when the two centres coincide (lines 117-120); `calculate_object_collision_direction` returns ZERO to mean "not colliding" (line 130). Callers cannot tell them apart.

Consequences verified in the source:
- `resolve_object_collision` (line 235) treats ZERO as no-collision, sets `amount = ZERO`, returns false — so two exactly concentric shapes (a maximally deep overlap) are never separated.
- Player::on_structure_ramp_collision has an explicit `else if (direction == Vector2F::ZERO) { throw std::exception("No collision direction."); }` (Player.cpp:346-349), so a projectile spawning exactly at a ramp's centre takes down the process.

The comparison is exact float equality under /fp:fast (confirmed FloatingPointModel=Fast in all four ArtAttack configurations), while `MattMath::are_equal(a, b, epsilon)` (MattMath.h:59) already exists and is not used here.
findings.suggestion: Signal failure out of band (bool return + out-param, or std::optional once the standard is bumped) instead of encoding it in the value. For the concentric case pick a deterministic fallback axis rather than reporting no collision.
findings.verify_note: Read CollisionTools.cpp:109-134 and 231-239; read Player.cpp:340-352 for the throw; confirmed /fp:fast in ArtAttack.vcxproj (four FloatingPointModel=Fast entries).

findings.title: calculate_object_collision_depth heap-clones a polymorphic shape and runs the full resolver to answer one comparison
findings.suggestion: Special-case RECTANGLE/RECTANGLE to `RectangleF::intersection` and skip the clone entirely — that covers the dominant player-vs-structure case. Long term, return depth from the narrow phase so direction, depth and resolution all come from one query per pair per frame.
findings.verify_note: Read CollisionTools.cpp:270-281 and 209-229; read Player.cpp:576-638 to confirm the four call sites and the double resolution; confirmed Shape::clone is pure virtual returning unique_ptr at MattMath.h:85.

findings.title: The same narrow-phase intersection test runs three times per colliding pair before any resolution, and each pair is processed twice per frame
findings.detail:
For one player-vs-object contact I traced four full `intersects` evaluations before the bracket even starts: Player::is_colliding (Player.cpp:148-185), then `calculate_object_collision_direction`'s guard (CollisionTools.cpp:128), then `resolve_object_collision`'s guard (line 235), then 40 more inside the bracket. Each is a virtual call plus a `dynamic_cast` (MattMath.cpp:119-136) plus, for triangle/quad/rotated-rect, a `std::vector` allocation (MattMath.cpp:339).

On top of that, Level::update_level_logic processes every player↔collision-object pair twice: once in the player loop (Level.cpp:222-241, calling both `player->on_collision` and `other_object->on_collision`) and again in the collision-object loop (Level.cpp:258-273, calling the same two in the other order). The collision-object↔collision-object loop (Level.cpp:275-293) likewise iterates both orderings with only an `object == object_2` self-guard, no i<j.

The redundancy is structural: each function is written to be independently safe, so none can trust its caller.
findings.suggestion: Produce a contact once in the broad/narrow phase and thread it through on_collision, and dedup pairs so each is resolved exactly once per frame.
findings.verify_note: Read CollisionTools.cpp:125-134 and 231-261, Player.cpp:140-200, and Level.cpp:180-300 in full to confirm both the repeated tests and the double pair traversal.

findings.title: CollisionTools is a namespace in class costume with global-scope tuning constants and an all-raw-pointer API
findings.detail:
Every member is static, the class has no state, and `CollisionTools() = default;` (line 13) exists only so `CollisionTools ct;` compiles — a Java-style utility class. EricsonMath, in the same module group, correctly uses `namespace EricsonMath { ... }`, so the module is internally inconsistent on the most basic structural choice.

`constexpr int BRACKET_ITERATIONS = 40;` and `constexpr float ITERATION_POWER = 1.5f;` (lines 7-8) sit at **global** namespace scope in a public header transitively included by Player and much of the game — names that generic, unqualified, are a collision hazard, and there is no way for a game or a test to tune them.

The API surface is all raw pointers: `resolve_object_collision(Shape* collider, const Shape* collidee, ...)` mutates `collider` in place via `offset()` yet is indistinguishable from a signature that takes ownership or accepts null. Nothing null-checks either argument. Nothing guards `collider == collidee` — passing the same shape twice would burn all 40 iterations translating an object away from itself and never separate; the only self-pair guard lives in the caller (Level.cpp:283), not in the library. Finally, all ~10 Player call sites discard the bool return.
findings.suggestion: `namespace collision_tools { ... }` with the constants inside it (or moved to an anonymous namespace in the .cpp, since only the .cpp uses them). Change parameters to `Shape&` / `const Shape&` so non-null and non-owning are in the type system and `assert(&collider != &collidee)` becomes possible. Mark the resolver `[[nodiscard]]` and collapse the twin overload.
findings.verify_note: Read CollisionTools.h in full and EricsonMath.h:11 for the namespace contrast; confirmed the self-pair guard is in Level.cpp:283 and that Player.cpp:282-339, 548-573 ignore the return.

findings.title: Two dead `collider_aabb` locals, one inside the 40-iteration loop
findings.detail:
`bracket_object_collision` (line 35) and `bracket_object_collision_generic` (line 58) both open with `RectangleF collider_aabb = collider->get_bounding_box();` and never read the variable. Line 35 is inside the function invoked once per bracket iteration, so it is 40 discarded virtual `get_bounding_box()` calls per resolution — and for RectangleRotated that call walks four stored points.

These are C4189 under /W4, which the project sets (WarningLevel=Level4 in all four configs) — but `TreatWarningAsError` appears in neither ArtAttack.vcxproj nor MattMathTests.vcxproj, so the warning has simply been ignored.
findings.suggestion: Delete both lines. Turn on TreatWarningAsError (or at least /we4189 /we4100 /we4018) so dead locals in hot loops surface at build time.
findings.verify_note: Read CollisionTools.cpp:32-69 confirming neither local is referenced again; grepped both vcxproj files for TreatWarningAsError (absent) and WarningLevel (Level4 x4 in ArtAttack).

findings.title: bracket_object_collision: leading bool parameter, magic i==1 sentinel, and per-iteration pow()
findings.detail:
`bool bracket_object_collision(bool colliding, int i, Shape* collider, const Vector2F& collider_direction)` — the sole caller computes the flag inline (line 62), so the call reads `bracket_object_collision(collider->intersects(collidee), i, collider, dir)` with no indication of what the leading boolean means. The returned bool means "keep going", not "collided": two booleans with opposite senses in one 20-line function. `else if (i == 1)` encodes "first iteration" as a magic loop index (and is unreachable — see the bracket-failure finding).

Lines 40 and 50 call unqualified `pow(ITERATION_POWER, static_cast<float>(i))` — relying on `<math.h>` dumping `::pow` into the global namespace via pch.h rather than `std::pow` — once per iteration, where a running multiply by 1/1.5f would do. (Correcting one reviewer: it is 40 pow calls per resolution, not 80 — only one branch executes per iteration.)
findings.suggestion: Fold the step function into the loop: hoist the first-iteration early-out above it, then `float step = 1.0f; for (...) { step /= ITERATION_POWER; ... }` — no bool parameter, no i==1 sentinel, no pow.
findings.verify_note: Read CollisionTools.cpp:32-69; confirmed only one of the two pow branches runs per iteration.

findings.title: Three unguarded divisions produce NaN for degenerate geometry, and the downstream clamps and comparisons silently swallow it
findings.detail:
