1. `barycentric` (729-743): `float denom = d00 * d11 - d01 * d01; v = (...)/denom; w = (...)/denom;` — zero for any collinear or zero-area triangle. `test_point_triangle` (746-752) then evaluates `v >= 0.0f && w >= 0.0f && (v + w) <= 1.0f` on NaNs, every comparison is false, and a degenerate triangle silently claims every point is outside it. This is live: MattMath.cpp:449 `triangle_point_intersect` forwards straight to `test_point_triangle`.

2. `closest_pt_point_segment` (756-767): `t = dot(c - a, ab) / dot(ab, ab);` — a zero-length segment gives 0/0 = NaN, and the clamps `if (t < 0.0f)` / `if (t > 1.0f)` are both false for NaN, so `d` becomes (NaN, NaN). Live via MattMath.cpp:333-340 `circle_segment_intersect`, whose `distance(...) <= radius` is then false — a degenerate segment silently reports no intersection.

3. `closest_pt_point_triangle` (line 348): `float denom = 1.0f / (va + vb + vc);` — same degeneracy, no guard.

Triangles and segments come from level JSON via LevelObjectBuilder with no non-degeneracy validation, so this is reachable by editing a level file, and the failure mode is a silent hole in the world rather than a diagnostic. /fp:fast is set in all four configs, which licenses the compiler to assume no NaNs, so the "silently false" behaviour is not even reliably reproducible across optimisation levels.
findings.suggestion: Guard each denominator against a near-zero magnitude and return a defined fallback (degenerate triangle → not contained; zero-length segment → t = 0, d = a). Better, validate geometry at load time in LevelObjectBuilder using the `signed_2D_tri_area` already implemented at line 688, and reject with a message naming the level file and object.
findings.verify_note: Read EricsonMath.cpp:308-352, 729-767; confirmed the live call paths at MattMath.cpp:336 (closest_pt_point_segment) and MattMath.cpp:449 (test_point_triangle); confirmed /fp:fast in the vcxproj.

findings.title: intersect_moving_AABB_AABB reports a hit when the relative velocity is zero on a separating axis
findings.detail:
The per-axis blocks are gated on `if (v.x < 0.0f)` / `if (v.x > 0.0f)` (lines 572, 586) and the y equivalents (606, 620). When a component of `v = vb - va` is exactly zero, **no separation test runs on that axis at all**. With `tfirst = 0.0f` and `tlast = 1.0f` untouched (547-548), the `tfirst > tlast` checks never fire and the function returns 1.

Concrete: `a` at x∈[0,10], `b` at x∈[100,110], overlapping in y, `va == vb` so `v = (0,0)`. The early `test_AABB_AABB` at line 540 correctly says they do not overlap; both axis blocks are skipped; the function returns 1, claiming contact over [0,1]. Two boxes moving in lockstep 90 units apart are reported as colliding.

This is a faithful transcription of a known erratum in the 3D original, preserved by the hand-unrolling. It is also the engine's only swept-collision routine and has zero callers anywhere (verified by grep, including MattMathTests) — so fast projectiles tunnel with nothing to catch them, and the one routine that would fix that is both unused and wrong.
findings.suggestion: Add the zero-velocity case per axis: with no relative motion, any existing separation on that axis is permanent, so `else { if (b_max.x < a_min.x || b_min.x > a_max.x) return false; }`. Then either wire the function into projectile integration or delete it so it stops looking like available functionality.
findings.verify_note: Read EricsonMath.cpp:535-640 in full and confirmed no else-branch for v == 0 on either axis; grepped the repo for callers — none outside EricsonMath.{h,cpp}.

findings.title: Circular dependency between the geometry-types module and the intersection-algorithm module
findings.detail:
EricsonMath.h includes MattMath.h (line 8) because every signature takes MattMath types; MattMath.cpp includes EricsonMath.h and implements much of its intersection surface by forwarding down to it — verified at MattMath.cpp:179 (test_AABB_AABB), 185/190 (test_circle_AABB), 249 (test_segment_AABB), 308/315 (test_circle_triangle), 336 (closest_pt_point_segment), 449 (test_point_triangle), 572 (test_2D_segment_segment).

Neither module can be extracted or reused without the other — a direct blocker on the reusable-engine goal. It is compounded by MattMath.cpp being a single ~4500-line translation unit holding the value types, the `Shape` polymorphic dispatch (with its dynamic_cast switch at 119-136), and the free-function intersection table.
findings.suggestion: Three strictly-upward layers: math/types (Vector2F, RectangleF, Circle, Triangle, Quad, Segment, RectangleRotated — no knowledge of intersection), math/intersect (free functions over those types; the EricsonMath content, renamed for what it does), collision/ (Shape polymorphism, contacts, solver). Only then can the math be lifted out of this project.
findings.verify_note: Read EricsonMath.h:1-10 and grepped MattMath.cpp for `EricsonMath::` — nine forwarding call sites confirmed at the lines listed.

findings.title: Two EPSILON constants 100x apart and a duplicated dead clamp, both visible in the same translation units
findings.detail:
`EricsonMath::EPSILON = 0.000001f` (EricsonMath.h:75) coexists with `MattMath::EPSILON = 0.0001f` (MattMath.h:46), and EricsonMath.h includes MattMath.h. EricsonMath.cpp has file-scope `using namespace MattMath;` and `using namespace EricsonMath;`. The unqualified `EPSILON` at EricsonMath.cpp:665-666 resolves to the 1e-6 value today only because functions defined with a qualified-id search their own namespace first; move that code into a `namespace EricsonMath { }` block and it silently binds the 100x-larger value with no diagnostic. `MattMath::are_equal(a, b, epsilon = EPSILON)` bakes the loose value in as a default, so the two tolerances are already applied inconsistently across the collision code.

EricsonMath::EPSILON is used at exactly one site (test_segment_AABB); every other predicate in the file is exact float comparison under /fp:fast — e.g. `test_2D_segment_segment` uses strict `a1 * a2 < 0.0f` / `a3 * a4 < 0.0f` (705, 712), so segments that touch exactly at an endpoint or are collinear report no intersection.

`EricsonMath::clamp` (EricsonMath.h:88, cpp:354-365) duplicates `MattMath::clamp` (MattMath.h:51) and is dead: grep finds no callers anywhere including the tests, while `closest_pt_point_AABB` (428-448) and `closest_pt_point_OBB` (781-782) each hand-inline the same three lines instead.

REJECTED sub-claim: one reviewer stated MattMathTests/MathTests.cpp would be a hard ambiguity error because it does `using namespace MattMath; using namespace EricsonMath;`. It defines its own EPSILON_F constants (MathTests.cpp:14-16) and never names EPSILON or clamp unqualified, so nothing is ambiguous today.
findings.suggestion: Delete EricsonMath::clamp and EricsonMath::EPSILON. Keep one tolerance, expressed per-operation and named for its purpose and its world-space units. Route the sign tests in test_2D_segment_segment through it rather than comparing to exact zero.
findings.verify_note: Read EricsonMath.h:75-88, MattMath.h:44-60, EricsonMath.cpp:354-365 and 655-725; grepped for clamp callers (none) and read MathTests.cpp:1-20 to check the claimed ambiguity.

findings.title: MattMath::AABB is a typedef for RectangleF, so every AABB entry point re-derives min/max and the type name lies
findings.detail:
`typedef MattMath::RectangleF AABB;` (MattMath.h:301). RectangleF is position+size; every Ericson routine wants min/max corners, so five functions each open with the same two lines — test_AABB_AABB (286-289), sq_dist_point_AABB (394-395), closest_pt_point_AABB (426-427), intersect_moving_AABB_AABB (567-570), test_segment_AABB (647-648).

Worse, the two names are freely interchangeable with no compiler distinction, and the header uses both for the same type in adjacent declarations: `test_AABB_AABB` takes `const RectangleF&` (EricsonMath.h:77-78) while `intersect_moving_AABB_AABB` (113-114) and `test_segment_AABB` (119-120) take `const AABB&`.
findings.suggestion: Make `struct AABB { Point2F min, max; }` a real type in the types layer with explicit conversions to/from RectangleF. The intersection layer then takes AABB and does no conversion; the rendering/layout layer keeps RectangleF; the conversion happens once at the boundary.
findings.verify_note: Read MattMath.h:301 and the five listed EricsonMath.cpp functions; confirmed the mixed spelling across EricsonMath.h:77-120.

findings.title: Half the EricsonMath API returns results through out-parameters, several unwritten on the failure path
findings.detail:
Seven of fifteen public functions use non-const reference out-params: test_circle_AABB(…, Point2F& p), closest_pt_point_AABB(…, Point2F& q), test_circle_triangle(…, Point2F& p), intersect_moving_AABB_AABB(…, float& tfirst, float& tlast), test_2D_segment_segment(…, float& t, Point2F& p), barycentric(…, float& u, float& v, float& w), closest_pt_point_segment(…, float& t, Point2F& d).

The file is inconsistent with itself: closest_pt_point_triangle (83-86) returns Point2F by value while closest_pt_point_AABB (99-100) writes into `q`. Point2F is two floats, so there is no efficiency argument.

Worse, the bool+out-param ones do not write on failure. test_2D_segment_segment's comment promises "compute and return intersection t value along ab and intersection position p", but the `return 0` at line 724 leaves both untouched. MattMath.cpp:576-581 already relies on that: `float t; Point2F p; return segments_intersect(a, b, t, p);` — `t` is uninitialised and survives only because the result is discarded. Any future caller of the four-arg form that reads `t` after a false return reads garbage.
findings.suggestion: Return values: `Point2F closest_pt_point_AABB(...)`, `struct Barycentric { float u, v, w; }`, `struct SegmentHit { float t; Point2F point; }` returned as std::optional. At minimum, write the out-params on all paths so a stale read is impossible.
findings.verify_note: Read EricsonMath.h:77-142 and EricsonMath.cpp:697-725; read MattMath.cpp:576-581 to confirm the uninitialised local (never read, so no live UB).

findings.title: Roughly 40% of the EricsonMath module is commented-out dead code, including a competing type system
findings.detail:
EricsonMath.h lines 13-74 are a commented-out parallel math library — `struct Vector`, `typedef Vector Point`, `struct AABB`, `struct Sphere`, `struct OBB`, plus eleven commented declarations. EricsonMath.cpp lines 1-281 are one contiguous commented block, with further blocks at 451-479 (a duplicate sq_dist_point_AABB), 494-530 (test_triangle_AABB, which contains literal `...` and could never have compiled) and 551-565 (the 3-axis loop that lines 572-638 replace by hand). The trailing `// 132` at line 788 is a page number from the book.

This is not just untidiness: a reader opening the intersection module sees two definitions of AABB (a commented struct here, a live typedef in MattMath.h:301) and two Vector types, and has to work out which is real. The commented 3-axis loop at 551-565 is also the template that produced the still-live `i < 3` bug in closest_pt_point_OBB.

On top of that, four declared functions have zero callers anywhere including MattMathTests: test_circle_circle (which uses the correct squared-distance form, while the live MattMath::circles_intersect uses a sqrt), intersect_moving_AABB_AABB, clamp, closest_pt_point_OBB.
findings.suggestion: Delete the commented blocks — git is the archive. Delete the four unreferenced functions, or fix and test them. If intersect_moving_AABB_AABB is kept, note its x and y blocks (572-604, 606-638) are the same 30 lines with .x/.y swapped.
findings.verify_note: Read EricsonMath.h and EricsonMath.cpp in full; grepped the repo (ArtAttack + MattMathTests) for the four function names — no callers.

findings.title: bool-returning functions return integer literals 0 and 1 throughout
findings.detail: The signatures were modernised to `bool` but the bodies kept the book's C-style int returns — e.g. test_AABB_AABB ends `if (...) return 0; if (...) return 0; return 1;` (292-295). Every site listed above does the same. This survives /W4 silently and reads as if the functions still return counts. Line 541 compounds it: `tfirst = tlast = 0.0f; return 1;` — chained assignment plus int return in one statement.
findings.suggestion: Mechanical replace with `false`/`true` across the file.
findings.verify_note: Read all the listed lines in EricsonMath.cpp.

findings.title: test_segment_AABB takes p1 by value while p0 is by const reference
findings.detail:
```cpp
bool test_segment_AABB(const MattMath::Point2F& p0,
	const MattMath::Point2F p1, const MattMath::AABB& b);
```
Matched by the definition at EricsonMath.cpp:644-645. It is the only by-value parameter in the entire header, so it is plainly a dropped `&` rather than a decision. The top-level `const` on a by-value parameter is also meaningless in the declaration. The one live caller, MattMath.cpp:249, passes `segment.point_1` — a member, so the copy is pure waste.
findings.suggestion: `const MattMath::Point2F& p1` in both the header and the .cpp.
findings.verify_note: Read EricsonMath.h:119-120, EricsonMath.cpp:644-645, MattMath.cpp:249.

findings.title: Pure math free functions lack [[nodiscard]], and the header includes <cmath> it does not need
findings.detail:
Every function in the header is a pure value computation over trivially-copyable structs, yet none is [[nodiscard]] — discarding the result of `test_AABB_AABB` is always a bug and should not compile. Nothing prevents adding it today.

Header hygiene: line 9 `#include <cmath>` — no declaration in the header needs it; the std::abs/std::max/std::min uses are all in the .cpp (579, 583, 656-659), which currently relies on pch.h for them. That dependency is fragile because MattMathTests compiles EricsonMath.cpp directly against its own pch.h. The header also pulls in all of MattMath.h when forward declarations would suffice for a file that only declares functions.

constexpr/noexcept are blocked today by Vector2F's non-constexpr operators (MattMath.h:500-506) and are a follow-up, not an immediate change.
findings.suggestion: Add [[nodiscard]] to the fourteen non-void functions. Move <cmath> into the .cpp and add the direct includes it needs. Revisit constexpr once MattMath's operators are.
findings.verify_note: Read EricsonMath.h in full and confirmed no declaration requires <cmath>; checked MattMathTests/MathTests.cpp:5-6 compiles EricsonMath.cpp directly.

findings.title: partition() divides by num_partitions with no validation — zero is a hardware fault, negative silently returns nothing
findings.detail:
```cpp
int elements_per_partition = num_elements / num_partitions;
int remainder = num_elements % num_partitions;
```
Neither argument is checked. `num_partitions == 0` is integer division by zero — undefined behaviour, a fault on x86. `num_partitions < 0` gives a negative quotient, the loop condition `i < num_partitions && i < num_elements` is false immediately, and an **empty** vector is returned; the callers then dispatch zero draw tasks and render nothing, with no diagnostic. This is a public utility in a library that is supposed to be reusable, with no stated precondition anywhere.

REJECTED sub-claim, repeated by four reviewers: that this path is live because `ThreadPool::_max_num_threads` is default-initialised to -1 (ThreadPool.h:26). ThreadPool has no default constructor — the only declared one is `ThreadPool(int min, int max)` (ThreadPool.h:12) — and the sole construction site passes NUM_THREADS_MAX (Game.cpp:236). The -1 member initialiser is never observable. The missing validation is real; the claimed live trigger is not.

The partition arithmetic itself is correct: I checked remainder distribution and the `i < num_elements` guard for 0, 5/3, 17/16 and n < partitions.
findings.suggestion: `if (num_partitions <= 0) throw std::invalid_argument(...)` (or clamp to 1) and `if (num_elements <= 0) return {};` at the top. Also give ThreadPool's members a sane default rather than -1, and make them const.
findings.verify_note: Read Partitioner.cpp in full, ThreadPool.h in full (no default ctor), and grepped for ThreadPool construction — Game.cpp:236 only, passing NUM_THREADS_MIN/MAX.

findings.title: The int/size_t partition overload pair narrows silently and is ambiguous for every other integer type
findings.detail:
```cpp
std::vector<std::pair<int, int>> partition(int num_elements, int num_partitions) const;
std::vector<std::pair<int, int>> partition(size_t num_elements, int num_partitions) const;
```
The size_t overload's entire body is `return partition(static_cast<int>(num_elements), num_partitions);` (Partitioner.cpp:26) — an unchecked narrowing cast, so a container larger than INT_MAX yields a negative count and the silent-empty behaviour above. The overload exists only so call sites can pass `.size()` without a warning; it suppresses the warning rather than fixing the type.

The pair also only disambiguates for exactly `int` and exactly `size_t`. Any other integer type (unsigned int, long, uint32_t on this toolchain) needs an integral conversion to reach either candidate, both at the same rank, so the call is ambiguous and fails to compile — a trap for the next caller.

Returning signed pairs then forces signed/unsigned comparisons at both call sites: `for (int i = 0; i < partitioned_players.size(); i++)` (Level.cpp:386) and `for (int i = 0; i < partitioned_mobjects.size(); i++)` (MenuPage.cpp:140), both C4018 under /W4 — advisory only, since TreatWarningAsError is set nowhere.
findings.suggestion: One function taking and returning size_t, and a named result type: `struct IndexRange { size_t begin; size_t end; };` — `.first`/`.second` at Level.cpp:391-392 and MenuPage.cpp:146 tell the reader nothing. Delete the int overload; mark it [[nodiscard]].
findings.verify_note: Read Partitioner.h and Partitioner.cpp in full; read Level.cpp:379-399 and MenuPage.cpp:125-150 for the loop types.

findings.title: A stateless one-function class is heap-allocated and threaded through four layers as a non-owning pointer
findings.detail:
`class Partitioner` has zero data members; both methods are const and pure. Despite that it is heap-allocated once (Game.cpp:255 `std::make_unique<Partitioner>()`), stored as `std::unique_ptr<Partitioner>` (Game.h:75), published into the service locator (GameData.h:43-44, 61; GameData.cpp:148-156), threaded through LevelBuilder's constructor and member (LevelBuilder.h:24, 38; LevelBuilder.cpp:14, 21, 82), into Level's constructor and member (Level.h:80, 147; Level.cpp:30, 52), fetched ad hoc by MenuPage (MenuPage.cpp:130), and passed again at GameStates.cpp:120. GameData.h includes Partitioner.h, so effectively every TU sees it.

Four non-owning `const Partitioner*` aliases exist whose validity rests on the undocumented assumption that Game::_partitioner outlives every Level and MenuPage; none is documented as non-owning and none is null-checked before use (Level.cpp:383, MenuPage.cpp:135). The payoff for that surface is nothing, because there is no state to share.

For the engine-reuse goal specifically: a partitioning utility should not require an object graph to call.
findings.suggestion: Delete the class. Free functions in a namespace. That removes a member from GameData, a constructor parameter and member from LevelBuilder and Level, and an include from three headers.
findings.verify_note: Grepped every Partitioner/_partitioner reference in the repo and read Partitioner.h; all the plumbing sites listed are from that grep output.

findings.title: Partitioner + ThreadPool + index ranges is a hand-rolled parallel_for duplicated at both call sites
findings.detail:
Both users perform the identical six-step ritual. Level::draw_active_level (Level.cpp:378-399): read num_threads, partition(size, num_threads), loop over result, add_task capturing the index, wait_for_tasks_to_complete. MenuPage::draw_mobjects_in_viewports (MenuPage.cpp:125-150): the same code with a different body function. Both then rely on the partition index implicitly lining up with a deferred-context index and a SpriteBatch index in parallel vectors — a correspondence expressed nowhere in a type.

The two sites also disagree about capture semantics: Level captures `partitioned_players` **by value** into every lambda (Level.cpp:388, a vector copy per task per frame), MenuPage captures `partitioned_mobjects` and `command_lists` **by reference** (MenuPage.cpp:142-143). Both are correct only because of the join four lines later, which is documented nowhere. One site pays for safety it does not need; the other relies on an invariant it does not state.

A further note on the MenuPage site: `command_lists` holds raw owning COM pointers released by hand at MenuPage.cpp:162, and draw_mobject_in_viewports throws (`throw std::exception("Failed to finish command list")`, MenuPage.cpp:120), so an exception between creation and release leaks every command list. ComPtr is already used elsewhere in the codebase.
findings.suggestion: Put `parallel_for(size_t count, fn(begin, end, worker))` on ThreadPool. It owns the split, the dispatch and the join, and passing `worker` explicitly stops the deferred-context/SpriteBatch lookup being an implicit index correspondence. Both call sites collapse to one line and Partitioner disappears. Use ComPtr for the command lists.
findings.verify_note: Read Level.cpp:374-399 and MenuPage.cpp:110-163 side by side; confirmed the differing captures and the shared wait_for_tasks_to_complete.

findings.title: The class named "Partitioner" does no spatial partitioning, and the engine has no broad phase at all
findings.detail:
In a 2D engine, "partitioner" names a spatial index. This class splits [0, n) into contiguous index ranges for thread scheduling. Meanwhile the thing the name promises does not exist anywhere: Level::update_level_logic (Level.cpp:180-293) is three nested loops — players x collision_objects, collision_objects x players, collision_objects x collision_objects — with no acceleration structure and no ordering. Every pair is narrow-phase tested, and because the first two loops cover the same pairs in both orderings, each player/object pair is tested and dispatched to `on_collision` **twice per frame**; the object/object loop likewise runs both orderings with only an `object == object_2` self-guard.

Each of those tests is the virtual + dynamic_cast + (for non-rect shapes) allocating path, and each resolved contact then triggers the 40-iteration bracket. With a paint-heavy level dominated by projectiles, the quadratic term caps projectile count long before rendering does. Note also that ThreadPool/Partitioner are used only to parallelise *drawing* (Level.cpp:374-399); the genuinely quadratic part of the frame is single-threaded.
findings.suggestion: Rename the current class to what it is (RangeSplitter / IndexRange) and build the abstraction the name was reserving: a uniform grid broad phase producing a deduplicated candidate pair list, queried per object. Level bounds are already known (Level::is_object_out_of_bounds), so a grid is the cheapest correct fit.
findings.verify_note: Read Partitioner.h/.cpp and Level.cpp:180-300 in full; confirmed the double traversal of player/object pairs and the absence of any i<j or spatial guard.

findings.title: partition() returns fewer partitions than requested, without reserve, and the result is copied per task
findings.detail:
The loop guard is `i < num_partitions && i < num_elements`, so the result size is min(num_partitions, num_elements) — the function silently does not honour its own parameter, and nothing in the header says so. Both call sites happen to iterate `result.size()` and survive, but any caller that indexes a per-thread resource array by num_threads would be wrong.

The final size is known exactly up front yet there is no `reserve`, so this reallocates two or three times per call, once per draw pass per frame. `push_back(std::make_pair(start, end))` constructs a temporary where `emplace_back(start, end)` would construct in place. Level then captures the whole returned vector by value into each of N lambdas (Level.cpp:388), so with N partitions that is N more copies per frame of data that is constant for the frame.
findings.suggestion: `reserve(min(num_partitions, num_elements))` and `emplace_back`. Document (and assert) the shortfall behaviour, or pad with empty ranges so the result size always equals the requested count and the worker-index correspondence holds. Capture only `partitioned[i]` in each lambda, not the whole vector.
findings.verify_note: Read Partitioner.cpp:4-22 and Level.cpp:385-397 for the by-value capture.

findings.title: Seven global predicates form a hand-maintained taxonomy the compiler cannot check; five are dead and one is duplicated verbatim elsewhere
findings.detail:
is_player, is_dead_player, is_projectile, is_team_a_projectile, is_team_b_projectile, is_structure, is_structure_ramp are inline free functions at **global** scope, each a hand-written `||` chain. is_projectile lists ten enumerators; is_team_a_projectile and is_team_b_projectile are the same five-element list with the suffix swapped. There is no COUNT sentinel, no static_assert, and no exhaustive switch, so adding an enumerator compiles cleanly while silently dropping out of every predicate — a new projectile type would pass through paint tiles and never be counted.

A repo-wide grep confirms **five of the seven have zero call sites**: only is_structure (Level.cpp:238, Player.cpp:146) and is_structure_ramp (Player.cpp:197) are used. Meanwhile Level::count_projectiles (Level.cpp:665-675) contains a verbatim ten-term reimplementation of is_projectile, with the local variable named identically to the free function it duplicates. So the logic exists in at least two places and the reusable copy is the dead one.

is_player deliberately excludes PLAYER_TEAM_A_DEAD/B_DEAD — a false-negative waiting to happen for any caller that reads the name as "is this a player", with the distinction invisible at the call site. The enum also carries two undocumented null values, DEFAULT and NONE (lines 27-28), with no stated difference.
findings.suggestion: Replace Level.cpp:665-675 with `if (is_projectile(type)) count++;`. Put the predicates in a namespace, mark them [[nodiscard]] constexpr, and derive them from a single table with a static_assert on its size so adding an enumerator has exactly one edit site. Rename is_player to is_live_player. Longer term these vanish once kind and team are separate data.
findings.verify_note: Read collision_object_type.h in full; grepped every predicate name across ArtAttack — only is_structure and is_structure_ramp have callers; read Level.cpp:658-682 for the duplicate.

findings.title: Ramp orientation encoded as a collision category, duplicating what the shape already knows, and half of it is an empty TODO
findings.detail:
STRUCTURE_RAMP_LEFT and STRUCTURE_RAMP_RIGHT encode which way a slope faces as a collision *category*, information the triangle geometry already carries. The duplication then drives control flow: Player::on_structure_ramp_collision (Player.cpp:245-358) branches on the enum to decide which face is a solid wall (the `side_wall_collision` expression at Player.cpp:258-261) — a decision the triangle's edge normals answer directly.

Worse, I confirmed the STRUCTURE_RAMP_LEFT branch is an empty `// TODO` (Player.cpp:273-276) while the RIGHT branch is fully implemented, and the `else` falls through to `throw std::exception("Invalid ramp type.")`. So half the feature does not exist while its enum tag is fully wired through the engine's collision interface, and a left ramp silently does nothing after the enum dispatch.
findings.suggestion: Delete both enumerators and derive slope handling from the contact normal — a surface whose dot with up falls in the walkable band is a ramp regardless of facing, and arbitrary slopes then work for free. If distinct *material* behaviour is needed (jump-through, ice), that is a surface property on the collider, not a collision category.
findings.verify_note: Read collision_object_type.h:9-10 and Player.cpp:245-358; confirmed the empty TODO branch for STRUCTURE_RAMP_LEFT and the fully-written RIGHT branch.

findings.title: MText and MTextDropShadow disable viewport culling with a hardcoded return true
findings.suggestion: Text already knows its font and string; use SpriteFont::MeasureString, cache the extents on set_text/set_scale (they only change then, so it is not a per-frame cost), and test that rectangle. Implement it once on a shared base rather than twice.

findings.title: Text scaling uses scale.x only while position uses both axes, so text drifts out of its layout on non-uniform resolution changes
findings.detail:
```cpp
void MText::scale_size_and_position(const Vector2F& scale)
{
	this->set_position(this->get_position() * scale);   // both axes
	this->set_scale(this->get_scale() * scale.x);       // x only
}
```
Same asymmetry in MTextDropShadow::scale_size_and_position (317-320), where _shadow_offset scales by both axes but _shadow_scale by scale.x alone, while MTexture::scale_size_and_position (180-183) scales its rectangle by both components. A change from 1920x1080 to 1280x1024 gives scale = (0.667, 0.948): textures shrink ~5% more in x than y, glyphs shrink 33% while their y positions shrink only 5%, and drop shadows detach from their glyphs.

Because each call *multiplies* into the existing scale, the error compounds across successive resolution changes and the authored design coordinates are destroyed — the layout cannot round-trip. This runs from 26 call sites across MainMenu/EndMenu/PauseMenu/ResultsMenu.
findings.suggestion: Author UI once in a fixed virtual resolution and never mutate widget geometry; apply the resolution mapping at draw time as a single scale+letterbox transform folded into the Camera. scale_size_and_position and scale_objects_to_new_resolution both disappear, resolution changes become lossless, and non-uniform aspect gets one explicit policy instead of two accidental ones.
findings.verify_note: Read Mh.cpp:78-84, 180-183, 252-256, 315-321; grepped scale_objects_to_new_resolution — 26 call sites across the four menu files.

findings.title: scale_objects_to_new_resolution divides by the previous resolution with no zero guard
findings.suggestion: `if (prev_resolution.x <= 0.0f || prev_resolution.y <= 0.0f) return;` at the top. Better, store the design resolution and always scale from that base rather than compounding relative factors.
findings.verify_note: Read Mh.cpp:78-84 and the three scale_size_and_position implementations it drives; did not verify reachability of a zero prev_resolution.

findings.title: Most of MContainer's API is dead, and get_children returns a deep copy of a vector the caller cannot safely hold
findings.suggestion: Delete the unused methods. If they return, define them against an owning `vector<unique_ptr<MObject>>`, drop the duplicated name key, and return `const vector<...>&`.
findings.verify_note: Grepped remove_child / remove_all_children / get_children / get_child_count across ArtAttack — no hits outside Mh.cpp/Mh.h; read Mh.cpp:44-77.

findings.title: The UI widget hierarchy inherits the game-object interface, which hardcodes DirectX::SpriteBatch at its root
findings.detail:
`class MObject : public IGameObject` (Mh.h:8). IGameObject (read in full) is the simulation-object interface: `update()`, two `draw()` overloads typed on `DirectX::SpriteBatch*` and `MattMath::Camera`, and `is_visible_in_viewport()`. So menu buttons are game objects.

The interface-segregation violation is visible in the implementations: three of the four concrete widgets have a no-op update() — MTexture (Mh.cpp:158-161 `return;`), MText (274-277 `// do nothing`), MTextDropShadow (339-342 `return;`). Only MContainer::update does anything, and all it does is forward.

The deeper problem for the stated goal is that IGameObject bakes a specific D3D11 helper class into the root of both the UI and the simulation hierarchies. There is no rendering abstraction to swap, so nothing below IGameObject is portable. The same leak shows up higher: MenuPage's public API traffics in `std::vector<std::pair<MObject*, ID3D11SamplerState*>>` (MenuPage.cpp:124-125), putting a raw D3D sampler in the UI-tree interface, and z-order is expressed as the arrangement of two container members (_texture_container before _text_container) replicated across eight menu classes rather than as data — while MTexture already inherits an unused layer_depth.
findings.suggestion: Separate the interfaces: a UI node needs layout/draw/hit_test, a simulation object needs update/draw. Whatever they share should be a narrow `Drawable { void draw(Renderer&) const; }` where Renderer is an engine-owned interface, not DirectX::SpriteBatch*. That single substitution is the prerequisite for the engine being reusable. Then put render state and a sort key on the node so ordering is authored data, not class layout.
findings.verify_note: Read IGameObject.h in full, Mh.h:8-29, the three no-op update() bodies in Mh.cpp, and MenuPage.cpp:100-150 for the sampler-in-the-API and per-pair Begin/End.

findings.title: Non-virtual MObject::draw(SpriteBatch*, Viewport) is hidden by the draw overrides in every derived class
findings.detail:
MObject declares `void draw(DirectX::SpriteBatch*, const MattMath::Viewport&);` non-virtually (Mh.h:15) alongside the two pure-virtual draw overloads (23-24). MContainer (50-51), MTexture (93-94), MText (132-133) and MTextDropShadow (161-162) each redeclare the virtual pair **without** `using MObject::draw;`, so ordinary name hiding removes the Viewport overload from their scope: `MTexture t; t.draw(sb, viewport);` does not compile. It works today only because the sole caller holds an `MObject*` (MenuPage.cpp:112).

Mixing a non-virtual convenience overload into a virtual overload set is a hazard that should not ship in a public base class. Related constness inconsistency in the same interface: is_visible_in_viewport is const but draw is not, even though every implementation only reads — MTexture::draw just forwards to TextureObject::draw.
findings.suggestion: Make the viewport adapter a free function rather than a member, which sidesteps hiding entirely; the render loop already knows its viewport and should build the Camera once outside the widget loop. Independently, make IGameObject::draw const.
findings.verify_note: Read Mh.h in full — confirmed no `using MObject::draw;` in any derived class — and Mh.cpp:18-21 for the adapter body.

findings.title: MWidget is a pure pass-through layer whose only content is one setter that all three leaves forward away
findings.detail:
MWidget re-declares the same four pure virtuals already pure on MObject — scale_size_and_position (64 vs 20), update (66 vs 22), both draw overloads (67-68 vs 23-24), is_visible_in_viewport (69 vs 25) — and adds exactly one thing: `virtual void set_colour(const MattMath::Colour&) = 0;`. Its only non-declaration content is a constructor forwarding to MObject (Mh.cpp:130-134).

And set_colour is not behaviour either: all three leaves implement it as a one-line forward to a base they already inherit — MTexture → SpriteSheetObject::set_colour (Mh.cpp:176-179), MText → Text::set_colour (283-286), MTextDropShadow → TextDropShadow::set_colour (348-351). Four levels (IGameObject → MObject → MWidget → leaf) all declaring the same four signatures so that one setter can be re-exported under a different name.

The repeated `override = 0` re-declarations at MObject (22-25) and MWidget (64-69) are pure noise — inheriting a pure virtual already keeps a class abstract — and restating draw in MObject is what starts the name-hiding chain above. `~MWidget() override = default;` (62) is the only user-declared destructor among the five classes; it suppresses MWidget's implicit move operations while its siblings keep theirs, and buys nothing since IGameObject already has a virtual destructor.
findings.suggestion: Delete MWidget and derive the leaves from MObject directly. Delete the redundant `override = 0` lines and `~MWidget() override = default;`.
findings.verify_note: Read Mh.h:8-72 and the three set_colour forwarders in Mh.cpp.

findings.title: Defaulted default constructors exist solely to build widgets in an invalid state
findings.detail:
`MObject() = default;` (11), `MContainer() = default;` (34), `MWidget() = default;` (60), `MTexture() = default;` (77), `MText() = default;` (115), `MTextDropShadow() = default;` (141). A default-constructed MTexture inherits `DrawObject::_resource_manager = nullptr` and `MObject::_name = "error_name"` — the name literal is itself an admission that the state is invalid, and a widget with no ResourceManager cannot draw anything.

No call site in the codebase default-constructs any of these (every use passes the full constructor: MainMenu.cpp:1322/1368, EndMenu.cpp:137, ResultsMenu.cpp:77, PauseMenu.cpp:120, …), so these constructors exist purely to make a broken object reachable.

Relatedly, none of MObject/MWidget/MContainer declares or deletes its copy operations despite being polymorphic bases. Copying an MContainer duplicates _children, giving two containers holding the same raw non-owning pointers; assigning through an `MWidget&` slices — and MTexture inherits two independent polymorphic hierarchies, so a slice through either leaves the other half stale.
findings.suggestion: Remove the `= default` default constructors (a user-declared constructor already suppresses the implicit one). Delete the copy operations on MObject — widgets are identity objects referenced by pointer, not values.
findings.verify_note: Read Mh.h in full and DrawObject.h:7-20 (default ctor, ResourceManager member); confirmed the full-constructor call sites via the add_child/make_unique greps.

findings.title: Widget constructors take 11-14 positional parameters with a bool flag buried mid-tail
findings.detail:
MTexture takes 11 parameters, MText 12, MTextDropShadow 14. To set layer_depth you must spell out every preceding default. `bool hidden` sits at position 7 of 11 (position 9 of 14 for MTextDropShadow), so `MTexture(n, s, f, r, rm, c, true)` is unreadable at the call site — and it is the same flag already present on `MObject(const std::string&, bool hidden = false)` and `MWidget(..., bool hidden = false)`. The adjacent floats (rotation, scale, shadow_scale) and the two Colours are positionally swappable with no compile error.

The last several parameters are identical across all three widgets and are only forwarded to DrawObject.
findings.suggestion: Introduce a `DrawParams` aggregate carrying colour/rotation/origin/effects/layer_depth and pass one struct. Replace `bool hidden` with `enum class Visibility { visible, hidden };`.
findings.verify_note: Read Mh.h:74-165 and DrawObject.h:12-17 to confirm the forwarded tail.

findings.title: Mh.h uses Text, ResourceManager, colour_consts and SpriteEffects without including any of their headers
findings.detail:
Mh.h includes only IGameObject.h, TextureObject.h and TextDropShadow.h. But `class MText final : public MWidget, public Text` (line 112) inherits Text, whose header is never included — it arrives only because TextDropShadow.h:4 happens to include Text.h (verified). Reorder or refactor that chain and Mh.h stops compiling. Same for `ResourceManager*` (82, 120, 146), `colour_consts::WHITE` (83), `DirectX::SpriteEffects` (87) and `MattMath::Viewport` (15), all reached transitively.

Conversely TextureObject.h is pulled in for MTexture alone and TextDropShadow.h for MTextDropShadow alone, so every TU that only wants MContainer compiles the whole sprite-sheet and font stack.

The filename and prefix are their own problem: Mh.h/Mh.cpp hold the entire retained-mode UI layer (MObject, MContainer, MWidget, MTexture, MText, MTextDropShadow) under a two-letter name, with a one-letter type prefix, in no namespace, flat in the same directory as Level.cpp and CollisionTools.cpp. A consumer of this engine cannot tell from the file tree that a UI system exists.
findings.suggestion: Include what you use (Text.h, ResourceManager.h, Colour.h). Split the framework (MObject/MContainer/MWidget) from the three concrete widgets, move them under ui/ with matching vcxproj filters, and put them in a namespace.
findings.verify_note: Read Mh.h:1-7 and 112, and TextDropShadow.h:1-6 confirming the transitive Text.h include.

findings.title: MenuHighlight base holds a raw MWidget* into a unique_ptr owned by the derived class
findings.detail:
```cpp
private:
	MWidget* _highlighted_widget = nullptr;
```
MenuHighlight is always used as a *base* (EndMenuPage, the MainMenu page classes, PauseMenu), and the pointer is always set to the address of an object owned by a unique_ptr **member of the derived class** — e.g. `set_highlighted_widget(this->_change_teams.get())` where _change_teams is EndMenu.h:68. C++ destroys derived members before base subobjects, so the pointer is dangling for the whole of ~MenuHighlight, by construction, in every page.

Severity lowered from the reviewers' "high": MenuHighlight has no destructor body and nothing dereferences the pointer during teardown, so there is no live use-after-free. It is a structural hazard — one added log line or assert away from one — not a current defect. There is also no null guard before `get_highlighted_widget()->get_name()` in the update paths.

Note this file is outside the math-collision module group; it surfaced because it consumes Mh.h.
findings.suggestion: Store the highlighted widget's name (or an index into an ordered navigable list) and resolve against the container — the navigation code already compares get_name() string literals anyway. Or make MContainer own the widgets and hold MenuHighlight as a member declared after the container rather than as a base.
findings.verify_note: Read MenuHighlight.h in full and EndMenu.h:55-77 for the derived-member ownership and declaration order.

findings.title: Shape is a polymorphic base with public implicit copy-assignment, and every core value type inherits it
findings.detail:
`struct Shape` declares `virtual ~Shape() = default` and nine pure virtuals, but neither deletes nor protects copy construction/assignment, so `Shape& operator=(const Shape&)` is implicitly public. Combined with the raw `Shape*` API CollisionTools exposes, `*collider = *collidee;` inside a resolution routine would compile and silently slice a Circle into a RectangleF's Shape subobject.

The already-paid cost is layout: RectangleF, Circle, Triangle, Quad and RectangleRotated all carry a vptr, so none is trivially copyable or constant-initialisable, and they cannot be passed in registers. These are the engine's fundamental value types and they are copied constantly in the collision path — CollisionTools.cpp:15, 35, 58, 139-140 and EricsonMath.cpp:286-289, 394-395, 426-427, 647-648 each build one or more temporaries per call, and `get_bounding_box()` returns a polymorphic type by value on every invocation. The polymorphism also forces the dynamic_cast double-dispatch chain (MattMath.cpp:119-136) and the `clone()`/unique_ptr dance in calculate_object_collision_depth.

Note this file is outside the math-collision module group but is the direct cause of costs inside it.
findings.suggestion: Minimal: `protected: Shape(const Shape&) = default; Shape& operator=(const Shape&) = default;` to close the slicing hole without changing layout. Structural, and better for the engine goal: drop the inheritance, make the shapes plain aggregates, and move dispatch to a tagged variant or a free-function overload set — that kills the vptr, the dynamic_casts, and the need for clone().
findings.verify_note: Read MattMath.h:68-92 and MattMath.cpp:119-136; confirmed the temporary construction sites in CollisionTools.cpp and EricsonMath.cpp listed.

findings.title: No LanguageStandard set in either vcxproj, so the project builds as C++14 and works around missing standard facilities
findings.detail:
Neither ArtAttack.vcxproj nor MattMathTests.vcxproj contains a `<LanguageStandard>` element (verified by grep), so MSVC defaults to /std:c++14. That is not a cosmetic setting — it is the direct cause of several findings in this module:

- `EricsonMath::clamp` exists (and duplicates `MattMath::clamp`, and is dead) because std::clamp is C++17.
- Nine of fifteen EricsonMath functions signal failure through a bool plus out-params because std::optional is C++17.
- `resolve_object_collision` has a twin overload whose only purpose is to declare a throwaway local, for the same reason.
- `constexpr` globals in the CollisionTools header get a per-TU copy without `inline constexpr`.

Also absent from both projects: `TreatWarningAsError`. WarningLevel is Level4 in all four ArtAttack configurations (and only Level3 in the test project), so /W4 is advisory — which is why the dead locals at CollisionTools.cpp:35/58 (C4189), the unused `view` parameters in Mh.cpp (C4100), and the signed/unsigned loops at Level.cpp:386 and MenuPage.cpp:140 (C4018) have all accumulated unaddressed.
findings.suggestion: Set `<LanguageStandard>stdcpp20</LanguageStandard>` in both vcxproj files — a grep shows zero C++17-or-later features in use, so nothing breaks — then delete the workarounds it was hiding. Turn on TreatWarningAsError, or at minimum /we4189 /we4100 /we4018, so /W4 stops being decoration.
findings.verify_note: Grepped both vcxproj files for LanguageStandard (absent), TreatWarningAsError (absent), WarningLevel (Level4 x4 / Level3 x4) and FloatingPointModel (Fast x4).

findings.title: Player::draw mutates object state and runs concurrently on the same Player from several thread-pool threads
findings.detail:
Merges 3 candidates (all reported this). Verified end to end. `Player::draw(SpriteBatch*, const Camera&)` is non-const and writes: `this->_animation_state = new_animation_state;` (:59), `TextureObject::set_sprite_sheet_name(info.sprite_sheet)` (:62), `TextureObject::set_element_name(...)` (:63), `set_animation_strip_and_reset(...)` (:65, which also resets `_frame_index`/`_time_elapsed`), `set_frame_time(...)`/`set_frame_time_to_default()` (:66-73), and unconditionally `TextureObject::set_effects(effects)` (:83) and `AnimationObject::set_effects(effects)` (:86).

The concurrency is real, and it is worse than the candidates described — `Level::draw_active_level` (Level.cpp:382-397) partitions the PLAYER list, not the viewport list: `_partitioner->partition(this->_player_objects->size(), num_threads)` with `NUM_THREADS_MAX = 16` (Game.h:14). `Partitioner::partition` (Partitioner.cpp:10) caps the loop at `i < num_elements`, so an N-player match produces exactly N partitions and N concurrent `ThreadPool::add_task` submissions. `ThreadPool::add_task` uses the real Win32 pool (`SubmitThreadpoolWork`, ThreadPool.cpp:47). Each task then runs `draw_player_view_level`, which loops over EVERY player (Level.cpp:534-540: `for (auto& object : *this->_player_objects) { ... object->draw(sprite_batches->at(i), camera); }`).

So in any 2+ player match, `Player::draw` for the same instance executes on N threads simultaneously. `SpriteSheetObject::_sheet_name` and `_element_name` are `std::string` (SpriteSheetObject.h:25-26); concurrent unsynchronised assignment to a `std::string` is a torn write on the heap pointer / SSO buffer, i.e. potential heap corruption, not merely a stale frame.

Separately, even single-threaded this is a design defect: clip selection belongs in `update()` (called once per frame), not `draw()` (called once per viewport). A player who is off-screen in every viewport never changes animation clip at all, because `Level` guards the call with `is_visible_in_viewport`.
findings.suggestion: Move the whole `calculate_animation_state()` / strip-swap / effects block into `Player::update()`, and make both `draw` overrides `const` so the compiler enforces purity. Long term `IGameObject::draw` should be const across the engine — a parallel command-list recorder is only safe if the record path is read-only.
findings.verify_note: Read Player.cpp:47-90, Level.cpp:375-400 and 491-593, Partitioner.cpp:4-27, ThreadPool.cpp:38-58, Game.h:13-14, SpriteSheetObject.h:24-27. Confirmed N partitions for N players and that each task draws all players.

findings.title: update_and_get_player_inputs returns a positionally compacted vector that Level indexes by player ordinal
findings.suggestion: Return a fixed-size, slot-indexed container — `std::array<PlayerInputData, MAX_PADS>` — emitting an entry for every pad slot with `connection` set correctly and axes zeroed when absent. Then index == pad index always, and `Player` can react to a drop-out (freeze / prompt to reconnect) instead of being silently reassigned.
findings.verify_note: Read PlayerInput.cpp:119-138 and 96-117, PlayerInputData.h:7-23, Level.cpp:188-213, GameStates.cpp:141-145 and 348-359.

findings.title: Spawn points chosen with the global player index into per-team spawn arrays; unchecked operator[] on JSON data
findings.detail:
Merges 5 candidates. `build_players` keeps one counter `i` incremented once per player (:64) but uses it to index two separate per-team arrays (:32, :36):

```
if (setting.team == player_team::A) { position = team_a_spawns[i]; }
else                                { position = team_b_spawns[i]; }
```

With teams ordered A,B,A,B the team-A players take `team_a_spawns[0]` and `[2]` while `[1]` and `[3]` are never used. The correct index is a per-team running counter. This is a live behavioural bug today, not just latent.

The bounds hazard is real but I verified it is NOT currently reachable: `team_a_spawns`/`team_b_spawns` come straight from level JSON via `LevelLoadedInfo::get_team_a_spawns()` with no size validation and `operator[]` is unchecked, but all three shipped levels declare exactly 4 spawns per team (I parsed close_quarters.json, king_of_the_hill.json, turbulence.json — all `{team_a: 4, team_b: 4}`) and the max player count is 4, so `i` maxes at 3. Any level authored with fewer spawns for one team is an immediate OOB read feeding `Player::_respawn_position` for the whole match.

Also verified: `MenuPlayerSettings::team` defaults to `player_team::NONE` and `num` to `-1` (MenuPlayerSettings.h:9-11); the `else` branch silently treats NONE as team B, and `team_colours.get_team_colour(NONE)` at :50/:56 then throws mid-build.
findings.suggestion: Track `team_a_index`/`team_b_index` separately, switch explicitly on `setting.team` with an error branch for `NONE`, and validate up front that each team's spawn list is at least as long as that team's player count — throwing a diagnostic that names the level file — rather than relying on `operator[]`.
findings.verify_note: Read PlayerBuilder.cpp:13-67, LevelLoadedInfo.h:17-18, MenuPlayerSettings.h:7-12. Parsed all three level JSONs and counted spawn entries (4/4 each), confirming the OOB is latent but the wrong-spawn selection is live.

findings.title: Dead players keep firing: the weapon is never gated on player_state
findings.detail:
`Player::update()` branches on `_state` and only runs movement/animation while ALIVE (:698-711), but the weapon lives entirely outside that branch. `Level::update_level_logic` calls it unconditionally for every player (Level.cpp:204-210), and `Player::update_weapon_and_get_projectiles() const` (:742-750) just forwards `this->get_input()` to `Weapon::update_and_get_projectiles`. I read `Weapon::update_and_get_projectiles` (Weapon.cpp:168-186) and `check_if_shooting_and_ammo_update` (Weapon.cpp:188-233): neither knows anything about `player_state`.

Result: a dead player holding the right trigger keeps spawning projectiles for the whole `RESPAWN_DELAY` (3 s), from `get_center()` — frozen at the death position because `update_movement()` is skipped. `Player::draw` early-returns at :49-52, so the player and gun are invisible. An invisible corpse turret. The weapon's shoot sound also keeps playing (`handle_shoot_sound`, Weapon.cpp:231).
findings.suggestion: Gate it in `Player::update_weapon_and_get_projectiles()`: return an empty vector when `_state == player_state::DEAD`, or pass a neutral `PlayerInputData{}` so timers still tick but nothing fires. Also call `stop_sounds()` on death (:704-708 currently only plays the death wave).
findings.verify_note: Read Player.cpp:696-750, Level.cpp:203-210, Weapon.cpp:168-233. No player_state check anywhere in that chain.

findings.title: Player inherits SpriteSheetObject/DrawObject twice (non-virtual diamond) — two divergent copies of all draw state
findings.detail:
Merges 2 candidates. `class Player final : public MovingObject, public ICollisionGameObject, public AnimationObject, public TextureObject`. I confirmed `AnimationObject : public SpriteSheetObject` (AnimationObject.h:7), `TextureObject : public SpriteSheetObject` (TextureObject.h:6), `SpriteSheetObject : public DrawObject` (SpriteSheetObject.h:6), all non-virtual.

So every `Player` physically contains two `SpriteSheetObject` and two `DrawObject` subobjects: two `ResourceManager* _resource_manager`, two `_colour`, two `_draw_rotation`, two `_origin`, two `_effects`, two `_layer_depth` (DrawObject.h:36-41), two `_sheet_name`/`_element_name` (SpriteSheetObject.h:25-26). A `Player*` → `DrawObject*` conversion is ambiguous and ill-formed, so a Player can never be handled generically as a drawable — a hard blocker for the reusable-engine goal.

The two copies are deliberately initialised to different values (Player.cpp:29 passes `DEFAULT_PLAYER_COLOUR` to the AnimationObject branch, :31 passes `team_colour` to the TextureObject branch), and every access must be hand-qualified to pick a side — `TextureObject::set_effects(effects); AnimationObject::set_effects(effects);` at :83/:86 is the same value written twice or they diverge. `MovingObject` adds a third, never-rendered `_rotation` (MovingObject.h:56), which is why `respawn()`'s `MovingObject::set_rotation(0.0f)` (:996) is a visual no-op.
findings.suggestion: Replace inheritance with composition: `Sprite _uniform;` and `AnimatedSprite _body;` as members, each owning its own draw params, with one authoritative transform on the entity. An entity is not a sprite — it has sprites.
findings.verify_note: Read Player.h:63-64, AnimationObject.h:7, TextureObject.h:6, SpriteSheetObject.h:6/24-27, DrawObject.h:7/35-41, MovingObject.h:53-57, Player.cpp:26-45 and 76-90.

findings.title: Player is a god class: simulation, rendering, audio, camera, input, weapon and game rules in one type
findings.detail:
Player.h declares ~90 member functions and 22 data members; Player.cpp is 1263 lines. In one type it owns: kinematics (`MovingObject` velocity/dx, `update_movement`, `do_jump`, `_air_time`), a ground/air state machine (`player_move_state`, `is_on_ground`, `is_on_ramp`, `on_no_collision`), collision response for eight directions plus ramps and jump-through platforms (`on_top_collision` … `on_structure_ramp_collision`, Player.cpp:245-639), two full sprite hierarchies plus clip selection (`calculate_animation_state`, `get_animation_info`), audio (`SoundBank* _sound_bank`, four hardcoded cue names from `player_consts`), view state that belongs to the renderer (`MattMath::Camera _camera` Player.h:140, `MattMath::Viewport _viewport` :161), input state (`PlayerInputData _input` :152), weapon ownership (`std::unique_ptr<Weapon> _primary` :142), and Splatoon rules (`_team`, `_team_colour`, `_health`, `_respawn_timer`, `_score`, per-weapon damage constants).

This is the central engine-reuse blocker for this module group: to get a moving, animated, colliding character in a different game you must take teams, respawn timers, ammo, a debug HUD flag and a splatoon damage table with it.
findings.suggestion: Decompose into engine parts plus a thin game script: `RigidBody2D` (position/velocity/integration), `CharacterController2D` (ground/air state machine driven by an abstract action set), `SpriteAnimator` (a state→clip table with no knowledge of 'player'), `AudioEmitter`, `CameraTarget`. `Player` then becomes ~150 lines of game glue composing them.
findings.verify_note: Read all of Player.h (255 lines) and Player.cpp (1263 lines). Member and responsibility inventory is accurate.

findings.title: Player caches a raw SoundBank* that Game::OnDeviceLost destroys underneath it
findings.suggestion: Stop caching. Either look the bank up through the `ResourceManager*` at each call site, or have `reset_all_sounds` reset only the instances (not the owning `unique_ptr`) so device-lost recovery re-initialises in place instead of destroying objects other code points at.
findings.verify_note: Read Player.cpp:44, Player.h:168, ResourceManager.cpp:86-126, Game.cpp:269-287. Confirmed reset_all_sounds destroys the owned SoundBank and OnDeviceLost leaves the state tree alive.

findings.title: STRUCTURE_RAMP_LEFT collision branch is an empty // TODO — left ramps are silently non-solid
findings.suggestion: Either implement the mirrored case (collapse the RIGHT arm to one `if (direction is any of DOWN/RIGHT/DOWN_LEFT/DOWN_RIGHT)` and parameterise on ramp side), or make `LevelObjectBuilder` reject `STRUCTURE_RAMP_LEFT` so a broken level fails loudly at load rather than silently at play.
findings.verify_note: Read Player.cpp:245-359, LevelObjectBuilder.cpp:145-160, collision_object_type.h:9/80/86, king_of_the_hill.json (only RAMP_RIGHT present), StructureRampLeft.h (fully commented out).

findings.title: 'No collision direction' guard is unreachable; a non-intersection is laundered into DIRECTION_RIGHT and resolved as a real ramp contact
findings.detail:
Merges 3 candidates (including the dead `is_on_ramp` local). Verified the whole chain:

- `CollisionTools::calculate_object_collision_direction` returns `Vector2F::ZERO` exactly when the shapes are not intersecting (CollisionTools.cpp:128-131).
- Player.cpp:250 immediately feeds that through `Vector2F::direction_to_8_cardinal_direction`, which starts `float angle = direction.angle();` → `std::atan2(0.0f, 0.0f)` → `0.0f` (MattMath.cpp:1749-1752), landing in the first bucket and returning `Vector2F::DIRECTION_RIGHT` (MattMath.cpp:1870-1876). It can never return ZERO.

So the `else if (direction == Vector2F::ZERO) throw` at :346-349 is dead code, the trailing `else throw` at :350-353 is also unreachable (UP/UP_LEFT/UP_RIGHT consumed at :254, LEFT at :258, and DOWN/RIGHT/DOWN_LEFT/DOWN_RIGHT all handled), and the real failure mode is silent: a 'not touching' result becomes DIRECTION_RIGHT, hits the branch at :289-297, and snaps the player down onto the ramp with `set_velocity_y(0)`.

Same function, :271-272: `bool is_on_ramp = ...` is computed and never referenced again, and shadows the member function `Player::is_on_ramp()` (:1246) for the rest of the scope. That is MSVC C4189 under the project's /W4 — evidence warnings are not being read.
findings.suggestion: Test `direction == Vector2F::ZERO` immediately after :248, before the cardinal snap, and return early. Make `direction_to_8_cardinal_direction` propagate ZERO for a zero-length input instead of silently answering RIGHT — that trap applies to every caller. Delete the dead local.
findings.verify_note: Read Player.cpp:245-359, CollisionTools.cpp:125-134, MattMath.cpp:1749-1752 and 1870-1905. Traced atan2(0,0)==0 into the first bucket.

findings.title: on_no_collision() omits ON_CEILING, so the player stays flagged 'on ceiling' for the whole fall
findings.suggestion: Add `move_state == player_move_state::ON_CEILING` to the condition, or better `if (is_on_ground() || move_state == ON_CEILING)` so a newly added grounded state cannot be forgotten here. Separately, have `Level` distinguish 'supported from below' from 'touched any structure' before deciding to call `on_no_collision`.

findings.title: respawn() leaves _prev_rectangle and _health_regen_timer stale, and hardcodes 1.0f instead of STARTING_HEALTH
findings.detail:
Merges 3 candidates, with their consequences corrected. `respawn()` resets position, rotation, velocity, dx, health, ammo and state, but not `_move_state`, `_prev_rectangle`, `_air_time`, `_damage_sound_timer` or `_health_regen_timer`.

I verified that most of the alarming consequences the reviewers claimed do NOT occur:
- The 'free jump on respawn' and 'ramp-gravity slam' claims are WRONG. While dead, `Player::is_colliding` returns false (:151-154), so `player_colliding_with_structure` is false every frame and `Level` calls `on_no_collision()` (Level.cpp:245-248), which converts ON_GROUND/ON_DROP_DOWN_GROUND/ON_RAMP_* to IN_AIR long before the respawn. `_air_time` is only read in the JUMPING branch and is zeroed by `do_jump` on the next jump, so it is harmless.

What IS real:
- `_prev_rectangle` still holds the death rectangle. `respawn()` runs from `update()` at Level.cpp:193, before the collision pass (Level.cpp:222) and before `update_prev_rectangle()` (Level.cpp:255). So for the whole respawn frame `on_structure_jump_through_collision` evaluates `_prev_rectangle.get_bottom() <= other_rect.get_top()` (:372) against a position from wherever the player died — the player can snap onto, or drop through, the platform under the spawn point.
- `_health_regen_timer` keeps accumulating while dead (the regen block at :732-740 is outside the state branch), so on respawn the 5 s `HEALTH_REGEN_DELAY` is already satisfied and regen is live from frame one.
- `this->_health = 1.0f;` (:999) and the regen cap `if (this->_health > 1.0f)` (:735-737) both duplicate `player_consts::STARTING_HEALTH` (player_consts.h:34), which is already 1.0f. Retuning STARTING_HEALTH silently desynchronises all three.
findings.suggestion: Factor a `reset_transient_state()` called by both the constructor and `respawn()`, covering `_prev_rectangle = _rectangle`, `_health_regen_timer = 0.0f`, `_damage_sound_timer`, `_move_state = IN_AIR`, and `_health = player_consts::STARTING_HEALTH`. That makes it impossible to add a member and forget one of the two paths.
findings.verify_note: Read Player.cpp:148-185, 360-388, 696-741, 993-1003; Level.cpp:188-256. Traced that on_no_collision fires every dead frame, which invalidates the free-jump and ramp-gravity consequences the reviewers asserted.

findings.title: Two divergent damage tables — Player hardcodes its own and ProjectileDetails::player_damage is dead data; health is never clamped at zero
findings.detail:
Merges 3 candidates. `on_projectile_collision` (:645-690) is a 35-line if/else chain mapping the collision enum back to constants in `player_consts` (`SPRAY_DAMAGE` … `MIST_DAMAGE`, player_consts.h:65-69). Meanwhile every projectile already carries `ProjectileDetails::player_damage` (projectile_details.h:13), populated per weapon in projectile_consts.h and exposed via `Projectile::get_player_damage()` (Projectile.cpp:295-298). I grepped the whole tree: `get_player_damage` has ZERO call sites outside its own definition — the entire per-projectile damage configuration is dead.

The two tables disagree in sign convention and magnitude: spray 0.01 vs -0.1; jet 0.334 vs -0.5; rolling 0.015 vs **-1000.0**; ball 0.201 vs -0.1; mist 0.01 vs -0.05. Whichever a maintainer edits, half the time nothing happens.

This also forces `Player` to enumerate every weapon type — adding a weapon means editing `collision_object_type`, `Projectile::is_matching_collision_object_type`, `Player::on_collision` (:199-222, which hand-writes 'is this an enemy projectile' as ten enum comparisons duplicating `is_team_a_projectile`/`is_team_b_projectile` in collision_object_type.h) and `Player::on_projectile_collision`. Four places, none compiler-checked, with a runtime `throw` as the fallthrough. That is the game-logic-welded-into-the-entity problem in its purest form.

Also confirmed: `_health` is clamped only on the upper side (:735-738). Nothing clamps at zero, so multiple hits in one frame drive it arbitrarily negative, and that value goes straight to the HUD via `get_health()` (Level.cpp:563).
findings.suggestion: Delete the `*_DAMAGE` constants from `player_consts.h` and make the projectile the single source of truth — add `get_damage()` to the collision interface (or a small `DamageEvent` payload) so the player does `_health = std::max(0.0f, _health - other->get_damage())`. Fix the sign convention while you are there. Replace the hostility ladder with a `{kind, team}` tag plus an `is_hostile(a, b)` query.
findings.verify_note: Read Player.cpp:186-244 and 645-690, player_consts.h:65-69, projectile_details.h:13, projectile_consts.h:20-101, Projectile.cpp:93-119 and 295-298. Grepped get_player_damage tree-wide: definition only.

findings.title: ResourceManager getters return nullptr for a missing key (the catch block is dead), and Player dereferences the result unchecked
findings.detail:
Merges 3 candidates. `ResourceManager::get_sound_bank` is:
```
try { return this->_sound_banks[sound_bank_name].get(); }
catch (const std::out_of_range&) { ... throw std::out_of_range(error); }   // ResourceManager.cpp:91-102
```
`std::map::operator[]` default-inserts on a missing key and never throws `std::out_of_range`, so the catch is dead code, the function returns `nullptr` for an unknown bank, and the map is polluted with a null entry. `get_texture` (:7-19), `get_sprite_font` (:27-38) and `get_sprite_sheet` (:46-58) have the identical defect. (`get_level_info` at :66-78 correctly uses `.at()`.)

`Player` stores that unchecked at :44 and dereferences it at :687 (damage), :707 (death), :880 (jump) and :1002 (respawn) — a null deref on the first jump if the bank is missing. Not hypothetical: `.gitignore` excludes `*.wav`/`*.xwb`, so a fresh clone has no audio assets.

Compounding it, `player_consts::SOUND_BANK` is the hardcoded literal `"sound_bank_1"` (player_consts.h:55) while the level declares its own bank in JSON (`LevelLoadedInfo::get_sound_bank_name`, used by `Level`). A reusable Player has no business knowing that "sound_bank_1" exists.
findings.suggestion: Change the getters to `find()` + explicit throw naming the missing key, so a missing resource is a real error at load time. Then null-check `_sound_bank` once at construction and fail loudly, or degrade to a null-sink SoundBank. Longer term the bank name should come from the builder/level data, not from `player_consts`.
findings.verify_note: Read ResourceManager.cpp:1-126 and Player.cpp:44/687/707/880/1002. Confirmed operator[] usage and the unreachable catch in four of five getters.

findings.title: Sixteen private accessors with no callers, plus two dead members and a duplicate input setter
findings.detail:
Merges 4 candidates. I grepped the whole tree for each. These `Player` members have exactly one occurrence — their own definition — and are private so unreachable from outside: `set_player_num` (Player.cpp:1167), `set_team` (:1122), `get_primary` (:1142), `set_primary` (:1147), `get_secondary` (:1152), `set_secondary` (:1157), `set_team_colour` (:1127), `set_viewport` (:1132), `set_input` (:1137), `set_health` (:1087), `alter_health` (:1092), `set_respawn_timer` (:1097), `alter_respawn_timer` (:1102), `set_score` (:1107), `alter_score` (:1112), `get_score` (:1117), `set_showing_debug` (:1162). ~90 lines of dead code.

Two members die with them: `int _score = 0;` (Player.h:148) is never read or written outside its three dead accessors — the per-player scoring the header advertises does not exist. `wep_type _secondary_type` (Player.h:159) is written once by the constructor and never read; `PlayerBuilder.cpp:55` hardcodes `wep_type::GRENADE_STD` for it, so there is no secondary-weapon feature at all.

`void set_input(const PlayerInputData&)` (Player.h:230, Player.cpp:1137-1140) is byte-identical to the public `set_player_input` (Player.h:99, Player.cpp:922-925) — `this->_input = input;` twice under two names and two access levels. Two setters for one field becomes a correctness hazard the moment one grows a side effect.

This matters beyond tidiness: a reader of the 255-line header cannot tell which dozen members actually participate in behaviour. Note the inconsistency it already creates — `on_projectile_collision` writes `this->_health -= SPRAY_DAMAGE;` directly (:652) rather than using `alter_health`.
findings.suggestion: Delete all sixteen accessors, `_score`, `_secondary_type` and the `wep_type secondary` constructor parameter. Reintroduce a setter only when a caller actually exists.
findings.verify_note: Grepped each name across ArtAttack/. Every one resolves only to its Player.h declaration and Player.cpp definition.

findings.title: Frame time is a raw const float* to a heap float, stored twice per Player; team colour stored three times; viewport is a stale snapshot
findings.detail:
Merges 4 candidates. Three separate duplications of the same state on one object:

1. `const float* _dt = nullptr;` (Player.h:170), dereferenced blind in `float Player::get_dt() const { return *this->_dt; }` (:692-695). The pointee is a single heap float — `Game.h` holds `std::unique_ptr<float> _dt`, `Game.cpp:244-245` does `make_unique<float>(0.f)` and hands out `.get()`, and `Game::update` writes through it at Game.cpp:90. The same pointer is ALSO stored in `AnimationObject::_dt` (AnimationObject.h:49, initialised from Player.cpp:27) and dereferenced independently there. Two non-owning copies of one pointer, both unvalidatable, in exchange for a heap allocation for one float. Nothing in Player.h documents that it is non-owning, must outlive the Player, or must be non-null.

2. `MattMath::Colour _team_colour` (Player.h:160) is the same value that is passed into `TextureObject` (stored as `DrawObject::_colour`) at Player.cpp:31 and into the `Weapon` at PlayerBuilder.cpp:50. Three copies, all write-once, none coherently updatable — `set_team_colour` touches only Player's and is itself dead.

3. `MattMath::Viewport _viewport` (Player.h:161) is a construction-time snapshot of `viewport_manager->get_player_viewport(setting.num)` (PlayerBuilder.cpp:57-58). `ViewportManager::get_player_viewport` computes it from the manager's CURRENT `_layout` and resolution (ViewportManager.cpp:84-88) — a derived value, not an identity. The layout demonstrably changes underneath it: `Level::draw_zoom_out_level_component` calls `_viewport_manager->set_layout(screen_layout::ONE_PLAYER)` (Level.cpp:619) and never restores it. `Player::set_viewport` exists but is private and never called. The only reader is `DebugText.cpp:28`, which therefore reports a stale viewport after any zoom-out or resolution change.
findings.suggestion: Pass dt by value — `void update(float dt)` on `IGameObject` — deleting `Player::_dt`, `AnimationObject::_dt`, `Weapon::_dt`, `Level::_dt`, the `float*` in `GameData` and the `unique_ptr<float>` in `Game`, plus a whole class of lifetime questions, and making the engine testable with a fixed dt. Store the team colour once. Delete `_viewport`/`get_viewport`/`set_viewport` and have `DebugText` ask `ViewportManager` for `player->get_player_num()`.
findings.verify_note: Read Player.h:140-172, AnimationObject.h:49, Game.cpp:87-98 and 236-261, PlayerBuilder.cpp:40-60, ViewportManager.cpp:79-104, Level.cpp:609-625, DebugText.cpp:18-42.

findings.title: const member functions mutate the owned Weapon through unique_ptr, where const does not propagate
findings.detail:
Merges 3 candidates. `std::unique_ptr::operator->` yields a non-const `Weapon&` from a const `Player`, so three commands are declared as queries:
- `void Player::update_weapon_position() const { this->_primary->set_player_center(...); }` (:641-644)
- `std::vector<std::unique_ptr<ICollisionGameObject>> Player::update_weapon_and_get_projectiles() const` (:742-750) — forwards to `Weapon::update_and_get_projectiles`, a non-const member (Weapon.h:36) that advances shoot timers, spends ammo, plays sounds and constructs projectiles. The most mutating operation in the module, declared const.
- `void Player::stop_sounds() const { this->_primary->stop_sounds(); }` (:1048-1051)

This is what lets `void Level::update_level_logic(...) const` (Level.cpp:180) drive an entire frame of simulation while claiming to be const — it calls `object->update_weapon_and_get_projectiles()` (:205) and `object->update_weapon_position()` (:254) on `const auto&` players. `const` currently carries no information anywhere in this call graph, so the compiler cannot catch a genuine mistake, and it is a direct blocker on ever sharing entities across threads safely (see the draw-race finding). `PlayerBuilder::build_players(...) const` has the same hole via `_weapon_builder`.
findings.suggestion: Drop `const` from all three. That will correctly force `Level::update_level_logic` and its loop variables to become non-const, restoring `const` as a meaningful signal. If a const-preserving handle is wanted, wrap `_primary` in a small propagate-const pointer.

findings.title: Player's per-frame state is only valid if the caller invokes six methods in one exact, undocumented order
findings.detail:
Merges 2 candidates. To advance one player by one frame `Level` must call, in this order: `set_player_input` (Level.cpp:192), `update` (:193), `set_camera` (:201), `update_weapon_and_get_projectiles` (:205), the whole collision pass (:222-243) including `on_no_collision` (:247), then `update_weapon_position` (:254) and `update_prev_rectangle` (:255). None of it is expressed in a type or a comment; it lives only in the caller.

The failure modes are silent, not loud:
- `on_structure_jump_through_collision` decides pass-through by `this->_prev_rectangle.get_bottom() <= other_rect.get_top()` (:372). Call `update_prev_rectangle()` before the collision pass instead of after and `_prev_rectangle == _rectangle`, so the player falls through every drop-down platform.
- `update_weapon_position()` must run after collision resolution has moved `_rectangle`, or the weapon renders at the pre-resolution position.
- `on_no_collision()` is the only thing that transitions the player out of `ON_GROUND`; omitting it leaves the player able to jump in mid-air forever. It exists purely so the caller can report 'I checked every structure and none touched you' — information the collision system already has and should not be relaying by hand.

For a reusable engine this is the opposite of an interface: the entity's invariants are the caller's responsibility.
findings.suggestion: Collapse the sequence into the entity: one `update(const FrameContext&)` that snapshots its own previous transform and repositions its own weapon, with grounded-ness derived from the collision system's contact set for this frame. Projectile spawning should go through a spawner/command queue rather than a return value the caller must remember to drain.

findings.title: The 'raw' input layer is hardwired to four XInput pads and already speaks game verbs
findings.detail:
Merges 2 candidates. `RawPlayerInput` — the supposedly raw layer — has fields named `jump_button`, `jump_trigger`, `primary_shoot`, `secondary_shoot`, `show_debug`, `pause_menu` (PlayerInput.h:19-24), with the binding baked in at PlayerInput.cpp:27-32 (`result.jump_button = pad.buttons.a; result.primary_shoot = pad.triggers.right; result.show_debug = pad.buttons.back; ...`).

There is no keyboard, no mouse, no rebinding, no way to add a fifth player, and no way for a different game to define different actions. For a project whose stated goal is a reusable 2D engine, this is a hard ceiling: `jump` and `shoot` should never appear in engine code.

The pad count 4 is a bare literal in four places — `RawPlayerInput _prev_inputs[4]` (PlayerInput.h:34), `RawPlayerInput current[4]` and both `for (int i = 0; i < 4; i++)` loops (PlayerInput.cpp:121-127) — even though a `player_input_consts` namespace (PlayerInput.h:8-13) already exists as the obvious home for a named constant. DirectXTK's real bound is `GamePad::MAX_PLAYER_COUNT`, which is 8 under GDK; nothing static-asserts the relationship.
findings.suggestion: Two layers: an `InputDevice` interface producing a device-neutral `DeviceState` of axes and buttons, and a data-loaded `ActionMap` producing `ActionState { axis(action), down(action), pressed(action) }`. Player count comes from device enumeration, not a literal.
findings.verify_note: Read PlayerInput.h:8-39 and PlayerInput.cpp:17-36/119-138. Confirmed GamePad.h is only included via pch.h:64.

findings.title: PlayerInputData carries derived state alongside its source, plus raw stick values that leak the device into gameplay
findings.detail:
Merges 2 candidates. The struct holds `x_movement` (derived from `left_analog_stick.x`), `shoot_angle` and `shoot_direction` (both derived from `right_analog_stick`), a `shoot_direction_requested` flag guarding the direction value, and `connection` — then also ships the raw `left_analog_stick` and `right_analog_stick` it derived them from. `calculate_player_input` (PlayerInput.cpp:96-114) computes the three derived fields and then copies the raw sticks in as well. Nothing enforces that the four stay consistent, and every field is independently settable by any consumer.

`connection` is always `CONNECTED` (:111) because disconnected pads are filtered out entirely, so it carries no information (see the compaction finding).

The leak is the concrete harm: `Player::update_movement` reaches past the semantic layer — `const bool analog_stick_down = this->_input.left_analog_stick.y > DROP_DOWN_ANALOG_THRESHOLD;` (Player.cpp:762-763). 'Drop through a platform' is therefore permanently a left-thumbstick gesture that can never be a key, a button, or a rebound control. Deadzone policy is now split across three layers: `GamePad::DEAD_ZONE_CIRCULAR` (PlayerInput.cpp:20), `STICK_DEADZONE = 0.5f` (PlayerInput.cpp:86-97), and this 0.8 threshold inside the entity.
findings.suggestion: Reduce the struct to intent-level fields — add a `drop_down` action computed in `calculate_player_input` where the stick threshold belongs, replace the direction/angle/requested triple with an optional direction, and delete `connection` and the two raw stick fields (their only other reader is the debug dump at DebugText.cpp:33-34).
findings.verify_note: Read PlayerInputData.h:7-23, PlayerInput.cpp:86-117, Player.cpp:756-764, DebugText.cpp:29-34.

findings.title: Stick deadzone applied twice and never rescaled, so x_movement jumps discontinuously from 0 to 0.5
findings.detail:
`GetState(gamepad_num, GamePad::DEAD_ZONE_CIRCULAR)` (:20) already applies XInput's deadzone AND rescales the surviving range to 0..1. The code then applies a second, larger threshold on top without rescaling:
```
if (std::fabs(current.left_analog_stick.x) > STICK_DEADZONE)   // 0.5f
{ result.x_movement = current.left_analog_stick.x; }           // raw value, not remapped
else { result.x_movement = 0.0f; }
```
So `x_movement` snaps from 0 straight to ±0.5 — half the stick's usable travel is dead and there is no fine speed control. `X_INITIAL_VELOCITY * x_input` (Player.cpp:769) means the smallest possible starting speed is exactly half the maximum starting speed. The same untranslated 0.5 threshold gates the aim stick at :97.
findings.suggestion: Pick one deadzone. If you keep the manual one, request `GamePad::DEAD_ZONE_NONE` and rescale: `x = sign(x) * (|x| - DZ) / (1 - DZ)`. Also 0.5 is enormous for a movement axis — 0.15-0.25 is typical.
findings.verify_note: Read PlayerInput.cpp:17-36 and 86-97, Player.cpp:766-770, player_consts.h:27.

findings.title: is_colliding and on_collision disagree: Player only accepts structures but its handler expects projectiles
findings.detail:
