`Player::is_matching_collision_object_type` returns `is_structure(other_type)` (:142-147), so `Player::is_colliding` can never return true for a projectile. Yet `Player::on_collision` (:186-244) has a full projectile branch and ends in `throw std::exception("Invalid collision object type.")`.

It only works because `Level::update_level_logic` calls the handler on both participants whenever either predicate passed — Level.cpp:233-236 (`player->is_colliding(other)` → both handlers) and Level.cpp:268-272 (`object->is_colliding(player)` → both handlers). So `Player::on_collision` routinely receives objects that `Player::is_colliding` explicitly rejected, and the callee's correctness depends on the exact shape of the caller's loop. It is also why the same pair is resolved twice per frame.

The fragility is concrete: add any object whose `is_colliding` accepts a player but which `Player::on_collision` does not enumerate, and the game throws from inside the collision loop. (I checked — `PaintTile::is_colliding` (PaintTile.cpp:84-109) has NO type filter at all and would trigger exactly this; it survives only because paint tiles live inside `StructurePaintable::_paint_tiles` rather than in `Level::_collision_objects`.)

The same 25-line 'AABB check, then if other is a rectangle return true, then narrow phase' body is copy-pasted verbatim in Player.cpp:148-185, PaintTile.cpp:84-109 and all five Projectile* classes.
findings.suggestion: Take collision filtering out of the objects. A `CollisionWorld` with layer/mask bitsets decides candidate pairs, a broad+narrow phase produces a `ContactManifold{a, b, normal, depth}`, and each object gets exactly one `on_contact(const Contact&)` per pair per frame. That deletes seven copies of the same predicate.
findings.verify_note: Read Player.cpp:142-244, Level.cpp:222-293, Projectile.cpp:93-119, PaintTile.cpp:84-114, StructurePaintable.h:53.

findings.title: PlayerBuilder depends on menu types and hardcodes per-player configuration, so customisation is impossible by construction
findings.detail:
`PlayerBuilder.h:5` includes `MenuLevelSettings.h`, so constructing a gameplay entity depends on the menu system's state object — a UI type reaching into entity construction. In the body, the secondary weapon is the literal `wep_type::GRENADE_STD` (:55) and appearance is the literal `DEFAULT_ANIMATION_INFO` (:42), so no per-player customisation is possible even though the constructor accepts both.

The class is also called a Builder but is a one-shot factory function with six parameters and one member, and that member is pointless — see the WeaponBuilder finding.
findings.suggestion: Take a plain `const std::vector<PlayerSpawnRequest>&` (team, player_num, weapon, appearance) that neither the menu nor the level loader owns. Secondary weapon and appearance come from the request, not from literals in the factory.
findings.verify_note: Read PlayerBuilder.h:1-27 and PlayerBuilder.cpp:13-67, MenuLevelSettings.h.

findings.title: build_players returns unique_ptr<vector<unique_ptr<Player>>> — a heap allocation and a null state wrapping an already-movable container
findings.detail:
Merges 2 candidates. `PlayerBuilder.cpp:21` does `auto players = std::make_unique<std::vector<std::unique_ptr<Player>>>();` and `:66` returns it. The outer `unique_ptr` adds an allocation, an indirection, and a nullable state that no caller checks, around a type that is already move-only and cheap to move — a plain local plus `return players;` would be identical in cost thanks to NRVO.

The cost is paid at every use site: `Level.h:95-105` stores four members this way (`_non_collision_objects`, `_collision_objects`, `_player_objects`, `_viewport_dividers`), all defaulted to `nullptr`, and Level.cpp dereferences them everywhere (`*this->_player_objects` at :190, 222, 252, 262, 308, 639; `->at(i)` at :503, 508, 555-577). `Level() = default;` exists (Level.h:57), so a default-constructed Level with null members is a reachable state and every one of those dereferences is a null deref waiting to happen.
findings.suggestion: Return `std::vector<std::unique_ptr<Player>>` by value and store it by value in `Level`. The container can never be null and `*this->_player_objects` becomes `_player_objects` everywhere.
findings.verify_note: Read PlayerBuilder.h:15-21, PlayerBuilder.cpp:21/66, Level.h:94-106.

findings.title: Player constructor takes 16 positional parameters, with two adjacent same-typed enums that can be silently swapped
findings.detail:
The signature mixes geometry, animation info, a service pointer, identity (`player_num`, `team`), two `wep_type` enums PLUS an already-built `unique_ptr<Weapon>`, colour, viewport, a `const float* dt`, respawn position, and five sprite-drawing defaults. The call site (PlayerBuilder.cpp:40-60) is a 20-line unlabelled argument list.

Two specific hazards I verified: `wep_type primary` and `wep_type secondary` are separated only by the weapon pointer, so swapping them compiles silently; and `primary` is passed alongside the already-constructed `primary_weapon`, so the same fact is supplied twice and can disagree. Four parameters (`rotation`, `origin`, `effects`, `layer_depth`) are pure pass-through to the two sprite bases and are never supplied by any caller.

The body then does its own content lookup: `this->_sound_bank = resource_manager->get_sound_bank(SOUND_BANK);` where `SOUND_BANK` is the literal `"sound_bank_1"` — the entity hardcodes which asset bundle exists.
findings.suggestion: Take one `CharacterDef` (size, movement tuning, animation set, audio cues) plus a spawn descriptor `{position, team, player_num, viewport}` and already-resolved dependencies, with the builder doing all name→resource resolution. Drop `wep_type primary` — ask the weapon. Drop `wep_type secondary` until a secondary weapon exists.
findings.verify_note: Read Player.h:67-83, Player.cpp:9-45, PlayerBuilder.cpp:40-60.

findings.title: player_move_state conflates 'what surface am I on' with 'what motion am I performing'
findings.detail:
One enum mixes two orthogonal axes: contact (`ON_GROUND`, `ON_DROP_DOWN_GROUND`, `ON_RAMP_LEFT`, `ON_RAMP_RIGHT`, `ON_CEILING`) and motion (`JUMPING`, `DROPPING_DOWN`, `IN_AIR`). Consequently every 'am I grounded' test is a four-way OR, written three times: `is_on_ground()` (Player.cpp:1238-1244), `is_on_ramp()` (:1246-1250) and again inline in `on_no_collision` (:1256-1259) — which is precisely why `ON_CEILING` was forgotten in the third copy.

The surface identity is also encoded in the collision TYPE of the thing touched (`STRUCTURE_RAMP_LEFT`/`RIGHT`), which is what forces `on_structure_ramp_collision` to be a 115-line type/direction ladder with an empty branch and four copy-pasted bodies, and what forces the `RAMP_GRAVITY_MULTIPLIER = 20.0f` hack at Player.cpp:820-828 (2000 × 20 = 40,000 px/s² to keep the player stuck to a slope).
findings.suggestion: Split into a `GroundContact { bool grounded; Vector2F normal; const ICollisionGameObject* surface; }` produced by the collision system — the normal makes ramps fall out for free, deleting the RAMP_LEFT/RIGHT collision types, the per-ramp branch and the gravity multiplier — plus a small `motion_state { grounded, jumping, falling, dropping }`.

findings.title: MovingObject is 30 protected virtual accessors over three fields, inherited where a member belongs
findings.detail:
`MovingObject` has three data members (`_velocity`, `_dx`, `_rotation`, :54-56) and 30 protected `virtual` one-line accessors over them (:17-51). Exactly one is ever overridden anywhere in the codebase: `Player::get_velocity() const override` (Player.h:104), and it is overridden not to change behaviour — the body is `return MovingObject::get_velocity();` (Player.cpp:935-938) — but purely to widen access from protected to public so `DebugText.cpp:25` can read it. The class pays for a vtable and 30 virtual slots to achieve what a public member would.

Worse, the virtual layer is bypassed inconsistently within a single file: Player.cpp calls `MovingObject::get_velocity_x()`, `MovingObject::set_velocity_x(...)`, `MovingObject::alter_velocity_y(...)` with explicit qualification throughout (:767-853), which SUPPRESSES virtual dispatch, while other functions in the same file call the same accessors through `this->` (:606, :624, :910, :1009).

It is also inherited rather than composed: a Player is not a moving object, it has a velocity. Note this is what makes the diamond four-way instead of three-way.
findings.suggestion: Make it a plain value type (`struct RigidBody2D { Vector2F velocity, delta; }`) held as a member, non-virtual, and delete `Player::get_velocity` and every `MovingObject::` qualification. `_rotation` should not live here at all — it duplicates `DrawObject::_draw_rotation` and is never rendered.
findings.verify_note: Read MovingObject.h in full, Player.h:104, Player.cpp:935-938 and the qualified/unqualified call sites at 606, 624, 767-853, 910, 1009. Grepped for other overrides — none.

findings.title: Player.h includes CollisionTools.h for nothing and pulls the audio stack, rapidjson and D3D into every consumer
findings.detail:
Merges 2 candidates. `#include "CollisionTools.h"` (Player.h:14) — `CollisionTools` appears nowhere in the header; the only uses are in Player.cpp. `#include "SoundBank.h"` (:13) exists solely for the raw member `SoundBank* _sound_bank = nullptr;` (:168), which a forward declaration satisfies; SoundBank.h itself drags in `<Audio.h>` and `rapidjson/document.h`. `#include "Weapon.h"` (:8) pulls `ProjectileBuilder.h`, `WeaponDetails.h`, `TextureObject.h` → `ResourceManager.h` → D3D.

`Level.h` includes `Player.h`, so every translation unit that touches a level parses the JSON library, the audio library, D3D and the whole weapon/projectile system. With all first-party sources sitting flat in one directory and no library target, there is no place where 'engine' ends and 'game' begins — Player.h is where they fuse.
findings.suggestion: Drop the `CollisionTools.h` include outright and forward-declare `class SoundBank;`. Structurally: split into `engine/` (math, shapes, collision world, sprites, input, audio, resources, threading) and `game/` (player, weapons, projectiles, paint, menus), build `engine` as a static library, and forbid engine headers from including anything under `game/`. That boundary is what makes 'reusable engine' checkable rather than aspirational.
findings.verify_note: Read Player.h in full — no CollisionTools reference in the header. Confirmed SoundBank is only used as a raw pointer member.

findings.title: PlayerInput.h and PlayerBuilder.h are not self-contained — they compile only via the PCH and accidental transitive includes
findings.detail:
`PlayerInput.h` uses `DirectX::GamePad` in the constructor (:31) and the member (:38) but includes only `<vector>`, `PlayerInputData.h` and `MattMath.h`. I grepped the tree: the only `#include "GamePad.h"` anywhere is `pch.h:64`. Compile this header first in any TU without the PCH and it fails.

`PlayerBuilder.h` names `LevelLoadedInfo` (:17) and `ResourceManager` (:19) without including either — it resolves only because one of `Player.h`/`ViewportManager.h` transitively reaches `ResourceManager.h`, which itself includes `LevelLoadedInfo.h`. Removing one unrelated include anywhere in that chain breaks it.

For a project whose goal is a shippable reusable engine, headers that cannot be included standalone are a hard blocker.
findings.suggestion: Add `#include "GamePad.h"` to PlayerInput.h; forward-declare `class LevelLoadedInfo;` and `class ResourceManager;` in PlayerBuilder.h (both are used only as pointers). Verify with a build step that compiles each header alone with the PCH disabled.
findings.verify_note: Read PlayerInput.h and PlayerBuilder.h in full; grepped GamePad.h tree-wide (pch.h:64 only).

findings.title: PlayerInputData.h squats on the include guard that PlayerInput.h's own #endif comment claims
findings.detail:
`PlayerInputData.h:1-2` is `#ifndef PLAYER_INPUT_H / #define PLAYER_INPUT_H`. `PlayerInput.h:1-2` is `#ifndef PLAYERINPUT_H / #define PLAYERINPUT_H` but its closing line 41 reads `#endif // !PLAYER_INPUT_H` — it does not match its own `#define`.

Today this works, but `PlayerInput.h:5` includes `PlayerInputData.h`. The moment anyone 'tidies' PlayerInput.h's guard to match its trailing comment, `PlayerInputData.h` becomes a silently empty header and `PlayerInputData` vanishes with a confusing cascade of errors. The guard name also does not correspond to the file name, unlike every other header in the directory.
findings.suggestion: Rename PlayerInputData.h's guard to `PLAYER_INPUT_DATA_H` and fix PlayerInput.h's trailing comment. Or, since pch.h already uses `#pragma once` and the project is MSVC-only, switch all first-party headers to `#pragma once` and remove the bug class entirely.
findings.verify_note: Read both headers in full; the guard collision and the mismatched #endif comment are exactly as described.

findings.title: Ramp collisions resolve via a 40-iteration bisection with a dynamic_cast in the innermost loop
findings.detail:
`on_structure_ramp_collision` calls `CollisionTools::resolve_object_collision(&this->_rectangle, other->get_shape(), ...)` at :282, :291, :300 and :339. Ramps are triangles, so the rect/rect fast path at CollisionTools.cpp:244-248 is skipped and it falls into `bracket_object_collision_generic(..., BRACKET_ITERATIONS)` with `BRACKET_ITERATIONS = 40` (CollisionTools.h:7).

Each of the 40 iterations does `collider->intersects(collidee)`, and `Shape::intersects` dispatches through a `dynamic_cast` chain (MattMath.cpp:119-136) — an RTTI lookup in the innermost loop — plus a `pow(1.5f, i)` call (CollisionTools.cpp:40 or :50) and a `get_bounding_box()` returning `RectangleF` by value (:35, :58).

The iteration count is also nonsense at the tail: step size is `1/1.5^i`, so at i=40 that is ~8.6e-8 of the object's size — about 4.5e-6 px for a 52 px-wide player, far below float resolution at world coordinates in the thousands. Everything past roughly iteration 20 is pure waste.
findings.suggestion: Replace the bisection with an analytic push-out for rect-vs-right-triangle (compute the ramp surface y at the player's x and snap), and give `Shape` a proper double-dispatch or shape-type-indexed function table instead of `dynamic_cast`. If a search must survive, cut it to ~8 iterations with a precomputed step table.
findings.verify_note: Read CollisionTools.cpp:32-69 and 231-268, CollisionTools.h:7-8, MattMath.cpp:119-136. Confirmed the triangle path avoids the AABB fast path.

findings.title: Every corner collision heap-allocates a cloned Shape just to measure penetration depth
findings.detail:
All four diagonal handlers call `CollisionTools::calculate_object_collision_depth(...)` (:578, :592, :610, :628), which is implemented as:
```
std::unique_ptr<Shape> collider_copy = collider->clone();   // CollisionTools.cpp:275
resolve_object_collision(collider_copy.get(), collidee, collision_direction, amount);
return amount;
```
So each corner contact performs a heap allocation, a virtual clone, and a FULL collision resolution on the copy (including the 40-iteration bisection for non-rectangles) purely to measure a penetration depth that for two AABBs is `RectangleF::intersection(a, b)` — two subtractions. `on_bottom_left_collision`/`on_bottom_right_collision` are the common case of landing on a platform edge, so this runs repeatedly every frame for every player.
findings.suggestion: Compute the MTV directly: for rect/rect take the intersection extents; for the general case add a non-mutating, non-allocating `Shape::penetration_depth(const Shape*, const Vector2F&)`. Nothing here needs a clone.
findings.verify_note: Read Player.cpp:576-639 and CollisionTools.cpp:270-281.

findings.title: Player update and draw perform string-keyed std::map lookups every frame to find the sprite sheet and animation strip
findings.detail:
`AnimationObject::update()` (called from Player.cpp:702 every frame) goes `get_animation_strip()` → `get_sprite_sheet()` → `ResourceManager::get_sprite_sheet(_sheet_name)`, a `std::map<std::string, ...>` lookup (ResourceManager.cpp:46-58), then a second string-keyed lookup into the sheet's animation strips.

`Player::draw` repeats it: `TextureObject::draw` (:84) resolves the sheet and then the frame by name, and `AnimationObject::draw` (:87) resolves the sheet and the source rectangle via the strip. That is roughly 2 lookups per player per update and ~4 per player per viewport — 4 players × 4 viewports is ~64 red-black-tree traversals with string comparisons per frame for players alone, and the identical path runs for every projectile, which can number in the hundreds. The result is invariant between animation-state changes.

Note this also compounds the draw-race finding: `ResourceManager::get_sprite_sheet` uses non-const `map::operator[]` on a shared map from N threads, so a missing key would be a concurrent insert.
findings.suggestion: Resolve the `SpriteSheet*` and `const AnimationStrip*` once (at construction and again in the animation-state transition) and cache the pointers. Longer term, key resources by an opaque handle produced at load time rather than `std::string`, and use `unordered_map` at minimum.
findings.verify_note: Read Player.cpp:47-90/696-711, AnimationObject.h:48-56, ResourceManager.cpp:46-58, ResourceManager.h map declarations.

findings.title: Death is detected one frame late, and health regen / debug toggle run while dead
findings.detail:
Merges 2 candidates. `Player::update()` tests `if (this->_health <= 0.0f)` at :704, but damage is applied in `on_projectile_collision`, which `Level` invokes at Level.cpp:271 — AFTER every player's `update()` has already run (Level.cpp:193). So lethal damage taken on frame N is not noticed until frame N+1. During the intervening draw pass in the same tick, the player still renders alive, `get_collision_object_type()` still returns `PLAYER_TEAM_A`/`_B` rather than the `_DEAD` variants, and `is_colliding` still reports live collisions.

Separately, the debug toggle (:726-729) and the health-regen block (:732-740) sit OUTSIDE the `_state` if/else chain, so they execute for dead players too. `_health_regen_timer` accumulates for the whole 3 s `RESPAWN_DELAY`, so on respawn the 5 s `HEALTH_REGEN_DELAY` is already satisfied and regen is live from frame one — the delay only ever applies to the first hit of a life.

I rejected one sub-claim the reviewers made: `_damage_sound_timer` starting at 0.0f does not silence 'the first hit a player ever takes' in general, only a hit landing within the first 0.25 s of the match, since the timer accumulates every alive frame.
findings.suggestion: Check for death at the point damage is applied (and clamp at zero there) so state, collision type and rendering agree within one frame. Move the regen and debug blocks inside the ALIVE branch and reset `_health_regen_timer` in `respawn()`.
findings.verify_note: Read Player.cpp:645-741 and 96-127, Level.cpp:188-193 and 258-273. Confirmed damage lands after update; corrected the overstated damage-sound claim.

findings.title: player_consts.h is a dumping ground: per-TU dynamically-initialised strings, dead constants, and a stale duplicate of the level countdown UI block
findings.detail:
Merges 4 candidates. Three problems in one file.

1. **Per-TU copies.** ~13 `const std::string`s (:49-62) and six `const PlayerAnimationInfo` aggregates each holding three `std::string`s (:80-121) sit at namespace scope in a header. `const` at namespace scope gives internal linkage, so every TU that transitively includes Player.h gets its own copy — ~18 dynamically-constructed `std::string`s per TU at static-init time, before `main`, for pure compile-time data. `Player::get_animation_info` hands out references into Player.cpp's private copies; safe today, but a different address from what any other TU sees for the same logical constant. `DEFAULT_TEAM_COLOUR = colour_consts::GRAY` is worse — that is itself parsed from a hex `std::string` at static-init, a cross-header static-init-order dependency for a fixed RGB triple.

2. **Stale duplicate of level UI constants.** :71-78 declare `COUNTDOWN_TEXT`, `COUNTDOWN_FONT_NAME`, `COUNTDOWN_COLOUR`, `COUNTDOWN_SHADOW_COLOUR`, `COUNTDOWN_SCALE`, `COUNTDOWN_SHADOW_OFFSET`, `COUNTDOWN_TEXT_WIDTH/HEIGHT` — level-start UI settings with nothing to do with a Player. They duplicate `level_consts` (Level.h:35-42) with DIFFERENT values: font `gill_sans_mt_bold_72` vs `_144`, scale 1.0 vs 2.0, shadow offset {2,2} vs {5,5}. Level.cpp uses `using namespace level_consts;`, so the player copies have zero readers — and if any TU ever pulls in both using-directives, every `COUNTDOWN_*` reference becomes ambiguous.

3. **Dead constants:** `DEFAULT_COLLISION_BOUNDS` (:23), `STARTING_DX` (:24), `STARTING_VELOCITY` (:25), `JUMP_POWER` (:33) — no call sites. Spelling is also inconsistent within the file: `const std::string DEFAULT_SHEET` (:49) vs `const static std::string COUNTDOWN_TEXT` (:71); `constexpr auto DEFAULT_TEAM` hides the type for no benefit.
findings.suggestion: Delete the COUNTDOWN block and the four dead constants. Move to `inline constexpr std::string_view` / `inline constexpr` aggregates (C++17) so there is one object across the program with zero dynamic init. Longer term, replace the asset-name literals with a data-driven `CharacterDef { size; MovementTuning; AnimationSet; AudioCues; }` loaded from JSON, so an engine user defines a character in data rather than by editing a C++ header.
findings.verify_note: Read player_consts.h in full and Level.h:35-48. Confirmed the value divergence between the two COUNTDOWN blocks and grepped the four dead constants.

findings.title: Inconsistent float-zero comparison for the same velocity, plus an unnamed 600.0f walk/run threshold
findings.detail:
Merges 3 candidates. `update_movement` mixes epsilon and exact comparison of the same two values within one if/else chain: `are_equal(MovingObject::get_velocity_x(), 0.0f) && x_input != 0.0f` (:767) versus `MovingObject::get_velocity_x() > 0.0f && are_equal(x_input, 0.0f)` (:802). `calculate_animation_state` then tests the same velocity with a bare exact compare: `if (velocity_x == 0.0f)` (:1010).

The project builds with `<FloatingPointModel>Fast</FloatingPointModel>` in all four configurations (verified in ArtAttack.vcxproj), and `MattMath::EPSILON` is 1e-4, so a velocity of 5e-5 is 'zero' to the movement code and non-zero to the animation code — the player is treated as stopped for physics while playing the walk clip.

`600.0f` (:1014) is an unnamed walk/run threshold sitting between the named `X_INITIAL_VELOCITY` (100) and `MAX_VELOCITY.x` (800) in `player_consts`. Same category: `player_and_weapon_rect.inflate(Vector2F(200.0f, 200.0f))` (:919) is an unnamed culling margin that exists only because the player's `_rectangle` covers the body while `draw` also renders `_primary` — a hand-tuned guess whose failure mode is invisible pop-in rather than a compile error.

Also in the same chain and genuinely wrong: the two opposite-direction branches (:790-800) apply BOTH `X_DEACCELERATION * dt * x_input` and `X_ACCELERATION * dt * x_input` and, unlike the same-direction branches above them, never clamp to `±MAX_VELOCITY.x`.
findings.suggestion: Use `are_equal(v, 0.0f)` everywhere for velocity. Move `600.0f` and the cull margin into `player_consts` as named constants (and better, derive the cull bounds as the union of `_rectangle` and `_primary->get_draw_bounds()`). Collapse the seven-branch chain into one signed-acceleration computation followed by a single clamp.
findings.verify_note: Read Player.cpp:756-866, 916-921, 1004-1021; player_consts.h:26-29; grepped ArtAttack.vcxproj for FloatingPointModel (Fast in all four configs).

findings.title: get_player_move_state_string omits DROPPING_DOWN and allocates a std::string per call
findings.detail:
Merges 2 candidates. `player_move_state` has eight enumerators (Player.h:22-32); the switch handles seven. `DROPPING_DOWN` is missing, so the debug overlay reports `"invalid"` whenever the player is dropping through a jump-through platform — exactly the state you would be debugging. It is a reachable state, set at Player.cpp:845.

Because there is no `default` label and an enumerator is unhandled, MSVC at /W4 emits C4062 here. The project sets `Level4` but never `TreatWarningAsError` (verified in the vcxproj), which is why this and the C4189 dead local at :271 have gone unnoticed.

The function also returns `std::string` by value from string literals, heap-allocating once per player per frame for the debug overlay. There is a stray `;` after the switch's closing brace.
findings.suggestion: Add `case player_move_state::DROPPING_DOWN: return "dropping_down";`, return `const char*` (the literals have static storage duration), and keep the switch `default`-less so C4062 keeps guarding it as the enum grows. Turn on warnings-as-errors, or at least read them.
findings.verify_note: Read Player.h:22-32, Player.cpp:835-845 and 1216-1236; grepped the vcxproj (WarningLevel Level4 ×4, no TreatWarningAsError).

findings.title: direction.h and direction_lock.h are dead files, and direction.h would break any TU that also uses MattMath
findings.detail:
Merges 3 candidates. I grepped the whole tree: neither header is `#include`d by any source file — the only references are `ArtAttack.vcxproj:195-196` and the two matching `.filters` entries.

`direction.h` is not merely dead, it is a landmine. It declares a global-scope `enum class direction { TOP_LEFT, TOP, ..., BOTTOM_RIGHT }` (nine anchor positions) whose name collides with `MattMath::direction { NONE, UP, DOWN, LEFT, RIGHT, UP_LEFT, ... }` (a compass enum). `Player.cpp:5` has `using namespace MattMath;` and then uses the unqualified name as a TYPE at :366 (`direction dir = velocity.get_direction();`), :606 and :624. Including direction.h anywhere into that TU makes every one of those an ambiguity error. The same file also uses `direction` as a VARIABLE name at :247 and :488, so within one file the identifier is a type in some scopes and a local in others.
findings.suggestion: Delete both headers and their vcxproj/filters entries. If a nine-way anchor is wanted later, name it `anchor_point` and namespace it. Rename the `Vector2F direction` locals in Player.cpp to `collision_direction`.
findings.verify_note: Read both headers; grepped the tree for `direction.h` and `direction_lock` — only vcxproj and filters hits. Read MattMath.h:12-23 for the colliding enum and Player.cpp:5/247/366/488/606/624.

findings.title: FLT_MIN used as an 'unset' sentinel for frame_time and compared with exact != under /fp:fast
findings.detail:
Merges 2 candidates.
```
// if frame_time is FLT_MIN, then the frame_time will be set to the default
float frame_time = FLT_MIN;
```
consumed at Player.cpp:66 as `if (info.frame_time != FLT_MIN) { set_frame_time(...); } else { set_frame_time_to_default(); }`.

Three problems: (1) a sentinel inside the value domain instead of an explicit optional; (2) exact float `!=` in a project built with `/fp:fast` in all four configurations, three lines of code away from `update_movement` which correctly uses `are_equal(...)` for its float comparisons; (3) `FLT_MIN` is the smallest positive NORMAL float (~1.18e-38), a perfectly legal (if absurd) frame time, and `<cfloat>` is not included by player_consts.h — it arrives transitively.
findings.suggestion: `std::optional<float> frame_time;` once the project moves off its implicit C++14. Until then, an explicit `bool use_default_frame_time = true;` field, or a negative default with `frame_time <= 0.0f` meaning 'use the strip default'. Add `#include <cfloat>` if the constant survives.
findings.verify_note: Read player_consts.h:8-16 and 80-121, Player.cpp:57-74; confirmed no <cfloat> include and /fp:fast in the vcxproj.

findings.title: Pause and debug toggles fire on button RELEASE while their comments say press, and three if/else blocks that reduce to one assignment each
findings.suggestion: Either fix both to `current.X && !previous.X` to match jump, or correct the comments so the intent is unambiguous. Collapse the three blocks to direct assignments.
findings.verify_note: Read PlayerInput.cpp:38-117 and Player.cpp:726-729.

findings.title: PlayerBuilder heap-allocates a stateless WeaponBuilder in order to make a static call
findings.detail:
Merges 2 candidates. `PlayerBuilder::PlayerBuilder() { this->_weapon_builder = std::make_unique<WeaponBuilder>(); }` backs `std::unique_ptr<WeaponBuilder> _weapon_builder = nullptr;` (PlayerBuilder.h:23), used as `this->_weapon_builder->build_weapon(...)` (:47).

`WeaponBuilder` has no data members at all and its single function is `static` (WeaponBuilder.h:10-22). So this is a heap allocation, an owning pointer and a pointer dereference purely to make a static call. It also silently makes `PlayerBuilder` non-copyable and leaves a nullable member that the `const` `build_players` dereferences without checking. The constructor also assigns in the body rather than in the member-init list.
findings.suggestion: Delete the member and the constructor, and write `WeaponBuilder::build_weapon(...)` at :47. Since `WeaponBuilder` is a stateless bag of one static function, it should be a namespace, not a class.
findings.verify_note: Read PlayerBuilder.h:10-24, PlayerBuilder.cpp:8-11 and 47, WeaponBuilder.h in full.

findings.title: Three by-value accessors deep-copy whole vectors, and a range-for binds non-const refs into the temporary
findings.suggestion: Make the three accessors return `const std::vector<T>&`, then write `const auto& team_a_spawns = ...;` and `for (const auto& setting : ...)`. Zero copies, and no reliance on lifetime extension.
findings.verify_note: Read PlayerBuilder.cpp:21-27, LevelLoadedInfo.h:16-18, MenuLevelSettings.h:14.

findings.title: const RectangleF& bound to a by-value temporary, then the identical temporary recomputed nine lines later
findings.detail:
Merges 2 candidates.
```
const RectangleF& other_rect = other->get_shape()->get_bounding_box();   // :371
bool was_above = this->_prev_rectangle.get_bottom() <= other_rect.get_top();
...
const RectangleF& rect = other->get_shape()->get_bounding_box();         // :380
this->_rectangle.set_position_y_from_bottom(rect.get_top());
```
`Shape::get_bounding_box()` returns `RectangleF` by VALUE (MattMath.h, and every override). Binding a `const&` is legal via lifetime extension, but it reads as a borrowed reference into `other` — the single most common way this pattern becomes a dangling reference when someone later returns it or stores it in a member. `other_rect` and `rect` are the same value under two names, obtained by two virtual calls.
findings.suggestion: Compute it once as a value — `const RectangleF other_rect = other->get_shape()->get_bounding_box();` — and use it at both sites. Reserve `const T&` for things that genuinely outlive the expression.
findings.verify_note: Read Player.cpp:360-388 and MattMath.h's Shape::get_bounding_box declaration (returns by value).

findings.title: The no-camera draw overload omits the team-colour layer, the facing flip and the dead check
findings.suggestion: Delegate: `draw(sprite_batch, Camera::DEFAULT_CAMERA);`. Better, drop the two-overload scheme from `IGameObject` entirely — `Camera::DEFAULT_CAMERA` already expresses 'no camera', so one method suffices.
findings.verify_note: Read Player.cpp:47-95; grepped Level.cpp — only the camera overload is ever called.

findings.title: Constructor drops animation_info.frame_time and starts _animation_state inconsistent with the strip it loaded
findings.detail:
The constructor forwards `animation_info.sprite_sheet`/`animation`/`uniform_texture` to the two sprite bases (:27-31) but silently ignores `animation_info.frame_time`. The only place `frame_time` is ever honoured is `draw()` (:66-73), and only on a state CHANGE — so a caller passing a custom `frame_time` gets it dropped until the state happens to change.

`_animation_state` is declared `= player_animation_state::IDLE` (Player.h:154) while `PlayerBuilder` constructs every player with `DEFAULT_ANIMATION_INFO` (PlayerBuilder.cpp:42), which is the WALK strip (`DEFAULT_ANIMATION_STRIP = "player_right_walk"`, player_consts.h:50/80-86). The object therefore starts claiming IDLE while displaying the walking animation.

Graded low because I traced that it self-corrects: `_move_state` starts as `IN_AIR` and velocity is zero, so the first `calculate_animation_state()` returns JUMPING ≠ IDLE and the transition block repairs it on the first draw. But construct a Player grounded at zero velocity and the walk strip renders while idle indefinitely.
findings.suggestion: Apply the full `animation_info` — including `frame_time` — through one private `apply_animation_info(const PlayerAnimationInfo&)` used by both the constructor and the state transition, and initialise `_animation_state` from that same info instead of hardcoding IDLE. Point `DEFAULT_ANIMATION_INFO` at `ANIMATION_INFO_IDLE`.
findings.verify_note: Read Player.cpp:9-45/47-90/1004-1047, Player.h:153-154, player_consts.h:49-51/80-121, PlayerBuilder.cpp:42.

findings.title: get_velocity is overridden only to widen protected access to public
findings.detail: `const MattMath::Vector2F& get_velocity() const override;` is declared in Player's PUBLIC section and its body is a bare forward: `return MovingObject::get_velocity();` (Player.cpp:935-938). It changes no behaviour — it exists solely because `MovingObject`'s accessors are `protected` and `DebugText.cpp:25` needs to read the velocity. That is access laundering dressed as polymorphism, and it is the only override of any of the 30 `MovingObject` virtuals in the entire codebase.
findings.suggestion: Drop `virtual` from the `MovingObject` accessor block, make the getters public and the mutators protected, and delete `Player::get_velocity`. Then remove the `MovingObject::` qualification from every call site in Player.cpp (they suppress dispatch anyway).
findings.verify_note: Read Player.h:104, Player.cpp:935-938, MovingObject.h:16-51, DebugText.cpp:25. Grepped for other overrides of MovingObject members — none.

findings.title: get_collision_object_type recomputes a two-level switch, and can throw, on every collision-pair test
findings.detail:
This virtual re-derives a value from two members that change at most a few times per match, and its default arms `throw std::exception(...)`. `Level::update_level_logic` calls it once per (collision object, player) pair — `Projectile::is_matching_collision_object_type` calls `other->get_collision_object_type()` (Projectile.cpp:96) for every projectile against every player (Level.cpp:268), and `Player::is_colliding` does the mirror for every object (Player.cpp:145). With 4 players and a few hundred live projectiles that is thousands of calls per frame on a throwing function the optimiser cannot inline across the vtable.

It also means an invalid `player_team`/`player_state` surfaces as an exception thrown from a getter deep inside the collision loop rather than at the point the bad value was set. Graded low because the per-call cost is small; the design smell (throwing query, derived-state recomputation) is the real point.
findings.suggestion: Store the derived `collision_object_type` as a member updated in `set_state`/`set_team` — the only two mutators. Better still, replace the 23-value cross-product enum with a `{category, team}` pair so the type is a trivial field read.
findings.verify_note: Read Player.cpp:96-127 and 142-185, Projectile.cpp:93-119, Level.cpp:222-293.

findings.title: Raw C array with the literal 4 repeated five times, a redundant constructor loop, and a per-frame heap allocation
findings.detail:
Merges 3 candidates. `RawPlayerInput _prev_inputs[4]` (PlayerInput.h:34), `RawPlayerInput current[4]` (:121) and two `for (int i = 0; i < 4; i++)` loops (:122, :127) — the magic 4 appears five times with no named constant, even though `player_input_consts` (PlayerInput.h:8-13) is the obvious home for a `MAX_PADS`.

The constructor body is dead code: `for (auto& _prev_input : this->_prev_inputs) { _prev_input = RawPlayerInput(); }` — `RawPlayerInput` has NSDMIs on every member (PlayerInput.h:17-25), so the array is already correctly initialised before the body runs; the loop default-constructs and copy-assigns four times for nothing. The loop variable is named `_prev_input`, a leading-underscore name the rest of the codebase reserves for members.

`update_and_get_player_inputs` also constructs a fresh `std::vector<PlayerInputData>` every frame (:126) with no `reserve`, so it heap-allocates and reallocates (1→2→4) on the way to at most four elements, every frame, forever — and the result is copied again into `GameLevel::update`'s local (GameStates.cpp:141-142).
findings.suggestion: `std::array<RawPlayerInput, player_input_consts::MAX_PADS> _prev_inputs{};`, iterate with `.size()`, and delete the constructor body entirely: `PlayerInput(DirectX::GamePad* gamepad) : _gamepad(gamepad) {}`. Returning a fixed-size `std::array` also fixes the index-mapping bug reported separately and removes the allocation.
findings.verify_note: Read PlayerInput.h in full, PlayerInput.cpp:8-15 and 119-138, GameStates.cpp:141-142.

findings.title: Debug-overlay visibility is a boolean on the character entity, toggled inside its simulation update
findings.detail:
`if (this->_input.toggle_debug) { this->_showing_debug = !this->_showing_debug; }` inside `Player::update`, read back by `Level::draw_player_view_level` at Level.cpp:572 to decide whether to run `DebugText::draw_debug_info`, and also passed into `_primary->draw(..., this->_showing_debug)` at Player.cpp:89.

Whether a developer overlay is on screen is a property of the debug tooling and the view, not of a simulated character. It forces the flag to replicate per player and forces `get_showing_debug`/`set_showing_debug` into the entity's API (Player.h:115, 246 — the setter is dead).
findings.suggestion: Give the engine a `DebugOverlay` subsystem owning its own visibility keyed by view index, subscribing to a `toggle_debug` action. `Player` should not know a debug HUD exists.
findings.verify_note: Read Player.cpp:89/726-729, Player.h:115/149/246, Level.cpp:571-578.

findings.title: PlayerInputData copied redundantly — once into a local that is then bypassed, and three more times through the by-value weapon API
findings.detail:
Merges 2 candidates. `update_movement` opens with `const PlayerInputData input = this->_input;` (:758), uses it for exactly one field (`input.x_movement`, :759), and then goes back to the member directly for the next two reads (`this->_input.left_analog_stick.y` :762, `this->_input.jump_pressed` :764). The copy buys nothing and misleads.

`Player::update_weapon_and_get_projectiles` passes `this->get_input()` (a `const&`) into `Weapon::update_and_get_projectiles(PlayerInputData input, ...)` — by VALUE (Weapon.h:36, and again in the `RelativeVelocityWeapon` override at Weapon.h:164) — which then passes it by value again into `update_movement_and_rotation(PlayerInputData input, ...)` (Weapon.h:110) and `check_if_shooting_and_ammo_update(PlayerInputData input, ...)` (Weapon.h:106). Three full-struct copies (~56 bytes each) per player per frame for a parameter nobody mutates. Graded low — the cost is trivial; the point is that four signatures are wrong by default.
findings.suggestion: Delete the local at :758 (bind `const PlayerInputData& input = this->_input;` if a short name is wanted) and change all four `Weapon` signatures to `const PlayerInputData&`.
findings.verify_note: Read Player.cpp:742-764, Weapon.h:35-39/104-112/162-166, Weapon.cpp:168-233, PlayerInputData.h:7-23.

findings.title: Player owns a unique_ptr<Weapon> but declares no special members, and never null-checks the weapon it is handed
findings.detail:
`Player` owns `std::unique_ptr<Weapon> _primary` (Player.h:142) plus three raw non-owning pointers and declares no destructor, no copy operations and no move operations. The implicit copy is deleted by the `unique_ptr` — correct, but by accident. The implicit MOVE operations are declared and not deleted (every base is at least copyable), so `Player p2 = std::move(p1);` compiles and leaves `p1` fully live with `_primary == nullptr`, while every use of `_primary` is unguarded (Player.cpp:89, 94, 643, 745, 1000, 1050, 1179).

The constructor also takes `std::unique_ptr<Weapon> primary_weapon` and stores it (:32) without checking for null, even though the class dereferences it at seven sites and nothing in the API says a weapon is mandatory.

Graded low, not medium: Players live in a `vector<unique_ptr<Player>>` and are never relocated, and `PlayerBuilder` always supplies a weapon, so neither hole is currently reachable.
findings.suggestion: Declare intent explicitly — `Player(const Player&) = delete; Player& operator=(const Player&) = delete; Player(Player&&) = delete; Player& operator=(Player&&) = delete;` — and throw/assert in the constructor body if `_primary == nullptr`, so the invariant is enforced once instead of assumed at seven call sites.
findings.verify_note: Read Player.h:63-83/142, Player.cpp:32 and all seven _primary dereferences, PlayerBuilder.cpp:40-62, Level.h:101-102.

findings.title: No LanguageStandard element, so the project silently builds as C++14 on toolset v145
findings.detail:
Several candidates in this group proposed `std::optional`, `std::string_view`, `inline constexpr` and designated initialisers as fixes, all of which are unavailable. I grepped the vcxproj: `<PlatformToolset>v145</PlatformToolset>` in all four configurations, `<WarningLevel>Level4</WarningLevel>` ×4, `<ConformanceMode>true</ConformanceMode>` ×4, `<FloatingPointModel>Fast</FloatingPointModel>` ×4 — and no `<LanguageStandard>` element at all, so MSVC defaults to `/std:c++14`. There is also no `<TreatWarningAsError>`, which is why the C4189 at Player.cpp:271 and the C4062 at Player.cpp:1218 have gone unnoticed.

A 2026 toolset building a 2014 standard is leaving `optional`, `string_view`, `inline` variables, structured bindings, `if constexpr` and guaranteed copy elision on the table — several of which are the natural fix for findings above.
findings.suggestion: Add `<LanguageStandard>stdcpp20</LanguageStandard>` (or at minimum `stdcpp17`) to all four configurations, and turn on `<TreatWarningAsError>true</TreatWarningAsError>` once the existing /W4 backlog is cleared.
findings.verify_note: Grepped ArtAttack.vcxproj for PlatformToolset, WarningLevel, FloatingPointModel, LanguageStandard, ConformanceMode, TreatWarningAsError. LanguageStandard and TreatWarningAsError are absent.

findings.title: stop_sounds() throws for Sniper and Bucket, terminating the process at the end of every round
findings.detail: `Weapon::stop_sounds() const` (Weapon.cpp:252-257) is non-virtual and unconditionally calls `get_sound_effect_instance_name()` (Weapon.cpp:258-277), whose switch handles only SPRAYER, ROLLER and MISTER and ends in `default: throw std::exception("Weapon::get_sound_effect_instance_name() - invalid weapon type")`. SNIPER and BUCKET are buildable (WeaponBuilder.cpp:22, :34) and selectable in the weapon-select menu (MainMenu.cpp:1589, :1601). They dodge the throw during play only because WeaponSniper.cpp:28-35 and WeaponBucket.cpp:28-35 override `handle_shoot_sound` to use `play_wave`; neither overrides `stop_sounds`, which is not virtual anyway. The path is unconditional and hit every match: Level.cpp:135 `this->stop_player_sounds();` on the ACTIVE->ZOOM_OUT transition -> Level.cpp:323-329 loops every player -> Player.cpp:1048-1050 -> `_primary->stop_sounds()`. There is no try/catch anywhere on the tick path (grep of Main.cpp and Game.cpp finds none), so the exception reaches std::terminate. Merged from four independent reports.
findings.suggestion: Stop keying sound identity off `wep_type`. Resolve the looping instance name (or nullptr/empty for wave-based weapons) once in the Weapon constructor from data in `WeaponDetails`, and make `stop_sounds()` a no-op when there is none. A teardown path must never throw. Adding an explicit SNIPER/BUCKET case plus `virtual stop_sounds()` is the minimum patch, but the data-driven fix removes the whole class of bug.
findings.verify_note: Read Weapon.cpp:252-277 (switch + throw), Weapon.h:44 (non-virtual), WeaponSniper.h:22 / WeaponBucket.h:23 (only handle_shoot_sound overridden), WeaponBuilder.cpp:22/:34, MainMenu.cpp:1589/:1601, Level.cpp:135 and :323-329, Player.cpp:1048-1050. Grepped Main.cpp/Game.cpp for try/catch: none.

findings.title: Weapon::draw mutates shared per-object state and is executed concurrently on several render threads
findings.detail:
`Weapon::draw` is non-const and writes four members of its own base subobjects before issuing the batch call: `TextureObject::set_element_name(get_details().frame_name)` (Weapon.cpp:61, assigns `SpriteSheetObject::_element_name`, a `std::string` - SpriteSheetObject.h:26), `DrawObject::set_origin`, `set_effects`, `set_draw_rotation` (:62-64), and again in the debug branch (:71-78). `WeaponRoller::draw` additionally writes `_colour` (WeaponRoller.cpp:90-97).

That object is shared across threads. `Level::draw_active_level` (Level.cpp:379-399) partitions the players and submits one `ThreadPool` task per partition; `Partitioner::partition` (Partitioner.cpp:4-22) yields one partition per player while players <= threads, and `ThreadPool` is a real Win32 pool with `SetThreadpoolThreadMaximum(16)` (ThreadPool.cpp:15-18). Each task runs `Level::draw_player_view_level`, which at Level.cpp:534-540 loops over **all** `_player_objects` - so with N players, player 0's `Player::draw` (Player.cpp:47-89) and therefore `this->_primary->draw(...)` is entered by N threads simultaneously. Unsynchronised concurrent write/write on a `std::string` is UB and can tear the pointer/size/capacity triple.

Downstream is worse: `SpriteSheetObject::get_sprite_sheet()` reaches `ResourceManager::get_sprite_sheet`, which is `this->_sprite_sheets[name]` - `std::map::operator[]`, a mutating call - from all those threads at once (ResourceManager.cpp:46-58).
findings.suggestion: Make drawing a pure read. Compute element name / origin / effects / rotation / colour into locals and pass them as arguments to a `const` `TextureObject::draw(...)`, then declare `Weapon::draw` and the whole `IGameObject::draw` chain `const` so the compiler enforces it. Separately, change `ResourceManager::get_*` and `SpriteSheet::draw` to use `find()`/`at()` so lookups cannot mutate the container. Resolving the `SpriteSheet*` and `SpriteFrame` once at construction removes both the race and the per-frame lookups.
findings.verify_note: Read Weapon.cpp:36-82, WeaponRoller.cpp:59-115, SpriteSheetObject.h (private std::string _element_name), DrawObject.h:34-40, Level.cpp:379-399 and :490-540, Partitioner.cpp, ThreadPool.cpp:4-47 (Win32 pool, max 16 threads), Player.cpp:47-89, ResourceManager.cpp:46-58.

findings.title: Weapon is a god class welded to DirectX and to Splatoon's team/player concepts - the core obstacle to engine reuse
findings.detail:
Merging four related design reports, all verified:

1. `class Weapon : public TextureObject` (Weapon.h:14) - a weapon *is* a sprite frame. Weapon.h therefore transitively pulls in SpriteSheetObject.h -> DrawObject.h -> ResourceManager.h -> D3D/SpriteBatch, so the whole weapon module compiles against DirectX. A weapon with two sprites, no sprite, or particle-only presentation cannot exist.
2. One type owns six responsibilities: rendering (`draw`, Weapon.cpp:36-82), input interpretation (`update_movement_and_rotation` reads `input.shoot_direction_requested` / `input.shoot_angle`, Weapon.cpp:283-285), ammo economy (`_ammo`/`_ammo_timer`, :217-227), fire timing (`_shoot_timer` vs `_details.shoot_interval`, :202), audio (owns a `SoundBank*`, names per-team instances, :236-277), and object spawning (owns a `ProjectileBuilder`, returns owned `ICollisionGameObject`s, :313-328). None of the pure arithmetic (ammo regen, fire rate) can be unit-tested without a live `ResourceManager` with loaded sheets and sound banks.
3. The base constructor takes `player_team team, int player_num, const Colour& team_colour, wep_type type` and stores all four (Weapon.h:135-138). `player_team` is a closed A/B/NONE enum; `_player_num` exists only to index eight hardcoded sound names; `_team_colour` is a paint rule. All four are forwarded verbatim into `ProjectileBuilder::build_projectiles` (Weapon.cpp:319-327) - the weapon is a conduit for game rules it never uses.
4. Both update entry points take the game's gamepad struct `PlayerInputData` by value (Weapon.h:36, 106, 110) and read exactly three of its thirteen fields. An AI turret or replay system would have to fabricate a `PlayerInputData` including a `connection_state` (PlayerInputData.h:7-23) to pull a trigger.
findings.suggestion: Decompose: an immutable `WeaponDefinition` (already almost `WeaponDetails`), a `FireControl { bool try_fire(dt); }`, an `AmmoPool`, a data-driven audio policy, and a separate render component that consumes an emitted `WeaponRenderState`. Replace `PlayerInputData` with a tiny engine-level `WeaponIntent { bool fire; bool aim_requested; float aim_angle; }` that the game maps onto in one place. Replace team/player/colour with one opaque `OwnerId` plus a game-supplied spawn payload forwarded untouched. Rendering becomes a member/observer, not a base class.
findings.verify_note: Read the whole of Weapon.h and Weapon.cpp; confirmed the inheritance from TextureObject, the six responsibility clusters at the cited lines, the four game-specific members at Weapon.h:135-138 forwarded at Weapon.cpp:319-327, and PlayerInputData.h's 13 fields against the three actually read (Weapon.cpp:194, 283-285).

findings.title: The base class switches on wep_type to name sounds, so Weapon knows the full list of its own subclasses
findings.detail:
`Weapon::get_sound_effect_instance_name()` is `switch (this->get_type())` returning `SPRAYER_SOUND_DETAILS.get_sound_name(...)` / `ROLLER_...` / `MISTER_...` with a throwing default. This is an enum switch standing in for polymorphism, located *in the base class*: adding a sixth weapon requires editing Weapon.cpp, and two of the five existing subclasses deliberately fall into the throwing default. Meanwhile `WeaponDetails::shoot_sound_name` (WeaponDetails.h:47) is populated for all five weapons but read only by Sniper and Bucket (WeaponSniper.cpp:32, WeaponBucket.cpp:32).

The same shape produces two byte-identical 6-line overrides: `WeaponSniper::handle_shoot_sound` (WeaponSniper.cpp:28-35) and `WeaponBucket::handle_shoot_sound` (WeaponBucket.cpp:28-35) are character-for-character the same. The difference they encode - one-shot crack vs continuous hiss - is a property of the *sound asset*, not of the class. It is also why `_sound_bank` and `_details` had to be made `protected` (Weapon.h:47-48).
findings.suggestion: Add `enum class shoot_sound_mode { NONE, ONE_SHOT, LOOPED; }` plus the resolved instance name to `WeaponDetails`, implement `handle_shoot_sound` once branching on data, and delete both overrides, the type switch, and the three separate `*_SOUND_DETAILS` tables. `_sound_bank`/`_details` can then go back to private, and `stop_sounds()` becomes total (see the critical finding).
findings.verify_note: Read Weapon.cpp:258-277, WeaponSniper.cpp:28-35 and WeaponBucket.cpp:28-35 (identical bodies), WeaponDetails.h:47, Weapon.h:47-48.

findings.title: All weapon tuning is a compile-time C++ table in a header while the rest of the content pipeline is data-driven JSON
findings.detail:
weapon_consts.h holds twelve namespace-scope aggregates (`DETAILS_DEFAULT` :14, `DETAILS_RELATIVE_DEFAULT` :30, `DETAILS_SPRAYER` :36, `DETAILS_RELATIVE_SPRAYER` :52, `SPRAYER_SOUND_DETAILS` :58, `DETAILS_SNIPER` :70, `DETAILS_ROLLER` :86, `ROLLER_SOUND_DETAILS` :102, `DETAILS_MISTER` :114, `DETAILS_RELATIVE_MISTER` :130, `MISTER_SOUND_DETAILS` :136, `DETAILS_BUCKET` :148, `DETAILS_RELATIVE_BUCKET` :164) built by positional aggregate initialisation with field names only in trailing comments. Changing a fire rate recompiles the game, while levels and sound banks already load from rapidjson (`SoundBank::load_from_json`, `LevelObjectBuilder`).

The positional style has already drifted: `DETAILS_DEFAULT` (:16-20) has five unlabelled leading values, and `DETAILS_ROLLER` sets `starting_vel_length` to `0.0f` (:92) against a struct default of `1100.0f` (WeaponDetails.h:41) with no explanation. The table also couples to the projectile table at namespace scope - `nozzle_offset` is `projectile_consts::DETAILS_SPRAY.size.x / 2.0f` (:40, and likewise :74, :90, :118, :152).

Separately, every one of these is `static` at namespace scope in a header, i.e. internal linkage: one dynamically-initialised copy **per translation unit**. `WeaponDetails` has five `std::string` members (WeaponDetails.h:43-47) and `SoundEffectInstanceWeaponDetails` has eight (WeaponDetails.h:23-30), so each TU runs ~50 `std::string` constructions before `main`. weapon_consts.h reaches Weapon.h:7 -> all five Weapon*.h -> WeaponBuilder.h -> PlayerBuilder.h, and Player.h -> Level.h onwards, so this is multiplied a dozen-plus times.
findings.suggestion: Move weapon definitions to `weapons.json` loaded into a `WeaponRegistry`, mirroring how levels load - the engine ships the struct and the registry, the game ships the data. As an interim step, declare the tables `extern const` in the header and define them once in a `weapon_consts.cpp`; once the project moves off its default C++14 (see the vcxproj finding), `inline constexpr` with `std::string_view` removes the dynamic initialisation entirely.
findings.verify_note: Read all of weapon_consts.h and WeaponDetails.h; confirmed `static` linkage on every aggregate, the std::string member counts, the unlabelled DETAILS_DEFAULT block, the roller's 0.0f starting_vel_length against the struct default, and the projectile_consts cross-references.

findings.title: _sound_bank comes from a lookup that silently returns nullptr on a bad name and is then dereferenced unguarded every frame
findings.suggestion: Fail loudly at construction: `if (!_sound_bank) throw std::runtime_error("weapon sound bank '" + details.sound_bank_name + "' not loaded");`, and assert `resource_manager != nullptr` on the same line. Independently, `ResourceManager::get_sound_bank`/`get_sprite_sheet` must use `find()`/`at()` so a missing key is reported rather than inserted.
findings.verify_note: Read Weapon.cpp:32-33 and the five deref sites; read ResourceManager.cpp:90-101 and :46-58 confirming operator[] inside a dead try/catch; counted the six "sound_bank_1" literals in weapon_consts.h.

findings.title: Dead players keep firing, burning ammo and looping the shoot sound from the corpse
findings.detail: `Level::update_level_logic` (Level.cpp:189-212) calls `object->update_weapon_and_get_projectiles()` for every player unconditionally, and `Player::update_weapon_and_get_projectiles` (Player.cpp:742-750) forwards straight to `_primary->update_and_get_projectiles(get_input(), ...)` with no `player_state` check. `Player::update` (Player.cpp:696-721) only branches ALIVE/DEAD for movement and leaves `_input` untouched while dead. `Player::draw` early-returns when DEAD (Player.cpp:49-52), so the weapon disappears visually while `Weapon::check_if_shooting_and_ammo_update` keeps running: it spends ammo, spawns projectiles from the death position, and `handle_shoot_sound` (Weapon.cpp:231, 236-251) keeps the looping effect playing for the whole respawn delay. `Player::respawn` calls `reset_ammo()` (Player.cpp:1000), which hides the ammo half of the symptom.
findings.suggestion: Gate it in `Player::update_weapon_and_get_projectiles`: `if (_state != player_state::ALIVE) { _primary->stop_sounds(); return {}; }`. Better for the engine goal, give `Weapon` an explicit `set_active(bool)` so "this weapon should not act this frame" is expressible at the weapon API instead of being every caller's responsibility. Note the `stop_sounds()` call must be made non-throwing first.
findings.verify_note: Read Level.cpp:189-212, Player.cpp:742-750, Player.cpp:696-721, Player.cpp:47-52, Player.cpp:992-1002, Weapon.cpp:188-251.

findings.title: Looping shoot sound is only ever stopped from inside the per-frame update, so it survives pause and outlives the weapon
findings.detail:
`handle_shoot_sound` (Weapon.cpp:236-251) is the only place a looping effect is started or stopped, and its sole call site is Weapon.cpp:231 inside `check_if_shooting_and_ammo_update`. `Weapon` declares no destructor, so the acquired looping `SoundEffectInstance` (owned by the `SoundBank`, which outlives the level) has no automatic release path.

Verified consequences:
- Pause: GameStates.cpp:143-148 sets `game_level_state::PAUSE_MENU`, and the ACTIVE branch (GameStates.cpp:181-185) is the only caller of `_level->update`. Pausing while holding fire leaves the loop running for the duration of the pause menu.
- Teardown: `stop_player_sounds()` has exactly one caller, Level.cpp:135, on the round-timer transition. The pause-menu RESTART and QUIT paths (GameStates.cpp:200-207) and the end-menu paths (GameStates.cpp:248, 258, 268, 278, 286) call only `stop_music()`, then destroy the level and its `Player`s and `Weapon`s. Since the `SoundBank` lives in the `ResourceManager`, the instance keeps looping and the only name that could stop it died with the weapon.
findings.suggestion: RAII: give `Weapon` a small `ScopedLoopingSound` member that stops in its destructor, so every teardown path releases automatically and `Level::stop_player_sounds` / `Player::stop_sounds` become unnecessary. Add explicit `on_activated()`/`on_deactivated()` lifecycle hooks driven by `GameLevel`'s state transitions rather than inferring audio state as a side effect of the shoot check. The destructor must not throw - fix the SNIPER/BUCKET switch first.
findings.verify_note: Read Weapon.cpp:229-257 (only call site), Weapon.h (no destructor declared), GameStates.cpp:130-215 and :240-290, Level.cpp:61-64, :135, :323-329.

findings.title: Fire rate is quantised to the tick rate (shoot_interval 0.0f / 0.0001f) and nothing caps live projectiles feeding an all-pairs collision loop
findings.detail:
`DETAILS_SPRAYER.shoot_interval = 0.0f` (weapon_consts.h:41) and `DETAILS_ROLLER.shoot_interval = 0.0001f` (:91), against the gate `if (get_shoot_timer() > get_shoot_interval() && ...)` with `set_shoot_timer(0.0f)` on fire and `alter_shoot_timer(dt)` at the end (Weapon.cpp:202-227). With an interval below `dt`, these weapons emit exactly one projectile per update tick, so DPS and paint rate are a function of the simulation tick rate, not wall-clock time.

The volume this produces meets a brute-force collision phase. Spray projectiles live 5 s (`projectile_consts.h:32 delete_timer = 5.0f`), and `Level::update_level_logic` (Level.cpp:255-290) runs `for (object : _collision_objects) for (object_2 : _collision_objects)` - a full O(n^2) all-pairs `is_colliding` sweep with no broad phase, on top of an O(players x n) pass. Four continuously-firing sprayers put the live list into the high hundreds, i.e. ~10^5-10^6 virtual `is_colliding` calls per frame.

The roller is pure churn: `shoot_interval 0.0001f` with `DETAILS_ROLLING.delete_timer = 0.000001f` (projectile_consts.h:66) heap-allocates a full `ProjectileRolling` every tick purely to stamp paint, then destroys it the same tick.

Secondary timing defects at the same site: the reset-to-zero discards overshoot, so the real interval is always `shoot_interval + dt` (sniper's configured 1.0 s is 61 frames = 1.017 s at 60 Hz), and `>` rather than `>=` means the very first update after construction never fires.
findings.suggestion: Give every weapon a real non-zero interval in seconds, increment the timer at the top of the update, compare with `>=`, and on fire do `alter_shoot_timer(-get_shoot_interval())` (or a `while` loop) so leftover time carries over and the rate is tick-rate independent. Cap live projectiles per player with a recycling pool. For the roller, replace the one-tick throwaway projectile with a direct paint call.
findings.verify_note: Read weapon_consts.h:41 and :91, Weapon.cpp:202-227, projectile_consts.h delete_timer values (5.0f spray/jet/mist/ball, 0.000001f rolling), Level.cpp:255-290 confirming the nested all-pairs loop with no broad phase.

findings.title: Shoot sound is re-issued or re-stopped every frame instead of on state change, with a tree lookup and XAudio2 round-trips each time
findings.detail: `handle_shoot_sound` is called unconditionally once per weapon per tick (Weapon.cpp:231) and does full work on both branches with no edge detection. Firing branch: `get_sound_effect_instance_name()` runs a switch, then `SoundBank::play_effect` (SoundBank.cpp:29-37) does a `std::map<std::string,...>` lookup keyed on e.g. "sprayer_a0" followed by `SetVolume`, `SetPitch`, `SetPan`, `Play`. Idle branch: `stop_effect` -> `SoundEffectInstance::Stop(true)` (SoundBank.cpp:38-41), which in DirectXTK issues `IXAudio2SourceVoice::Stop` + `FlushSourceBuffers` unconditionally on an already-idle voice, plus the same map lookup. Four idle players cost four map lookups and four XAudio2 stop/flush round-trips every frame, forever. None of it is needed - the instance is fixed for the weapon's whole life.
findings.suggestion: Resolve and cache the `SoundEffectInstance*` in the constructor, keep a `bool _sound_playing`, and touch the voice only on transitions. Zero lookups, zero redundant XAudio2 calls, and it removes the throwing type switch as a side effect.
findings.verify_note: Read Weapon.cpp:229-251, SoundBank.cpp:29-41 (play_effect does get_sound_effect_instance + 4 voice calls; stop_effect calls Stop unconditionally), SoundBank.cpp:74 get_sound_effect_instance.

findings.title: RelativeVelocityWeapon is a whole subclass carrying two data fields, and it duplicates the parent's update loop
findings.detail: `RelativeVelocityWeapon` adds exactly one member: `RelativeWeaponDetails _rel_details` = `{ add_player_velocity add_vel; float player_vel_amount; }` (WeaponDetails.h:15-19). For that it introduces a second hierarchy layer, a 14-parameter constructor, and a duplicate update loop: `Weapon::update_and_get_projectiles` (Weapon.cpp:168-186) and `RelativeVelocityWeapon::update_and_get_projectiles` (Weapon.cpp:576-595) are identical apart from `this->shoot(dir)` vs `this->shoot(dir, player_velocity)`. `Weapon::shoot` (Weapon.cpp:313-328) and `RelativeVelocityWeapon::shoot` (:552-574) are likewise the same eight-argument `build_projectiles` call with a different velocity computation. Three weapons derive from it, two do not - a split that exists purely because of where two floats live.
findings.suggestion: Fold `add_vel`/`player_vel_amount` into `WeaponDetails` and delete `RelativeVelocityWeapon`. Better, replace the enum+scalar with a single `Vector2F inherit_owner_velocity {0,0}` and compute `launch = dir * speed + owner_velocity * inherit_owner_velocity` unconditionally - no branch, no subclass, no duplicated update or shoot, and `NONE` becomes `{0,0}` (which also fixes the enum-fallthrough bug reported separately).
findings.verify_note: Read Weapon.h:145-183, WeaponDetails.h:15-19, and diffed Weapon.cpp:168-186 against :576-595 and :313-328 against :552-574.

findings.title: add_player_velocity::NONE silently falls into the Y_ONLY branch and adds the player's vertical velocity
findings.suggestion: Use `switch (add_player_vel)` with an explicit `case add_player_velocity::NONE: break;` and no `default:`, so /W4 C4062 flags the next enumerator added. Same treatment for the other exhaustive-by-assumption chains in the module. The `Vector2F inherit_owner_velocity` redesign removes the branch entirely.
findings.verify_note: Read Weapon.cpp:528-550, WeaponDetails.h:7-19, weapon_consts.h:30-34/:52-56/:130-134/:164-168, Weapon.h:182. Downgraded from 'high' because it is latent - no shipped configuration reaches the wrong branch.

findings.title: Base and derived declare same-named virtuals with different signatures - nothing overrides, everything hides
findings.detail:
`Weapon` declares `virtual shoot(const Vector2F&) const` (Weapon.h:96-97) and `virtual calculate_projectile_launch_velocity(const Vector2F&, float) const` (:99-101). `RelativeVelocityWeapon` declares same-named functions with different signatures (`shoot(dir, player_velocity)` :177-179; `calculate_projectile_launch_velocity(dir, speed, player_vel, add_vel, amount)` :170-175), also `virtual`, neither `override`. These are new virtuals that merely *hide* the base names in the derived scope.

So `Weapon::shoot(dir)` remains a live virtual that, invoked on a WeaponSprayer/Mister/Bucket through a `Weapon*`, silently produces a launch velocity with no owner-velocity contribution - the entire point of the subclass. It is unreachable today only because `RelativeVelocityWeapon` also overrides `update_and_get_projectiles`, which is why that function had to be duplicated at all. All four are `virtual` while nothing overrides any of them: four vtable slots for no polymorphism.

Related at the same site: `RelativeVelocityWeapon::update_and_get_projectiles` calls two virtuals through explicit class qualification - `Weapon::update_movement_and_rotation(...)` (Weapon.cpp:582) and `Weapon::check_if_shooting_and_ammo_update(...)` (:585) - which suppresses virtual dispatch. `update_movement_and_rotation` is genuinely overridden elsewhere (WeaponRoller.cpp:29). The base's own version correctly uses `this->` (Weapon.cpp:174, 177). No current subclass is affected, but any future subclass of `RelativeVelocityWeapon` overriding either hook would be silently ignored.
findings.suggestion: Collapse to one virtual with the full parameter set: `virtual Vector2F calculate_launch_velocity(const Vector2F& dir, const Vector2F& owner_velocity) const` (base ignores the second argument) and one non-virtual `shoot(dir, owner_velocity)` that calls it. Then `update_and_get_projectiles` exists once, `RelativeVelocityWeapon` genuinely overrides, and the qualified calls become `this->`. Mark every intended override `override` - the compiler would have caught all of this immediately.
findings.verify_note: Read Weapon.h:96-101 and :163-179, Weapon.cpp:168-186, :313-336, :552-595, WeaponRoller.cpp:29. Downgraded from 'high': the hiding is a genuine trap but no current call path reaches the wrong function.

findings.title: WeaponBuilder is a stateless static switch that must be edited to add a weapon, yet is heap-allocated and called through a pointer
findings.detail:
Three verified problems in 15 lines. (1) `build_weapon` is `static` (WeaponBuilder.h:14) and the class has no state, yet `PlayerBuilder.h:23` holds `std::unique_ptr<WeaponBuilder> _weapon_builder`, `PlayerBuilder.cpp:10` does `make_unique<WeaponBuilder>()`, and `PlayerBuilder.cpp:47` calls `this->_weapon_builder->build_weapon(...)` - an instance call to a static function through a heap-allocated empty object. (2) `WeaponBuilder.cpp:16-40` is a hardcoded switch over five `wep_type` values with `default: throw std::exception("Invalid weapon type")`; adding a weapon means editing this file, so the factory is closed for extension. (3) `WeaponBuilder.h:4-8` includes all five concrete weapon headers, so touching WeaponMister.h recompiles PlayerBuilder, Player and everything downstream.

The same anti-pattern is one level down: `ProjectileBuilder` (ProjectileBuilder.h:11-44) has zero data members, a defaulted ctor, one `const` method and one `static` method, yet every `Weapon` heap-allocates its own (`std::make_unique<ProjectileBuilder>()`, Weapon.cpp:32), stores it (Weapon.h:122), and hands it out as a raw borrowed pointer via `get_projectile_builder()` (Weapon.h:115, Weapon.cpp:488-491). `Weapon.h:11` includes ProjectileBuilder.h, which includes all five concrete projectile headers - so every TU that touches a weapon compiles the entire projectile hierarchy.
findings.suggestion: Replace `WeaponBuilder` with a registry the game populates: `register_weapon(id, factory_fn)` at startup (or from the weapons JSON), so concrete weapon headers are included only by the one TU that registers them. Make `ProjectileBuilder`'s functions free functions in a namespace and delete `_proj_builder`, `get_projectile_builder()` and the ProjectileBuilder.h include from Weapon.h. Both classes are namespaces wearing a class costume.
findings.verify_note: Read WeaponBuilder.h, WeaponBuilder.cpp, ProjectileBuilder.h:11-44, PlayerBuilder.h:23, PlayerBuilder.cpp:8-11 and :47-54, Weapon.h:11/:115/:122, Weapon.cpp:32/:488-491.

findings.title: WeaponRoller::draw is a 57-line copy-paste of Weapon::draw for an 8-line colour tint
findings.detail: `WeaponRoller::draw` reproduces `Weapon::draw` (Weapon.cpp:36-82) line for line - same `get_draw_pos()`, same `calculate_sprite_origin(..., LEFT_CENTER)`, same invert_x/invert_y -> `SpriteEffects` ladder, same four `set_*` calls, same debug-nozzle block. The only difference is WeaponRoller.cpp:90-97, choosing `get_team_colour()` vs `colour_consts::WHITE`. `_shooting_this_update` was made a protected data member of `Weapon` (Weapon.h:50) solely to feed this. Both copies also carry the identical unreachable `invert_x` branches (see the dead-state finding). The override is declared `private` in WeaponRoller.h:28-29 while the base declaration is public (Weapon.h:31), and it drops the base's `bool debug = false` default argument - default arguments on virtuals bind statically, so the effective default depends on the static type of the pointer used.
findings.suggestion: Add `protected: virtual MattMath::Colour get_draw_tint() const { return colour_consts::WHITE; }` to `Weapon`, override that in `WeaponRoller`, and delete `WeaponRoller::draw` entirely. Keep override access identical to the base declaration and never redeclare or omit a default argument on a virtual.
findings.verify_note: Diffed WeaponRoller.cpp:59-115 against Weapon.cpp:36-82; read WeaponRoller.h:22-30 (private overrides, no default arg) against Weapon.h:31-32.

findings.title: SoundEffectInstanceWeaponDetails hardcodes 2 teams x 4 players as eight named string fields plus a throwing nested switch
findings.suggestion: Delete the struct and the accessor. The naming convention is perfectly regular, so derive the name: `sound_id + '_' + team_char + std::to_string(index)`. Better, have the audio layer hand the weapon an opaque `SoundEffectInstance*` handle resolved once at construction, so no per-frame string naming happens at all and the 2x4 limit disappears with the three constant tables.
findings.verify_note: Read WeaponDetails.h:21-33, WeaponDetails.cpp:4-40, weapon_consts.h:58-68/:102-112/:136-146, Weapon.cpp:236-238. Note: one reviewer's claim that the *default* values of `_team`/`_player_num` reach the throw is misleading - `Weapon` has no default constructor, so both always come from the caller.

findings.title: 13/14-parameter constructors with five dead trailing parameters, copy-pasted across six classes
findings.detail:
`Weapon`'s constructor takes 13 parameters and `RelativeVelocityWeapon`'s 14 (Weapon.h:148-161). The trailing five - `color`, `rotation`, `origin`, `effects`, `layer_depth` - are forwarded to `TextureObject` (Weapon.cpp:21-22) and **never supplied by any caller**: `WeaponBuilder::build_weapon` passes exactly 7 arguments in all five branches (WeaponBuilder.cpp:18-37). They are then re-declared verbatim in all five concrete weapon headers (WeaponSprayer.h:16-20, WeaponSniper.h:16-20, WeaponRoller.h:16-20, WeaponMister.h:16-20, WeaponBucket.h:16-20) and re-forwarded verbatim in all five .cpp files - roughly 60 lines of pure pass-through.

Three of the five are worse than unused: `draw` unconditionally overwrites origin, effects and rotation every frame (Weapon.cpp:62-64; WeaponRoller.cpp:86-88), so passing anything but the defaults does nothing. And `rotation` is *not* used to initialise `Weapon::_rotation` - that member is absent from the ctor init list (Weapon.cpp:23-30) and keeps its NSDMI of `0.0f` (Weapon.h:128). Since `_rotation` is the aim angle driving `get_draw_pos`, `get_nozzle_pos`, `facing_left` and the launch direction, constructing a weapon with `rotation = PI` yields a weapon aiming right.

The leading parameters are also a fixed bundle repeated eight times: `(team, player_num, team_colour, type, player_center, resource_manager, dt)`.
findings.suggestion: Delete the five trailing parameters from `Weapon`, `RelativeVelocityWeapon` and all five subclasses. Group the rest into one `struct WeaponSpawnContext` passed by const reference so each concrete constructor is a single line and adding a dependency touches one struct rather than six headers and six .cpp files. If an initial aim angle is genuinely wanted, add one `float aim_rotation` that actually initialises `_rotation`.
findings.verify_note: Read Weapon.h:17-29 and :148-161, Weapon.cpp:8-34 (init list has no _rotation), WeaponBuilder.cpp:16-40 (7 args everywhere), all five Weapon*.h/.cpp constructors, Weapon.cpp:62-64 and WeaponRoller.cpp:86-88.

findings.title: check_if_shooting_and_ammo_update: a bool-returning 'check' that mutates four subsystems including audio
findings.detail: The name promises two responsibilities; the body has four: fire-rate gating and ammo spend (:202-215), ammo regen and timer advance (:218-227), the `_shooting_this_update` flag (:229), and starting/stopping a looping sound effect (:231) - all inside a function whose return value is "did we fire". You cannot ask "can this weapon fire?" without playing a sound, which is exactly why the pause and death paths above leak audio. It also carries a vestigial alias chain `bool normal_gun_ok_to_shoot = ...; bool ok_to_shoot = normal_gun_ok_to_shoot;` (:194-197) and two open-coded clamps written as mutate-then-test through four accessor calls (:209-213, :220-224).
findings.suggestion: Split into `bool FireControl::try_fire(dt)` (pure timing), `AmmoPool::try_consume(amount)` + `AmmoPool::tick(dt)` (pure arithmetic - and unit-testable in MattMathTests, which none of this currently is), and a `WeaponAudio::on_firing_changed(bool)` driven by the coordinator after the fact. The weapon's `update` becomes four readable calls with no hidden side effects.
findings.verify_note: Read Weapon.cpp:188-235 line by line and confirmed all four side-effect clusters and the alias chain.

findings.title: handle_shoot_sound's two bool arguments are bound in the order opposite to their parameter names
findings.detail:
The declaration is `virtual void handle_shoot_sound(bool shooting_this_update, bool holding_shoot)` (Weapon.h:52). The only call site is:
```
this->_shooting_this_update = ok_to_shoot && this->get_ammo() > 0.0f;
this->handle_shoot_sound(result, this->_shooting_this_update);
```
So the parameter named `shooting_this_update` receives `result` (a shot was actually fired) and the parameter named `holding_shoot` receives the member named `_shooting_this_update`. The member is itself misnamed - it means "trigger held and ammo remains", deliberately ignoring the fire-interval gate. Because both arguments are `bool`, a transposition compiles silently, and `WeaponSniper`/`WeaponBucket` branch on the first argument only (WeaponSniper.cpp:30, WeaponBucket.cpp:30) - one "tidy-up" swap would make the sniper fire its wave sound every frame the trigger is held. The same unlabelled-bool problem is in `play_effect(sound_name, true, ...)` (:242, `true` = loop) and `stop_effect(sound_name, true)` (:249, :256, `true` = immediate).

Downstream, `WeaponRoller::draw` tints the roller from `_shooting_this_update` (WeaponRoller.cpp:90), so the roller reads as firing on frames where the interval blocked the shot.
findings.suggestion: Rename the member to `_trigger_held_with_ammo` and the parameters to `fired_this_update` / `trigger_held`, matching the call site - or better, pass a single `enum class shoot_sound_event { fired, held, idle }` so the impossible `(true, false)` combination cannot be expressed. Use named enums (`sound_loop`, `stop_mode`) for the SoundBank booleans.
findings.verify_note: Read Weapon.h:52, Weapon.cpp:229-251, WeaponSniper.cpp:28-35, WeaponBucket.cpp:28-35, WeaponRoller.cpp:90-97.

findings.title: Weapon stores a second copy of the ResourceManager pointer and overrides the base getter to return it
findings.detail: `Weapon.cpp:21-25` passes `resource_manager` into the `TextureObject` base, which stores it in `DrawObject::_resource_manager` (DrawObject.h:36), **and** stores it again in `Weapon::_resource_manager` (Weapon.h:124). `Weapon.h:118` then declares `ResourceManager* get_resource_manager() const override;` whose whole body is `return this->_resource_manager;` (Weapon.cpp:500-503). Because `SpriteSheetObject::get_sprite_sheet()` resolves the manager through that virtual, `DrawObject::_resource_manager` becomes permanently dead state inside every `Weapon` while still looking live. Two aliases of one non-owning pointer with no single source of truth: any future fix that reseats one silently misses the other, and a reader cannot tell from the header which is authoritative.
findings.suggestion: Delete `Weapon::_resource_manager` and the `get_resource_manager` override and use the inherited accessor. Longer term, once rendering is decomposed out of `Weapon`, the weapon should be handed already-resolved handles and not know about `ResourceManager` at all.
findings.verify_note: Read Weapon.cpp:20-30 and :500-503, Weapon.h:118/:124, DrawObject.h:19-36 (virtual get_resource_manager, private _resource_manager).

findings.title: Weapon caches three raw non-owning pointers into objects that OnDeviceRestored destroys and rebuilds
findings.detail:
`Weapon` caches for its whole life `SoundBank* _sound_bank` (Weapon.h:47), `const float* _dt` (:123) and `ResourceManager* _resource_manager` (:124), set at Weapon.cpp:24-25 and :33, with no documented lifetime contract. All three owners are rebuilt by `Game::create_device_dependent_resources()`: `this->_resource_manager = std::make_unique<ResourceManager>();` (Game.cpp:238, which destroys every `SoundBank` it owned) and `this->_dt = std::make_unique<float>(0.f);` (Game.cpp:243). That function is re-run wholesale by `Game::OnDeviceRestored()` (Game.cpp:281-286).

Crucially `Game::OnDeviceLost()` (Game.cpp:268-279) does not tear down game state - the `_states` it resets is `std::unique_ptr<DirectX::CommonStates>` (Game.h:62), while the state machine is the separate `std::unique_ptr<State> _state` (Game.h:66). So the level, its players and their weapons survive the device-lost/restored cycle holding three dangling pointers, and the next frame executes `const float dt = *this->_dt;` (Weapon.cpp:193) on freed memory. The weapon also propagates the stale pointers into every projectile it spawns (Weapon.cpp:319-327, :565-573).
findings.suggestion: Pass `float dt` as a parameter to `update_and_get_projectiles` instead of caching a `const float*` - the call already threads other per-frame data down that path. For the manager pointers, either make `create_device_dependent_resources` genuinely idempotent (reuse the existing `ResourceManager`/`_dt` and only re-create D3D-dependent contents) or have `OnDeviceLost` tear the state machine down so nothing can hold stale pointers across the boundary.
findings.verify_note: Read Weapon.h:47/:123-124, Weapon.cpp:20-34/:193/:319-327/:565-573, Game.cpp:236-243/:268-286, Game.h:62-66 confirming _states is CommonStates and _state is the separate state machine.
