findings.verify_note: Read ResourceManager.cpp:27-38 and 91-102, SpriteSheet.cpp:105, and every literal-bearing construction site in MainMenu.cpp/PauseMenu.cpp/EndMenu.cpp/ResultsMenu.cpp. Confirmed "stage_test_1" at MainMenu.cpp:1927 is never produced by update_stage_select_visuals.

findings.title: Every menu frame spins up the thread pool, partitioner and a 16-entry command-list array to draw two objects
findings.detail: Every page's `draw()` builds the same 2-element vector and hands it to `draw_mobjects_in_viewports`, which per frame: allocates `std::vector<ID3D11CommandList*> command_lists(16, nullptr)` (128); allocates a partition vector via `Partitioner::partition(2, 16)` (134-135); submits two thread-pool tasks — and `ThreadPool::add_task` takes `std::function` BY VALUE and then heap-copies it again into `new std::function<void()>(task)` (ThreadPool.cpp:39-40), so four allocations plus two `CreateThreadpoolWork` calls; blocks on `wait_for_tasks_to_complete()` which does `WaitForThreadpoolWorkCallbacks` + `CloseThreadpoolWork` per item; then two `FinishCommandList` + two `ExecuteCommandList` + two `Release`. All to issue on the order of ten sprite draws. On the main menu (one viewport, ~6 widgets) this is pure overhead on the critical path of every frame.
findings.suggestion: Draw menus directly on the immediate context with one `Begin`/`End` pair per sampler state. If the deferred path must be kept for symmetry with `Level`, skip the thread pool below a threshold and reuse a persistent `command_lists` buffer instead of reallocating per frame.
findings.verify_note: Read MenuPage.cpp:124-164, ThreadPool.cpp:37-57 (function taken by value then heap-copied), Partitioner.cpp. All costs present as described.

findings.title: Background music is owned by individual pages — eight pages restart it in init(), one page stops it
findings.detail: `this->play_effect(MUSIC, true, MUSIC_VOLUME);` is the last statement of `init()` in all eight main-menu pages (MainMenu.cpp:107, 276, 566, 857, 1124, 1407, 1734, 1969), and exactly one place stops it: `MainMenuStageSelect::update` calls `stop_effect(MUSIC, true)` when the level is about to load (1815). Menu music is a property of being in the menu, not of any individual screen, so its lifetime is an emergent property of eight independent calls plus whatever de-duplication `SoundBank` happens to do. `MainMenuTitle` even declares `std::unique_ptr<DirectX::SoundEffectInstance> _music` (MainMenu.h:138) that is never assigned anywhere — its only mention is the commented-out `//this->_music->Stop();` at MainMenu.cpp:55. Wiring that member up the obvious way would be a double delete: the only source of a `SoundEffectInstance*` here is `SoundBankObject::get_sei()`, which borrows from a `std::map<std::string, std::unique_ptr<SoundEffectInstance>>` owned by `SoundBank`.
findings.suggestion: Start and stop the music in `GameMenu`, the owner of the whole menu session, or introduce a small `MusicDirector` that pages request states from. Delete the dead `_music` member — behaviour that spans screens must not live on a screen.
findings.verify_note: grep for play_effect/stop_effect/_music across MainMenu.cpp confirmed all eight init sites, the single stop at 1815, that `_music` is never assigned, and the commented-out line 55. Read SoundBankObject.h:29-30 confirming get_sei returns a borrowed raw pointer.

findings.title: MenuLevelSettings is shared mutable state with an order-dependent API and stored derived data
findings.detail: The per-player setters index `_player_settings[player_index]` unchecked while the vector is sized only by the separate `set_player_count` (9-25), so the object carries an implicit protocol — count first, then per-player fields — that the caller must know. `MainMenuPlayerCount::update` performs the dance four times over: `set_player_count(1); set_player_team(0, A); set_screen_layout(ONE_PLAYER); set_player_num(0, 0);` (MainMenu.cpp:899-913, repeated at 915-950 for 2/3/4 players). `screen_layout` is pure derived data — it is a function of player count — yet it is stored (MenuLevelSettings.h:35) and hand-set at four sites, so the two can disagree. Meanwhile `MainMenuData` holds a `MenuLevelSettings*` that eight pages read and write across transitions, and three page constructors reassign it as a side effect (MainMenu.cpp:1137-1142, 1420-1425, 1767-1772).
findings.suggestion: Make it an immutable value produced by a builder, compute `screen_layout` from `player_count` at the point of use, and pass the finished value to `GameLevel` instead of sharing a pointer to a half-filled object across the whole menu flow.
findings.verify_note: Read MenuLevelSettings.h/.cpp in full and MainMenu.cpp:897-950. Confirmed the four hand-set screen_layout calls and the three side-effecting constructors.

findings.title: Half-built layout grid in MenuPage that most pages route around with absolute pixel constants
findings.detail: `MenuPage` offers `_widget_position {150,150}`, `_widget_size {300,75}`, `_widget_spacing {250,150}` (58-60) plus `calculate_widget_position(int h_index, int v_index)` (26) — a notional grid with no concept of alignment, wrapping or content size. Only three of the twelve pages ever set the size (EndMenu.cpp:147, PauseMenu.cpp:130, 286), the value is write-mostly, and the defaults are load-bearing by accident: `ResultsMenuInitial::init` never calls `set_widget_size` yet computes its team-B percentage X from it — `calculate_center_position(this->get_widget_size().x, DEFAULT_RESOLUTION.x) + TEAM_B_PERCENTAGE_X_OFFSET` (ResultsMenu.cpp:150-152) — so the results layout silently depends on the `{300, 75}` literal chosen for main-menu items, and (1920-300)/2 + 325 = 1135 only 'works' because two unrelated magic numbers cancel. Contrast the team-A label two statements earlier (ResultsMenu.cpp:133), positioned correctly from `_team_a_fill->get_rectangle().get_position()`. Meanwhile `MainMenuOptions::init` reads the value into a local it never uses (MainMenu.cpp:457, a C4189 under /W4). Other pages abandon the grid entirely: `PROCEED_POSITION = {725,750}`, `HEADING_POSITION = {800,235}`, `WINNER_POSITION = {750,400}` (ResultsMenu.h:44-46); `_ready` positioned as `_background->get_rectangle().get_center() - Vector2F(400, 100)` (MainMenu.cpp:1946).
findings.suggestion: Either commit to a real layout system on `MContainer` (stack/anchor + margin, measured content size) or delete the grid and be honest about absolute coordinates. Derive the team-B percentage from `_fill_box`/`calculate_team_b_fill_top_right_position()` like everything else on that page. Delete the unused local at MainMenu.cpp:457.
findings.verify_note: Read MenuPage.h:18-30/58-60 and MenuPage.cpp:12-42. grep for set_widget_size found only three call sites. Read ResultsMenu.cpp:129-153 and MainMenu.cpp:453-467 confirming the unused local.

findings.title: Two unreachable validation branches, both of which throw a raw pointer
findings.suggestion: Delete both branches — the mutual exclusivity is established by construction, so there is no error condition left to report. If a defensive check is genuinely wanted, compute it before the dispatch chain and `throw std::logic_error(...)` by value. Never `throw new`.
findings.verify_note: Read MenuInput.cpp:36-129 and traced the boolean derivation at lines 40-46 — the conjunctions are unsatisfiable both by the else-if ordering and by construction. grep confirmed these are the only two `throw new` sites.

findings.title: Unguarded pointer from an enum switch with no default in update_team_select_visuals
findings.suggestion: Add `default: selected_widget = nullptr; break;` plus a guard before the `set_colour`, matching the error-frame handling the two sibling functions already use.
findings.verify_note: Read MainMenu.cpp:1258-1290, 1577-1626, 1852-1883 and player_team.h. Confirmed the missing default, the present defaults in both siblings, and that ArtAttack.vcxproj sets no TreatWarningAsError.

findings.title: all_players_confirmed() is vacuously true when player_count is 0
findings.detail: `for (int i = 0; i < get_player_count(); i++) { if (...) return false; } return true;` returns true when the count is zero. `MainMenuTeamSelect::update` checks it every frame regardless of whether any input arrived (1215-1222), so a zero-player page would transition to `MainMenuWeaponSelect` on its first update; `MainMenuWeaponSelect::all_players_confirmed()` (1555-1565) has the identical shape and would immediately advance to `MainMenuStageSelect`, whose input loop `for (int i = 0; i < num_inputs && i < player_count; i++)` (1790) never executes with `player_count == 0`, leaving a stage-select screen that ignores all input. `MenuLevelSettings` default-constructs with `_player_count = 0` (MenuLevelSettings.h:34) and `GameStates.cpp:206-208` and `284-286` both build `settings.settings = MenuLevelSettings()`. Not reachable today because both of those pair it with `main_menu_screen::HOME`, but nothing in `GameMenu::init` (GameStates.cpp:19-62) checks that a TEAM_SELECT/WEAPON_SELECT entry point comes with a non-zero player count.
findings.suggestion: Guard the transition on `get_player_count() > 0 && all_players_confirmed()`, and have `GameMenu::init` assert/reject a mid-way screen whose `MenuLevelSettings` has no players.
findings.verify_note: Read MainMenu.cpp:1215-1246, 1555-1565, 1784-1795, GameStates.cpp:19-62 and 196-212/280-290. Confirmed the vacuous-true and that the zero-player object is only ever paired with HOME today.

findings.title: Back from weapon select in a 1-player game skips the Player Count page it came from
findings.suggestion: Send the 1-player case to `MainMenuPlayerCount` to match the forward path. Structurally, hold a navigation stack so BACK is `pop()`.
findings.verify_note: Read MainMenu.cpp:897-913 (forward path) and 1445-1462 (back path). Asymmetry confirmed.

findings.title: Select-page widgets are built with hardcoded placeholder content even though the loaded selection is known one line earlier
findings.detail: `MainMenuWeaponSelect::init()` reads the persisted selection at 1675 (`state.type = get_level_settings()->get_player_weapon(i)`) and then builds all three widgets against a hardcoded Sprayer: `set_sprite_frame("sprayer")` (1695), `"Sprayer"` (1702), `weapon_description(wep_type::SPRAYER)` (1713). The correct values come from `update_weapon_select_visuals()` (1577-1626), which `init()` never calls. It is masked only because `StateContext::update()` runs before `draw()` and `update()` ends by calling `update_weapon_select_visuals()` (1509) — a coincidence of frame ordering, not a design. `MainMenuTeamSelect::init()` has the same gap: it loads `state.team = get_player_team(i)` (1349-1350) but builds the widgets with the unselected frames `"team_select_a"`/`"team_select_center"`/`"team_select_b"` (1371, 1380, 1388) and never calls `update_team_select_visuals()`.
findings.suggestion: Call `update_weapon_select_visuals()` / `update_team_select_visuals()` at the end of `init()` so the page is correct before its first draw, and construct the widgets from the loaded state rather than a placeholder.
findings.verify_note: Read MainMenu.cpp:1310-1408 and 1637-1735 in full. Neither init() calls its visuals-refresh function; both seed _select_states from persisted settings first.

findings.title: menu_element, both its converters, MainMenuTitle::_music, and two data-class accessors are entirely unreferenced
findings.detail: `menu_element.h` defines a 22-value enum whose ONLY references in the codebase are `MainMenuModeSelect::convert_mode_to_element` (MainMenu.h:201, MainMenu.cpp:744-759) and `MainMenuPlayerCount::convert_player_count_to_element` (MainMenu.h:221, MainMenu.cpp:1010-1026) — both `private static` and both called from nowhere. This is the half-finished ID-based widget identity system the string comparisons should have used; it was started, abandoned, and left in the build. As written it is also a project-global enum hardcoding one specific game's screens (`MAIN_MENU_TEAM_DEATHMATCH`, `PAUSE_MENU_CONFIRMATION_NO`), which does not scale past this project. Other dead code in the same module: `MainMenuTitle::_music` (MainMenu.h:138), never assigned, only mentioned in the commented-out `//this->_music->Stop();` at MainMenu.cpp:55; `MenuData::get_menu_data()` (MenuData.h:14, MenuData.cpp:26-28) and `GameData::get_game_data()` (GameData.cpp:122), both of which just `return this` and have zero callers; and the unused local `Vector2F widget_size = this->get_widget_size();` at MainMenu.cpp:457.
findings.suggestion: Delete menu_element.h, both converters, `_music`, both `return this` accessors and the unused local. If widget identity is wanted it should be per-page (`enum class Item` nested in the page) or an opaque handle returned by `add_item()`, never a project-global enum of every screen's buttons.
findings.verify_note: grep for menu_element, convert_mode_to_element, convert_player_count_to_element, _music, get_menu_data and get_game_data across all first-party .h/.cpp — every one has zero call sites beyond its own definition.

findings.title: Signed loop counters compared against .size(), inconsistently with the rest of the same file
findings.detail: `for (int i = 0; i < inputs.size(); i++)` — `int` vs `std::vector::size_type`, C4018 under /W4. Sites: MainMenu.cpp:50, EndMenu.cpp:32, ResultsMenu.cpp:266, MenuPage.cpp:140, GameStates.cpp:322. The rest of the module already does it correctly with an explicit cast (`int num_inputs = static_cast<int>(inputs.size());` at MainMenu.cpp:134, 303, 648, 883, 1157, 1441, 1787), so these are straightforward oversights — the same loop written two ways in one file. The reverse narrowing also occurs: MenuPage.cpp:103-108 iterates `size_t i` and passes it to `apply_player_viewport(int player_num, ...)` (C4267). None of these can overflow at these sizes, but `ArtAttack.vcxproj` sets `WarningLevel Level4` with no `TreatWarningAsError` in any of the four configurations, so the noise accumulates and masks warnings that matter. Several of these loops need no index at all — `ResultsMenuInitial::check_for_continue_input` (ResultsMenu.cpp:263-274) is a hand-written linear search that `std::any_of` expresses in one line, and the module contains zero uses of `<algorithm>`.
findings.suggestion: Use `size_t` or the explicit cast the rest of the file uses; prefer range-for where the index is unused and `std::any_of` for the search. Turn on `TreatWarningAsError` for at least C4018/C4267 so these cannot silently reappear.
findings.verify_note: Read each cited loop and grepped the vcxproj for TreatWarningAsError (absent) and WarningLevel (Level4 in all four configs).

findings.title: const member functions that mutate the objects they own, applied inconsistently
findings.detail: `const` means nothing here because the mutation goes through an owned `unique_ptr`, so the compiler cannot object. `ResultsMenuInitial::update_fill_box() const`, `update_team_a_fill() const`, `update_team_b_fill() const` (ResultsMenu.h:105-107, .cpp:214-252) call `_team_a_fill->set_width(width)` and `_team_b_fill->set_position_from_top_right_origin(...)` — they are the animation tick, the most mutating thing on the page. `MainMenuOptions::update_full_screen_selection_text() const` (MainMenu.h:180, .cpp:609-622) calls `_full_screen_value->set_text(...)` while its sibling `update_resolution_selection_text()` (602-607) does the identical thing and is NOT const — the qualifier is not even applied consistently to the same operation. `MainMenuTeamSelect::set_level_settings() const` (1225-1235), `MainMenuWeaponSelect::set_level_settings() const` (1511-1518) and `MainMenuStageSelect::set_level_settings() const` (1847-1851) write the shared `MenuLevelSettings` the whole level build depends on. The const propagation is lost in the first place because every `get_*_data() const` returns a NON-const pointer (MainMenu.cpp:18-21, PauseMenu.cpp:35-38, EndMenu.cpp:16-19, ResultsMenu.cpp:18-21).
findings.suggestion: Drop `const` from anything that changes what the page displays or the settings it feeds forward — the qualifier is actively misleading. Where a genuinely read-only accessor is wanted, return `const T*`.
findings.verify_note: Read every cited declaration and definition. All const-qualified as claimed, and all mutate through owned pointers or shared state.

findings.title: Aggregate getters return by value where const& belongs, forcing whole-container and struct copies
findings.detail: `std::vector<MenuPlayerSettings> MenuLevelSettings::get_player_settings() const` (MenuLevelSettings.h:14, .cpp:4-7) copies the entire vector; its one caller iterates it read-only — `PlayerBuilder.cpp:27` `for (auto& setting : settings.get_player_settings())` — a full heap copy per level build, bound by non-const reference so any write would be silently discarded into a temporary. `set_player_setting(int, MenuPlayerSettings)` (h:24) takes the struct by value then copies it again into the vector (.cpp:62-65). `ResultsMenuData::get_level_end_info() const` (ResultsMenuData.h:14) and `ResultsMenuInitial::get_level_end_info() const` (ResultsMenu.h:101, .cpp:275-278) each return `LevelEndInfo` by value — a copy of a copy of an aggregate containing a `TeamColour` plus two floats — and `update_team_a_fill`/`update_team_b_fill` call it every frame (ResultsMenu.cpp:228, 241) just to read one float that is fixed from `init()` onward. `init()` itself already holds `const LevelEndInfo end_info` at line 75 and then re-fetches two more full copies at 116 and 127. `ViewportManager::get_all_viewports()` (ViewportManager.cpp:89-103) likewise builds a fresh vector and is called once per MObject per frame from MenuPage.cpp:99-100.
findings.suggestion: Return `const std::vector<MenuPlayerSettings>&` and `const LevelEndInfo&`; take `const MenuPlayerSettings&` in the setter; use `const auto&` at PlayerBuilder.cpp:27; reuse the `end_info` local at ResultsMenu.cpp:116/127; cache the viewport list in `ViewportManager` and invalidate it in `set_layout`.
findings.verify_note: Read MenuLevelSettings.h/.cpp, LevelEndInfo.h, ResultsMenuData.h, ResultsMenu.cpp:73-127/214-278, PlayerBuilder.cpp:20-35 and ViewportManager.cpp:89-103. All by-value returns and repeated calls present as described.

findings.title: Select pages rebuild every widget's frame, colour and text from string literals every frame
findings.detail: `MainMenuTeamSelect::update()` ends with an unconditional `update_team_select_visuals()` (1223), which first calls `deselect_and_unconfirm_all_widgets()` (1291-1309) to set all three frames and three colours per player, then immediately overwrites one of them (1262-1289). `set_sprite_frame` takes `const std::string&`, so every literal materialises a temporary `std::string`; `"team_select_center"` (18 chars), `"team_select_a_selected"` (22) and `"team_select_center_selected"` (27) all exceed MSVC's 15-char SSO buffer, so each is a malloc/free pair. That is roughly two dozen string constructions per frame for state that only changes on a button press. `get_player_count()` is also re-evaluated as the loop condition and chains three pointer hops (MainMenu.cpp:22-26) per iteration. Same pattern in `update_weapon_select_visuals` (1577-1626, called unconditionally at 1509) and `update_stage_select_visuals` (1852-1883, called at 1845). Compounding it, `weapon_description(wep_type)` (1736-1755) returns `std::string` **by value** from 70-100 character `const static std::string` constants (MainMenu.h:84-89), and `update_weapon_select_visuals` calls it per player per frame (1623-1624) then copy-assigns into the widget via `TextObject::set_text` (TextObject.cpp:80-82).
findings.suggestion: Make the visual refresh event-driven — only call `update_*_visuals()` when a select state actually changed this frame. Return `const std::string&`/`const char*` from `weapon_description`, hoist `int player_count = get_player_count();` out of the loop conditions, and store the descriptions in a `constexpr const char*` table instead of dynamically-initialised namespace-scope strings.
findings.verify_note: Read MainMenu.cpp:1215-1309, 1494-1636, 1736-1755, 1845-1891 plus MainMenu.h:84-89 and TextObject.cpp:79-82. The unconditional per-frame refresh, the reset-then-overwrite, and the by-value description return are all as described.

findings.title: Viewport list is rebuilt per widget per frame, and Begin/End is issued per widget per viewport
findings.suggestion: Have `ViewportManager` cache the viewport array and return `const std::vector<Viewport>&`, invalidated in `set_layout`/on resolution change. Restructure the draw so viewports are the outer loop and widgets are grouped by sampler state inside a single `Begin`/`End`.
findings.verify_note: Read MenuPage.cpp:99-115, ViewportManager.cpp:52-103 and Mh.cpp:18-21. All as described. (Separately noted while reading: get_all_viewports pushes get_player_viewport(4) rather than (3) for the three-player case — outside this module's scope but worth a look.)

findings.title: Drawing API uses pointer-to-vector parameters, a reference out-parameter, and a six-argument signature
findings.detail: The three protected draw helpers are the widest API surface `MenuPage` exposes to subclasses, and every part of the shape is wrong. `draw_mobjects_in_viewports(std::vector<std::pair<MObject*, ID3D11SamplerState*>>* mobjects)` (43-44) takes a POINTER to a container it never modifies and never null-checks; all twelve call sites do `draw_mobjects_in_viewports(&mobjects)` on a local built that frame. `draw_mobject_in_viewports(ID3D11DeviceContext*, ID3D11CommandList*& command_list, SpriteBatch*, MObject*, ID3D11SamplerState* = nullptr)` (38-41) produces the command list through a reference out-parameter written by `FinishCommandList(FALSE, &command_list)` (MenuPage.cpp:117) — a COM object's sole reference deposited into a caller's container slot by a function that cannot know whether the slot already held one; double-assignment would leak silently, prevented today only by `Partitioner::partition` producing disjoint ranges. `draw_range_of_mobjects_in_viewports` (46-50) is six positional parameters, four of them raw container pointers of identical shape, trivially transposable with no compiler complaint.
findings.suggestion: Take `const std::vector<...>&` (or a span) for inputs, RETURN a `Microsoft::WRL::ComPtr<ID3D11CommandList>` rather than writing through a reference, and bundle the three parallel per-thread resource vectors into a single `DeferredDrawResources` struct passed by reference.
findings.verify_note: Read MenuPage.h:38-50 and MenuPage.cpp:89-178, plus all twelve `&mobjects` call sites. Confirmed the reference is bound to `command_lists->at(i)` at MenuPage.cpp:176.

findings.title: A generic confirmation dialog is hardcoded to two questions via an enum declared in a protected section
findings.detail: `PauseMenuPage` declares `protected: enum class confirmation_type { RESTART, QUIT };` (55-59) purely so `PauseMenuInitial` can name it when constructing `PauseMenuConfirmation` (PauseMenu.cpp:70-79). `PauseMenuConfirmation` then switches on it twice — once for the prompt text (`get_question_text`, PauseMenu.cpp:362-374) and once for the resulting action (233-245). A yes/no dialog is the most obviously reusable widget in any UI toolkit, and this one cannot ask a third question without editing an enum in a base class it does not belong to plus two switches. Worse, `PauseMenuConfirmation`'s constructor is PUBLIC but its parameter type is protected in the base (PauseMenu.h:85), so no code outside the hierarchy can name the type — a public API that no public caller can invoke. The name also collides conceptually with the unrelated `confirmation_state` (confirmation_state.h) used for per-player select state.
findings.suggestion: `ConfirmationPage(std::string question, std::function<void()> on_yes, std::function<void()> on_no)` — no enum, no switches, reusable by every screen. Move the type to namespace scope if it must stay, and rename one of the two to remove the `confirmation_type`/`confirmation_state` collision.
findings.verify_note: Read PauseMenu.h in full (enum in the protected section, public ctor at line 85 taking it) and PauseMenu.cpp:208-268, 362-374. Both switches present.

findings.title: MContainer stores raw non-owning child pointers, and every page declares containers before the widgets they point at
findings.detail: `MContainer::add_child(MObject* child)` (Mh.h:36, Mh.cpp:40) stores raw, non-owning pointers into `std::vector<std::pair<std::string, MObject*>> _children`, undocumented. The children are `unique_ptr` members of the page, and every page declares the containers FIRST, so reverse-order destruction destroys all the widgets before the containers holding pointers to them: MainMenu.h:133-137, 149-155, 166-175, 192-200, 212-220, 245-251, 280-285, 310-316; PauseMenu.h:73-79, 90-97; EndMenu.h:64-72; ResultsMenu.h:86-96. Benign only because `~MContainer` is implicit and a vector of raw pointers touches nothing — but `MContainer` already declares `remove_child`/`remove_all_children` (Mh.h:37-39), so one teardown call in a destructor makes every page a use-after-free. Related and load-bearing but unstated: `MainMenuTeamSelect::init()` (1345-1400) and `MainMenuWeaponSelect::init()` (1671-1728) hand raw pointers to `widgets->player_a` etc. to the containers WHILE `_player_widgets` is still being `push_back`-ed. This survives only because `_player_widgets` is `vector<unique_ptr<PlayerWidgets>>` (MainMenu.h:250, 284) — the extra indirection means reallocation moves the `unique_ptr`s, not the widgets. Change it to `vector<PlayerWidgets>`, the obvious 'simplification', and every registered child pointer dangles on the next `push_back`.
findings.suggestion: Make ownership explicit: have `MContainer` own its children (`vector<unique_ptr<MObject>>`) with pages keeping observing raw pointers, or at minimum rename to `add_observer`/document non-ownership and declare the containers LAST so destruction order matches the pointer graph. Comment `_player_widgets` explaining that the unique_ptr indirection is required for pointer stability.
findings.verify_note: Read Mh.h:31-51 and Mh.cpp:40, every cited member declaration block, and MainMenu.cpp:1345-1400/1671-1728 confirming children are registered mid-push_back.

findings.title: MenuHighlight and SoundBankObject are public mixin bases with public non-virtual destructors
findings.detail: `MenuHighlight` (MenuHighlight.h:8-30) declares no destructor at all, and `SoundBankObject` (SoundBankObject.h:7-36) likewise — both get an implicit PUBLIC NON-VIRTUAL destructor. Both expose nothing but a constructor and protected members, i.e. they are implementation mixins, yet every page inherits them PUBLICLY: `class MainMenuPage : public MenuPage, public SoundBankObject` (MainMenu.h:110), `class MainMenuHome final : public MainMenuPage, public MenuHighlight` (141, and the same at 158, 184, 204), `class PauseMenuPage : public MenuPage, public MenuHighlight, public SoundBankObject` (PauseMenu.h:44), EndMenu.h:42, ResultsMenu.h:64. Destruction through `unique_ptr<State>` is safe because `State` declares `virtual ~State()` (State.h:8), but `delete static_cast<SoundBankObject*>(page)` is UB the public interface permits, and the implicit `MainMenuHome* -> MenuHighlight*` conversion is available to any caller for no benefit. Related: `MenuHighlight::_highlighted_widget` (MenuHighlight.h:27) is a raw pointer into a `unique_ptr` member of the DERIVED page (`set_highlighted_widget(this->_play.get())`, MainMenu.cpp:274), so as a base it is destroyed after the members it points into — dangling for the duration of `~MenuHighlight`, harmless only because that destructor is trivial today.
findings.suggestion: Make both mixins private bases and give them `protected: ~MenuHighlight() = default;` — deletion through the mixin becomes a compile error while derived use stays legal. Document `_highlighted_widget` as non-owning.
findings.verify_note: Read MenuHighlight.h, SoundBankObject.h, State.h and all six page class declarations. No destructor declared in either mixin; State.h:8 does declare `virtual ~State() = default`.

findings.title: get_highlighted_widget() is dereferenced unguarded in seven update() bodies, by a class that null-checks it everywhere else
findings.detail: Every highlight-driven page starts with `std::string highlighted_element = this->get_highlighted_widget()->get_name();` — MainMenu.cpp:135-136, 304-305, 649-650, 884-885; PauseMenu.cpp:50-51, 219-220; EndMenu.cpp:29-30. `MenuHighlight::_highlighted_widget` defaults to `nullptr` (MenuHighlight.h:27), and the class's own `highlight_widget`/`unhighlight_widget` (MenuHighlight.cpp:6-22) both begin with `if (widget == nullptr) return;` — so the author knew it could be null. `get_highlighted_widget()` returns it raw and every caller dereferences it. The only thing preventing a crash is that each `init()` remembers to call `set_highlighted_widget` (MainMenu.cpp:274, 564, 855, 1122; PauseMenu.cpp:174, 330; EndMenu.cpp:210). A new page that forgets, or an `update()` that runs before `init()`, is an immediate null dereference.
findings.suggestion: Bind the highlight in the `MenuHighlight` constructor or assert it on entry to `update()`. Better, replace the stringly-typed identity with an ordered item list plus index so there is no pointer to be null.
findings.verify_note: Read MenuHighlight.h/.cpp in full (null checks in highlight/unhighlight, none in get_highlighted_widget) and all seven dereference sites plus all seven set_highlighted_widget calls.

findings.title: Three duplicate two-argument constructors whose extra parameter re-does what the caller already did
findings.detail: `MainMenuTeamSelect`, `MainMenuWeaponSelect` and `MainMenuStageSelect` each declare a second constructor taking `MenuLevelSettings*`. All three bodies are one line — `this->get_main_menu_data()->set_level_settings(settings);` (MainMenu.cpp:1137-1142, 1420-1425, 1767-1772). But the only caller, `GameMenu::init`, has already stored that exact pointer into the same `MainMenuData` before transitioning: `set_main_menu_data_ptrs()` runs at GameStates.cpp:23 and does `_menu_data->set_level_settings(_menu_level_settings.get())` (GameStates.cpp:65), and then GameStates.cpp:51/55/59 pass `this->_menu_level_settings.get()` — the identical pointer — to the two-argument overload. The overloads are pure noise, and two constructors that differ only in whether they re-assign shared state invite the paths to drift.
findings.suggestion: Delete the two-argument overloads and use the single-argument form at GameStates.cpp:50-60; the level settings pointer is already installed on the shared `MainMenuData`.
findings.verify_note: Read all three constructor definitions and GameStates.cpp:19-70. The pointer passed to the two-arg overload is the same `_menu_level_settings.get()` already installed by set_main_menu_data_ptrs.

findings.title: check_for_continue_input returns an int sentinel of -1 that the caller only tests for presence
findings.detail: `static int ResultsMenuInitial::check_for_continue_input(const std::vector<ProcessedMenuInput>&)` (ResultsMenu.h:104, .cpp:263-274) returns the index of the first proceeding input or `-1`. The sole caller throws the index away: `int continue_input = this->check_for_continue_input(menu_inputs); if (continue_input != -1) { ... }` (ResultsMenu.cpp:58-60). The return type encodes information nobody wants, in a form the type system cannot check — nothing stops a future caller from subscripting with the sentinel. The same anti-pattern is `GameLevel::check_for_pause_input` (GameStates.cpp:345-357), whose result IS consumed as an index and feeds directly into the pause-menu out-of-bounds hazard.
findings.suggestion: Return `bool` here since only presence is used (`std::any_of` expresses the whole body in one line). Where the index genuinely is needed, return `std::optional<size_t>` so 'no input' cannot be accidentally used as a subscript.
findings.verify_note: Read ResultsMenu.cpp:55-66 and 263-274, and GameStates.cpp:345-357. Confirmed the caller discards the index and that the pause-input variant feeds the OOB path.

findings.title: Bare positional bool arguments at the end of 9-14 parameter constructor calls
findings.detail: `MTextDropShadow`'s constructor has fourteen parameters (Mh.h:142-156) with eight defaulted, and the menus routinely pass a naked `true` in the ninth slot to mean 'hidden': `make_unique<MTextDropShadow>("ready", "READY?", ANNOUNCEMENT_FONT, ..., SHADOW_COLOUR, HEADING_SHADOW_OFFSET, true)` (MainMenu.cpp:1942-1951). Same at ResultsMenu.cpp:129-138, 140-149, 155-164, 166-175. Nothing at the call site says what `true` means, and swapping it with an adjacent compatible argument is not a compile error. The habit runs through the module's own APIs too: `MainMenuOptions::apply_fullscreen_setting(bool fullscreen)` (MainMenu.h:181) with its `if (fullscreen) {...} else // windowed` body, and `play_effect(name, bool loop, float volume, ...)` / `stop_effect(name, bool immediate)` (SoundBankObject.h:18-20) called as `play_effect(MUSIC, true, MUSIC_VOLUME)` and `stop_effect(MUSIC, true)` (MainMenu.cpp:107, 1815).
findings.suggestion: Replace trailing bools with named enums (`enum class visibility { visible, hidden }`, `window_mode`, `playback`), and give `MTextDropShadow` a config struct instead of fourteen positional parameters.
findings.verify_note: Read Mh.h:142-156 (fourteen parameters) and every cited call site. The bare `true` in the hidden slot is present at all five construction sites.

findings.title: Applying options rewrites the whole save file twice and swallows the failure
findings.detail:
```cpp
this->get_save()->set_resolution_and_save(this->_resolution_selection);   // line 329
...
this->get_save()->set_full_screen_and_save(fs);                           // line 343
```
Each performs a complete `fopen("wb")` + RapidJSON serialise + `fclose` of the whole save file (Save.cpp:58-83, 101-111), so one Apply truncates and rewrites the file twice; between the two writes the on-disk state is inconsistent (new resolution, old fullscreen flag). The failure path is invisible: `Save::save_to_file()` returns `void` and only `std::cout`s "Save was unsuccessful." (Save.cpp:94-96), which goes nowhere in a `wWinMain` GUI app. The menu then changes the window and the in-memory resolution regardless, so the user sees the setting applied and finds it reverted on next launch with no explanation.
findings.suggestion: Add a `Save::set_resolution_and_fullscreen(...)` that mutates both fields and writes once, returning a `bool` the menu checks — on failure, revert the in-memory selection and surface an on-screen message. Write to a temp file and rename for atomicity.
findings.verify_note: Read Save.cpp:57-111 — write_save_file does the full fopen/serialise/fclose, save_to_file is void and only prints, and both setters call it.

findings.title: If add_task throws mid-loop, already-submitted workers keep references into a stack frame that is unwinding
findings.detail: The lambdas submitted at MenuPage.cpp:142-149 capture `partitioned_mobjects` and `command_lists` BY REFERENCE; both are locals of `draw_mobjects_in_viewports` (128, 134-135). Correctness depends on reaching `wait_for_tasks_to_complete()` at line 150. But `ThreadPool::add_task` throws `std::runtime_error("Failed to create thread pool work object.")` (ThreadPool.cpp:42-45) when `CreateThreadpoolWork` fails — AFTER earlier iterations already called `SubmitThreadpoolWork` (line 46). That exception unwinds the frame, destroying `command_lists` and `partitioned_mobjects` while live workers are still writing through references to them. The already-created `PTP_WORK` handles also stay in `_work_items`, and the `new std::function` at ThreadPool.cpp:39-40 leaks outright on that path (its `delete` at line 64 only runs on the success path). Low severity because `CreateThreadpoolWork` failing is a rare OOM condition.
findings.suggestion: Make the wait unconditional with an RAII scope guard whose destructor calls `wait_for_tasks_to_complete()`, so no exit path can leave workers pointing at a dead frame. In `add_task`, hold the task in a `unique_ptr` and only `release()` after `CreateThreadpoolWork` succeeds.
findings.verify_note: Read MenuPage.cpp:124-164 (by-reference captures of two locals) and ThreadPool.cpp:37-65 (throw after prior SubmitThreadpoolWork, leaked new std::function on the failure path).

findings.title: load_from_json freads into a 1-byte allocation using sizeof(unique_ptr) as the buffer size, leaks it, and never checks fopen
findings.detail:
Merged from four independent reports; all four describe the same six lines and all four are correct.

```cpp
FILE* fp = fopen(json_path, "rb");            // 72: result never checked
auto read_buffer = std::make_unique<char>();  // 74: allocates exactly ONE char
FileReadStream is(fp, read_buffer.get(), sizeof(read_buffer)); // 75: sizeof(unique_ptr<char>) == 8
Document d; d.ParseStream(is);
fclose(fp);
read_buffer.release();                        // 81: drops ownership without deleting
```
I read the vendored stream to confirm the consequence. external/rapidjson/include/rapidjson/filereadstream.h:66-81 `Read()` does `readCount_ = std::fread(buffer_, 1, bufferSize_, fp_);` and then, when `readCount_ < bufferSize_`, `buffer_[readCount_] = '\0';`. With bufferSize_==8 and a 1-byte allocation that is a 7-byte heap overflow on every refill, repeated for the whole file. It also forces the parser to refill 8 bytes at a time.

`release()` abandons the allocation (author meant `reset()`, which was itself unnecessary). `fopen` is unchecked and rapidjson's `RAPIDJSON_ASSERT(fp_ != 0)` compiles out under NDEBUG, so a missing file gives `fread(nullptr)` then `fclose(nullptr)`.

The identical five lines exist verbatim in ArtAttack/SoundBank.cpp:150-161 (I read it; same `make_unique<char>()` + `sizeof(read_buffer)` + `release()`), so this is two sites, not one. Live at startup via ResourceLoader.
findings.verify_note: Read SpriteSheet.cpp:70-90 and SoundBank.cpp:150-161 (identical). Read external/rapidjson/include/rapidjson/filereadstream.h:66-85 to confirm fread(buffer_, 1, bufferSize_, fp_) plus the buffer_[readCount_] write.

findings.title: Device-lost/restore destroys ResourceManager and the dt float, leaving every live drawable holding a freed pointer
findings.detail:
`DrawObject::_resource_manager` (DrawObject.h:36) and `Drawer::_resource_manager` / `Drawer::_dt` (Drawer.h:30-31) and `AnimationObject::_dt` (AnimationObject.h:49) are non-owning raw pointers captured at construction and never re-seated.

I read Game.cpp. `OnDeviceLost()` resets the sprite batches, resets `_states` (which is `CommonStates`, not the state machine) and calls `reset_all_textures/sprite_fonts/sounds`. It does NOT tear down `Game::_state` (Game.h:67, `std::unique_ptr<State>`), so the whole live object graph survives. `OnDeviceRestored()` then calls `create_device_dependent_resources()`, which at Game.cpp:238-245 does:
```cpp
this->_resource_manager = std::make_unique<ResourceManager>();  // old one destroyed
this->_dt = std::make_unique<float>(0.f);                       // old float destroyed
```
The `unique_ptr` assignments free the old objects. `GameData` is re-pointed; every already-constructed `Player`, `Visual`, `PaintTile`, `Text`, `TextDropShadow`, `InterfaceGameplay` and `DebugText` is not. The next `TextureObject::draw` → `SpriteSheetObject::get_sprite_sheet()` (SpriteSheetObject.cpp:33) dereferences freed memory, as does `Drawer::get_dt()` (Drawer.cpp:30).

The root cause is the design: nothing in `DrawObject`'s or `Drawer`'s API states that the pointer is non-owning, how long it must outlive the object, or who re-seats it. This is exactly the coupling that blocks the engine-reuse goal — every drawable holds a mutable back-pointer to a global service.
findings.suggestion: Short term: do not recreate `ResourceManager` and the dt float on device restore — keep the objects and only reload their GPU-side contents in place. Long term: delete `DrawObject::_resource_manager` entirely; drawables should hold resolved handles and receive whatever they need through the draw call, and frame time should be a `float` parameter to `update(float dt)` rather than a heap-allocated float whose address is threaded through ~26 headers.
findings.verify_note: Read Game.cpp:238-287 (create_device_dependent_resources reassigns both unique_ptrs; OnDeviceLost does not reset Game::_state), Game.h:67, DrawObject.h:36, Drawer.h:30-31, Drawer.cpp:28-31.

findings.title: SpriteSheet stores a borrowed ID3D11ShaderResourceView* with no AddRef that ResourceManager releases underneath it
findings.detail:
```cpp
ID3D11ShaderResourceView* _texture = nullptr;   // SpriteSheet.h:63
SpriteSheet::SpriteSheet(ID3D11ShaderResourceView* texture) : _texture(texture) {}
```
The pointer originates from `ResourceManager::get_texture()` (ResourceManager.cpp:12) as a bare `.Get()` off a `ComPtr` — no AddRef. `ResourceManager::reset_all_textures()` (ResourceManager.cpp:112-118) calls `.Reset()` on every texture, and `Game::OnDeviceLost` calls it. `_sprite_sheets` is not cleared, so every surviving `SpriteSheet` then holds a dangling COM pointer that it passes straight to `SpriteBatch::Draw` at SpriteSheet.cpp:103, 124, 145, 166.

This is the only long-lived raw COM pointer in the codebase — `ResourceManager` itself uses `ComPtr` correctly.

Secondary: `SpriteSheet` has a user-declared constructor but no destructor, so the implicit move constructor is generated and copies `_texture` without nulling the source. Currently latent (sheets live in `unique_ptr` and are never moved), so it is a hardening point, not a live bug.
findings.suggestion: Store `Microsoft::WRL::ComPtr<ID3D11ShaderResourceView> _texture;` — assignment AddRefs, so the texture cannot die while a sheet holds it. Delete the copy constructor and default the move so the borrowing story is stated rather than inferred.
findings.verify_note: Read SpriteSheet.h:63, SpriteSheet.cpp:9-13 and 102-174, ResourceManager.cpp:7-19 and 112-118, Game.cpp:269-280.

findings.title: All four ResourceManager getters use map::operator[] wrapped in a catch that can never fire, so a missing asset returns nullptr and every render call site dereferences it
findings.detail:
Reported by five reviewers; all correct. `get_texture` (7-19), `get_sprite_font` (27-38), `get_sprite_sheet` (46-58) and `get_sound_bank` (91-102) are all this shape:
```cpp
try { return this->_sprite_sheets[sprite_sheet_name].get(); }
catch (const std::out_of_range&) { throw std::out_of_range("SpriteSheet ... not found."); }
```
`std::map::operator[]` never throws `out_of_range` — it default-inserts and returns `nullptr`. The catch block is unreachable dead code and the documented contract is a fiction. (`get_level_info` at :66-78 gets it right with `.at()`, so the codebase disagrees with itself in the same file.)

Every consumer in the rendering module dereferences the result unchecked: SpriteSheetObject.cpp:33-34, TextureObject.cpp:24-26 and :43-45, AnimationObject.cpp:26, :33, :52, TextObject.cpp:29-30 and :49-50, DebugText.cpp:106-115, InterfaceGameplay.cpp:66-73, 113-120, 153-156, 183-188. So one misspelled or unshipped asset name becomes a null dereference mid-frame on a worker thread instead of a diagnosable load error — and the names involved are hardcoded literals in engine-level headers (`interface_consts::SPRITE_SHEET`, `TIMER_FONT`, `debug_text_consts::DEBUG_FONT`).

It also makes the getters non-const and inserting, which is what turns a missing-name mistake into a shared-map mutation from the parallel draw pass.
findings.suggestion: Use `.at()` inside the try so the catch becomes live, or better `find()` + an explicit throw naming the key. Then mark all four getters `const` and have them return `const T*`. Add a startup validation pass in `ResourceLoader` that resolves every name the engine hardcodes, so failures surface once at load.
findings.verify_note: Read ResourceManager.cpp in full; confirmed operator[] in all four getters and .at() in get_level_info. Traced the dereference sites listed.

findings.title: Both name-keyed draw overloads look frames up with map::operator[], so a typo draws nothing silently and the overloads cannot be const
findings.detail:
`this->_sprite_frames[frame_name].get_source_rectangle()` at SpriteSheet.cpp:105 and :126.

`operator[]` default-constructs on a miss. `SpriteFrame`'s default `_source_rectangle` is `{0,0,0,0}` (SpriteFrame.h:21), so a misspelled frame name in code or level JSON produces an invisible sprite with no error, no assert and no log, plus a permanent junk entry in the atlas. Contrast `get_animation_strip` (SpriteSheet.cpp:17) on the same class, which uses `.at()` and throws — two lookups, opposite failure semantics.

Because `operator[]` is non-const these two overloads cannot be `const`, while the two `const RECT*` overloads directly below them (SpriteSheet.cpp:134-174) are. That single choice is what forces the entire chain above — `TextureObject::draw`, `SpriteSheetObject::get_sprite_sheet`, `DrawObject::get_resource_manager` — to hand out non-const pointers out of const methods.

On severity I am downgrading the reviewers' "heap corruption today" framing. `draw_player_view_level` genuinely runs on N thread-pool workers sharing one `SpriteSheet` (see the concurrency finding), but every frame name actually used at runtime exists in sprite_sheet_1.json (I checked "pixel" at line 209 and "health_box" at line 378), so `operator[]` is not currently restructuring the tree. The race is latent behind a content typo, not active.

I also reject one sub-claim attached to this by two reviewers: `SpriteFrame::get_source_rectangle()` returning `&_source_rectangle` is not a live hazard — DirectXTK's `SpriteBatch::Draw` copies the source rect into its own sprite record, and `_sprite_frames` is only reassigned wholesale in `load_from_json`, which does not run concurrently with drawing.
findings.suggestion: `find()` + throw naming the missing frame, or `.at()`. Mark both overloads `const`. Best: resolve frame names to an index/handle once at load so the render path never touches a string or a map, which removes the mutability and the per-draw lookup together.
findings.verify_note: Read SpriteSheet.cpp:92-174 and SpriteSheet.h:19-59 (const asymmetry between the two overload pairs), SpriteFrame.h:21. Grepped sprite_sheet_1.json for the two hardcoded HUD frame names — both present, which is why I downgraded the active-corruption claim.

findings.title: draw() is a mutating operation on shared objects, and the same object is drawn concurrently by every viewport thread
findings.detail:
`IGameObject::draw` is non-const (IGameObject.h:11-12) and the render path exploits it.

I verified the dispatch. `Level::draw_active_level` partitions the player list and adds one thread-pool task per partition, each running `draw_player_view_level`. But `draw_player_view_level` then loops over **all** `_player_objects`, `_collision_objects` and `_non_collision_objects` for its viewport, calling `object->draw(...)`. So in 2-4 player split-screen the same `Player` instance has `draw()` entered concurrently by up to 4 threads.

`Player::draw` (Player.cpp:47-90) writes during draw:
```cpp
this->_animation_state = new_animation_state;
TextureObject::set_sprite_sheet_name(info.sprite_sheet);   // std::string assignment
TextureObject::set_element_name(info.uniform_texture);     // std::string assignment
set_animation_strip_and_reset(info.sprite_sheet, info.animation); // 2 more strings + _frame_index + _time_elapsed
set_frame_time(info.frame_time);
TextureObject::set_effects(effects);
AnimationObject::set_effects(effects);
```
while other threads read those same members in `SpriteSheetObject::get_sprite_sheet()` and `AnimationObject::get_source_rectangle()`. Concurrent write/read of a `std::string` that outgrows SSO is a use-after-free of the string buffer, not merely a stale frame. A torn `_frame_index` read makes `AnimationStrip::get_frame_rect` throw (AnimationStrip.cpp:30-33) from inside `ThreadPool::work_callback`, which invokes `(*task)()` with no try/catch (ThreadPool.cpp:60-65) — that terminates the process and leaks the task.

Same shape at `TextDropShadow::draw` (separate finding), `PaintTile::draw` (PaintTile.cpp:34-70, `set_colour` + `_splash.set_rectangle_center` on shared tile state) and `Weapon::draw` (Weapon.cpp:36-66, `set_element_name`/`set_origin`/`set_effects`/`set_draw_rotation`).

This is the single biggest structural obstacle to the engine goal: the renderer is parallel but nothing below `IGameObject` is const or read-only.
findings.suggestion: Make `IGameObject::draw` and everything it reaches `const`, and move every state transition into `update()` — starting with hoisting the animation-state block out of `Player::draw`. Per-viewport values that genuinely vary (effects, view rect) belong in a draw-parameter struct passed by value. Separately, wrap `ThreadPool::work_callback`'s invocation in try/catch so a task exception cannot terminate the process.
findings.verify_note: Read Level.cpp:375-400 (per-partition task dispatch) and 510-600 (each task loops over all objects), Player.cpp:47-90, IGameObject.h, ThreadPool.cpp:60-65, PaintTile.cpp:32-70, Weapon.cpp:36-66.

findings.title: TextDropShadow::draw renders by mutating and restoring its own base state, on an object shared across all render threads
findings.suggestion: Give `TextObject` a private `draw_with(SpriteBatch*, const Camera&, const Colour&, const Vector2F& position, float scale) const` and have `TextDropShadow::draw(...) const` call it twice. No mutation, const-correct, thread-safe, exception-safe. Store the shadow scale as a multiplier of the text scale so the pair cannot desync.
findings.verify_note: Read TextDropShadow.cpp:28-52 and TextDropShadow.h:36-38, Level.cpp:737-745 (const method, unique_ptr member) and its call site inside the threaded draw_player_view_level.

findings.title: TextDropShadow::draw hides rather than overrides TextObject::draw — the const qualifier differs and no override keyword catches it
findings.suggestion: Add `const` and `override` to both and drop the redundant `virtual`. That requires making the body const, which the mutate-restore finding independently demands. Then apply `override` mechanically across the whole render hierarchy and enable `/w14263 /w14266` so MSVC flags hidden virtuals under the existing /W4.
findings.verify_note: Read TextObject.h:21-23 (both const) and TextDropShadow.h:24-25 (neither const, neither override, both parameters misspelled) and TextDropShadow.cpp:28,49.

findings.title: InterfaceGameplay is a Splatoon HUD welded into what is presented as an engine class
findings.detail:
This derives `Drawer` and sits in the rendering layer, but every part of it is game content:

- Asset identity is hardcoded in the header: `SPRITE_SHEET = "sprite_sheet_1"`, `EMPTY_BOX_FRAME = "health_box"`, `FILL_FRAME = "pixel"`, `TIMER_FONT = "gill_sans_mt_bold_48"`, `RESPAWN_TIMER_FONT = "gill_sans_mt_bold_144"` (lines 18, 26-31). Renaming an atlas is a code change and a rebuild of everything that includes this header.
- Layout is compile-time: `RIGHT_MARGIN`, `AMMO_TOP_MARGIN`, `TOP_RIGHT_BOX_SIZE`, and `TIMER_SCALE_FACTOR = 1920.0f`, which bakes in a reference resolution with no comment saying so.
- The API is nine loose game-domain parameters ending in `float respawn_timer, bool show_respawn_timer`, and it takes a raw `ID3D11SamplerState*` — the HUD knows about D3D pipeline state objects.
- Line 5 includes `player_team.h` and `InterfaceDraw` carries a `player_team` member, so "there are teams" is baked into the type.

An engine has widgets; a game has a health bar. This is the clearest instance in the module of game logic living where reusable code should be.
findings.suggestion: Split into (a) engine widgets — a `ProgressBar { RectangleF bounds; FrameId background, fill; Colour tint; float fraction; }` and a `Label { FontHandle; std::string; Vector2F anchor; float scale; Colour text, shadow; }`, plus anchor/margin layout in normalised units — and (b) a game-side `GameplayHud` that owns a list of those widgets built from a data file (the level JSON pipeline already exists) and updated from `Player`. The sampler state belongs to the renderer, not to a HUD signature.
findings.verify_note: Read InterfaceGameplay.h in full and InterfaceGameplay.cpp in full.

findings.title: DebugText, an engine-level overlay, includes Player.h and hardcodes knowledge of ~18 game-specific fields
findings.detail:
`DebugText.h:7` is `#include "Player.h"` and the sole API is `draw_debug_info(SpriteBatch*, const Player* player, int num_projectiles) const`.

DebugText.cpp:21-102 reaches into `Player` for `get_input()`, `get_rectangle()`, `get_center()`, `get_velocity()`, `get_camera()`, `get_viewport()`, `get_input_x_movement()`, `get_input_shoot_direction()`, `input.shoot_angle`, `input.left_analog_stick`, `input.right_analog_stick`, `get_input_primary_shoot()`, `get_input_jump_pressed()`, `get_input_jump_held()`, `get_move_state()`, `get_state()`, `get_player_move_state_string()`, and switches on `player_state::ALIVE/DEAD` at :93-101. It also takes `num_projectiles`, a level-wide statistic, as a parameter.

The dependency points the wrong way: the debug renderer knows the game object instead of the game object describing itself. Adding one debug field means editing the renderer. And because `DebugText.h` is pulled in by `Level.h`, every TU that reaches `Level.h` compiles the whole `Player` hierarchy.

DebugText.cpp:113-131 also hand-rolls drop-shadow text (draw at `pos + offset` in black, then at `pos` in grey) — precisely what `TextDropShadow` already does. `DEBUG_FONT = "courier_new_bold_16"` hardcodes an asset name into an engine header.
findings.suggestion: `class DebugOverlay { void add_line(std::string); void draw(SpriteBatch*, const TextStyle&) const; void clear(); }` with zero knowledge of `Player` — it renders a `vector<string>`. Give game objects `void append_debug_lines(DebugOverlay&) const` so `Player` formats its own fields and `Level` supplies the projectile count. Font/colour/spacing arrive as a `TextStyle` value. Reuse the shared text-draw path instead of re-implementing the shadow. The header only needs `class Player;` regardless.
findings.verify_note: Read DebugText.h and DebugText.cpp in full; confirmed the include, the pointer-only usage in the declaration, and every field access listed.

findings.title: The render hierarchy is inheritance where composition belongs, and Player ends up with two complete copies of all render state
findings.detail:
`DrawObject` (colour/rotation/origin/effects/depth/`ResourceManager*`) → `SpriteSheetObject` (+ two name strings) → sibling leaves `TextureObject` and `AnimationObject`. These are pure state bags with no polymorphic behaviour, yet they are inherited rather than held.

The cost is visible at Player.h:63-64:
```cpp
class Player final : public MovingObject, public ICollisionGameObject,
                     public AnimationObject, public TextureObject
```
`AnimationObject` and `TextureObject` both derive `SpriteSheetObject` → `DrawObject` **non-virtually**, so every `Player` contains two independent copies of `_resource_manager`, `_colour`, `_draw_rotation`, `_origin`, `_effects`, `_layer_depth`, `_sheet_name`, `_element_name`. `Player::draw` keeps them in sync by hand — `TextureObject::set_effects(effects)` at :83 and `AnimationObject::set_effects(effects)` at :86, the same value written twice; the sheet name is set on the texture copy at :62-63 and on the animation copy at :65.

The two bases also declare `draw` overload sets with identical signatures (TextureObject.h:20-32 vs AnimationObject.h:34-46), so every call from `Player` must be explicitly qualified or it is ambiguous. Storing the non-owning `ResourceManager*` twice per player also doubles the dangling surface of the device-restore bug.

Same shape at Visual.h:8 (`IGameObject` + `TextureObject`), Projectile.h and Mh.h's menu widgets.
findings.suggestion: Make render state a value type held by composition: `struct Sprite { SheetHandle sheet; FrameId frame; Colour tint; Vector2F origin; float rotation; SpriteEffects effects; float depth; };` and `class SpriteAnimator { AnimationId clip; int frame; float elapsed; bool paused; };`. `Player` then *has* a `Sprite` and *has* a `SpriteAnimator` and iterates a small list of layers in `draw`. No diamond, no duplicated state, no qualified-call gymnastics, and the state becomes inspectable and serialisable.
findings.verify_note: Read Player.h:63-64, Player.cpp:47-90, DrawObject.h, SpriteSheetObject.h, TextureObject.h, AnimationObject.h. Confirmed non-virtual inheritance and the duplicated set_effects calls.

findings.title: Renderables store resource names, so every draw costs 2-3 string-keyed std::map lookups through a chain of virtual getters
findings.suggestion: Names are load-time data. Have `ResourceManager` issue opaque handles (indices into contiguous arrays) at load, and have renderables store the handle plus a resolved `const AnimationStrip*`, invalidated only in `set_animation_strip_and_reset`. Resolution happens once, in the builder/loader layer that can report a missing asset usefully. This also makes the render path const and thread-safe for free.
findings.verify_note: Read SpriteSheetObject.cpp:31-35, TextureObject.cpp:21-54, AnimationObject.cpp:24-28/81-107/139-159, TextObject.cpp:27-62, and the per-viewport loops in Level.cpp:510-600.

findings.title: const accessors hand out a mutable ResourceManager*, so the entire const-marked draw path performs writes to shared containers
findings.detail:
```cpp
virtual ResourceManager* get_resource_manager() const;   // DrawObject.h:20
ResourceManager* Drawer::get_resource_manager() const;   // Drawer.h:17
```
A const member function returning a non-const pointer to a collaborator, and here it is load-bearing rather than incidental. `TextureObject::draw(...) const` (TextureObject.cpp:21-34) uses it to obtain a non-const `SpriteSheet*` and call the non-const `SpriteSheet::draw`, which does `_sprite_frames[frame_name]`. `TextObject::draw(...) const` uses it to call `ResourceManager::get_sprite_font`, which is non-const because it does `_sprite_fonts[font_name].get()`.

So every `const` marker on the draw path is a guarantee that is simply false, and it is exactly the guarantee that any future reasoning about the parallel renderer would rest on. Making these honest is a prerequisite for the threading being correct, not a tidiness exercise.
findings.suggestion: Make the four `ResourceManager` getters const, using `.at()`, returning `const SpriteFont*` / `const SpriteSheet*`. Then `DrawObject::get_resource_manager() const` returns `const ResourceManager*` and `_resource_manager` becomes `const ResourceManager*` in both `DrawObject` and `Drawer`.
findings.verify_note: Read DrawObject.h:20, DrawObject.cpp:22-25, Drawer.h:17, TextureObject.cpp:21-34, TextObject.cpp:27-62, ResourceManager.cpp:27-58.

findings.title: Including DrawObject.h drags RapidJSON, XAudio2, SoundBank and the game's level_stage enum into every renderable
findings.detail:
`DrawObject.h:5` includes `ResourceManager.h`. I read ResourceManager.h:1-10 — it includes `<map>`, `<string>`, `SpriteSheet.h`, `level_stage.h`, `LevelLoadedInfo.h`, `<Audio.h>` and `SoundBank.h`. And `SpriteSheet.h:6` includes `rapidjson/document.h`.

Since `DrawObject` is the root of the entire render hierarchy, every file that draws anything transitively compiles RapidJSON's document parser, the DirectXTK audio engine, the game's sound-bank type, and `level_stage` — an enum of game modes. A texture-drawing base class cannot be compiled without the game's mode list and an audio library.

The root cause is that `DrawObject` stores a `ResourceManager*` at all: every drawable holds a pointer to the god-object that also owns sounds and level metadata.
findings.suggestion: (1) Remove `ResourceManager*` from `DrawObject` — drawables hold resolved handles and receive what they need through the draw call, and the header dependency disappears. (2) Split `ResourceManager` along asset lines (`TextureCache`, `FontCache`, `SpriteSheetCache`, `SoundCache`, `LevelInfoCache`) behind narrow interfaces, and move JSON parsing out of `SpriteSheet.h` into a `SpriteSheetLoader.cpp` so RapidJSON never appears in a public header. Forward-declare `SpriteBatch`, `SpriteFont` and `ID3D11ShaderResourceView`.
findings.verify_note: Read DrawObject.h:1-6, ResourceManager.h:1-10, SpriteSheet.h:1-8.

findings.title: SpriteSheet is three classes in one: atlas data, JSON loader, and sprite renderer
findings.detail:
The class simultaneously holds the data (`map<string, SpriteFrame>`, `map<string, unique_ptr<AnimationStrip>>`, `ID3D11ShaderResourceView*`), parses it (`load_from_json` plus the two static decoders at SpriteSheet.cpp:20-68, which is why `rapidjson/document.h` is in the header), and renders it (five `draw` overloads at :92-174 calling `SpriteBatch::Draw` directly).

That conflation is why the class cannot be `const`, cannot be unit-tested without D3D and a file on disk, and forces RapidJSON on every consumer. It also means the atlas owns the *policy* of how a sprite is drawn: those five overloads are the engine's entire public rendering vocabulary, each a positional list of 6-9 defaulted arguments that every caller re-specifies.
findings.suggestion: Three types. `SpriteSheet` = immutable atlas (texture handle + `vector<SpriteFrame>` + `vector<AnimationStrip>` + name→index tables, all const after load, safely shareable across render threads). A free `load_sprite_sheet(...)` in a .cpp = JSON → `SpriteSheet`, so the format is swappable and the header has no parser dependency. `SpriteRenderer` = the only thing that talks to `SpriteBatch`, taking `const SpriteSheet&` + a `SpriteDrawParams` struct.
findings.verify_note: Read SpriteSheet.h and SpriteSheet.cpp in full.

findings.title: No rule about who owns SpriteBatch Begin/End — four incompatible conventions across the rendering code
findings.detail:
Batch lifetime is decided ad hoc in four different ways, all verified:

- `InterfaceGameplay::draw_gameplay_interface` begins and ends the batch twice inside one call (`Begin(); draw_timer(); End();` at :26-28, then `Begin(SpriteSortMode_Deferred, nullptr, sampler_state); ... End();` at :30-46), and needs a caller-supplied `ID3D11SamplerState*` to do it.
- `DebugText::draw_debug_info` begins and ends its own (DebugText.cpp:109, :136).
- `Level::draw_countdown_text` wraps its one drawable in its own (Level.cpp:740-745).
- `TextureObject::draw`, `AnimationObject::draw`, `Visual::draw`, `TextObject::draw` all assume the caller has already begun one (Level.cpp begins at :513, loops, ends at :553).

So whether you may call a given `draw` depends on undocumented per-class knowledge, and the sort mode / sampler / blend state a drawable renders under is invisible at its call site. Two of the four also flush mid-frame, which is a real cost: a normal player viewport pays 3 Begin/End cycles, rising to 5 with debug text and the countdown active. (I am correcting the reviewer's flat "five per player per frame" — debug and countdown are conditional.)
findings.suggestion: Introduce a `Renderer`/`SpriteBatchScope` that owns `Begin`/`End` and the pipeline state. Every drawable gets `void draw(Renderer&, const Camera&) const` and only submits; nothing below the renderer calls `Begin`/`End` or sees an `ID3D11SamplerState*`. Where a different state block is genuinely needed (point-clamped UI), express it as a named pass the renderer opens.
findings.verify_note: Read InterfaceGameplay.cpp:15-47, DebugText.cpp:109/136, Level.cpp:513-553 and 737-745. Counted the conditional branches to correct the per-frame Begin/End claim.

findings.title: AnimatedSprite is entirely dead code and a line-for-line fork of AnimationObject — including both of its bugs
findings.detail:
A repo-wide grep for the identifier finds it only in its own two files, the two `.vcxproj` entries (lines 182 and 296), and `#include "AnimatedSprite.h"` at AnimationObject.h:5 — and `AnimationObject.cpp` never names the type, so even that include is spurious (it serves only to pull in `SpriteSheet.h` transitively).

It is not merely unused, it is a fork of the class that replaced it. Compare AnimatedSprite.cpp:59-122 with AnimationObject.cpp:81-138: `update`, `reset`, `stop`, `play`, `pause`, `is_paused`, `set_frame_index` are the same algorithm over the same five members, including the same `if`-instead-of-`while` timing bug, the same `reset()`-does-not-clear-`_paused` bug, and the same `throw std::exception("Invalid frame index.")`. Every timing fix has to be made twice and one will be missed.

The galling part is that the dead copy is the better design: it is a *component* you hold, and it caches `SpriteSheet*` + `const AnimationStrip*` at construction (AnimatedSprite.h:43-44) instead of doing two string map lookups per call.

I am rejecting one attached sub-claim: a reviewer flagged `set_animation_strip` (AnimatedSprite.cpp:103-109) not resetting `_frame_index` as a live crash when switching to a shorter strip. The analysis is right but the class is never constructed anywhere, so there is no reachable path.
findings.suggestion: Two coherent options. (a) Delete AnimatedSprite.h/.cpp and their vcxproj entries, and change AnimationObject.h:5 to include `AnimationStrip.h` directly. (b) Keep it, rename to `SpriteAnimator`, delete `AnimationObject`, and have everything that animates *hold* one — which also removes one arm of the `Player` diamond and the per-frame lookups. Do not leave both.
findings.verify_note: Grepped the whole tree for AnimatedSprite (only self-references + vcxproj + the AnimationObject.h include). Read both files in full and diffed the state machine against AnimationObject.cpp.

findings.title: Health bar fill width is never clamped and player health is only clamped at the top, so a dead player renders an inverted destination RECT
findings.detail:
```cpp
Vector2F fill_size = Vector2F(size.x - 2.0f * border, size.y - 2.0f * border);
fill_size.x *= health;                       // :127 — no clamp
RectangleI fill_rect = RectangleI(..., static_cast<int>(fill_size.x), ...);
```
I traced the value. `health` comes straight from `Player::get_health()` at Level.cpp:563. Player health is clamped only at the top — Player.cpp:735-737 caps regen at 1.0f — while the damage path just subtracts with no floor (`_health -= SPRAY_DAMAGE/JET_DAMAGE/ROLLING_DAMAGE/BALL_DAMAGE/MIST_DAMAGE` at Player.cpp:652, 658, 664, 670, 676). A hit that takes health from 0.05 to negative is routine. `Player::update` then flags DEAD at :704 but leaves `_health` negative until `respawn()` resets it to 1.0f at :999, up to 3 seconds later — and `draw_gameplay_interface` runs unconditionally every one of those frames (Level.cpp:560-569).

With `health` negative, `fill_size.x` is negative, `RectangleI` gets a negative width, and `RectangleI::get_win_rect()` (MattMath.cpp:2043-2052) computes `right = x + width`, which is less than `left`. `SpriteBatch::Draw` receives an inverted destination rect.

`draw_ammo` (:80) has the identical missing clamp and is safe only because `Weapon` happens to pre-clamp ammo. The UI layer is the last line of defence and should not depend on that.
findings.suggestion: Clamp at the point of use — `const float fraction = std::clamp(health, 0.0f, 1.0f);` (needs the C++17 bump; see the LanguageStandard finding) — and separately floor `Player::_health` at 0 in the damage path so the real bug surfaces at its source. Note `draw_ammo` and `draw_health` are otherwise identical apart from the fill colour; they should be one `draw_bar(...)`.
findings.verify_note: Read InterfaceGameplay.cpp:49-143, Level.cpp:560-569, grepped every _health write in Player.cpp (only the regen path clamps), read RectangleI::get_win_rect at MattMath.cpp:2043-2052.

findings.title: reset() does not clear _paused, so any object that finishes a non-looping animation is frozen forever afterwards
findings.suggestion: Make `reset()` mean reset: `_frame_index = 0; _time_elapsed = 0.0f; _paused = false;` and keep `stop()` as `reset(); _paused = true;`. `PaintTileSplash::reset_and_play()` then collapses to a plain `reset()`.
findings.verify_note: Read AnimationObject.cpp:81-125 and 144-151, PaintTile.cpp:176-180, Player.cpp:65. Grepped sprite_sheet_1.json for looping flags — one false at line 119, the rest true.

findings.title: Frame advance uses `if` not `while` and frame_time is never validated, so fast strips drift and a zero frame_time poisons the accumulator
findings.suggestion:
Drain the accumulator and reject nonsense input:
```cpp
while (_frame_time > 0.0f && _time_elapsed >= _frame_time) { _time_elapsed -= _frame_time; advance_one_frame(); }
```
Validate `frame_time > 0` in the JSON decoder so a malformed sheet fails at load. Replace the `FLT_MIN` sentinel with `std::optional<float>`.
findings.verify_note: Read AnimationObject.cpp:81-107 and 152-159, AnimationStrip.h:22, SpriteSheet.cpp:61-62, Player.cpp:64-70. Checked ArtAttack.vcxproj for FloatingPointModel (Fast in all four configs) before rejecting the FLT_MIN sub-claim.

findings.title: draw_respawn_timer ignores resolution scaling and rounds differently from draw_timer, giving a visible off-by-one on every death
findings.detail:
The two timer renderers in the same class disagree on both scaling and rounding.

`draw_timer` (:144-173) computes `float scale = resolution.x / TIMER_SCALE_FACTOR;`, passes it to `DrawString`, and scales the shadow offset with it (`pos + (TIMER_SHADOW_OFFSET * scale)`).

`draw_respawn_timer` (:175-199) does neither — `DrawString(sprite_batch, text.c_str(), (pos + RESPAWN_TIMER_SHADOW_OFFSET).get_xm_vector(), ...)` passes no scale argument at all, so it defaults to 1.0. In 2-player split-screen the match timer shrinks to 0.5x while the respawn counter stays full size; at 4K the respawn counter stays tiny.

Rounding differs too: `static_cast<int>(std::ceil(timer))` at :158 versus `static_cast<int>(timer) + 1` at :186. Those agree only for non-integral positive values. `Player::_respawn_timer` is initialised to exactly `RESPAWN_DELAY = 3.0f` (Player.h:151, player_consts.h:43) and is not decremented on the frame the player dies — `Player::update` takes the ALIVE branch and sets DEAD at :704-706, and the DEAD branch that decrements (:714) only runs from the next frame. So the first respawn frame renders `int(3.0) + 1 = 4` for a 3-second delay.
findings.suggestion: Give `draw_respawn_timer` the same `scale` treatment and use `std::ceil`. Better, both functions are "draw a scaled number with a drop shadow" — extract one helper taking font, value, position, colours and scale, and delete the duplicate.
findings.verify_note: Read InterfaceGameplay.cpp:144-199. Read Player.h:151, player_consts.h:43 (RESPAWN_DELAY 3.0f) and Player.cpp:704-719 to confirm the decrement ordering.

findings.title: SpriteFrame parses origin and rotated-packing from the atlas JSON and then throws both away; _source_rectangle2 is never even written
findings.detail:
`SpriteSheet::decode_sprite_frames_json` (SpriteSheet.cpp:34-44) carefully parses two optional fields and passes them to the constructor, which stores them (SpriteFrame.cpp:11-12, 18-19). Nothing ever reads them back — the class's only accessor is `get_source_rectangle()` (SpriteFrame.h:19), there is no `get_origin()` or `is_rotated()`, and grep finds no other use of `_origin`/`_rotated` anywhere.

So an atlas entry marked `"rotated": true` — meaning the packer stored it turned 90 degrees to save space — is drawn unrotated, i.e. visibly wrong, with no warning. The schema is live: sprite_sheet_1.json:141 already carries a `"rotated": false` entry, so the first `true` produces a corrupt sprite. Per-frame authored pivots are likewise ignored, which is part of why `Weapon` and `Drawer` each hand-roll a `calculate_sprite_origin`.

Separately, `MattMath::RectangleI _source_rectangle2` (line 23) is declared, default-initialised to `ZERO`, and never written by either constructor or either `set_source_rectangle` overload (SpriteFrame.cpp:28-38). It is a half-finished duplicate representation; the `2` suffix is the tell. The second constructor (`SpriteFrame(position, size, ...)`, SpriteFrame.h:14-18) also has no callers — only the `RectangleI` one is used, at SpriteSheet.cpp:43.
findings.suggestion: Either implement or delete. To implement: expose `get_origin()`/`is_rotated()`, use the pivot as the default draw origin, and in the draw path add -pi/2 to the rotation and swap the destination extents when rotated. To delete: strip `_origin`, `_rotated`, the unused constructor, the JSON parsing at SpriteSheet.cpp:34-42, and `_source_rectangle2`. Silently ignoring data you bothered to parse is worse than not parsing it.
findings.verify_note: Read SpriteFrame.h and SpriteFrame.cpp in full, SpriteSheet.cpp:20-47. Grepped for _origin/_rotated/_source_rectangle2 reads — none. Confirmed "rotated" at sprite_sheet_1.json:141.

findings.title: set_draw_rotation_by_rectangle_rotated is an empty stub and Visual's RectangleRotated constructor silently discards the rotation
findings.suggestion: Implement it — `_draw_rotation = rect.get_angle();` — and call it from the `Visual` constructor along with `set_origin(_rectangle.get_size() / 2.0f)`. If you are not implementing it now, delete both the stub and the `Visual` overload so callers get a compile error rather than a silently wrong image.
findings.verify_note: Read DrawObject.cpp:66-69, Visual.cpp:22-35, MattMath.cpp:4456-4463 (both get_rectangle_rotated_to_axis and get_angle exist). Grepped for callers of the setter — none. Confirmed LevelObjectBuilder.cpp:188/236 use the RectangleF overload.

findings.title: AnimationObject's constructor calls virtual functions and does two resource lookups on a half-built object
findings.detail:
```cpp
AnimationObject::AnimationObject(const float* dt, ...) :
	SpriteSheetObject(sheet_name, animation_strip_name, ...), _dt(dt)
{
	this->_frame_time = this->get_animation_strip()->get_frame_time();   // :21
}
```
`get_animation_strip()` (:24-28) calls `get_sprite_sheet()` and `get_element_name()`, both declared `virtual` in SpriteSheetObject.h:20-21. During this constructor the dynamic type is `AnimationObject`, so any override in a derived class is silently bypassed and the object gets a `_frame_time` from the wrong strip. No warning; the failure mode is a wrong animation speed.

It also bakes in an undocumented ordering requirement: no `AnimationObject` — and therefore no `Player`, `Projectile` or `PaintTileSplash` — may be constructed before `ResourceLoader::load_all_resources()` has populated that specific sheet *and* that specific strip. On violation, `ResourceManager::get_sprite_sheet` returns nullptr (see that finding) and this is a null dereference during object construction, from a virtual call, in a constructor.

`_frame_time` is itself a denormalised cached copy of `AnimationStrip::_frame_time` that must be manually re-synced via `set_frame_time_to_default()` whenever the strip changes.
findings.suggestion: Never call virtuals from a constructor. Resolve the strip outside the object and inject it: `AnimationObject(const float* dt, const AnimationStrip& strip, ...) : ..., _strip(&strip), _frame_time(strip.get_frame_time()) {}`. Holding the resolved `const AnimationStrip*` also removes two string map lookups from `update()` and `get_source_rectangle()` on every object every frame.
findings.verify_note: Read AnimationObject.cpp:16-28 and SpriteSheetObject.h:19-23 (get_sprite_sheet and get_element_name are both virtual).

findings.title: Every class in the render hierarchy has a public defaulted constructor that produces a permanently unusable object
findings.detail:
`DrawObject() = default` (DrawObject.h:11), `SpriteSheetObject() = default` (SpriteSheetObject.h:9), `TextureObject() = default` (TextureObject.h:9), `AnimationObject() = default` (AnimationObject.h:10), `TextObject() = default` (TextObject.h:9), `Text() = default` (Text.h:9), `TextDropShadow() = default` (TextDropShadow.h:9), `Visual() = default` (Visual.h:11), plus `PaintTileSplash() = default` (PaintTile.h:26).

All leave `DrawObject::_resource_manager == nullptr`, and `AnimationObject` additionally leaves `_dt == nullptr` and `_frame_time == 0.0f`. `DrawObject` exposes no setter for `_resource_manager` — `SpriteSheetObject` only has name setters — so such an object can never be brought into a valid state through the public or protected API. It is guaranteed to null-deref on first use: `TextureObject::draw` → `get_sprite_sheet()` → `get_resource_manager()->...` (SpriteSheetObject.cpp:33), and `AnimationObject::update` → `*this->_dt` (AnimationObject.cpp:88, reached because `_paused` defaults to false).

This is not purely theoretical plumbing. `PaintTile.h:83` declares `PaintTileSplash _splash;` by value, so every `PaintTile` passes through a state where its splash has a null `_dt`; PaintTile.cpp:25 move-assigns a real one over it in the constructor *body*, so the window is currently closed by luck rather than by construction.

Compare `Drawer`, which at least has `set_resource_manager`/`set_dt` — inconsistent, and those accept nullptr silently anyway.
findings.suggestion: Delete the defaulted constructors from the render hierarchy, and have `PaintTile` initialise `_splash` in its member-initialiser list rather than assigning in the body. Take the manager as `ResourceManager&` so "absent" is not representable. If a container needs default-constructibility, the container should hold `optional`/`unique_ptr`.
findings.verify_note: Read every listed header line, SpriteSheetObject.cpp:31-35, AnimationObject.cpp:81-88, PaintTile.h:26/83 and PaintTile.cpp:25-27.

findings.title: DrawObject declares a virtual destructor and none of the other four special members — the hierarchy is slice-prone and unmovable
findings.detail:
```cpp
class DrawObject
{
public:
    virtual ~DrawObject() = default;   // :10
    DrawObject() = default;            // :11
```
Declaring the destructor suppresses the implicit move constructor and move assignment, so the whole hierarchy — `SpriteSheetObject`, `TextureObject`, `AnimationObject`, `TextObject`, `Text`, `TextDropShadow`, `Visual`, `Player` and the menu widgets — is non-movable; every apparent move silently degrades to a copy of two `std::string`s plus the rest.

Meanwhile copy construction and copy assignment stay implicitly public on a class with virtual functions and a public non-final base, so `Text& t = some_drop_shadow; t = some_text;` compiles and slices: the shadow's colour/offset/scale survive while the `Text`/`TextObject` subobject is overwritten.

`AnimationStrip` (AnimationStrip.h:6-27) has the mirror problem: implicitly copyable while handing out `&_frame_rects[i]` (AnimationStrip.cpp:34), so a copy-assignment invalidates every pointer previously returned.

Rule of five in the strictest sense — the base declares one of the five and none of the other four.
findings.suggestion: Apply the polymorphic-base recipe on `DrawObject` (and mirror it on `Drawer`, `SpriteSheet`, `AnimationStrip`): `virtual ~DrawObject() = default;` public, and `protected:` defaulted copy/move constructor and assignment. Protected copy/move keeps derived classes copyable while making slicing through a base reference ill-formed, and restores move semantics.
