findings.verify_note: Read DrawObject.h:7-42 (only the destructor among the five is declared), AnimationStrip.h:6-27 and AnimationStrip.cpp:28-35.

findings.title: Drawer is a base class with a public non-virtual destructor whose entire helper API is dead code
findings.detail:
`Drawer` has no virtual functions and no user-declared destructor, so its implicit destructor is public and non-virtual — yet it is used purely as an implementation-inheritance base (`class DebugText : public Drawer`, `class InterfaceGameplay : public Drawer`). Currently latent because both are held as concrete `unique_ptr`s in `Level`, but `delete static_cast<Drawer*>(p)` is silent UB with no diagnostic, which is a landmine in a codebase meant to be subclassed by others.

Everything it contributes beyond two raw pointers is unused. Grep-verified: `set_resource_manager` and `set_dt` (Drawer.h:14-15) have no callers; both `calculate_draw_rectangle` overloads (Drawer.cpp:33-53) have no callers except each other; `calculate_sprite_origin` (Drawer.cpp:55-67) has no callers. `calculate_draw_rectangle` also reimplements the world-to-screen transform that `Camera::calculate_view_rectangle` already provides, and does it with a *different* camera representation (`Vector3F` packing x/y/zoom) from the `MattMath::Camera` every other renderer uses.

Meanwhile `Weapon::calculate_sprite_origin` (Weapon.cpp:88-101) is a functionally identical reimplementation in a class that does not derive from `Drawer`, called from Weapon.cpp:42, :73 and WeaponRoller.cpp. (Correcting the reviewers: it is not byte-for-byte — Weapon spells out `TOP_LEFT` and adds a `default:` — but it is the same function.) So the inheritance is not even succeeding at sharing the one thing it exists to share, because all three helpers are non-static, non-const members that touch no member state and therefore need an instance to call.

After removing the dead code, `Drawer` is a struct with two raw pointers.
findings.suggestion: Delete `calculate_draw_rectangle` (Camera owns that transform) and `set_resource_manager`/`set_dt`. Move `calculate_sprite_origin` to a free function in a small rendering-utility header and delete the `Weapon` copy. Then dissolve `Drawer` as a base class — pass a `DrawContext { const ResourceManager* resources; float dt; }` value to the two consumers. In the meantime add `protected: ~Drawer() = default;`.
findings.verify_note: Read Drawer.h and Drawer.cpp in full and Weapon.cpp:88-101. Grepped the tree for calculate_draw_rectangle / Drawer::calculate_sprite_origin / set_resource_manager — no external callers.

findings.title: protected virtual AnimationObject::update() has the same signature as IGameObject::update(), so Player::update overrides both at once
findings.detail:
```cpp
protected:
    virtual void update();     // AnimationObject.h:21
```
Identical signature to `IGameObject::update()` (IGameObject.h:10, public pure virtual). `Player final : MovingObject, ICollisionGameObject, AnimationObject, TextureObject` (Player.h:63-64) inherits both, so its single `void update() override;` overrides two unrelated virtuals simultaneously — one an interface contract meaning "advance the whole game object", the other an implementation detail meaning "advance the animation frame".

It does not blow up today only because every derived class remembers the explicit qualified call (`AnimationObject::update();` in Player.cpp and each of the four Projectile subclasses). The moment anything inside `AnimationObject` calls unqualified `update()`, or a new derived class forgets the qualified call, you get infinite recursion or a permanently frozen animation with no diagnostic. Nothing overrides `AnimationObject::update` in the virtual sense, so the `virtual` buys nothing and creates the collision.
findings.suggestion: Rename it to say what it does and drop `virtual`: `void advance_animation();`. That removes the accidental override and makes the five call sites read correctly. The same reasoning applies to the `virtual` on the `draw` overloads in AnimationObject.h:34-46 and TextureObject.h:20-32, which shadow `IGameObject::draw` by name in every multiply-inheriting concrete class.
findings.verify_note: Read AnimationObject.h:21, IGameObject.h:10, Player.h:63-64. Confirmed the qualified AnimationObject::update() calls in the derived classes.

findings.title: Class Text exists only to widen the access of four setters, implemented as pointless forwarding overrides
findings.suggestion: Replace the whole body with `using TextObject::set_text;` etc. and delete Text.cpp. Better: decide whether those setters should be public on `TextObject` in the first place — a text object you cannot set the text of is odd — and delete `Text` entirely, reparenting `TextDropShadow` and `MText` onto `TextObject`.
findings.verify_note: Read Text.h, Text.cpp, TextObject.h:31-34, DrawObject.h:27-31 in full.

findings.title: draw_ammo and draw_health are the same 45 lines twice, plus redundant re-lookups and double string formatting
findings.detail:
`draw_ammo` (:49-96) and `draw_health` (:97-143) are identical apart from the parameter name, one local name (`empty_box_rect` vs `empty_rect`) and the final fill colour (`team_colour` vs `HEALTH_COLOUR`). Both compute `size` from `TOP_RIGHT_BOX_SIZE * resolution`, build a `RectangleI` from four `static_cast<int>`, fetch `SPRITE_SHEET`, draw `EMPTY_BOX_FRAME` in WHITE, compute `border`, build `fill_pos`/`fill_size`, scale `fill_size.x` by the fraction, and draw `FILL_FRAME`.

Both also re-fetch the identical sprite sheet pointer into the same variable for no reason — :88-89 repeats :66-67, and :135-136 repeats :113-114 — paying a second string map lookup each.

`draw_timer` builds the same string twice (`std::to_string(static_cast<int>(std::ceil(timer))).c_str()` at :158 and :167), doing two `ceil` calls per player per frame; `draw_respawn_timer` at :186 correctly hoists it into a local, so the two functions in the same class disagree. (Downgrading the reviewers' "two heap allocations" — a 2-3 character string fits MSVC's SSO, so the waste is real but small.)
findings.suggestion: One `draw_bar(SpriteBatch*, const Vector2F& viewport_size, float fraction, const Colour& fill, const Vector2F& position) const`, with `draw_ammo`/`draw_health` as one-line callers — then promote it out of this class into a reusable `ProgressBar` widget per the HUD finding. Delete the duplicate lookups and hoist the timer string.
findings.verify_note: Read InterfaceGameplay.cpp:49-199 line by line and diffed the two functions.

findings.title: Roughly 25 virtual accessors and draw overloads across the render bases, of which two are ever actually overridden
findings.detail:
DrawObject.h:20-31 declares eleven `virtual` one-line accessors. SpriteSheetObject.h:19-23 adds five more. TextureObject.h:20-32 and AnimationObject.h:34-46 each declare five `virtual` `draw` overloads.

A grep for `override` on these signatures across the first-party tree finds only two: `set_colour` (Mh.h, PaintTile.h:40, Text.h:22 — and the `Text` one is the useless forwarder) and `get_resource_manager` (Weapon.h). No getter is ever overridden, and none of the ten `draw` overloads is overridden — `MTexture::draw`/`MText::draw` override `IGameObject::draw`, a different signature, and then call these qualified.

Cost: every `Player`, `Projectile`, `PaintTile`, `Structure` and menu widget carries vtable slots for accessors that return a float, and the per-sprite draw path makes indirect calls the optimiser cannot inline — on the hot loop in `draw_player_view_level`, a per-sprite tax for zero polymorphism.
findings.suggestion: Strip `virtual` from all of them, keeping it only where a real override exists (and reconsider even `Weapon::get_resource_manager` — that override suggests the dependency should be a constructor parameter, not a virtual hook). Mark the pure getters `[[nodiscard]]` while you are in there.
findings.verify_note: Read DrawObject.h:20-31, SpriteSheetObject.h:19-23, TextureObject.h:20-32, AnimationObject.h:34-46. Grepped for override across the tree.

findings.title: IGameObject is a fat interface that hardwires DirectX types and a non-const draw into every game object
findings.suggestion: Split by responsibility: `IUpdatable { void update(float dt); }` and `IRenderable { void draw(Renderer&, const Camera&) const; RectangleF bounds() const; }`. Culling belongs to the renderer/scene computed from `bounds()`, not reimplemented per object. Collapse the two draw overloads into one. Replace `SpriteBatch*` with an abstract `Renderer&` so the object graph does not name a DirectX type, and make `draw` const.
findings.verify_note: Read IGameObject.h in full, Visual.cpp:38-52, TextDropShadow.cpp:49-52, Level.cpp:375 and 737.

findings.title: Sprite sheet JSON is parsed with zero validation, so a malformed file is undefined behaviour in Release
findings.detail:
`load_from_json` does `d.ParseStream(is)` and never calls `d.HasParseError()`. It then does `Value& sprite_frames = d["sprite_frames"];` and `d["animation_strips"]` with no `HasMember` check.

`decode_sprite_frames_json` (:20-47) indexes `frame["name"]`, `frame["position"]["x"]`, `frame["size"]["w"]` and calls `GetString`/`GetInt`/`GetFloat` with no type checks. `decode_animation_strips_json` (:49-68) does the same for `first_frame`/`frame_count`/`frame_time`/`looping`. RapidJSON guards all of these with `RAPIDJSON_ASSERT`, which is a no-op under NDEBUG — and Release defines NDEBUG. So a truncated or hand-edited sheet does not produce an error message, it reads past `MemberEnd()`.

`frame_count` and `frame_time` are also never range-checked before being handed to `AnimationStrip`, which is the upstream cause of two other findings here (zero frame_time poisoning the animation accumulator, and an unvalidated `frame_count` driving an unreserved allocation loop).
findings.suggestion: After `ParseStream`, `if (d.HasParseError()) throw` with `GetParseError_En(d.GetParseError())` and `GetErrorOffset()`. Add a `require_member(v, "name")` helper that checks `HasMember` plus the expected `Is*()` and throws a message naming the file, the frame and the field. Validate `frame_count > 0` and `frame_time > 0` before constructing `AnimationStrip`.
findings.verify_note: Read SpriteSheet.cpp:20-90 in full; no HasParseError, no HasMember, no Is*() checks anywhere.

findings.title: AnimationStrip trusts frame_count from JSON, allocates unreserved, keeps a redundant count, and has a default ctor that can only throw
findings.detail:
Four related defects in one small class:

1. `calculate_all_frame_rects()` (:50-57) `push_back`s `_frame_count` times with no `reserve`, so a strip reallocates log2(n) times at load.
2. `_frame_count` comes straight from `strip["frame_count"].GetInt()` (SpriteSheet.cpp:61) with no validation. A negative value yields an empty strip whose every `get_frame_rect()` then throws; a huge value attempts that many RECTs.
3. `calculate_frame` (:17-26) re-validates an index against `_frame_count` even though its only caller is a loop bounded by `_frame_count` — a branch that can never fire — and it throws from inside the constructor, which runs inside `SpriteSheet::load_from_json`, so a bad sheet aborts resource loading via an exception nobody catches. `get_frame_rect` (:28-35) then validates against `_frame_count` but indexes `_frame_rects`, two values that agree only by constructor convention.
4. `AnimationStrip() = default` (AnimationStrip.h:9) leaves `_frame_count == 0`, so the guard in `get_frame_rect` is true for every index including 0 — a default-constructed strip's entire public surface is a guaranteed exception. Nothing default-constructs one (they are built only at SpriteSheet.cpp:64), so this is cleanup rather than a live bug.

Separately, `calculate_frame` hardcodes a single uniform-width horizontal row (`frame.offset(frame_index * frame.width, 0)`) with no way to express a grid, wrapped or non-uniform atlas, and one `frame_time` for the whole clip — a real limitation for a reusable engine.
findings.suggestion: Validate `frame_count > 0` and `frame_time > 0` in the decoder, with a message naming the strip. `reserve(_frame_count)` before the loop. Drop `_frame_count` and use `_frame_rects.size()` as the single source of truth, which removes the redundant check. Delete the default constructor. Longer term, model a clip as an explicit ordered list of `FrameId`s plus timing, so any packing layout works.
findings.verify_note: Read AnimationStrip.h and AnimationStrip.cpp in full, SpriteSheet.cpp:53-66. Confirmed no default construction exists anywhere.

findings.title: Constructors of 9-15 parameters with long runs of interchangeable defaulted floats, while the parameter-object struct the project already wrote sits unused
findings.detail:
`TextDropShadow`'s constructor takes 13 parameters, nine defaulted, including four consecutive interchangeable floats (`scale`, `shadow_scale`, `rotation`, `layer_depth`) and two interchangeable pairs (`color`/`shadow_color`, `shadow_offset`/`origin`). Transposing any of them compiles cleanly and produces a subtly wrong render. `MTextDropShadow` (Mh.h) makes it 15 by inserting a bare `bool hidden` into the middle of the float run, so the call site reads as a naked `true`.

The same shape recurs at Visual.h:12-20 and :22-30, TextureObject.h:10-17, SpriteSheetObject.h:10-17, AnimationObject.h:11-19, TextObject.h:10-19, and four times in `SpriteSheet::draw` (SpriteSheet.h:19-59).

The project already knows the answer and did not apply it: `InterfaceGameplay.h:37-45` declares `struct InterfaceDraw` bundling exactly these fields, and a grep across all first-party sources finds it referenced at precisely one place — its own declaration. It is never constructed. Meanwhile `draw_gameplay_interface` takes nine loose positional parameters including four adjacent floats (`health, ammo, timer, ..., respawn_timer`) — swapping health and ammo silently swaps the two bars. The trailing `float respawn_timer, bool show_respawn_timer` is a textbook `std::optional<float>`. `InterfaceDraw` also disagrees with the real signature (`Vector2I resolution` vs `const Vector2F&`) and carries a `player_team` the function does not take — which is the only reason the header includes `player_team.h`.

Also: the argument actually passed as `resolution` is `player_vp.get_size()` (Level.cpp:558), a *viewport* size, so the parameter name is wrong in split-screen, which is the normal case. And `draw_gameplay_interface` is non-const while all four helpers it delegates to are const, despite mutating nothing.
findings.suggestion: Introduce `struct DrawStyle { Colour colour; float rotation; Vector2F origin; SpriteEffects effects; float layer_depth; }` and `struct ShadowStyle { Colour colour; Vector2F offset; float scale; }` and pass those. Either finish the `InterfaceDraw` refactor — `void draw(SpriteBatch*, ID3D11SamplerState*, const InterfaceDraw&, std::optional<float> respawn_timer) const` — or delete the struct and the `player_team.h` include. Rename `resolution` to `viewport_size` throughout. Replace `bool hidden` with `enum class visibility`.
findings.verify_note: Read TextDropShadow.h:10-22, InterfaceGameplay.h:37-60, InterfaceGameplay.cpp:15-47, Level.cpp:556-569. Grepped the whole tree for InterfaceDraw — declaration only.

findings.title: The origin field has no defined coordinate space, and Weapon feeds world-space values into a texture-space parameter
findings.suggestion: Make the pivot explicit and typed. Store it as a normalised `Vector2F` in [0,1] of the frame and convert to texel space in the single place that calls `SpriteBatch::Draw`, or take it from `SpriteFrame::_origin` — already parsed from the atlas and currently discarded — so it is authored in texture space by construction. Remove the untyped `set_origin` from the public surface.
findings.verify_note: Read DrawObject.h:39, TextureObject.cpp:21-69, Weapon.cpp:36-66 and Weapon.cpp:88-101. Confirmed get_details().size is the world-space draw rectangle size used for both the destination rect and the origin.

findings.title: Namespace-scope `const static std::string`/`Colour`/`Vector2F` in headers give a dynamically-initialised copy per translation unit
findings.suggestion: With the language standard bumped to C++17, use `inline constexpr` for anything literal and `inline const` for the rest, giving one object across the program. Give `Vector2F` and `Colour` constexpr constructors so they can be `inline constexpr` too. Prefer `inline constexpr std::string_view` over `std::string` for the asset names.
findings.verify_note: Read InterfaceGameplay.h:10-35 and DebugText.h:9-19; confirmed the mix of constexpr and const static, and that both headers reach Level.h.

findings.title: No LanguageStandard is set, so the project silently builds as C++14 and the fixes several findings need are unavailable
findings.detail:
I grepped the vcxproj: `PlatformToolset` is `v145` and `ConformanceMode` is `true` in all four configurations, but there is no `<LanguageStandard>` element anywhere. MSVC therefore defaults to `/std:c++14`.

This is not cosmetic — it is why several natural fixes in this module are currently unavailable: `std::clamp` for the unclamped HUD bars, `std::optional<float>` for the `FLT_MIN` frame-time sentinel and the `respawn_timer`/`show_respawn_timer` pair, `inline` variables for the header constants above, `std::string_view` for asset names, and designated initialisers (C++20) for the giant defaulted constructor lists. A grep for `std::optional`, `string_view`, `if constexpr` and `std::clamp` across the first-party sources returns zero hits, so nothing depends on staying at C++14.

Also worth noting from the same file: `FloatingPointModel` is `Fast` in all four configurations, which the codebase then combines with exact float equality comparisons (`info.frame_time != FLT_MIN`, Player.cpp:66).
findings.suggestion: Set `<LanguageStandard>stdcpp20</LanguageStandard>` (or at minimum `stdcpp17`) in all four configurations and fix the fallout in one pass. Consider `TreatWarningAsError` for new code, since /W4 warnings are currently accumulating unread (the unused parameter in the `set_draw_rotation_by_rectangle_rotated` stub is one).
findings.verify_note: Grepped ArtAttack.vcxproj for LanguageStandard (absent), PlatformToolset (v145 x4), ConformanceMode (true x4), FloatingPointModel (Fast x4). Grepped the sources for C++17 library features — none used.

findings.title: Wrong-case include of Colour.h, plus heavy headers included where forward declarations suffice
findings.detail:
`InterfaceGameplay.h:7` is `#include "colour.h"` but the file on disk is `Colour.h` (I listed the directory to confirm — only `Colour.h`, `TeamColour.h`, `TeamColour.cpp`). This resolves only because NTFS is case-insensitive; it is a hard build break on any case-sensitive filesystem, which for a project whose stated goal is a reusable engine is a portability failure hiding in one character. Every other TU spells it correctly (`DrawObject.h:4`, `SpriteSheet.h:5`). It is also redundant — line 6 already pulls `ResourceManager.h` → `SpriteSheet.h` → `Colour.h` — as are `MattMath.h` (line 8, already via `Drawer.h:7`) and `ResourceManager.h` (already via `Drawer.h:5`).

`DebugText.h` has the same shape: line 7 includes the full `Player.h` where the only use is `const Player*` in a declaration, so `class Player;` would do; line 5 includes `ResolutionManager.h` for a `const ResolutionManager*` member; line 6's `MattMath.h` is already provided by `Drawer.h:7`. As written, every TU reaching `DebugText.h` via `Level.h:11` compiles the whole `Player` hierarchy and rebuilds when any of it changes.
findings.suggestion: Fix `"colour.h"` → `"Colour.h"` or delete it as redundant. In `DebugText.h`, replace the `Player.h` and `ResolutionManager.h` includes with forward declarations and move the real includes into the .cpp. Drop the redundant `MattMath.h`/`ResourceManager.h` from both headers, and `player_team.h` once `InterfaceDraw` is dealt with.
findings.verify_note: Listed ArtAttack/ and confirmed the file is Colour.h. Read InterfaceGameplay.h:1-8, DebugText.h:1-33 (Player used only as a pointer parameter), Drawer.h:1-7.

findings.title: SpriteFont's UTF-8 DrawString overload uses a per-font conversion buffer, and fonts are shared singletons drawn from every render thread
findings.detail:
Both `TextObject::draw` overloads pass `this->_text.c_str()` — a `const char*` — which selects DirectXTK's UTF-8 `DrawString` overload (SpriteFont.h:51-55). That overload converts UTF-8 to UTF-16 into a scratch buffer owned by the font's pImpl, lazily allocated and grown on demand.

The buffer is per-`SpriteFont`, and fonts are shared singletons handed out by `ResourceManager`. Text drawing happens inside `draw_player_view_level`, which runs as one task per partition on the thread pool: `Level::draw_countdown_text`, `InterfaceGameplay::draw_timer`/`draw_respawn_timer` (InterfaceGameplay.cpp:156-198) and `DebugText::draw_debug_info` (DebugText.cpp:115-131) all call `DrawString` on the same font from different threads. Concurrent conversions would overwrite each other's buffer, and a grow would reallocate under another thread's feet.

I am marking this uncertain rather than confirmed: only the DirectXTK *header* is vendored here (packages/directxtk_desktop_2019.2023.10.31.1/include/SpriteFont.h), so I could confirm the const UTF-8 overloads exist and that only a `unique_ptr<Impl>` backs them, but I could not read the implementation to verify the shared-buffer claim in this tree. The threading exposure is confirmed; the library-internal mechanism is not.
findings.suggestion: Store text as `std::wstring` (or cache a converted wstring alongside `_text`, invalidated in `set_text`) and call the `wchar_t` overload, which does no shared-buffer conversion. That also removes a `MultiByteToWideChar` call from the hot path. Confirm against the DirectXTK source you are actually linking before deciding how urgent this is.
findings.verify_note: Read TextObject.cpp:27-62 and SpriteFont.h:40-60 in the vendored package (UTF-8 overloads exist, const, backed by unique_ptr<Impl>). The DirectXTK .cpp is not in this tree, so the shared conversion buffer could not be verified here. Threading exposure confirmed from Level.cpp:375-400 and 556-590.

findings.title: Destination rects truncate position and size independently rather than rounding edges, giving seams and an asymmetry across x=0
findings.verify_note: Read TextureObject.cpp:35-39, MattMath.cpp:823-829 (four static_cast<int>) and 2043-2052 (right = x + width). Did not verify the paint-grid geometry, hence the downgrade.

findings.title: calculate_sprite_origin silently folds NO_ROTATION into TOP_LEFT, and the rotat_origin field it exists for is never read anywhere
findings.suggestion: Make the switch total and let the compiler police it — drop `default:`, list all four cases, and have `NO_ROTATION` assert or map explicitly. Then either wire `ProjectileDetails::rotat_origin` into the projectile draw path or delete the field and its six initialisers.

findings.title: draw_debug_info: unguarded 1/dt, two different bool formats in adjacent lines, gratuitous copies, and per-frame string churn
findings.detail:
Several small defects in one function:

- Line 82: `std::to_string(1.0f / this->get_dt())` with no guard. `Drawer::get_dt()` (Drawer.cpp:28-31) dereferences `_dt` unconditionally on a pointer that defaults to nullptr, and `Game::_dt` starts at 0.0f (Game.cpp:244) and is only written in `update()`, which the fixed-timestep loop can skip while render always runs. The result is `"inf"` — harmless output, but it is the same unguarded pointer every `Drawer` subclass uses with no stated contract. (Correcting the reviewers: `1.0f/0.0f` gives inf under IEEE regardless of /fp:fast.)
- Lines 70-79 format `primary_shooting` as `"true"`/`"false"` via an eight-line if/else, while lines 84-85 format two other bools through `std::to_string(bool)`, which resolves to the `int` overload and prints `"1"`/`"0"`. Three booleans, two formats, in the same block.
- Lines 23-28 copy `RectangleF`, `Vector2F`, `Camera` and `Viewport` from accessors that already return `const&`.
- `std::vector<std::string> lines;` with ~20 `push_back`s and no `reserve`, rebuilt from scratch every call, inside the parallel render pass. The `operator+` chains at :46-68 do allocate for the longer lines (the short `to_string` results fit MSVC's SSO, so I am not repeating the reviewers' "60+ allocations" figure).
- An index loop over a container only ever read front-to-back (:111).
- `Level.cpp:574` recomputes `count_projectiles()` — a full linear scan — once per player rather than once per frame.
findings.suggestion: `const float dt = get_dt(); lines.push_back("fps: " + (dt > 0.0f ? std::to_string(1.0f/dt) : std::string("--")));`. One `bool_str` helper for all three booleans. `const auto&` for the four reference getters. `lines.reserve(20)` and a range-for. Keep the vector as a member and rebuild in place. Hoist `count_projectiles()` out of the per-player loop.
findings.verify_note: Read DebugText.cpp:18-137 and Drawer.cpp:28-31, Game.cpp:244, Level.cpp:570-578.

findings.title: throw std::exception("literal") is an MSVC extension that does not compile on any other toolchain — 54 sites
findings.detail:
```cpp
throw std::exception("frame_index out of range");   // AnimationStrip.cpp:21 and :32
throw std::exception("Invalid frame index.");       // AnimationObject.cpp:131
throw std::exception("Invalid frame index.");       // AnimatedSprite.cpp:115
throw std::exception("Failed to finish command list"); // Level.cpp
```
Standard `std::exception` has no `const char*` constructor; only MSVC's implementation provides one. Every one of these is a hard compile error on libstdc++/libc++. I counted 54 occurrences across the first-party .cpp files (the reviewers said 58 — the count differs slightly depending on whether headers are included, but the order of magnitude is right). For a codebase whose stated purpose is a reusable 2D engine, this single idiom pins it to one compiler.

The type is also wrong: an out-of-range frame index is `std::out_of_range`, and catching anything meaningfully is impossible when everything throws the same base type. `ResourceManager` already throws `std::out_of_range` for the analogous case, so the codebase is inconsistent with itself.
findings.suggestion: `throw std::out_of_range("AnimationStrip::get_frame_rect: frame_index " + std::to_string(frame_index) + " not in [0, " + std::to_string(_frame_count) + ")");` and equivalents elsewhere. `<stdexcept>` is already in pch.h. Fixing all 54 is mechanical and unblocks any future cross-platform build.
findings.verify_note: Read AnimationStrip.cpp:17-35, AnimationObject.cpp:126-134, AnimatedSprite.cpp:110-118. Counted 54 `std::exception("` sites across ArtAttack/*.cpp.

findings.title: map<string, unique_ptr<AnimationStrip>> adds a heap indirection for a plain value type, next to a map that gets it right
findings.detail:
```cpp
std::map<std::string, SpriteFrame> _sprite_frames;                       // :61 — correct
std::map<std::string, std::unique_ptr<AnimationStrip>> _animation_strips; // :62
```
`AnimationStrip` (AnimationStrip.h:19-23) is `vector<RECT>` + `RectangleI` + `int` + `float` + `bool` — an ordinary movable value type with no virtual functions and no derived classes. The `unique_ptr` buys nothing (`std::map` already guarantees reference stability) and costs an extra allocation per strip plus a pointer chase on every `get_frame_rect`. SpriteSheet.cpp:64-65 does `make_unique<AnimationStrip>(...)` where `emplace(name, AnimationStrip{...})` would do.

The two containers are declared one line apart and disagree about the idiom, which is the tell that it was not a deliberate choice.
findings.suggestion: `std::map<std::string, AnimationStrip> _animation_strips;` (or `unordered_map` — nothing depends on ordering), with `get_animation_strip` returning `const AnimationStrip*` from `.at()`. Same for the decoder's return type.
findings.verify_note: Read SpriteSheet.h:60-68, SpriteSheet.cpp:49-68, AnimationStrip.h:18-27 (no virtuals, no derived classes).

findings.title: Visual and MTexture are the same class written twice, and Visual is final yet exposes a protected member
findings.detail:
`Visual` (Visual.h:8-41) and `MTexture` (Mh.h) have the same shape: both are `IGameObject` + `TextureObject` plus a `RectangleF _rectangle`; both implement `update()` as a no-op; both implement the two `draw` overloads by forwarding to `TextureObject::draw(batch, _rectangle, camera)`; both implement `is_visible_in_viewport` as `_rectangle.intersects(view)`. `MTexture` adds only a name and a hidden flag.

Smaller contradiction in the same header: `class Visual final` (line 8) declares `_rectangle` as `protected` (line 40). Nothing can derive from it, so protected is meaningless — it should be private.
findings.suggestion: One `SpriteInstance` type — `{ Sprite visual; RectangleF bounds; float rotation; }` — used by both level content and UI, with the UI layer adding name/visibility by *wrapping* it rather than re-deriving. Make `_rectangle` private in the meantime.
findings.verify_note: Read Visual.h and Visual.cpp in full; compared against the MTexture declaration in Mh.h.

findings.title: AudioEngine is destroyed before the ResourceManager that owns its WaveBanks and SoundEffectInstances
findings.detail: Members destruct in reverse declaration order. `_resource_manager` is declared at Game.h:65 and `_audio_engine` at Game.h:74, so on every shutdown `_audio_engine` dies FIRST and `_resource_manager` second. `ResourceManager::_sound_banks` (ResourceManager.h:53) is `std::map<std::string, std::unique_ptr<SoundBank>>`; `SoundBank` owns `std::unique_ptr<DirectX::WaveBank> _wave_bank` (SoundBank.h:39) and `std::map<std::string, std::unique_ptr<DirectX::SoundEffectInstance>>` (SoundBank.h:41). DirectXTK requires the AudioEngine to outlive every WaveBank / SoundEffectInstance — their destructors unregister themselves from the engine. So `g_game.reset()` (Main.cpp:226) runs ~WaveBank and ~SoundEffectInstance against a freed AudioEngine on every normal exit. `Game::~Game()` (Game.cpp:23-29) calling `_audio_engine->Suspend()` does not help: the destructor body runs BEFORE member destruction, not after.
findings.suggestion: Declare `_audio_engine` first (before `_resource_manager`/`_resource_loader`) so it dies last, and better, stop relying on declaration order: add an explicit `Game::shutdown()` that does `_resource_manager.reset(); _resource_loader.reset();` and only then `_audio_engine.reset()`, with a comment stating the DirectXTK constraint.
findings.verify_note: Read Game.h:59-76 (declaration order), ResourceManager.h:46-54, SoundBank.h:38-42, Game.cpp:23-29, Main.cpp:226. Ordering is exactly as described.

findings.title: OnDeviceRestored reconstructs every subsystem, turning the entire live object graph into dangling pointers
findings.detail:
`Game::OnDeviceRestored()` (Game.cpp:282-287) unconditionally re-runs `create_device_dependent_resources()`, which is not a GPU-resource hook at all — it reassigns `_thread_pool` (:236), `_resource_manager` (:239), `_resource_loader` (:241), `_dt = std::make_unique<float>(0.f)` (:244), `_viewport_manager` (:247), `_states` (:252), `_partitioner` (:255), each assignment destroying the previous object, then republishes the new addresses into `GameData`.

Nothing in the live world re-reads GameData. Raw pointers are snapshotted once at construction: `Level.h:118 ViewportManager*`, `:119 ResourceManager*`, `:140 const float* _dt`, `:141 ID3D11SamplerState* _sampler_state` (obtained from the `CommonStates` that `OnDeviceLost` destroys at Game.cpp:276), `:146 ThreadPool*`, `:147 const Partitioner*`. Eleven headers cache `const float* _dt` (AnimationObject.h, AnimatedSprite.h, Drawer.h, LevelBuilder.h, Level.h, LevelObjectBuilder.h, PaintTile.h, Player.h, Projectile.h, StructurePaintable.h, Weapon.h). A single TDR/driver-update during gameplay therefore frees the float that every one of them reads on the next update, plus the thread pool the render path is mid-flight in.
findings.suggestion: Split into (a) device-dependent GPU objects recreated on restore (SpriteBatches, CommonStates, textures) and (b) device-independent services created exactly once in `initialize()` and never reassigned (ThreadPool, ResourceManager registry, ViewportManager, Partitioner, frame delta). Services that must be recreated should be repaired in place (`_resource_manager->recreate_gpu_resources(device)`) so their identity is stable, or reached through an accessor rather than a snapshotted raw pointer.
findings.verify_note: Read Game.cpp:218-287 line by line; every listed assignment is present and unconditional. Confirmed the raw-pointer members in Level.h:118-147 and counted 11 headers holding `const float* _dt` by grep (the candidates' '26 headers' figure was wrong; corrected here).

findings.title: Save-file parse writes an 8-byte read into a 1-byte heap allocation and never checks anything
findings.detail:
NOTE: outside the platform file list, but this is the first thing `wWinMain` does (Main.cpp:99) so it is a platform-startup defect.

```
FILE* fp = fopen(json_path, "rb");             // NULL never checked
auto read_buffer = std::make_unique<char>();    // ONE byte
FileReadStream is(fp, read_buffer.get(), sizeof(read_buffer)); // sizeof(unique_ptr)==8, not the buffer size
Document d; d.ParseStream(is);                  // HasParseError() never checked
fclose(fp);
read_buffer.release();                          // leaks the allocation
auto resolution = Vector2I(d["resolution"]["x"].GetInt(), ...); // unchecked member access
```
rapidjson is told the buffer is 8 bytes when it is 1 — a guaranteed 7-byte heap overflow on every launch. `read_buffer.release()` then leaks it. A truncated or hand-edited `save_data.json` makes `d["resolution"]` assert/UB. `check_if_save_file_exists()` (Save.cpp:33-42) makes the NULL `fp` unlikely but not impossible (file deleted between the check and the open, or unreadable).
findings.suggestion: `auto read_buffer = std::make_unique<char[]>(N);` and pass `N`. Check `fp != nullptr` and `d.HasParseError()`, guard every member access with `HasMember`/`IsObject`, drop the `release()`, and fall back to default `SaveData` on any failure instead of propagating.
findings.verify_note: Read Save.cpp:12-42 directly. `std::make_unique<char>()` (no [] and no size) and `sizeof(read_buffer)` on a unique_ptr are both exactly as described.

findings.title: Deferred contexts are raw AddRef'd COM pointers that are never released — 16 leaked contexts, rule-of-5 violation on vendor code
findings.detail:
`create_deferred_contexts` (DeviceResources.cpp:716-730) puts raw `ID3D11DeviceContext*` (refcount 1 from `CreateDeferredContext`) into `std::unique_ptr<std::vector<ID3D11DeviceContext*>> _deferred_contexts` (DeviceResources.h:128). A grep for `->Release()` across ArtAttack/ finds only GameStates.cpp:329 and MenuPage.cpp:162 (both command lists) plus a commented-out line in Main.cpp:55 — the contexts are never released. `~DeviceResources() = default` (DeviceResources.h:32) destroys a vector of raw pointers and nothing else, so all 16 leak and pin the D3D device for the process lifetime.

Every other COM object in this class is a `ComPtr` (DeviceResources.h:95-105); these are the sole exception. This is an owning resource grafted onto vendor code that still has `= default` destructor and `= default` move operations (:34-35). Two secondary leaks in the same function: `make_unique` at :718 replaces the old vector unconditionally, so a second call leaks the previous batch; and the `throw std::runtime_error` at :726 abandons the contexts already created in the loop.
findings.suggestion: `std::vector<Microsoft::WRL::ComPtr<ID3D11DeviceContext>> m_deferredContexts;` (drop the pointless unique_ptr<vector<>> indirection), pass `ReleaseAndGetAddressOf()`, `clear()` first, and use `ThrowIfFailed` for consistency with the rest of the file. Then the defaulted destructor is correct again. Better still, move the pool out of the vendored file entirely so DeviceResources.h/.cpp stay upstream-updatable.
findings.verify_note: Read DeviceResources.cpp:716-745, DeviceResources.h:32-38 and 95-128, and grepped all of ArtAttack/*.cpp for `Release()` — only the two command-list sites exist.

findings.title: HandleDeviceLost never touches the deferred-context pool, so restore builds SpriteBatches on contexts of a destroyed device
findings.detail: `HandleDeviceLost` (DeviceResources.cpp:418-453) resets the RTV/DSV, swap chain, `m_d3dContext`, `m_d3dAnnotation`, `m_d3dDevice` and `m_dxgiFactory`, recreates the device, then calls `OnDeviceRestored()`. `_deferred_contexts` is not in that list, and `create_deferred_contexts` is called from exactly one place — `Game::initialize` (Game.cpp:52). So after a device-removed event the vector still holds 16 contexts owned by the destroyed device, and `Game::OnDeviceRestored` → `create_device_dependent_resources` immediately does `std::make_unique<SpriteBatch>(this->_device_resources->get_deferred_context(i))` (Game.cpp:229) on them. `Game::clear()` (Game.cpp:136-149) then calls `OMSetRenderTargets`/`RSSetViewports` on the same stale contexts every frame. The reset list predates the author's deferred-context addition and was never updated.
findings.suggestion: Clear the pool at the top of `HandleDeviceLost` (before `m_d3dDevice.Reset()`) and recreate it at the end of `CreateDeviceResources()` from a remembered count, so the pool's lifetime is structurally tied to the device rather than to one call in `Game::initialize`.
findings.verify_note: Read DeviceResources.cpp:418-453 (full reset list — no `_deferred_contexts`), 716-730, and Game.cpp:49-56, 226-232, 282-287.

findings.title: get_deferred_context is declared noexcept but throws std::out_of_range — the bounds check is a guaranteed std::terminate
findings.suggestion: Drop `noexcept`, take `std::size_t index`, null-check the container, and delete the redundant manual check in favour of `at()`. Separately fix MenuPage.cpp:175-176 to index by partition/thread rather than by object.
findings.verify_note: Read DeviceResources.cpp:737-745 and DeviceResources.h:88 (both noexcept). Read MenuPage.cpp:124-178: `command_lists(deferred_contexts->size(), nullptr)` at :128, `partitioner->partition(mobjects->size(), num_threads)` at :135, and `get_deferred_context(i)` / `at(i)` with the mobject index at :175-176. Whether a page actually exceeds 16 widgets I did not enumerate, but nothing bounds it.

findings.title: OnDeviceLost frees SpriteBatches and CommonStates but leaves the raw-pointer mirrors GameData published
findings.suggestion: Delete the parallel `vector<SpriteBatch*>` mirror entirely — expose `const std::vector<std::unique_ptr<SpriteBatch>>&` or build the raw view on demand — so there is no second copy to forget. Until then, clear `_sprite_batches_ptrs` and null every observer GameData published in `OnDeviceLost`.
findings.verify_note: Read Game.cpp:269-280, Game.h:72-73, Game.cpp:224-234 (`set_sprite_batches(&this->_sprite_batches_ptrs)`), GameData.h:58-59, Level.h:141.

findings.title: calculate_viewport's layout cases fall through — an out-of-range player index silently gets another layout's geometry
findings.detail:
Every outer `case` ends with an inner `switch (player_num)` whose `default:` is `break`, and there is no `break`/`return` after the inner switch:

- TWO_PLAYER (:166-183) inner `default: break;` at :181-182 falls into `case THREE_PLAYER:` at :184
- THREE_PLAYER (:184-207) inner `default: break;` at :205-206 falls into `case FOUR_PLAYER:` at :208
- FOUR_PLAYER (:208-237) inner `default: break;` at :235-236 falls into `default:` at :238, which returns a fullscreen viewport

So `calculate_viewport(TWO_PLAYER, 2, …)` returns the THREE_PLAYER top-left quadrant, and `calculate_viewport(THREE_PLAYER, 3, …)` returns the FOUR_PLAYER bottom-right quadrant (a duplicate of what THREE_PLAYER already gives player 1). A bad index produces plausible-looking but wrong geometry instead of a diagnosable failure, and MSVC emits no implicit-fallthrough warning even at /W4. Callers pass unvalidated indices: `Level.cpp:503` passes `get_player_num()` straight from level data, `MenuPage.cpp:107-108` passes a `size_t` loop counter. This is also the mechanism behind the `get_player_viewport(4)` bug reported separately.
findings.suggestion: Replace the whole 90-line double switch with one static table of normalised rects — `static constexpr struct { float x, y, w, h; } LAYOUTS[4][4]` indexed by `[layout][player]` and multiplied by `screen_size`. That removes the fall-through by construction and makes a 6-player layout a data edit. Bounds-check `player_num` against `get_player_count_from_layout(layout)` and assert rather than returning fullscreen.
findings.verify_note: Read ViewportManager.cpp:154-245 in full and traced each fall-through path by hand.

findings.title: get_all_viewports asks for player 4 to fill the empty 3-player quadrant and receives a fullscreen viewport
findings.suggestion: The empty quadrant is index 1 of the FOUR_PLAYER layout: `result.push_back(calculate_viewport(screen_layout::FOUR_PLAYER, 1, res));`. Also reorder THREE_PLAYER so 1 = top-right and 2 = bottom-left — the current 0=TL, 1=BR, 2=BL is surprising on its own.
findings.verify_note: Read ViewportManager.cpp:90-104 and 154-245; traced index 4 through the fall-through chain. Read MenuPage.cpp:99-115 to confirm the consumer. Corrected the candidates' claim that the widget is 'drawn stretched fullscreen' — the RSSetViewports for i=3 is the bottom-right quadrant, only the layout rect is fullscreen.

findings.title: Camera scroll border clamps min above max, inverting the dead zone at the shipped default resolution
findings.detail:
```
clamp_ref(result.top,    MIN_BORDER_TOP,    viewport_size.y / 2.0f);
clamp_ref(result.bottom, MIN_BORDER_BOTTOM, viewport_size.y / 2.0f);
```
`MattMath::clamp_ref` (MattMath.cpp:49-59) is `if (value < min) value = min; else if (value > max) value = max;` — it never validates `min <= max`, and when they are inverted the MIN wins and the result exceeds the requested maximum.

At the default 1280x720 (ResolutionManager.h:25) with a 2-player layout each viewport is 1280x360 (ViewportManager.cpp:166-180). `MIN_BORDER_TOP = MIN_BORDER_BOTTOM = 250` (CameraTools.h:15,17) but `viewport_size.y / 2 = 180`, so top = 0.2*360 = 72 → 250 and bottom = 0.4*360 = 144 → 250; combined 500 inside a 360px viewport. `calculate_camera` (CameraTools.cpp:19-20) then yields `top_edge = ty + 250` and `bottom_edge = ty + 110` — bottom is 140px ABOVE top, so the `else if (player_center.y > bottom_edge)` branch at :29 is unreachable whenever the first fires and the camera pins the player 250px from the top of a 360px viewport instead of following them.

4-player at 1280x720 gives 640x360 viewports, so BOTH axes break (`MIN_BORDER_LEFT/RIGHT = 400 > 320`). I checked 1920x1080: 2-player (1920x540) gives 500 < 540 and 4-player (960x540) gives 800 < 960 and 500 < 540 — both just fit. So this is specifically the default resolution in every multiplayer layout.
findings.suggestion: Only apply the pixel floor when it fits: clamp the border to at most `0.45f * viewport_size` AFTER applying the minimum, or drop the absolute pixel minimums entirely and keep only the ratios — resolution-independence is what an engine wants. Separately, `MattMath::clamp`/`clamp_ref` should assert `min <= max` instead of silently picking one.
findings.verify_note: Read CameraTools.cpp:74-91, CameraTools.h:9-19, MattMath.cpp:49-59, ViewportManager.cpp:166-237, ResolutionManager.h:25. Worked the arithmetic for 1280x720 and 1920x1080 at 2P and 4P; the candidates' claim is right for 720p and (they did not check) does not reproduce at 1080p.

findings.title: AdjustWindowRect and GetClientRect results are both computed and discarded; the backbuffer is sized from the save file
findings.detail:
```
RECT rc = { 0, 0, res_ivec2.x, res_ivec2.y };
AdjustWindowRect(&rc, WS_OVERLAPPEDWINDOW, FALSE);   // rc never used again
...
hwnd = CreateWindowExW(0, ..., WS_OVERLAPPEDWINDOW,
    CW_USEDEFAULT, CW_USEDEFAULT, res_ivec2.x, res_ivec2.y, ...);   // OUTER size = raw resolution
```
`CreateWindowExW` takes the outer size, which is precisely what `AdjustWindowRect` exists to compute. For 1280x720 with a standard caption+border the client area ends up roughly 1264x681. Then Main.cpp:202 calls `GetClientRect(hwnd, &rc)` and discards that too, and `Game::initialize` (Game.cpp:38-40) passes `get_resolution_ivec()` — the saved enum, not the client rect — to `DeviceResources::SetWindow`. The swap chain is created at 1280x720 for a 1264x681 client and `DXGI_SCALING_STRETCH` (DeviceResources.cpp:321) resamples it every frame: a non-integer downscale of a pixel-art game.

The fullscreen branch is worse: a `WS_POPUP` window created at the saved resolution and then `ShowWindow(hwnd, SW_SHOWMAXIMIZED)` (:191) sized to the monitor **work area** (taskbar excluded). The resulting WM_SIZE is dropped because `DeviceResources::SetWindow` has not run yet (`WindowSizeChanged` early-returns on `!m_window`, DeviceResources.cpp:397-398), so the backbuffer stays at the saved resolution regardless of the monitor. Same shape at MainMenu.cpp:334-340 and 427-451, which pass the raw resolution to `SetWindowPos`.
findings.suggestion: Create the window with `rc.right - rc.left, rc.bottom - rc.top`, then call `GetClientRect` and drive `SetWindow`/`initialize` from that. For borderless fullscreen, query the monitor via `MonitorFromWindow` + `GetMonitorInfo` and `SetWindowPos` to `rcMonitor` exactly, rather than relying on SW_SHOWMAXIMIZED for a popup. One source of truth for render size: the client rect.
findings.verify_note: Read Main.cpp:146-207 (rc computed at :150, never read; GetClientRect at :202, never read), Game.cpp:38-40, DeviceResources.cpp:321 (DXGI_SCALING_STRETCH) and :385-398, MainMenu.cpp:334-340 and 427-451.

findings.title: create_window_size_dependent_resources is an empty stub, so any window resize desyncs viewports from the backbuffer
findings.detail:
```
void Game::create_window_size_dependent_resources() const
{
    auto size = _device_resources->GetOutputSize();   // computed, never used
}
```
The entire body is an unused local (C4189 under /W4, silently accumulating because `TreatWarningAsError` is unset). It is called from three places (Game.cpp:57, 202, 286) and does nothing.

Meanwhile `WndProc` WM_SIZE / WM_EXITSIZEMOVE (Main.cpp:299-318) → `on_window_size_changed` → `DeviceResources::WindowSizeChanged` DOES resize the swap chain and rebuild `m_screenViewport` (DeviceResources.cpp:395-415, 381), and the windowed style is `WS_OVERLAPPEDWINDOW` so the user can resize freely down to 320x200 (`WM_GETMINMAXINFO`, Main.cpp:320-326). But nothing updates `ResolutionManager` — `set_resolution` is only ever called from Main.cpp:100 and MainMenu.cpp:324. Every viewport (`ViewportManager.cpp:19, 49, 58, 66, 87, 126`), the camera dead zone, split-screen dividers, `MenuPage::get_float_resolution` (:190-193) and `Level` (Level.cpp:90, 152, 156) still compute against the stale saved enum. After a resize the split-screen geometry is clipped off the backbuffer with no diagnostic. There are two conflicting sources of truth for 'screen size' and the empty stub makes it look like the resize path is handled.
findings.suggestion: Pick one authority. Either drop WS_THICKFRAME|WS_MAXIMIZEBOX so the client size cannot change behind the engine's back, or make the swap chain the authority: a Display service exposing `backbuffer_size()` plus a resize event that ViewportManager, cameras and UI subscribe to, with the resolution enum used only as an input when creating/resizing the window.
findings.verify_note: Read Game.cpp:264-267 and 197-205, Main.cpp:162 (WS_OVERLAPPEDWINDOW), 299-326, DeviceResources.cpp:381, 395-415, and grepped `set_resolution(` across ArtAttack/ — only Main.cpp:100 and MainMenu.cpp:324 call it.

findings.title: apply_player_viewport(int) mutates the immediate context from a thread-pool worker and configures a batch belonging to a different context
findings.suggestion: Delete this overload and the `_sprite_batch` / `_device_resources` members (ViewportManager.h:47-48) — a viewport calculator has no business owning a device or a batch. Keep only the overloads that take the context and batch explicitly, which is what the rest of the draw code already uses. Move `set_layout` out of the draw path.
findings.verify_note: Read ViewportManager.cpp:45-70 and .h:21-32,46-48, Game.cpp:224-232 and 247-249, Level.cpp:595-651. Grepped `apply_player_viewport(` — the 1-arg overload has exactly one live caller, Level.cpp:620, inside the thread-pool lambda at Level.cpp:601.

findings.title: clear() records into all 16 deferred contexts every frame; 12 of them are never flushed, so their command buffers grow unbounded
findings.detail:
`Game::clear()` loops over every deferred context and records `OMSetRenderTargets` (:136-140) and `RSSetViewports` (:146-149) into it, every frame. But only contexts `[0, partition_count)` ever get `FinishCommandList`: `Level::draw_active_level` (Level.cpp:379-399) partitions `_player_objects` (max 4) over `get_max_num_threads()` = 16, and `Partitioner::partition` caps the partition count at `num_elements` (Partitioner.cpp:10 — `i < num_partitions && i < num_elements`), so only those tasks reach `deferred_contexts->at(i)->FinishCommandList(...)` (Level.cpp:587).

A deferred context's recorded command buffer is only handed off and freed by `FinishCommandList`. Contexts 4..15 therefore accumulate two recorded commands per frame — 7,200 per minute — for the entire session, and every one is wasted since nothing executes them. In a 1-player level that is 15 of 16 contexts growing forever.
findings.suggestion: Do not touch deferred contexts in `clear()` at all. Bind the render target and viewport inside the recording function, on the specific context that thread is about to `FinishCommandList` (`Level::draw_player_view_level`, `MenuPage::draw_mobject_in_viewports`). `clear()` should only clear the RTV on the immediate context.
findings.verify_note: Read Game.cpp:124-152, Level.cpp:375-400 and 491-592, Partitioner.cpp:1-27. The partition cap at num_elements is exactly as described, so ≤4 contexts are flushed during gameplay.

findings.title: No <LanguageStandard> in any configuration, so the whole engine compiles as C++14
findings.detail:
All four ItemDefinitionGroup blocks set `WarningLevel=Level4`, `ConformanceMode=true` and `FloatingPointModel=Fast` (lines 91/94/96, 113/116/117, 134/139/141, 160/165/166) but none sets `<LanguageStandard>`, so MSVC v145 falls back to `/std:c++14`. Everything the platform layer needs is therefore unavailable: `std::clamp` (CameraTools.cpp:85-88 hand-rolls it via the out-param `clamp_ref` that causes the inverted-dead-zone bug), `[[fallthrough]]` (ViewportManager.cpp:183/207 fall through silently), `std::string_view` (ResolutionManager.cpp:94-121 heap-allocates up to four std::strings per lookup), `[[nodiscard]]`, `std::optional`, `inline` variables (so `viewport_consts` in ViewportManager.h:10-16 gets a dynamically-initialised copy per TU), and structured bindings.

There is also no `<TreatWarningAsError>` and no `<MultiProcessorCompilation>`, so /W4 findings such as the C4018 at DeviceResources.cpp:740 and the C4189 at Game.cpp:266 accumulate unnoticed, and 81 TUs compile serially.
findings.suggestion: Add `<LanguageStandard>stdcpp20</LanguageStandard>` and `<MultiProcessorCompilation>true</MultiProcessorCompilation>` in a shared `common.props` imported by all four configurations, instead of four hand-maintained copies. Turn on `<TreatWarningAsError>` once the existing /W4 backlog is cleared.
findings.verify_note: Grepped ArtAttack.vcxproj for LanguageStandard / TreatWarningAsError / MultiProcessorCompilation — zero hits; WarningLevel, ConformanceMode and FloatingPointModel=Fast confirmed at the four sites listed.

findings.title: Game is a god object: platform host, device-lost sink, root state machine and owner of twelve unrelated subsystems
findings.detail:
`class Game final : public DX::IDeviceNotify, public StateContext` simultaneously is (1) the Win32/D3D host (DeviceResources, StepTimer, clear/present), (2) the device-lost listener, (3) the root application state machine — by *inheriting* StateContext, an is-a claim that is false and that makes `transition_to` public on any `Game*` — and (4) the owner of CommonStates, ResourceLoader, ResourceManager, a heap `float`, GamePad, ViewportManager, ThreadPool, a `vector<unique_ptr<SpriteBatch>>` plus a hand-maintained parallel `vector<SpriteBatch*>` (Game.h:72-73), AudioEngine, Partitioner, and a `GameData*` service locator it populates with pointers to all of the above (Game.cpp:36, 60, 234, 237, 240, 243, 245, 250, 253, 256).

Nothing here is reusable: taking the platform layer to another game means taking the audio engine, the sprite-batch pool and the resource loader with it. `Main.cpp:208` then hardcodes the game's first screen into the entry point (`transition_to(std::make_unique<GameMenu>(...))`). Most of the lifetime bugs in this module — the audio destruction order, the OnDeviceRestored subsystem churn, the dangling `_sprite_batches_ptrs` — are direct consequences of this one class owning everything.
findings.suggestion: Split into an `Engine`/`Application` (window + device + timer + frame loop + present, nothing else), a `Services` container of subsystem interfaces constructed and injected explicitly, and a `StateMachine` **member** rather than a base class. The game supplies its initial state; the engine never names GameMenu or any game type.
findings.verify_note: Read Game.h in full and Game.cpp:32-66, 218-261. Every listed member and every `set_*` publication is present.

findings.title: Frame delta is a heap-allocated unique_ptr<float> whose raw pointer is threaded through eleven classes
findings.detail:
`std::unique_ptr<float> _dt = nullptr;` — allocated at Game.cpp:244, published as a raw `float*` via `_data->set_dt(this->_dt.get())` (:245), written each update by `*this->_dt = elapsedTime;` (:90). Eleven headers cache it as `const float* _dt`: AnimationObject.h, AnimatedSprite.h, Drawer.h, LevelBuilder.h, Level.h, LevelObjectBuilder.h, PaintTile.h, Player.h, Projectile.h, StructurePaintable.h, Weapon.h. None documents the pointer as non-owning, none can tell whether it is still valid, and reassigning `_dt` on device restore (Game.cpp:244) frees it out from under all eleven.

The root cause is that `State::update()`/`draw()` are nullary (State.h) and `StateContext::update()/draw()` forward without arguments (StateContext.h:12-13), so frame time has nowhere to travel except as ambient global state. The same shape forces the renderer to be looked up through GameData: `GameLevel::draw` fetches `get_deferred_contexts()` and `get_sprite_batches()` from the locator (GameStates.cpp:311-317) because `draw()` cannot be handed a render target.
findings.suggestion: Change the interface to `virtual void update(float dt) = 0;` and `virtual void draw(Renderer& r) = 0;` and thread both down explicitly. dt then has no lifetime at all and the renderer becomes an injected parameter rather than something any object can reach.
findings.verify_note: Read Game.h:66, Game.cpp:87-98 and 244-245, StateContext.h:7-17, GameStates.cpp:303-330. Counted the `const float* _dt` holders by grep: 11 files, not the '~26' the candidates claimed — corrected.

findings.title: Raw D3D11 contexts and command lists are the public draw API, and the record/execute/Release protocol is copy-pasted
findings.detail:
Because `DeviceResources` exposes `std::vector<ID3D11DeviceContext*>* get_deferred_contexts()` (line 87), every drawing entry point in the game speaks raw D3D11: `Level::draw` and friends take `std::vector<ID3D11DeviceContext*>*, std::vector<ID3D11CommandList*>*, std::vector<SpriteBatch*>*` (Level.h:83-85). The same protocol — fetch contexts, allocate `vector<ID3D11CommandList*>(n, nullptr)`, hand the raw pointers down, then loop `ExecuteCommandList` + `->Release()` skipping nulls — is written twice verbatim at GameStates.cpp:311-330 and MenuPage.cpp:127-163, with the leaf `FinishCommandList` calls scattered at Level.cpp:587, Level.cpp:646 and MenuPage.cpp:117, each guarded by its own `throw std::exception("Failed to finish command list")`. Command lists are released by raw `->Release()`, so any early return or exception between `FinishCommandList` and the loop leaks them — and Level.cpp:590 throws from inside a thread-pool worker, which is `std::terminate` on its own.

A game object should never see `ID3D11` anything if the engine is to be reusable or ever ported.
findings.suggestion: Introduce a `Renderer` facade owning the context pool and command lists: `renderer.record(view_index, [&](DrawList&){ ... })` plus one `renderer.flush()` that executes and releases (via ComPtr) in a single place. Level and MenuPage then take a `Renderer&` and D3D11 stays behind the platform boundary.
findings.verify_note: Read DeviceResources.h:86-88, GameStates.cpp:303-330, MenuPage.cpp:124-178, Level.cpp:491-651. Both copies of the protocol and all three FinishCommandList sites are as described.

findings.title: Window and display-mode management lives inside a menu screen, duplicating Main.cpp and bypassing ExitGame()
findings.detail:
`MainMenuOptions::apply_fullscreen_setting` (:427-451) calls raw Win32 `SetWindowLongPtr(hWnd, GWL_STYLE, WS_POPUP / WS_OVERLAPPEDWINDOW)`, `SetWindowLongPtr(GWL_EXSTYLE, …)`, `SetWindowPos` and `ShowWindow` on the HWND it pulls out of GameData. The resolution-apply path does its own `SetWindowPos(..., res_i.x, res_i.y, SWP_NOMOVE|SWP_NOZORDER)` at :334-340. Quitting is `DestroyWindow(this->get_main_menu_data()->get_window())` at :167.

All three duplicate logic that already exists in the platform layer (Main.cpp:154-196 does the same style/size branch at creation) and bypass `ExitGame()` (Main.cpp:410-413), which is declared `extern` in Game.cpp:4, prototyped at Main.cpp:30, and — per grep — called from nowhere. None of the three notifies DeviceResources or ViewportManager that anything changed. A UI screen in the game layer is the only place that knows how to change display mode, so the engine cannot offer that capability to any other game.
findings.suggestion: Add `Window::set_mode(WindowMode, Vector2I size)` and `Application::request_exit()` to the platform layer; the options menu calls those and nothing else. The window owns the HWND, styles and ShowWindow, and raises a resize event the display/viewport services consume.
findings.verify_note: Read MainMenu.cpp:160-169, 315-353, 420-451; grepped `ExitGame` — declared at Game.cpp:4 and Main.cpp:30, defined at Main.cpp:410, zero call sites.

findings.title: wWinMain has no try/catch, so any asset, save or D3D failure aborts with no diagnostic
findings.detail:
There is not a single `try`/`catch` in Main.cpp, yet the code it calls throws routinely: `DX::ThrowIfFailed` (pch.h:99-105) throws `com_exception` from every D3D call in DeviceResources.cpp; `create_deferred_contexts` throws `std::runtime_error` (DeviceResources.cpp:726); `StepTimer`'s constructor throws (StepTimer.h:29-37); `ViewportManager::get_viewport_dividers` throws (`ViewportManager.cpp:150`); the level/JSON builders and the render path throw `std::exception("literal")` in dozens of places (Level.cpp:500, 590, 616, 649; MenuPage.cpp:96, 120).

`g_game->initialize(...)` (:207) and `g_game->tick()` (:222) are both unguarded, so a missing `textures/` folder or a malformed level JSON produces an unhandled-exception abort with no indication of what was missing. Worse, `Level.cpp:590` and `MenuPage.cpp:120` throw from inside a thread-pool callback — that is `std::terminate` outright, which a `wWinMain` handler would never even see. `throw std::exception("literal")` is also an MSVC-only extension.
findings.suggestion: Wrap the body of `wWinMain` in `try { ... } catch (const std::exception& e) { MessageBoxA(nullptr, e.what(), "Fatal error", MB_ICONERROR); return 1; }`. Independently, catch at the top of every thread-pool task body, store an `exception_ptr`, and rethrow after `wait_for_tasks_to_complete`. Replace `std::exception("literal")` with `std::runtime_error`.
findings.verify_note: Read Main.cpp in full (no try/catch anywhere), pch.h:99-105, StepTimer.h:18-41, DeviceResources.cpp:726, ViewportManager.cpp:150, Level.cpp:587-591 inside the lambda dispatched at Level.cpp:601.

findings.title: Game explicitly defaults move operations while three external observers hold pointers into it
findings.suggestion: `Game(Game&&) = delete; Game& operator= (Game&&) = delete;` alongside the already-deleted copies. Longer term, move `RegisterDeviceNotify(this)` out of the constructor into `initialize()` so a half-constructed Game is never published, and stop publishing the address of a member container.
findings.verify_note: Read Game.h:19-26, Game.cpp:20 and 234, DeviceResources.h:125-126, StateContext.h:14.

findings.title: Window message handlers dereference _gamepad and _audio_engine unguarded, and messages arrive before initialize()
findings.detail:
`on_activated()` checks the pointer (`if (this->_gamepad)`, :161) but its three siblings do not:
```
void Game::on_deactivated() const { this->_gamepad->Suspend(); }                          // :165-169
void Game::on_suspending()  const { this->_gamepad->Suspend(); _audio_engine->Suspend(); } // :171-176
void Game::on_resuming()          { _timer.ResetElapsedTime(); _gamepad->Resume(); _audio_engine->Resume(); } // :178-184
```
The ordering makes this reachable: WM_CREATE installs the `Game*` into GWLP_USERDATA (Main.cpp:246-252) *inside* `CreateWindowExW` (:156/162), `ShowWindow` runs at :191/195 and synchronously delivers WM_ACTIVATEAPP and WM_SIZE, but `_audio_engine` is not created until `initialize` (Game.cpp:47) and `_gamepad` until :59 — and `initialize` is not called until Main.cpp:207. A WM_ACTIVATEAPP with `wParam == 0` (window created behind another app) or WM_SIZE(SIZE_MINIMIZED) during startup is an immediate null dereference. `WM_POWERBROADCAST`/PBT_APMQUERYSUSPEND (Main.cpp:343-350) has the same exposure. The lone guard in `on_activated` is evidence that this was hit once and only the branch that fired was patched.

`on_window_size_changed` survives the same window purely by luck: `WindowSizeChanged` early-returns on `!m_window` (DeviceResources.cpp:397-398).
findings.suggestion: Do not publish `this` to GWLP_USERDATA until the object is usable — create the window with `lpCreateParams = nullptr`, call `initialize()`, then `SetWindowLongPtr`. That eliminates the whole class of half-constructed-callback bugs rather than sprinkling null checks. Failing that, guard every handler uniformly with one `_initialized` flag.
findings.verify_note: Read Game.cpp:157-184 (the asymmetry is exactly as described), Game.cpp:32-66 (creation order), Main.cpp:154-207 and 246-252, DeviceResources.cpp:395-398.

findings.title: Audio device loss is detected and then deliberately discarded
findings.suggestion: Implement the standard recovery, or — if ignoring it is genuinely intended — delete the `if` and write a comment saying why. An empty conditional body reads as unfinished work. For a reusable engine, surface it as an `on_audio_device_lost()` hook.
findings.verify_note: Read Game.cpp:87-98 verbatim.

findings.title: convert_resolution_to_ivec returns {-1,-1} for an unknown value while every sibling converter falls back to 1280x720
findings.detail:
`default: return {-1, -1};` (:60-62). The three sibling converters all fall back to a valid resolution: `convert_string_to_resolution` → S_1280_720 (:119), `convert_vec_to_resolution` → S_1280_720 (:148), `convert_ivec_to_resolution` → S_1280_720 (:173). `convert_resolution_to_string` returns the literal string `"-1x-1"` (:90), which round-trips back through `convert_string_to_resolution` to 1280x720 — so the two halves of one round trip disagree about the sentinel.

A `{-1,-1}` flows straight into `RECT rc = {0, 0, -1, -1}` and `CreateWindowExW(..., -1, -1, ...)` (Main.cpp:146-164) and into `SetWindow(hwnd, -1, -1)` (Game.cpp:38-40), where `static_cast<UINT>(m_outputSize.right - m_outputSize.left)` (DeviceResources.cpp:275) becomes 0xFFFFFFFF before the `std::max<UINT>(…, 1u)` clamp lets it through. It also poisons every viewport division in ViewportManager. Nothing checks for a negative extent anywhere.
findings.suggestion: Make all five converters agree on one policy. `screen_resolution` is a scoped enum with four values, so `default:` is unreachable for well-formed input — make it loud (assert / `throw std::invalid_argument`) plus a 1280x720 fallback. Silently returning a negative size is the worst of the options.
findings.verify_note: Read ResolutionManager.cpp:47-175 in full, Main.cpp:146-164, Game.cpp:38-40, DeviceResources.cpp:275-276.

findings.title: The resolution table is hand-written five times here and duplicated again in Save
findings.detail:
Five parallel encodings of the same four rows: `convert_resolution_to_ivec` (:47-63), `convert_resolution_to_string` (:76-92), `convert_string_to_resolution` (:94-121, an if/else chain calling the previous function four times, each returning a fresh heap `std::string` — up to four allocations per lookup), `convert_vec_to_resolution` (:123-150), `convert_ivec_to_resolution` (:152-175, which hard-codes 1280/720/1920/… a second time so the pixel dimensions live in two places that can drift). `Save.cpp:112-152` duplicates two of them again, declared as private members of an unrelated class in Save.h.

All four private converters are `const` non-static member functions that never touch `this` — free functions wearing a `this` pointer. (Note: `convert_resolution_to_string` is correctly `static` in ResolutionManager.h:21, contrary to what some reviewers claimed.)
findings.suggestion: One `static constexpr std::array<ResolutionInfo, N>` of `{screen_resolution id, int w, int h, std::string_view name}` with lookup helpers over it. Save serialises the id or the name and calls the shared lookup. Supporting 21:9 or arbitrary sizes becomes a table edit rather than seven function edits.
findings.verify_note: Read ResolutionManager.cpp:47-175 and ResolutionManager.h:21-36 in full; read Save.cpp:12-32 and confirmed the Save-side duplicates exist.

findings.title: Resolution is a closed hardcoded list of four 16:9 modes, never validated against the actual display
findings.detail:
Nothing in the codebase queries the display: I grepped all of ArtAttack/ for `GetSystemMetrics`, `EnumDisplaySettings`, `GetMonitorInfo`, `MonitorFromWindow` and `GetDisplayModeList` — zero hits. The only adapter/output enumeration that ever existed is commented out at Main.cpp:39-81.

So the options menu walks the enum blindly (`MainMenu.cpp:572` reads `static_cast<int>(screen_resolution::MAX)` and cycles), and selecting 3840x2160 on a 1080p panel creates an oversized window with no check. A user whose native mode is not one of the four hardcoded 16:9 entries can never match it, and a saved resolution is never validated on load. Combined with the `{-1,-1}` sentinel above, an out-of-range value produces a negative window size rather than a clamp.
findings.suggestion: Enumerate supported modes from `IDXGIOutput::GetDisplayModeList` at startup, populate the options menu from that list, validate any saved resolution against it, and clamp to the monitor's current mode on mismatch.
findings.verify_note: Grepped all of ArtAttack/ for the five display-query APIs — no matches. Read Main.cpp:39-81 (commented-out adapter enumeration) and MainMenu.cpp:572.

findings.title: The five file-scope globals are declared in exactly the reverse of their dependency order, saved only by one hand-written reset()
findings.suggestion: Move all five into a local struct (or plain locals in dependency order) inside `wWinMain` so destruction order is the declared member order and is compiler-enforced, and pass its address through `lpCreateParams` as is already done for `Game*`. Add a `ComScope` RAII type for `CoInitializeEx`/`CoUninitialize` so every exit path releases.

findings.title: The active State is destroyed after every service it borrows, because it lives in a base subobject
findings.detail:
C++ destroys derived-class members first (reverse declaration order) and base subobjects last. On `g_game.reset()` (Main.cpp:226) the order is: `_partitioner`, `_audio_engine`, `_sprite_batches_ptrs`, `_sprite_batches`, `_thread_pool`, `_data`, `_viewport_manager`, `_gamepad`, `_state` (the dead one), `_dt`, `_resource_manager`, `_resource_loader`, `_states`, `_timer`, `_device_resources` — and only THEN `~StateContext` → `~GameLevel` → `~Level` → `~Player`.

So the entire live object graph is destructed after every service it points at has been freed: `Level` holds `ThreadPool*` (Level.h:146), `const Partitioner*` (:147), `ViewportManager*` (:118), `ResourceManager*` (:119), `const float* _dt` (:140), `ID3D11SamplerState*` (:141). Today the game-object destructors are implicit and happen not to touch those pointers, so it does not crash — but it becomes UB the first time a `Level` or `Player` destructor logs, stops a sound, or releases a GPU resource, which is a normal thing to add.
findings.suggestion: Explicitly tear the state machine down first: reset the state at the top of `Game::~Game()` (Game.cpp:23), before any member destructor runs. Longer term `Game` should HOLD a `StateContext` rather than BE one — composition makes this ordering explicit and expressible.
findings.verify_note: Read Game.h:16 and 59-76, StateContext.h:7-17, Level.h:118-147, Main.cpp:226. The ordering claim follows from the standard; the 'not currently a crash' qualifier is mine — I did not find user-written destructors on Level/Player.

findings.title: DestroyWindow is called from inside a menu update, and tick() then renders and presents on the dead HWND
findings.detail:
`DestroyWindow(this->get_main_menu_data()->get_window());` is the Exit menu item, invoked from a menu page's `update()` — i.e. from inside `Game::tick()` → `_timer.Tick(update)` → `StateContext::update()`. `DestroyWindow` is synchronous: WM_DESTROY/WM_NCDESTROY are delivered and the handle is invalid before it returns, and `WndProc`'s WM_DESTROY handler only calls `PostQuitMessage(0)` (Main.cpp:363-365), which unwinds nothing.

Control therefore returns into `Game::tick()`, which unconditionally calls `render()` (Game.cpp:82) → `clear()` → `_device_resources->Present()` on a swap chain whose HWND no longer exists. `DeviceResources::m_window` still holds the dead handle and `Present` calls `UpdateColorSpace()` whenever the factory is stale (DeviceResources.cpp:499-502), which does `if (!GetWindowRect(m_window, &windowBounds)) throw std::system_error(...)` (DeviceResources.cpp:630-631) — and there is no try/catch anywhere. Main.cpp never calls `DestroyWindow` itself and there is no path that tells DeviceResources the window died.
findings.suggestion: Route quit through the existing `ExitGame()` helper (Main.cpp:410) so the message loop drains normally, then destroy the window and the Game in `wWinMain` after the loop. If `DestroyWindow` must stay in the state, `Game::tick()` needs a shutdown check before `render()`.
findings.verify_note: Read MainMenu.cpp:165-168, Game.cpp:75-84, Main.cpp:363-365 and 410-413, DeviceResources.cpp:456-504 and 620-631. The exact behaviour of Present on a destroyed HWND I did not run; the UpdateColorSpace throw path is definite given a stale factory.

findings.title: get_camera_adjusted_player_viewport_rect multiplies by camera scale where it must divide
findings.suggestion: `vp.width / scale, vp.height / scale`, with a guard against `scale == 0.0f` (a lerp to a degenerate camera or a zero-width `view_rectangle` in `calculate_camera_from_view_rectangle` would produce inf/NaN that then poisons every `is_visible_in_viewport` comparison). Add a test at scale 0.5 asserting the world rect doubles.
findings.verify_note: Read ViewportManager.cpp:29-43, MattMath.cpp:4092-4180 (scale semantics), Level.cpp:505-540 and 150-159, CameraTools.cpp:8-72 (scale never modified). Downgraded from the candidates' 'high' because it is unreachable today — no code path produces a per-player camera with scale != 1.

findings.title: NUM_THREADS_MAX = 16 is an unnamespaced header constant that fixes four unrelated decisions, with no reference to hardware
findings.detail:
`constexpr int TARGET_FPS = 60; constexpr int NUM_THREADS_MIN = 1; constexpr int NUM_THREADS_MAX = 16;` sit at global namespace scope in a header included by most of the project, and `NUM_THREADS_MAX` simultaneously means: the deferred-context count (Game.cpp:52), the SpriteBatch pool size (Game.cpp:224-232), and the ThreadPool ceiling (Game.cpp:236). `std::thread::hardware_concurrency()` appears nowhere in the codebase (grepped).

The real parallelism is bounded by player count (max 4), because `Partitioner::partition` caps the partition count at `num_elements` (Partitioner.cpp:10). So on any machine running a 1-player level, 15 deferred contexts and 15 DirectXTK SpriteBatch objects are constructed and never used — each SpriteBatch carries its own dynamic vertex buffer (4096 sprites), so several MB of GPU-visible memory is allocated to serve at most 4 of them. `Game::clear()` then re-binds state on all 16 every frame (see the separate finding).
findings.suggestion: Compute the worker count once as `std::clamp(std::thread::hardware_concurrency(), 1u, MAX_VIEWS)` and size contexts, batches and pool from it. Make it a constructor parameter of the engine rather than a header constant — a reusable engine cannot know the game's player cap. Wrap `TARGET_FPS` and friends in a namespace or an engine config struct.
findings.verify_note: Read Game.h:12-14 and Game.cpp:52, 224-236; read Partitioner.cpp:1-27; grepped for `hardware_concurrency` — no hits. The exact per-SpriteBatch byte figure the candidates quoted I did not verify.

findings.title: pch.h forces the whole DirectXTK 3D surface into all 81 TUs of a 2D-only game, and doubles as the engine's error header
findings.detail:
The PCH includes `BufferHelpers.h`, `Effects.h`, `GeometricPrimitive.h`, `GraphicsMemory.h`, `Keyboard.h`, `Model.h`, `Mouse.h`, `PostProcess.h`, `PrimitiveBatch.h`, `ScreenGrab.h`, `VertexTypes.h`, `WICTextureLoader.h`. I grepped every first-party .h/.cpp under ArtAttack/ for `GeometricPrimitive`, `PostProcess`, `PrimitiveBatch`, `ScreenGrab`, `GraphicsMemory`, `Keyboard`, `Mouse`, `BasicEffect`, `IEffect`, `VertexPosition`, `CreateWICTextureFromFile` and `Model` — the only hits are the `#include` lines in pch.h itself. `Model.h` and `Effects.h` are among the heaviest headers in the toolkit, and this project explicitly constructs DeviceResources with `DXGI_FORMAT_UNKNOWN` depth because it 'Renders only 2D' (Game.cpp:12-14). There is no `MultiProcessorCompilation` in the vcxproj, so the cost is serialised.

Separately, pch.h *defines* the engine's error vocabulary — `DX::com_exception` and `DX::ThrowIfFailed` (:79-106) — so any module wanting those helpers must also pull in d3d11_1.h and dxgi1_6.h. That is why pure-math code starts with `#include "pch.h"` and why MattMathTests can only reach it by #including the .cpp files.
findings.suggestion: Cut the PCH to what is used: CommonStates.h, DDSTextureLoader.h, DirectXHelpers.h, GamePad.h, SimpleMath.h, SpriteBatch.h, SpriteFont.h. Move `com_exception`/`ThrowIfFailed` to a small `dx_error.h`, and let platform-free modules (MattMath, EricsonMath, CollisionTools) compile with no PCH at all — a precondition for the engine ever being a linkable library. Also raise `_WIN32_WINNT` from 0x0601 (Windows 7, pch.h:10).
findings.verify_note: Read pch.h in full; grepped ArtAttack/**/*.{h,cpp} for the twelve symbols — the only matches are pch.h's own include lines.

findings.title: The viewport abstraction is hardwired to 'players' and to exactly four split-screen arrangements
findings.detail:
`enum class screen_layout { ONE_PLAYER, TWO_PLAYER, THREE_PLAYER, FOUR_PLAYER }` is the only vocabulary the viewport service has, and it propagates through the whole API: `apply_player_viewport(int player_num)`, `get_player_viewport(int player_num)`, `get_camera_adjusted_player_viewport_rect(int player_num, …)`, `get_player_count_from_layout` (ViewportManager.h:27-52). The game sets it from a menu choice and `Level::draw_zoom_out_level_component` flips it mid-render (Level.cpp:619).

A reusable engine cannot express a picture-in-picture minimap, a security-camera view, a render-to-texture pass or a 6-player layout with this API, because a viewport is *defined* as 'the thing player N looks through'. This is game-specific vocabulary welded into what should be the platform layer.
findings.suggestion: Model views generically: a `ViewSet` of indexed `View { Viewport rect; Camera camera; }` with `add_view` / `view(i)` / `count()`. Split-screen for N players becomes a game-side helper that populates a ViewSet from a generic layout table; the word 'player' disappears from the platform layer.
findings.verify_note: Read screen_layout.h, ViewportManager.h:25-59, ViewportManager.cpp:84-121, Level.cpp:619.

findings.title: Sprite-sheet names and a colour for split-screen dividers are declared in the viewport header, as per-TU const std::strings
findings.suggestion: `ViewportManager` should return only geometry (`std::vector<RectangleF> divider_rects() const`); the sheet name, frame name and colour move to game-side UI content, ideally the level/theme JSON. Drop the Colour.h dependency from the header. If they must stay, use `inline constexpr std::string_view` (needs C++17) or `extern const` declared here and defined once in the .cpp.
findings.verify_note: Read ViewportManager.h:1-16 and GameData.h:9. The internal-linkage claim follows from the standard; the header is transitively included nearly project-wide via GameData.h.

findings.title: Game::update(StepTimer const&) hides the inherited public StateContext::update() behind a private overload
findings.detail: `StateContext` exposes `void update() const;` (StateContext.h:12). `Game` declares `void update(DX::StepTimer const& timer);` in its **private** section (Game.h:51). Name lookup in a derived class stops at the first scope containing the name, so `StateContext::update()` is entirely hidden on any `Game` object — and hidden behind a private overload, so an external `game.update()` is an access error rather than a call to the base. Game.cpp:91 has to work around its own hiding by writing `StateContext::update();` explicitly inside `Game::update`. The same shape almost recurs with `Game::render()` vs `StateContext::draw()` (Game.cpp:115).
findings.suggestion: Rename the private one to `update_frame(DX::StepTimer const&)` or `step`, or add `using StateContext::update;` if the overload set is intended. `StateContext::update()/draw()` are the polymorphic entry points and would be better as virtuals on StateContext than as names shadowed by a derived class.
findings.verify_note: Read Game.h:49-57, StateContext.h:9-17, Game.cpp:87-98 (the explicit `StateContext::update();` qualification at :91 is present).

findings.title: Viewports are recomputed on every query, including a heap allocation per widget per frame from worker threads
findings.detail:
