`ViewportManager` caches nothing. `get_player_viewport` (:84-88) calls `_resolution_manager->get_resolution_vec()` — itself a switch plus a `Vector2I`→`Vector2F` construction (ResolutionManager.cpp:47-74) — and then runs the 90-line layout switch, on every call. Viewports change only when the layout or resolution changes, at most once per level load.

Call sites are per-frame or hotter: Level.cpp:82 and :198 (per player per update), Level.cpp:505, 510, 544 (per player per frame in the record path), and worst, `MenuPage::draw_mobject_in_viewports` (MenuPage.cpp:99-100) calls `get_all_viewports()` — which heap-allocates a fresh `std::vector<Viewport>` — once for **every MObject drawn**, on worker threads, every frame. `get_viewport_dividers()` (:123-152) allocates a fresh vector per call too.
findings.suggestion: Compute the viewport set and divider rects once in `set_layout()` (and on a resolution-change notification) into a fixed `std::array<Viewport, 4>` plus a count, and return `const Viewport&` / `const std::vector<RectangleF>&`. That also removes the per-call dependency on `_resolution_manager` from the multi-threaded draw path.
findings.verify_note: Read ViewportManager.cpp:84-152, ResolutionManager.cpp:6-15 and 47-74, MenuPage.cpp:88-115 (get_all_viewports is inside draw_mobject_in_viewports, which is called once per mobject from :174), Level.cpp:80-85, 196-201, 505-544.

findings.title: com_exception::what() returns a shared function-local static buffer, and its converting constructor is not explicit
findings.suggestion: Mark the constructor `explicit`, and either derive from `std::runtime_error` with the message formatted in the constructor (it owns a refcounted copy, so `what()` becomes trivially correct) or store a `char m_str[64]` member instead of a function-local static.
findings.verify_note: Read pch.h:79-106. Downgraded from the candidates' 'critical/data race': they argued two ThreadPool workers race on the buffer, but ThrowIfFailed is only reached from DeviceResources.cpp and ResourceLoader (main thread) — the thread-pool tasks throw plain `std::exception`, so the concurrent-race scenario is overstated. The aliasing/lifetime defect is real regardless.

findings.title: The frame loop keeps updating, rendering and presenting while minimized or occluded
findings.detail:
The loop calls `g_game->tick()` whenever `PeekMessage` finds nothing, with no minimized check. `WndProc` does track `s_minimized` (Main.cpp:238, 282-298) but uses it only to suspend audio/gamepad, never to skip the frame, and `Game::render()` (Game.cpp:103-121) unconditionally clears, draws and presents.

`DeviceResources::Present` (DeviceResources.cpp:456-504) ignores `DXGI_STATUS_OCCLUDED` — it is a success code, so `ThrowIfFailed` passes it through. With flip-model presentation on an occluded or minimized window, `Present(1, 0)` stops blocking on vsync, so the loop spins as fast as the CPU allows, re-recording 16 command lists and re-submitting draws for a frame nobody sees.
findings.suggestion: Skip `tick()` (or at least `render()`) while `s_minimized` is set. Capture the `Present` HRESULT and, on `DXGI_STATUS_OCCLUDED`, switch to `Present(0, DXGI_PRESENT_TEST)` plus a short sleep until it returns S_OK.
findings.verify_note: Read Main.cpp:211-224 and 281-298, Game.cpp:103-121, DeviceResources.cpp:456-504. Note this loop and Present body are both unmodified Microsoft template code, so it is inherited rather than authored — but the 16-context re-record per spin is the author's addition, which is what raises the cost.

findings.title: const member functions across Game mutate device, audio and input state; the const is meaningless and inconsistently applied
findings.detail:
`on_activated() const` resumes the gamepad, `on_deactivated() const` and `on_suspending() const` suspend gamepad and audio, `clear() const` issues `ClearRenderTargetView`/`OMSetRenderTargets`/`RSSetViewports` on the device and all 16 deferred contexts, `on_window_moved() const` and `on_window_size_changed(...) const` call `_device_resources->WindowSizeChanged(...)` which resizes the swap chain. All compile because `const std::unique_ptr<T>::operator->` still yields a non-const `T*` — const on Game does not propagate through the pointers.

The tell is `on_resuming()` (Game.cpp:178), which is NOT const and does the exact mirror of `on_suspending() const`, differing only by `_timer.ResetElapsedTime()`. The qualifiers communicate nothing and actively mislead — they say 'this does not change the game' about the functions that reconfigure the swap chain.
findings.suggestion: Drop `const` from all of these; they are commands. Reserve `const` for genuine observers. If you want the compiler to help, hold non-owning dependencies through a propagate_const-style wrapper rather than relying on convention.
findings.verify_note: Read Game.h:39-57 and Game.cpp:124-205, 264-267. The const/non-const asymmetry between on_suspending and on_resuming is exactly as described.

findings.title: Game declares a dead unique_ptr<State> _state duplicating the one StateContext already owns
findings.detail: `std::unique_ptr<State> _state = nullptr;` — `Game` inherits `StateContext` (Game.h:16), which owns the real `std::unique_ptr<State> _state` privately (StateContext.h:16) and manages it through `transition_to` (called from Main.cpp:208). I grepped Game.cpp for `_state\b`: zero hits — the member is never assigned, read, or reset. It is a leftover that makes the header lie about where the current state lives, in the exact class a reader opens to answer 'who owns the current state?'. (It does not shadow — the base member is private — it is a silently unused duplicate.)
findings.suggestion: Delete the line. If derived classes genuinely need to inspect the active state, give `StateContext` a `const State* get_state() const` rather than a second member. While there, the `= nullptr` initialisers on every `unique_ptr` member (Game.h:59, 62, 64-69, 71, 74-75) are redundant.
findings.verify_note: Grepped Game.cpp for `_state\b` — no matches (only `_states`, the CommonStates member). Read Game.h:67 and StateContext.h:16.

findings.title: convert_vec_to_resolution compares floats with == under /fp:fast, and both vec overloads are dead code
findings.detail:
`if (vec == this->convert_resolution_to_vec(screen_resolution::S_1280_720))` — `Vector2F::operator==` is exact float equality (the codebase has `MattMath::are_equal(a, b, EPSILON)` for the epsilon case and does not use it here), and the project compiles with `FloatingPointModel=Fast` in all four configurations. The specific values 1280/720/1920/1080/2560/1440/3840/2160 are all exactly representable in binary32 so it works today, but only by accident — it stops working the moment a value such as 1366x768 scaled by a DPI factor is added.

Both `set_resolution(const Vector2F&)` and `set_resolution(const Vector2I&)` are additionally dead: a grep for `set_resolution` across ArtAttack/ finds only Main.cpp:100 and MainMenu.cpp:324, both passing a `screen_resolution` enum.
findings.suggestion: Delete the `Vector2F` and `Vector2I` overloads and their two private converters — ~50 lines of untested dead code with a latent float-equality trap. If a vec lookup is needed later, compare integer dimensions against the single constexpr table proposed above.
findings.verify_note: Read ResolutionManager.cpp:32-45 and 123-175; grepped `set_resolution(` across ArtAttack/ — only the two enum call sites exist. Confirmed FloatingPointModel=Fast in all four vcxproj configs.

findings.title: Five dead globals/locals/functions in Main.cpp plus roughly 100 lines of commented-out code
findings.detail:
(1) `std::unique_ptr<SimpleMath::Vector2> g_screen_resolution` (:24) is never assigned or read — its only uses are commented out at :106-107 and :142-143, yet it sits in the list of process-lifetime owners next to four live ones. (2) `AdjustWindowRect(&rc, ...)` (:150) computes an adjusted rect neither `CreateWindowExW` call uses. (3) `GetClientRect(hwnd, &rc)` (:202) overwrites `rc`, which is never read again. (4) `static bool s_fullscreen = g_save->get_fullscreen();` (:239) is referenced only inside the commented-out ALT+ENTER block (:367-397), so it is an unused variable that nonetheless runs a thread-safe-static guard on every WndProc call and makes the window procedure depend on `g_save` existing before the first message. (5) `ExitGame()` (:410-413) is declared `extern` in Game.cpp:4, prototyped at Main.cpp:30, and called from nowhere.

Commented-out blocks: :39-81, :106-107, :129-143, :167-179, :198, :206, :367-397.

Separately, the identity is stale and inconsistent: `LPCWSTR g_szAppName = L"Colour Wars"` (:27, a mutable extern global in Hungarian notation) with window class `L"ChromaClashWindowClass"` repeated verbatim at :123, :156 and :162, in a project called ArtAttack.
findings.suggestion: Delete all five and the commented-out blocks (git has them). Settle on one product name as `constexpr wchar_t APP_NAME[]` / `WINDOW_CLASS[]` in an anonymous namespace, and collapse the fullscreen/windowed CreateWindowExW and ShowWindow branches into style/ex-style/show variables so the call appears once.
findings.verify_note: Read Main.cpp in full; verified each of the five and grepped `ExitGame` for call sites (none). Items (2) and (3) are also the substance of the AdjustWindowRect finding above; listed here for completeness of the cleanup.

findings.title: CameraTools is a stateless class used as a namespace, heap-allocated per Level through a unique_ptr
findings.detail:
`CameraTools` has no data members. `calculate_camera` is a `const` non-static member that reads only its four parameters (CameraTools.cpp:8-72) — the only reason it is not already `static` is that it was not marked. `calculate_camera_scroll_border` already is static. Yet `Level` owns one on the heap: `std::unique_ptr<CameraTools> _camera_tools` (Level.h:113), constructed with `std::make_unique<CameraTools>()` (Level.cpp:56) purely to call a pure function at Level.cpp:80 and :196. Same shape as `CollisionTools` elsewhere in the codebase: a namespace written as a type, then given an owner because everything else in the file has one.

Its policy is also unconfigurable: the border ratios and pixel minimums are `constexpr` in `camera_consts` (CameraTools.h:9-17), so no game or level can supply its own follow behaviour.
findings.suggestion: `namespace camera_tools { MattMath::Camera calculate_camera(...); }` — the `camera_consts` namespace is already right there — and delete `Level::_camera_tools` and the make_unique. If a real camera abstraction is wanted, make it a `CameraController` owning target/bounds/translation/scale with injectable policy and explicit modes (Follow, FitRect, Lerp), which would also absorb the zoom logic currently inlined in `Level::update` (Level.cpp:150-159).
findings.verify_note: Read CameraTools.h and .cpp in full, Level.h:113, Level.cpp:56, 80-85, 196-201, 150-159. Rejected one candidate's sub-claim that the unique_ptr indirection is 'an indirect call the compiler cannot inline' — it is a direct non-virtual call and fully inlinable; the cost is the allocation and the conceptual noise, not the call.

findings.title: Bounds clamping silently returns an out-of-bounds camera when the viewport is larger than camera_bounds, and ignores camera scale
findings.detail:
Two related gaps in the bounds correction. (1) It uses `if (left < bounds.left) ... else if (right > bounds.right)` per axis. When the viewport is larger than `camera_bounds` — a small level, or one player at 3840x2160 — both conditions hold; only the first fires and the returned camera still violates the bounds it was asked to respect, with no assert and no way for the caller to know. `Level::update_level_logic` feeds the result straight into `object->set_camera(camera)` (Level.cpp:196-201).

(2) The rectangle is built from raw `viewport_size` (screen pixels) against `camera_bounds` (world units): `RectangleF(new_cam.translation.x, new_cam.translation.y, viewport_size.x, viewport_size.y)`. `prev_camera.scale` is carried into `new_cam` at :23 but never consulted, so the world extent should be `viewport_size / scale`. Currently harmless because per-player cameras always run at scale 1.0, but it is the mirror of the `* scale` bug in `ViewportManager::get_camera_adjusted_player_viewport_rect` and breaks the moment zoom is added or CameraTools is reused.
findings.suggestion: Compute `const Vector2F world_size = viewport_size / prev_camera.scale;` once at the top (guarding scale == 0) and use it for both the scroll-border edges and the bounds rectangle. Handle the viewport-larger-than-bounds case explicitly (centre on the bounds) and assert the postcondition.
findings.verify_note: Read CameraTools.cpp:8-91 and Level.cpp:196-201. Both gaps are real; graded low rather than the candidates' medium/high because neither is reachable at the current call sites (scale is always 1.0 and levels are larger than viewports in shipped content, though nothing enforces either).

findings.title: Redundant std::move around make_unique, plus the hand-maintained parallel sprite-batch vector
findings.detail:
```
this->_sprite_batches[i] = std::move(
    std::make_unique<SpriteBatch>(this->_device_resources->get_deferred_context(i)));
```
`std::make_unique` already returns a prvalue; wrapping it in `std::move` is a no-op at best and pessimising where copy elision would otherwise apply. The loop also maintains `_sprite_batches_ptrs` in lockstep (`:231`) purely so `:234` can publish `&this->_sprite_batches_ptrs` as a `std::vector<SpriteBatch*>*` through `GameData::set_sprite_batches` — handing every consumer a mutable pointer to a Game member container (and the source of the dangling-mirror bug reported separately).

Same file, `float elapsedTime = float(timer.GetElapsedSeconds());` (Game.cpp:89) is a C-style functional cast where the codebase uses `static_cast` everywhere else (ResolutionManager.cpp:71-72, Main.cpp:148), and `elapsedTime` is the only camelCase local in the file.
findings.suggestion: Drop the `std::move` and use `static_cast<float>`. Replace the parallel vector with a single accessor returning `const std::vector<std::unique_ptr<SpriteBatch>>&` or a span-like view so there is nothing to keep in sync.
findings.verify_note: Read Game.cpp:87-98 and 218-234 verbatim.

findings.title: Game.h relies on transitive includes and offers two entry points for setting the same GameData pointer
findings.detail:
Header hygiene: Game.h declares `std::unique_ptr<ResourceLoader>` (:64), `std::unique_ptr<ViewportManager>` (:69) and `std::unique_ptr<Partitioner>` (:75) but includes none of ResourceLoader.h / ViewportManager.h / Partitioner.h. It compiles only because GameData.h (included at Game.h:6) happens to pull all three in (GameData.h:6, 9, 11); reordering the includes breaks the build.

API duplication: `initialize(GameData*)` (:29) sets `_data` at Game.cpp:34, and `set_game_data(GameData*)` (:47) sets the same field at Game.cpp:70. Main.cpp calls both — `set_game_data` at :110, `initialize` at :207 — so there are two entry points for one invariant and no way to tell which is authoritative.
findings.suggestion: Include the three headers explicitly, or forward-declare the classes (Game's destructor is already out-of-line, so forward declarations work for the unique_ptr members). Delete `set_game_data` and take GameData in the constructor or in `initialize` only.
findings.verify_note: Read Game.h in full (includes are DeviceResources.h, StepTimer.h, GameData.h, ResourceManager.h, StateContext.h, ThreadPool.h, Audio.h) and GameData.h:1-12 (which does include all three). Read Game.cpp:32-34 and 68-71, Main.cpp:110 and 207.

findings.title: ViewportManager.h drags DeviceResources.h, MattMath.h and Colour.h into nearly every TU, and ships three near-identical overloads
findings.detail:
The header includes ResolutionManager.h, DeviceResources.h, MattMath.h and Colour.h (:4-8), yet `ResolutionManager`, `DX::DeviceResources` and `DirectX::SpriteBatch` appear only as pointer members/parameters (:21-23, 46-48) and could all be forward-declared. Because GameData.h:9 includes this header, the ~4000-line MattMath.h and the D3D-heavy DeviceResources.h are pulled into essentially the whole project.

The three `apply_player_viewport` overloads (:27, :28-30, :31-32) have bodies that are the same three lines with different sources for the context and batch (ViewportManager.cpp:45-70); the 1-arg version silently uses ambient state and is the subject of a separate finding. `get_player_count_from_layout` (:52, defined :106-121) is a `const` member that never touches `this`.
findings.suggestion: Forward-declare `class ResolutionManager;`, `namespace DX { class DeviceResources; }`, `namespace DirectX { class SpriteBatch; }` and move the includes to the .cpp. Delete the ambient overload and collapse the remaining two into one with a defaulted batch parameter. Make `get_player_count_from_layout` a static free function.
findings.verify_note: Read ViewportManager.h in full and ViewportManager.cpp:45-70, 106-121; confirmed GameData.h:9 includes it.

findings.title: screen_resolution::MAX aliases a real enumerator rather than being a past-the-end sentinel
findings.suggestion: `enum class screen_resolution : std::uint8_t { S_1280_720, …, S_3840_2160, COUNT };` and iterate `< COUNT`, updating MainMenu.cpp:572 accordingly. Better still, drive the menu from the single constexpr resolution table proposed for ResolutionManager rather than from enum arithmetic.
findings.verify_note: Read screen_resolution.h and grepped `screen_resolution::MAX` — one use, MainMenu.cpp:572.

findings.title: ExecuteCommandList/FinishCommandList request full state restore in the level path and not in the menu path
findings.detail:
`immediate_context->ExecuteCommandList(command_lists[i], TRUE)` (GameStates.cpp:328) passes `RestoreContextState = TRUE`, the documented expensive path, once per player per frame. `Level::draw_player_view_level` (Level.cpp:587) and `draw_zoom_out_level_component` (Level.cpp:646) likewise pass `TRUE` to `FinishCommandList`. The identical operation in the menu path passes `FALSE` (MenuPage.cpp:117 and :161), so the two halves of the engine disagree about whether the restore is needed.

Nothing depends on it: `Game::clear()` re-binds the render target and viewport on every context at the start of every frame (Game.cpp:129-149), so the saved state is discarded immediately.
findings.suggestion: Pass `FALSE` everywhere and set state explicitly at the start of each recording, which the code already does. Wrap the execute-and-release loop in one helper so the flag exists in a single place.
findings.verify_note: Read GameStates.cpp:311-330, MenuPage.cpp:117 and 154-163, Level.cpp:587 and 646, Game.cpp:124-152. The TRUE/FALSE split is exactly as described.

findings.title: No [[nodiscard]] on any observer in the platform layer, including ones that allocate or throw
findings.detail: Every query in this module is discardable: `ResolutionManager::get_resolution_ivec/get_resolution_vec/get_resolution_string/get_resolution/convert_resolution_to_string` (ResolutionManager.h:12-22); `ViewportManager::get_layout/get_player_viewport/get_all_viewports/get_camera_adjusted_player_viewport_rect/get_viewport_dividers/get_fullscreen_d3d11_viewport` (ViewportManager.h:26-43); `CameraTools::calculate_camera` (CameraTools.h:24); `DeviceResources::get_deferred_contexts/get_deferred_context` (DeviceResources.h:87-88). Several are non-trivial — `get_all_viewports` builds a vector, `get_viewport_dividers` builds a vector and can throw (ViewportManager.cpp:150). This matters more than usual here because `apply_*` vs `get_*` naming is the only signal distinguishing commands from queries, and the three `apply_player_viewport` overloads are easy to confuse with the getters.
findings.suggestion: Once /std:c++17 is set (see the vcxproj finding), mark all of the above `[[nodiscard]]`.
findings.verify_note: Read ResolutionManager.h, ViewportManager.h, CameraTools.h and DeviceResources.h:86-88 — no attribute appears on any of them.

findings.title: rapidjson read buffer is a 1-byte allocation sized with sizeof(unique_ptr) — heap overrun on every JSON load, then leaked
findings.suggestion: Delete all four copies and write ONE helper — `rapidjson::Document parse_json_file(const char* path)` — that opens with a checked/RAII FILE*, uses `char buf[65536]` (or `std::vector<char>`) with its real size, and returns the document. Drop every `.release()`.
findings.verify_note: Read all four call sites and rapidjson/filereadstream.h:44-79. sizeof on a unique_ptr object is unambiguously the pointer size; make_unique<char>() is a single-object allocation. release() does not delete.

findings.title: fopen result unchecked and ParseStream result never inspected — a missing or malformed asset is UB in Release, not an error
findings.detail:
Merged from 4 candidates. `FILE* fp = fopen(json_path, "rb");` is passed straight into `FileReadStream` with no null test. `FileReadStream`'s only guard is `RAPIDJSON_ASSERT(fp_ != 0)` (filereadstream.h:45), which is plain assert. I confirmed ArtAttack.vcxproj lines 138 and 164 define NDEBUG for both Release configs, so in Release a missing file gives `fread(buf, 1, 8, nullptr)` then `fclose(nullptr)`.

`d.ParseStream(is)` returns a ParseResult that is discarded everywhere; a grep of the first-party tree finds zero uses of `HasParseError`/`GetParseError`. The subsequent member lookups are also unguarded: SoundBank.cpp:163-166 `d["waves"]`, `d["sound_effect_instances"]`, `d["create_effect_instance_for_each_wave"].GetBool()`; SoundBank.cpp:125-126 `effect["name"]`, `effect["wave"]`; Save.cpp:25-26 `d["resolution"]["x"].GetInt()`, `d["fullscreen"].GetBool()`. rapidjson's `operator[](const Ch*)` on a missing member asserts (compiled out) and returns a shared static NullValue, on which `.GetInt()`/`.GetBool()` assert again and read garbage.

Save.cpp is the worst case because save/save_data.json is the one file here that is genuinely untrusted: `write_save_file` opens it with "wb" (Save.cpp:60), truncating immediately, so a crash mid-write leaves a zero-length file that `check_if_save_file_exists()` happily reports as present.

Same at SpriteSheet.cpp:72-88 and LevelLoadedInfo.cpp:96-110.
findings.suggestion: In the shared loader from the previous finding: check `fp != nullptr` and throw naming the path; check `d.ParseStream(is).IsError()` and report `GetParseErrorCode()` + `GetErrorOffset()`; guard each member with `HasMember` + the matching type predicate. For Save specifically, any failure should fall back to `SaveData{}` defaults and rewrite the file rather than propagate.
findings.verify_note: Read all four loaders, rapidjson/filereadstream.h:44-46, and ArtAttack.vcxproj (NDEBUG at lines 138/164, no LanguageStandard, WarningLevel4, no TreatWarningAsError).

findings.title: Four resource getters use map::operator[] inside a catch(out_of_range) that can never fire — a miss silently inserts a null entry and returns nullptr
findings.suggestion: Use `.at()` (or `find()` + explicit throw carrying the key) in all four, mark them `const` and `[[nodiscard]]`, and delete the try/catch wrappers — `.at()`'s own throw is strictly better than one that discards the original message. Collapse the four near-identical bodies into one `template <class Map> auto& lookup(const Map&, const std::string&, const char* kind)`.
findings.verify_note: Read ResourceManager.cpp in full. operator[] on std::map is specified to default-insert, never to throw out_of_range. get_level_info at line 71 uses .at() and is const, proving the author knew the right form.

findings.title: Mutating map lookups run concurrently on thread-pool workers during parallel draw — genuine data race
findings.detail:
`get_sprite_sheet` calls `this->_sprite_sheets[sprite_sheet_name]`, a non-const mutating operation, and it sits on the parallel draw path. I traced the full chain:

  Level::draw_active_level (Level.cpp:386-397) -> ThreadPool::add_task, one task per partition
    -> Level::draw_player_view_level (worker thread) -> object->draw(...)
    -> TextureObject::draw (TextureObject.cpp:24, 43) -> SpriteSheetObject::get_sprite_sheet (SpriteSheetObject.cpp:31-35)
    -> ResourceManager::get_sprite_sheet

Multiple worker threads therefore invoke `operator[]` on the SAME `std::map` simultaneously with no synchronisation. Even when no insertion occurs this is a data race by the standard's rules (non-const member on a shared object); if any name misses, one thread rebalances the red-black tree while others walk it.

`SpriteSheet::draw` is the same shape one level down: non-const, `this->_sprite_frames[frame_name]` at SpriteSheet.cpp:105 and :126, invoked from the same worker threads. `MenuPage::draw_mobjects_in_viewports` (MenuPage.cpp:124-150) reaches the identical path for menus.
findings.suggestion: Make every read-only accessor genuinely read-only and `const` (`.at()`/`find()` on a const map) and mark `SpriteSheet::draw` const. That removes the race with no lock. Enforce it by handing draw code a `const ResourceManager&` so a mutating lookup will not compile.
findings.verify_note: Read Level.cpp:375-400 (add_task per partition, lambda calls draw_player_view_level), TextureObject.cpp:24/43, SpriteSheetObject.cpp:31-35, ResourceManager.cpp:46-58, SpriteSheet.cpp:92-132.

findings.title: reset_all_* null out the mapped values but keep the keys, turning "released" into a silent nullptr, and dangle every cached SoundBank*
findings.suggestion: `.clear()` the maps so lookups fail loudly, remove `reset_all_sounds()` from the device-lost path entirely, and delete the redundant `reset_all_instances()` call. Longer term, give GPU-backed caches a real `reload(ID3D11Device1*)` that restores objects in place so cached pointers stay valid.
findings.verify_note: Read ResourceManager.cpp:104-126, SoundBank.cpp:180-187, Game.cpp:269-280, and grepped Level.cpp for _sound_bank (cached raw at line 59, used at 63/73/74/134/136/147/171).

findings.title: OnDeviceRestored rebuilds ThreadPool / ResourceManager / ResourceLoader / _dt, leaving every cached raw pointer in the live scene dangling
findings.detail:
Merged from 3 candidates. `Game::OnDeviceRestored()` (Game.cpp:282-287) just calls `create_device_dependent_resources()`, which is not a device-resource function — it unconditionally REPLACES every long-lived service:

    _thread_pool      = std::make_unique<ThreadPool>(NUM_THREADS_MIN, NUM_THREADS_MAX); // :236
    _resource_manager = std::make_unique<ResourceManager>();                            // :239
    _resource_loader  = std::make_unique<ResourceLoader>(...);                          // :241
    _dt               = std::make_unique<float>(0.f);                                   // :244
    _viewport_manager = std::make_unique<ViewportManager>(...);                         // :247
    _states           = std::make_unique<CommonStates>(device);                         // :252
    _partitioner      = std::make_unique<Partitioner>();                                // :255

Each assignment destroys the previous object. The new addresses are republished into the root `GameData`, but `OnDeviceLost` (269-280) does NOT tear down the state tree, so every live object still holds the address it cached at construction: `SoundBankObject::_resource_manager` (SoundBankObject.h:35), `Level::_sound_bank` (Level.cpp:59), and every `MenuData`-family object, which is a by-value SNAPSHOT of the 13-pointer bag taken via `GameData::GameData(const GameData*)` (GameData.cpp:4-20).

The `_dt` case is the cleanest proof: `Game::update` writes `*this->_dt = elapsedTime;` (Game.cpp:90) into the NEW float while every consumer still reads the OLD, freed one. Verified by grep: only lines 89-90, 244-245 touch `_dt`.

I graded this high rather than critical because it needs a device-lost event (TDR, driver reset, RDP session change) to trigger — but when it does, the entire scene is on freed memory.
findings.suggestion: Split `create_device_dependent_resources()` into a one-time `create_services()` called only from `initialize`, and a `recreate_device_resources()` called on restore that reloads GPU CONTENTS into the existing manager, preserving object identity. Independently, stop passing frame time as `float*` — pass it by value into `update(float dt)`.
findings.verify_note: Read Game.cpp:218-290 and grepped for _dt (lines 89-90, 244-245 only). Confirmed OnDeviceLost does not touch the state tree and OnDeviceRestored calls create_device_dependent_resources unchanged.

findings.title: work_callback invokes the task with no exception handling — an escaping throw terminates the process and leaks the task
findings.verify_note: Read ThreadPool.cpp:60-65, Level.cpp:585-607 (throw at 590, add_task at 601), MenuPage.cpp:117-150 (throw at 120, add_task at 142).

findings.title: ThreadPool owns raw Win32 handles and declares a destructor but does not delete copy — the implicit copy ctor double-closes every handle
findings.detail:
Merged from 2 candidates. The class holds `PTP_POOL _pool`, `PTP_CLEANUP_GROUP _cleanup_group`, `TP_CALLBACK_ENVIRON _callback_environment` and `std::vector<PTP_WORK> _work_items` (ThreadPool.h:27-30), and `~ThreadPool()` (ThreadPool.cpp:30-36) closes all of them. No copy or move operation is deleted or defined, so the compiler-generated copy constructor and copy assignment are available and `ThreadPool b = a;` compiles into a double `CloseThreadpool` of the same handle. (The moves are suppressed by the user-declared destructor, so the class is copyable-but-not-movable — the worst combination.)

It cannot be correctly copied or moved even in principle: `add_task` registers work against `&_callback_environment` BY ADDRESS (ThreadPool.cpp:41) and `SetThreadpoolCallbackPool(&_callback_environment, _pool)` (line 26) was performed on the original address. The object is pinned in memory and nothing in the header says so.

Also verified: both constructor throw paths (ThreadPool.cpp:12 and :24) fire AFTER `InitializeThreadpoolEnvironment` succeeded at line 8, and neither calls `DestroyThreadpoolEnvironment` — the destructor does not run for a constructor that threw.
findings.suggestion: Add `ThreadPool(const ThreadPool&) = delete; ThreadPool& operator=(const ThreadPool&) = delete;` and explicitly delete the moves (or wrap each handle in its own RAII type so the destructor becomes `= default` and the ctor throw paths clean up automatically).
findings.verify_note: Read ThreadPool.h in full and ThreadPool.cpp:4-36. No copy/move declarations exist; the destructor is user-declared.

findings.title: The engine's resource loader hardcodes this one game's entire asset manifest, including its game-mode enum
findings.suggestion: Make the manifest data: `void load_manifest(const std::filesystem::path&)` reading `{type, id, path}` entries. The project already has rapidjson wired up and sounds/sound_bank_1.json proves the pattern works. Wrap each entry individually, collect failures, and substitute a placeholder asset so a missing file degrades rather than terminates.
findings.verify_note: Read ResourceLoader.cpp/.h in full and grepped the whole tree for callers: the only external call is Game.cpp:258 load_all_resources(). Every other reference is ResourceLoader calling itself.

findings.title: The game-mode enum `level_stage` is baked into the engine's asset cache as a map key type
findings.detail:
`ResourceManager` — the engine's asset cache — `#include`s `level_stage.h` (line 7) and stores `std::map<level_stage, std::unique_ptr<LevelLoadedInfo>> _level_infos;` (line 52), with `get_level_info(level_stage)` / `add_level_info(level_stage, ...)` (lines 32-35). `level_stage` enumerates this game's three maps plus a menu concept.

Every other resource type in the same class is keyed by `std::string`, so this is not even internally consistent — it exists only so game code can write `get_level_info(settings.get_stage())`. `ResourceLoader.h:6` inherits the dependency, and so does every TU that includes `GameData.h`. The engine literally knows a game mode is called King of the Hill.
findings.suggestion: Key level definitions like every other asset — by an `AssetId` (string or interned handle). Delete `level_stage` from ResourceManager and ResourceLoader; let the game map its own `level_stage` -> asset id in game-side code (a table in LevelBuilder or in the manifest).
findings.verify_note: Read ResourceManager.h:1-55 and level_stage.h include at line 7, _level_infos at line 52. Confirmed all four other caches are std::string-keyed.

findings.title: GameData is a 13-pointer service locator that is also inherited as a base by five game-specific data bags, with no virtual destructor
findings.detail:
Merged from 3 candidates. `GameData` holds raw non-owning pointers to `Save`, `ResolutionManager`, `HWND`, `float* _dt`, `ResourceLoader`, `ResourceManager`, `GamePad`, `DeviceResources`, `ViewportManager`, `CommonStates`, `std::vector<SpriteBatch*>*`, `ThreadPool` and `const Partitioner*` — 13 members, every engine service in one struct, handed to essentially everything. Any class that needs frame time also gets the D3D device and the gamepad, so nothing here can be unit-tested or reused in isolation.

(Two candidates said "12 pointers"; the actual count is 13 members, one of which is an HWND handle.)

Then it is INHERITED: `class MenuData : public GameData` (MenuData.h:7), which adds `MenuInput* _input`, which is in turn the base of MainMenuData/PauseMenuData/ResultsMenuData/EndMenuData. `GameData` has no destructor at all, hence a public non-virtual one; deletion through a `GameData*` is UB, and `GameData::get_game_data()` even hands out a `GameData*` to `this`.

Construction goes through `explicit GameData(const GameData* game_data)` (GameData.cpp:4-20), a hand-written field-by-field copy calling 13 getters. That is exactly what the implicit copy constructor already does, and it must be edited every time a service is added — forgetting silently drops a pointer. Its pointer parameter also makes slicing invisible: `MenuData::MenuData(const GameData*)` passes a derived pointer and the derived state is dropped with no diagnostic. And it means each menu holds a SNAPSHOT of the pointers, not a view, which is what makes the device-restore finding above fatal.
findings.suggestion: Add `protected: ~GameData() = default;` so base-pointer deletion cannot compile. Replace the pointer-taking ctor with the implicit copy ctor. Strategically: split into narrow interfaces (`IAssetRegistry`, `IJobSystem`, `IAudioSystem`, `Clock`) injected per-class, and make `MenuData` HOLD services rather than BE them.
findings.verify_note: Read GameData.h/.cpp in full (13 private members, no destructor, get_game_data returns this at GameData.cpp:122-125) and MenuData.h (public inheritance).

findings.title: Game frees every service before its StateContext base destroys the State that points at them
findings.detail:
`class Game final : public DX::IDeviceNotify, public StateContext` (Game.h:16). C++ destroys members first, base subobjects last. So `g_game.reset()` (Main.cpp:226) runs `~Game()`, then members in reverse declaration order (`_partitioner`, `_audio_engine`, `_sprite_batches`, `_thread_pool`, `_viewport_manager`, `_gamepad`, `_state`, `_dt`, `_resource_manager`, `_resource_loader`, `_states`, `_device_resources`), and only THEN `~StateContext()`, which destroys `StateContext::_state` (StateContext.h:16) — the live scene graph.

So the entire game state tree is torn down AFTER the ResourceManager, ThreadPool, AudioEngine, SpriteBatches, CommonStates and DeviceResources it points at have been freed. `Level::_sound_bank` (cached at Level.cpp:59), `Level::_thread_pool`, `SoundBankObject::_resource_manager` are all dangling at that moment.

It does not crash today only because nothing dereferences during teardown. `Level::stop_music()` already exists at Level.cpp:61-64 and does `this->_sound_bank->stop_effect(...)`; the day someone writes the obvious `~Level() { stop_music(); }` this becomes a use-after-free at every exit. For a project whose goal is a reusable engine, "shutdown works because no destructor does anything" is not a shutdown design.
findings.suggestion: Destroy the state tree explicitly and FIRST: give `StateContext` a `clear_state()` and call it at the top of `~Game()`, or stop inheriting `StateContext` and hold it as the last-declared member. Document the required teardown order in the header either way.
findings.verify_note: Read Game.h:16 and 59-76, StateContext.h (private unique_ptr<State> _state, virtual dtor), Main.cpp:226-228, Level.cpp:59-64. C++ destruction order (members before bases) is standard.

findings.title: add_task leaks the heap-allocated std::function when CreateThreadpoolWork fails, and copies the task twice
findings.verify_note: Read ThreadPool.cpp:38-48 and Level.cpp:386-397 (partitioned_players captured by value).

findings.title: Thread counts unvalidated and cast to DWORD; SetThreadpoolThreadMinimum's BOOL discarded; _work_items unsynchronised
findings.detail:
Merged from 3 candidates.

    SetThreadpoolThreadMaximum(_pool, static_cast<DWORD>(max_num_threads));
    SetThreadpoolThreadMinimum(_pool, static_cast<DWORD>(min_num_threads));

1. No validation that `min > 0`, `max > 0`, or `min <= max`. The members are `int` defaulted to `-1` in the header (ThreadPool.h:25-26); a negative value casts to a ~4-billion DWORD. Win32 requires min <= max. The two adjacent same-typed int parameters are also trivially transposable at the call site.
2. `SetThreadpoolThreadMinimum` returns BOOL and is the one call here that can genuinely fail (it must create persistent threads immediately). The result is discarded, so the pool can silently come up under-provisioned while `get_max_num_threads()` — used at Level.cpp:379 and MenuPage.cpp:131 to size partitions and index `sprite_batches`/`deferred_contexts` — keeps reporting the requested value.
3. `_work_items` (ThreadPool.h:27) is a bare `std::vector` mutated by `add_task` and cleared by `wait_for_tasks_to_complete` with no mutex and no documented threading contract. Safe today only because both are called from the main thread.

Currently saved only by the call site passing NUM_THREADS_MIN=1, NUM_THREADS_MAX=16 (Game.h:13-14, verified).
findings.suggestion: Take the counts as `unsigned` (or a `ThreadPoolConfig { unsigned min, max; }` so they cannot be transposed), assert `0 < min <= max` and throw otherwise, and check the BOOL: `if (!SetThreadpoolThreadMinimum(...)) { CloseThreadpool(_pool); throw ...; }`. Document in the header that add/wait are main-thread-only.
findings.verify_note: Read ThreadPool.cpp:4-28, ThreadPool.h:25-30, Game.h:13-14, Level.cpp:379, MenuPage.cpp:131.

findings.title: load_save_file detects that writing the default save file failed, prints it, then parses the file anyway
findings.suggestion: Make `save_to_file()` return `bool` and propagate it. If the write failed, keep the in-memory `SaveData{}` defaults and return WITHOUT parsing. Null-check every fopen. Write saves atomically (tmp file + rename) so a crash cannot destroy existing settings.
findings.verify_note: Read Save.cpp:33-99 and directory_consts.h:11; grepped ArtAttack.vcxproj for PostBuildEvent/Copy/xcopy — no matches.

findings.title: std::cout << ctime_s(...) prints the errno_t return code, not the timestamp
findings.suggestion: `if (ctime_s(buffer, sizeof(buffer), &legacy_start) == 0) std::cout << buffer << ...;`, or drop the C API for `std::put_time`. Route diagnostics through `OutputDebugStringA` or a real logger rather than `std::cout` from an engine class.
findings.verify_note: Read Save.cpp:85-99. ctime_s's signature returning errno_t is unambiguous.

findings.title: WaveBank::CreateInstance returns nullptr for an unknown wave; the catch(out_of_range) never fires and the null is stored under a valid key
findings.detail:
Merged from 3 candidates.

    try { sound_effect_instances[name] = this->_wave_bank->CreateInstance(wave.c_str()); }
    catch (const std::out_of_range& e) { throw std::out_of_range("Wave with name " + wave + " not found"); }

I verified in packages/directxtk_desktop_2019.2023.10.31.1/include/Audio.h that `CreateInstance` (lines 336-339) returns `std::unique_ptr<SoundEffectInstance>` and that `WaveBank::Find(const char*)` returns `int` (line 362) — the name-resolution path. DirectXTK returns nullptr on a miss rather than throwing `std::out_of_range`. So both catch blocks here (116-119 and 137-140) are dead code, and a typo in sounds/sound_bank_1.json stores a live map key with a null value.

That null survives every downstream guard: `get_sound_effect_instance` (74-84) uses `.at()`, which SUCCEEDS because the key exists, and returns `.get()` == nullptr. Every caller dereferences it unchecked — `play_effect` lines 33-37 does `sei->SetVolume(...)`, and `stop_effect`/`pause_effect`/`resume_effect`/`set_effect_*`/`get_effect_state`/`is_effect_looping` (39-73) are all one-line `get_sound_effect_instance(x)->Method()`.

Same dead-catch shape at play_wave (19-26) — `WaveBank::Play(const char*, float, float, float)` returns `void` (Audio.h:334) and cannot throw out_of_range — so a misspelled wave name is a permanent SILENT no-op in Release. I checked the current data and every name used in code does exist in sound_bank_1.json, so nothing is broken today; but nothing would tell you if it were.

Downgraded from high: it takes a data-authoring error to trigger.
findings.suggestion: `auto inst = _wave_bank->CreateInstance(wave.c_str()); if (!inst) throw std::runtime_error("wave '" + wave + "' not in wave bank"); sound_effect_instances.try_emplace(name, std::move(inst));`. Delete the dead catches. Have `get_sound_effect_instance` throw on a null mapped value so failure surfaces at the lookup. For play_wave, resolve via `Find()` and fail loudly on -1.
findings.verify_note: Read SoundBank.cpp:16-148 and Audio.h:317-362 (CreateInstance -> unique_ptr, Play -> void, Find -> int). Also read sounds/sound_bank_1.json: 24 waves + 24 named instances, create_effect_instance_for_each_wave true.

findings.title: Default constructors on SoundBankObject and SoundBank leave dependencies null with no way to repair them
findings.detail:
Merged from 4 candidates.

`SoundBankObject() = default;` (SoundBankObject.h:10) leaves `_resource_manager == nullptr` (line 35). Every method funnels through `get_sound_bank()` (SoundBankObject.cpp:14-17), which is `return this->_resource_manager->get_sound_bank(...)` with no null test. The class provides `set_sound_bank_name` (line 32) but NO setter for the resource manager, so a default-constructed object can never be made valid.

`SoundBank() = default;` (SoundBank.h:15) is the same: `_wave_bank` stays null (line 39) while `play_wave` does `_wave_bank->Play(...)` (SoundBank.cpp:21) and `decode_sound_effect_instances_json` does `_wave_bank->CreateInstance(...)` (line 113). No setter exists.

Even the intended path is two-phase: `SoundBank(std::move(wb))` then a separate `sb->load_from_json(...)` (ResourceLoader.cpp:161-164), so the object exists with no waves in between.

All four current derived classes pass both arguments, so this is latent rather than live — but it is a trap left armed. The half-initialised case composes badly with the `operator[]` finding: a valid manager plus the default `_sound_bank_name == ""` makes `get_sound_bank("")` INSERT an empty-named entry and return nullptr.

Minor in the same header: `std::string _sound_bank_name = "";` (line 34) — the default constructor already yields an empty string.
findings.suggestion: Delete both `= default` constructors and the `= ""` initialiser. Take `ResourceManager&` so null is not expressible, and make SoundBank construction total via a factory that returns a fully-loaded object or fails.
findings.verify_note: Read SoundBankObject.h/.cpp and SoundBank.h/.cpp in full, plus ResourceLoader.cpp:152-168.

findings.title: SoundBankObject is inheritance-as-implementation-reuse: 12 one-line forwarders grafted onto four UI page classes, public base with a non-virtual destructor
findings.detail:
Merged from 3 candidates. The whole class is a `std::string` + a `ResourceManager*` plus twelve protected members that each forward one call. SoundBankObject.cpp:23-72 is 50 lines of nothing but:

    void SoundBankObject::play_wave(const std::string& wave_name, float volume, float pitch, float pan) const
    { this->get_sb()->play_wave(wave_name, volume, pitch, pan); }

Every signature is a second copy of the corresponding `SoundBank` signature, so any API change is a two-file edit.

It is inherited PUBLICLY by four unrelated UI classes, which I verified by grep:
  MainMenu.h:110    class MainMenuPage : public MenuPage, public SoundBankObject
  PauseMenu.h:44    class PauseMenuPage : public MenuPage, public MenuHighlight, public SoundBankObject
  EndMenu.h:42      class EndMenuPage : public MenuPage, public MenuHighlight, public SoundBankObject
  ResultsMenu.h:64  class ResultsMenuPage : public MenuPage, public SoundBankObject

Its entire interface is `protected`, so it exists solely to be inherited — the `is-a` relation public inheritance advertises is false (a menu page is not a sound bank object). It declares no destructor, so it gets a public non-virtual one and `delete static_cast<SoundBankObject*>(page)` compiles as UB. Safe today only because pages are owned as `unique_ptr<State>` and `State` has a virtual destructor.
findings.suggestion: Composition: give the page a member holding the resolved `SoundBank*` (or an `AudioSystem&`) and call `_audio->play_effect(...)`. That deletes SoundBankObject.cpp entirely and removes a base class from four multiple-inheritance hierarchies. If the mixin survives, at minimum make its destructor `protected: ~SoundBankObject() = default;`.
findings.verify_note: Read SoundBankObject.h/.cpp in full; grepped for the four class declarations and confirmed the base clauses.

findings.title: Every audio call re-resolves the SoundBank by string through ResourceManager — two tree lookups per sound operation
findings.detail:
SoundBank* SoundBankObject::get_sound_bank() const
    { return this->_resource_manager->get_sound_bank(this->_sound_bank_name); }

All twelve wrappers (SoundBankObject.cpp:23-72) call `get_sb()` individually, so every `play_wave`/`play_effect`/`get_effect_state` first walks `ResourceManager::_sound_banks` — a `std::map<std::string, ...>` and, via `operator[]`, a MUTATING call, which is also the concurrency finding — and then walks `SoundBank::_sound_effect_instances` (48 entries per sound_bank_1.json). Two string-keyed red-black tree traversals per sound operation, for a pointer that is fixed at construction.

`Level` and `Weapon` already do the right thing and cache the pointer once (Level.cpp:59, Weapon.cpp). `SoundBankObject` is the outlier.
findings.suggestion: Resolve once in the constructor (and in `set_sound_bank_name`) into a `SoundBank*` member; `get_sound_bank()` becomes a member read.
findings.verify_note: Read SoundBankObject.cpp in full, ResourceManager.cpp:91-102, Level.cpp:59, sound_bank_1.json (24 waves + 24 named instances = 48 map entries).

findings.title: Weapon audio does a string-keyed map lookup plus SetVolume/SetPitch/SetPan/Play on every update tick
findings.suggestion: Cache the `SoundEffectInstance*` on the Weapon (the name is fixed by team + slot + weapon type, none of which change after construction) and only touch it on a state transition — track the previous shooting state and call Play/Stop only when it flips. Set volume/pitch/pan once at setup.
findings.verify_note: Read Weapon.cpp:225-277 (handle_shoot_sound called unconditionally at line 231), SoundBank.cpp:29-38, Level.cpp:65-75 and 163-175.

findings.title: No asset-handle abstraction: assets are re-resolved by string map lookup on every draw
findings.detail:
Merged from 2 candidates. Every accessor takes `const std::string&` and returns a raw non-owning pointer, and consumers store the NAME rather than the resolved asset. Verified chain: `TextureObject::draw` (TextureObject.cpp:24, 43) calls `SpriteSheetObject::get_sprite_sheet()` (SpriteSheetObject.cpp:31-35), a `std::map<std::string, unique_ptr<SpriteSheet>>` lookup keyed on `_sheet_name`; `SpriteSheet::draw` then does a SECOND `std::map<std::string, SpriteFrame>` lookup keyed on the frame name (SpriteSheet.cpp:105, 126).

Because `Level::draw_player_view_level` redraws the world once per player viewport, the cost is roughly `objects x players x 2` red-black-tree walks with string compares per frame, all recomputing a constant. There is also no way to detect a typo'd asset name at build time.

All five caches are `std::map` (ordered) although nothing needs ordered iteration.
findings.suggestion: Introduce `AssetHandle<T>` (index or shared_ptr<const T>) resolved once by the registry. `SpriteSheetObject` should hold `AssetHandle<SpriteSheet>` resolved in its constructor, not `std::string _sheet_name`. Keep the string lookup as a one-time `resolve(AssetId) -> Handle` used at load/build time only. If a name cache remains, `unordered_map` fits better.
findings.verify_note: Read ResourceManager.h, SpriteSheetObject.cpp, SpriteSheet.cpp:92-132, TextureObject.cpp (get_sprite_sheet at lines 24 and 43).

findings.title: ResourceManager is five copy-pasted caches; adding a resource type means editing three classes plus OnDeviceLost
findings.detail:
The class is the same six-line pattern instantiated five times — `_textures`, `_sprite_fonts`, `_sprite_sheets`, `_level_infos`, `_sound_banks` — each with `add_X`, `get_X`, and (for three of them) `reset_all_X`. Lines 27-38 vs 46-58 vs 91-102 are identical modulo the member name and one string literal. The three `reset_all_*` bodies (104-126) differ only in the member and the spelling of reset.

Adding shaders or particle definitions requires touching ResourceManager.h, ResourceManager.cpp, ResourceLoader.h, ResourceLoader.cpp, and `Game::OnDeviceLost` (Game.cpp:277-279) which hand-enumerates the reset calls — a list that has already drifted (two of the five caches have no reset at all).
findings.suggestion: One `template <class T> class AssetCache` plus a type-erased registry (`unordered_map<type_index, unique_ptr<IAssetCache>>`) exposing `get<T>(AssetId)` / `add<T>(...)` / `for_each_cache(fn)`. `OnDeviceLost` becomes one loop instead of a hand-written list.
findings.verify_note: Read ResourceManager.cpp in full (126 lines, five caches) and Game.cpp:269-280.

findings.title: Engine headers are not self-contained — they compile only behind this project's pch — and drag rapidjson into every TU
findings.detail:
Merged from 1 candidate, verified against pch.h.

(a) NOT SELF-CONTAINED. `ResourceManager.h` names `Microsoft::WRL::ComPtr<ID3D11ShaderResourceView>` (line 48), `std::unique_ptr` (50-53) and `DirectX::SpriteFont` (line 22) while including only <map>, <string>, SpriteSheet.h, level_stage.h, LevelLoadedInfo.h, <Audio.h>, SoundBank.h. I read pch.h: it is what supplies <wrl/client.h> (line 34), <d3d11_1.h> (36), <memory> (49) and SpriteFont.h (75). `SpriteSheet.h` is worse — it names `ID3D11ShaderResourceView`, `DirectX::SpriteBatch`, `RECT` and `std::unique_ptr` with none of them included. A header that only compiles behind one specific .vcxproj's pch is unusable outside it, which is fatal to the stated engine-reuse goal.

(b) TRANSITIVE WEIGHT. `GameData.h -> ResourceLoader.h -> ResourceManager.h -> SoundBank.h -> <rapidjson/document.h>` compiles a JSON library into every TU that includes GameData.h — which, since `GameData*` is the universal parameter, is nearly all of them — purely so two PRIVATE member declarations (SoundBank.h:45-47) can name `const rapidjson::Value&`. `SoundBank.h:10` includes `MattMath.h` and uses no MattMath type in the header (it is there so the .cpp's `using namespace MattMath;` finds `clamp`). `ResourceManager.h:9` includes <Audio.h> although it names no audio type. `Save.h:4,7` include <iostream> and <rapidjson/document.h> although neither appears in that header. All 13 GameData members are pointers/handles, so GameData.h needs no concrete engine headers at all.
findings.suggestion: Make every engine header compile standalone (add a self-contained-header check to the build). Forward-declare (`class ResourceManager;`, `namespace DirectX { class AudioEngine; }`) instead of including where only pointers/references appear; use rapidjson/fwd.h — already vendored — for the `Value` parameters; move the .cpp-only includes out of the headers.
findings.verify_note: Read pch.h in full (lines 34, 36, 49, 74-75 supply wrl/d3d11_1/memory/SpriteFont+SpriteBatch), ResourceManager.h, SpriteSheet.h, SoundBank.h, Save.h, ResourceLoader.h.

findings.title: Thread-pool tasks capture caller stack locals by reference with no RAII guarantee that the wait is reached
findings.detail:
std::vector<ID3D11CommandList*> command_lists(deferred_contexts->size(), nullptr);   // :128 stack local
    auto partitioned_mobjects = partitioner->partition(mobjects->size(), num_threads);   // :134 stack local
    for (int i = 0; i < partitioned_mobjects.size(); i++)
        thread_pool->add_task([this, i, &partitioned_mobjects, mobjects, deferred_contexts,
            &command_lists, sprite_batches]() { ... });                                   // :142-148 BY REFERENCE
    thread_pool->wait_for_tasks_to_complete();                                            // :150

Two stack locals are captured by reference into work items running on OS thread-pool threads; their validity depends entirely on line 150 being reached. It can be skipped: `add_task` itself throws on `CreateThreadpoolWork` failure (ThreadPool.cpp:44), and the task bodies throw (`throw std::exception("Failed to finish command list")`, MenuPage.cpp:120). Either unwinds past line 150 while tasks 0..i-1 are still writing into `command_lists` — a cross-thread write into a destroyed stack frame. Nothing waits on unwind: `ThreadPool` has no scope guard and its destructor is not reached (the pool is owned by Game).

The analogous `Level::draw_active_level` (Level.cpp:386-397) captures `partitioned_players` BY VALUE and `command_lists` as a caller-owned raw pointer. The two sites disagree about the rule, which is the underlying problem: there is no stated contract about what a task may capture.
findings.suggestion: Make the wait un-skippable with RAII: a `ThreadPool::TaskBatch batch(pool);` whose destructor calls `wait_for_tasks_to_complete()`, with `add_task` on the batch. Then state in the header that tasks may capture references to anything outliving the batch, and stop copying `partitioned_players` at Level.cpp:388.
findings.verify_note: Read MenuPage.cpp:100-164 and Level.cpp:375-400. Confirmed the capture-list difference and the throw at MenuPage.cpp:120.

findings.title: Menu page constructors call a sibling base's member function from the mem-initializer list; correctness depends only on base-clause order
findings.detail:
MainMenuPage::MainMenuPage(MainMenuData* data) :
        MenuPage(data),
        SoundBankObject(main_menu_consts::SOUND_BANK, this->get_resource_manager()),
        _data(data)
    {}

`this->get_resource_manager()` is `MenuPage::get_resource_manager()` (MenuPage.h:35), which reads `MenuPage`'s data pointer. This is a member call on a partially-constructed object from inside a mem-init list. It works ONLY because `MenuPage` precedes `SoundBankObject` in the base clause (`class MainMenuPage : public MenuPage, public SoundBankObject`, MainMenu.h:110) — bases initialise in base-clause order, not in the order written in the mem-init list.

Reordering the base names reads as a cosmetic edit, produces no compiler warning, and would make this read an uninitialised pointer and dereference garbage. Same pattern in the other three menu hierarchies: PauseMenu.h:44, EndMenu.h:42, ResultsMenu.h:64.
findings.suggestion: Use the constructor argument directly — `SoundBankObject(main_menu_consts::SOUND_BANK, data->get_resource_manager())` — which has no ordering dependency. Apply to all four menu page hierarchies.
findings.verify_note: Read MainMenu.cpp:9-16, MenuPage.h:35, and grepped all four base clauses (MainMenu.h:110, PauseMenu.h:44, EndMenu.h:42, ResultsMenu.h:64) — MenuPage is first in every one.

findings.title: SpriteSheet caches a borrowed, non-AddRef'd ID3D11ShaderResourceView* that reset_all_textures() frees underneath it
findings.detail:
`SpriteSheet` stores `ID3D11ShaderResourceView* _texture = nullptr;` (SpriteSheet.h:63) and hands it to `SpriteBatch::Draw` in all four draw overloads (SpriteSheet.cpp:103, 124, 146, 167). The pointer comes from `ResourceManager::get_texture(...)` via `ResourceLoader::load_sprite_sheet` (ResourceLoader.cpp:119-120), and `get_texture` returns `_textures[name].Get()` — a BORROWED raw pointer with no AddRef. The only reference is the ComPtr inside `ResourceManager::_textures`.

`Game::OnDeviceLost()` (Game.cpp:277) calls `reset_all_textures()`, which does `texture.second.Reset()` for every entry, dropping the last reference and destroying the SRV — while every `SpriteSheet::_texture` still points at it. `_sprite_sheets` is NOT reset, so the sheets survive holding freed COM objects. Any draw between device-lost and device-restore passes a dead object to `SpriteBatch::Draw`.

Second vector: `add_texture` (ResourceManager.cpp:21-25) does `_textures[name] = texture`, releasing whatever was previously under that key, so reloading a texture under an existing name silently invalidates every SpriteSheet holding the old pointer.

Graded medium: the window between device-lost and the (wholesale) manager replacement on restore is narrow.
findings.suggestion: Store `Microsoft::WRL::ComPtr<ID3D11ShaderResourceView> _texture` in SpriteSheet, and make `add_texture`/`get_texture` take and return ComPtr so the refcount reflects the actual sharing.
findings.verify_note: Read SpriteSheet.h:60-64, SpriteSheet.cpp draw overloads, ResourceLoader.cpp:111-125, ResourceManager.cpp:7-25 and 112-118, Game.cpp:269-280.

findings.title: AudioEngine is declared after ResourceManager, so it is destroyed BEFORE the SoundBanks that own its WaveBank and voices
findings.detail:
Member order puts `_resource_manager` at Game.h:65 and `_audio_engine` at Game.h:74. Reverse-order destruction therefore frees the AudioEngine FIRST and the ResourceManager — which owns the SoundBanks, which own `unique_ptr<DirectX::WaveBank>` and `unique_ptr<SoundEffectInstance>` (SoundBank.h:39, 41) — second.

Those DirectXTK objects are constructed with a raw `AudioEngine*` (Audio.h:320 `WaveBank(AudioEngine*, const wchar_t*)`) and unregister from the engine in their destructors. This is precisely the ordering DirectXTK warns against.

It survives today only because DirectXTK defends itself — `AudioEngine`'s destructor notifies every registered object and nulls their engine pointer. So this is a latent bug rescued by a third-party defensive path, with nothing in this codebase documenting the dependency. `~Game()` (Game.cpp:23-29) only calls `_audio_engine->Suspend()`, which does not address it.
findings.suggestion: Move `_audio_engine` above `_resource_manager` in Game.h so it outlives it, and add a comment stating the invariant. Better, release the resource manager's sound banks explicitly in `~Game()` so the ordering is expressed in code rather than in declaration position.
findings.verify_note: Read Game.h:59-76 (declaration order), SoundBank.h:39-41, Audio.h:317-322. The rescue mechanism is DirectXTK's, not this project's.

findings.title: SoundBank conflates immutable asset data with runtime voices, forcing per-team/per-player-slot voice names into the data file
findings.detail:
`SoundBank` owns both a `unique_ptr<WaveBank>` (an immutable asset, line 39) and `map<string, unique_ptr<SoundEffectInstance>> _sound_effect_instances` (mutable runtime voices, line 41), keyed by name. Because there is no voice pool, the game must pre-declare one instance per emitter BY NAME. I read sounds/sound_bank_1.json: lines 32-127 declare `sprayer_a0..a3`, `sprayer_b0..b3`, `roller_a0..b3`, `mister_a0..b3` — the cross product of weapon x team x player slot, 24 hand-written entries.

Supporting a fifth player, a third team, or a fourth weapon means editing a JSON asset plus the code tables that mirror it. `decode_sound_effect_instances_json` (SoundBank.cpp:99-148) additionally creates an instance for EVERY wave when `create_effect_instance_for_each_wave` is true (it is, line 29 of the JSON), so all 24 waves get voices whether or not anything plays them — 48 live SoundEffectInstances at startup.
findings.suggestion: Split the concepts. `SoundAsset` = immutable wave data, shared and const. `AudioSystem` = runtime, owning a voice pool: `VoiceHandle play(SoundId, const PlayParams&)`, `stop(VoiceHandle)`, with voice stealing when exhausted. An emitter holds a handle acquired at fire time; nobody names a voice, and the data file lists sounds only.
findings.verify_note: Read SoundBank.h in full, SoundBank.cpp:99-148, and sounds/sound_bank_1.json in full (24 waves, create_effect_instance_for_each_wave: true, 24 named instances following the a0-a3/b0-b3 pattern).

findings.title: No mixer or bus concept: music is just a looping sound effect and there is no master or category volume
findings.detail:
The whole audio API is per-instance: `play_effect(name, loop, volume, pitch, pan)`, `set_effect_volume(name, volume)`. Music goes through the identical path — `Level::update` does `this->_sound_bank->play_effect(this->_music_name, true, this->_music_volume);` (Level.cpp:73) with the track name and volume stored as plain Level members, and menus do the same with hardcoded constants.

I grepped the entire first-party tree for `SetMasterVolume` — zero hits — and there is no category/bus anywhere. An Options screen therefore physically cannot offer a working volume slider without touching every call site, and music is held fully decoded in a wave bank rather than streamed.
findings.suggestion: Add buses (`Master`, `Music`, `SFX`, `UI`), each with a gain multiplied into every routed voice, and persist the gains through the settings store. Play music through a streaming path (DirectXTK `SoundStreamInstance`) owned by a small `MusicPlayer` with `play(track, fade)` / `stop(fade)`, so Level and every menu page stop carrying a track name and a magic volume constant.
findings.verify_note: Read SoundBank.h:20-32, Level.cpp:65-75. Grepped ArtAttack/ for SetMasterVolume — no matches.

findings.title: const is meaningless on SoundBank: const methods start and stop playback and hand out mutable pointers to owned state
findings.detail:
Merged from 2 candidates. `play_wave`, `play_effect`, `stop_effect`, `pause_effect`, `resume_effect`, `set_effect_volume/pitch/pan` are all declared `const` (SoundBank.h:20-30) yet every one mutates the audio objects the class owns. They get away with it because `get_sound_effect_instance(...) const` (SoundBank.cpp:74-84) returns a NON-const `SoundEffectInstance*` obtained from `_sound_effect_instances.at(...).get()` — a const member handing out a mutable handle to its own state.

The fiction is copied wholesale into `SoundBankObject` (all 12 methods const, SoundBankObject.h:16-30) and then propagates outward: `void Level::stop_music() const` (Level.cpp:61-64) is a const member that stops audio. `const` in this codebase therefore carries no information — a reader cannot use it to reason about what a call does, and the compiler cannot help.
findings.suggestion: Drop `const` from every method that changes playback state, and give `get_sound_effect_instance` a const overload returning `const SoundEffectInstance*` plus a non-const overload for the mutable pointer. If a component needs to trigger audio from a const context, that is the const context's bug.
findings.verify_note: Read SoundBank.h:20-35, SoundBank.cpp:16-88, SoundBankObject.h:16-30, Level.cpp:61-64.

findings.title: Content locations are CWD-relative paths as namespace-scope std::string objects in a header, with no post-build asset copy
findings.suggestion: Resolve an asset root once at startup from `GetModuleFileNameW` + parent (or a CLI/env override) into a small `Paths`/VFS service with mount points. Put the save file under %LOCALAPPDATA% via `SHGetKnownFolderPath`. Add a post-build content copy so the exe is standalone. Make the constants `constexpr const char*` (works under C++14) or `inline constexpr std::string_view` after the standard bump.
findings.verify_note: Read directory_consts.h in full; grepped ArtAttack.vcxproj for PostBuildEvent/Copy — none. Counted the literal lengths myself against the MSVC 15-char SSO threshold to correct the reviewer's claim.

findings.title: Save duplicates ResolutionManager's resolution tables verbatim, and the two halves disagree about failure
findings.detail:
Merged from 3 candidates, with the line numbers corrected. `Save::convert_ivec_to_resolution` (Save.cpp:112-135) duplicates `ResolutionManager::convert_ivec_to_resolution` (ResolutionManager.cpp:152-175), and `Save::convert_resolution_to_ivec` (Save.cpp:136-152) duplicates `ResolutionManager::convert_resolution_to_ivec` (ResolutionManager.cpp:47-63) — one candidate cited 46-61 for the latter; the correct range is 47-63. Same four hardcoded pairs, same silent fallback to S_1280_720, same `default: return {-1,-1}`.

The cause is visible: both ResolutionManager copies are PRIVATE (ResolutionManager.h:24 `private:`, converters at 27 and 35), so `Save` could not call them and copied them instead. ResolutionManager has two further copies of the same table in `convert_resolution_to_string` (81-88) and `convert_vec_to_resolution` (98-119) — four copies of one table across two files.

The two halves also disagree about failure: reading an unrecognised resolution silently downgrades to 720p with no warning, while writing an unrecognised enum emits `{"x":-1,"y":-1}` into save/save_data.json, which the reader maps back to 720p. A user's resolution can be reset with zero diagnostic.

Both Save copies are non-static `const` member functions (Save.h:34-38) that read no member — they are pure functions on `screen_resolution`.
findings.suggestion: Delete Save's two copies. Own the table once: a `constexpr` array of `{screen_resolution, w, h, label}` next to the enum with free functions `to_extent` / `from_extent` / `to_string`. Serialise the enum by NAME so an unknown value round-trips as an explicit parse error instead of silently becoming 720p.
findings.verify_note: Read Save.cpp:112-152 and Save.h:34-38; grepped ResolutionManager.cpp (converters at 47-63 and 152-175, plus string/vec copies at 81-88 and 98-148) and ResolutionManager.h (both are private).

findings.title: ResourceLoader's entire public API is dead code, and GameData carries a ResourceLoader* nobody reads
findings.detail:
Merged from 2 candidates. Ten public methods exist (`load_texture`, `load_texture_from_directory`, `load_sprite_font`, `load_sprite_font_from_directory`, `load_sprite_sheet`, `load_sprite_sheet_from_directory`, `load_level_info`, `load_level_info_from_directory`, `load_sound_bank`, `load_sound_bank_from_directory`). I grepped the whole first-party tree: the ONLY external call into this class anywhere is `Game.cpp:258 this->_resource_loader->load_all_resources();`. Every other reference is ResourceLoader calling itself.

Meanwhile `GameData` stores, sets and exposes a `ResourceLoader* _resource_loader` (GameData.h:27-28, 53) whose only reader in the entire codebase is `GameData`'s own copy constructor (GameData.cpp:9) — so a useless dependency and its transitive headers are propagated to every TU that includes GameData.h.

There is also a confusing overload set split across access levels: public `load_level_info(const std::string&, level_stage) const` (line 35) and private `load_level_info() const` (line 53).

The `*_from_directory` twins double the API purely to concatenate a directory, a name and a hardcoded extension.
findings.suggestion: Decide what the class is. If lazy/streaming loading is wanted, expose it through the registry (`AssetRegistry::load(AssetId)` / `load_async(...) -> JobHandle`) and drop the per-type public methods. If not, make everything private except `load_all_resources()` and remove `ResourceLoader*` from `GameData` entirely.
findings.verify_note: Grepped ArtAttack/ for _resource_loader, get_resource_loader, load_texture(, load_sprite_font(, load_sound_bank(, load_level_info(, load_texture_from_directory. Only external caller is Game.cpp:258; only reader of GameData::_resource_loader is GameData.cpp:9.

findings.title: load_sprite_font catches every std::exception and rethrows out_of_range with the original diagnostic destroyed
findings.suggestion: Catch narrowly and chain: `catch (const std::exception& e) { throw std::runtime_error("failed to load SpriteFont '" + font_name + "' from " + font_path + ": " + e.what()); }`. Pick one error policy for the whole class and apply it to load_texture / load_sprite_sheet / load_sound_bank / load_level_info too.
findings.verify_note: Read ResourceLoader.cpp:54-101 and pch.h:79-106 (com_exception derives from std::exception).

findings.title: ResourceLoader's const qualifiers are arbitrary — identical operations are half const, half not
findings.detail:
void load_texture(...) const;        // :17
    void load_sprite_font(...);          // :22   not const
    void load_sprite_sheet(...) const;   // :28
    void load_level_info(...) const;     // :35
    void load_sound_bank(...);           // :40   not const

All five do the same thing — build a resource and hand it to `_resource_manager->add_*` — and none mutates a `ResourceLoader` member. The split is a coin flip and it propagates: `load_textures()`/`load_level_info()` are const (lines 51, 53) because what they call is, while `load_fonts()`/`load_sounds()` (52, 54) are not, which forces `load_all_resources()` (15) to be non-const.

`const` here is also actively misleading: `load_texture(...) const` writes into the shared ResourceManager through a raw pointer. Marking a member const while it mutates the entire asset cache communicates the opposite of the truth.
findings.suggestion: Make them all non-const (they all mutate the world), or better, take the ResourceManager as a parameter so the mutation is visible in the signature: `void load_texture(ResourceManager& out, const std::filesystem::path&) const;`. The latter also makes ResourceLoader stateless and testable.
findings.verify_note: Read ResourceLoader.h in full and cross-checked every definition in ResourceLoader.cpp.

findings.title: No <LanguageStandard> is set, pinning the project to MSVC's C++14 default, and /W4 output is demonstrably unread
findings.detail:
I grepped the vcxproj: `WarningLevel>Level4` and `ConformanceMode>true` appear in all four configurations (lines 91/96, 113/117, 134/141, 160/166), but there is NO `<LanguageStandard>` element anywhere, so MSVC defaults to /std:c++14. That is why the codebase hand-rolls `MattMath::clamp` instead of `std::clamp`, cannot use `std::filesystem` for the path handling flagged elsewhere, cannot use `std::string_view` for directory_consts, cannot use `try_emplace`, and has no `[[nodiscard]]` (grep: zero hits across all first-party files).

There is also no `<TreatWarningAsError>`. The proof that /W4 output is being ignored is `GameData.cpp:142-146`, an unreachable duplicated `return` that C4702 would flag in optimised builds, sitting in committed code.

Also note both Debug configs define `_DEBUG` (lines 93, 115) and both Release configs define `NDEBUG` (138, 164) — which is what disarms every `RAPIDJSON_ASSERT` in the JSON findings above.
findings.suggestion: Set `<LanguageStandard>stdcpp20</LanguageStandard>` (or at minimum stdcpp17) in all four configurations, then sweep for the now-available replacements: std::clamp, std::filesystem::path, string_view constants, [[nodiscard]], try_emplace. Triage the current /W4 output once and turn on TreatWarningAsError for new code.
findings.verify_note: Grepped ArtAttack.vcxproj for LanguageStandard/WarningLevel/ConformanceMode/TreatWarningAsError/PreprocessorDefinitions — Level4 and ConformanceMode present in all four configs, LanguageStandard and TreatWarningAsError absent. Grepped all first-party files for 'nodiscard' — zero hits.

findings.title: NUM_THREADS_MAX = 16 is hardcoded and drives three unrelated quantities regardless of hardware or workload
findings.suggestion: Derive from `std::max(1u, std::thread::hardware_concurrency())` capped by the actual maximum parallel work, and allocate deferred contexts + SpriteBatches to match. If a fixed cap is wanted, name it for what it bounds instead of reusing one constant for three unrelated quantities.
findings.verify_note: Read Game.h:12-14, Game.cpp:218-261 (resize to NUM_THREADS_MAX at 224-232, pool at 236), Level.cpp:379-383, MenuPage.cpp:131.

findings.title: `Save` conflates persistence, schema, display policy and console logging; it is really an unversioned settings file
findings.detail:
`SaveData` contains exactly `{screen_resolution resolution; bool fullscreen;}` — application display settings, not save-game data. I read the on-disk form: save/save_data.json is a single line, `{"resolution":{"x":1920,"y":1080},"fullscreen":false}`, with no schema version field, so the format can never be migrated.

The class simultaneously does file I/O (`load_from_json`, `write_save_file`), owns the resolution enum<->pixel mapping (the duplicated tables above), and logs to `std::cout` from a windowed app with no console. `set_resolution_and_save` / `set_full_screen_and_save` (Save.cpp:101-111) hard-wire the write policy into every setter, so changes cannot be batched or deferred. The path is a fixed relative constant, so multiple profiles or a per-user location are impossible.

Minor in the same header: `SaveData _save_data = SaveData();` (line 29) spells out a redundant copy-initialisation where the members' default initialisers already do the job.
findings.suggestion: Split into (a) a POD `Settings` struct with a `version` field, (b) a `SettingsStore` serialising it to a path supplied at construction (resolved through a platform path service), and (c) a logging facade. Setters mutate `Settings`; an explicit `store.save(settings)` performs I/O.
findings.verify_note: Read Save.h in full, Save.cpp in full, and save/save_data.json (52 bytes, no version field).

findings.title: load_texture does a QueryInterface and GetDesc whose results are discarded, and the QI can reject valid textures
findings.suggestion: Delete lines 66-70 outright. If the dimensions are wanted later, return them from the function rather than computing them into a dead local.
findings.verify_note: Read ResourceLoader.cpp:54-73. texture_desc has no reader; texture has no other use.

findings.title: char-to-wchar_t path conversion via iterator range is wrong for any byte >= 0x80
findings.detail:
std::wstring(texture_path.begin(), texture_path.end()).c_str()

`std::wstring(first, last)` widens each `char` by integral conversion. On MSVC `char` is signed, so any byte >= 0x80 sign-extends into the 0xFF80-0xFFFF range rather than the intended character. It also materialises a temporary wstring on every load. Three sites: line 62 (texture), 91-92 (sprite font), 158-159 (wave bank).

DOWNGRADED from the reviewers' medium. Two candidates described this failing on "an accented user directory" or "any non-ASCII in a user's install path" — that is not reachable here. Every path fed to these calls is built by concatenating a `directory_consts` literal, an asset-name literal and an extension literal (ResourceLoader.cpp:79, 107, 131-132, 148, 172-173), all CWD-relative and pure ASCII. The construct is genuinely wrong, but it cannot misbehave with the current inputs, so this is a cleanup rather than a defect.
findings.suggestion: Store asset paths as `std::wstring`/`std::filesystem::path` end-to-end so no conversion is needed (`directory_consts` becomes `const wchar_t*`). If a conversion is genuinely required, use `MultiByteToWideChar(CP_UTF8, ...)`.
findings.verify_note: Read all three conversion sites and traced every path construction (lines 79, 107, 131-132, 148, 172-173) back to ASCII literals in directory_consts.h. The construct is wrong; the described failure mode is not currently reachable, hence the downgrade.

findings.title: get_thread_pool contains a duplicated, unreachable return
findings.suggestion: Delete line 145 and both `get_*_data()` self-returning accessors. Since the class has no invariants at all — 13 raw pointers, 26 trivial accessors, no validation — consider making it a `struct` of public members and deleting GameData.cpp entirely.
findings.verify_note: Read GameData.cpp:142-146 verbatim. Grepped the tree for get_game_data(/get_menu_data( — only the declarations and definitions, no callers.

findings.title: Game declares a second, unused `_state` member that shadows the one its StateContext base owns
findings.detail:
`class Game final : public DX::IDeviceNotify, public StateContext` (Game.h:16), and `StateContext` already owns the current state as a private `std::unique_ptr<State> _state = nullptr;` (StateContext.h:16). Game.h:67 then declares its own `std::unique_ptr<State> _state = nullptr;`.

I grepped Game.cpp for `_state`: the only hits are lines 252, 253 and 276, all of which are `_states` (the CommonStates member). Game's own `_state` is never read or written anywhere. The real state is managed entirely through the inherited `StateContext::transition_to`. Two same-named, same-typed members owned by different subobjects of one class make it impossible to tell from the header who owns the current state — which is what makes the destruction-order finding above hard to see.
findings.suggestion: Delete Game.h:67.
findings.verify_note: Read Game.h:59-76 and StateContext.h:16. Grepped Game.cpp for _state — only _states matches at 252/253/276.

findings.title: Abbreviation-alias accessors (get_sb, get_sei) are pure forwarders with no external callers
findings.detail:
DirectX::SoundEffectInstance* get_sound_effect_instance(const std::string&) const;
    DirectX::SoundEffectInstance* get_sei(const std::string&) const;   // identical

mirrored in SoundBankObject.h:13-14 (`get_sound_bank`/`get_sb`) and :29-30. `SoundBankObject::get_sb` is literally `return this->get_sound_bank();` and `get_sei` is `return this->get_sound_effect_instance(...);`.

I grepped all first-party files: `SoundBank::get_sei` (SoundBank.cpp:85) and `SoundBankObject::get_sei` (SoundBankObject.cpp:69) have ZERO callers anywhere. `get_sb` is called only from inside SoundBankObject.cpp's own forwarders. Four declarations exist for nothing, and they leak `DirectX::SoundEffectInstance*` out of the abstraction — the one thing that ties consumers to DirectXTK.
findings.suggestion: Delete `get_sei` at both declaration sites and `get_sb` (fold it into `get_sound_bank`, or better into a cached member per the performance finding). Also drop `get_sound_effect_instance` from both public/protected surfaces.
findings.verify_note: Grepped ArtAttack/ for get_sei( and get_sb( — every hit is a declaration, a definition, or an internal SoundBankObject forwarder. No external callers.

findings.title: _wave_names is effectively a parameter promoted to a member
