findings.detail: `std::vector<std::string> _wave_names;` is assigned exactly once, at SoundBank.cpp:168 (`this->_wave_names = decode_wave_names_json(waves);`) and read exactly once, at SoundBank.cpp:107 (`for (auto& wave : this->_wave_names)`) from `decode_sound_effect_instances_json`, which is called on the very next statement (line 169) inside the same function. Nothing else in the codebase touches it. It keeps the 24 wave-name strings from sounds/sound_bank_1.json alive for the whole process lifetime for no reason, and it is the only thing preventing `decode_sound_effect_instances_json` from being `static` like its sibling `decode_wave_names_json` already is.
findings.suggestion: Make it a local in `load_from_json` and pass it to `decode_sound_effect_instances_json(json, wave_names, create_for_each)`, which then becomes static.
findings.verify_note: Read SoundBank.cpp in full; _wave_names appears only at lines 107 and 168, and SoundBank.h:40.

findings.title: clamp_levels mutates three out-parameters, and the valid ranges are re-stated in four places
findings.detail:
void SoundBank::clamp_levels(float& volume, float& pitch, float& pan)
    { volume = clamp(volume, 0.0f, 1.0f); pitch = clamp(pitch, -1.0f, 1.0f); pan = clamp(pan, -1.0f, 1.0f); }

Called only to overwrite the caller's own by-value parameters (SoundBank.cpp:18 and :32). Then `set_effect_volume`/`set_effect_pitch`/`set_effect_pan` (51-65) re-implement the same three clamps inline, so the range knowledge lives in four places.

Related in the same signatures: `play_effect(name, bool loop, float volume, float pitch, float pan)` gives call sites like `play_effect("roller_a0", true, 0.5f, 0.0f, 0.0f)` where nothing says what `true` means, and pitch and pan share the same [-1,1] range so transposing them compiles and silently misbehaves. Every one of these signatures exists twice — once in SoundBank, once as a SoundBankObject forwarder — so any change is a two-file edit.

`clamp` here is `MattMath::clamp`, a hand-rolled `std::clamp` the project cannot use because no LanguageStandard is set (see the build-config finding).
findings.suggestion: `struct SoundParams { float volume = 1.0f, pitch = 0.0f, pan = 0.0f; SoundParams clamped() const; };` with the ranges declared once as constexpr, plus `enum class loop_mode { once, loop };` and `enum class stop_mode { fade, immediate };`. `play_effect(name, loop_mode::loop, {0.5f})` is self-documenting and un-transposable.
findings.verify_note: Read SoundBank.cpp:16-38, 51-65, 174-179 and SoundBank.h:20-32; confirmed the duplicate signature set in SoundBankObject.h:16-30.

findings.title: Four catch blocks bind an exception name they never use and discard the original what()
findings.detail:
`catch (const std::out_of_range& e)` at SoundBank.cpp:23, 80, 116 and 137 — `e` is unreferenced in all four, which is /W4 noise, and every block throws a freshly-constructed `out_of_range` that discards `e.what()`. Three of the four are also unreachable dead code per the earlier findings; only the one at line 80 (wrapping `.at()`) can actually fire, and that one is the one that throws away the real message.

In the same function (99-148): `std::string name = wave;` at line 109 is a full copy of `wave` used only as a map key, and `sound_effect_instances[name] = ...` default-constructs then move-assigns where `try_emplace` would construct once. `decode_wave_names_json` (89-97) `push_back`s into an unreserved vector when `json.Size()` is known up front.
findings.suggestion: Drop the unused `e` names, or append `e.what()` to the new message. Use `sound_effect_instances.try_emplace(wave, _wave_bank->CreateInstance(wave.c_str()))` and delete the `name` copy; add `wave_names.reserve(json.Size())`.
findings.verify_note: Read SoundBank.cpp in full; all four catch parameters are unreferenced and all four blocks construct new exceptions from scratch.

findings.title: C-era file handling: NULL, fopen-as-existence-check, unchecked fclose, duplicated 65536 literal, FILE* leaks on throw
findings.suggestion: `std::filesystem::exists(...)` and `nullptr`. `constexpr size_t WRITE_BUFFER_SIZE = 4096;` used in both places. Call `os.Flush()` explicitly then `return fclose(fp) == 0;`. Wrap every handle: `std::unique_ptr<FILE, int(*)(FILE*)> fp(fopen(p, "rb"), &fclose);`.
findings.verify_note: Read Save.cpp:33-99 (NULL at line 36, nullptr at 61, 65536 at 66 and 67, fclose unchecked at 81) and save/save_data.json (52 bytes).

findings.title: A name collision in the sound bank JSON aborts startup rather than being reported as a data error
findings.suggestion: Treat the collision as a warning (skip the duplicate, log the file and entry name) or make the two name spaces explicitly distinct. Include `json_path` in every message this loader produces.
findings.verify_note: Read SoundBank.cpp:99-148 and sounds/sound_bank_1.json (create_effect_instance_for_each_wave: true at line 29, 24 waves at 3-27).

findings.title: Namespace-scope unique_ptr globals outlive the Game they point into and are destroyed after CoUninitialize
findings.suggestion: Move these into `wWinMain` as locals in a small `AppContext` struct with a documented member order, so destruction is deterministic and precedes CoUninitialize. Delete `g_screen_resolution`.
findings.verify_note: Read Main.cpp:15-37 and 215-231. Only g_game is explicitly reset; CoUninitialize is at line 228.

findings.title: No [[nodiscard]] anywhere in the project, and Save::get_save_data is entirely dead
findings.detail:
A grep for `nodiscard` across all first-party files returns zero hits. The unambiguous candidates in this module are pure accessors whose return value is the point of the call: `ResourceManager::get_texture/get_sprite_font/get_sprite_sheet/get_level_info/get_sound_bank` (ResourceManager.h:17-40), `SoundBank::get_effect_state`/`is_effect_looping` (SoundBank.h:31-32), `ThreadPool::get_min_num_threads`/`get_max_num_threads` (ThreadPool.h:18-19), `Save::get_resolution`/`get_fullscreen` (Save.h:25-26) and all 13 `GameData::get_*`.

Relatedly, `Save::get_save_data()` (Save.h:23, Save.cpp:154-157) returns `SaveData` by value and has zero callers anywhere in the tree — the whole accessor is dead.

(`[[nodiscard]]` is C++17, so this depends on the LanguageStandard finding above.)
findings.suggestion: Bump the standard, then add `[[nodiscard]]` to every pure getter in the module. Delete `get_save_data` and the redundant `= SaveData()` initialiser at Save.h:29.
findings.verify_note: Grepped all first-party files for 'nodiscard' (zero hits) and for get_save_data (only the declaration at Save.h:23 and definition at Save.cpp:154).

findings.title: ThreadPool.h includes <iostream> and uses no stream facility
findings.detail: `#include <iostream>` at ThreadPool.h:7. I read both ThreadPool.h and ThreadPool.cpp in full — neither names `std::cout`, `std::cerr`, or any stream type. Since `GameData.h` includes `ThreadPool.h` and `GameData*` is the universal parameter, this drags the iostream machinery (and its static-initialisation cost) into nearly every translation unit in the project for nothing.
findings.suggestion: Delete the include.
findings.verify_note: Read ThreadPool.h and ThreadPool.cpp in full; no stream usage in either. GameData.h:10 includes ThreadPool.h.

findings.title: The pool churns a TP_WORK object plus a heap std::function per task per frame, with one global barrier for the whole engine
findings.detail:
Per task: one `new std::function` (copy-constructed from a by-value parameter, so two copies of the captures), the std::function's own internal allocation, and a `CreateThreadpoolWork`/`CloseThreadpoolWork` pair. TP_WORK objects are designed to be created once and re-submitted; here they are created and closed every frame.

Separately, `add_task` pushes into a single shared `std::vector<PTP_WORK> _work_items` and `wait_for_tasks_to_complete()` waits on and closes EVERY outstanding item. There is therefore exactly one task group in the entire engine: two subsystems cannot use the pool concurrently and no caller can wait on just its own work. `get_max_num_threads()` exists purely so callers can size their own partitions and index parallel arrays, which is why `Partitioner` exists as a separate injected service at all.

DOWNGRADED from the reviewers' high. One candidate claimed "2,000-6,000 heap allocations per second". I checked the call sites: `Level::draw_active_level` submits one task per partition, and `Partitioner::partition` is called with the player count (at most 4), so gameplay submits ~4/frame; `MenuPage` submits up to 16/frame; `Level::draw_zoom_out_level` submits exactly 1 (and computes an unused `num_threads` at Level.cpp:599). At 60fps that is roughly 240-960 dispatch allocations/second, not thousands. Real, but an order of magnitude smaller than stated.
findings.suggestion: Return a `JobHandle` from `dispatch(...)` so callers wait on their own group; keep per-group counters rather than one global vector. Pre-create the TP_WORK objects and re-submit them, and allocate job payloads from a per-frame linear allocator instead of `new std::function`. A `parallel_for(count, [](size_t worker_index, size_t begin, size_t end){...})` API would also absorb Partitioner and own the worker-index-to-deferred-context mapping that three call sites currently duplicate by hand.
findings.verify_note: Read ThreadPool.cpp:38-58, Level.cpp:375-400 (partition over player count) and 595-607 (single task, unused num_threads at 599), MenuPage.cpp:124-150 (up to get_max_num_threads tasks). Recomputed the allocation rate myself to correct the reviewer's figure.

findings.title: Gamepad input vector is compacted by connection state, then indexed by player number — out-of-bounds read on controller disconnect
findings.suggestion: Return a fixed 4-element array (or a vector always sized to the max player count) indexed by pad slot, with `connection` correctly set for absent pads, so slot index == player identity is an invariant across both input types and across frames. Then `check_for_pause_input` returns a real player number and every `inputs[n]` is safe. Until then use `.at()` in Level::update_level_logic and PauseMenu so the failure is loud.
findings.verify_note: Read GameStates.cpp:141-157/185/348-359, PlayerInput.cpp:95-138 (confirmed push_back only when connected, connection hardcoded CONNECTED), MenuInput.cpp:131-150 (same compaction), Level.cpp:180-213 (confirmed positional player_index subscript), PauseMenu.cpp:45-114 (confirmed inputs[player_num] unchecked).

findings.title: transition_to destroys the State whose update() is still on the stack — `delete this` at ~30 call sites
findings.verify_note: Read StateContext.cpp:20-25 (move-assign into _state confirmed). Grepped transition_to across ArtAttack/: 17 in GameStates.cpp, 21 in MainMenu.cpp, 4 in PauseMenu.cpp, 1 in Main.cpp. Traced GameStates.cpp:76-84, 206-215, 240-300 and PauseMenu.cpp:46-114 — confirmed no member is touched after the call today.

findings.title: transition_to publishes the new state before init(), has no null guard, and gives no exception guarantee
findings.detail:
Two further defects in the same three lines, distinct from the self-destruction issue and needing a different fix.

1. **No null guard.** `update()` and `draw()` both open with `if (this->_state == nullptr) return;` (StateContext.cpp:6-9, 14-17) and `_state` legitimately defaults to `nullptr` (StateContext.h:16) — so the class plainly contemplates a null state. But `transition_to` dereferences unconditionally at :23. `transition_to(nullptr)`, the natural way to tear a context down (and exactly the hook `~Game()` needs to fix its destruction order), is an immediate null dereference. The class is internally inconsistent about whether null is legal.

2. **New state installed before it is valid.** `_state = std::move(state)` publishes, then `_state->init()` runs. `GameLevel::init` (GameStates.cpp:105-127) calls `LevelBuilder::build_level`, which throws `std::exception` on any unexpected level JSON. If it throws, the previous state is already destroyed and `_state` is left holding a `GameLevel` whose `_level`, `_player_input` and `_menu_input` are all null — and `GameLevel::draw` dereferences `_level` unconditionally at :315.
findings.verify_note: Read StateContext.cpp:4-25 and StateContext.h:16; confirmed the null guards in update/draw and their absence in transition_to. Confirmed GameStates.cpp:125-126 build_level with no try/catch, and :315 unconditional _level deref.

findings.title: No exception handler exists anywhere on the path; a malformed level file or an out-of-bounds object terminates the process
findings.detail:
`GameLevel::init()` calls `this->_level = std::move(this->_level_builder->build_level(this->_settings));` (:125-126) with no try/catch. I traced the entire stack and there is no handler at any level: GameStates.cpp:125 → `StateContext::transition_to` (StateContext.cpp:20-25) → `Game::update` (Game.cpp:87-98) → `Game::tick` (Game.cpp:75-84) → `wWinMain` (Main.cpp:211-224). A grep of Main.cpp for `try`/`catch` returns exactly one hit, and it is the word "Entry point" in a comment on line 83.

The codebase throws liberally on this path — 58 `throw std::exception` sites project-wide, including `Level::update_level_logic` throwing `"Player out of bounds"` / `"Collision object out of bounds"` during *normal play* (Level.cpp:312, 319). So a player clipping out of the level, or a missing/malformed `levels/*.json`, produces `std::terminate` — instant process death, no message box, no log.

Worse: `Level::draw_player_view_level` throws `"Deferred context not created"` (Level.cpp:500) and `"Failed to finish command list"` (:590, :649) from *inside thread-pool worker lambdas*, and `ThreadPool::work_callback` (ThreadPool.cpp:60-65) is `void CALLBACK` with no try/catch — an exception escaping there is unconditionally `std::terminate`, and it can never be caught by the caller no matter what handlers are added upstream.
findings.suggestion: Wrap `build_level` in a try/catch in `GameLevel::init()` and fail back to the main menu with an on-screen error. Add a top-level try/catch around the message loop in `wWinMain`. Add a try/catch inside `ThreadPool::work_callback` that captures the exception into the work item so `wait_for_tasks_to_complete()` can rethrow on the calling thread. For an engine, unrecoverable termination on bad content is the worst possible failure mode.
findings.verify_note: Grepped try/catch in Main.cpp (only a comment matched). Read Game.cpp:75-98, StateContext.cpp:20-25, GameStates.cpp:105-127, ThreadPool.cpp:38-65 (work_callback has no handler), Level.cpp:296-322 and :491-651. Counted 58 `throw std::exception` sites.

findings.title: Game inherits StateContext, so subsystems die before the live state tree — and the audio engine dies before the sounds it owns
findings.detail:
`class Game final : public DX::IDeviceNotify, public StateContext` (Game.h:16) owns every engine subsystem as *members* (`_device_resources`:59, `_states`:62, `_resource_loader`:64, `_resource_manager`:65, `_dt`:66, `_gamepad`:68, `_viewport_manager`:69, `_thread_pool`:71, `_sprite_batches`:72, `_audio_engine`:74, `_partitioner`:75), while the live `GameLevel`/`Level`/`Player` tree is owned by the *base* `StateContext::_state` (StateContext.h:16).

C++ destroys derived members first, then base subobjects. At `g_game.reset()` (Main.cpp:226) the order is: `~Game()` body (Game.cpp:23-29, only suspends audio) → all 15 members in reverse declaration order → `~StateContext()` → the whole GameLevel/Level/Player/Weapon/Projectile graph. Every one of those objects holds raw non-owning `ResourceManager*`, `ThreadPool*`, `ViewportManager*`, `const float* _dt` pointers into members that are already gone. This part is latent — it survives only because no game object has a user-written destructor.

The **second half is not latent**: `_audio_engine` (:74) is destroyed before `_resource_manager` (:65), and `ResourceManager::_sound_banks` (ResourceManager.h:53) owns `std::unique_ptr<SoundBank>`, each of which owns a `std::unique_ptr<DirectX::WaveBank>` and a set of `SoundEffectInstance`s (SoundBank.h:33-40). DirectXTK requires all WaveBank/SoundEffect/SoundEffectInstance objects to be destroyed *before* the owning AudioEngine — `~SoundEffectInstance` calls back into the engine to return its voice. This happens on every clean exit.
findings.suggestion: (1) Give `StateContext` a `clear_state()` and call it as the first statement of `~Game()` so the state tree dies while its dependencies are alive; better, stop inheriting `StateContext` and hold one by composition declared *before* all subsystems. (2) Move `_audio_engine` to be declared before `_resource_manager`, or reset the resource manager explicitly at the top of `~Game()`.
findings.verify_note: Read Game.h:16-76 (member order verified line by line), Game.cpp:1-29 and :230-261, Main.cpp:207-230, StateContext.h:7-17, ResourceManager.h:37-53, SoundBank.h:12-40. Confirmed _audio_engine (74) is destroyed before _resource_manager (65) and that SoundBank owns the WaveBank.

findings.title: GameLevel::init captures device-dependent raw pointers for the whole life of the level and never refreshes them on device restore
findings.detail:
```cpp
this->_level_builder = std::make_unique<LevelBuilder>(
    this->get_data()->get_viewport_manager(),
    this->get_data()->get_dt(),                            // float* owned by Game::_dt
    this->get_data()->get_resource_manager(),
    this->get_data()->get_common_states()->PointClamp(),   // borrowed, un-AddRef'd
    ...);
```
`CommonStates::PointClamp()` returns a borrowed `ID3D11SamplerState*` whose lifetime is the `CommonStates` object. It is stored in the LevelBuilder, copied into the `Level`, and used every frame. `Game::OnDeviceLost` (Game.cpp:269-280) does `_states.reset()`; `Game::OnDeviceRestored` (Game.cpp:282-287) re-runs `create_device_dependent_resources()`, which allocates a brand-new `CommonStates` at a new address (Game.cpp:252) **and a brand-new `_dt` float** (Game.cpp:244), republishing both into the real `GameData`.

`GameLevel` implements no device-lost notification and `Game::OnDeviceRestored` does not re-`init()` the current state. After a device reset (driver update, TDR, some Alt-Tab paths) the running level draws with a freed sampler and integrates physics against a freed `float`.

The same snapshot problem exists one level up: `class MenuData : public GameData` (MenuData.h:7) and `GameData::GameData(const GameData*)` (GameData.cpp:4-20) copies all thirteen raw pointers by value, so `MainMenuData` (:6, :13), `PauseMenuData` (:153), `ResultsMenuData` (:172) and `EndMenuData` (:228) each hold their own frozen copy of `_common_states`, `_dt`, `_sprite_batches` and `_device_resources` taken at construction time.
findings.suggestion: Do not cache device-dependent handles in simulation objects — look them up through the resource manager at draw time, or hold a `ComPtr` and re-acquire on restore. Stop passing `const float*` for delta time entirely: pass `float dt` as an argument to `update(float)`. Route `IDeviceNotify` down to the active `State` so it can re-init. And make `MenuData` hold a `const GameData*` by composition rather than copy-inheriting the service bag.
findings.verify_note: Read GameStates.cpp:105-127, Game.cpp:230-287 (confirmed _dt and _states are both recreated in create_device_dependent_resources, which OnDeviceRestored calls), GameData.h:13-62, GameData.cpp:4-20 (confirmed all 13 pointers copied), MenuData.h:7. Confirmed neither GameLevel nor StateContext implements any device-notify hook.

findings.title: Splatoon rules are welded into the engine's core collision interface via collision_object_type
findings.detail:
`virtual collision_object_type get_collision_object_type() const = 0;` makes a 23-value enum that cross-multiplies class × team × weapon part of the fundamental collision contract. `collision_object_type.h:4-29` literally enumerates `PROJECTILE_MIST_TEAM_B`, `PROJECTILE_ROLLING_TEAM_A`, `PLAYER_TEAM_A_DEAD`, `STRUCTURE_RAMP_LEFT`, `PAINT_TILE`. Adding a sixth weapon adds two enumerators and forces edits to every if/else chain keyed on it; adding a third team is a combinatorial rewrite.

The header also ships the game's classification rules as eight inline free functions (`is_player`, `is_projectile`, `is_team_a_projectile`, `is_structure_ramp`, …, collision_object_type.h:31-88) — game rules living in an engine header — and those rules are then re-derived by hand anyway at the use sites (Player::on_collision, PaintTile::on_collision, StructurePaintable::on_collision, Level::count_projectiles).

For a project whose stated goal is a reusable 2D engine, this is the single largest obstacle to reusing the collision layer for anything else: the engine cannot describe a collision without naming Splatoon's weapons and teams.
findings.suggestion: The engine interface should carry only `get_shape()` and a numeric collision layer/mask bitfield used for broad-phase filtering; the game supplies the layer meanings. Identity ("is this an enemy projectile?") belongs to game-side data on the entity (team id, damage source), and the branching should be a response table or double dispatch rather than a type-tag ladder.
findings.verify_note: Read ICollisionGameObject.h:8-17 and the whole of collision_object_type.h (23 enumerators, 8 inline classification helpers, all game-specific).

findings.title: is_colliding lives on the interface, so every object implements the whole narrow phase — and the relation is not symmetric
findings.suggestion: Remove `is_colliding` from the interface. Leave `get_shape()` plus a layer mask and a cached AABB the level can read without dispatch; a `CollisionSystem` computes intersection once per pair and calls `on_collision` on each participant with the contact. Intersection logic then lives in exactly one place (`MattMath::Shape::intersects`, where it already is) and symmetry is structural rather than a convention each class must remember.
findings.verify_note: Read ICollisionGameObject.h:8-17, Structure.cpp:43-46 (confirmed `return false`), Level.cpp:180-322 and :375-400. Confirmed the seven separate is_colliding implementations by grep.

findings.title: IGameObject hardwires DirectX::SpriteBatch and MattMath::Camera into the root interface of every object in the engine
findings.suggestion: Invert the dependency: `virtual void draw(IRenderer&) const = 0;` where `IRenderer` owns the SpriteBatch and the active camera and exposes `draw_sprite(const Sprite&, const Transform&)`. Objects then never name a D3D or DirectXTK type, and the second overload disappears because "no camera" becomes an identity camera on the context — a value, not a virtual. This is the single change that makes the object layer renderer-agnostic and therefore reusable.
findings.verify_note: Read IGameObject.h:1-16 and ICollisionGameObject.h:1-19. Confirmed the camera-less forwarders in Player.cpp:91-95 and the camera-only call sites at Level.cpp:518-540.

findings.title: StateContext holds one state with no stack, forcing GameLevel to hand-roll overlay machinery three times
findings.detail:
`StateContext` has a single `std::unique_ptr<State> _state` and one operation, `transition_to` (replace). There is no push/pop, no way to query the current state, and no notion of an overlay sitting on top of a still-live state.

But pause/results/end menus *are* overlays over a live level, so `GameLevel` re-implements the missing feature by hand three times: `_pause_menu`, `_results_menu`, `_end_menu` are three separate `unique_ptr<StateContext>` members, each with its own action enum and data object (GameStates.h:60-69), each constructed inline in the middle of `GameLevel::update` (GameStates.cpp:150-162, 169-181, 225-236), and `GameLevel::draw` (:332-345) switches over `_state` to pick which of the three to draw on top of the level. `GameMenu` does it a fourth time with its own `_menu` context (GameStates.h:25).

This is also why `game_level_state` (GameStates.h:36-44) conflates three unrelated axes: two load-warmup frames, one simulation state, and three overlay identities. PAUSE_MENU/RESULTS/END_MENU are not states of the level — the level is still drawn underneath them (:311-330 runs before the overlay switch).
findings.suggestion: Give the engine a state stack: `push`, `pop`, `replace`, `top()`. Add `blocks_update_below()` / `blocks_draw_below()` to `State`; `update()` walks top-down until something blocks, `draw()` walks bottom-up. PauseMenu then becomes `push(make_unique<PauseMenu>(...))` over a live GameLevel and `pop()` resumes it, and the three duplicated context/action/data triples plus half of `game_level_state` collapse to nothing.
findings.verify_note: Read StateContext.h:7-17 (single _state, only transition_to, no accessor), GameStates.h:25/36-44/60-69, and GameStates.cpp:150-162, 169-181, 225-236, 303-346.

findings.title: The state layer is bidirectionally coupled to every concrete screen; GameStates.h compiles the whole game
findings.detail:
`GameStates.h` includes `MenuLevelSettings.h`, `GameData.h`, `LevelBuilder.h`, `PauseMenu.h`, `ResultsMenu.h`, `MainMenu.h`, `EndMenu.h`, `PlayerInput.h`. `GameData.h:4-11` in turn pulls `ResolutionManager.h`, `Save.h`, `ResourceLoader.h`, `ResourceManager.h`, `DeviceResources.h`, `ViewportManager.h`, `ThreadPool.h`, `Partitioner.h`, and `LevelBuilder.h` pulls `Level.h` → `Player.h`, `Weapon.h`, `CollisionTools.h`, plus d3d11/dxgi. Anything touching the state machine compiles the entire game.

Of the members that need those headers, every one except `MenuLevelSettings _settings` (:56) is behind a `unique_ptr` and needs only a forward declaration.

The transition graph is also hardcoded in the leaves and cyclic at the concrete-type level: `GameMenu` constructs `GameLevel` (GameStates.cpp:82) and `GameLevel` constructs `GameMenu` at five sites (:212, :253, :263, :273, :291). Each state must know its siblings' concrete types *and* their exact constructor signatures. For an engine, `State`/`StateContext` should ship alone and concrete screens should be game code.
findings.suggestion: Forward-declare the unique_ptr'd types, declare `~GameMenu();`/`~GameLevel();` in the header and `= default` them in the .cpp, and move heavy includes into the .cpp. Break the cycle by making transitions symbolic — states name a target by id or return a registered factory — so `GameLevel.cpp` never includes `GameMenu`. Split GameStates.h into GameMenu.h / GameLevel.h.
findings.verify_note: Read GameStates.h:1-76 and GameData.h:1-12. Confirmed the GameMenu↔GameLevel construction cycle at GameStates.cpp:82 and 212/253/263/273/291, and that only _settings is a by-value member.

findings.title: Non-virtual diamond: Player physically contains two complete DrawObject subobjects
findings.detail:
`class Player final : public MovingObject, public ICollisionGameObject, public AnimationObject, public TextureObject`. I traced the chain: `AnimationObject : public SpriteSheetObject` (AnimationObject.h:7), `TextureObject : public SpriteSheetObject` (TextureObject.h:6), `SpriteSheetObject : public DrawObject` (SpriteSheetObject.h:6) — all non-virtual inheritance.

So a `Player` contains **two** `DrawObject` subobjects: two `_resource_manager`, two `_colour`, two `_draw_rotation`, two `_origin`, two `_effects`, two `_layer_depth`, plus two `_sheet_name`/`_element_name` from `SpriteSheetObject`. Any unqualified `set_colour(...)` or `get_origin()` inside Player is ambiguous, and every qualified one silently mutates only half the object — which is why the code is littered with `this->AnimationObject::draw(...)` / `this->TextureObject::draw(...)` (Player.cpp:91-95, Structure.cpp:35-38, ProjectileBall.cpp:47-50).

`Player` also mixes in `MovingObject`'s `_rotation`, giving one Player three rotation floats for one concept. `Projectile.h:19-21` has the same shape.

I am flagging this from the MovingObject/interface review because it is the structural reason the object layer is unusable as engine code.
findings.suggestion: Stop expressing "has a sprite" and "has an animation" as base classes. Introduce one `Sprite` value type owning transform + tint + origin + effects + layer depth, with a source that is either a static frame or an animation strip, and hold it by composition (`Sprite _sprite;`). Player then has one colour, one origin, one rotation, and `draw` needs no qualification to disambiguate.
findings.verify_note: Read Player.h:63-64 and grepped the inheritance chain: AnimationObject.h:7 and TextureObject.h:6 both derive non-virtually from SpriteSheetObject.h:6, which derives from DrawObject.h:7. Confirmed Projectile.h:19 has the same mixin set.

findings.title: GameLevel::draw does raw D3D11 command-list submission — GPU backend code inside a flow-control State
findings.suggestion: Introduce a Renderer that owns the deferred contexts, the SpriteBatch pool, and command-list recording+submission; `State::draw(Renderer&)` should only record. `ID3D11CommandList*` and `ExecuteCommandList` must not appear above the platform layer. In the interim: use `std::vector<Microsoft::WRL::ComPtr<ID3D11CommandList>>` (the project already uses ComPtr at ResourceManager.h:48), make it a member sized to the max player count and `assign(n, nullptr)` each frame, use a range-for, pass the cached local, and pass FALSE for RestoreContextState.
findings.verify_note: Read GameStates.cpp:303-346, Level.cpp:354-400/491-651, Partitioner.cpp:1-27 (confirmed the `i < num_elements` cap), Game.h:12-14, Game.cpp:52. Confirmed ResourceManager.h:48 uses ComPtr.

findings.title: Member declaration order is inverted: every menu's data is destroyed before the StateContext holding raw pointers to it
findings.detail:
Members are destroyed in reverse declaration order, and all four menu groups are declared the wrong way round.

`GameMenu` (:24-30): `_menu` (25) is declared *before* `_menu_input` (26), `_menu_data` (27), `_menu_level_settings` (28) and `_is_ready_to_load_level` (29). Destruction therefore frees `_is_ready_to_load_level`, `_menu_level_settings`, `_menu_data`, `_menu_input` — and only *last* destroys `_menu`, the `StateContext` owning a `MainMenuTitle`/`MainMenuHome`/… whose page holds a raw `MainMenuData*` to the already-freed `_menu_data`, which itself held raw pointers to the already-freed settings and flag.

`GameLevel` repeats it three times: `_pause_menu`(60) before `_pause_menu_action`(61)/`_pause_menu_data`(62); `_results_menu`(64) before `_results_menu_action`(65)/`_results_menu_data`(66); `_end_menu`(67) before `_end_menu_action`(68)/`_end_menu_data`(69). And `_menu_input`(63) is destroyed before both `_results_menu`(64) and `_end_menu`(67), whose pages reach it through `MenuData::_input`.

Nothing crashes today only because no menu page has a non-default destructor — the same "correct by luck" property as the transition_to finding. The ordering is load-bearing and undocumented.
findings.suggestion: Declare owned data strictly before the things that point at it, so destruction unwinds dependents first: `_menu_input`, `_menu_data`, `_menu_level_settings`, `_is_ready_to_load_level`, *then* `_menu`. Far better: have pages obtain the data through an accessor on the parent rather than storing a raw back-pointer, so there is nothing to go stale.
findings.verify_note: Read GameStates.h:24-30 and 55-70 and verified the declaration order line by line against C++ reverse-order destruction. Confirmed MenuData.h:16 stores a raw MenuInput* and GameData.cpp:4-20 stores raw service pointers.

findings.title: Menu sub-objects are rebuilt in reverse dependency order and are never released when the overlay closes
findings.detail:
```cpp
this->_pause_menu_action = std::make_unique<pause_menu_action>(NONE);  // :150 frees the OLD action
this->_pause_menu_data   = std::make_unique<PauseMenuData>(..., _pause_menu_action.get()); // :153 frees the OLD data
this->_pause_menu        = std::make_unique<StateContext>();           // :159 frees the OLD menu
```
The assignments are the exact reverse of the dependency order. At :150 the previous `pause_menu_action` is deleted while the previous `_pause_menu_data` — still alive — holds a pointer to it, and the previous `_pause_menu`'s page still holds a pointer to that data. Only at :159 is the top of the chain released. Identical shape at :169-181 (results) and :225-236 (end menu). I checked and nothing dereferences through the stale pointers in that window, so this is a latent hazard rather than an active bug — hence `low`.

The related lifetime sloppiness is more visible: on `RESUME` (:197-199) the code sets `_state = ACTIVE` and nothing else, so the whole pause-menu tree, its data and its stale `RESUME` action stay alive until the next pause press — which then rebuilds a `StateContext`, a `PauseMenuData` and a `PauseMenuInitial` (loading its widget tree) mid-frame, a visible hitch at the exact moment the player pauses. The RESULTS objects are likewise never freed once END_MENU is entered. `GameMenu::_is_ready_to_load_level` is never reset to false either.
findings.suggestion: Tear down top-down before rebuilding bottom-up (`_pause_menu.reset(); _pause_menu_data.reset(); _pause_menu_action.reset();`), or better: build the overlay objects once in `init()` and `reset()` them on entry, and release them explicitly on exit so ownership matches lifetime.
findings.verify_note: Read GameStates.cpp:145-239. Confirmed the assignment order, confirmed RESUME at :197-199 only sets _state, and confirmed no reset of any overlay member anywhere in the file.

findings.title: MAX sentinel aliases the last enumerator, so generate_random_team_colour can never return BLUE_YELLOW
findings.detail:
```cpp
enum class team_colour_enum { BLUE_ORANGE, PINK_GREEN, BLUE_YELLOW, MAX = BLUE_YELLOW };
```
`MAX` is 2, i.e. the last *valid* value, not a count. TeamColour.cpp:28-29 then does:
```cpp
int enum_max = static_cast<int>(team_colour_enum::MAX);   // == 2
int random = rand() % enum_max;                            // yields 0 or 1 only
```
so `case 2: return BLUE_YELLOW;` (TeamColour.cpp:36-37) is unreachable and one of the three colour schemes never appears in a match.

I checked the two other `MAX`-style sentinels several reviewers claimed had "the same off-by-one shape" and **they are correct**: `wep_type::MAX_PRIM_WEP = RANDOM_PRIMARY` is genuinely one past the last primary (BUCKET), so `rand() % MAX_PRIM_WEP` at MainMenu.cpp:1521 is right; `level_stage::MAX_STAGE = RANDOM` is one past CLOSE_QUARTERS, so MainMenu.cpp:1894 is right. `team_colour_enum` is the odd one out because `BLUE_YELLOW` is a real palette rather than a RANDOM placeholder.
findings.suggestion: Replace the sentinel with a one-past-the-end `COUNT` after `BLUE_YELLOW`, index a `static constexpr std::array<TeamColour, COUNT>` instead of the switch, and delete `get_team_colours`'s duplicate switch. That gives one mapping instead of two and makes the bug impossible to reintroduce.
findings.verify_note: Read TeamColour.h:17-23 and TeamColour.cpp:26-56. Read wep_type.h and level_stage.h in full plus MainMenu.cpp:1521 and 1893-1898 to settle the contradiction between reviewers — those two sentinels are one-past-the-end and correct.

findings.title: rand() is never seeded anywhere in the project, so every random choice is identical on every launch
findings.detail:
There are exactly three `rand()` call sites in the whole first-party tree — TeamColour.cpp:29, MainMenu.cpp:1521 (random weapon), MainMenu.cpp:1894 (random stage) — and a repo-wide grep for `srand` returns **zero** hits. `rand()` without seeding behaves as if `srand(1)` was called, so the team colour, the RANDOM_PRIMARY weapon roll and the random stage produce the exact same sequence on every run of the game.

Secondary issues at the same line: `rand() % n` is biased when `n` does not divide `RAND_MAX+1` (MSVC's `RAND_MAX` is only 32767), the global generator is not injectable so no test can control it, and `rand()` shares hidden global state with a codebase that runs a Windows thread pool.
findings.suggestion: Do not seed `rand()` — replace it. Put one `std::mt19937` in the engine, seeded once from `std::random_device`, behind `int random_int(int lo, int hi)` using `std::uniform_int_distribution`, and route all three call sites through it. An engine should own its RNG so gameplay is reproducible and testable.
findings.verify_note: Grepped `srand|rand\(\)` across ArtAttack/: exactly three rand() sites, zero srand. Confirmed TeamColour.cpp:29 is one of them.

findings.title: Missing break after case END_MENU, and case QUIT declares a non-trivial local with no braces
findings.detail:
Two switch defects in `GameLevel::update`, plus one that makes them hard to spot.

1. The `case game_level_state::END_MENU:` compound block closes at :297 with **no `break;`** and falls straight into `default: break;` at :298-299. Every other case in that switch terminates explicitly (FIRST_UPDATE `return` :135, ACTIVE `break` :187, PAUSE_MENU :215, RESULTS :238), so this is an inconsistency rather than a deliberate fallthrough — and it becomes a real bug the moment a `game_level_state` is inserted between END_MENU and `default`.

2. `case pause_menu_action::QUIT:` (:206-213) declares `MainMenuMidwayLoadSettings settings;` at :208 with no braces around the case body. `MainMenuMidwayLoadSettings` (MainMenu.h:104-109) contains a `MenuLevelSettings`, which contains `std::vector<MenuPlayerSettings> _player_settings` (MenuLevelSettings.h:33) — a non-trivially-initialised local inside a switch scope. It compiles only because QUIT is the last label in that switch; adding any case after it is an immediate hard error C2360. The structurally identical END_MENU cases at :246-293 all correctly brace their bodies.

3. The *deliberate* fallthrough at :137-138 (`SECOND_UPDATE` → `ACTIVE`) is marked only by the comment `//no break here so it goes to active`. MSVC has no `-Wimplicit-fallthrough`, so nothing distinguishes the intentional one from the accidental one at :297.
findings.suggestion: Add `break;` at :297. Brace the QUIT case body like its siblings. Once the project moves off C++14 (see the LanguageStandard finding), mark :138 `[[fallthrough]];` so the deliberate case is machine-checkable.
findings.verify_note: Read GameStates.cpp:128-301 in full — confirmed no break at :296-297 and that :206-213 has no braces. Read MenuLevelSettings.h:1-37 confirming the std::vector member that makes the QUIT local non-trivial.

findings.title: FIRST_UPDATE/SECOND_UPDATE warm-up hack is defeated by the fixed-timestep loop and causes a black flash
findings.suggestion: Delete both states and fix the root cause: call `_timer.ResetElapsedTime()` after `GameLevel::init()` and after each rebuild at :202 and :279 — that is exactly what `StepTimer::ResetElapsedTime()` exists for. It also removes the two special cases from `GameLevel::draw` and the black flash with them.
findings.verify_note: Read GameStates.cpp:128-139/303-309/200-205/276-283, Game.cpp:62-98, and StepTimer.h:95-150 — confirmed the fixed-timestep while-loop, the max-delta clamp, and that GetElapsedSeconds is the fixed step.

findings.title: 27 protected virtual accessors over three fields, with exactly one override in the entire codebase — and it is a no-op
findings.detail:
`MovingObject` holds two `Vector2F` and a `float` and declares 27 `virtual` protected one-line accessors plus `virtual ~MovingObject() = default`. I grepped every `override` in the project: the only override of any of them is `Player::get_velocity` (Player.h:104), whose entire body is
```cpp
const Vector2F& Player::get_velocity() const { return MovingObject::get_velocity(); }   // Player.cpp:935-938
```
A pure pass-through whose only effect is to widen access from `protected` to `public` for one caller, `DebugText.cpp:25`. `using MovingObject::get_velocity;` would do that with no vtable.

Cost: a vptr and a 28-entry vtable on every object that mixes it in. `Player` (Player.h:63) and `Projectile` (Projectile.h:19) already carry a vptr from `IGameObject`, so they pay two, and projectiles are spawned continuously (Level.cpp:204-210).

It is also an active trap in two directions. The scalar and derived accessors bypass the virtual entirely — `get_velocity_x()` (:20-23), `get_unit_velocity()` (:52-55), `get_velocity_magnitude()` (:56-59) and `get_velocity_angle()` (:60-63) all read `_velocity` directly rather than calling `get_velocity()`. And most call sites explicitly qualify (`MovingObject::set_velocity_y(0.0f)`, `MovingObject::alter_velocity_y(...)`), suppressing dispatch anyway. If anyone ever writes a *real* override, `obj.get_velocity().x` and `obj.get_velocity_x()` will silently disagree and the qualified call sites will silently ignore it.

The public virtual destructor also advertises `delete static_cast<MovingObject*>(p)`, which for `Player` is a different subobject address than the allocation — yet nothing anywhere holds a `MovingObject*`.
findings.suggestion: Drop `virtual` from all 27 accessors and define them inline in the header; make the destructor `protected` and non-virtual to document "mixin, never deleted through this base" and remove the vptr. Replace `Player::get_velocity` with `using MovingObject::get_velocity;`. Best: replace the class entirely with a plain aggregate held by composition (`struct Kinematics { MattMath::Vector2F velocity; };`) — in an engine this is a component, not a base class. Note `_dx` is not state at all: it is recomputed and consumed within one integration step (Player.cpp:852-856, Projectile.cpp:275-276), so it and its 12 accessors should be a local variable.
findings.verify_note: Read MovingObject.h:1-60 (counted 27 virtual accessors, not the 30 several reviewers claimed) and MovingObject.cpp in full. Grepped `override` in Player.h — only get_velocity at :104 comes from MovingObject. Read Player.cpp:935-938 confirming the pass-through body, and DebugText.cpp:25 confirming the sole public caller.

findings.title: get_unit_velocity()/get_unit_dx() divide by zero for a stationary object — but both are dead code
findings.suggestion: Delete the four unused accessors, or guard in `Vector2F::normalized()`/`normalize()`: if `length_squared()` is below an epsilon, return `Vector2F::ZERO`. Do not paper over it at the MovingObject layer only — `normalized()` has other callers.
findings.verify_note: Read MovingObject.cpp:52-63/100-111 and MattMath.cpp:1724-1734 (no zero guard confirmed). Grepped get_unit_velocity/get_unit_dx/get_velocity_angle/get_dx_angle across ArtAttack/ — only the declarations and definitions matched, zero call sites. Grepped FloatingPointModel in ArtAttack.vcxproj.

findings.title: Two-phase construction with no guard: update() and draw() dereference members that only init() creates
findings.detail:
`GameMenu`'s constructors (:4-18) create only `_game_data`, `_menu_data` and `_menu_level_settings`. `_menu_input`, `_is_ready_to_load_level` and `_menu` exist only after `init()` (:21-26). But `update()` dereferences unconditionally:
```cpp
this->_menu->update();                 // null unique_ptr if init() did not run
if (*this->_is_ready_to_load_level)    // null deref
```
and `draw()` (:87) does the same. `GameLevel` is identical: the constructor (:95-99) sets only `_game_data` and `_settings`; `_player_input`, `_menu_input`, `_level_builder` and `_level` all come from `init()` (:107-126), yet `update()` dereferences `_player_input` at :142 and `draw()` dereferences `_level` at :315. `_pause_menu_action`, `_results_menu_action` and `_end_menu_action` are dereferenced without a guard at :193, :220 and :243.

Nothing enforces the ordering. `State::init()` is a public pure virtual peer of `update`/`draw` (State.h:11-13) with no stated ordering; the only thing that makes it work is that `StateContext::transition_to` happens to call it (StateContext.cpp:24) — which is also the line that leaves a half-built state installed when it throws.

Worse, `GameMenu`'s constructor builds `_menu_data` (:6) whose three back-pointers stay null until `set_main_menu_data_ptrs()` patches them at :24. And `GameLevel::init` needs nothing that is not already available in the constructor — it only reads `get_data()` and `_settings` — so the two-phase split buys literally nothing there.
findings.suggestion: Do the work in the constructors and delete `init()` from the `State` interface; the context then constructs a fully valid state before publishing it, which also fixes the exception hole in `transition_to`. If a post-construction hook is genuinely needed to know the context, pass the `StateContext&` to the constructor instead of `set_context`.
findings.verify_note: Read GameStates.cpp:4-127 and 189-243, State.h:9-19, StateContext.cpp:20-25. Confirmed every listed dereference is unguarded and that GameLevel::init uses only get_data() and _settings.

findings.title: Child-to-parent signalling is four heap-allocated scalars whose raw addresses are handed to sub-states
findings.detail:
```cpp
std::unique_ptr<bool>                _is_ready_to_load_level;   // :29,  created GameStates.cpp:23
std::unique_ptr<pause_menu_action>   _pause_menu_action;        // :61,  created :150
std::unique_ptr<results_menu_action> _results_menu_action;      // :65,  created :169
std::unique_ptr<end_menu_action>     _end_menu_action;          // :68,  created :225
```
Four separate heap allocations for one `bool` and three 4-byte enums, each existing only so a raw `bool*` / `pause_menu_action*` can be handed to a child state (`_menu_data->set_is_ready_to_load_level(_is_ready_to_load_level.get())`, :68-69; `PauseMenuData(..., _pause_menu_action.get())`, :157). The child writes through the borrowed pointer (`*this->get_pause_menu_data()->get_action() = pause_menu_action::RESUME;`, PauseMenu.cpp:57) and the parent polls it next frame (`pause_menu_action action = *this->_pause_menu_action;`, :193).

A plain value member has an equally stable address, so the allocation buys nothing — while the `unique_ptr` obscures that these are just mutable out-flags, adds four null states that must be created in `init()`, and makes correctness depend on the member declaration order and the reassignment order, both of which are wrong (see the two ordering findings). `Game::_dt` being a `unique_ptr<float>` (Game.h:66) is the same anti-pattern.
findings.suggestion: Make them plain value members (`bool _is_ready_to_load_level = false; pause_menu_action _pause_menu_action = NONE;`) — the existing `.get()` hand-off becomes `&_flag` and everything still compiles. Better: have sub-states *return* a result from `update()` (a small tagged transition request) rather than scribbling into a borrowed cell in their owner.
findings.verify_note: Read GameStates.h:29/61/65/68, GameStates.cpp:23/68-69/150-157/169-176/225-231/193/220/243, PauseMenu.cpp:53-80. Confirmed Game.h:66 uses unique_ptr<float> for dt.

findings.title: GameLevel::update is a 174-line nested switch containing five copy-pasted return-to-menu blocks
findings.suggestion: Extract `void GameLevel::return_to_menu(main_menu_screen screen, const MenuLevelSettings& settings)` and `void GameLevel::restart_level()`. Once transitions are values rather than side effects (see the transition_to finding), each menu-action case collapses to a single returned transition request and the nested switch disappears entirely.
findings.verify_note: Read GameStates.cpp:128-301 in full and diffed the five menu-return blocks and two restart blocks by hand.

findings.title: State has init() but no on_exit(), so _level->stop_music() is hand-duplicated at seven sites and skipped on app exit
findings.detail:
`State` (State.h:11-13) declares `update`, `draw`, `init` — an entry hook with no matching exit hook. So every path that leaves the level must remember `this->_level->stop_music();` by hand: seven copies at the lines above. Forgetting an eighth when a transition is added later leaks a playing music instance over the menu.

More importantly, `Level` declares no destructor (I checked Level.h — only `void stop_music() const;` at :92, no `~Level`), so the one exit path that cannot be hand-patched is skipped: quitting the app mid-level. `Main.cpp:213-224` breaks out on WM_QUIT, `g_game.reset()` (:226) destroys `Game`, `_audio_engine` (Game.h:74) is destroyed before `_resource_manager` (Game.h:65) which owns the still-playing `SoundEffectInstance`s, and the `Level` that started them is destroyed after both via the StateContext base. Releasing a resource is the destructor's job, not seven call sites'.
findings.suggestion: Two independent fixes; do both. (1) Add `virtual void on_enter() {}` / `virtual void on_exit() {}` to `State`, invoked by `StateContext` around the transition — engine-level lifecycle, not a per-state convention. (2) Stop the music in `~Level()`; the sound instance it started is its resource. With (2) all seven call sites vanish immediately and the app-exit path becomes correct too.
findings.verify_note: Read State.h:1-20 (no exit hook), grepped stop_music in GameStates.cpp (7 sites, all listed) and Level.h (declared at :92, no destructor declared in the class). Read Main.cpp:211-230 and Game.h:59-76 for the exit path.

findings.title: No LanguageStandard is set, so the project builds as C++14 and several correct fixes are unavailable
findings.detail:
`ArtAttack.vcxproj` sets `WarningLevel` Level4, `ConformanceMode` true and `FloatingPointModel` Fast in all four configurations (:91/94/96, :113/116/117, :134/139/141, :160/165/166), but **never sets `<LanguageStandard>`** — a grep for it returns nothing. MSVC therefore falls back to `/std:c++14`.

That is not theoretical: I grepped all first-party `.cpp`/`.h` for `nodiscard`, `std::optional`, `string_view`, `if constexpr` and `[[fallthrough]]` and got **zero** hits. The codebase has never used a C++17 feature, and several of the right fixes in this module group are currently unavailable: `[[fallthrough]]` for the deliberate fall-through at GameStates.cpp:137-138, `std::optional<std::size_t>` for `check_for_pause_input`'s -1 sentinel (GameStates.cpp:348-359), `inline constexpr` for `team_colour_consts` (TeamColour.h:25-42), and `[[nodiscard]]` on the pure queries of `IGameObject`/`ICollisionGameObject`/`MovingObject`.

`TreatWarningAsError` is also set in neither project, so the /W4 warnings this code does generate (e.g. C4018 at GameStates.cpp:321) accumulate silently.
findings.suggestion: Add `<LanguageStandard>stdcpp20</LanguageStandard>` (or stdcpp17) to a shared `.props` sheet imported by both projects, replacing the four hand-maintained near-identical ItemDefinitionGroup blocks. Enable `TreatWarningAsError` at least for new code. Given `/fp:fast` is on everywhere, also confirm it is actually wanted — this codebase relies on float comparison helpers.
findings.verify_note: Grepped LanguageStandard/FloatingPointModel/TreatWarningAsError/WarningLevel/ConformanceMode in ArtAttack.vcxproj — LanguageStandard and TreatWarningAsError absent, the others confirmed at the quoted lines. Grepped all first-party .cpp/.h for five C++17 features: zero matches.

findings.title: Namespace-scope const TeamColour objects in a header: one internally-linked, dynamically-initialised copy per translation unit
findings.suggestion: Make `Colour`'s float/int constructors `constexpr`, then declare these `inline constexpr TeamColour BLUE_ORANGE{...}` (C++17 — see the LanguageStandard finding). That gives one shared compile-time constant with no static-init ordering exposure and no per-TU duplication. Where constexpr is impossible, declare `extern const` in the header and define once in a .cpp. Same treatment for `colour_consts`.
findings.verify_note: Read TeamColour.h:25-42, Colour.h:300-320, and MattMath.h:586-614 confirming Colour's constructors are user-provided and non-constexpr (so not a literal type). Grepped TeamColour.h's includers.

findings.title: Exactly-two-teams is baked into struct member names and has propagated into engine-facing interfaces
findings.detail:
`struct TeamColour { MattMath::Colour team_a; MattMath::Colour team_b; }` with `player_team { A, B, NONE }` (player_team.h:4-9). Because the team count is encoded in member *names*, it cannot be varied — and it has spread well beyond this struct: `IPaintableGameObject.h` defines `struct PaintTotal { float team_a; float team_b; }` on an *interface*; `LevelEndInfo.h` carries `team_a_area`/`team_b_area` plus a set of `team_a_*`/`team_b_*`/`winning_*`/`losing_*` accessors that all assume a two-way comparison; `Level.h:136-137` has separate `_team_a_spawns`/`_team_b_spawns` vectors; and `collision_object_type` doubles every projectile enumerator by team.

Free-for-all, three teams, or solo play are all structurally impossible without touching every one of these. For a codebase whose stated goal is a reusable 2D engine, hard-coding the team count into an interface (`PaintTotal`) is the wrong side of the engine/game line.
findings.suggestion: `using TeamId = int;` (or a strong typedef) plus `struct TeamPalette { std::vector<MattMath::Colour> colours; const MattMath::Colour& operator[](TeamId) const; }`. `PaintTotal` becomes a small vector or map keyed by TeamId; `LevelEndInfo` becomes a sorted `std::vector<TeamScore>` with `winner() == front()`; spawns become `std::vector<std::vector<Vector2F>>` indexed by TeamId.
findings.verify_note: Read TeamColour.h:7-15 and player_team.h in full. Confirmed the team_a/team_b duplication in collision_object_type.h and the TeamColour by-value members at Level.h:128, PaintTile.h:81, StructurePaintable.h:54. PaintTotal/LevelEndInfo member names taken from the reviewers and consistent with the grep of _team_colours usage; not opened line by line.

findings.title: The dependency container is a 13-pointer service locator that is also a polymorphic base with a non-virtual destructor
findings.detail:
`GameData` is a bag of 13 raw pointers (:49-61), all defaulting to `nullptr` and each populated by a separate `set_*` call scattered through `Game::initialize` (Game.cpp:32-66), `create_device_dependent_resources` (Game.cpp:230-256) and `wWinMain`. Its destructor is public, implicit and **non-virtual** — yet it is used as a base class: `MenuData : public GameData` (MenuData.h:7) adds a `MenuInput*`; `MainMenuData`, `PauseMenuData`, `ResultsMenuData`, `EndMenuData` each add more. `GameData::get_game_data()` (:46) hands out an upcast `GameData*`, so any `delete` through it is UB (avoided today only because nothing does it), and any `GameData` copy from a `MenuData*` silently slices `_input` off.

Using inheritance to bolt an extra field onto a container makes the *dependency-injection mechanism itself* polymorphic, which is backwards. And the consumers chase it unchecked: `GameLevel::draw` (:311-319) does `get_data()->get_device_resources()->get_deferred_contexts()` and `->GetD3DDeviceContext()` with no null check anywhere, so a forgotten or reordered setter is a null dereference on the render path with no diagnostic.

A state that needs a ResourceManager and a MenuInput should say so in its signature, not receive a 13-pointer bag and reach into it.
findings.suggestion: Mark `GameData` `final` and stop deriving from it; per-screen state (`MenuInput*`, `MenuLevelSettings*`, action flags) belongs to the State that owns it, passed as explicit constructor parameters. If it must stay a base, give it a protected non-virtual destructor so delete-through-base is a compile error. At minimum, assert the whole bag is populated at the end of `Game::initialize`.
findings.verify_note: Read GameData.h in full (13 pointer members, no virtual destructor, get_game_data at :46), GameData.cpp:1-20, MenuData.h:1-19, and GameStates.cpp:311-319 confirming the unchecked chains.

findings.title: get_for_deletion is a read-only self-destruct flag with no way to request destruction and no owner of lifetime
findings.suggestion: The world owns lifetime. Give the engine an entity handle and a `World::destroy(Handle)` command queue drained at a defined point in the frame; anything — the object itself, a collision response, an out-of-bounds check — can enqueue a destroy. `get_for_deletion` then disappears from the interface entirely.
findings.verify_note: Read ICollisionGameObject.h:8-17 and Level.cpp:290-322. Confirmed the swap-erase loop and the adjacent throw-based out-of-bounds handling.

findings.title: throw std::exception("literal") is an MSVC-only extension, used at 58 sites — a hard portability wall for the engine
findings.detail:
`default: throw std::exception("Invalid team.");` The standard `std::exception` has **no `const char*` constructor**; the one-argument form is an MSVC extension. A grep for `throw std::exception` across the first-party tree returns **58** occurrences, including on live paths: this one is reached from `PaintTile::on_collision` (PaintTile.cpp:39-64) and `PlayerBuilder` (PlayerBuilder.cpp:50, 56), and `Level::update_level_logic` uses it for out-of-bounds (Level.cpp:312, 319).

For a project whose stated goal is a reusable 2D engine, none of this compiles on gcc/clang. Interestingly the newest code in the repo already knows better — `RectangleRotated::set_x_axis` (MattMath.cpp:4365) throws `std::invalid_argument`, so the correct pattern exists and just has not been applied backwards.

Separately, this particular throw is questionable on its merits: `player_team` has only A, B and NONE, and NONE is a legitimate value (`PaintTile::_team` defaults to it), so "invalid team" is a programming error rather than a runtime condition.
findings.suggestion: Replace all 58 with `std::runtime_error` / `std::invalid_argument` / `std::logic_error` taking `std::string`, which compile everywhere. For this specific function, decide once what NONE means: either it is a precondition violation (assert) or it has a defined neutral colour — currently it is treated as both, depending on which of the two same-named functions you call.
findings.verify_note: Read TeamColour.cpp:13-24. Counted 58 `throw std::exception` sites by grep across first-party .cpp/.h. Confirmed MattMath.cpp:4365 uses std::invalid_argument, showing the newer pattern.

findings.title: Culling is delegated to each object, producing unimplementable stubs, one permanently-invisible object, and an infinite recursion
findings.detail:
`virtual bool is_visible_in_viewport(const MattMath::RectangleF& view) const = 0;` forces every implementer to own frustum culling, and there is no `get_bounds()` on the interface — so the level physically cannot see where anything is, and a quadtree or grid can never be layered on without touching every derived class. `Level::draw_player_view_level` consequently makes one virtual call per object per viewport per frame across three unsorted lists (Level.cpp:516-540), and the zoom-out path gave up entirely and culls nothing (Level.cpp:629-642).

The implementations show the interface is wrong. Most are the identical one-liner `return this->_rectangle.intersects(view);` (PaintTile.cpp:151, 199; ProjectileBall.cpp:53; ProjectileJet.cpp:52; ProjectileMist.cpp:54; ProjectileSpray.cpp:54; Structure.cpp:41; Visual.cpp:52) with Player differing only by an inflate (Player.cpp:916-921). And three are broken:
- `ProjectileRolling::is_visible_in_viewport` (ProjectileRolling.cpp:44-47) is a hard `return false;` — a rolling projectile tells the renderer it is *never* on screen, so it is never drawn.
- `MText`/`MTextDropShadow` (Mh.cpp:278-282, 343-347) are `return true;` under `TODO: implement text bounding box`, because a text widget cannot cheaply compute its own bounds.
- **`MTexture::is_visible_in_viewport` (Mh.cpp:162-165) is `return this->is_visible_in_viewport(view);` — unconditional infinite recursion, i.e. a stack-overflow crash the moment it is called.** That one is outside this module group's files but is a `critical`-grade bug in its own right and should be routed to whoever owns Mh.cpp.
findings.suggestion: Objects expose data, the renderer decides: `virtual const MattMath::RectangleF& get_bounds() const = 0;` returning a cached AABB the object updates when it moves. The scene performs the intersection test once, over a flat array of rects with no virtual calls, and can later swap the linear scan for a spatial index without touching a single object. UI widgets simply report their layout rect. Fix ProjectileRolling and Mh.cpp:162 immediately regardless.
findings.verify_note: Read IGameObject.h:13 and grepped every is_visible_in_viewport implementation with 4 lines of context. Confirmed ProjectileRolling.cpp:46 `return false;`, Mh.cpp:164 self-recursive call, Mh.cpp:281/346 `return true;` TODOs, and the Level.cpp:516-540 linear scan.

findings.title: check_for_pause_input returns a magic -1 and hand-rolls a search the standard library already provides
findings.suggestion: Return `std::optional<int>` (C++17) or at minimum introduce `constexpr int NO_PAUSING_PLAYER = -1;` instead of the bare literal. Implement with `std::find_if` + `std::distance`. Make the returned value a genuine player number by fixing the input vector to be slot-indexed (see the critical finding).
findings.verify_note: Read GameStates.cpp:145-146 and 348-359. Grepped first-party sources for std::optional and found none; no <algorithm> usage in this file.

findings.title: Interface mandates two draw overloads; the camera-less one is dead for every game object and non-const for all of them
findings.detail:
Every implementer must supply both `draw(SpriteBatch*, const Camera&)` and `draw(SpriteBatch*)`. The one-argument form is only ever called by the `Mh` UI widget tree, `PaintTile.cpp:70` and `StructurePaintable.cpp:56/59`; the level renderer only uses the camera form (Level.cpp:520, 529, 538, 550). So `Player::draw(SpriteBatch*)` (Player.cpp:91-95), `ProjectileSpray/Jet/Ball/Mist/Rolling::draw(SpriteBatch*)` and `Structure::draw(SpriteBatch*)` are hand-written forwarders that exist only because the interface demands them — one extra dead function per new object type.

Both overloads are also **non-const**, although the primitives underneath are already const: `TextureObject::draw(...) const` (TextureObject.h:20-31) and all five `AnimationObject::draw(...) const` overloads (AnimationObject.h:34-46). The concrete overrides are pure forwarders to those const functions. The gratuitous non-const then infects the whole render path — `Level::draw_active_level(...) const` has to hold non-const object pointers just to draw them, which is a large part of why const is broken throughout Level.
findings.suggestion: Collapse to one `virtual void draw(...) const = 0;`. "No camera" is the identity camera — a value, not a second virtual. Do not use a virtual with a default argument, since defaults bind statically and would be a second trap. Anything that genuinely mutates during draw (animation frame advance) should do it in `update()`.
findings.verify_note: Read IGameObject.h:11-12. Confirmed the const draw primitives are one layer down and that the concrete overrides forward to them (Player.cpp:91-95, Structure.cpp:35-38). Confirmed the camera-form-only call sites at Level.cpp:518-540.

findings.title: Stateless all-static class is heap-allocated via unique_ptr to call its static functions, and two of its three functions are dead
findings.detail:
`class TeamColourTools` has no data members and three static functions. Yet `LevelBuilder.h:29` declares `std::unique_ptr<TeamColourTools> _team_colour = nullptr;`, `LevelBuilder.cpp:23` does `this->_team_colour = std::make_unique<TeamColourTools>();`, and `LevelBuilder.cpp:36` then calls a *static* member through the instance: `const TeamColour team_colours = _team_colour->generate_random_team_colour();`. A heap allocation, an owning smart pointer and a lifetime to reason about, all for zero bytes of state.

I grepped all first-party files: `TeamColourTools::get_team_colours` (:51) and `TeamColourTools::get_team_colour` (:53) have **zero callers**. `generate_random_team_colour` is called from exactly one place. Because `get_team_colours` is dead, `team_colour_enum` (:17-23) is never used to select anything — the player cannot choose a colour scheme, and the enum exists only to be miscounted by `generate_random_team_colour`.

The dead static `get_team_colour` also takes `TeamColour` **by value** (two non-trivially-copyable `Colour`s) and returns by value, duplicating the member function at :14 which returns `const Colour&`.
findings.suggestion: Delete the class. Make `generate_random_team_colour` a free function in a `team_colour` namespace, delete the two dead statics, and remove `LevelBuilder::_team_colour` and its allocation entirely. Then either wire `team_colour_enum` into the menu as a real option or delete it too. (`CollisionTools` has the identical all-static-class shape and deserves the same treatment.)
findings.verify_note: Read TeamColour.h:44-55 and TeamColour.cpp:26-70. Grepped TeamColourTools:: across ArtAttack/ — only the three definitions and the single LevelBuilder.cpp:36 call matched; get_team_colours and the static get_team_colour have no callers. Confirmed LevelBuilder.h:29 and LevelBuilder.cpp:23.

findings.title: Two same-named team-to-colour lookups with opposite failure policies — but the divergent one is dead code
findings.suggestion: Delete `TeamColourTools::get_team_colour` and `get_team_colours` entirely. Keep one lookup, on the data type. Decide the NONE contract explicitly — for a palette lookup a neutral colour is the more useful answer than an exception, given `PaintTile::_team` defaults to NONE.
findings.verify_note: Read TeamColour.cpp:13-24 and 58-70 and player_team.h. Grepped TeamColourTools::get_team_colour across ArtAttack/ — zero call sites, which is why I downgraded the claimed scoring bug.

findings.title: StateContext::update()/draw() are const yet drive the entire mutable simulation
findings.suggestion: Drop `const` from both — that is honest and is a prerequisite for making `update()` perform a deferred state swap. Do the same for `Level::update_level_logic`. If const-correctness through owning pointers matters (it should, for an engine), use a `propagate_const`-style wrapper so the compiler enforces the intent rather than the annotation being decorative.
findings.verify_note: Read StateContext.h:12-13, StateContext.cpp:4-19, Game.cpp:87-98, and Level.cpp:180-322 confirming the const member mutates _collision_objects.

findings.title: Dead duplicate member Game::_state, one character away from the live member _states
findings.detail:
`std::unique_ptr<State> _state = nullptr;` is declared as a private member of `Game`, but `Game` already inherits `StateContext` (Game.h:16), which owns the one and only real state in `StateContext::_state` (StateContext.h:16). Grepping `_state` in Game.cpp returns exactly three hits — lines 252, 253 and 276 — and all three are the *unrelated* member `_states` (the `CommonStates`). `Game::_state` is never assigned, never read, never reset; it is a leftover from before Game was refactored to inherit StateContext.

Severity is `low` because it has no behavioural effect (three reviewers graded it high/medium). It is worth fixing because a reader of Game.h concludes Game owns the state directly (it does not), and because a member named `_state` sitting one character from a live member named `_states` is a typo waiting to compile silently.
findings.suggestion: Delete Game.h:67. While you are there, rename `_states` to `_common_states` so no member differs from another only by a trailing `s`.
findings.verify_note: Read Game.h:16 and :62-67. Grepped `_state` in Game.cpp — only three hits, all `_states` at 252/253/276.

findings.title: set_context is public with one legitimate caller, get_context() const hands out a mutable pointer, and neither class suppresses copy/move
findings.detail:
`void set_context(StateContext* context);` is public (State.h:14). A grep across all first-party files shows exactly one caller: `StateContext::transition_to` (StateContext.cpp:23). Any code holding a `State*` can silently re-parent a state to a different context.

`StateContext* get_context() const;` (State.h:16, protected — several reviewers wrongly called it public) is a const member returning a **non-const** pointer, so a `const State` can call `get_context()->transition_to(...)` and replace itself; the const is meaningless.

Neither `State` nor `StateContext` deletes copy or move, so the invariant "`_context` points at the object whose `_state` unique_ptr holds me" has no type-system protection. `Game` then explicitly opts in with `Game(Game&&) = default; Game& operator=(Game&&) = default;` (Game.h:22-23) — moving a `Game` would move the `StateContext` base's unique_ptr to a new address while the state's `_context` still pointed at the moved-from husk, and would leave `_device_resources->RegisterDeviceNotify(this)` (Game.cpp:20) pointing at that husk too. `Game` is `final` and constructed once (Main.cpp), so the move operations exist for no reason and are wrong.
findings.suggestion: Make `set_context` private with `friend class StateContext;`, or remove it and pass the context to the `State` constructor. Return `const StateContext*` from the const overload. Delete copy and move on both `State` and `StateContext`, and remove `Game(Game&&) = default;` / `operator=(Game&&) = default;` — a device-notify registrant is not movable.
findings.verify_note: Read State.h in full (confirmed get_context is protected at :15-16, not public as claimed) and State.cpp. Grepped set_context — the only caller is StateContext.cpp:23. Read Game.h:22-23 and Game.cpp:20.

findings.title: GameMenu::init's screen switch has no default; an unmatched value leaves a null inner state that renders nothing forever
findings.detail:
`init()` creates `this->_menu = std::make_unique<StateContext>();` (:26) and relies on the switch at :28-62 to populate it. The switch currently covers all eight `main_menu_screen` enumerators (MainMenu.h:92-102) but has no `default:` and no post-condition check. If `_screen` ever holds a value not listed — a new enumerator, or a garbage value read back from `MainMenuMidwayLoadSettings::screen` — `_menu` is left with a null `_state`. `StateContext::update()`/`draw()` then hit their null guards (StateContext.cpp:6, 14) and return silently, giving a game that runs at full framerate showing a cleared screen with no exception, no log and no assert.

Graded `low` rather than medium because all eight enumerators *are* currently handled, and MSVC's C4062 ("enumerator in switch is not handled", level 4, active when there is no default label) would fire at /W4 if one were added — though warnings are not errors in this project.

The switch also has inconsistent arity: five branches pass only `_menu_data.get()`, three (TEAM_SELECT :51-52, WEAPON_SELECT :55-56, STAGE_SELECT :59-60) also pass `_menu_level_settings.get()` — despite `MainMenuData` already carrying the settings pointer via `set_level_settings` at :66, making the second argument redundant.
findings.suggestion: Add `default: throw std::logic_error("unhandled main_menu_screen");`, or assert in debug with a fallback to TITLE. Better: give every page a uniform constructor taking one `MainMenuData*` (which already carries the settings) and replace the switch with a registry keyed by `main_menu_screen`, so adding a screen without wiring it fails at startup rather than rendering a blank screen.
findings.verify_note: Read GameStates.cpp:19-70 and MainMenu.h:92-102 (exactly 8 enumerators, all covered). Confirmed StateContext.cpp:6/14 null guards and GameStates.cpp:66 already setting the settings pointer on _menu_data.

findings.title: std::move applied to a prvalue return value, defeating copy elision
findings.detail: Three sites do `this->_level = std::move(this->_level_builder->build_level(this->_settings));`. `LevelBuilder::build_level` already returns `std::unique_ptr<Level>` **by value** (LevelBuilder.h:26), so the expression is already a prvalue. Wrapping it in `std::move` turns it into an xvalue and blocks elision into the assignment. MSVC /W4 does not diagnose this; clang and gcc emit `-Wpessimizing-move`.
findings.suggestion: `this->_level = this->_level_builder->build_level(this->_settings);` at all three sites.
findings.verify_note: Read GameStates.cpp:125-126, 202-203, 279-280 and grepped LevelBuilder.h:26 confirming the by-value unique_ptr return.

findings.title: #include "colour.h" but the file on disk is Colour.h — compiles only because NTFS is case-insensitive
findings.detail:
`TeamColour.h:5` is `#include "colour.h"`. `ls` confirms the file on disk is `Colour.h` (capital C) and there is no lowercase variant. This resolves on Windows/MSVC and nowhere else.

A repo-wide grep for `#include "colour.h"` returns exactly two offenders: TeamColour.h:5 and InterfaceGameplay.h:7. Every other include site spells it correctly. For a project whose stated goal is a reusable engine, a header that cannot be included on a case-sensitive filesystem is a hard portability wall and a two-character fix that MSVC will never tell you about.
findings.suggestion: Fix both sites to `#include "Colour.h"`, and do a one-off audit across the tree for any other mismatch between `#include "X"` spellings and the actual filenames.
findings.verify_note: Listed ArtAttack/*olour*.h — only Colour.h and TeamColour.h exist, no lowercase colour.h. Grepped `#include "colour.h"` — exactly two hits: TeamColour.h:5 and InterfaceGameplay.h:7.

findings.title: Dead GameMenu::get_data(), redundant value-initialisers, and three include-guard end comments that name the wrong macro
findings.detail:
Three small cleanups in the module's headers.

1. `GameData* GameMenu::get_data() const` is declared at GameStates.h:33 and defined at GameStates.cpp:90-93, but nothing calls it — `GameMenu::order_level_creation` reaches for `this->_game_data` directly (:82) and `GameMenu::init` goes through `_menu_data->get_gamepad()`. Every `get_data()` call in the file (:108-120, :154, :173, :212, :229, :253, :263, :273, :291, :311-319) is inside a `GameLevel` method. `GameLevel` has a byte-identical accessor that *is* used 18 times.

2. `MenuLevelSettings _settings = MenuLevelSettings();` (GameStates.h:56) writes an explicit value-initialiser where nothing at all would do. The member is also commented `// need this to pass to GameLevel` at :24, which is an admission that the state machine has no way to carry shared services and each state smuggles the pointer through by hand.

3. Three include guards have end comments naming a different macro than the guard: `#endif // !GAMELEVEL_H` for guard `GAMESTATES_H` (GameStates.h:76); `#endif // !STATECONTEXTGENERIC_H` for guard `STATECONTEXT_H` (StateContext.h:19); `#endif // !TEAM_COLOURS_H` for guard `TEAMCOLOUR_H` (TeamColour.h:57). Stale comments from renamed files.
findings.suggestion: Delete the unused `GameMenu::get_data()` and the redundant `= MenuLevelSettings()`. Replace the hand-written include guards with `#pragma once` (this is an MSVC-only project and pch.h already uses it) so the comments cannot drift again. Hoist the `GameData*` into `State` or `StateContext` so states obtain services from their context rather than each re-declaring the member.
findings.verify_note: Read GameStates.h in full and grepped every `get_data()` occurrence in GameStates.cpp — all 24 are in GameLevel methods. Verified the three guard/comment mismatches by reading GameStates.h:1/76, StateContext.h:1/19, TeamColour.h:1/57.

findings.title: Duplicate MattMath.h include, raw pointers where references are meant, no [[nodiscard]] on any query, misnamed predicate
findings.detail:
Four small header hygiene issues on the collision interface.

1. **Duplicate include.** `ICollisionGameObject.h:4` includes `IGameObject.h`, which already includes `MattMath.h` at IGameObject.h:4; line 6 then includes `"MattMath.h"` again. MattMath.h is 1139 lines and pulls `SimpleMath.h`, `<d3d11.h>` and `<vector>`, while nothing in these interfaces needs more than `RectangleF`, `Camera` and `Shape`. `DirectX::SpriteBatch` is used only as a pointer and could be forward-declared.

2. **Pointers where references are meant.** `is_colliding(const ICollisionGameObject* other)` and `on_collision(const ICollisionGameObject* other)` take pointers, but null is not a meaningful argument and not one of the ~10 implementations checks for it (Player.cpp:148-185, PaintTile.cpp:84-109, ProjectileSpray.cpp:56, ProjectileJet.cpp:54, ProjectileBall.cpp:55, ProjectileMist.cpp:56, ProjectileRolling.cpp:48). Same for `DirectX::SpriteBatch*` in IGameObject.h:11-12.

3. **No `[[nodiscard]]` anywhere.** I grepped all first-party sources: zero occurrences. Pure queries like `is_colliding`, `get_collision_object_type`, `get_shape`, `get_for_deletion`, `is_visible_in_viewport` and all 27 MovingObject getters can be called and silently discarded. (Requires C++17 — see the LanguageStandard finding.)

4. **Misnamed predicate.** `get_for_deletion()` returns a bool; it should be `is_marked_for_deletion()`.

5. **Copy not suppressed.** `IGameObject`, `ICollisionGameObject`, `State` and `MovingObject` all declare a virtual destructor and stop there, which suppresses implicit *move* but leaves implicit *copy*. Given two `ICollisionGameObject&`, `a = b;` compiles and slices. For `MovingObject`, which carries `_velocity`/`_dx`/`_rotation`, that would half-copy physics state.
findings.suggestion: Remove the duplicate MattMath.h include; split MattMath.h into per-type headers and include only what each interface needs; forward-declare `namespace DirectX { class SpriteBatch; }`. Take `const ICollisionGameObject&` and `SpriteBatch&`. Add `[[nodiscard]]` to every pure query. Rename `get_for_deletion`. Add protected/deleted copy and move to every abstract base.
findings.verify_note: Read ICollisionGameObject.h and IGameObject.h in full (duplicate MattMath.h confirmed). Grepped nodiscard across first-party .cpp/.h — zero hits. Confirmed no implementation of is_colliding null-checks its argument.

findings.title: get_shape() hands out a raw interior pointer with no lifetime contract, while the same interface defines the deletion protocol
findings.detail:
`virtual const MattMath::Shape* get_shape() const = 0;` returns the address of a member shape (e.g. `Player::get_shape` returns `this->get_collision_rectangle()`, Player.cpp:128-131). Nothing in the signature or a comment says how long it is valid, whether it may be stored, whether it survives `update()`, or whether it can be null.

The *same interface* declares `get_for_deletion()` at :16, and `Level::update_level_logic` acts on it by swap-erasing entries out of `_collision_objects` mid-frame (Level.cpp:296-305) — which destroys the object and would dangle any `Shape*` obtained from it earlier. `Level` also `push_back`s newly spawned projectiles into that same vector while the frame is in progress (Level.cpp:209), invalidating references into it.

I checked and no current caller holds a `Shape*` across either operation, so this is an undocumented contract rather than a live bug — hence `low`. `CollisionTools::resolve_object_collision` taking a *mutable* `Shape*` and mutating it in place makes the contract genuinely ambiguous, though.
findings.suggestion: Return `const Shape&` so it cannot be null and is harder to store casually, and document the validity window on the interface. Longer term, separate collision geometry from the object so the broad phase can own it in a contiguous array with stable handles rather than pointers into scattered heap objects.
