findings.verify_note: Read ICollisionGameObject.h:15-16 and Level.cpp:204-213 and 290-322. Confirmed the swap-erase and mid-frame push_back; confirmed no caller currently retains a Shape* across them.

findings.title: Unqualified atan2 can silently round-trip through double
findings.detail:
`return atan2(this->_velocity.y, this->_velocity.x);` (:62) and the same for `_dx` (:110). `atan2` is unqualified. `<cmath>` comes in via pch.h and MattMath.h, and MSVC also injects the C `<math.h>` names into the global namespace, so this resolves — but which overload wins is implementation-dependent. If `::atan2` (the `double(double,double)` C function) is selected, both float arguments are promoted to double, the computation happens in double, and the result is narrowed back to float.

Graded `low` in part because both functions are dead code (see the get_unit_velocity finding — `get_velocity_angle` and `get_dx_angle` have zero callers), so there is no measurable cost today.
findings.suggestion: Use `std::atan2(...)` and include `<cmath>` in MovingObject.cpp directly rather than relying on the precompiled header — or delete both functions, since nothing calls them.
findings.verify_note: Read MovingObject.cpp:60-63 and 108-111. Confirmed via grep that get_velocity_angle and get_dx_angle have no callers outside their own definitions.

findings.title: A level-wide-constant TeamColour is stored by value in every PaintTile
findings.detail:
`TeamColour _team_colours = TeamColour();` — 32 bytes (two 4-float `Colour`s), copied into every paint tile. `StructurePaintable` holds `std::vector<PaintTile> _paint_tiles` (StructurePaintable.h:53), generated as a grid over every paintable surface, and `PaintTile::on_collision` reads `_team_colours.get_team_colour(...)` on the collision path (PaintTile.cpp:39-64).

The value is fixed for the entire level — chosen once at LevelBuilder.cpp:36 — so the same two colours are duplicated across every tile and pulled through cache in the tile update/draw/scoring loops. `Level` (Level.h:128) and `StructurePaintable` (StructurePaintable.h:54) each hold their own copy too.

Graded `low` because I have not measured the tile count; the fix is cheap either way and `PaintTile` is the most numerous object type in the game, so its footprint is worth auditing as a whole.
findings.suggestion: Store a `const TeamColour*` (8 bytes) or a small palette index in `PaintTile`, with the single `TeamColour` owned by `Level`. Better still, resolve the tile's colour once when its team changes rather than looking it up through a per-tile copy on every collision.
findings.verify_note: Read PaintTile.h:81, StructurePaintable.h:53-54, Level.h:128, PaintTile.cpp:39-64, LevelBuilder.cpp:36. Confirmed the by-value storage at all three sites; tile count not measured, hence low.

findings.title: Copy-paste bug: ProjectileMist registers itself as projectile_type SPRAY
findings.detail:
`ProjectileMist`'s ctor initialiser list was copied from `ProjectileSpray.cpp:19-22` and the type tag was never changed:

```cpp
DiffusingProjectile(velocity, team, player_num, team_colour,
    SPRAY, dt, resource_manager,          // <-- should be MIST
    DETAILS_MIST, DIFFUSION_DETAILS_MIST, ...)
```

`Projectile::_type` feeds `Projectile::get_collision_object_type()` (Projectile.cpp:154-192), which switches on `_type`, so every mist projectile in the game reports `PROJECTILE_SPRAY_TEAM_A/B`. Consequences: `collision_object_type::PROJECTILE_MIST_TEAM_A` and `_B` are dead enum values that never occur at runtime; `Player::on_projectile_collision` (Player.cpp:645-690) applies `SPRAY_DAMAGE` instead of `MIST_DAMAGE` to mist hits; every hand-written `PROJECTILE_MIST_*` branch in `PaintTile::on_collision`, `StructurePaintable::on_collision` and `Level::count_projectiles` is unreachable. This is exactly the failure mode the 5-way projectile copy-paste (see the ProjectileSpray/Jet/Ball/Mist/Rolling finding) invites.
findings.suggestion: Change `SPRAY` to `MIST` at ProjectileMist.cpp:20. Better: remove the parameter entirely — make `projectile_type` a `virtual projectile_type get_type() const` or a static trait on the concrete class so the tag cannot disagree with the class, or drop the enum and put the `collision_object_type` in `ProjectileDetails` next to the rest of the per-projectile data.

findings.title: Five Projectile subclasses are ~90% byte-identical; the whole family should be one class + a data table
findings.detail:
`ProjectileSpray.cpp` (91 lines), `ProjectileJet.cpp` (89), `ProjectileBall.cpp` (89), `ProjectileMist.cpp` (90) and `ProjectileRolling.cpp` (82) — ~440 lines total — are the same file five times. Each holds a private `MattMath::RectangleF _rectangle`, and each defines byte-identical bodies for `draw(sprite_batch, camera)`, `draw(sprite_batch)`, `is_visible_in_viewport`, `get_shape`, `is_colliding`, plus a ctor that differs only in which `DETAILS_*` constant it forwards and a 12-line `update()` that differs only by an `inflate_to_size(calculate_diffusion_size())` line. The five headers are identical except the class name and base (`Projectile` vs `DiffusingProjectile`); ProjectileSpray.h:9 / ProjectileMist.h:9 even use `= delete` for the default ctor while the other three use `= default`, for no reason.

All the real variation already lives in data: `projectile_consts.h:14-106` holds `DETAILS_SPRAY/JET/ROLLING/MIST/BALL` and `DIFFUSION_DETAILS_SPRAY/MIST`. `ProjectileRolling` is the only genuine behavioural variant (empty draw, `is_visible_in_viewport` returns false).
findings.suggestion: Delete all ten files. Move `_rectangle`, `draw`, `is_visible_in_viewport`, `get_shape` and the generic `update()` into `Projectile`; keep `DiffusingProjectile::update()` as the one override that inflates. Construct instances as `Projectile(DETAILS_X, ...)` / `DiffusingProjectile(DETAILS_X, DIFFUSION_DETAILS_X, ...)` from a `projectile_type -> details` lookup table, so adding a projectile is a table row rather than two new files.

findings.title: The same 32-line is_colliding narrow-phase boilerplate is copy-pasted into 7 classes
findings.detail:
Identical body — type filter, `AABB_intersects`, "if the other object is a rectangle return true", `Shape::intersects` — appears verbatim at:

- Player.cpp:148-184
- PaintTile.cpp:84-109 (same minus the type filter)
- ProjectileSpray.cpp:56-87
- ProjectileJet.cpp:54-85
- ProjectileBall.cpp:55-86
- ProjectileMist.cpp:56-87
- ProjectileRolling.cpp:48-79

~220 duplicated lines, right down to the comments (`// aabb check`, `// if the other object is a rectangle, then we have a collision`). Note the shared shortcut is also shared-wrong: `if (other_shape_type == shape_type::RECTANGLE) return true;` is only valid when `*this* is also a rectangle — when `this` is a triangle or circle an AABB overlap with a rectangle is reported as a real collision. Because it is copied seven times, fixing that bug means seven edits.
findings.suggestion: Put the entire algorithm in one free function `bool narrow_phase_collides(const Shape* a, const Shape* b)` (or a non-virtual `ICollisionGameObject::is_colliding` that calls a virtual `should_test_against(other)` type filter). Each class then supplies only its type predicate. Removing the copies also lets the `shape_type::RECTANGLE` shortcut bug be fixed in one place.

findings.title: Twelve byte-identical menu draw() bodies across four files
findings.suggestion: Move `std::unique_ptr<MContainer> _texture_container` and `_text_container` into `MenuPage` and give `MenuPage` a single non-virtual `draw()` that builds the pair list from them. All twelve overrides disappear; pages that need extra layers can override and call the base.

findings.title: Four menu *_consts namespaces redefine the same fonts, shadow offsets, colours and sound names
findings.detail:
`main_menu_consts` (MainMenu.h:14-90), `pause_menu_consts` (PauseMenu.h:11-42), `results_menu_consts` (ResultsMenu.h:9-62) and `end_menu_consts` (EndMenu.h:11-40) each independently declare the identical set:

- `DEFAULT_RESOLUTION = {1920,1080}` (MainMenu.h:16, PauseMenu.h:13, ResultsMenu.h:11, EndMenu.h:13)
- `ITEM_FONT = "gill_sans_mt_bold_48"`, `HEADING_FONT = "gill_sans_mt_bold_72"`, `DETAIL_FONT = "gill_sans_mt_bold_36"` (×4)
- `SHADOW_COLOUR`, `TITLE_SHADOW_OFFSET {6,6}`, `HEADING_SHADOW_OFFSET {2.5,2.5}`, `ITEM_SHADOW_OFFSET {1.5,1.5}`, `DETAIL_SHADOW_OFFSET {1,1}` (×4 — a 5-line block repeated verbatim)
- `SOUND_BANK = "sound_bank_1"`, `DIRECTION_SOUND = "UI_Clicks14"`, `CONFIRM_SOUND = "UI_Clicks01"`, `CANCEL_SOUND = "UI_Clicks17"` (×4)
- `STANDARD_HIGHLIGHT = WHITE`, `STANDARD_UNHIGHLIGHT = BLUE` (MainMenu.h:31-32, PauseMenu.h:20-21, EndMenu.h:24-25)

~60 duplicated declarations. Worse, they are namespace-scope `const std::string` / `const Colour` objects in headers, so each of the ~30 TUs that include them gets its own copy with dynamic initialisation at startup.
findings.suggestion: Create one `ui_theme.h` holding the shared font names, shadow offsets, palette and UI sound names, and leave only the genuinely page-specific values (`MODE_SELECT_WIDGET_SPACING`, `RESULTS_MENU_FILL_BOX_SIZE`, weapon descriptions, …) in the per-menu namespaces. Declare the strings `inline constexpr std::string_view` (or `constexpr const char*`) so there is one object, not one per TU.

findings.title: is_projectile / is_team_a_projectile predicates exist but four call sites re-inline the 10-way disjunction
findings.detail:
`collision_object_type.h` already provides `is_projectile` (:43-55), `is_team_a_projectile` (:57-64) and `is_team_b_projectile` (:66-73). They are ignored at every site that needs them:

- `Level::count_projectiles` (Level.cpp:665-675) rewrites the exact body of `is_projectile` into a local `bool is_projectile = ...` — and shadows the function name while doing it.
- `StructurePaintable::on_collision` (StructurePaintable.cpp:68-78) rewrites the same 10-term disjunction as `is_offensive_projectile`.
- `Player::on_collision` (Player.cpp:199-221) rewrites both `is_team_a_projectile` and `is_team_b_projectile` inline.
- `PaintTile::on_collision` (PaintTile.cpp:116-133) rewrites both again to derive `other_team`.

~60 duplicated lines, and each is a place a new projectile type must be added by hand. `PaintTile`'s copy also throws `std::exception("...is not a projectile")` on the miss, so it doubles as a type check.
findings.suggestion: Replace all four bodies with the existing predicates, and add the one missing helper `player_team projectile_team(collision_object_type)` (returns A/B/NONE) so `PaintTile::on_collision` and `Player::on_collision` stop deriving team from the enum by hand. Better still: put `player_team` and a category tag on the object itself rather than cross-multiplying class × team into a 23-value enum.

findings.title: Colour.h maintains the same 149 colour names as three parallel hand-written tables (~450 lines)
findings.detail:
The one list of HTML colour names is written out three times:

1. `colour_consts::html` (Colour.h:8-158): 149 `const std::string NAME = "rrggbb";`
2. `colour_consts` (Colour.h:160-308): 149 `const MattMath::Colour NAME = { html::NAME };`
3. `colour_consts::colour_from_name` (Colour.h:315-352 and preceding): a 149-branch `if (name == "NAME") return colour_consts::NAME;` chain, linear-scanned on every JSON colour lookup in `LevelObjectBuilder`.

Adding or renaming a colour means three coordinated edits, and a typo in table 3 silently falls through to `return colour_consts::WHITE;`. These are also namespace-scope non-inline `const std::string`/`const Colour` objects in a header included nearly everywhere — ~300 dynamically-initialised objects per translation unit.
findings.suggestion: Write the list once as an X-macro or a `constexpr std::array<std::pair<std::string_view, uint32_t>, N>` and generate the named constants plus the lookup from it. Make the lookup a `std::unordered_map`/binary search over the sorted table instead of a 149-branch chain, and mark the constants `constexpr`/`inline`.

findings.title: Five parallel conversion ladders over the same four-entry resolution table
findings.detail:
The set {1280x720, 1920x1080, 2560x1440, 3840x2160} is written out five separate times in 130 lines:

- `convert_resolution_to_ivec` (:47-63) — switch returning `{1280,720}` etc.
- `convert_resolution_to_string` (:76-92) — switch returning `"1280x720"` etc.
- `convert_string_to_resolution` (:94-121) — 4-branch if-chain
- `convert_vec_to_resolution` (:123-150) — 4-branch if-chain
- `convert_ivec_to_resolution` (:152-175) — 4-branch if-chain that *re-hardcodes the literals a second time* (`if (vec.x == 1280 && vec.y == 720)`), so the numbers now live in two places and can drift.

Adding a resolution requires five edits plus an enum entry.
findings.suggestion: Declare one `static constexpr struct { screen_resolution e; int w, h; const char* name; } RESOLUTIONS[]` and implement all five functions as linear scans over it (the string form can be built with the width/height rather than stored). ~130 lines collapse to ~30, and a new resolution becomes one table row.

findings.title: The convex-polygon intersection algorithm is hand-copied four times, and 42 forwarding overloads implement an N x N dispatch matrix
findings.detail:
Two overlapping duplications in one file:

(a) The identical "AABB reject -> A contains any vertex of B -> B contains any vertex of A -> any edge pair intersects" algorithm is written out four times with only the vertex accessors changed:
- `rectangle_triangle_intersect` (:193-227)
- `rectangle_rotated_rectangle_intersect` (:260-297)
- `triangle_rectangle_rotated_intersect` (:453-487)
- `rectangles_rotated_intersect` (:619-660)
~150 lines. A further three functions (`rectangle_quad_intersect` :231-244, `triangle_quad_intersect` :409-423, `quad_rectangle_rotated_intersect` :545-560) are the same "split quad into triangles, loop" reduction copied three times.

(b) `MattMath.cpp` contains 42 `X::intersects(const Y&)` member definitions (RectangleF :888-918, Circle :3364-3390, Triangle :3549-3581, Quad :3988-4020, Segment :4054-4060, RectangleRotated :4237-4263), essentially all 3-line forwarders to the free function with the argument order flipped — e.g. `bool Triangle::intersects(const RectangleF& other) const { return rectangle_triangle_intersect(other, *this); }`. `MattMath.h` declares 48 `bool intersects(` overloads. On top of that sits `Shape::intersects` (:119-136), a `dynamic_cast`-per-branch dispatcher.

The pairwise matrix is what forces every new shape (RectangleRotated was added recently) to add ~7 new free functions plus ~7 overloads on every existing shape.
findings.suggestion: (a) Write one `bool convex_polygons_intersect(const Point2F* a, size_t na, const Point2F* b, size_t nb)` (or a proper SAT implementation) and have every polygon-vs-polygon case call it after an AABB reject; the quad cases become `for (tri : quad.get_triangles())` over that one function. (b) Give `Shape` a virtual `get_vertices()`/`get_edges()` and dispatch generically, or keep an explicit `shape_type x shape_type` function-pointer table, instead of an O(N^2) hand-written overload matrix.

findings.title: TextureObject and AnimationObject duplicate the same five draw overloads
findings.suggestion: Move the camera-to-view conversion overloads into `SpriteSheetObject` as non-virtual, expressed in terms of two pure-virtual primitives `draw_primitive(SpriteBatch*, const RectangleI&)` and `draw_primitive(SpriteBatch*, const Vector2F&, float)`. `TextureObject` and `AnimationObject` then implement one function each instead of five.

findings.title: WeaponRoller re-implements Weapon::draw and update_movement_and_rotation instead of overriding a small hook
findings.detail:
`WeaponRoller::draw` (WeaponRoller.cpp:59-115, 57 lines) is a verbatim copy of `Weapon::draw` (Weapon.cpp:35-82, 48 lines) — same `get_draw_pos`/`RectangleF`, same `calculate_sprite_origin(..., LEFT_CENTER)`, same 12-line `SpriteEffects` flip ladder, same debug-nozzle block — with exactly one addition, lines 90-97:

```cpp
if (this->_shooting_this_update) DrawObject::set_colour(this->get_team_colour());
else                             DrawObject::set_colour(colour_consts::WHITE);
```

Similarly `WeaponRoller::update_movement_and_rotation` (:29-57) copies `Weapon::update_movement_and_rotation` (Weapon.cpp:274-306); only the two `set_rotation` values differ (`PI/4` / `3PI/4` vs `0` / `PI`) plus one `set_gun_player_aligned(true)`.

Separately, `Weapon::calculate_sprite_origin` (Weapon.cpp:88-101) is a byte-for-byte duplicate of `Drawer::calculate_sprite_origin` (Drawer.cpp:55-67), which already exists as a shared helper.
findings.suggestion: Keep one `Weapon::draw` and add a `virtual Colour get_tint_colour() const` hook that the roller overrides; add `virtual float get_aim_rotation(bool facing_right) const` for the rotation. Delete `Weapon::calculate_sprite_origin` and use `Drawer::calculate_sprite_origin` (or promote it to a free function in a `sprite_tools` header, since neither class needs to be a base for it).

findings.title: RelativeVelocityWeapon duplicates Weapon::shoot and Weapon::update_and_get_projectiles wholesale
findings.detail: `RelativeVelocityWeapon::shoot` (Weapon.cpp:551-572) repeats the whole 11-argument `build_projectiles` call from `Weapon::shoot` (Weapon.cpp:311-326); the only difference is which `calculate_projectile_launch_velocity` overload computes the velocity. `RelativeVelocityWeapon::update_and_get_projectiles` (Weapon.cpp:574-595) repeats `Weapon::update_and_get_projectiles` (Weapon.cpp:168-186) verbatim apart from passing `player_velocity` into `shoot`. ~45 duplicated lines — and because the two `shoot`s have different signatures they do not override each other, so the base overload is silently hidden rather than replaced.
findings.suggestion: Make `update_and_get_projectiles` non-virtual on `Weapon` and give it one virtual extension point: `virtual Vector2F calculate_launch_velocity(const Vector2F& dir, const Vector2F& player_velocity) const`. `RelativeVelocityWeapon` then overrides that one function and both duplicated bodies disappear.

findings.title: Five Weapon subclasses are pure data forwarding; the SoundEffectInstance details struct triples the same 8-string table
findings.detail:
`WeaponSprayer.cpp:8-27`, `WeaponMister.cpp:8-27` and `WeaponBucket.cpp:8-27` are byte-identical 20-line ctors apart from the `DETAILS_*` / `DETAILS_RELATIVE_*` pair they forward; `WeaponSniper.cpp:9-27` and `WeaponRoller.cpp:9-27` are the same minus the relative details. Their headers (WeaponSprayer.h, WeaponMister.h, WeaponBucket.h, WeaponSniper.h, WeaponRoller.h) are identical 12-line ctor declarations with the class name swapped. `WeaponSniper::handle_shoot_sound` (WeaponSniper.cpp:28-35) and `WeaponBucket::handle_shoot_sound` (WeaponBucket.cpp:28-35) are byte-identical 7-line bodies.

Related data duplication: `SoundEffectInstanceWeaponDetails` (WeaponDetails.h:21-33) declares eight separately-named string fields `shoot_sound_name_a0..a3, b0..b3`, requiring the 36-line nested switch `get_sound_name` (WeaponDetails.cpp:55-91) to index them; `weapon_consts.h` then writes the same `{weapon}_{team}{index}` table out three times as literals (`SPRAYER_SOUND_DETAILS` :58-67, `ROLLER_SOUND_DETAILS` :102-111, `MISTER_SOUND_DETAILS` :136-145).
findings.suggestion: Delete all ten Weapon* files and construct weapons directly from a `wep_type -> {WeaponDetails, RelativeWeaponDetails*, sound-instance prefix}` table in `WeaponBuilder`. Where `handle_shoot_sound` genuinely differs (one-shot vs looped), make it a `bool looping_shoot_sound` flag in `WeaponDetails` rather than a subclass. Replace the eight named strings with `std::array<std::string, 8>` indexed by `team * 4 + index` — `get_sound_name` becomes one line — or drop the table entirely and build the name as `prefix + (team == A ? "_a" : "_b") + std::to_string(index)`, since the strings are already mechanical.

findings.title: Two divergent projectile-damage tables; the ProjectileDetails one is dead code
findings.detail:
Damage per projectile is specified twice, with different values:

- `player_consts.h:65-69`: `SPRAY_DAMAGE = 0.01f; JET_DAMAGE = 0.334f; ROLLING_DAMAGE = 0.015f; BALL_DAMAGE = 0.201f; MIST_DAMAGE = 0.01f;`
- `projectile_consts.h:20,33,54,67,80,101`: `player_damage` per `ProjectileDetails` = `0.0, -0.1, -0.5, -1000.0, -0.05, -0.1` (note the sign flip and the wildly different magnitudes).

`Projectile::get_player_damage()` (Projectile.h:51, Projectile.cpp:295-298) exists to read the second table — a repo-wide grep shows it is called from nowhere. Instead `Player::on_projectile_collision` (Player.cpp:645-690) hand-writes a 5-branch `if/else` over `collision_object_type` to pick a `player_consts` constant, with the same `//this->_health_regen_timer = 0.0f;` comment copy-pasted into all five branches. So the authoritative damage number depends on which table you happen to read, and (per the ProjectileMist finding) mist actually takes the SPRAY branch.
findings.suggestion: Delete the `*_DAMAGE` constants from `player_consts.h` and replace the whole 5-branch ladder with `this->_health -= projectile->get_player_damage();` — after `dynamic_cast`/interface-widening the collidee to `Projectile`, or by putting `get_player_damage()` on `ICollisionGameObject` with a 0 default. Fix the sign convention in `ProjectileDetails::player_damage` while doing it.

findings.title: draw_ammo and draw_health are the same 47-line function twice
findings.detail:
`InterfaceGameplay::draw_ammo` (:49-96) and `InterfaceGameplay::draw_health` (:97-143) are line-for-line identical — same `TOP_RIGHT_BOX_SIZE` computation, same `RectangleI` construction with four `static_cast<int>`, same `EMPTY_BOX_FRAME` draw, same border/fill maths, same redundant second `get_sprite_sheet(SPRITE_SHEET)` lookup — differing only in the fill fraction (`fill_size.x *= ammo;` vs `*= health;`) and the fill colour (`team_colour` vs `HEALTH_COLOUR`). ~47 duplicated lines.

`draw_timer` (:144-173) and `draw_respawn_timer` (:175-199) likewise duplicate the "DrawString at pos+shadow_offset in shadow colour, then DrawString at pos" pattern, which `TextDropShadow::draw` (TextDropShadow.cpp:24-44) already implements.
findings.suggestion: Collapse to one `draw_bar(SpriteBatch*, const Vector2F& resolution, const Vector2F& position, float fraction, const Colour& fill_colour) const` and call it twice. Route the two timer draws through the existing `TextDropShadow`/`Text` objects instead of calling `SpriteFont::DrawString` twice by hand.

findings.title: PlayerInput and MenuInput are the same class written twice; both hardcode the pad count four times each
findings.detail: `PlayerInput::update_and_get_player_inputs` (PlayerInput.cpp:119-137) and `MenuInput::update_and_get_menu_inputs` (MenuInput.cpp:131-149) are structurally identical 19-line functions — poll 4 pads into a `Raw*[4]`, for each connected pad run `calculate_*_input(current[i], _prev_inputs[i])`, push, then `_prev_inputs[i] = current[i]`. The two constructors (PlayerInput.cpp:8-15, MenuInput.cpp:7-14) are also the same loop. Both files hardcode the literal `4` four times rather than using `std::size(_prev_inputs)` or a named constant, and both classes carry their own `GamePad* _gamepad` and `_prev_inputs[4]`.
findings.suggestion: Extract `template <class Raw, class Processed> class GamepadPoller` holding `GamePad*`, `std::array<Raw, MAX_PADS> _prev`, and one `poll(F&& process)` that does the loop; `PlayerInput` and `MenuInput` then reduce to their `get_raw_input` and `calculate_*_input` functions. Replace the four literal `4`s per file with one `constexpr int MAX_PADS`.

findings.title: JSON rectangle-parsing block duplicated verbatim; ProjectileBuilder repeats the same make_unique 9 times
findings.detail:
Two builder duplications:

(a) `LevelObjectBuilder::build_collision_object` contains the same 20-line `rectangle` / `rectangle_tlbr` parsing block twice, byte-identical including the `throw std::exception("Invalid rectangle type")` fallthrough: lines 120-139 (Structure branch) and 163-182 (StructurePaintable branch). The surrounding per-type blocks also repeat `json["sheet_name"].GetString(), json["frame_name"].GetString(), ..., colour_consts::colour_from_name(json["colour"].GetString())` four times (:141-148, :215-225, :252-259, and `build_non_collision_object` :271-279). `build_collision_objects` (:285-296) and `build_non_collision_objects` (:298-307) are the same loop twice.

(b) `ProjectileBuilder::build_projectiles` (ProjectileBuilder.cpp:23-113) has four `case` blocks (SPRAY/JET/ROLLING/BALL) that are identical 16-line `vector + push_back(make_unique<ProjectileX>(RectangleF(position, DETAILS_X.col_rect_size), velocity, team, player_num, team_colour, dt, resource_manager, rotation, origin, effects, layer_depth)); return` bodies. `build_mist_projectiles` (:116-201) then repeats the same 14-line `push_back` five more times, differing only in the rotation applied to the velocity (`0`, `+PI/12`, `-PI/12`, `+PI/6`, `-PI/6`). ~200 duplicated lines across the two functions.

Note also line 145 and 219 pass `&rectangle` — the address of a function-local — into the object constructors.
findings.suggestion: (a) Extract `static RectangleF parse_rectangle(const rapidjson::Value&)` and a `SpriteSpec parse_sprite(const rapidjson::Value&)` for the sheet/frame/colour triple; make `build_collision_objects`/`build_non_collision_objects` one template. (b) In `ProjectileBuilder`, once the Projectile family is collapsed (see that finding) the whole switch becomes one `make_unique<Projectile>(details_for(type), ...)`; the mist spread becomes `for (float a : {0.0f, PI/12, -PI/12, PI/6, -PI/6})`.

findings.title: Scene-drawing loops exist in three copies, one of which is 88 lines of commented-out code
findings.detail:
`Level` draws the same object lists three times:

- `Level::draw_player_view_level` (:491-589) — three `for (object : *this->_X) if (object->is_visible_in_viewport(camera_view)) object->draw(sprite_batch, camera);` loops over `_non_collision_objects`, `_collision_objects`, `_player_objects`.
- `Level::draw_zoom_out_level_component` (:609-650) — the same three loops with the visibility test dropped.
- `Level.cpp:402-489` — an 88-line commented-out earlier `draw_active_level` containing a third copy of the same three loops plus the interface/debug/countdown draw sequence. It is stale (it calls `object->draw(camera)` with a signature that no longer exists) and is the kind of dead duplicate that makes the live code hard to trust.

Separately, the D3D command-list boilerplate `if (ctx->GetType() != D3D11_DEVICE_CONTEXT_DEFERRED) throw ...` + `FinishCommandList` + `if (FAILED(hr)) throw ...` is copy-pasted into three functions across two files: MenuPage.cpp:156-159 & 179-183, Level.cpp:498-501 & 583-588, Level.cpp:614-617 & 646-650. `MenuPage::draw_mobjects_in_viewports` (MenuPage.cpp:186-226) and `Level::draw_active_level` (Level.cpp:375-399) are also the same partition-then-thread-pool-then-wait dance twice.
findings.suggestion: Extract `draw_objects(SpriteBatch*, const Camera&, const RectangleF* cull_view)` taking the cull rect as optional, and call it three times from each draw path. Delete the commented-out block at :402-489 (git has it). Extract the deferred-context/FinishCommandList boilerplate into one RAII `DeferredRecording` helper in an engine-level header that both `Level` and `MenuPage` use, and extract the partition+dispatch+wait sequence into one `ThreadPool::parallel_for(count, fn)`.

findings.title: Six StructureRamp files are 100% commented out but still compiled and still listed in the vcxproj
findings.detail:
`StructureRamp.cpp` (27 lines), `StructureRamp.h` (23), `StructureRampLeft.cpp` (20), `StructureRampLeft.h` (21), `StructureRampRight.cpp` (20), `StructureRampRight.h` (21) contain nothing but `#include "pch.h"` followed by the entire class commented out with `//`. They are still in `ArtAttack.vcxproj`, so three empty translation units are compiled every build. The live ramp code is elsewhere: `LevelObjectBuilder.cpp:227-259` builds ramps as a plain `Structure` with a `TriangleRightAxisAligned` shape and a `STRUCTURE_RAMP_LEFT/RIGHT` enum tag, and `StructureRampLeft`/`Right` were themselves already duplicate-by-copy — identical ctors differing only in which enum they pass to `StructureRamp`.

This matters for the reusable-engine goal: a fresh reader has to work out which of the two ramp representations is real.
findings.suggestion: Delete all six files and their `<ClCompile>`/`<ClInclude>` entries from ArtAttack.vcxproj. If the class is wanted later, git history has it. If ramps do become first-class, the Left/Right split should be one class with a `bool` or an axis enum, not two subclasses that differ by one constructor argument.

findings.title: Team A / Team B accessor pairs duplicated across LevelEndInfo, TeamColour and ResultsMenu
findings.detail:
The two-team model is hardcoded as method pairs instead of a `player_team` parameter:

- `LevelEndInfo::team_a_ratio` / `team_b_ratio` (:18-33) — identical bodies, one character different.
- `team_a_percentage` / `team_b_percentage` (:34-41).
- `team_a_percentage_string` / `team_b_percentage_string` (:42-61) — 10-line bodies duplicated verbatim (the `find('.')` / `substr` truncation).
- `ResultsMenuInitial::update_team_a_fill` / `update_team_b_fill` (ResultsMenu.cpp:224-249) — same 10-line body; the B version just adds one reposition call.
- `TeamColour::get_team_colour(player_team)` (TeamColour.cpp:140-151) and `TeamColourTools::get_team_colour(TeamColour, player_team)` (TeamColour.cpp:185-197) are two implementations of the same switch that disagree on error handling (`throw` vs silently returning team A).

~70 duplicated lines. This is also the engine-vs-game boundary problem in miniature: two teams are baked into the shape of the API (and into `IPaintableGameObject`'s `PaintTotal{team_a, team_b}`), so a third team would mean editing every one of these pairs.
findings.suggestion: Parameterise on `player_team`: `float ratio(player_team) const`, `float percentage(player_team) const`, `std::string percentage_string(player_team) const`, and store areas as an array indexed by team rather than two named floats. Delete one of the two `get_team_colour` implementations. Doing this now is what makes a third team (or a free-for-all mode) a data change rather than a refactor.

findings.title: No <LanguageStandard> anywhere: the whole engine is stuck on /std:c++14
findings.detail: None of the four ItemDefinitionGroup/ClCompile blocks (lines 87-98, 109-119, 130-143, 156-169) sets <LanguageStandard>, and neither does MattMathTests.vcxproj. MSVC's vcxproj default is /std:c++14, so despite the v145 toolset the codebase cannot use anything from C++17/20. This is confirmed by absence, not just by the project file: grepping all 197 first-party sources for std::optional, std::string_view, if constexpr, std::clamp, std::scoped_lock, structured bindings, and inline variables returns zero hits. It is the root enabler of several other findings here - notably that ~780 namespace-scope `const std::string`/`const Colour` objects in headers cannot be `inline constexpr`, that `std::string_view` cannot replace the stringly-typed resource keys, and that `[[nodiscard]]` is unavailable on the ~344 const getters. /Zc:__cplusplus is already passed (lines 97, 118, 142, 167), so __cplusplus reports 201402L honestly and nothing is masking the problem.
findings.suggestion: Add <LanguageStandard>stdcpp20</LanguageStandard> (and <LanguageStandard_C>stdc17</LanguageStandard_C>) to a shared .props sheet imported by both projects. Nothing in the codebase depends on C++14 semantics; the only C++17-ish construct in the tree today is std::size() in the vendor-supplied DeviceResources.cpp, which already compiles as an MSVC extension.

findings.title: The 'engine' is ConfigurationType=Application, so it can never be linked by anything - including its own tests
findings.detail: All four configurations declare <ConfigurationType>Application</ConfigurationType>. The project therefore emits no .lib, and there is no second project separating engine from game. The consequence is visible in the test project: MattMathTests/MattMathTests.vcxproj:173 declares a ProjectReference to ArtAttack.vcxproj, but because there is no library to link, MattMathTests/MathTests.cpp:5-6 does `#include "..\ArtAttack\MattMath.cpp"` and `#include "..\ArtAttack\EricsonMath.cpp"`, and MattMathTests/CollisionToolsTests.cpp:3 does `#include "..\ArtAttack\CollisionTools.cpp"`. The ProjectReference's only effect is to force a full game-EXE build before the tests run. Only 3 of the 81 translation units are reachable by tests at all, and the stated goal (a reusable 2D engine) is structurally impossible: there is nothing a second game could consume.
findings.suggestion: Split into three projects sharing one .props sheet: ArtAttackEngine (StaticLibrary - DeviceResources, StepTimer, MattMath, CollisionTools, ThreadPool, Partitioner, ResourceManager, SpriteSheet, State/StateContext, Drawer, ViewportManager), ArtAttackGame (Application - Level, Player, Weapon*, Projectile*, Menu*, TeamColour, collision_object_type), and Tests linking the engine lib. Delete the #include-a-.cpp hack once the lib exists.

findings.title: Unit tests compile MattMath.cpp with /fp:precise while the game compiles it with /fp:fast - tests validate different arithmetic than ships
findings.detail: ArtAttack.vcxproj sets <FloatingPointModel>Fast</FloatingPointModel> in all four configs (lines 94, 116, 139, 165). MattMathTests.vcxproj sets no FloatingPointModel at all in any of its four ItemDefinitionGroups, so it compiles at the default /fp:precise. Because the tests textually include the implementation (MathTests.cpp:5 `#include "..\ArtAttack\MattMath.cpp"`, CollisionToolsTests.cpp:3 `#include "..\ArtAttack\CollisionTools.cpp"`), the exact same source is compiled twice under different floating-point contraction, reassociation and NaN/denormal rules. The tests assert with epsilons as tight as 1e-6 (MathTests.cpp:14 `constexpr float EPSILON_F = 0.000001f;`, CollisionToolsTests.cpp:10). A green test suite therefore does not tell you the shipping build behaves the same way - and CollisionTools' bisection push-out (BRACKET_ITERATIONS=40) is precisely the kind of iterative float code where /fp:fast reassociation changes results. The same drift applies to /arch:SSE2, which ArtAttack sets on Win32 (lines 95, 140) and the test project never sets.
findings.suggestion: Move FloatingPointModel, EnableEnhancedInstructionSet, ConformanceMode, WarningLevel and LanguageStandard into a single shared Common.props imported by both .vcxproj files, so the tests cannot drift from the build under test. Better still, link a real engine .lib so there is only one compilation of MattMath.cpp in existence.

findings.title: /W4 with no TreatWarningAsError, and the test project silently compiles at /W3 with -permissive- off
findings.detail: ArtAttack sets <WarningLevel>Level4</WarningLevel> and <ConformanceMode>true</ConformanceMode> in all four configs, but <TreatWarningAsError> appears nowhere in either project file (grep returns 0). /W4 is therefore purely advisory and warnings accumulate unnoticed - the recon sweep already identified live C4018 signed/unsigned comparisons at ArtAttack/MainMenu.cpp:50, ArtAttack/Level.cpp:386, ArtAttack/EndMenu.cpp:32, ArtAttack/MenuPage.cpp:140 and ArtAttack/ResultsMenu.cpp:266. Meanwhile MattMathTests.vcxproj:98,113,130,149 uses <WarningLevel>Level3</WarningLevel> and sets no <ConformanceMode> at all, so test code - which textually includes engine source - is checked under strictly weaker rules than the engine, and non-conforming constructs can pass the tests and fail the game build. There is also no <MultiProcessorCompilation> in either project, so all 81 TUs build serially.
findings.suggestion: Add <TreatWarningAsError>true</TreatWarningAsError>, <MultiProcessorCompilation>true</MultiProcessorCompilation>, ConformanceMode and WarningLevel Level4 to a shared .props. Fix the existing warnings first (they are a small, bounded list), then turn the switch on so the count can only go down.

findings.title: PCH includes 13 DirectXTK headers that are never used, and omits <string>/<vector>/<map> which almost everything uses
findings.detail: pch.h is force-included into all 81 TUs. Of its 19 DirectXTK includes (lines 59-77), grepping the entire first-party tree for the corresponding APIs finds zero uses of: BufferHelpers.h (line 59, no CreateStaticBuffer), DirectXHelpers.h (62, no SetDebugObjectName/MapGuard), Effects.h (63, no BasicEffect/IEffect/EffectFactory), GeometricPrimitive.h (65), GraphicsMemory.h (66), Keyboard.h (67), Model.h (68), Mouse.h (69), PostProcess.h (70), PrimitiveBatch.h (71), ScreenGrab.h (72, no SaveDDSTextureToFile), VertexTypes.h (76), WICTextureLoader.h (77, no CreateWICTextureFromFile). Model.h and Effects.h are the two heaviest headers in DirectXTK. Only CommonStates.h, DDSTextureLoader.h, GamePad.h, SimpleMath.h, SpriteBatch.h and SpriteFont.h earn their place. Conversely the PCH's STL section (lines 42-52) omits <string>, <vector> and <map> even though 34 of 81 .cpp files use std::string, 28 use std::vector, and only 5 headers bother to include <string> explicitly - so those are being pulled in accidentally through DirectXTK's own includes.
findings.suggestion: Delete the 13 unused DirectXTK includes and add <string>, <vector>, <map>, <functional>. Then, since the PCH is the only thing holding the build together (see the self-containment finding), keep it as a build accelerator rather than a dependency-injection mechanism.

findings.title: 40 headers are not self-contained: they name DirectX/Win32 types with no include, and compile only because /Yu force-injects pch.h
findings.detail: IGameObject.h includes only "MattMath.h" yet its pure-virtual interface is declared as `virtual void draw(DirectX::SpriteBatch* sprite_batch, const MattMath::Camera& camera) = 0;` (line 11). Nothing in its include closure declares DirectX::SpriteBatch - it resolves purely because MSVC's /Yu"pch.h" has already injected SpriteBatch.h into every TU. I ran the closure check across all 105 headers: 39 first-party headers (plus vendor DeviceResources.h) name a symbol whose header they do not include. Representative sites: Player.h, Projectile.h, Structure.h, StructurePaintable.h, PaintTile.h, TextureObject.h, TextObject.h, TextDropShadow.h, Visual.h, Mh.h, AnimatedSprite.h, AnimationObject.h, SpriteSheet.h, SpriteSheetObject.h, DrawObject.h, MenuPage.h, ViewportManager.h, Weapon.h + all 5 Weapon*.h + all 5 Projectile*.h (DirectX::SpriteBatch / SpriteEffects); GameData.h and Game.h (CommonStates, GamePad, HWND, SpriteBatch); ResourceManager.h (SpriteFont, Microsoft::WRL); MenuInput.h and PlayerInput.h (GamePad). For a project whose goal is a reusable engine this is fatal: a consumer cannot `#include "Player.h"` without first reproducing ArtAttack's exact pch.h.
findings.suggestion: Make every header compile standalone. Cheapest mechanical fix: add the missing includes (or, for pointer-only uses like `DirectX::SpriteBatch*`, forward-declare `namespace DirectX { class SpriteBatch; }` in one small fwd.h). Then add a build step or a Debug-only .cpp that includes each header first-and-alone to keep the property from regressing.

findings.title: rapidjson/document.h is parsed by 60 of 81 TUs because a JSON Document is stored by value in a header
findings.detail: LevelLoadedInfo.h:5 includes "rapidjson/document.h" and line 34 stores `rapidjson::Document _json_doc;` as a by-value member, so the include is mandatory there. ResourceManager.h:7 then includes LevelLoadedInfo.h even though it only ever handles the type behind indirection - `std::map<level_stage, std::unique_ptr<LevelLoadedInfo>> _level_infos;` (line 51) and `const LevelLoadedInfo* get_level_info(level_stage) const;` (line 33), both of which a forward declaration satisfies. ResourceManager.h is reached by 52 of 81 TUs, and Save.h:7 (`#include <rapidjson/document.h>`) adds more. Net: I measured 60 of 81 translation units transitively parsing rapidjson/document.h - a ~2,700-line header that itself drags in reader.h, allocators.h, encodings.h and internal/*. Roughly three quarters of the build pays for the JSON parser to load two level files. Save.h is worse: it includes rapidjson/document.h but contains no rapidjson type at all (verified - the only occurrence in Save.h is the #include itself); it is used solely by Save.cpp.
findings.suggestion: Give LevelLoadedInfo a pimpl (or store the parsed data in plain structs and drop the Document entirely - the level is parsed once at load). Forward-declare LevelLoadedInfo in ResourceManager.h and move the include into ResourceManager.cpp. Delete Save.h:7 outright and put the include in Save.cpp where it is actually used. Also note the inconsistency: Save.h uses <rapidjson/document.h> while LevelBuilder.h:11, LevelLoadedInfo.h:5 and LevelObjectBuilder.h:6 use "rapidjson/document.h".

findings.title: Colour.h duplicates 302 dynamically-initialised const objects and a 152-line function into each of 58 TUs
findings.detail: Colour.h declares 149 `const std::string` at namespace scope (lines 10-157) and 153 `const MattMath::Colour` constructed from those strings (lines 160-307), then a `static MattMath::Colour colour_from_name(const std::string& name)` (lines 315-466) that is a 150-branch chain of `if (name == "ALICE_BLUE") return ...`. Namespace-scope `const` gives internal linkage in C++, and `static` on the function does too, so every including TU gets its own private copy: 149 std::string constructions + 153 Colour constructions running before main() and 302 destructor registrations at exit, plus a full codegen of the 152-line function. I measured Colour.h reaching 58 of 81 TUs, so that is roughly 17,500 duplicated dynamically-initialised objects and 58 copies of the lookup function in the binary. The pattern is repeated across the codebase - I counted ~780 namespace-scope const non-literal objects in 55 headers, concentrated in Colour.h (301), MainMenu.h (53), Weapon.h (28), ResultsMenu.h (25), InterfaceGameplay.h (24), PauseMenu.h (22), player_consts.h (22), Mh.h (21), EndMenu.h (20), Level.h:33-49 and directory_consts.h:9-13. Note directory_consts.h spells it `const static std::string` while Colour.h spells it `const std::string` - the same thing, written two ways.
findings.suggestion: With C++17 (see the LanguageStandard finding) these become `inline constexpr std::string_view` for the hex literals and `inline constexpr Colour` for the colours - one object, external linkage, zero dynamic init. colour_from_name should move to Colour.cpp as a single non-inline function backed by a static sorted table or a constexpr map, not 150 string compares. The string-keyed colour lookup is itself a smell worth removing.

findings.title: GameData.h drags in 8 concrete headers for 13 members that are all raw pointers
findings.detail: GameData.h:4-11 includes ResolutionManager.h, Save.h, ResourceLoader.h, ResourceManager.h, DeviceResources.h, ViewportManager.h, ThreadPool.h and Partitioner.h. Every one of its 13 data members (lines 49-61) is a pointer - `Save* _save`, `ResolutionManager* _resolution_manager`, `HWND _window`, `float* _dt`, `ResourceLoader*`, `ResourceManager*`, `DirectX::GamePad*`, `DX::DeviceResources*`, `ViewportManager*`, `DirectX::CommonStates*`, `std::vector<DirectX::SpriteBatch*>*`, `ThreadPool*`, `const Partitioner*` - and every accessor returns or takes a pointer. Not one of these includes is required by the header; all eight could be forward declarations. Because ResourceManager.h is in that list, GameData.h transitively pulls in rapidjson/document.h, DirectXTK's <Audio.h>, and <iostream> (via Save.h:4). This is the service-locator hub of the whole program, so it lands in Game.h, GameStates.h, LevelBuilder.h, Level.h, Weapon.h and Player.h.
findings.suggestion: Replace all 8 includes with forward declarations (`class Save; class ResourceManager; namespace DX { class DeviceResources; } namespace DirectX { class GamePad; class CommonStates; class SpriteBatch; }`) plus <vector> and <windows.h> for HWND. Longer term the pointer-bag itself should be replaced by explicit constructor dependencies, but the include cleanup is a zero-risk first step.

findings.title: The entire codebase contains exactly one forward declaration - the root cause of the header coupling
findings.detail: `class StateContext;` at State.h:4 is the only forward declaration in all 105 headers (verified by grep for a leading `class X;` pattern). Everything else includes the full definition, whether it needs it or not. The measurable result: mean transitive header closure per TU is 21 headers; Main.cpp reaches 105 and GameStates.cpp 103; MattMath.h and shape_type.h reach 68 of 81 TUs, SpriteFrame.h/AnimationStrip.h/Colour.h 55-58, SoundBank.h and LevelLoadedInfo.h 53-56, ResourceManager.h 52. Editing SpriteFrame.h - a small value type - rebuilds two thirds of the project. The codebase already proves it knows how (State.h works fine), it just never applies the technique anywhere else.
findings.suggestion: Adopt the rule 'include only what the header's declarations require by value/base; forward-declare everything used only by pointer or reference'. The highest-leverage targets are GameData.h, ResourceManager.h, Level.h (17 includes), Player.h (11), LevelBuilder.h (10) and Weapon.h (9). A single fwd.h for the DirectXTK types used by pointer (SpriteBatch, SpriteFont, GamePad, CommonStates) covers most of the remainder.

findings.title: The math library has a D3D11 type baked into it, forcing d3d11.h into 68 of 81 TUs
findings.detail: MattMath.h:6 includes <d3d11.h>, and the reason is MattMath::Viewport: line 786 `Viewport(const D3D11_VIEWPORT& viewport);`, line 789 `D3D11_VIEWPORT get_d3d_viewport() const;`, line 790 `const D3D11_VIEWPORT* get_d3d_viewport_ptr() const;`, line 799 `Viewport& operator=(const D3D11_VIEWPORT&);`. MattMath.h is the single most-included first-party header (68 of 81 TUs), so one graphics-API-specific struct in an otherwise pure 2D math library taxes the entire build and makes the math module - the one part of the engine that is genuinely reusable and genuinely unit-tested - non-portable. The implementation compounds it: MattMath.cpp:3215 is `return reinterpret_cast<const D3D11_VIEWPORT*>(this);`, i.e. MattMath::Viewport is silently type-punned as a D3D11_VIEWPORT, which is only 'safe' as long as nobody adds a member or changes field order.
findings.suggestion: Move Viewport out of MattMath into the presentation layer (ViewportManager or a new GraphicsTypes.h), or keep a plain `struct Viewport { float x,y,w,h,minz,maxz; }` in MattMath and put the D3D11 conversion in a free function in the D3D layer. Then delete MattMath.h:6 and drop d3d11.h from 68 TUs. Replace the reinterpret_cast with explicit field-by-field conversion regardless.

findings.title: <Audio.h> (XAudio2) is parsed by 56 of 81 TUs via ResourceManager.h
findings.detail: ResourceManager.h:8 does `#include <Audio.h>` - DirectXTK's audio header, which pulls in the XAudio2 redist headers via the USING_XAUDIO2_REDIST define from the NuGet targets. Nothing in ResourceManager.h uses a DirectXTK audio type directly; the sound support goes through `std::map<std::string, std::unique_ptr<SoundBank>> _sound_banks;` (line 53) and SoundBank.h is included separately on line 10. Because ResourceManager.h reaches 52 TUs and Game.h adds more, I measured Audio.h being parsed by 56 of 81 translation units. Combined with the rapidjson finding, the two heaviest third-party headers in the project are both in the include closure of three quarters of the build for no reason.
findings.suggestion: Delete ResourceManager.h:8 and let SoundBank.h own the audio dependency (and forward-declare SoundBank in ResourceManager.h so even that is confined to ResourceManager.cpp).

findings.title: ThreadPool.h includes <iostream> it never uses and leaks raw <windows.h> into every consumer
findings.detail: ThreadPool.h:7 includes <iostream>; ThreadPool.cpp contains no std::cout/cerr/endl (the only console output in the codebase is Save.cpp:47,51,90,93,97). <iostream> is one of the heaviest STL headers and injects a static std::ios_base::Init object into every TU that sees it. Save.h:4 does the same thing - it includes <iostream> and <chrono> for the benefit of Save.cpp, not the header. Between them 17 of 81 TUs parse <iostream> for nothing. Separately, ThreadPool.h:5 includes <windows.h> at header scope so that PTP_WORK/TP_CALLBACK_ENVIRON/PTP_POOL can appear as members (lines 27-30); every consumer of the thread pool therefore inherits the full Win32 macro soup. It only works today because pch.h defines WIN32_LEAN_AND_MEAN/NOMINMAX first - a header this one relies on but does not include.
findings.suggestion: Delete ThreadPool.h:7 and Save.h:4-5 (move <iostream>/<chrono> to the .cpp files). For ThreadPool, pimpl the Win32 handles so the header exposes only `void add_task(std::function<void()>)` and `void wait_for_tasks_to_complete()` - that also makes it swappable for a std::thread or std::jthread implementation, which is what a portable engine wants.

findings.title: Four hand-maintained copies of the compiler settings have visibly drifted apart
findings.detail: Lines 86-180 are four near-identical ItemDefinitionGroup blocks with no shared .props sheet (there is no .props file anywhere in the repo). They have drifted: (a) <EnableEnhancedInstructionSet>StreamingSIMDExtensions2</EnableEnhancedInstructionSet> appears at line 95 (Debug|Win32) and 140 (Release|Win32) but is absent from both x64 blocks; (b) <GuardEHContMetadata>true</GuardEHContMetadata> appears only at line 168 (Release|x64), so three of four configurations lack the hardening; (c) `WIN32` is defined in the x64 preprocessor lists at lines 115 and 164; (d) the identical AdditionalIncludeDirectories, AdditionalDependencies, Manifest DPI and /Zc:__cplusplus settings are each written out four times. The AdditionalDependencies list is also stale boilerplate - comdlg32.lib, advapi32.lib, shell32.lib and oleaut32.lib are not used by anything in this project. The project still declares ToolsVersion="14.0" (line 2) with no <VCProjectVersion>, while MattMathTests.vcxproj:22 declares <VCProjectVersion>17.0</VCProjectVersion>.
findings.suggestion: Create Directory.Build.props or a Common.props at the repo root holding everything the four blocks share (include dirs, warning level, conformance, /Zc:__cplusplus, /Zc:preprocessor, LanguageStandard, FloatingPointModel, MultiProcessorCompilation, TreatWarningAsError), import it from both .vcxproj files, and leave only genuinely per-config settings (Optimization, UseDebugLibraries) in the ItemDefinitionGroups. Drop ToolsVersion="14.0" and set VCProjectVersion to match the test project.

findings.title: All audio assets are gitignored, so a fresh clone cannot run the game
findings.detail: .gitignore lines 366-368 ignore `*.wav`, `*.xwb` and `*.mp3`. I verified with git ls-files: ArtAttack/sounds tracks only `sound list.txt`, `sound_bank_1.json`, `sound_bank_1/XWBTool.exe`, `sound_bank_1/cmd.txt` and `unused/wave_bank_1.json`. The directory on disk confirms it - ArtAttack/sounds/sound_bank_1/ contains XWBTool.exe and cmd.txt and nothing else. The compiled XACT wave bank the SoundBank loader needs is not in the repository. Since player_consts.h:57-64 names DAMAGE_SOUND/DEATH_SOUND/JUMP_SOUND/RESPAWN_SOUND and Level.h:45-49 names COUNTDOWN_SOUND/ZOOM_OUT_SOUND, and the loader throws on missing resources, the project as cloned cannot start a level. This makes the repo unbuildable-to-runnable for anyone but the author, which for a project meant to demonstrate a reusable engine is the single most damaging piece of repo hygiene here.
findings.suggestion: Either commit the .xwb wave bank (add `!ArtAttack/sounds/**/*.xwb` and `!ArtAttack/sounds/**/*.wav` negations), or use Git LFS for audio, or add a documented fetch/build step (there is already a cmd.txt next to XWBTool.exe describing the build). Whichever you choose, add a README that says how to get a clone into a runnable state - there is currently no README or LICENSE in the repo at all.

findings.title: No asset deployment step: the built exe only runs under the VS debugger
findings.detail: directory_consts.h:9-13 uses relative paths `./textures/`, `./levels/`, `./fonts/`, `./save/save_data.json`, `./sounds/`. The vcxproj has no <OutDir> override, no PostBuildEvent, no <Content>/<CopyToOutputDirectory> items, and no asset ItemGroup beyond two <Image> entries (lines 386-389: directx.ico and textures\sprite_sheet_1.dds - one of the six top-level textures, and it is only there for the resource compiler). With the default OutDir the exe lands in $(SolutionDir)Debug\ or $(SolutionDir)x64\Debug\, where none of ./textures, ./levels, ./fonts, ./save or ./sounds exist. The app runs only because Visual Studio's debugger defaults the working directory to $(ProjectDir). Meanwhile the XAudio2 NuGet targets do copy xaudio2_9redist.dll next to the exe, so the output directory is half-populated and looks deployable.
findings.suggestion: Add a <Content Include="levels\**;textures\*.dds;fonts\*.spritefont;sounds\**"> group with <CopyToOutputDirectory>PreserveNewest</CopyToOutputDirectory>, or a PostBuildEvent robocopy. Then verify by running the exe directly from the output folder rather than F5.

findings.title: 105 headers use ad-hoc #ifndef guards with collision-prone global macro names; three vendor headers use #pragma once
findings.detail: Guard style is inconsistent and the names are unsafe for a library meant to be embedded in someone else's build. BorderThickness.h:1-2 uses `#ifndef BORDER_THICKNESS` / `#define BORDER_THICKNESS` - not even suffixed _H, and a plausible identifier for a UI type in a consuming project. Other guards occupy extremely generic global macro names with no project prefix: TEXT_H (Text.h), LEVEL_H, STATE_H, SAVE_H, PLAYER_H, WEAPON_H, STRUCTURE_H, GAME_H, VISUAL_H, COLOUR_H, DIMENSION_H, DIRECTION_H, PROJECTILE_H. Naming is also internally inconsistent - ANIMATEDSPRITE_H vs ANIMATED_SPRITE style is applied at random across ~65 of the 105 headers. PlayerInputData.h uses `PLAYER_INPUT_H` while PlayerInput.h uses `PLAYERINPUT_H`: they do not collide today but are one rename apart from silently eliding a header. Trailing #endif comments have drifted from their guards (LevelLoadedInfo.h defines LEVELLOADEDINFO_H but its #endif comment says LEVEL_LOADED_INFO_H; StateContext.h:2 defines STATECONTEXT_H but its #endif says STATECONTEXTGENERIC_H; IPaintableGameObject.h defines IPAINTABLEGAMEOBJECT_H, #endif says IPAINTABLE_H). Meanwhile the three Microsoft-supplied headers (pch.h, DeviceResources.h, StepTimer.h) all use #pragma once, so the project already mixes both conventions.
findings.suggestion: Switch every first-party header to `#pragma once` (MSVC, clang and gcc all support it, and it is what the vendor files in this same directory already do). That removes 105 global macro names from the preprocessor namespace and makes the drifted #endif comments moot. If you prefer guards for portability reasons, prefix them all with ARTATTACK_ and generate them from the path.

findings.title: Six source files that are 100% commented out are still compiled as part of the build
findings.detail: StructureRamp.h/.cpp, StructureRampLeft.h/.cpp and StructureRampRight.h/.cpp are listed as project items (ClInclude lines 252-254, ClCompile lines 348-350) and are in the filters file (lines 126-128, 211-213). I measured their content: the three headers have 0 non-comment non-blank lines and the three .cpp files have exactly 1 each - `#include "pch.h"`. StructureRamp.h opens with `//#ifndef STRUCTURE_RAMP_H` and every subsequent line is commented. So the build compiles three empty translation units, and the four headers among them are the only first-party headers with no include guard of any kind (because the guard is commented out too). Ramps are actually built as plain `Structure` objects with a TriangleRightAxisAligned shape in LevelObjectBuilder.cpp:144-177, so these files are not a work-in-progress that something depends on - they are abandoned.
findings.suggestion: Delete all six files and their vcxproj/filters entries. Git remembers them. The same applies to the ~840 lines of commented-out code elsewhere (MattMath.cpp ~254 lines, EricsonMath.cpp ~233, MattMath.h:303-352 dead Matrix/Vector templates, Player.cpp:307-335 and 391-420, Level.cpp:331-353, Main.cpp:39+).

findings.title: Two filters cover 6 of 200 project items - all 193 sources sit flat in one directory with no engine/game boundary
findings.detail: The filters file declares exactly two filters, "Common" (lines 4-6) and "Assets" (lines 7-10). "Common" is applied only to the four Microsoft-supplied files (StepTimer.h, DeviceResources.h/.cpp) and "Assets" to directx.ico, sprite_sheet_1.dds and settings.manifest. Every other ClInclude/ClCompile entry - all 105 headers and 81 sources - has no <Filter> element and appears at the project root. On disk it is the same: ArtAttack/ is one flat directory containing DeviceResources.cpp, MattMath.cpp, ThreadPool.cpp, Player.cpp, WeaponSniper.cpp and MainMenu.cpp side by side. There is no physical or logical line anywhere between 'engine' (device/timer/math/collision/threadpool/resources/state/sprite) and 'game' (Splatoon-specific players, weapons, projectiles, teams, menus). Given the stated goal, this is the structural expression of the problem: nobody can tell what they would need to take with them, and nothing stops game concepts leaking into engine types (which they have - see collision_object_type.h enumerating PROJECTILE_SPRAY_TEAM_A inside the core ICollisionGameObject interface, and ResourceManager.h:33 keying a cache on level_stage).
findings.suggestion: Move files into real directories (engine/platform, engine/math, engine/render, engine/resources, engine/core, game/...) and regenerate the filters from the paths. Do this at the same time as splitting the static library - the directory layout is what makes the library split obvious and enforceable.

findings.title: Test project hardcodes a versioned NuGet path, has no packages.config, and its PCH is an empty stub
findings.detail: All four ItemDefinitionGroups put `..\packages\directxtk_desktop_2019.2023.10.31.1\include` on the include path literally. The test project has no packages.config of its own (MattMathTests/ contains only the two test .cpp, pch.h/.cpp and the project files), so nothing restores that package for it - it works purely because ArtAttack/packages.config happens to pin the identical version. Bump DirectXTK and the test project breaks with a missing-header error that points at nothing obvious. Separately, all four configs set <PrecompiledHeader>Use</PrecompiledHeader> with <PrecompiledHeaderFile>pch.h</PrecompiledHeaderFile>, but MattMathTests/pch.h is the untouched wizard stub - guard, a comment saying 'add headers that you want to pre-compile here', and nothing else - so the PCH provides zero benefit while still costing a Create pass. And <ProjectName>UnitTests</ProjectName> (line 27) disagrees with both the directory and the .vcxproj filename, so the solution shows a project name that matches nothing on disk.
findings.suggestion: Add a packages.config to the test project (or migrate both projects to PackageReference so the version lives in one place), replace the hardcoded path with the $(directxtk...) property the NuGet targets define, either populate pch.h or set PrecompiledHeader to NotUsing, and make ProjectName match the directory.

findings.title: A file the program rewrites on every run is tracked in git, so the tree is dirty after each launch
findings.detail: git ls-files ArtAttack/save returns save_data.json and save_data.txt. Save.cpp opens SAVE_FILE_PATH (directory_consts.h:12, "./save/save_data.json") for writing and rewrites it whenever resolution or fullscreen changes, and Main.cpp calls load_save_file() at startup. Running the game therefore modifies a tracked file, so `git status` is dirty after every session and real changes get lost in the noise. save_data.txt appears to be a superseded copy of the same data that nothing reads. Related repo clutter, all verified tracked: 84 of the 103 files under ArtAttack/textures live in a directory literally named "old textures"; ArtAttack/fonts/"unuseed fonts" (sic) holds 20 unused .spritefont files; ArtAttack/levels/unused/ and ArtAttack/sounds/unused/ are tracked; and three third-party tool executables are committed - ArtAttack/textures/texconv.exe, ArtAttack/fonts/MakeSpriteFont.exe, ArtAttack/sounds/sound_bank_1/XWBTool.exe.
findings.suggestion: Ship a save_data.default.json as the tracked template, gitignore the live save, and have Save::load_save_file() copy the default on first run (it already has check_if_save_file_exists()). Delete the 'old textures', 'unuseed fonts', levels/unused and sounds/unused directories and the three committed EXEs - document the tool versions in a README instead. While you are in .gitattributes, note it is the untouched VS template (`* text=auto` with every other rule commented out); add explicit `*.dds binary`, `*.spritefont binary`, `*.xwb binary`, `*.exe binary` so line-ending normalisation can never be attempted on assets.

findings.title: App identity is two renames stale: window titled "Colour Wars", class "ChromaClashWindowClass"
findings.detail: `LPCWSTR g_szAppName = L"Colour Wars";` (Main.cpp:28) is the window caption the user actually sees, and `wcex.lpszClassName = L"ChromaClashWindowClass"` (Main.cpp:123, plus CreateWindowExW calls at :156 and :162 and four commented copies at :167-181) names the registered window class. The project went ColourWars -> ChromaClash -> ArtAttack; both dead names are still shipping. `g_szAppName` also carries Hungarian notation (`sz` = zero-terminated *narrow* string) on an `LPCWSTR`, which is wrong even by Hungarian's own rules, and Hungarian appears literally nowhere else in the 197 first-party files.
findings.suggestion: Hoist a single `constexpr wchar_t APP_NAME[] = L"Art Attack";` and `APP_WINDOW_CLASS[] = L"ArtAttackWindowClass";` into an engine-level header (or, better for a reusable engine, make both parameters the host app passes in). Delete the `g_sz` prefix.

findings.title: Colour.h contains no Colour type - only `namespace colour_consts` - and breaks the file-naming rule it sits next to
findings.detail: `Colour.h` is 469 lines and its only top-level declaration is `namespace colour_consts` (line 6) holding 149 hex strings and ~153 `MattMath::Colour` objects. The `Colour` struct itself lives in `MattMath.h:586-645`. So `#include "Colour.h"` reads as "give me the Colour type" and gives you constants instead. Meanwhile every other constants-only header in the repo is snake_case and named `*_consts.h`: `directory_consts.h`, `player_consts.h`, `weapon_consts.h`, `projectile_consts.h`. `Colour.h` is the sole PascalCase constants file.
findings.suggestion: Rename the file to `colour_consts.h` to match its four siblings and its own namespace. Update the ~20 includes. This also removes the ambiguity that produced the case-mismatched `#include "colour.h"` sites (see separate finding).

findings.title: Three `#include` directives use the wrong case and only compile because of Windows' case-insensitive filesystem
findings.detail: `TeamColour.h:5` is `#include "colour.h"` but the file is `Colour.h`. Same bug at `InterfaceGameplay.h:7` (`#include "colour.h"`) and `Level.cpp:2` (`#include "level.h"` for `Level.h`). These are the only three case-mismatched first-party includes in the tree - I enumerated every `#include "..."` and checked it against the real filename. They resolve today purely because NTFS is case-insensitive; they are hard errors on any case-sensitive filesystem, which matters the moment this "reusable engine" is built in CI on Linux, in WSL, or under a case-sensitive Dev Drive.
findings.suggestion: Fix to `#include "Colour.h"` and `#include "Level.h"` (or to `colour_consts.h` if you take the rename above). Worth adding a CI check that greps includes against `ls` output, since this class of bug is invisible locally.

findings.title: `enum projectile_type` is the codebase's only unscoped enum and dumps SPRAY/JET/ROLLING/MIST/BALL into the global namespace
findings.detail: `enum projectile_type { SPRAY, JET, ROLLING, MIST, BALL };` at Projectile.h:10-16 has no `class`. Every other enum in the repo - all 25 of them (`collision_object_type`, `shape_type`, `wep_type`, `player_team`, `level_state`, `menu_direction`, `diffusion_type`, `add_player_velocity`, ...) - is `enum class`. Because Projectile.h is pulled in transitively by Weapon.h, Player.h and Level.h, the bare identifiers `SPRAY`, `JET`, `ROLLING`, `MIST` and `BALL` are visible in most of the program. `weapon_consts.h:24` and :45 already rely on this (`projectile_type proj_type = SPRAY;`, `SPRAY, //projectile_type`), and `Projectile.h:75` does `projectile_type _type = SPRAY;`.
findings.suggestion: Make it `enum class projectile_type` and qualify the ~15 use sites (`projectile_type::SPRAY`). While you are there, move it into its own `projectile_type.h` to match the existing one-enum-per-snake_case-header convention used by `shape_type.h`, `wep_type.h`, `player_team.h` etc.

findings.title: Boolean accessors split between `get_x()` and `is_x()` with no rule; the worst offender is on a core engine interface
findings.detail:
`virtual bool get_for_deletion() const = 0;` (ICollisionGameObject.h:16) reads as "fetch the for-deletion" rather than a question, and it sits on the interface every collidable object in the engine implements. It is not an isolated slip - the codebase has two competing conventions for bool accessors:
  `get_` form: `ICollisionGameObject.h:16` / `Player.h:97` / `Projectile.h:47` / `PaintTile.h:76` / `Structure.h:33` (`get_for_deletion`), `AnimationStrip.h:16` (`get_looping`), `Mh.h:18` (`get_hidden`), `Save.h:26` (`get_fullscreen`), `Player.h:109-111,115,227` (`get_input_primary_shoot`, `get_input_jump_pressed`, `get_input_jump_held`, `get_showing_debug`, `get_facing_right`), `Weapon.h:73,75,79` (`get_invert_x`, `get_invert_y`, `get_gun_player_aligned`).
  `is_` form: `AnimatedSprite.h:35` / `AnimationObject.h:28` (`is_paused`), `IGameObject.h:13` (`is_visible_in_viewport`), `ICollisionGameObject.h:12` (`is_colliding`), `Player.h:250-251` (`is_on_ground`, `is_on_ramp`), `SoundBank.h:32` (`is_effect_looping`).
So `AnimationStrip::get_looping()` and `SoundBank::is_effect_looping()` ask the same question two ways.
findings.suggestion: One rule: bool accessors read as predicates. `get_for_deletion` -> `is_flagged_for_deletion`, `get_looping` -> `is_looping`, `get_hidden` -> `is_hidden`, `get_fullscreen` -> `is_fullscreen`, `get_facing_right` -> `is_facing_right`, `get_showing_debug` -> `is_showing_debug`, `get_invert_x/y` -> `is_x/y_inverted`, `get_gun_player_aligned` -> `is_gun_player_aligned`, `get_input_jump_pressed` -> `is_jump_pressed`.

findings.title: `_dx` is a 2D vector, producing the nonsense accessors `get_dx_x()` / `set_dx_x()` / `get_dx_magnitude()`
findings.detail: `MattMath::Vector2F _dx` (MovingObject.h:55) is a per-frame displacement vector, but `dx` universally means "change in x" - a scalar. The result is a whole accessor family that reads as gibberish: `get_dx()` returns a Vector2F, `get_dx_x()` (line 34), `get_dx_y()` (35), `set_dx_x(float x)` (38), `alter_dx_x` (42), `get_unit_dx()` (45), `get_dx_magnitude()` (46), `get_dx_angle()` (47). "the x of the change-in-x" and "the magnitude of the change-in-x" are not sentences. The name also leaks into constants - `player_consts.h:24` has `const MattMath::Vector2F STARTING_DX = { 0.0f, 0.0f };`.
findings.suggestion: Rename the member and its 14 accessors to `_displacement` / `get_displacement()` / `get_displacement_x()` / `get_displacement_magnitude()` (or `_frame_delta` if you prefer). `STARTING_DX` -> `STARTING_DISPLACEMENT`. This is a mechanical rename with no behaviour change and it makes MovingObject readable for the first time.

findings.title: `alter_*` mutators name their delta parameter after the field, so call sites read as assignment
findings.detail:
The codebase has an `alter_x(delta)` idiom meaning "add delta to x", but half the declarations name the parameter as if it were the new value:
  Wrong: `Weapon.h:85 void alter_ammo(float ammo);` (adds to ammo), `Weapon.h:82 void alter_shoot_timer(float dt);` and `:88 void alter_ammo_timer(float dt);` (parameter is a delta that happens to usually be dt, so the name hardcodes one caller's argument), `Projectile.h:65 void alter_timer(float time);`, `MovingObject.h:25 alter_velocity(const Vector2F& velocity)`, `:37/:41 alter_dx(const Vector2F& dx)`, `:51 alter_rotation(float rotation)`.
  Right: `Player.h:232 void alter_health(float change);`, `:236 alter_respawn_timer(float change)`, `:240 alter_air_time(float change)`, `:244 alter_score(int change)`.
A reader hitting `alter_ammo(0.007f)` next to `set_ammo(0.007f)` has no way to tell them apart from the signatures.
findings.suggestion: Two changes: (1) rename the verb to something unambiguous - `add_ammo` / `add_to_shoot_timer`, or drop them for `operator+=`-style helpers; (2) name every parameter `delta` or `change`, matching the four Player.h declarations that already get it right. Never name a delta `dt`.

findings.title: `Mh.h` and its `M`-prefixed classes are unguessable; the prefix even yields the word "mobject" in API names
findings.detail: `Mh.h` declares `MObject`, `MContainer`, `MWidget`, `MTexture`, `MText`, `MTextDropShadow` - the entire UI widget system. Nothing in the file, the filename, or any comment says what `M` or `h` stand for. The prefix has already metastasised into method names that read as a real (wrong) word: `MenuPage.h:38 draw_mobject_in_viewports(...)`, `:43 draw_mobjects_in_viewports(std::vector<std::pair<MObject*, ID3D11SamplerState*>>* mobjects)`, `:46 draw_range_of_mobjects_in_viewports(...)`. Compare the rest of the repo, which never abbreviates a type prefix like this (`SpriteSheetObject`, `TextureObject`, `AnimationObject`, `SoundBankObject`). For a codebase whose stated goal is a reusable engine, a public UI layer named `Mh` is a non-starter.
findings.suggestion: Rename file to `MenuWidgets.h` (or split per class) and the types to `MenuObject`, `MenuContainer`, `MenuWidget`, `MenuTexture`, `MenuText`, `MenuTextDropShadow`. Method names become `draw_widget_in_viewports` / `draw_widgets_in_viewports`. If the widgets are meant to be engine-general rather than menu-specific, drop the prefix entirely: `UiObject`, `UiContainer`, `UiWidget`.

findings.title: Cryptic acronym aliases `get_sb()` and `get_sei()` duplicate the spelled-out getters, and both forms are in live use
findings.detail: `SoundBankObject.h:65-66` declares both `SoundBank* get_sound_bank() const;` and `SoundBank* get_sb() const;`. Lines 81-82 do the same for `get_sound_effect_instance()` / `get_sei()`. `SoundBank.h:34-35` repeats the `get_sound_effect_instance` / `get_sei` pair. These are not deprecated leftovers - call-site counts across the .cpp files are `get_sb()` 12 vs `get_sound_bank()` 8, and `get_sei()` 2 vs `get_sound_effect_instance()` 14. So a reader must learn both spellings, and `sei` is an acronym that appears nowhere else in 28k lines.
findings.suggestion: Delete `get_sb()` and `get_sei()`; rewrite their 14 call sites to the full names. If the motivation was line length, that is what a local `auto* bank = get_sound_bank();` is for.

findings.title: `RectangleRotated` half-extent API: ambiguous `hw`, self-contradictory `half_y_width`, and axes typed as `Point2F`
findings.detail:
Three separate naming defects in one struct:
  1. `Vector2F _hw_extents` (line 1117) and `void set_half_extents(const Point2F& hw_extents)` (1083) - `hw` could be half-width, height-width, or hardware. The getter at 1075 says `get_half_extents` while the member says `hw_extents`; pick one word.
  2. `float get_half_y_width() const;` (line 1077) - "the half y width" is a contradiction. Its sibling is `get_half_x_width()` (1076) and there is a `get_half_width(int axis)` (1078).
  3. `Point2F get_x_axis() const;` (1072), `get_y_axis()` (1073), `get_half_extents()` (1075) all return `Point2F` while the backing members are `Vector2F _x_axis` (1115), `_y_axis` (1116), `_hw_extents` (1117). An axis is a direction and a half-extent is a size; neither is a point. This only compiles because `MattMath.h:33` has `typedef Vector2F Point2F`, so the type system cannot catch the mixup.
Also `RectangleF get_rectangle_rotated_to_axis() const;` (1100) - unparseable without reading the body.
findings.suggestion: `_hw_extents` -> `_half_extents` everywhere including parameter names. `get_half_x_width()` -> `get_half_extent_x()`, `get_half_y_width()` -> `get_half_extent_y()`, `get_half_width(int axis)` -> `get_half_extent(int axis)`. Change the return types of `get_x_axis`/`get_y_axis`/`get_half_extents` to `Vector2F`. Rename `get_rectangle_rotated_to_axis` to say what it produces, e.g. `get_axis_aligned_local_rectangle()`.

findings.title: MattMath gives four types two names each via typedefs, and one struct is camelCase in an all-snake_case namespace
findings.detail:
Alias sprawl: `typedef Vector2F Point2F;` (line 33), `typedef MattMath::RectangleF AABB;` (301), `typedef RectangleRotated OBB;` (1136). The consequence is that the same type is spelled differently depending on which file you are in - `EricsonMath.h:113,119-120` takes `const MattMath::AABB&` while `MattMath.h:96` takes `const MattMath::RectangleF&` for the identical type, and `EricsonMath.h:83-99` uses `Point2F` where `MattMath.h:80` uses `Vector2F`. `Point2F` in particular destroys type safety for the whole shape library (see the RectangleRotated finding).
Separately, `struct Viewport` (line 766) declares `float x, y, width, height` in snake_case and then `float minDepth = 0.0f;` / `float maxDepth = 1.0f;` (774-775) in camelCase - the only camelCase data members in first-party code. The camelCase spelling then propagates through `MattMath.cpp:3152-3294` (`minDepth(minDepth)`, `this->maxDepth`, ~20 sites) and the ctor defaults at `MattMath.h:780,783,785`.
findings.suggestion: Delete `Point2F` and use `Vector2F` (or make it a real distinct type, not a typedef, if you want point-vs-vector safety). Keep `AABB`/`OBB` only if you commit to them as *the* names and rename `RectangleF`/`RectangleRotated` away; otherwise delete the aliases and fix EricsonMath's signatures. Rename `minDepth`/`maxDepth` to `min_depth`/`max_depth`.

findings.title: Four overlapping direction/anchor enums, three of them in headers nothing includes
findings.detail:
The repo has four enums covering the same conceptual space:
  - `::direction` (`direction.h:4-15`): TOP_LEFT..BOTTOM_RIGHT, 9 anchor values.
  - `MattMath::direction` (`MattMath.h:12-22`): NONE, UP, DOWN, LEFT, RIGHT, UP_LEFT... - a compass, unqualified-name-identical to the above.
  - `menu_direction` (`MenuInput.h:94-101`): UP/DOWN/LEFT/RIGHT/NONE.
  - `rotation_origin` (`rotation_origin.h:4-10`): CENTER, TOP_LEFT, LEFT_CENTER, NO_ROTATION - anchors again.
I grepped every include and every use site: `direction.h` is included by zero files, and its values are referenced zero times. Same for `dimension.h` (enum `dimension { X, Y }`) and `direction_lock.h` (enum `direction_lock { LOCKED, UNLOCKED }`) - both are orphans with no includers and no uses. So three of the eight snake_case enum headers are dead weight whose names actively collide with live concepts.
findings.suggestion: Delete `direction.h`, `dimension.h`, `direction_lock.h` (and their vcxproj entries). Rename `MattMath::direction` -> `MattMath::cardinal_direction` so it says what it is, and keep `menu_direction` and `rotation_origin` as-is. If a 9-way anchor type is ever needed, call it `anchor_point`, not `direction`.

findings.title: Six files named after classes that do not exist - StructureRamp/Left/Right are 100% commented out but still in the vcxproj
findings.detail: `StructureRamp.h` (23 lines), `StructureRamp.cpp` (26), `StructureRampLeft.h` (21), `StructureRampLeft.cpp` (20), `StructureRampRight.h` (21), `StructureRampRight.cpp` (20). I counted non-comment non-blank lines: 0, 1, 0, 0, 0, 0. There is no `StructureRamp` class anywhere; ramps are actually built as plain `Structure` with a `TriangleRightAxisAligned` shape at `LevelObjectBuilder.cpp:144-177`. All six files are listed in `ArtAttack.vcxproj:252-254` and `:348-350`, so the build compiles six empty translation units and anyone browsing Solution Explorer sees a ramp class hierarchy that is fiction. Note the JSON level format at `LevelObjectBuilder.cpp:144` also keys on `type == "StructureRamp"`, a type name with no corresponding class.
findings.suggestion: Delete all six files and their vcxproj entries. If ramps deserve a class later, add it then. Meanwhile rename the JSON discriminator from `"StructureRamp"` to something honest like `"ramp"`, since the JSON `type` strings elsewhere (`"Structure"`, `"StructurePaintable"`, `"Visual"`) are C++ class names and this one is not.

findings.title: Player has two names for its input setter and a `_primary` member whose getter returns something else entirely
findings.detail:
Two distinct defects in one class:
  1. `std::unique_ptr<Weapon> _primary = nullptr;` (line 142) is the weapon *object*, but `wep_type get_primary() const;` (217) and `void set_primary(wep_type primary);` (218) operate on `_primary_type` (line 158). So `_primary` and `get_primary()` refer to different members of different types. A reader calling `get_primary()` expecting the Weapon gets an enum.
  2. `void set_player_input(const PlayerInputData& input);` is public at line 99 while `void set_input(const PlayerInputData& input);` is private at line 230, and the getter is `get_input()` at line 122. Three names, one concept.
Also in the same header: the ctor parameter is `const MattMath::Viewport& view_port` (line 76, and `Player.cpp:18`) while the member and setter are `_viewport` / `set_viewport` (161, 225) - the same word spelled two ways inside one class.
findings.suggestion: `_primary` -> `_primary_weapon`; `get_primary`/`set_primary` -> `get_primary_weapon_type`/`set_primary_weapon_type` (same for `_secondary`). Collapse `set_player_input` and `set_input` into one `set_input`. Fix `view_port` -> `viewport`.

findings.title: Three different naming schemes for "the screen resolution as a vector", plus a duplicated private converter
findings.detail:
The same two operations are named three ways across three classes:
  - `ResolutionManager.h:12-13`: `get_resolution_ivec()` -> Vector2I, `get_resolution_vec()` -> Vector2F. "vec" silently means float; "ivec" is GLSL vocabulary that appears nowhere else here.
  - `MenuPage.h:54-55`: `get_float_resolution()` -> Vector2F, `get_int_resolution()` -> Vector2I. Adjective moved to the front, abbreviations expanded.
  - `Save.h:34-37`: private `convert_ivec_to_resolution` / `convert_resolution_to_ivec`, byte-identical in name and purpose to `ResolutionManager.h:27,35` - the same converter written privately in two classes.
A fourth spelling shows up in `MainMenu.cpp:448` where the local is `res_i`.
