findings.suggestion: Settle on one pair - `get_resolution_pixels()` returning Vector2I and `get_resolution_size()` returning Vector2F - and expose them only on `ResolutionManager`. `MenuPage` should forward, not rename. Move the `screen_resolution <-> vector` conversions into one place (they belong with `screen_resolution.h`, not duplicated in `Save` and `ResolutionManager`).

findings.title: Five bare global constants with generic names leak from widely-included headers
findings.detail: `CollisionTools.h:7-8` declares `constexpr int BRACKET_ITERATIONS = 40;` and `constexpr float ITERATION_POWER = 1.5f;` at global scope, and `Game.h:12-14` declares `constexpr int TARGET_FPS = 60;`, `NUM_THREADS_MIN = 1;`, `NUM_THREADS_MAX = 16;`. These are the only five global-scope constants in the entire codebase - I checked every header - because everything else lives in a `*_consts` namespace (`player_consts`, `weapon_consts`, `projectile_consts`, `level_consts`, `camera_consts`, `viewport_consts`, `menu_input_consts`, `player_input_consts`, `debug_text_consts`, `main_menu_consts`, `interface_consts`, `directory_consts`, `colour_consts`, `team_colour_consts`). `CollisionTools.h` is included by `Player.h`, so `BRACKET_ITERATIONS` and `ITERATION_POWER` - two of the most collision-prone identifiers imaginable - are visible across most of the program.
findings.suggestion: Wrap them: `namespace collision_consts { constexpr int RESOLUTION_BRACKET_ITERATIONS = 40; constexpr float BRACKET_STEP_DECAY = 1.5f; }` and `namespace game_consts { constexpr int TARGET_FPS = 60; ... }`. Note `ITERATION_POWER` is also a name that does not describe what it does (it is the decay base for the bisection step size).

findings.title: `rectangle_rotated_rectangle_intersect` parses two ways and its name order is the reverse of its parameters
findings.detail: `bool rectangle_rotated_rectangle_intersect(const MattMath::RectangleF& rect, const MattMath::RectangleRotated& rotated_rect);` (MattMath.h:117, defined MattMath.cpp:260). The name reads as `rectangle_rotated` + `rectangle` - i.e. (RectangleRotated, RectangleF) - but the parameters are (RectangleF, RectangleRotated). Every sibling in the family puts the types in argument order: `circle_rectangle_rotated_intersect` (141), `triangle_rectangle_rotated_intersect` (156), `quad_rectangle_rotated_intersect` (167), `segment_rectangle_rotated_intersect` (175), `point_rectangle_rotated_intersect` (178). So this one function is backwards, and the call sites prove the confusion is live: `MattMath.cpp:918` calls `rectangle_rotated_rectangle_intersect(*this, other)` from `RectangleF::intersects` while `MattMath.cpp:4239` calls `rectangle_rotated_rectangle_intersect(rect, *this)` from `RectangleRotated::intersects` - two orderings for one function.
findings.suggestion: Rename to `rectangle_rectangle_rotated_intersect` so it matches both its parameter order and its five siblings. The corresponding test at `MattMathTests/MathTests.cpp:356` should be renamed with it.

findings.title: `level_mode` is accessed as "game_mode"; `player_num` vs `player_index` vs `num` means three things across the codebase
findings.detail:
Two related naming lies in one small class:
  1. `void set_game_mode(level_mode game_mode);` / `level_mode get_game_mode() const;` (lines 17-18) storing `level_mode _game_mode` (32). The type is called a *level* mode, the accessor a *game* mode, and the enum values are `STANDARD_MODE, TEAM_DEATHMATCH, DEATHMATCH, PRACTICE` (`level_mode.h:6-9`) - note `STANDARD_MODE` carries a redundant `_MODE` suffix its three siblings do not.
  2. `void set_player_num(int player_index, int player_num);` (line 29) takes both concepts as ints in one call, and `MenuLevelSettings.cpp:82-84` shows they are genuinely different (`_player_settings[player_index].num = player_num`). `MenuPlayerSettings.h:48` names the field just `num`. Meanwhile `ViewportManager.h:78-90` uses `player_num` as a 0-based viewport *index*, `Player.h:113,156` stores `_player_num` seeded from `player_consts::DEFAULT_PLAYER_NUM = 0`, and `Weapon.h:19,58,136` passes `player_num` through to sound-instance selection (`shoot_sound_name_a0..b3`).
  Also `void set_screen_layout(screen_layout screen_layout);` (line 22) - the only parameter in the repo that shadows its own type name.
findings.suggestion: Pick `level_mode`/`get_level_mode` or `game_mode`/`game_mode` and be consistent; drop the `_MODE` suffix from `STANDARD_MODE`. Then split the player identifiers: `player_index` (0..3 slot, used for arrays/viewports) vs `gamepad_index`, and rename `MenuPlayerSettings::num` accordingly. Rename the shadowing parameter to `layout`.

findings.title: The snake_case-file/PascalCase-file split has a rule, and two files break it - plus abbreviated struct fields
findings.detail:
The de-facto convention is: PascalCase filename = declares a class/struct of that name (`WeaponDetails.h` -> `WeaponDetails`, `PlayerInputData.h` -> `PlayerInputData`, `MenuPlayerSettings.h` -> `MenuPlayerSettings`, `BorderThickness.h` -> `BorderThickness`); snake_case filename = enums and constants only (`shape_type.h`, `wep_type.h`, `player_team.h`, `weapon_consts.h`, ...). Two files break it: `projectile_details.h` declares `struct ProjectileDetails`, `enum class diffusion_type` and `struct DiffusionDetails`, and `player_consts.h:8-16` declares `struct PlayerAnimationInfo` inside a constants header. Compare `WeaponDetails.h`, which is the exact same kind of file, correctly named.
Inside `ProjectileDetails` the fields are also abbreviated inconsistently: `rotation_origin rotat_origin` (line 11 - "rotat" is not a word) and `Vector2F col_rect_size` (15 - "col" reads as column or colour, it means collision) sit beside fully spelled `wind_resistance`, `player_damage`, `animation_strip_name`.
findings.suggestion: Rename `projectile_details.h` -> `ProjectileDetails.h` and move `PlayerAnimationInfo` out of `player_consts.h` into `PlayerAnimationInfo.h`. Fix the fields: `rotat_origin` -> `rotation_origin_mode` (it cannot be `rotation_origin`, that is the type), `col_rect_size` -> `collision_rect_size`.

findings.title: `wep`/`proj` truncations appear only where the full word would have been just as short
findings.detail:
`wep_type.h` declares `enum class wep_type` with member `MAX_PRIM_WEP = RANDOM_PRIMARY` (line 17) - in a codebase whose classes are `Weapon`, `WeaponBucket`, `WeaponSprayer`, `WeaponBuilder`, `WeaponDetails`, and whose constants namespace is `weapon_consts`. So the type is `wep_type` but literally everything around it says `weapon`. The truncation spreads: `Weapon.h:141 get_wep_rotation_origin_offset` (defined `Weapon.cpp:157`), `Weapon.h:122 std::unique_ptr<ProjectileBuilder> _proj_builder` (a `ProjectileBuilder` in a file that spells `Projectile` out everywhere else), `WeaponDetails.h:45 projectile_type proj_type`, `Weapon.h:68 get_starting_vel_length`, `Weapon.h:174-175 add_player_vel / player_vel_amount`, `Weapon.h:91-92 get_draw_pos / get_nozzle_pos`, `Weapon.h:116 get_dt_ptr`, `MainMenu.cpp:1693,1712` widget suffixes `"_wep_icon"` / `"_wep_desc"`. `player_consts.h:48` has `DEFAULT_SECONDARY = wep_type::GRENADE_STD`.
Relatedly, `main_menu_consts` (MainMenu.h) contains both `WEAPON_DESCRIPTION_FONT` (line 26) and `SPRAYER_DESC`/`SNIPER_DESC`/... (84-89) plus `WEAPON_DESC_X_OFFSET` (73) - the same word abbreviated and not, three lines apart.
findings.suggestion: Global rename: `wep_type` -> `weapon_type` (and the file to `weapon_type.h`), `MAX_PRIM_WEP` -> `MAX_PRIMARY_WEAPON`, `_proj_builder` -> `_projectile_builder`, `proj_type` -> `projectile_type_id`, `get_starting_vel_length` -> `get_starting_velocity_length`, `add_player_vel` -> `add_player_velocity_mode`, `get_draw_pos`/`get_nozzle_pos` -> `..._position`, `GRENADE_STD` -> `GRENADE_STANDARD`, `*_DESC` -> `*_DESCRIPTION`. None of these truncations save a meaningful number of characters.

findings.title: en-GB `Colour` type with en-US `color` parameters throughout, and two `COLOR` constants among ~200 `COLOUR` ones
findings.detail: The type is `MattMath::Colour`, the namespace is `colour_consts`, members are `_colour`, setters are `set_colour` - but nearly every constructor parameter that takes one is spelled `color`. Representative: `DrawObject.h:13 const MattMath::Colour& color = colour_consts::WHITE` assigned at `DrawObject.cpp:14 _colour(color)`. Same in `AnimatedSprite.h:15,23`, `AnimationObject.h:15`, `TextureObject.h:84`, `TextObject.h:120`, `Visual.h:16,26`, `SpriteSheet.h:22,33,43,54`, `Mh.h:83,121,147-148` (where `MTexture` takes `color` at :83 and declares `set_colour` at :99), `Player.cpp`, `PaintTile.cpp:14,159`. In constants the split is 2 vs ~200: `DebugText.h:15-16` `DEBUG_COLOR` / `DEBUG_SHADOW_COLOR` against `COUNTDOWN_COLOUR`, `TITLE_TEXT_COLOUR`, `HEALTH_COLOUR`, `TIMER_COLOUR`, `DIVIDER_COLOUR` and the whole of `colour_consts`. `MattMath.h:641 get_sm_colour()` returns a `DirectX::SimpleMath::Color`, so one expression carries both spellings.
findings.suggestion: Pick en-GB (the type already is) and rename every `color` parameter to `colour`, plus `DEBUG_COLOR` -> `DEBUG_COLOUR` and `DEBUG_SHADOW_COLOR` -> `DEBUG_SHADOW_COLOUR`. The DirectX-facing spellings (`SimpleMath::Color`, `Colors::Black`) stay as they are - they are not yours.

findings.title: `fullscreen` vs `full_screen` inconsistent inside a single class
findings.detail: `SaveData::fullscreen` (Save.h:14, one word), `Save::get_fullscreen()` (26, one word), `Save::set_full_screen_and_save(bool full_screen)` (27, two words). `MainMenu.h:177` then stores `bool _full_screen_selection` and `MainMenu.cpp` uses widget names `"full_screen"` / `"full_screen_value"`, while `Main.cpp` branches on `Save::get_fullscreen`. Also note `set_full_screen_and_save` and `set_resolution_and_save` (line 24) encode a side effect in the name, which means there is no way to set the value without persisting - a design smell the name is honest about but should not need to be.
findings.suggestion: Standardise on the one-word `fullscreen` (matching the Win32/DXGI vocabulary): `set_fullscreen(bool fullscreen)`, `_fullscreen_selection`, widget name `"fullscreen"`. Separate the persistence: `set_fullscreen()` + an explicit `save_to_file()` call, which already exists at line 22.

findings.title: Include guards: 10 files whose `#endif` comment names a different macro, one of them a typo, plus two spelling schemes
findings.detail:
I compared the `#ifndef` macro to the trailing `#endif // !X` comment in all 88 headers. Ten disagree, so the comment misdirects anyone matching up a long file:
  `PauseMenuData.h`: guard `PAUSEMENUDATA_H`, comment `PAUSEMENUDATE_H` ("DATE" typo)
  `GameStates.h`: `GAMESTATES_H` vs `GAMELEVEL_H` | `StateContext.h`: `STATECONTEXT_H` vs `STATECONTEXTGENERIC_H` | `MenuHighlight.h`: `MENUHIGHLIGHT_H` vs `MENUPAGEHIGHLIGHT_H` | `TeamColour.h`: `TEAMCOLOUR_H` vs `TEAM_COLOURS_H` | `IPaintableGameObject.h`: `IPAINTABLEGAMEOBJECT_H` vs `IPAINTABLE_H` | `LevelLoadedInfo.h`: `LEVELLOADEDINFO_H` vs `LEVEL_LOADED_INFO_H` | `PlayerInput.h`: `PLAYERINPUT_H` vs `PLAYER_INPUT_H` | `ResolutionManager.h`: `RESOLUTIONMANAGER_H` vs `RESOLUTION_H` | `ViewportManager.h`: `VIEWPORTMANAGER_H` vs `VIEWPORT_H`.
The guards themselves also use two schemes for PascalCase filenames - run-together (`LEVELLOADEDINFO_H`, `MENUPAGE_H`, `SOUNDBANKOBJECT_H`) and underscored (`LEVEL_END_INFO_H`, `MENU_PLAYER_SETTINGS_H`, `THREAD_POOL_H`, `WEAPON_DETAILS_H`) - so `PlayerInput.h` guards `PLAYERINPUT_H` while `PlayerInputData.h` guards `PLAYER_INPUT_H`, a name that by the other scheme belongs to `PlayerInput.h`. `BorderThickness.h` guards `BORDER_THICKNESS` with no `_H` at all, and `CollisionTools.h:1` is `#ifndef  COLLISION_TOOLS_H` with a double space.
findings.suggestion: Replace all of them with `#pragma once` - MSVC v145 supports it, it is what `Game.h`/`StepTimer.h`/`DeviceResources.h` effectively want, and it makes every one of these divergences unrepresentable. If guards must stay, generate them mechanically from the filename (underscored + `_H`) and drop the `#endif` comments.

findings.title: Misspellings in a test name, a constant, and two asset paths
findings.detail:
Four concrete misspellings I confirmed by grep across code and assets:
  1. `MattMathTests/CollisionToolsTests.cpp:58` `TEST_METHOD(test_rectagle_triangle_collision)` - "rectagle". It is one of only two test methods in that file (the other, line 15, spells it correctly).
  2. `ArtAttack/player_consts.h:29` `constexpr float X_DEACCELERATION = 2500.0f;` - "deacceleration" is not a word; it is deceleration. Used at `Player.cpp:792,798,804,813`.
  3. `ArtAttack/levels/turebulence.pub` - "turebulence", next to correctly-spelled `turbulence.json` and `king_of_the_hill.pub` / `close_quarters.pub`.
  4. `ArtAttack/fonts/unuseed fonts/` - "unuseed", where `textures/old textures/` and `sounds/unused/` and `levels/unused/` are the same idea spelled three other ways.
Also worth noting: `MathTests.cpp:76 TEST_METHOD(test_test_2D_segment_segment)` has a doubled "test" because the function under test is `test_2D_segment_segment`.
findings.suggestion: Fix as: `test_rectangle_triangle_collision`; `X_DECELERATION`; rename the file to `turbulence.pub`; rename the folder to `unused fonts` (or better, delete it along with `textures/old textures/`, `levels/unused/`, `sounds/unused/` - and drop the spaces from directory names). For the test, `test_segment_segment_intersection_2d`.

findings.title: The test project has three different names, and its test classes shadow the namespaces containing them
findings.detail:
`MattMathTests.vcxproj:28` sets `<ProjectName>UnitTests</ProjectName>` while line 25 sets `<RootNamespace>MattMathTests</RootNamespace>`, the file/folder is `MattMathTests`, and `ArtAttack.sln:8` registers it as `"MattMathTests"`. Build output is `UnitTests.dll` (visible in the checked-in `MattMathTests/Debug/UnitTests.*` artifacts). So the same project is called three things depending on where you look, and the name that actually appears in Visual Studio's Solution Explorer is the one nobody wrote down.
Inside, `MathTests.cpp:22-23` declares `namespace EricsonMathTests { TEST_CLASS(EricsonMathTests)` - class name identical to enclosing namespace - and `:156 TEST_CLASS(MattMathTests)` collides with the project name. The file `MathTests.cpp` also covers two modules (MattMath and EricsonMath) while `CollisionToolsTests.cpp` covers one, so the file names do not predict contents either.
findings.suggestion: Delete the `<ProjectName>` override so all four names agree on `MattMathTests`. Split `MathTests.cpp` into `MattMathTests.cpp` and `EricsonMathTests.cpp`, and name the TEST_CLASSes after what they test rather than after their namespace (`ShapeIntersectionTests`, `ClosestPointTests`, ...).

findings.title: UI logic branches on opaque string literals "dm"/"tdm" while their siblings are spelled out - and `menu_element` exists but is bypassed
findings.detail:
`MainMenu.cpp:663-733` and the widget-name array at `:787-817` identify game modes as `"standard"`, `"tdm"`, `"dm"`, `"practice"` - two spelled out, two reduced to initialisms, in the same if/else ladder (`if (highlighted_element == "standard") ... else if (highlighted_element == "tdm") ... else if (highlighted_element == "dm")`). Nothing in the file expands them. Meanwhile `menu_element.h:14-17` already defines `MAIN_MENU_STANDARD_MODE`, `MAIN_MENU_TEAM_DEATHMATCH`, `MAIN_MENU_DEATHMATCH`, `MAIN_MENU_PRACTICE`, and `MainMenu.cpp:744-753 convert_mode_to_element` converts to them - so the typed enum exists and the comparison logic ignores it in favour of string literals. `MainMenu.cpp:1927` also references widget `"stage_test_1"`, whose level file lives in `levels/unused/test_1.json`.
The `menu_element` enum itself is only half-populated: it has `MAIN_MENU_*` and `PAUSE_MENU_*` prefixes but no entries for the Results or End menus, which exist (`ResultsMenu.h`, `EndMenu.h`) and drive their own string comparisons.
findings.suggestion: At minimum rename the literals to `"team_deathmatch"` / `"deathmatch"`. Better: finish the job `menu_element` started - key widgets by the enum, add `RESULTS_MENU_*` and `END_MENU_*` entries, and delete the string comparisons (there are ~51 of them per the module recon). A reusable menu system cannot be built on ad-hoc string identity.

findings.title: `InterfaceGameplay` reverses its own method's word order and overloads the most loaded word in C++
findings.detail:
`class InterfaceGameplay : public Drawer` (line 47) declares `void draw_gameplay_interface(...)` (line 52) - the class says "Interface Gameplay", its own method says "gameplay interface". Its constants namespace is `interface_consts` (line 10) and its companion struct is `InterfaceDraw` (line 37), reversing the order again. Worse, "Interface" in C++ means abstract base class - this codebase uses that meaning three doors down in `IGameObject`, `ICollisionGameObject`, `IPaintableGameObject`. This class is a heads-up display.
Same reversal habit shows up elsewhere: `SpriteSheetObject.h:69` stores `_element_name` with `get_element_name()` (63) while its subclass `TextureObject.h:82` calls the identical string `frame_name`, `SpriteSheet.h:20,31` calls it `frame_name`, and `AnimationObject.h:13` calls it `animation_strip_name` - three names for the key into one map.
findings.suggestion: Rename the class to `GameplayHud` (file `GameplayHud.h`), the namespace to `hud_consts`, the struct to `HudDrawParams`, and the method to `draw(...)`. Separately, settle `element_name` vs `frame_name`: `SpriteSheetObject` should call it `_element_name` and so should everyone else, or all of them should say `frame_name`.

findings.title: `_source_rectangle2` - a numeric-suffix placeholder name shipped as a member
findings.detail:
`SpriteFrame.h:21-23`:
```
RECT _source_rectangle = { 0, 0, 0, 0 };

MattMath::RectangleI _source_rectangle2 = MattMath::RectangleI::ZERO;
```
Two members holding the same rectangle in two representations, the second distinguished only by the digit `2`. `get_source_rectangle()` (line 19) returns the `RECT` one; `_source_rectangle2` is written by `set_source_rectangle` (27-30) and never read outside. The `2` tells a reader nothing about which to use or why both exist.
Similar numeric-placeholder naming in the assets: `textures/sprite_sheet_1.json` frames `projectile_1`, `projectile_2`, `projectile_3`, `cloud_1`, `cloud_2`, `player_1_right`, `player_2_right`, `splash_1`, `square_white_4`, `square_white_32` - the trailing numbers mean size in some cases and variant index in others.
findings.suggestion: If both representations are genuinely needed, name them for their type/purpose: `_source_rect_win32` and `_source_rect` (or store only `MattMath::RectangleI` and convert on demand in `get_source_rectangle`). Given `_source_rectangle2` appears to be write-only, deleting it is likely correct - verify against `SpriteFrame.cpp` first.

findings.title: The core collision interface identifies objects with an enum of this game's content
findings.detail:
`ICollisionGameObject` — the engine's fundamental collidable abstraction — includes `collision_object_type.h` (line 5) and exposes `virtual collision_object_type get_collision_object_type() const = 0;` (line 14). That enum (collision_object_type.h:4-29) is a flat cross-product of class x team x weapon: `PLAYER_TEAM_A`, `PLAYER_TEAM_B_DEAD`, `PROJECTILE_SPRAY_TEAM_A`, `PROJECTILE_MIST_TEAM_B`, `PAINT_TILE`, `STRUCTURE_RAMP_LEFT`, ... The header then ships 8 free predicates (`is_team_a_projectile`, `is_dead_player`, ...) at lines 31-88 that hardcode the same content.

Consequence: every collidable in any future game must declare itself as one of *this* game's 23 types. Adding a weapon means editing an engine header and recompiling every TU that touches collision. Adding a third team is a combinatorial edit. It also forces the same if/else identity ladder to be rewritten in every object (Player.cpp:186-244, PaintTile.cpp:114-140, StructurePaintable.cpp:64-102, Level.cpp:238, Level.cpp:713-715).

This is the single most pervasive engine/game inversion in the repo: the game's content model *is* the engine's type system.
findings.suggestion: Replace the enum with data the engine does not interpret: a `CollisionLayer`/`CollisionMask` bitset plus an opaque game-owned tag (e.g. `uint32_t user_type` or a `void*`/`std::any` payload). The engine filters pairs by layer/mask; the *game* decides what `PROJECTILE_SPRAY_TEAM_A` means by casting/inspecting its own tag in its own `on_collision`. Move `collision_object_type.h` out of the engine entirely into game/ as `game_collision_tags.h`.

findings.title: There is no engine target: one Application project, 193 files flat in one directory, 2 filters
findings.detail:
All four configurations set `<ConfigurationType>Application</ConfigurationType>` (lines 29, 36, 43, 51). The project emits an .exe and no .lib, so there is literally nothing another game could link against. All 193 first-party .h/.cpp files live in a single flat `ArtAttack/` directory, and `ArtAttack.vcxproj.filters` declares exactly two filters (`Common`, `Assets`) covering 6 of ~200 items — `Game.h`, `Level.h`, `Player.h`, `MattMath.h`, `weapon_consts.h` and `CollisionTools.h` are all siblings with no grouping.

The cost is already visible: `MattMathTests` cannot link the engine and instead `#include`s implementation .cpp files (MathTests.cpp:5-6 includes `..\ArtAttack\MattMath.cpp` and `EricsonMath.cpp`; CollisionToolsTests.cpp:3 includes `CollisionTools.cpp`). Only 3 of ~81 TUs are testable at all, precisely because there is no library boundary.

Every other finding in this sweep is downstream of this one: with no compilation boundary, nothing *stops* game concepts leaking into engine headers, so they all have.
findings.suggestion: Split into three MSBuild targets sharing a common `.props`: `MattMath` (StaticLibrary, zero deps), `ArtAttackEngine` (StaticLibrary, depends on MattMath + DirectXTK), `ArtAttackGame` (Application, depends on Engine). Mirror that on disk (see notes). The moment the engine is a static lib, a game include from an engine .cpp becomes a link/compile error instead of a silent coupling.

findings.title: `Level` is both the only scene abstraction and the complete paint-battle ruleset
findings.detail:
There is no engine-level `Scene`/`World` type; `Level` is it, and it is entirely this game. Its constructor (Level.h:58-80) takes `const TeamColour&`, `level_stage stage`, `const std::vector<Vector2F>& team_a_spawns`, `const std::vector<Vector2F>& team_b_spawns`. Its members include `TeamColour _team_colours` (:128), `level_stage _stage = level_stage::KING_OF_THE_HILL` (:129), `_team_a_spawns`/`_team_b_spawns` (:136-137). `level_consts` (:31-52) hardcodes a 240-second match timer, a 3-second countdown, the countdown font `gill_sans_mt_bold_144`, and the sound cue names `"smash_countdown"`/`"slide_whistle_up"`.

`level_state` (:22-29) — `START_COUNTDOWN/ACTIVE/ZOOM_OUT/OVERVIEW/FINISHED` — is this game's match flow, not a generic scene lifecycle. And `Level::get_level_end_info()` (Level.cpp:706-735) is the win condition: it walks `_collision_objects`, filters `type == STRUCTURE_PAINTABLE`, `dynamic_cast<IPaintableGameObject*>`, and sums `paint.team_a`/`paint.team_b`.

So the generic responsibilities that *should* be engine (own the object lists, step them, run broad/narrow phase, dispatch collisions, cull, draw through viewports, delete dead objects) are welded to the game responsibilities (two teams, spawns, paint scoring, match timer, zoom-out celebration).
findings.suggestion: Extract an engine `Scene` owning `std::vector<std::unique_ptr<IGameObject>>` + the collision/update/draw pipeline, with virtual (or callback) hooks `on_pre_update/on_post_collision/is_finished/get_result`. Then `PaintBattleScene : Scene` in game/ holds `TeamColour`, spawns, the match timer and `get_level_end_info()`. The engine must not know the word 'team'.

findings.title: An interface named `IPaintableGameObject` with a hardcoded two-team score sits alongside the engine's core interfaces
findings.detail:
The whole file is:
```
struct PaintTotal { float team_a = 0.0f; float team_b = 0.0f; };
class IPaintableGameObject { virtual PaintTotal get_paint_total() const = 0; };
```
It sits in the same flat directory as `IGameObject.h` and `ICollisionGameObject.h`, is named to match them, and is included by `Level.h:17` — i.e. the scene type consumes it directly. Exactly two teams are baked into the interface's return type, so a 3-team or free-for-all mode cannot even be expressed. `IPaintableGameObject` is a *Splatoon territory-control scoring hook* wearing an engine interface's name.

Related: `PaintTile.h:51-84` and `PaintTile.h:10-21` (`paint_tile_consts` with `SHEET_NAME = "sprite_sheet_1"`, `SPLASH_ANIMATION_STRIP_NAME = "splash_1"`) implement the paint grid as `ICollisionGameObject`s, so paint is physically inside the collision layer.
findings.suggestion: Move `IPaintableGameObject.h` and `PaintTile.*` into game/paint/. Replace `PaintTotal{team_a, team_b}` with something the game owns, e.g. `std::vector<float> coverage_by_faction` or `std::map<FactionId, float>`. The engine side needs no interface at all — the game can hold its own `std::vector<PaintableSurface*>`.

findings.title: The resource cache is keyed on this game's three map names, and the asset manifest is compiled C++
findings.detail:
`ResourceManager` — the engine's asset cache — includes `level_stage.h` (:7) and keys its level cache on it: `const LevelLoadedInfo* get_level_info(level_stage stage) const` (:32), `void add_level_info(level_stage stage, ...)` (:34), `std::map<level_stage, std::unique_ptr<LevelLoadedInfo>> _level_infos` (:52). `level_stage` (level_stage.h:4-11) is `{ KING_OF_THE_HILL, TURBULENCE, CLOSE_QUARTERS, RANDOM }` — literally the names of this game's three maps. Every other cache in the class is keyed by `std::string`; only levels got a game-specific enum.

Compounding it, the *entire* asset manifest is hardcoded in `ResourceLoader.cpp`: `load_textures()` loads one sheet, `"sprite_sheet_1"` (:19); `load_fonts()` names 7 specific `gill_sans_*`/`courier_new_bold_16` fonts (:23-31); `load_sounds()` loads `"sound_bank_1"` (:35); `load_level_info()` maps three literal filenames to three enum values (:40-42). Shipping a fourth map, renaming a font, or adding a second atlas requires editing engine source and recompiling.
findings.suggestion: Key `_level_infos` by `std::string` like every other cache, and delete `level_stage.h` from the engine (the game's stage-select menu can carry its own enum or just strings). Replace the hardcoded `load_textures/load_fonts/load_sounds/load_level_info` bodies with a data-driven manifest (e.g. `content/manifest.json` listing textures, fonts, sound banks, levels) that `ResourceLoader::load_all_resources()` iterates.

findings.title: The platform entry point includes the game's state header and constructs `GameMenu` directly
findings.detail:
`Main.cpp` is otherwise pure platform bootstrap (window class, message pump, WndProc, CoInitialize) — i.e. engine. But line 6 is `#include "GameStates.h"`, which transitively pulls in `MainMenu.h`, `PauseMenu.h`, `ResultsMenu.h`, `EndMenu.h`, `LevelBuilder.h` and therefore the whole game; and line 208 hardcodes the game's first screen:
```
g_game->transition_to(std::make_unique<GameMenu>(g_game_data.get()));
```
There is no seam where a different game plugs in its own initial state. Also stale from two prior repos: the window title is `LPCWSTR g_szAppName = L"Colour Wars";` (:27) and the window class is `L"ChromaClashWindowClass"` (:123, :156, :162) — neither matches ArtAttack, and both are hardcoded in engine bootstrap rather than supplied by the app.
findings.suggestion: Give the engine a small entry-point shim: `int run_game(HINSTANCE, std::unique_ptr<IApplication>)` where `IApplication` supplies the window title/class, the default resolution and `create_initial_state()`. `main.cpp` in game/ becomes ~10 lines constructing `ArtAttackApp`. Move `g_szAppName` into that app description.

findings.title: The level file format itself only has room for exactly two teams
findings.detail:
`LevelLoadedInfo` is the engine's parsed-level-file type, and its public surface is `std::vector<MattMath::Vector2F> get_team_a_spawns() const;` / `get_team_b_spawns() const;` (:17-18), backed by `static std::vector<Vector2F> decode_team_spawns_json(const rapidjson::Value&)` (:36-37). The on-disk format matches — `levels/king_of_the_hill.json` has `"spawn_locations": { "team_a": [...], "team_b": [...] }`.

The rest of the class is genuinely generic (`get_out_of_bounds_rectangle`, `get_camera_bounds_rectangle`, `get_collision_objects_json`, `get_sound_bank_name`) — which is exactly why the two team accessors are a violation: they contaminate an otherwise reusable level-file abstraction with a two-faction assumption. A single-player platformer loading this format has to invent a fake 'team_b'. Note the file format also carries `zoom_out_start_bounds`/`zoom_out_finish_bounds` (LevelLoadedInfo.h:23-24), which exist solely to drive this game's end-of-match camera pull-back.
findings.suggestion: Make the engine level format carry named, arbitrary-count spawn groups: `const std::vector<Vector2F>& get_spawn_group(const std::string& name)` over a JSON `"spawn_groups": { "team_a": [...], "team_b": [...] }`. Move `zoom_out_*_bounds` into a game-defined `"game_data"` blob the engine passes through opaquely.

findings.title: Level loading is a closed if/else over four hardcoded type strings — no registration point
findings.detail:
`build_collision_object` (lines 15-180) is `std::string type = json["type"].GetString();` followed by `if (type == "Structure")`, `if (type == "StructurePaintable")`, `if (type == "StructureRamp")`, then `throw std::exception("Invalid collision object type")`. `build_non_collision_object` (182-200) is the same shape with a single `"Visual"` branch. Each branch also re-parses the rectangle with a copy-pasted `HasMember("rectangle") / HasMember("rectangle_tlbr")` block (lines 37-56 duplicated at 80-99), and does a nested string->enum if/else for `collision_type` (24-35, 70-78, 148-159).

So the level loader — which is the one piece of the engine a content-driven game most needs to extend — cannot be extended without editing it. A second game shipping a `Ladder` or `MovingPlatform` object has to modify engine source. The builder is also already coupled to game types by include: `LevelObjectBuilder.h:7` includes `StructurePaintable.h`, and the signature takes `const TeamColour& team_colours` (:20-21, :34-35).
findings.suggestion: Invert it into a registry: `LevelObjectBuilder` holds `std::map<std::string, std::function<std::unique_ptr<ICollisionGameObject>(const rapidjson::Value&, const BuildContext&)>>` and exposes `register_type(name, factory)`. The game registers `"StructurePaintable"` at startup; the engine registers only truly generic types. Factor the rectangle/`rectangle_tlbr` parsing into one `parse_rectangle(const Value&)` helper. Drop `TeamColour` from the signature — pass it inside a game-owned `BuildContext`.

findings.title: The engine's split-screen viewport manager hardcodes this game's texture atlas and frame names
findings.suggestion: Make divider appearance a `ViewportManager` construction parameter (`DividerStyle{sheet, frame, colour, thickness}`) supplied by the game, defaulting to a 1x1 white pixel the engine itself owns. More broadly, no engine header should contain a string literal naming a content file — route all of them through a game-supplied style/theme struct or the content manifest.

findings.title: Every game object in the engine is compiled against DirectXTK's SpriteBatch and MattMath::Camera
findings.suggestion: Introduce a thin engine `IRenderer`/`SpriteDrawList` interface (`draw_sprite(texture, src_rect, dst_rect, colour, rotation, origin, depth)`) with a DirectXTK implementation, and have objects submit to that. Move culling out of objects into the scene (objects expose `get_bounds()`; the scene tests against the view rect once). This also unblocks headless tests of game logic.

findings.title: The input layer emits this game's verbs directly, with a fixed XInput button map and no keyboard
findings.detail:
`PlayerInputData` is the engine's only input payload, and every field is a game verb: `jump_pressed`, `jump_held`, `shoot_angle`, `shoot_direction`, `primary_shoot`, `secondary_shoot`, `toggle_debug`, `toggle_pause_menu` (lines 9-19). The mapping is hardcoded in `PlayerInput::get_raw_input` (PlayerInput.cpp:27-32): `result.jump_button = pad.buttons.a; result.jump_trigger = pad.triggers.left; result.primary_shoot = pad.triggers.right; result.secondary_shoot = pad.buttons.rightShoulder; result.show_debug = pad.buttons.back; result.pause_menu = pad.buttons.start;`.

There is no action-map indirection, no rebinding, no keyboard or mouse path at all (`DirectX::Keyboard`/`Mouse` appear nowhere in the codebase), and the player count is baked in as raw `4`s: `RawPlayerInput _prev_inputs[4]` (PlayerInput.h:34) and `RawPlayerInput current[4]; for (int i = 0; i < 4; i++)` (PlayerInput.cpp:121-128). A second game gets 'jump' and 'shoot' whether it wants them or not, and cannot be played without a gamepad.
findings.suggestion: Split into engine `RawInputState` (per-device sticks/buttons/keys, N devices) plus a game-defined action enum bound through an `InputMap` the game registers (`bind(action::JUMP, gamepad_button::A)`, loadable from the save file for rebinding). `PlayerInputData` and its verbs move to game/. Add a keyboard/mouse device so the engine is not gamepad-only.

findings.title: Game UI state classes inherit from the engine's service-locator, so engine wiring is a base class of game data
findings.detail:
`class MenuData : public GameData` (MenuData.h:7), then `MainMenuData : public MenuData` (MainMenuData.h:8), `PauseMenuData`, `ResultsMenuData`, `EndMenuData` — a 3-deep inheritance chain rooted in `GameData`, which is the engine's 12-pointer service bag (`Save*`, `ResolutionManager*`, `float* _dt`, `ResourceManager*`, `GamePad*`, `DeviceResources*`, `ViewportManager*`, `CommonStates*`, `std::vector<SpriteBatch*>*`, `ThreadPool*`, `const Partitioner*`, `HWND`; GameData.h:49-61).

This is inheritance used for field concatenation, and it runs the wrong way across the boundary: game screens *are-a* engine service locator. Each level slices a copy of all 12 pointers (`GameData::GameData(const GameData*)`, GameData.cpp:4-20), so `MainMenuData` carries three copies' worth of engine plumbing. Nothing polymorphic is ever done with the base — `GameData` has no virtuals and no virtual destructor, so any `delete` through a `GameData*` is UB.

(Incidentally `GameData::get_thread_pool()` contains a duplicated unreachable `return this->_thread_pool;` at GameData.cpp:144-145.)
findings.suggestion: Compose, don't inherit: `class MainMenuData { EngineServices* _services; MenuInput* _input; MenuLevelSettings* _settings; bool* _ready; };`. Rename `GameData` to `EngineServices` (or better, split it — most consumers want 2-3 of the 12 pointers, not all of them) and move it engine-side with no game type ever deriving from it.

findings.title: The engine colour palette ships this game's team colours, and every drawable includes it
findings.suggestion: Delete the `TEAM_*` block from `Colour.h` and define those five colours in game/paint/team_colours.h next to `TeamColour`. While there, make the palette `constexpr`/`inline constexpr` so it costs nothing per TU, and stop including the full palette from `DrawObject.h` (forward-declare `Colour` or include a minimal `colour_type.h`).

findings.title: The engine's debug overlay is compiled against `Player` and a projectile count
findings.detail:
An on-screen dev overlay is a canonical engine feature, but `DebugText.h` does `#include "Player.h"` (:7) and its only public method is `void draw_debug_info(SpriteBatch*, const Player* player, int num_projectiles) const;` (:29). The body (DebugText.cpp:21-102) reads `player->get_input()`, `get_input_shoot_direction()`, `get_input_primary_shoot()`, `get_input_jump_pressed()`, `get_move_state()`, `get_player_state()` and switches on `player_state::ALIVE/DEAD`. `Level.h:11` includes it and `Level.h:144` owns one.

So the engine's diagnostic facility cannot display anything about a game that has no `Player`, no jump, and no projectiles — and `Player.h` (with its weapons, teams and animation states) is dragged into the engine include graph by a debug widget. The generic 40% of it (`dt`, `fps`, camera, resolution, viewport) is unusable independently.
findings.suggestion: Reduce `DebugText` to an engine `DebugOverlay` with `add_line(const std::string&)` / `add_line(const char* label, float value)` and a `draw(SpriteBatch*)` that renders whatever was pushed this frame. Keep dt/fps/camera/resolution as engine-supplied lines. The game pushes its own player/projectile lines from `PaintBattleScene`. Drop the `Player.h` include.

findings.title: Content roots are hardcoded relative paths with no mount point, and the built exe is not standalone
findings.suggestion: Introduce an engine `ContentPaths`/`FileSystem` object initialised from the executable directory (`GetModuleFileNameW`) with game-settable subroots, and pass it to `ResourceLoader` instead of the header constants. Move the save file to `SHGetKnownFolderPath(FOLDERID_RoamingAppData)/<AppName>/` and untrack `save/save_data.json`. Add a post-build content copy (or a `<Content>` item group) so the exe is standalone.

findings.title: All game tuning and content data is compiled into C++ headers, so content changes require rebuilding
findings.detail:
Levels are data (`levels/*.json`) but everything else is source. `weapon_consts.h:14-56` defines `DETAILS_SPRAYER` etc. as `static const WeaponDetails` aggregates carrying sizes, velocities, ammo costs, sprite frame names (`"sprite_sheet_1"`, `"sprayer"`), sound bank and cue names; `projectile_consts.h` does the same for 6 projectile types; `player_consts.h:20-121` holds gravity, jump velocity, per-weapon damage values (`SPRAY_DAMAGE`, `JET_DAMAGE`, ...), sound cue names and 5 `PlayerAnimationInfo` records naming animation strips.

The inconsistency is the tell: the engine already has a JSON pipeline (rapidjson, `LevelLoadedInfo`, `SpriteSheet::load_from_json`, `SoundBank::load_from_json`) and uses it for levels, atlases and sound banks — but not for the entities. Balancing a weapon is a full rebuild of ~81 TUs, and a second game inherits the pattern of writing content in headers. (These are also namespace-scope non-`constexpr` `const` objects in headers: one copy plus dynamic init per including TU.)
findings.suggestion: Move weapon/projectile/player definitions into `content/*.json` parsed by the existing builders (`WeaponBuilder`, `ProjectileBuilder`, `PlayerBuilder` already exist and would be the natural readers). Keep only genuinely structural constants in headers, and mark those `inline constexpr`.

findings.title: Split-screen layout is a hardcoded 1-4 player table with fall-through switches and an out-of-range lookup
findings.detail:
`screen_layout` (screen_layout.h:4-11) is `{ONE_PLAYER, TWO_PLAYER, THREE_PLAYER, FOUR_PLAYER}` and `calculate_viewport` (ViewportManager.cpp:154-240) is a hand-written nested switch table for each. There is no way to express 5+ views, a non-quadrant split, or a picture-in-picture minimap — an engine viewport module should compute a grid, not enumerate cases.

Worse, the outer switch has no `break`/`return` after each inner switch's `default: break;` (lines 181-184, 205-207, 235-237), so out-of-range player numbers silently fall through to the *next* layout's case and ultimately to `default: //1P screen` (:238). `get_all_viewports()` exploits this by accident: at lines 98-102, when `player_count == 3` it calls `this->get_player_viewport(4)` to add a filler 4th viewport — but valid indices are 0..3, so index 4 falls all the way through and returns a **fullscreen** viewport instead of the empty bottom-right quadrant. In 3-player mode the divider/filler viewport therefore covers the whole screen.
findings.suggestion: Replace the enum + switch table with `set_view_count(int n)` and a computed grid (`cols = ceil(sqrt(n))`, etc.), returning `Viewport` from arithmetic. Immediately: change line 101 to `get_player_viewport(3)`, and add `break;`/`return` after each inner switch so out-of-range indices are a hard error rather than a silent fullscreen viewport.

findings.title: Six fully commented-out game-object files are still compiled by the project
findings.detail:
`StructureRamp.h`, `StructureRampLeft.h`, `StructureRampRight.h` contain zero non-comment lines; the three matching .cpp files contain exactly one each (the `#include "pch.h"`). All six are still listed in `ArtAttack.vcxproj` (ClInclude at lines 252-254, ClCompile at 348-350), so three empty TUs are compiled every build. `LevelObjectBuilder.h:10-11` still carries the commented-out includes.

Meanwhile ramps *are* shipped, as plain `Structure` with a `TriangleRightAxisAligned` shape and a `STRUCTURE_RAMP_LEFT/RIGHT` enum tag (LevelObjectBuilder.cpp:144-177) — so the enum values in the engine-level `collision_object_type.h:9-10, 84-88` exist to tag objects whose dedicated classes were abandoned. The dead-class graveyard makes the engine/game split harder to reason about because it is unclear which abstractions are live.
findings.suggestion: Delete the six files and their vcxproj entries. If ramps stay as tagged `Structure`s, drop `STRUCTURE_RAMP_LEFT/RIGHT` and `is_structure_ramp()` from the shared enum in favour of the shape type (which already distinguishes triangles).

findings.title: Include filename case mismatches will break any non-Windows or case-sensitive build of the engine
findings.detail:
The file on disk is `Colour.h`. Seven includes spell it correctly (`DrawObject.h:4`, `MenuHighlight.h:4`, `ResultsMenu.h:5`, `SpriteSheet.h:5`, `ViewportManager.h:8`, `Weapon.h:9`, `player_consts.h:6`) but two spell it `#include "colour.h"` — `TeamColour.h:5` and `InterfaceGameplay.h:7`. MSVC on NTFS does not care; clang/gcc on a case-sensitive filesystem, or a case-sensitive CI checkout, will fail to find the header.

For a codebase whose stated goal is a reusable engine this matters more than it would for a one-off Windows game: it is a one-character blocker on ever compiling the engine anywhere else, and it will be found only after the rest of the port is done.
findings.suggestion: Fix both includes to `"Colour.h"`. Consider a lint/CI step that compiles with clang-cl or checks include casing, so the engine stays portable-by-default as the rest of the DirectX coupling is abstracted out.

findings.title: closest_pt_point_OBB loops over 3 axes in 2D and throws on every call; zero tests
findings.detail: `closest_pt_point_OBB(p, b, q)` — the only OBB support routine, added with the recent RectangleRotated/OBB work — contains `for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) { float dist = Vector2F::dot(d, b.get_axis(i)); ... }`. `RectangleRotated::get_axis` (ArtAttack/MattMath.cpp:4315-4327) is `if (axis==0) ... else if (axis==1) ... throw std::invalid_argument("Axis must be 0 or 1")`. The third iteration therefore throws unconditionally: the function can never return normally, for any input. It is declared in EricsonMath.h:141, has zero call sites in the engine, and has zero tests. A single test asserting the closest point on an axis-aligned OBB would have caught this on the day it was written. This is the clearest evidence that the RectangleRotated/OBB work shipped without behavioural coverage of its own primitives.
findings.suggestion: Change the loop bound to 2. Add a test class for the OBB primitives: closest point for a point inside the box (returns p), outside along +x axis, outside past a corner (clamps on both axes), and on a 45-degree-rotated box where the answer differs from the AABB answer.

findings.title: RectangleRotated(Segment, thickness) constructor always throws; no test constructs it
findings.detail: The constructor does `this->_x_axis = center_line.get_direction();` then `this->_y_axis = Vector2F::normal(this->_x_axis);` and then `if (!this->is_valid()) throw std::invalid_argument(...)`. But `Segment::get_direction()` (ArtAttack/MattMath.cpp:4063-4066) returns `point_1 - point_0` — un-normalised — while `axes_valid()` (4522-4537) requires `are_equal(_x_axis.length(), 1.0f, EPSILON)`. So this constructor throws for every segment whose length is not within 1e-4 of 1.0. Note the sibling 4-arg constructor at 4186 does call `_x_axis.normalize()`, so the two constructors disagree. Every RectangleRotated test in MattMathTests/MathTests.cpp (lines 356-403, 491-515, 629-662, 736-765, 783-830, 831-873) uses only the 4-arg constructor; the Segment overload has zero tests. This is the overload intended for paint trails / thick line segments, i.e. the reason OBBs were added.
findings.suggestion: Normalise in the Segment ctor (`_x_axis = Vector2F::unit_vector(center_line.get_direction())`) and add tests: construct from a segment of length 10 with thickness 2, assert `get_half_extents()`, `get_angle()`, the four corner points, and that a zero-length segment throws (`Assert::ExpectException<std::invalid_argument>`).

findings.title: RectangleRotated::is_valid() is a no-op during construction and no test exercises the invalid path
findings.detail: The 4-arg ctor calls `this->is_valid()` at line 4194 and only assigns `this->_points = this->calculate_points()` at line 4199 — after the check. `is_valid()` calls `edges_valid()` (4539), which does `std::vector<Segment> edges = this->get_edges();` built from `_points`, which at that moment is still the header's default-member-initialiser `{ Point2F::ZERO, Point2F::ZERO, Point2F::ZERO, Point2F::ZERO }` (ArtAttack/MattMath.h:1119-1120). Four zero-length edges: every `dot(...) == 0` perpendicularity check passes and every `get_length()` pair compares 0 == 0, so `edges_valid()` returns true unconditionally at construction time. Two thirds of the validation is dead. Zero tests call `is_valid()`, and there is no test that a malformed RectangleRotated is rejected — the suite only ever builds valid ones.
findings.suggestion: Compute `_points` before validating, then add tests for the rejection paths: non-perpendicular axes, zero half-extents, negative half-extents, and a valid case. Use `Assert::ExpectException<std::invalid_argument>`.

findings.title: FLT_EPSILON boundary cases are arithmetic no-ops: "just inside" and "just outside" are the same point
findings.suggestion: Use a relative offset (`std::nextafter(10.0f, 11.0f)` / `std::nextafter(10.0f, 9.0f)`) or, better, an explicit tolerance that matches the library's own `MattMath::EPSILON` and assert only distinctions coarser than it.

findings.title: Two negative boundary cases build their input and then assert nothing
findings.suggestion: Add the missing `Assert::IsFalse(...)` calls. More generally, a lint/review rule: every `// case` comment in these test bodies must be followed by at least one Assert before the next assignment to the same variable.

findings.title: The one regression test for ramp (rect-vs-triangle) collision is commented out, in the module being actively fixed
findings.detail: `test_rectagle_triangle_collision` (note the typo in the name) contains a 17-line commented-out block testing `RectangleF(220, 5878, 52, 120)` against `Triangle((200,6000),(400,6000),(400,5800))` — a player-sized box against a level-sized ramp, i.e. exactly the scenario the last few commits ("fix ramp-player collision", "adding OBB logic and tests") were about. It asserts `DIRECTION_DOWN_RIGHT` and a resolve amount of (-1,-1). It was disabled rather than fixed. What remains is a single 10x10-vs-10x10 case at the origin where every quantity is symmetric, so it cannot distinguish a correct implementation from one that mixes up x and y.
findings.suggestion: Restore the case with whatever the correct expected values are (derive them, don't read them off the implementation) and mark it `Assert::Fail("known bug: <link>")` if it genuinely fails, so the suite reports the defect instead of hiding it.

findings.title: 2 tests cover 2 of CollisionTools' 11 functions; every buggy branch is untested
findings.detail:
The whole CollisionTools suite is two methods exercising `calculate_object_collision_direction` and `resolve_object_collision` on symmetric axis-aligned cases. Untested, with defects visible on inspection:
- `calculate_containing_collision_direction` (ArtAttack/CollisionTools.cpp:91-107): `if (std::abs(x_distance) < std::abs(y_distance)) return compare_point_collision_depth_horizontal(...)` — inverted. When the vertical separation dominates it resolves horizontally.
- `resolve_object_AABB_collision` (ArtAttack/CollisionTools.cpp:209-229): `float larger = std::max(collision_direction.x, collision_direction.y); direction = collision_direction / larger;` uses signed max, not magnitude. For direction (-0.9, -0.1), `larger` is -0.1 and `direction` becomes (9, 1) — the collider is pushed out by 9x the overlap width. The two existing tests use directions (0.707,0.707) and (-1,0), the only two shapes of input for which this line happens to be harmless.
- `calculate_object_collision_direction_by_edge` (136-207): 12 branches, zero tests.
- `bracket_object_collision_generic` (55-69): the 40-iteration bisection push-out used for *every* non-rect-vs-rect resolution in the game, zero tests.
- `calculate_object_collision_depth`, `opposite_direction`: zero tests.
findings.suggestion: Table-drive it: for each ordered pair of shape types (rect, circle, triangle, quad, rotated-rect) and each of the 8 cardinal approach directions, assert the resolved shape no longer intersects and that `amount` has the expected sign and roughly the expected magnitude. That single table would catch all four issues above.

findings.title: Three ad-hoc epsilon constants tuned until the tests went green, at resolutions finer than the library's own EPSILON
findings.detail: The suite defines `EPSILON_F = 1e-6f`, `EPSILON_F_2 = 2e-6f`, `EPSILON_F_100 = 1e-4f` and picks between them per call site: `rectangle_segment_intersect` needs `EPSILON_F_2` for its negative case (line 335) while its positive case uses `EPSILON_F` (331); `quads_intersect` needs `EPSILON_F_2` (686); the rotated-rectangle cases need `EPSILON_F_100` (393, 658, 762, 816, 866). Nothing derives these — they are the smallest values that made each assertion pass. Meanwhile `MattMath::EPSILON` is `0.0001f` (ArtAttack/MattMath.h:46) and `are_equal` (ArtAttack/MattMath.cpp:93-96) uses it as the library's declared resolution, and `test_segment_AABB` adds its own `EricsonMath::EPSILON = 1e-6f` fudge (ArtAttack/EricsonMath.cpp:665-666). So most of these tests assert that the library distinguishes separations 100x smaller than it claims to resolve. They are pinning float noise, not behaviour.
findings.suggestion: Pick one tolerance derived from `MattMath::EPSILON`, test separations of e.g. 10*EPSILON (must not intersect) and -10*EPSILON (must intersect), and delete the sub-epsilon cases. If a specific sub-epsilon behaviour genuinely matters, document why in the test.

findings.title: Geometric results compared with exact float equality via Vector2F::operator==
findings.detail: The suite's dominant assertion form is `Assert::IsTrue(closest == Point2F(5.0f, 0.0f))`. `Vector2F::operator==` (ArtAttack/MattMath.cpp:1574-1577) is `this->x == other.x && this->y == other.y` — bit equality, no tolerance. These are compared against values that came out of divisions and square roots (`closest_pt_point_segment` does `t = dot(c-a,ab)/dot(ab,ab)` then `d = a + t*ab`; `closest_pt_point_triangle` similar). They pass today only because every test input is a small power-of-two-friendly integer coordinate. Any change to the order of operations inside those routines — including one the optimiser makes — flips them. Note the suite already knows better: `are_equal(p, Point2F(...), 0.1f)` is used at lines 457 and 542, and CollisionToolsTests uses `Assert::AreEqual(a, b, EPSILON_F)`. The three styles are mixed arbitrarily.
findings.suggestion: Standardise on `Assert::IsTrue(are_equal(actual, expected, tol))` with a named tolerance, or add a small `AssertVec2(expected, actual, tol)` helper and use it everywhere. Exact `==` should be reserved for tests *of* `operator==` itself.

findings.title: Tests compile the code under test with different codegen than the game ships with
findings.detail: ArtAttack.vcxproj sets, in all four configs, `<FloatingPointModel>Fast</FloatingPointModel>` (lines 94, 116, 139, 165), `<ConformanceMode>true</ConformanceMode>` (96, 117, 141, 166), `<WarningLevel>Level4</WarningLevel>`, and on Win32 `<EnableEnhancedInstructionSet>StreamingSIMDExtensions2</EnableEnhancedInstructionSet>` (95, 140). MattMathTests.vcxproj sets *none* of these: no FloatingPointModel (so /fp:precise), no ConformanceMode, `Level3`. MattMath.cpp and EricsonMath.cpp are therefore compiled twice with different float semantics — the tested build reassociates less and keeps more intermediate precision than the shipped build. Given the previous finding (1-ULP boundary assertions and exact float comparisons), this is not theoretical: the suite can be green while the identical source in ArtAttack.exe returns the other answer. Neither project sets `<LanguageStandard>` either, so both are stuck on the MSVC default of C++14.
findings.suggestion: Extract a shared `common.props` with LanguageStandard, FloatingPointModel, ConformanceMode, WarningLevel and TreatWarningAsError, and import it from both projects. The test project must never compile engine code under settings the engine does not use.

findings.title: Tests #include .cpp files, and the two test TUs are implicitly linked to each other
findings.detail: `MathTests.cpp` includes `..\ArtAttack\MattMath.cpp` and `..\ArtAttack\EricsonMath.cpp`; `CollisionToolsTests.cpp:3` includes only `..\ArtAttack\CollisionTools.cpp`. CollisionTools.cpp needs MattMath symbols, which it gets not from a library but from *the other test file's* translation unit. Rename or delete MathTests.cpp and CollisionToolsTests.cpp stops linking, for reasons nothing in its source explains. The root cause is that ArtAttack is `ConfigurationType=Application` (ArtAttack/ArtAttack.vcxproj) and produces no .lib, so the `<ProjectReference>` at MattMathTests.vcxproj:173 links nothing — it only forces a full rebuild of the game executable before every test run. It also means MattMath.cpp's file-scope statics (`Vector2F::ZERO`, `Camera::DEFAULT_CAMERA`, …) exist in two separate binaries.
findings.suggestion: Split the engine into `ArtAttackLib` (`ConfigurationType=StaticLibrary`) containing everything except `Main.cpp`, make `ArtAttack.exe` a thin app project linking it, and have MattMathTests link the lib and `#include` only headers. This is the single change that unlocks testing anything beyond MattMath.

findings.title: Empty TEST_METHOD reports as a passing test
findings.suggestion: Delete the placeholder or fill it in with cases that actually exercise the cross-product axis: a steeply sloped segment passing near a box corner, and a segment collinear with a box edge.

findings.title: The Shape dispatch layer every in-game collision goes through has zero tests
findings.detail: `Shape::intersects(const Shape* other)` is a `switch` on `other->get_shape_type()` doing `dynamic_cast` to the concrete type and re-dispatching (lines 119-136), with `default: throw std::invalid_argument("Shape type not recognized")`. `shape_type` includes a `NONE` member (ArtAttack/shape_type.h:11) which has no case, so any shape reporting NONE throws mid-frame. `Shape::AABB_intersects` (143-151) and the four free `shapes_intersect` / `shapes_AABB_intersect` wrappers (157-175) are equally untested. Every test in the suite calls the concrete free functions (`rectangle_triangle_intersect`, `quad_rectangle_rotated_intersect`, …) directly and bypasses this layer entirely — yet this layer is what `Player::is_colliding`, `CollisionTools::calculate_object_collision_direction` and `bracket_object_collision_generic` actually call. The suite tests the leaves and skips the trunk.
findings.suggestion: Add a `Shape*`-based matrix test: for all 25 ordered pairs of the five concrete shape types, construct one overlapping and one separated pair, call `shapes_intersect(a.get(), b.get())`, and assert symmetry (`a->intersects(b) == b->intersects(a)`) — symmetry alone is a strong oracle and needs no hand-derived expected values.

findings.title: Nine public types in MattMath.h have literally zero tests, including Camera and the entire matrix library
findings.detail:
MattMath.h declares roughly 512 member/free functions; the suite has 33 TEST_METHODs (one empty, two for CollisionTools). Types with no coverage of any kind:
- `MatrixF` + `Matrix3x3F` + free `add/subtract/multiply/divide/gaussian_elimination/transpose/identity/zero/determinant/equal_dimensions` (MattMath.h:684-765, 729-748) — ~40 pure, dependency-free, trivially testable functions. `is_invertible()` (MattMath.cpp:2631-2637) is `determinant(*this) != 0.0f`, exact float comparison on a determinant.
- `Camera` (1007-1045): `calculate_view_rectangle` (4 overloads), `calculate_intermediate_camera`, `calculate_camera_from_view_rectangle`, `calculate_view_position`, `calculate_view_scale`. Every pixel drawn goes through these; a round-trip test (`calculate_camera_from_view_rectangle` then `calculate_view_rectangle` returns the input) is three lines and does not exist.
- `TriangleRightAxisAligned` (895-914): `get_hypotenuse`, `get_hypotenuse_gradient`, `find_hypotenuse` — this is the shape the engine uses for every ramp (LevelObjectBuilder.cpp:144-177).
- `Colour` (586-645), `Vector2I` (354-400), `RectangleI` (508-565), `Viewport` (767-806), `Vector4F`, `Vector3F`: nothing.
- `RectangleF`: ~60 members, and the only thing tested is `rectangles_intersect`. `RectangleF::intersection` is untested despite `CollisionTools::resolve_object_AABB_collision` (CollisionTools.cpp:214) depending on it for every rect-vs-rect push-out.
findings.suggestion: Prioritise by blast radius, not by ease: Camera round-trips, RectangleF::intersection/union_of/contains, TriangleRightAxisAligned::get_hypotenuse, then the matrix library (which is pure and can be tested exhaustively for small sizes against hand-computed 2x2/3x3 results).

findings.title: Colour::saturate and Colour::desaturate are byte-identical; no Colour test exists to notice
findings.suggestion: Add a Colour test class: `set_from_hex("FF0000")` -> (1,0,0,1); `"FF000080"` -> alpha 0.5; `"#FF0000"`, `"GG0000"`, `""` -> defined behaviour (assert the exception or the fallback, but assert *something*); `saturate(2)` and `desaturate(2)` must move in opposite directions.

findings.title: No degenerate, NaN, or exception-path testing anywhere in the suite
findings.detail:
`grep ExpectException MattMathTests/` returns zero hits, and every shape in every test is well-formed with positive dimensions. Reachable, untested failure modes:
- `Vector2F::normalize()` and `normalized()` (MattMath.cpp:1724-1734) divide by length with no zero guard, producing NaN — while `Vector2F::unit_vector` (1852-1863) *does* guard and returns (1,0). Two functions with the same job and opposite behaviour on the same input; nothing pins either.
- `Vector2F::angle_between` (1808-1811) is `acos(dot(a,b) / (a.length()*b.length()))`; for near-parallel vectors the quotient can exceed 1.0 after rounding and `acos` returns NaN. `RectangleRotated::get_angle()` (4460-4462) is built directly on it, so a rotated rect aligned with +x can report a NaN angle.
- `EricsonMath::barycentric` (EricsonMath.cpp:729-743) divides by `denom = d00*d11 - d01*d01`, which is 0 for a collinear/degenerate triangle -> NaN -> `test_point_triangle` (746-752) silently returns false for every point.
- `Triangle::calculate_gradient` (3594-3603) divides by `x1 - x0` — infinite for a vertical edge — and throws for out-of-range indices.
- `Partitioner::partition(n, 0)` (ArtAttack/Partitioner.cpp:7) is integer division by zero.
No test covers zero-area rectangles, negative width/height rectangles (which `rectangle_point_intersect` at MattMath.cpp:252-258 silently treats as empty), zero-radius circles, zero-length segments, or coincident triangle vertices.
findings.suggestion: Add a dedicated `DegenerateInputTests` class: one test per primitive constructed degenerately, asserting either a documented result or a thrown exception. Decide and document whether MattMath is total (returns a sentinel) or partial (throws) — right now it is inconsistently both.

findings.title: Rotation and wraparound behaviour is tested only at the 8 exact axis directions; collinear segment overlap is never tested
findings.detail:
`test_8_cardinal_direction` feeds `direction_to_8_cardinal_direction` exactly the eight vectors that are already the answers. The implementation (ArtAttack/MattMath.cpp:1870-1906) is a chain of half-open angle ranges (`angle >= -PI/8 && angle < PI/8`, `>= PI/8 && < 3PI/8`, …) built on `atan2`, whose range is (-PI, PI]. The sector boundaries and the ±PI wraparound — the only places the chain can fall through or double-count — are untested. The rest of the rotation API (`Vector2F::rotate`, `rotate_vector`, `rotate_vector_by_ref`, `angle`, `angle_between`, `normal`, `unit_vec_from_angle`, `vec_from_angle_magnitude`, `to_radians`/`to_degrees`) has zero tests despite RectangleRotated being built entirely on it.
Separately, `test_segments_intersect` (766-782) claims to cover the identical-segment case, but that only passes because `MattMath::segments_intersect` special-cases `if (a == b)` at MattMath.cpp:565-570. The real gap — *partially overlapping collinear* segments, e.g. (0,0)-(10,0) vs (5,0)-(15,0) — returns **false** from `test_2D_segment_segment` (EricsonMath.cpp:705, `a1*a2 < 0.0f` fails when all signed areas are 0), and no test says whether that is intended.
findings.suggestion: Test `direction_to_8_cardinal_direction` at each sector boundary angle and at ±PI; add a round-trip property test `rotate_vector(v, a) rotated by -a == v`. Add explicit collinear-overlap and shared-endpoint cases for `segments_intersect` and pin whatever the intended answer is.

findings.title: RectangleRotated::operator== / operator!= are declared but never defined; no test uses them
findings.detail: `bool operator==(const RectangleRotated& other) const;` and `operator!=` are declared in the class body but `grep -rn "RectangleRotated::operator" ArtAttack/` returns nothing — there is no definition anywhere in the repo. Every other shape defines its comparison operators (Circle at MattMath.cpp:3351, Triangle at 3538, Quad at 3975, Segment at 4045, RectangleF at 863). This is a latent LNK2019 for the first caller. It has survived because the RectangleRotated tests only compare *intersection results* (bools) and never compare two rotated rectangles for equality — a gap that is itself worth closing, since `clone()` (4276-4279) and `offset()` (4269-4275) can only be meaningfully tested via equality.
findings.suggestion: Define the operators (compare center, both axes, and half-extents with `are_equal`, not `==`), then add tests for `clone()` returning an equal-but-distinct object and `offset()` shifting center and all four points by the same amount.

findings.title: intersect_moving_AABB_AABB: the only swept-collision routine, zero tests and zero call sites
findings.detail: `intersect_moving_AABB_AABB` is 105 lines of continuous-collision maths, half of it commented-out 3D source from the book (lines 551-565), returning `int` literals `0`/`1` through a `bool`. `grep -rn intersect_moving_AABB_AABB ArtAttack/` finds only its declaration (EricsonMath.h:113) and definition — it has no callers. It is also the routine that would fix the engine's tunnelling problem, since `Level::update_level_logic` currently does discrete overlap tests only. It is untested, so nobody can tell whether it works well enough to adopt. Similarly untested and unreachable from the tests: `barycentric`, `test_point_triangle`, `sq_dist_point_AABB`, `test_circle_circle`, `EricsonMath::clamp`, and the 2-arg overloads of `rectangle_circle_intersect`, `circle_triangle_intersect`, `circle_segment_intersect` (only the 3-arg out-param versions are exercised), plus `circle_point_intersect` and `triangle_point_intersect` which have no coverage at all.
findings.suggestion: Either test it (two boxes approaching head-on: assert tfirst; two boxes moving apart: assert false; already-overlapping: assert tfirst==tlast==0) and wire it into the projectile path, or delete it. Dead untested code in a collision library is a liability either way.

findings.title: Tests never run automatically: no CI, PCH configured but empty, versioned NuGet path hardcoded
findings.detail: There is no `.github/`, no pipeline file, no test script anywhere in the repo root — the 33 test methods run only when someone opens Visual Studio and clicks Run All. Neither project sets `TreatWarningAsError`, so nothing enforces the tests or the /W4 warnings. Supporting problems in the test project: all four configs set `<PrecompiledHeader>Use</PrecompiledHeader>` with `<PrecompiledHeaderFile>pch.h</PrecompiledHeaderFile>` against a `pch.h` that contains no includes at all (MattMathTests/pch.h:1-13) — pure build machinery for zero benefit, and a hazard because the code under test does `#include "pch.h"` too (ArtAttack/MattMath.cpp:1, ArtAttack/CollisionTools.cpp:1) which resolves to the *other*, DirectX-configuring `ArtAttack/pch.h`. The include directories hardcode `..\packages\directxtk_desktop_2019.2023.10.31.1\include` (lines 96, 111, 128, 147), which breaks on any package upgrade, and the test project has no packages.config of its own.
findings.suggestion: Add a CI workflow running `msbuild ArtAttack.sln` then `vstest.console.exe UnitTests.dll` on push. Set `PrecompiledHeader=NotUsing` in the test project (or actually populate pch.h). Replace the versioned NuGet path with the `$(...)` property the .targets file defines.

findings.title: Duplicated epsilon constants, shadowed namespaces, and expected values transcribed from the implementation
findings.detail:
`EPSILON_F = 0.000001f` is declared three times: `MathTestConstants::EPSILON_F` (line 14, then `using namespace MathTestConstants` at 19), `MattMathTests::EPSILON_F` (line 154, which shadows it for the whole MattMath test class), and `CollisionToolsTests::EPSILON_F` (MattMathTests/CollisionToolsTests.cpp:10). `TEST_CLASS(MattMathTests)` sits inside `namespace MattMathTests` inside a file that also does `using namespace MattMath` — three near-identical names in scope at once.
On derivation: `test_signed_2D_tri_area` (61-75) asserts `signed_2D_tri_area(a, b, c) == 100.0f` for a triangle with legs of 10 — whose area is 50. The function returns *twice* the signed area (EricsonMath.cpp:686-692 says so in a comment), so the expected value was read off the implementation rather than derived; the test's own comment ("a, b, c are in counter-clockwise order") is also wrong for this y-down coordinate system, where (0,0),(10,0),(0,10) is clockwise. A reader cannot tell from the test what the function is supposed to return.
findings.suggestion: One shared `test_constants.h` with a single tolerance. Rename the test namespace (e.g. `mattmath_tests`). Write expected values as expressions that show the derivation (`2.0f * 0.5f * 10.0f * 10.0f`) and fix the winding comments.

findings.title: Six ramp source files are 100% commented out yet still compiled and listed in the vcxproj
findings.detail: `StructureRamp.h/.cpp`, `StructureRampLeft.h/.cpp`, `StructureRampRight.h/.cpp` contain nothing but `//`-prefixed lines (every line of all six files except `#include "pch.h"` at the top of each .cpp). They are still declared in `ArtAttack/ArtAttack.vcxproj:252-254` (`<ClInclude>`) and `:348-350` (`<ClCompile>`), and in `ArtAttack.vcxproj.filters`. Every build therefore compiles three empty translation units. `LevelObjectBuilder.h:10-11` also carries the corresponding `//#include "StructureRampLeft.h"` / `//#include "StructureRampRight.h"` lines. Ramps are actually built as plain `Structure` with a `TriangleRightAxisAligned` in `LevelObjectBuilder.cpp:144-176`, so the class hierarchy these files describe was abandoned.
findings.suggestion: Delete all six files and their vcxproj/filters entries and the two commented includes in LevelObjectBuilder.h. If the ramp abstraction is wanted later, recover it from git history — that is what history is for.

findings.title: An entire unused linear-algebra sublibrary (MatrixF / Matrix3x3F / Vector4F) lives in the core math header
findings.detail: `MattMath.h:567-584` (Vector4F), `:684-748` (MatrixF + free functions `add/subtract/multiply/divide/gaussian_elimination/transpose/identity/zero/determinant/equal_dimensions`) and `:750-765` (Matrix3x3F) are implemented in `MattMath.cpp` `#pragma region Vector4F` (2142-2183), `#pragma region MatrixF` (2476-2983) and `#pragma region Matrix3x3F` (2985-3050) — roughly 615 lines of live code. I grepped every first-party file: `MatrixF`, `Matrix3x3F`, `VectorF`, `Vector4F`, `gaussian_elimination`, `determinant`, `transpose`, `identity`, `eigenvectors` have **zero** references outside MattMath.h/.cpp, including in MattMathTests. Immediately above it sits `#pragma region Matrix` (MattMath.cpp:1138-1306) and `#pragma region Vector` (:1308-1366) — 231 further lines that are entirely commented out, matching the commented-out `template<typename T> struct Matrix`/`struct Vector` declarations at `MattMath.h:303-352`. So the same abandoned idea exists in the file twice, once dead-by-comment and once dead-by-disuse. MattMath.h is the header every engine type includes, so this is compile cost paid by all 81 TUs.
findings.suggestion: Delete Vector4F, MatrixF, Matrix3x3F, the commented Matrix/Vector template blocks, and the `#pragma region Matrix`/`Vector` blocks in the .cpp. If a general matrix type is wanted for the engine later, it belongs in its own header with tests, not welded into the 1139-line MattMath.h that every game object pulls in.

findings.title: Collision-type predicates are written and never called, while call sites re-implement them as shadowing locals
findings.detail: `is_player` (:31), `is_dead_player` (:37), `is_team_a_projectile` (:57) and `is_team_b_projectile` (:66) have **zero** call sites anywhere in ArtAttack/ or MattMathTests/. Only `is_projectile` and `is_structure` are used at all (2 and 2 sites). Worse, the code that should be using them re-implements them by hand and shadows them: `Level.cpp:665-676` declares `bool is_projectile = type == PROJECTILE_SPRAY_TEAM_A || ... || type == PROJECTILE_MIST_TEAM_B;` — a local variable with the same name as the inline function declared in the header the file includes, spelling out the identical 10-term disjunction. The same shadowing pattern appears at `Player.cpp:271-272`, where `bool is_on_ramp = get_move_state() == ON_RAMP_LEFT || ... == ON_RAMP_RIGHT;` shadows the member function `Player::is_on_ramp()` (Player.cpp:1246) and is then never read (a /W4 C4189 unreferenced-local). Team-membership checks are likewise hand-written in `Player::on_collision` (Player.cpp:186-244) and `PaintTile::on_collision` (PaintTile.cpp:114-140) instead of calling `is_team_a_projectile`/`is_team_b_projectile`.
findings.suggestion: Replace the hand-rolled chains in Level.cpp:658-682, Player.cpp:186-244 and PaintTile.cpp:114-140 with calls to the existing predicates, then delete the shadowing locals. Longer term this whole flat 23-value enum is game logic sitting in an engine interface (ICollisionGameObject.h:12-16) and should be replaced by a type-id + team pair or virtual dispatch.

findings.title: Level has four write-only members, including a complete spawn-point pipeline that terminates in nothing
findings.detail: `Level.h:136-137` declare `std::vector<Vector2F> _team_a_spawns` / `_team_b_spawns`. They are initialised at `Level.cpp:47-48` from constructor parameters (`Level.cpp:18-19`), which are fed by `LevelBuilder.cpp:70-71` from `LevelLoadedInfo::get_team_a_spawns()/get_team_b_spawns()` (`LevelLoadedInfo.cpp:19-27`), which parse `"spawn_locations"` out of the level JSON via `decode_team_spawns_json` (`LevelLoadedInfo.cpp:86-93`). Neither member is ever read — grep for `_team_a_spawns` returns exactly the ctor-init and the declaration. A whole JSON→builder→object data path exists to populate two vectors nobody looks at (players actually respawn from `Player::_respawn_position`, set in PlayerBuilder). Same file: `_level_name` (`Level.h:116`, set at `Level.cpp:37`) is never read, and `std::vector<PlayerInputData> _player_inputs` (`Level.h:143`) is never touched at all — not written, not read.
findings.suggestion: Either wire spawn points into respawn (the obviously intended behaviour) or delete the member, the ctor parameters, the LevelBuilder plumbing, and LevelLoadedInfo::get_team_a_spawns/get_team_b_spawns/decode_team_spawns_json. Delete `_level_name` and `_player_inputs` outright.

findings.title: SpriteFrame stores three fields it never exposes, silently discarding per-frame origin and rotation from the atlas JSON
findings.detail: `SpriteFrame` has exactly one accessor, `get_source_rectangle()` (SpriteFrame.h:19). Its private members `_origin` (:24) and `_rotated` (:25) are written in both constructors (`SpriteFrame.cpp:11-12, 18-19`) and never read by anything. `_source_rectangle2` (:23) is never written *or* read — grep returns one hit, the declaration. Upstream, `SpriteSheet.cpp:27-44` goes to the trouble of parsing `frame["origin"]["x"]`, `frame["origin"]["y"]` and `frame["rotated"]` out of `sprite_sheet_1.json` and passing them into the constructor. So the sprite-atlas format supports rotated/offset frames, the loader reads them, and the data is dropped on the floor — a second dead data pipeline in the same codebase.
findings.suggestion: Delete `_source_rectangle2`. Then either add `get_origin()`/`is_rotated()` and honour them in SpriteSheet's draw calls (which is what the atlas format implies), or delete `_origin`/`_rotated` and stop parsing them in SpriteSheet.cpp:27-44.

findings.title: AnimatedSprite is a whole class superseded by AnimationObject and never instantiated
findings.detail: `AnimatedSprite` (AnimatedSprite.h, 48 lines; AnimatedSprite.cpp, 125 lines) is referenced exactly once outside its own two files: an `#include "AnimatedSprite.h"` at `AnimationObject.h:5` — and `AnimationObject` does not use it. `AnimationObject` (AnimationObject.h:7-56) is a verbatim re-implementation: identical private state (`_frame_index`, `_paused`, `_time_elapsed` vs AnimatedSprite.h:44-47) and an identical method set (`update/reset/stop/play/pause/set_frame_index/is_paused/set_animation_strip*`). Both files are compiled into every build (ArtAttack.vcxproj).
findings.suggestion: Delete AnimatedSprite.h/.cpp, the include at AnimationObject.h:5, and the vcxproj/filters entries. (Note the newer copy is the worse one — AnimationObject makes the animation state a base-class mixin inherited into Player and Projectile rather than a component; that is a separate design problem.)

findings.title: Three headers are in the project and included by nothing at all
findings.detail: I searched every .cpp and .h under ArtAttack/ for `#include "<name>"`. Three headers have zero includers: `dimension.h` (enum class dimension {X, Y}), `direction.h` (enum class direction {TOP_LEFT..BOTTOM_RIGHT}) and `direction_lock.h` (enum class direction_lock {LOCKED, UNLOCKED}). The enum names themselves also appear nowhere else — `grep -rn "\bdimension\b"` returns only the declaration. All three are listed in ArtAttack.vcxproj and .filters, so they show up in the Solution Explorer as if they were live engine types. `direction.h` is additionally a name collision trap: `MattMath.h:12` declares a *different* `direction`-flavoured concept, and a future `#include "direction.h"` would be ambiguous with it.
findings.suggestion: Delete dimension.h, direction.h and direction_lock.h and their vcxproj/filters entries.

findings.title: ~140 functions are declared and defined but never called; the largest clusters are Drawer, MovingObject, Colour and MattMath
findings.detail:
I extracted every identifier followed by `(` from ArtAttack/*.h and counted occurrences across all first-party .cpp/.h; ~140 names occur exactly twice (declaration + definition) and are therefore never called. Representative clusters:

- `Drawer.h:14-25`: `set_resource_manager`, `set_dt`, and **both** overloads of `calculate_draw_rectangle` (Drawer.cpp:33-53). The latter take `const Vector3F& camera` — a leftover x/y/zoom camera model replaced by `MattMath::Camera`; `Vector3F` now appears nowhere else in the codebase except these four signatures.
- `MovingObject.h:25-51`: `alter_velocity`, `alter_dx`, `alter_dx_x/y`, `alter_rotation`, `get_unit_velocity`, `get_velocity_magnitude`, `get_velocity_angle`, `get_unit_dx`, `get_dx_magnitude`, `get_dx_angle` — all `protected virtual`, none overridden, none called.
- `MattMath.h:616-641` (Colour): `get_red/green/blue/alpha`, `set_red/green/blue/alpha`, `saturate`, `desaturate`, `brighten`, `darken`, `invert`, `make_opaque`, `make_transparent`, `get_sm_colour`.
- One-offs: `GameData.h:46 get_game_data()` (returns `this`), `MenuData.h:14 get_menu_data()` (same), `ResourceLoader.h:19 load_texture_from_directory` (ResourceLoader.cpp:75-81 — its logic was inlined into `load_sprite_sheet_from_directory` at :131 instead), `ThreadPool.h:18 get_min_num_threads`, `Save.h:23 get_save_data`, `TeamColour.h:51 get_team_colours`, `MenuLevelSettings.h:18 get_game_mode`, `ResultsMenuData.h:15 set_level_end_info`, `Mh.h:39-41 remove_all_children/get_child_count/get_children`, `ViewportManager.h:26 get_layout`, `ViewportManager.h:43 get_fullscreen_d3d11_viewport`, `MattMath.h:790 get_d3d_viewport_ptr`.
- Two are dead stubs: `Level.h:152 draw_end_screen` (Level.cpp:696-699, body is `// TODO`) and `DrawObject.h:33 set_draw_rotation_by_rectangle_rotated` (DrawObject.cpp:66-69, body is `// TODO: Implement this function`).
findings.suggestion: Delete them. The systemic cause is a reflex of writing a get/set pair for every field before there is a caller (182 setters / 344 const getters across the headers) — for a reusable engine the public surface should be driven by what callers actually need, and `protected virtual` one-liners that nothing overrides are pure vtable cost.

findings.title: The precompiled header pulls in 13 unused DirectXTK headers, including the two heaviest ones
findings.detail: `pch.h:59-77` includes 19 DirectXTK headers. I grepped every first-party file (excluding pch.h and the vendor-supplied DeviceResources.cpp) for the identifying symbols of each. Zero hits for: `Model.h` (`Model`), `Effects.h` (`BasicEffect`/`IEffect`/`EffectFactory`), `GeometricPrimitive.h`, `PostProcess.h`, `PrimitiveBatch.h`, `ScreenGrab.h` (`SaveDDSTextureToFile`/`SaveWICTextureToFile`), `BufferHelpers.h` (`CreateStaticBuffer`/`ConstantBuffer`), `VertexTypes.h` (`VertexPosition*`), `WICTextureLoader.h` (`CreateWICTextureFromFile`), `Keyboard.h`, `Mouse.h`, `GraphicsMemory.h`, `DirectXHelpers.h` (`CreateShaderResourceView`/`SetDebugObjectName`/`MapGuard`). `Model.h` and `Effects.h` are the two largest headers in DirectXTK and they are 3D-only; this project is 2D sprite rendering. Every one of the 81 translation units pays for them.
