findings.suggestion: Cut pch.h down to what is used: CommonStates, DDSTextureLoader, GamePad, SimpleMath, SpriteBatch, SpriteFont, Audio. Also note `MattMathTests/pch.h` is an empty stub (12 lines, no includes) while `PrecompiledHeader=Use` is set in MattMathTests.vcxproj:93,108,123,142 — a PCH that precompiles nothing.

findings.title: Colour.h is a 469-line header-only blob of internal-linkage objects reaching most of the codebase, of which 130 of 153 colours are unused
findings.detail: `Colour.h` declares 153 namespace-scope `const std::string` HTML codes (`:10-467` inside `namespace html`, closing at `:158`), then 153 namespace-scope `const MattMath::Colour` objects built from them (`:160-313`), then a 152-line `static MattMath::Colour colour_from_name(const std::string& name)` (`:315-466`) that is a flat chain of 153 `if (name == "ALICE_BLUE") return colour_consts::ALICE_BLUE;` lines. Namespace-scope `const` in C++ has internal linkage, so **every TU that includes this header gets its own copy of all 306 objects plus its own copy of `colour_from_name`**, and pays a dynamic-initialisation pass at startup for 153 `std::string` constructions plus 153 hex-parsing `Colour` constructions. It reaches most of the codebase because `DrawObject.h:4` includes it, and DrawObject is the base of every drawable. Actual demand: only 23 distinct `colour_consts::X` names appear anywhere outside Colour.h itself, and the three shipped level JSONs between them use exactly 7 colour names (SADDLE_BROWN, TAN, GREY, WHITE, LIGHT_SKY_BLUE, DARK_GREY, DARK_SLATE_GREY). Because `colour_from_name` is `static` in a header, any TU that includes Colour.h without calling it also emits /W4 C4505.
findings.suggestion: Move the table into Colour.cpp behind a single `const Colour& colour_from_name(std::string_view)` that looks up a `static const std::unordered_map`, and make the handful of genuinely-referenced colours `inline constexpr` (C++17) so there is one object, not one per TU. The full 153-colour HTML table is a library concern, not something to paste into an engine header.

findings.title: Window resize handling is a no-op function whose entire body is an unused local
findings.suggestion: Either implement it (re-create the SpriteBatch pool and re-derive viewports from the new output size) or delete the function and its three call sites so the gap is visible rather than disguised as handled.

findings.title: ProjectileRolling is invisible by construction, making both of its draw overrides unreachable
findings.suggestion: If invisible is intentional, delete both draw overrides and add a one-line comment on `is_visible_in_viewport` saying why. If not, this is a missing feature that the empty bodies are hiding.

findings.title: Left-ramp collision is an empty `// TODO` branch while right-ramp is fully implemented
findings.suggestion: Either implement the mirrored case (it is the RIGHT block with the x-direction flipped) or make `LevelObjectBuilder` throw on STRUCTURE_RAMP_LEFT so the gap fails loudly at load time instead of at play time.

findings.title: ~2000 commented-out lines across the tree, 7% of the whole first-party codebase
findings.detail:
2007 of the 27,999 first-party lines are `//`-only. The large contiguous blocks, all of which are superseded implementations left in place beside their replacements:
- `EricsonMath.cpp:7-126` (120) and `:129-280` (152) — an old `Vector`/`AABB`/`Sphere` type set, plus `EricsonMath.h:13-73` (61 lines) of matching declarations.
- `MattMath.cpp:1138-1306` + `:1308-1366` (231) — the commented `Matrix`/`Vector` templates, matching `MattMath.h:303-352`.
- `Level.cpp:402-490` (89) — the previous single-threaded `draw_active_level`, sitting directly under the live deferred-context version at `:375-400`; and `Level.cpp:331-353` — the previous `Level::draw()`.
- `Player.cpp:391-483` (93) — the previous `on_structure_collision` body, above the live one at `:488`.
- `StructurePaintable.cpp:123-180` (58) — the previous edge-walking paint-tile generator.
- `Main.cpp:39-81` (43) — `get_adapters()`/`get_outputs()`/`get_adapter0_output0_rect()`; `Main.cpp:368-374+` — the ALT+ENTER fullscreen toggle.
- `MainMenu.cpp:55` — `//this->_music->Stop();`, the only reference to the member `MainMenu.h:138 std::unique_ptr<SoundEffectInstance> _music`, which is otherwise never assigned or used.
Having the old and new implementation of the same function adjacent in the same file is actively misleading when reading the code.
findings.suggestion: Delete all of it. It is in git. The specific hazard here is not disk space but that a reader of Level.cpp or Player.cpp cannot tell which of the two bodies is authoritative without checking indentation.

findings.title: Roughly 20 MB of superseded and source-only assets are tracked, including four parallel 'unused' directories
findings.detail:
`ResourceLoader::load_textures()` (ResourceLoader.cpp:17-20) loads exactly one thing: `./textures/sprite_sheet_1.dds` (+ `.json`). Everything else under the asset tree is dead weight tracked in git:
- `ArtAttack/textures/old textures/` — 41 `.dds` + matching `.png` pairs, 8.3 MB, superseded by the atlas.
- `ArtAttack/textures/sprite_sheet_1.png` (9.1 MB) and `sprite_sheet_1.xcf` (176 KB, GIMP project) sitting in the *runtime* asset directory next to the 2.2 MB `.dds` that is actually loaded.
- `ArtAttack/textures/new player textures/` — 13 PNGs, referenced by nothing.
- `ArtAttack/fonts/unuseed fonts/` [sic] — 24 `.spritefont` files, 2.4 MB. `ResourceLoader::load_fonts()` (ResourceLoader.cpp:21-33) loads 7, all from `fonts/`.
- `ArtAttack/levels/unused/` — base.json, level_0.json, structure_test_old.json, test_1.json.
- `ArtAttack/levels/*.pub` — three 113-121 KB Microsoft Publisher documents (352 KB total), one of them misspelled `turebulence.pub` against `turbulence.json`. Nothing in the code opens `.pub`.
- `ArtAttack/sounds/unused/wave_bank_1.json` — an obsolete copy of the sound-bank schema.
- `ArtAttack/save/save_data.txt` — a legacy two-line save format (`1920x1080` / `false`) alongside the live `save_data.json`. `directory_consts.h:11` only knows about the .json; nothing reads the .txt.
findings.suggestion: Delete all of the above from the working tree. Move genuine source art (the .xcf, the source PNGs) out of the runtime asset directory into an `art/` folder outside the copy-to-output path, or out of the repo entirely. A directory named 'unused' checked into a repo is a decision that was deferred rather than made.

findings.title: Three third-party tool EXEs and their cmd.txt notes are committed, while the audio assets they produce are gitignored — the app cannot run from a clone
findings.detail:
Committed binaries: `ArtAttack/textures/texconv.exe` (944 KB), `ArtAttack/fonts/MakeSpriteFont.exe` (41 KB), `ArtAttack/sounds/sound_bank_1/XWBTool.exe` (110 KB). Each sits beside a `cmd.txt` holding the single command line that was run by hand — e.g. `ArtAttack/textures/cmd.txt`: `texconv sprite_sheet_1.png -pmalpha -m 1 -f BC3_UNORM`; `ArtAttack/sounds/sound_bank_1/cmd.txt`: the 24-file `XWBTool -f -o sound_bank_1.xwb ...` invocation. That is an asset build pipeline stored as a note-to-self.

The consequence is worse than untidiness: `.gitignore:366-368` ignores `*.wav`, `*.xwb`, `*.mp3`, so `sounds/sound_bank_1/sound_bank_1.xwb` is not in the repo — and it is not in the working tree either (`sounds/sound_bank_1/` contains only XWBTool.exe and cmd.txt). `ResourceLoader.cpp:35` calls `load_sound_bank_from_directory(SOUNDS_DIRECTORY, "sound_bank_1")`, which builds `./sounds/sound_bank_1.xwb` at `:172` and loads it unconditionally during `load_all_resources()`. The tool to rebuild it is committed; the 24 `.wav` inputs are not. So a fresh clone cannot start, and neither can this working tree.

Also in the pile: `ArtAttack/sounds/sound list.txt`, a hand-maintained scratch list of which sounds are 'DONE' with entries like `Title\t?????` — and sure enough `MainMenu.h:78 TITLE_SOUND` is declared and never referenced.
findings.suggestion: Get the tools from a package (they ship with DirectXTK/DirectXTex) and turn the cmd.txt contents into an actual asset-build step (a script or a vcxproj custom build step), then delete the EXEs and cmd.txt files. Decide whether audio is source-controlled: either un-ignore the .wav/.xwb and commit them, or document how to obtain them. Right now the repo is not buildable-and-runnable by anyone, including its author.

findings.title: Three includes have the wrong case and only compile because NTFS is case-insensitive
findings.detail: `Level.cpp:2` is `#include "level.h"` — the file is `Level.h`. `InterfaceGameplay.h:7` and `TeamColour.h:5` are both `#include "colour.h"` — the file is `Colour.h`. These resolve on Windows and fail on any case-sensitive filesystem. For a project whose stated goal is a reusable engine, this is a hard block on ever building it anywhere but Windows, and it is the kind of thing that only surfaces after someone has invested a day in a port.
findings.suggestion: Fix the three include spellings. Worth a one-off audit: `grep -rn '#include "[a-z]' ArtAttack/` and check each hit against the actual filename.

findings.title: The DirectXTK project template's TODO comments were never cleaned up and now misdescribe the code
findings.detail:
Twelve of the fifteen TODOs in the codebase are untouched boilerplate from the DirectX 11 VS template: `Game.cpp:17` ('TODO: Provide parameters for swapchain format...'), `:62` ('TODO: Change the timer settings if you want something other than the default variable timestep mode' — the line above it *does* set fixed timestep, so the comment is now false), `:159, :167, :173, :183` (in `on_activated`/`on_deactivated`/`on_suspending`/`on_resuming`, all of which are implemented), `:204, :222, :271`; `Main.cpp:181, :200, :240`. They make it impossible to tell template scaffolding from real work items.

The three TODOs that *are* real all mark unimplemented functions: `DrawObject.cpp:68` (`set_draw_rotation_by_rectangle_rotated`, empty, never called), `Level.cpp:698` (`draw_end_screen`, empty, never called), `Mh.cpp:280` and `:345` ('TODO: implement text bounding box' — which is why `MWidget` size queries on text are unreliable). `Player.cpp:276` is the left-ramp gap reported separately.
findings.suggestion: Delete the twelve template TODOs. Keep only real work items, and where the work item is 'this function does nothing', delete the function instead of the comment.

findings.title: Three game modes, four weapon types and three collision-object types exist in enums with no implementation anywhere
findings.detail: `level_mode.h` declares STANDARD_MODE / TEAM_DEATHMATCH / DEATHMATCH / PRACTICE. `MainMenu.cpp:667` unconditionally calls `set_game_mode(level_mode::STANDARD_MODE)`; `MenuLevelSettings::get_game_mode()` (MenuLevelSettings.cpp:37) is never called by anything, so the mode is written and never read; `MainMenuModeSelect::convert_mode_to_element` (MainMenu.cpp:744-758), which switches over all four, is itself never called. Similarly `wep_type::MINE`, `CURLING` and `WATER` (wep_type.h:12-14) have zero references outside the enum, and `WeaponBuilder::build_weapon` throws on anything but the five real weapons. `collision_object_type::POWER_UP`, `DEFAULT` and `NONE` (collision_object_type.h:26-28) are never produced by any object. `Player::_secondary_type` (Player.h:159) is set from `PlayerBuilder.cpp:55` to `wep_type::GRENADE_STD` and never read; `PlayerInputData::secondary_shoot` (PlayerInputData.h:16) is read off the gamepad right-shoulder at `PlayerInput.cpp:30` and consumed by nobody — the whole secondary-weapon feature is an unwired stub.
findings.suggestion: Trim the enums to what is implemented. Aspirational enum values are worse than a TODO because switch statements and if-chains grow branches for them (MainMenu.cpp:744-758) that can never execute, and readers cannot tell reachable from unreachable.

findings.title: Every render worker draws every object, and draw() mutates the object — guaranteed data race
findings.suggestion: Split the render pass into a lock-free shape: (1) make `draw` a `const` operation on immutable per-frame state — move all the animation/effect/name mutation out of `draw` and into `update`, which runs single-threaded; (2) have each task record only its own slice, i.e. per-viewport visibility should not require re-walking global containers from N threads mutating shared objects. Longer term, produce an immutable per-frame render packet list during update and let workers consume it read-only.

findings.title: No exception barrier in the thread-pool callback — any task exception terminates the process and leaks the task
findings.suggestion: Wrap the invocation: `try { (*task)(); } catch (...) { /* capture into a per-task std::exception_ptr */ }` and store the `std::unique_ptr<std::function<void()>>` so the delete is exception-safe. Change `add_task` to return a handle (or `std::future<void>`) and have `wait_for_tasks_to_complete` rethrow the first captured exception on the calling thread.

findings.title: Device restore re-creates every engine service while live objects hold stale raw pointers to the old ones
findings.detail:
`Game::OnDeviceRestored()` (Game.cpp:282-287) calls `create_device_dependent_resources()` a second time. That function reallocates essentially the whole service layer and republishes it into `GameData`:

```cpp
this->_thread_pool = std::make_unique<ThreadPool>(...);      // :236  old pool freed
this->_resource_manager = std::make_unique<ResourceManager>(); // :239 old cache freed
this->_dt = std::make_unique<float>(0.f);                     // :244 old float freed
this->_viewport_manager = std::make_unique<ViewportManager>(...); // :247
this->_partitioner = std::make_unique<Partitioner>();          // :255
```

But every consumer cached a raw copy at construction time, not a handle to `GameData`. `Level` alone caches five of them (Level.h:117-119, 140, 146-147): `_viewport_manager`, `_resource_manager`, `_dt`, `_thread_pool`, `_partitioner`. `MenuData`/`GameData(const GameData*)` (GameData.cpp:4-20) takes a *snapshot copy* of all twelve pointers, so every menu page holds a second stale set. `const float* _dt` is threaded into ~26 headers (Player.h, Drawer.h, AnimationObject.h:49, ...).

After any device reset (driver update, TDR, `DXGI_ERROR_DEVICE_REMOVED` from `Present`, DeviceResources.cpp:485-493) the running `Level` dereferences a freed `float` every frame and calls into a freed `ThreadPool` and `ResourceManager`. Nothing in the codebase re-seeds those cached pointers.

The root cause is architectural: `GameData` (GameData.h:49-61) is a bag of 12 raw non-owning pointers used as a service locator, with no lifetime contract and no indirection through which owners can be swapped.
findings.suggestion: Split `create_device_dependent_resources` so that only genuinely device-dependent objects (SpriteBatches, CommonStates, textures) are recreated on restore; `_dt`, `_thread_pool`, `_partitioner`, `_resource_manager` and `_viewport_manager` must be created once in `initialize`. Better: stop passing frame time as `const float*` entirely (pass `float dt` to `update`), and hand out services as references resolved per-call from a single owner rather than cached raw pointers.

findings.title: 16 deferred contexts are raw COM pointers: never Released, never recreated on device loss
findings.suggestion: Store them as `std::vector<Microsoft::WRL::ComPtr<ID3D11DeviceContext>>` (drop the pointless `unique_ptr<vector<...>>` indirection), clear the vector at the top of `create_deferred_contexts`, and call `create_deferred_contexts` from `HandleDeviceLost` after `CreateDeviceResources()` — or make it part of `CreateDeviceResources` itself.

findings.title: Resource "getters" use map::operator[] — mutating lookup from render threads, dead catch blocks, silent nullptr on typo
findings.suggestion: Make all lookups `const` and use `find()`/`at()` with an explicit not-found path that throws a descriptive exception (or returns an engine-level `Result`). Mark the accessors `const`, which also makes the concurrent-read safety self-documenting. Delete the unreachable try/catch blocks. Consider interning resource names to integer handles so lookups are not string-keyed map probes on the render hot path.

findings.title: ThreadPool owns raw OS handles with a user destructor but implicitly-defaulted copy/move — double-free waiting to happen
findings.detail:
`ThreadPool` holds `PTP_POOL _pool`, `PTP_CLEANUP_GROUP _cleanup_group`, `TP_CALLBACK_ENVIRON _callback_environment`, and `std::vector<PTP_WORK> _work_items` (ThreadPool.h:27-30), declares `~ThreadPool()` which closes all of them (ThreadPool.cpp:30-36), and declares **no** copy/move operations. So copy construction and copy assignment are implicitly generated and shallow: two `ThreadPool` objects would own the same `PTP_POOL`/`PTP_CLEANUP_GROUP` and both destructors would call `CloseThreadpoolCleanupGroup`/`CloseThreadpool` on them.

Moving is worse than a plain double-free: `add_task` passes `&_callback_environment` to `CreateThreadpoolWork` (ThreadPool.cpp:41), so every outstanding work item holds the *address* of a member of the specific `ThreadPool` object. Any move (or the vector reallocation that a `std::vector<ThreadPool>` would perform) leaves live work items pointing at a dead callback environment.

Today it survives only because there is exactly one instance and it lives in a `unique_ptr` (Game.h:71) — accident, not design. For a reusable engine component this is exactly the class that must state its ownership contract.
findings.suggestion: `ThreadPool(const ThreadPool&) = delete; ThreadPool& operator=(const ThreadPool&) = delete;` and either delete the moves too or implement them properly (nulling the source handles). Better still, wrap each handle in a small RAII type so the destructor becomes `= default` and the rule of zero applies.

findings.title: add_task is not thread-safe, leaks the task closure on failure, and copies the std::function twice
findings.suggestion: Take the task by value and `std::move` it into a `std::unique_ptr<std::function<void()>>`; release it into the callback only after `CreateThreadpoolWork` succeeds. Guard `_work_items` with a `std::mutex` (or document single-producer as a hard precondition and assert it). Return a handle/`std::future` from `add_task`.

findings.title: Zoom-out draw spawns one task then immediately waits — and that worker drives the immediate context and mutates ViewportManager
findings.suggestion: Run the zoom-out path inline on the calling thread (no pool involvement), pass the deferred context explicitly so the immediate-context overload of `apply_player_viewport` is never reachable from a worker, and delete the unused `num_threads`. Move `set_layout` out of the draw path into the state transition that actually changes the layout.

findings.title: Process-wide globals and WndProc statics make a second engine instance impossible
findings.suggestion: Move the four globals into a local scope in `wWinMain` and store the engine pointer in `GWLP_USERDATA` only (it already is, Main.cpp:250) — then move the four `static bool`s into a per-window struct hanging off `GWLP_USERDATA`. Make the window-class name and asset roots configuration passed into engine init rather than header constants. Delete `g_screen_resolution` (unused) and `s_fullscreen` (dead).

findings.title: get_deferred_context is declared noexcept but throws — guaranteed std::terminate on a bad index
findings.suggestion: Drop the `noexcept` (and let it throw), or keep `noexcept` and return `nullptr` on a bad index. Cast the size: `index >= static_cast<int>(...->size())`. Add a null check on `_deferred_contexts`.

findings.title: ~300 dynamically-initialised namespace-scope objects plus a 150-branch static function, duplicated into every TU
findings.detail:
`Colour.h` is included transitively by almost every source file and contains, at namespace scope:

- 149 `const std::string` hex literals (Colour.h:10-158)
- 153 `const MattMath::Colour X = { html::X };` (Colour.h:160-312)

`Colour`'s constructor takes a `std::string` and parses hex at runtime, and `Vector2F`/`Colour` constructors are non-constexpr out-of-line functions (MattMath.h:407-413 shows the same pattern for `Vector2F`). `const` at namespace scope gives internal linkage, so **every one of the ~81 translation units gets its own private copy** of all 302 objects, each with its own dynamic initialiser. That is roughly 12,000 `std::string` constructions and 12,000 hex parses executed before `wWinMain`, plus the corresponding `.bss`/init-array bloat.

Worse, Colour.h:315-467 defines

```cpp
static MattMath::Colour colour_from_name(const std::string& name)
{
    if (name == "ALICE_BLUE") return colour_consts::ALICE_BLUE;
    ... ~150 more string comparisons ...
}
```

A 150-branch string-comparison chain compiled into every TU that includes the header, and O(n) at runtime.

The same header-constant idiom is repeated in `player_consts.h:20-63`, `interface_consts` (InterfaceGameplay.h:15-34), `viewport_consts` (ViewportManager.h:12-15), `MainMenu.h`, `Level.h:35-51` — with inconsistent spellings (`const` vs `const static`) that make no difference here but signal the author wasn't sure.
findings.suggestion: Give `Colour` a `constexpr` constructor over `uint8_t` channels and declare the constants `inline constexpr` (requires C++17 — the vcxproj sets no `<LanguageStandard>` so it is on the C++14 default; bumping to /std:c++20 is safe, there are zero C++17 idioms in the tree today). Move `colour_from_name` into a .cpp behind a single static lookup table. Delete the 149 hex strings entirely once colours are numeric.

findings.title: Cross-TU static initialisation order dependency on MattMath's dynamically-initialised class statics
findings.detail:
```cpp
const static MattMath::Vector2F DEBUG_POSITION = MattMath::Vector2F::ZERO;
```

`Vector2F::ZERO` is a class static declared at MattMath.h:488 and **defined in a different translation unit**, MattMath.cpp:1907: `const Vector2F Vector2F::ZERO = { 0.0f, 0.0f };`. Because `Vector2F` has user-provided, non-`constexpr`, out-of-line constructors (MattMath.h:407-413, defined in MattMath.cpp), it is not an aggregate and that definition is *dynamically* initialised, not constant-initialised.

So `DEBUG_POSITION` — an internal-linkage object created afresh in every TU that includes DebugText.h — has a dynamic initialiser that reads a dynamically-initialised object from another TU, with no ordering guarantee. It currently "works" only because zero-initialisation happens first and the intended value is also zero; the bug is invisible until someone writes `const static Vector2F FOO = Vector2F::ONE;` (MattMath.cpp:1908) or similar with a non-zero value.

The same class-static-with-dynamic-init pattern covers `RectangleF::ZERO` (MattMath.cpp:1134), `Vector2I::ZERO` (:1495), `Vector2F::ONE` (:1908), `RectangleI::ZERO` (:2138), `Camera::DEFAULT_CAMERA` (:4180 — itself initialised from `Vector2F::ZERO`, safe only because it is later in the same file).
findings.suggestion: Make `Vector2F`, `RectangleF`, `Colour` etc. literal types with `constexpr` constructors and declare the well-known values `static constexpr` in-class. Then all of these become constant-initialised and the ordering question disappears. As an interim fix, replace `DEBUG_POSITION = MattMath::Vector2F::ZERO` with `{ 0.0f, 0.0f }`.

findings.title: com_exception::what() returns a pointer to a shared static buffer it rewrites on every call
findings.suggestion: Store the formatted message in a `std::string` member built in the constructor and return `_msg.c_str()` — or derive from `std::runtime_error` and pass the formatted string to its constructor, which is what the modern DirectXTK template does.

findings.title: Thread count hardcoded to 16 at global namespace scope; real parallelism is capped at 4 and never measured
findings.suggestion: Move these into a namespaced engine-config struct supplied at init (default `std::thread::hardware_concurrency()`), size the deferred-context/SpriteBatch pool to the actual number of parallel render targets needed, and validate/clamp the ThreadPool constructor arguments. Guard `Partitioner::partition` against `num_partitions <= 0`.

findings.title: Partition index doubles as object index and as deferred-context / SpriteBatch / command-list index
findings.suggestion: Give each worker a single `RenderThreadContext { ID3D11DeviceContext*; SpriteBatch*; ID3D11CommandList** }` selected by *thread/partition* index, and iterate objects with a separate index. Then the number of drawables is decoupled from the size of the deferred-context pool. Pick one `FinishCommandList`/`ExecuteCommandList` restore policy and document it.

findings.title: Member declaration order destroys the ThreadPool after the resources its tasks use, and before the objects that hold pointers to it
findings.detail:
Members are destroyed in reverse declaration order. Declared order is `_device_resources`(59) … `_state`(67) … `_thread_pool`(71), `_sprite_batches`(72), `_sprite_batches_ptrs`(73), `_audio_engine`(74), `_partitioner`(75). So destruction is:

`_partitioner` → `_audio_engine` → `_sprite_batches_ptrs` → `_sprite_batches` → **`_thread_pool`** → `_data` → `_viewport_manager` → `_gamepad` → **`_state`** → `_dt` → `_resource_manager` → … → `_device_resources`.

Two inversions:
1. `_sprite_batches` (and `_partitioner`, `_audio_engine`) are destroyed **before** `~ThreadPool`. `~ThreadPool` calls `CloseThreadpoolCleanupGroupMembers(_cleanup_group, FALSE, nullptr)` (ThreadPool.cpp:32), i.e. it *waits* for outstanding callbacks — callbacks that would be running against already-freed SpriteBatches. The class provides no "is idle" invariant, so this is safe only because every current call site happens to call `wait_for_tasks_to_complete()` synchronously.
2. `_state` (which owns `GameMenu`/`GameLevel` → `Level`, and `Level` caches `ThreadPool* _thread_pool`, Level.h:146) is destroyed **after** `_thread_pool`. Any future cleanup in `~Level` that touches the pool is a use-after-free.

Separately, `Game(Game&&) = default;` / `Game& operator=(Game&&) = default;` (Game.h:22-23) are wrong for this class: the constructor registers `_device_resources->RegisterDeviceNotify(this)` (Game.cpp:20) and `Main.cpp:250` stores the `Game*` in `GWLP_USERDATA`. A move leaves both back-references pointing at the moved-from object.
findings.suggestion: Declare `_thread_pool` **last** so it is destroyed first, and declare `_state` before it. Delete the move operations on `Game` (it is a `final` class registered by address; it should be neither copyable nor movable).

findings.title: Unreachable duplicated return statement — proof that /W4 warnings are being ignored
findings.suggestion: Delete the duplicate line, then turn on `<TreatWarningAsError>true</TreatWarningAsError>` for both projects and fix the backlog. Move the four near-identical `ItemDefinitionGroup` blocks in ArtAttack.vcxproj into a shared `.props` sheet so warning settings cannot drift between configurations.

findings.title: Every JSON file is parsed through a 1-byte heap buffer that rapidjson is told is 8 bytes
findings.detail:
All four JSON loaders in the codebase share this exact block:

```cpp
FILE* fp = fopen(json_path, "rb");
auto read_buffer = std::make_unique<char>();          // allocates ONE char
FileReadStream is(fp, read_buffer.get(), sizeof(read_buffer));  // sizeof(unique_ptr) == 8 (x64)
```

`std::make_unique<char>()` allocates a single byte. `sizeof(read_buffer)` is `sizeof(std::unique_ptr<char>)` — 8 on x64, 4 on Win32 — not the buffer size. rapidjson's `FileReadStream::Read()` (external/rapidjson/include/rapidjson/filereadstream.h:66-80) then does `std::fread(buffer_, 1, bufferSize_, fp_)` followed by `buffer_[readCount_] = '\0'`, i.e. it writes up to 9 bytes into a 1-byte allocation, repeatedly, for the entire length of the file. This is a heap buffer overflow on every asset load in the program. It only appears to work because malloc's minimum bucket happens to absorb it.

Secondarily, `read_buffer.release()` (Save.cpp:23) relinquishes ownership *without* deleting — a leak on every call; the author almost certainly meant nothing at all here.

Identical sites: Save.cpp:14-23, LevelLoadedInfo.cpp:98-107, SoundBank.cpp:152-161, SpriteSheet.cpp:72-81. All four must be fixed; there is no shared helper.
findings.suggestion: Replace all four copies with one shared helper, e.g. `rapidjson::Document load_json_document(const std::string& path)`, that reads the whole file into a `std::vector<char>` / `std::string` and uses `rapidjson::Document::Parse(text.c_str())` (or `FileReadStream` with a real `std::array<char, 65536>`). Delete the `release()` calls.

findings.title: fopen result never checked in any of the four JSON loaders; NULL FILE* reaches fread in Release builds
findings.detail:
`FILE* fp = fopen(json_path, "rb");` is used with no null check at Save.cpp:14, LevelLoadedInfo.cpp:98, SoundBank.cpp:152 and SpriteSheet.cpp:72. The only thing standing between a missing file and `std::fread(buf, 1, 8, nullptr)` is `RAPIDJSON_ASSERT(fp_ != 0)` in FileReadStream's constructor — and `RAPIDJSON_ASSERT` is `#define RAPIDJSON_ASSERT(x) assert(x)` (external/rapidjson/include/rapidjson/rapidjson.h:437), which is compiled out under NDEBUG. Release builds therefore call `fread` and then `fclose` on a null FILE*, invoking the MSVC invalid-parameter handler and aborting with no message.

The most likely trigger is not exotic: `Save::load_save_file()` (Save.cpp:43-56) writes a default save when the file is missing, but `write_save_file` (Save.cpp:60) will itself fail if the `save/` *directory* doesn't exist (fopen "wb" does not create directories). It returns false, prints "Save was unsuccessful" to a console that does not exist (see separate finding), and `load_save_file` then unconditionally proceeds to `load_from_json` on the still-missing file. A deployed build without a `save/` folder hard-crashes before the window is created (Main.cpp:99 calls `g_save->load_save_file()` with no try/catch).
findings.suggestion: Check `fp` and throw a typed exception carrying the path, or return an empty/defaulted result. Wrap the whole startup asset load in Main.cpp in a try/catch that shows a `MessageBoxW` naming the missing file instead of aborting silently.

findings.title: No JSON access anywhere is guarded: zero HasParseError checks, zero type checks, ~60 raw operator[] + GetFloat/GetString
findings.detail:
A repo-wide grep for `HasParseError`, `IsObject()`, `IsArray()`, `IsInt`, `IsString` returns **zero** hits in first-party code. `HasMember` appears exactly 7 times, all in LevelObjectBuilder.cpp:38,45,81,88,108 and SpriteSheet.cpp:34,39.

So `d.ParseStream(is)` at Save.cpp:20, LevelLoadedInfo.cpp:104, SoundBank.cpp:158 and SpriteSheet.cpp:78 is never checked, and every subsequent access is unguarded. LevelLoadedInfo is the worst offender — the whole class is unguarded chained subscripts:

```cpp
return this->_json_doc["level_name"].GetString();                       // :17
this->_json_doc["level_bounds"]["out_of_bounds"]["x"].GetFloat()        // :33-36, x4 rects
return this->_json_doc["collision_objects"];                            // :66
return this->_json_doc["sound"]["music_volume"].GetFloat();             // :82
for (auto& spawn : json.GetArray())  spawn["x"].GetFloat()              // :89-91
```

rapidjson's `operator[](name)` on a missing key hits `RAPIDJSON_ASSERT(false)` (document.h:1231) and, with asserts compiled out in Release, returns a static `kNullType` value. `GetFloat()`/`GetString()` on that null then reinterpret the union with the corresponding `RAPIDJSON_ASSERT(IsNumber())` also compiled out — so a renamed or misspelled key yields **garbage geometry** in Release and `std::string(garbage_pointer)` for the string accessors. A truncated save/level file (interrupted write) does the same via the unchecked parse.

Other unguarded sites: Save.cpp:25-26, SoundBank.cpp:125,126,163,164,166, SpriteSheet.cpp:26,30-33,55,57-63,83,84, LevelObjectBuilder.cpp:19,23,40-43,59,60,65,133-134,142,162-167,170-171,176,185,189-196.
findings.suggestion: Add a small guarded-access layer (`get_float(v, "x")`, `require_object(v, "level_bounds")`, …) that throws a descriptive exception naming the file and JSON pointer path, and check `d.HasParseError()` / `GetParseError()` / `GetErrorOffset()` immediately after every `ParseStream`. Do not rely on RAPIDJSON_ASSERT — it does not exist in Release.

findings.title: Device-lost recovery destroys the ResourceManager, ThreadPool and dt that every live object holds by raw pointer
findings.detail:
`Game::create_device_dependent_resources()` is called from two places: `Game::initialize()` (Game.cpp:54) and `Game::OnDeviceRestored()` (Game.cpp:284). It unconditionally re-creates the owning `unique_ptr` members:

```cpp
this->_resource_manager = std::make_unique<ResourceManager>();   // :239
this->_resource_loader  = std::make_unique<ResourceLoader>(...); // :241
this->_dt               = std::make_unique<float>(0.f);          // :244
this->_viewport_manager = std::make_unique<ViewportManager>(...);// :247
this->_thread_pool      = std::make_unique<ThreadPool>(...);     // :236
this->_partitioner      = std::make_unique<Partitioner>();       // :255
this->_resource_loader->load_all_resources();                    // :258
```

Every live game object captured raw pointers to the *old* instances at construction time: `Level::_sound_bank` and `_resource_manager` (Level.cpp:59), `Player::_sound_bank` (Player.cpp:44), `StructurePaintable::_sound_bank` (StructurePaintable.cpp:34), `Weapon::_sound_bank` (Weapon.cpp:33), `DrawObject::_resource_manager` on every drawable, and the `const float* _dt` threaded through ~26 headers. After a device-lost/restore (driver reset, TDR, Alt-Tab on some drivers) every one of those pointers dangles — guaranteed use-after-free on the next frame if a level is in progress.

`OnDeviceLost` (Game.cpp:269-280) also calls `reset_all_textures/sprite_fonts/sounds` on a ResourceManager that is about to be thrown away entirely, so that work is pointless, and `load_all_resources()` re-reads every DDS and JSON from disk from scratch.
findings.suggestion: Split device-dependent GPU resource creation from the service objects. `ResourceManager`, `ThreadPool`, `Partitioner`, `_dt` and `ViewportManager` should be created once in `initialize()` and never re-created; only the D3D objects (SpriteBatches, CommonStates, textures, SpriteFonts) should be torn down and rebuilt on device loss, with the ResourceManager re-populating its existing map entries in place so the borrowed pointers stay valid.

findings.title: Four of five ResourceManager getters use map::operator[] inside a catch(out_of_range) that can never fire
findings.detail:
```cpp
ID3D11ShaderResourceView* ResourceManager::get_texture(const std::string& texture_name) {
    try { return this->_textures[texture_name].Get(); }        // :12  operator[] never throws
    catch (const std::out_of_range&) { ... throw std::out_of_range(error); }  // dead code
}
```

`std::map::operator[]` default-constructs a new entry for an unknown key and never throws, so the catch block is unreachable and the "Texture X not found" diagnostic is dead. What actually happens on a typo is that the map silently grows a null entry and the caller receives `nullptr`, which is then handed straight to `SpriteBatch::Draw` / `SpriteFont::DrawString`.

Same at get_sprite_font (:31), get_sprite_sheet (:51), get_sound_bank (:95). `get_level_info` (:71) correctly uses `.at()` — so the author knew the right idiom and applied it once out of five times.
findings.suggestion: Use `.at()` in all five, or better `find()` + an explicit `throw resource_not_found(name)`. Mark all five getters `const` (only `get_level_info` is, purely because it uses `.at()`).

findings.title: Resource lookup mutates shared std::maps and is called per-draw from thread-pool worker threads
findings.suggestion: Make every ResourceManager and SpriteSheet lookup `const` and non-mutating (`.at()` / `find()`), which removes the race entirely for read-only lookups. Better still for a per-frame hot path: resolve the `SpriteSheet*` and the `SpriteFrame` once at object construction and store them, instead of doing two string-keyed map lookups per sprite per frame.

findings.title: A misspelled frame_name in level JSON silently draws a 0x0 sprite instead of failing
findings.detail:
```cpp
sprite_batch->Draw(this->_texture, position.get_xm_vector(),
    this->_sprite_frames[frame_name].get_source_rectangle(), ...);
```

`operator[]` inserts a default-constructed `SpriteFrame`, whose `RECT _source_rectangle = { 0, 0, 0, 0 }` (SpriteFrame.h:21). The result is an invisible zero-area sprite, silently, every frame, forever — with the bogus entry now permanently cached in the map. The 91 `frame_name` strings across the three level JSONs and the ~40 hardcoded `"sprite_sheet_1"`/frame-name literals scattered through MainMenu.cpp, PauseMenu.cpp, EndMenu.cpp, InterfaceGameplay.cpp and player_consts.h are all validated only by this silent-failure path.

Note the inconsistency: `SpriteSheet::get_animation_strip` (SpriteSheet.cpp:17) uses `.at()` and throws for the same class of error. Two lookups in the same class, two opposite failure modes.

Second site: SpriteSheet.cpp:126 (the RectangleI destination overload).
findings.suggestion: Use `.at()` (or `find()` with a descriptive throw naming both the sheet and the frame). Given every frame name is fixed at load time, prefer resolving names to indices/pointers once during load so a bad name fails at startup, not silently at draw time.

findings.title: reset_all_* nulls map entries instead of erasing them, leaving booby-trapped keys that lookups happily return
findings.suggestion: Either `clear()` the maps (and make lookups fail loudly) or introduce a real two-phase resource handle with an explicit `is_loaded()` and a reload path. Do not leave null values behind keys that lookups treat as success.

findings.title: A wave name typo in sound_bank_1.json stores a null SoundEffectInstance that crashes later at play time
findings.detail:
```cpp
try { sound_effect_instances[name] = this->_wave_bank->CreateInstance(wave.c_str()); }
catch (const std::out_of_range& e) { throw std::out_of_range("Wave with name " + wave + " not found"); }
```

DirectXTK's `WaveBank::CreateInstance(const char* name, ...)` (packages/directxtk_desktop_2019.2023.10.31.1/include/Audio.h:338) returns a `unique_ptr` that is **null** when the name isn't in the wave bank — it deliberately does not throw, because titles commonly ignore missing assets. So the catch is dead code, a null instance is stored under a valid key, `get_sound_effect_instance` (:78, using `.at()`) reports success, and `play_effect` (:33-37) null-derefs on `sei->SetVolume(volume)` the first time that sound is triggered mid-gameplay.

The same dead `catch (const std::out_of_range& e)` wraps `_wave_bank->Play()` at :19-26 and appears again at :80-83 and :137-140; in all four the bound `e` is unused (a /W4 C4101 warning that nobody sees because `TreatWarningAsError` is not set).

This matters because sounds/sound_bank_1.json:2-28 is a hand-maintained list of 24 wave names duplicating the XWBTool command line in sounds/sound_bank_1/cmd.txt — two sources of truth for the same list, with nothing checking they agree.
findings.suggestion: Null-check the result of `CreateInstance` and throw naming the wave, the bank and the JSON path, at load time. Delete the four dead `catch (std::out_of_range)` blocks. Better: derive the wave name list from the wave bank itself (`WaveBank::Find`) rather than duplicating it in JSON.

findings.title: StructurePaintable stores a reference to a builder local; it dangles for the object's entire lifetime
findings.detail:
```cpp
std::vector<Segment> paintable_edges;                 // :107  function-local
if (json.HasMember("paintable_faces")) { ... paintable_edges.push_back(...); }
return std::make_unique<StructurePaintable>(..., paintable_edges, ...);  // :140
```

`StructurePaintable` binds that argument to a **reference member**: `const std::vector<MattMath::Segment>& _paintable_edges;` (StructurePaintable.h:56). `build_collision_object` returns immediately afterwards, destroying the vector, so the member dangles for the whole life of the level. `StructurePaintable` reads it during paint-tile generation (StructurePaintable.cpp:189-193). 24 objects across the three shipping levels are `StructurePaintable`.

Secondary: that reference member also implicitly deletes the `StructurePaintable() = default;` declared on line 28 of the same header.
findings.suggestion: Change the member to `std::vector<MattMath::Segment> _paintable_edges;` (by value) and move the argument in. If the edges are only needed during construction (they appear to be — tiles are generated in the ctor), take the parameter and drop the member entirely.

findings.title: Per-team spawn arrays are indexed with a shared global player counter, unchecked, and team NONE falls into team B
findings.suggestion: Keep separate `size_t a_index`/`b_index` counters, `switch` on the team with an explicit error for `NONE`, and use `.at()` (or check `size()` up front and throw naming the level and the required spawn count).

findings.title: The content manifest is hardcoded C++ inside the engine's loader; adding a level means editing engine code
findings.suggestion: Move the manifest into data — e.g. `assets/manifest.json` listing textures, fonts, sound banks and levels by name and path — and key `ResourceManager::_level_infos` on `std::string` like every other cache in the class. `ResourceLoader` then becomes generic: read manifest, load each entry.

findings.title: Everything is loaded eagerly at startup and there is no unload API at all — no resource scoping for an engine
findings.detail:
`ResourceManager`'s entire public surface is `add_*`, `get_*` and three `reset_all_*`. There is no `remove`, `unload`, `erase`, reference count, or resource-set/bundle concept. `load_all_resources()` (ResourceLoader.cpp:45-51) loads *all three* levels' `LevelLoadedInfo` (each keeping its full parsed rapidjson `Document` resident — 21 KB, 22 KB and 13 KB of JSON, plus the DOM overhead), the 2.2 MB sprite sheet, seven SpriteFonts and the entire wave bank at process start, and nothing is ever released until exit. Transitioning between levels (GameLevel/GameMenu in GameStates.cpp) never touches the resource manager.

That is defensible for a three-level student game; it is not defensible for a reusable engine, which is the stated goal. There is no way for a game to say "these assets belong to this level" and get them back.
findings.suggestion: Introduce a resource-scope/bundle handle (`ResourceScope scope = rm.open_scope("level:turbulence")`) whose destruction releases everything loaded through it, and make level info lazily loaded on first request rather than all three up front. At minimum, add `unload(name)` / `unload_all()` so the API is capable of the thing an engine has to do.

findings.title: Asset paths are CWD-relative literals with no post-build copy — the built exe cannot find its data
findings.suggestion: Resolve paths against the executable's directory (`GetModuleFileNameW` + parent) rather than the CWD, put the save file under `%LOCALAPPDATA%` (the tracked `ArtAttack/save/save_data.json` is currently rewritten on every launch, dirtying the working tree). Add `<Content Include>` items with `CopyToOutputDirectory` so the output folder is self-contained. Make the constants `inline constexpr std::string_view` or a small runtime-configurable `AssetPaths` service.

findings.title: No version or schema field in save or level data; an unrecognised resolution is silently downgraded and then written back
findings.detail:
`save/save_data.json` is `{"resolution":{"x":1920,"y":1080},"fullscreen":false}` and the three level JSONs have top-level keys `level_name, sound, spawn_locations, level_bounds, collision_objects, non_collision_objects` (verified across all three). Neither format carries a version.

Consequences, concretely:
- Old save read by new code: any field added later is simply absent, so `d["new_field"]` takes the unguarded-access path above — garbage in Release, assert in Debug. There is no migration hook.
- New save read by old code: `convert_ivec_to_resolution` (Save.cpp:112-135) matches four hardcoded pairs and `else return screen_resolution::S_1280_720;` — an unrecognised resolution is silently downgraded, and the very next `set_full_screen_and_save` writes 1280x720 back over the user's setting. Silent data loss with no way to detect it.
- `Save::write_save_file` also serialises the resolution as x/y integers while the in-memory type is the closed enum `screen_resolution` (screen_resolution.h:4-11), so the file format promises more than the code accepts.

Also still tracked next to it: `ArtAttack/save/save_data.txt` containing `1920x1080\nfalse` — a dead legacy save format with no reader anywhere in the codebase.
findings.suggestion: Add a `"version"` integer to both formats, check it on load, and fail loudly (or migrate explicitly) on mismatch. Preserve unknown values rather than silently rewriting them. Delete save_data.txt.

findings.title: The same rectangle/vector decode is hand-written ~10 times in three mutually inconsistent JSON dialects
findings.detail:
There is no shared decoding layer; each class writes its own. The same concept — a rectangle — is spelled three different ways in the data and decoded three different ways in code:

- `{"x","y","width","height"}` — LevelLoadedInfo.cpp:32-36, 40-44, 48-52, 57-61 (four copies) and LevelObjectBuilder.cpp:40-43, 83-86, 191-194 (three more).
- `{"left","top","right","bottom"}` — LevelObjectBuilder.cpp:47-51 and 90-94 (two copies of a `rectangle_tlbr` branch that **no shipping level uses** — verified: zero occurrences across all three level JSONs).
- `{"position":{"x","y"},"size":{"w","h"}}` — SpriteSheet.cpp:29-33, and `{"x","y","w","h"}` at SpriteSheet.cpp:56-60.

Likewise `Vector2F` decode is written out at LevelLoadedInfo.cpp:91, LevelObjectBuilder.cpp:47-50, SpriteSheet.cpp:36-37. The file-open-and-parse block is copy-pasted four times (see the heap-overflow finding) — meaning the single most serious bug in the pipeline has to be fixed in four places.

Also dead data: every one of the 91 collision/non-collision objects in the level JSONs carries a `"name"` field that `build_collision_object`/`build_non_collision_object` never read; and `sprite_sheet_1.json`'s `origin`/`rotated` are parsed into `SpriteFrame::_origin` and `_rotated` (SpriteSheet.cpp:36-41) which have no getter and are read by nothing (`_source_rectangle2` likewise) — parsed and discarded.
findings.suggestion: Add a `json_util` (or `JsonReader`) with `read_rect`, `read_vec2`, `read_float`, `read_string`, `read_array`, each taking the value plus a key and throwing a message that names the file and path. Pick one rectangle spelling and migrate the data files. Either consume `name`/`origin`/`rotated` or remove them from the schema.

findings.title: The pipeline's only diagnostics are std::cout in a /SUBSYSTEM:WINDOWS app, and one of them prints an errno_t
findings.detail:
`ArtAttack.vcxproj` sets `<SubSystem>Windows</SubSystem>` in all four configurations and nothing calls `AllocConsole`. The five `std::cout` statements in Save.cpp:47, 51, 90, 93, 97 — "Save file exists", "Save was unsuccessful", etc. — go to a stream with no attached console and are invisible in every build. They are the *only* logging in the entire asset pipeline; there is no OutputDebugString, no log file, no error UI (the two DeviceResources.cpp uses are vendor code).

Line 90 is additionally wrong on its own terms:
```cpp
char buffer[30];
std::cout << ctime_s(buffer, sizeof(buffer), &legacy_start) << " Saving...\n";
```
`ctime_s` returns `errno_t` and writes the timestamp into `buffer`. This prints `0 Saving...` — the intended `buffer` is never streamed.

Net effect: when asset loading fails, the user gets a silent process abort and the developer gets nothing.
findings.suggestion: Add a minimal logging facility (OutputDebugStringA plus a log file) and route load failures to a `MessageBoxW` naming the failing asset before exit. Fix line 90 to stream `buffer`, or drop `<chrono>`/`ctime_s` entirely.

findings.title: colour_from_name is a 150-branch string if-chain in a header that silently returns WHITE for unknown names
findings.suggestion: Replace with a single `const std::unordered_map<std::string, Colour>` defined in a .cpp, and return `bool try_colour_from_name(name, out)` or throw naming the unknown value so bad level data fails at load. Move the colour constant tables out of the header (`inline constexpr` or a .cpp with `extern` declarations).

findings.title: Only one of five loaders has any error handling, and it destroys the original error; narrow-to-wide path conversion is byte-copied
findings.suggestion: Use `std::filesystem::path` (available once the project moves off its default /std:c++14) for all path handling and widening. Catch narrowly and chain the original message (`std::throw_with_nested`, or append `e.what()`). Delete the unused texture-desc query. Collapse the from_directory overloads into one helper taking the extension.

findings.title: player_inputs is compacted to connected pads but indexed by player-object index (OOB read)
findings.suggestion: Stop compacting. Return a fixed `std::array<PlayerInputData, 4>` (or a vector sized to the player count) indexed by player slot, and use the already-present but currently dead `PlayerInputData::connection` field (ArtAttack/PlayerInputData.h:19; `calculate_player_input` unconditionally writes `connection_state::CONNECTED` at ArtAttack/PlayerInput.cpp:111, so DISCONNECTED is never produced) to mark absent pads. Then `Level::update_level_logic` looks up by `player->get_player_num()` and treats a disconnected pad as neutral input / auto-pause instead of indexing off the end.

findings.title: OnDeviceRestored reallocates the shared frame-time float, dangling every const float* _dt in the engine
findings.detail:
`Game::OnDeviceRestored()` calls `create_device_dependent_resources()`, which at ArtAttack/Game.cpp:244-245 does:

```
this->_dt = std::make_unique<float>(0.f);
this->_data->set_dt(this->_dt.get());
```

Assigning a new `unique_ptr` frees the old float. Every live object took a copy of the OLD raw pointer at construction time and keeps it forever: `Level::_dt` (ArtAttack/Level.h:140), `Player::_dt` (ArtAttack/Player.h:170), `Weapon::_dt` (ArtAttack/Weapon.h:123), `Projectile::_dt` (ArtAttack/Projectile.h:79), `PaintTile::_dt` (ArtAttack/PaintTile.h:82), `StructurePaintable::_dt` (ArtAttack/StructurePaintable.h:57), `AnimationObject::_dt` (ArtAttack/AnimationObject.h:49), `AnimatedSprite::_dt` (ArtAttack/AnimatedSprite.h:42), `Drawer::_dt` (ArtAttack/Drawer.h:31), `LevelBuilder`/`LevelObjectBuilder` (:32/:31). After a device-lost/restore (driver update, TDR, GPU hot-swap, remote-desktop transition) every `*this->_dt` read — e.g. `Player::get_dt()` ArtAttack/Player.cpp:692-694, `AnimationObject.cpp:88` — is a use-after-free that then multiplies velocities by garbage.

The same function also replaces `_thread_pool`, `_resource_manager`, `_resource_loader`, `_viewport_manager`, `_partitioner` and republishes them into `GameData`, while the live `Level` holds raw pointers to the old ones (ArtAttack/Level.h:117-119, 146-147) — so device restore during gameplay is a use-after-free across the whole object graph, not just for `_dt`.
findings.suggestion: Split `create_device_dependent_resources()` into genuinely device-dependent GPU objects (SpriteBatch, CommonStates, textures) and device-INdependent services (`_dt`, ThreadPool, Partitioner, ResourceManager instance) so restore only recreates the former. Better still: stop passing frame time as a heap-allocated `float*` at all — pass `float dt` down through `update(float dt)`, which removes 11 dangling-pointer members and the whole aliasing problem in one change.

findings.title: ResetElapsedTime() exists at exactly one site; every real stall path (level load, device restore, drag) is missing it
findings.detail:
`_timer.ResetElapsedTime()` is called once in the entire program, in `Game::on_resuming()`. `m_qpcMaxDelta` is fixed at 1/10 s (ArtAttack/StepTimer.h:39-40 `m_qpcMaxDelta = m_qpcFrequency.QuadPart / 10`) and `m_targetElapsedTicks = SecondsToTicks(1.0/60) = 166666`, so after any stall longer than 100 ms the next `Tick()` runs exactly `1000000 / 166666 = 6` back-to-back `update()` calls (ArtAttack/StepTimer.h:132-142) with no `render()` between them, and the excess wall-clock time is silently discarded.

Paths that stall for far more than 100 ms and do NOT reset the timer:
- `GameLevel::init()` — ArtAttack/GameStates.cpp:105-127: builds `LevelBuilder`, parses the level JSON and constructs every `PaintTile`. Worse, this runs *inside* the timer's update lambda: Main.cpp:222 `tick()` → Game.cpp:77 `_timer.Tick(...)` → Game.cpp:91 `StateContext::update()` → GameStates.cpp:73-77 `GameMenu::update` → `order_level_creation()` → `StateContext::transition_to` (ArtAttack/StateContext.cpp:20-25) → `init()`. Blocking file I/O is being performed from inside `while (m_leftOverTicks >= m_targetElapsedTicks)`.
- level rebuild on restart — ArtAttack/GameStates.cpp:202-204 (`pause_menu_action::RESTART`) and :279-282 (`end_menu_action::RESTART`).
- `Game::initialize()` — ArtAttack/Game.cpp:32-66; the `StepTimer` is constructed when `Game` is (`DX::StepTimer _timer = DX::StepTimer();` ArtAttack/Game.h:60, i.e. at Main.cpp:109), then `create_device_dependent_resources()` runs `_resource_loader->load_all_resources()` (Game.cpp:258) — the entire texture/font/audio load sits between the timer's first QPC sample and the first `Tick()`.
- `Game::OnDeviceRestored()` — Game.cpp:282-287, which re-runs the full resource load.
- WM_EXITSIZEMOVE — ArtAttack/Main.cpp:309-318; the window-drag modal loop only ticks on WM_PAINT.
- `Game::on_activated()` — Game.cpp:157-163; only the minimize/power path (`on_resuming`) resets.

Observable effect: after a level loads, six 1/60 physics steps execute invisibly — collision resolution, projectile spawning, camera follow and the countdown/music start (ArtAttack/Level.cpp:65-124) all advance ~100 ms of simulated time before one pixel is drawn, driven by a single input snapshot. `Level::update_level_logic` also `throw std::exception("Player out of bounds")` (Level.cpp:312, 319) during that invisible burst.
findings.suggestion: Call `_timer.ResetElapsedTime()` immediately after every blocking operation: at the end of `GameLevel::init()`, after each `build_level()` call, at the end of `Game::initialize()` and `Game::OnDeviceRestored()`, and in the WM_EXITSIZEMOVE handler. Structurally, `GameData` should expose the timer (or a `request_timer_reset()` flag) so states can reset it without reaching into `Game`. Longer term, move level loading off the update thread entirely so the fixed-step loop never contains disk I/O.

findings.title: FIRST_UPDATE/SECOND_UPDATE is a hand-rolled workaround for the missing timer reset, and it under-shoots
findings.suggestion: Delete `FIRST_UPDATE`/`SECOND_UPDATE` and call `_timer.ResetElapsedTime()` at the end of `GameLevel::init()` instead. If a "level is not ready to draw" concept is genuinely wanted, make it an explicit `bool _ready` that `draw()` uses to render a loading screen rather than presenting a cleared black buffer.

findings.title: Controller polling lives inside the fixed-step update, so sampling rate is welded to 60 Hz and varies 0..6 per displayed frame
findings.suggestion: Poll input once per `tick()`, before `_timer.Tick(...)`, into a per-frame snapshot with sticky `pressed`/`released` bits that are latched on poll and cleared after the update loop has consumed them. That decouples sample rate from simulation rate, makes taps unmissable regardless of refresh, and makes catch-up steps consume the same latched edge exactly once.

findings.title: Edge-detection history is per-consumer and only advances while that consumer is the active state
findings.detail:
`PlayerInput::_prev_inputs[4]` (ArtAttack/PlayerInput.h:34) and `MenuInput::_prev_inputs[4]` (ArtAttack/MenuInput.h:50) are each written only by their own `update_and_get_*_inputs()` (`this->_prev_inputs[i] = current[i];` PlayerInput.cpp:135, MenuInput.cpp:147). `GameLevel` owns one of each (ArtAttack/GameStates.h:59, 63) but polls `_player_input` ONLY in the ACTIVE branch (GameStates.cpp:141-142) and `_menu_input` ONLY while a pause/results/end page is updating. So "previous" does not mean "the previous frame" — it means "the last frame this particular state happened to run", which can be minutes ago.

Concrete failure: pause the game while holding A (jump). `toggle_pause_menu` fires on Start *release* (PlayerInput.cpp:53) so the menu opens with A still down. `_menu_input._prev_inputs` was last written when the pause menu was last open (or is all-false), so the first menu poll sees `current.proceed == true, previous.proceed == false` → no action, then latches `prev.proceed = true`. The instant the player lets go of the jump button, `proceed = prev_proceed && no_press_current` fires and `PauseMenuInitial::update` activates whatever is highlighted (ArtAttack/PauseMenu.cpp:59-81) — the player is thrown straight back into the game, or into the Restart/Quit confirmation, from a button press they made *before* the menu existed.

Neither class exposes any way to clear the history, so there is no way to fix it at the call sites either. Note DirectXTK already ships exactly the right tool: `GamePad::ButtonStateTracker` with `UP/HELD/RELEASED/PRESSED` and a `Reset()` (packages/directxtk_desktop_2019.../include/GamePad.h:219-282) — both classes reimplement it, worse, and drop the `Reset()`.
findings.suggestion: Sample the pad once per frame into a single shared snapshot (see the polling finding) so there is exactly one authoritative `previous`. Failing that, at minimum add `PlayerInput::reset()` / `MenuInput::reset()` that re-reads the current pad state into `_prev_inputs` without emitting edges, and call it on every state entry (`GameLevel` ACTIVE↔PAUSE_MENU transitions, `PauseMenuData`/`ResultsMenuData`/`EndMenuData` construction). Or just use `GamePad::ButtonStateTracker`.

findings.title: Results menu polls the pad every update but discards the resulting edge until two timers expire
findings.suggestion: Latch edges in a frame-level input snapshot with an explicit `consume()`, so a PROCEED that arrives while the UI is not accepting input either survives to the next frame or is dropped deliberately, rather than by accident of where the poll call sits relative to the gate.

findings.title: The on-screen FPS readout is a constant 60 by construction; the timer's real FPS counter is never used
findings.detail:
```
lines.push_back("dt: " + std::to_string(this->get_dt()));
lines.push_back("fps: " + std::to_string(1.0f / this->get_dt()));
```

In fixed-timestep mode `StepTimer::Tick` assigns `m_elapsedTicks = m_targetElapsedTicks` on every iteration (ArtAttack/StepTimer.h:136), so `GetElapsedSeconds()` returns a compile-time-determined constant. `Game::update` copies it into the shared float (ArtAttack/Game.cpp:89-90). With `SetTargetElapsedSeconds(1.0 / TARGET_FPS)` (Game.cpp:65, `TARGET_FPS = 60` at Game.h:12), `m_targetElapsedTicks = (uint64)(1.0/60 * 1e7) = 166666`, so `*_dt` is 0.0166666f forever and the debug overlay prints `fps: 60.000240` no matter what the machine is actually doing. The one number a developer would look at to diagnose a performance problem is hard-wired to the target.

`StepTimer::GetFramesPerSecond()` (ArtAttack/StepTimer.h:55) computes the genuine presented-frame rate and is never called anywhere in the codebase.

Secondary point for the engine goal: because `*_dt` is provably constant, every `* dt` in the simulation (`Player.cpp:734, 761, 873`, `Projectile.cpp:234`, `Weapon.cpp:193`, `Level.cpp:106, 130, 141, 163`) is multiplication by a literal written as if it were variable — the frame-rate independence is nominal, never exercised, and would break the first time the target rate changed (see the animation-stepping finding).
findings.suggestion: Plumb `_timer.GetFramesPerSecond()` (and ideally the measured wall-clock delta) through `GameData` and print that as `fps`; keep `dt` for the simulation step. Since the app is fixed-step, also consider naming the constant `FIXED_STEP_SECONDS` rather than deriving it from a variable called `TARGET_FPS`, which reads as a rendering target.

findings.title: Blocking vsync Present + fixed 60 Hz update, no interpolation, no tearing option: judder on >60 Hz and full redraw of unchanged frames
findings.detail:
`DeviceResources` is constructed with default flags:

```
_device_resources = std::make_unique<DX::DeviceResources>(
    DXGI_FORMAT_B8G8R8A8_UNORM, DXGI_FORMAT_UNKNOWN);
// TODO: ... Add DX::DeviceResources::c_AllowTearing to opt-in to variable rate displays.
```

The TODO was never actioned, so `c_AllowTearing` is off and `DeviceResources::Present()` takes the blocking branch `m_swapChain->Present(1, 0)` (ArtAttack/DeviceResources.cpp:464-470). Meanwhile `Game::render()` runs unconditionally after `Tick` (Game.cpp:82) and the simulation is pinned to 60 Hz.

Observable symptoms:
- 144 Hz display: `render()` presents 144 frames/s; `update()` runs 60 times/s, so state changes land on a 2-3-2-3 refresh pattern. Nothing interpolates between simulation states (there is no alpha anywhere; `Camera` positions come straight from `Player::get_camera()` at Level.cpp:508), so motion visibly judders — the game looks *worse* on the faster monitor.
- ~58% of those 144 frames are byte-identical redraws, yet each one still runs `clear()` re-binding RTV+viewport across all 16 deferred contexts (Game.cpp:136-149), re-partitions the players and dispatches thread-pool tasks that re-record every command list (`Level::draw_active_level` ArtAttack/Level.cpp:375-400). All of that CPU work produces no pixel change.
- Display that cannot do 60 (e.g. 50 Hz): each 20 ms tick alternates 1 and 2 update steps, so the simulation runs correct wall-clock speed but at an uneven cadence with no interpolation to hide it.
- Minimised/occluded: `Present` returns `DXGI_STATUS_OCCLUDED`, which is a SUCCESS code, so `ThrowIfFailed` passes and there is no early-out (DeviceResources.cpp:495-497). The vsync block disappears and the loop busy-spins re-rendering invisible frames at 100% of a core.
findings.suggestion: Three separable fixes: (1) pass `DX::DeviceResources::c_AllowTearing` and let the render rate float; (2) expose the fixed-step remainder (`m_leftOverTicks / m_targetElapsedTicks`) from `StepTimer` as an interpolation alpha and lerp camera/sprite transforms in `draw`, which is the standard fix and the one a reusable engine needs; (3) skip `render()` when no `update()` ran and the swap chain is occluded — track whether `GetFrameCount()` changed since the last present.

findings.title: Animation stepping consumes one frame per update instead of draining elapsed time; silently assumes dt < frame_time
findings.suggestion: Change `if` to `while` and guard against `frame_time <= 0` to avoid an infinite loop. Then delete one of the two copies — `AnimationObject` and `AnimatedSprite` are the same algorithm written twice.

findings.title: StepTimer.h is an unmodified vendor template: unmarked, not self-contained, no interpolation alpha, fixed 100 ms clamp
findings.detail:
I compared this file line-by-line against the stock DirectX 11 VS-template / DirectXTK `StepTimer.h`: the constructor member-init order, the `m_qpcMaxDelta = m_qpcFrequency.QuadPart / 10` comment, the 1/4-millisecond snap block at lines 120-130, the `TicksPerSecond = 10000000` constant and the whole `Tick()` template are all byte-identical to upstream. **There are no local edits.** That is itself worth reporting for three reasons:

1. Nothing marks it as third-party. It sits flat among the 193 first-party sources with no `// vendored from ...` banner and no version note, unlike `external/rapidjson`, so a future reader cannot tell it is not the author's code and will not know it can be re-synced upstream.
2. It is not self-contained: it uses `LARGE_INTEGER`, `QueryPerformanceFrequency` and `QueryPerformanceCounter` but includes only `<cmath>`, `<cstdint>`, `<exception>`. It compiles only because `pch.h:32` pulls in `<Windows.h>` first. A reusable engine header must not depend on the consumer's precompiled header.
3. Because it was never adapted, it lacks the two things this codebase actually needs: an accessor for the fixed-step remainder (`m_leftOverTicks / m_targetElapsedTicks`) to drive render interpolation, and a setter for `m_qpcMaxDelta`, which is a hard-coded private (line 40) that fixes the maximum catch-up burst at exactly 6 steps with no way to tune it.

Minor precision note: `SetTargetElapsedSeconds(1.0/60)` truncates to `m_targetElapsedTicks = 166666`, i.e. 60.00024 Hz rather than 60 — harmless here only because the snap window at line 127 (2500 ticks) is far larger than the error.
findings.suggestion: Move vendored files (`StepTimer.h`, `DeviceResources.h/.cpp`, `pch.h`) into an `external/` or `vendor/` folder with a provenance comment giving upstream URL and version, matching how `external/rapidjson` is already handled. Add `#include <Windows.h>` (or a minimal `<profileapi.h>`) to `StepTimer.h` so it stands alone, then add `double GetInterpolationAlpha() const` and `void SetMaxDelta(double seconds)` as clearly-marked local extensions.

findings.title: End-menu "Restart" replays the match with the wrong viewport layout and no split-screen dividers
findings.suggestion: Two separate fixes. (a) Stop mutating global render state from a draw path: `draw_zoom_out_level_component` should compute the fullscreen viewport locally (`ViewportManager::get_fullscreen_d3d11_viewport()` already exists) and apply it to the deferred context, instead of calling `set_layout`. Note the method is declared `const` (Level.h:173) yet mutates the manager — that const is a lie. (b) Make rematch go through one code path: extract a `GameLevel::build_and_enter_level()` that calls `set_layout(_settings.get_screen_layout())` and then `build_level`, and call it from `init()`, from `pause_menu_action::RESTART` (GameStates.cpp:200-205) and from `end_menu_action::RESTART`.

findings.title: Quit-to-main-menu from the pause menu leaves weapon loop sounds playing forever
findings.suggestion: Add `void Level::stop_all_sounds() const { stop_music(); stop_player_sounds(); }` and call that from every exit branch instead of `stop_music()`. Better still, give `Level` an actual destructor that stops everything it started, so no caller has to remember — the current design duplicates the teardown call at seven sites in `GameLevel::update` and gets it wrong at two of them.

findings.title: get_all_viewports() asks for viewport index 4 in a 3-player layout, so every menu draws a spurious 4th fullscreen copy
findings.suggestion: Change `get_player_viewport(4)` to `get_player_viewport(3)`. Add the missing `break;` after each layout case in `calculate_viewport` (lines 183, 207) so a bad `player_num` reaches the intended fallback instead of silently borrowing another layout's geometry — or better, make the function a table lookup returning `optional`/throwing on an out-of-range index rather than silently returning fullscreen.

findings.title: "Random" stage and "Random" weapon are resolved once and baked into MenuLevelSettings, so rematch is never random
findings.suggestion: Keep the user's selection (`RANDOM`) in `MenuLevelSettings` and resolve it at level-build time inside `LevelBuilder::build_level`, so each rematch re-rolls and the menus round-trip the real choice. Replace `rand() % N` with `std::uniform_int_distribution` over a seeded `std::mt19937` owned by the engine.

findings.title: Results-screen fill bars are sized in 1920-space after the widgets have already been scaled to the real resolution
findings.suggestion: Cache the resolution scale factor in `init()` (or store the scaled `RESULTS_MENU_TEAM_FILL_SIZE` once) and multiply `max_width` by it, or express the animation as a fraction of the already-scaled `_fill_box` width: `max_width = (_fill_box->get_rectangle().get_width() - 2*border_scaled) * score`. The general bug is that `scale_objects_to_new_resolution` is a one-shot mutation with no record of the scale, so any later absolute setter silently reintroduces design-space units.

findings.title: GameLevel declares every menu's data object after the state that points at it, so data dies first
findings.detail:
std::unique_ptr<Level> _level;                       // 57
    ...
    std::unique_ptr<StateContext> _pause_menu;           // 60
    std::unique_ptr<pause_menu_action> _pause_menu_action;// 61
    std::unique_ptr<PauseMenuData> _pause_menu_data;     // 62
    std::unique_ptr<MenuInput> _menu_input;              // 63
    std::unique_ptr<StateContext> _results_menu;         // 64
    std::unique_ptr<results_menu_action> _results_menu_action; // 65
    std::unique_ptr<ResultsMenuData> _results_menu_data; // 66
    std::unique_ptr<StateContext> _end_menu;             // 67
    std::unique_ptr<end_menu_action> _end_menu_action;   // 68
    std::unique_ptr<EndMenuData> _end_menu_data;         // 69

Members are destroyed in reverse declaration order, so the order is: `_end_menu_data`, `_end_menu_action`, `_end_menu`, `_results_menu_data`, `_results_menu_action`, `_results_menu`, `_menu_input`, `_pause_menu_data`, `_pause_menu_action`, `_pause_menu`. Every pointee dies before its pointer holder:
* `_end_menu_data` dies before `_end_menu`, whose live `EndMenuInitial` holds `EndMenuData* _data` (EndMenu.h:53).
* `_menu_input` dies before both `_pause_menu_data` (which stores `MenuInput*`, MenuData.h:16) and `_pause_menu` (whose pages call `get_menu_inputs()`).

The same inversion happens *mid-life*, on the second match, and there the dangling window is two live statements long:

    // GameStates.cpp:169-181
    this->_results_menu_action = std::make_unique<...>(NONE);   // old action freed HERE
    this->_results_menu_data   = std::make_unique<ResultsMenuData>(...);  // old data freed HERE
    this->_results_menu        = std::make_unique<StateContext>();        // old page freed only HERE

Between lines 169 and 178 the still-alive `ResultsMenuInitial` from match 1 holds a `ResultsMenuData*` to freed memory, which in turn holds a freed `results_menu_action*`.

This is currently latent only because none of the destructors happen to dereference. It is one added line in `~EndMenuPage`/`~MenuPage` away from a use-after-free.
findings.suggestion: Declare owners before borrowers (`_menu_input`, then `*_action`, then `*_data`, then the `StateContext`), and on re-entry destroy top-down explicitly: `_results_menu.reset(); _results_menu_data.reset(); _results_menu_action.reset();` before building the new ones. Structurally the better fix is to fold the action flag and the data into one object owned by the `StateContext` (or return an action enum from `State::update()`) so the ordering cannot be got wrong.

findings.title: Pause menu indexes the compacted menu-input vector with an index taken from a different, independently compacted vector
findings.suggestion: Put the gamepad slot into `ProcessedMenuInput`/`PlayerInputData` (they already carry a useless `connection` field that is unconditionally set to CONNECTED, MenuInput.cpp:127) and return a fixed 4-entry vector with a `connected` flag instead of compacting. Then look up by slot, not by position. As an immediate patch, bounds-check: `if (player_num < 0 || player_num >= static_cast<int>(inputs.size())) return;`.

findings.title: The root State is owned by a base class, so on app exit it outlives every service it borrows; Game::_state is dead code
findings.detail:
class Game final : public DX::IDeviceNotify, public StateContext
    { ...
        std::unique_ptr<DX::DeviceResources> _device_resources;   // 59
        std::unique_ptr<ResourceManager> _resource_manager;       // 65
        std::unique_ptr<State> _state = nullptr;                  // 67  <-- never used
        std::unique_ptr<ThreadPool> _thread_pool;                 // 71
        std::unique_ptr<DirectX::AudioEngine> _audio_engine;      // 74

Two problems.

1. `Game::_state` (line 67) is referenced nowhere in Game.cpp (grep for `_state` in Game.cpp returns only `_states`, the `CommonStates`). The live state actually lives in the private `StateContext::_state` base member. It is a dead, misleading member that also collides visually with `_states`.

2. Base-class subobjects are destroyed *after* members. So `g_game.reset()` (Main.cpp:226) destroys, in order, `_partitioner`, `_audio_engine`, `_thread_pool`, `_viewport_manager`, `_resource_manager`, `_device_resources` ... and only then `~StateContext()` destroys the live `GameLevel`, its `Level`, `Player`s and `Weapon`s — every one of which holds raw pointers into the already-destroyed `ResourceManager`/`SoundBank`/`ThreadPool`. Destroying `AudioEngine` before the `SoundEffect`/`SoundEffectInstance` objects it owns notifications for is explicitly unsupported by DirectXTK. Nothing crashes today only because none of those destructors dereference anything.

This is the app-exit branch of the teardown path: quitting from a live match tears the world down in exactly the wrong order.
findings.suggestion: Delete the dead `_state` member. Make `Game` *hold* a `StateContext` rather than inherit one (`std::unique_ptr<StateContext> _root_state;` declared first among the members, so it is destroyed first), or add an explicit `~Game()` body that does `StateContext::transition_to(nullptr)`-equivalent teardown of the state tree before any service is released. `Game` also declares `Game(Game&&) = default` (line 22) while the constructor calls `_device_resources->RegisterDeviceNotify(this)` (Game.cpp:20) — a move leaves DeviceResources pointing at a moved-from Game; that move should be deleted.

findings.title: transition_to deletes the currently-running state before initialising the new one; every call site is a self-delete
Every ResourceManager lookup uses map::operator[] inside a catch(out_of_range) that can never fire
findings.suggestion: Use `.at()` and let it throw, or `find()` + an explicit error. Make all five getters `const` (the maps then need `mutable`-free const lookup, which `.at()` gives you) so concurrent reads from thread-pool tasks are actually defined. Longer term, resolve resources to handles once at load time instead of doing a string map lookup per draw call per frame.

findings.title: End-of-match sound teardown throws for Sniper/Bucket, and nothing anywhere catches it
findings.suggestion: Give `Weapon` a sound name for every `wep_type` (or make the name a field of `WeaponDetails`, which already exists in weapon_consts.h) so teardown cannot throw. Independently, wrap `g_game->tick()` in a try/catch that logs and shows a message box before exiting — right now `/W4` warnings are unenforced (no `TreatWarningAsError`) and there is no crash reporting, so these are invisible until a player hits one. Note also `throw std::exception("literal")` is an MSVC-only extension; use `std::runtime_error`.

findings.title: Results screen positions the team-B percentage from a widget size it never sets
findings.detail:
this->_team_b_percentage->set_position(Vector2F(
        this->calculate_center_position(this->get_widget_size().x, DEFAULT_RESOLUTION.x) +
        TEAM_B_PERCENTAGE_X_OFFSET,
        this->calculate_team_b_fill_top_right_position().y));

`ResultsMenuInitial::init()` never calls `set_widget_size` / `set_widget_position` / `set_widget_spacing`, so `get_widget_size()` returns `MenuPage`'s unrelated hard-coded default `{ 300.0f, 75.0f }` (MenuPage.h:59). The x position of the team-B percentage text is therefore `(1920 - 300) / 2 + 325 = 1135` — a number that has nothing to do with this screen and that silently moves if anyone ever tunes the `MenuPage` default. The mirror image of the same smell is in `EndMenuInitial::init` (EndMenu.cpp:147), which *sets* `END_MENU_INITIAL_WIDGET_SIZE` and then never reads it.

`results_menu_consts` also carries five constants that are never referenced anywhere: `RESULTS_MENU_TEAM_FILL_Y_OFFSET` (ResultsMenu.h:25), `RESULTS_MENU_TITLE_Y_OFFSET` (32), `WINNER_TEXT_Y_OFFSET` (34), `TITLE_SHADOW_OFFSET`/`ITEM_SHADOW_OFFSET` (49, 51), `DIRECTION_SOUND`/`CANCEL_SOUND` (55, 57) — leftovers that make it impossible to tell which numbers actually drive the layout.
findings.suggestion: Either call `set_widget_size(...)` explicitly in `init()` with the value this screen intends, or drop the `get_widget_size()` dependency and write the intended x directly. Delete the unused constants. More broadly, `MenuPage`'s `_widget_position/_widget_size/_widget_spacing` are mutable per-page layout state on a shared base with defaults that no page actually wants — they belong in a small layout value type each page constructs.

findings.title: Half of LevelEndInfo is dead code, and it is also wrong: draws report 100%/0% and a 0-0 match yields NaN
findings.suggestion: Delete the six unused functions, or fix them: make the NONE branch return a sentinel/`optional`, guard the divisions the way `team_a_ratio` already does (LevelEndInfo.cpp:20-23), and drop the unreachable throws. `team_a_percentage_string` should also use `std::ostringstream`/`std::setprecision(1)` rather than `to_string` + `substr(0, find('.') + 2)` (lines 42-51), which produces garbage for NaN/inf and depends on the locale-free `to_string` format.

findings.title: Menu data classes inherit a hand-copied pointer bag; adding one service silently nulls it in every menu
findings.detail:
GameData::GameData(const GameData* game_data) :
        _save(game_data->get_save()),
        _resolution_manager(game_data->get_resolution_manager()),
        ... 13 members copied by hand ...

This reimplements the compiler-generated copy constructor, and takes a *pointer* rather than a reference so it can never be `= default`. `MenuData : public GameData` (MenuData.h:7) then snapshots the whole bag by value, and `EndMenuData`, `ResultsMenuData`, `PauseMenuData` and `MainMenuData` all inherit that. Consequences:

* Adding a 14th service to `GameData` and forgetting to extend this list leaves it `nullptr` in every single menu screen, with no compiler diagnostic. `Save::_dt`-style aliasing bugs are invisible.
* Nothing IS-A `GameData`. `EndMenuData` inheriting a service-locator so it can reach `get_resource_manager()` is inheritance used for `using`-namespace convenience. `MenuData::get_menu_data() { return this; }` (MenuData.cpp:26-29) and `GameData::get_game_data() { return this; }` are pure no-ops that exist only to paper over the confusion.
* Every `EndMenuData`/`ResultsMenuData` is a 13-pointer copy created per menu screen (GameStates.cpp:172, 228) — a snapshot that will silently go stale if anything ever calls a `GameData` setter after construction, which `Game::initialize` does (Game.cpp:36, 60, 253).

For a project whose stated goal is a reusable engine, this is the single biggest coupling problem in the menu layer: no menu screen can be reused or tested without dragging in `DeviceResources`, `ThreadPool`, `Partitioner` and `Save`.
