findings.suggestion: Delete `GameData(const GameData*)` and let the implicit copy constructor do it (take `const GameData&` if a converting constructor is genuinely wanted). Change `MenuData` to *hold* a `const GameData*` instead of inheriting it, and delete `get_menu_data()`/`get_game_data()`. Then narrow what each screen actually needs — `EndMenuInitial` uses only `ResourceManager*`, `ResolutionManager*`, `MenuInput*`, `CommonStates*` and the sprite-batch/deferred-context set; that is the real interface.

findings.title: MenuHighlight null-guards the two methods that cannot crash and leaves the one that can unguarded
findings.suggestion: Return early on a null highlight in each `update()`, or make `get_highlighted_widget()` return a reference and assert in `set_highlighted_widget`. Replace the string-name dispatch with a small `std::vector<MWidget*>` of menu entries plus an `size_t _index`, so up/down is `(_index + n - 1) % n` / `(_index + 1) % n` — that single change deletes the 100-line if/else ladders in `EndMenuInitial::update` (EndMenu.cpp:32-130) and `PauseMenuInitial::update` and makes the wrap-around impossible to get wrong.

findings.title: EndMenuInitial::update reads the highlight once outside the loop, plays the move sound before deciding, and has no back/ownership handling
findings.suggestion: Re-read the highlight inside the loop (or better, index-based selection as suggested for MenuHighlight); move `play_wave(DIRECTION_SOUND)` into `change_highlight` so it only fires when the highlight actually changes; add a BACK case; and decide explicitly whether the end menu is owned by one player (store the index like `PauseMenuData` does) or open to all, rather than leaving it as an accident of the loop. Use `size_t`/range-for for the loop to clear the C4018.

findings.title: Results and end-menu frames re-draw the entire level, unculled, on one worker thread, for as long as the menus are open
findings.suggestion: Draw the frozen level once into a cached command list (or a render target) when the level enters ZOOM_OUT/FINISHED and re-execute that while the menus are up, instead of re-recording it every frame. Delete the unused `num_threads`, and call `draw_zoom_out_level_component` directly rather than round-tripping through the pool for a single task. Then turn on `TreatWarningAsError` for at least a warning subset so this class of thing cannot accumulate.

findings.title: END_MENU case has no break and one pause case declares a local without braces
findings.detail:
Two latent landmines in the same switch.

1. The `game_level_state::END_MENU` case block (lines 240-297) ends without a `break;`. It currently falls into `default: break;` at lines 298-299, so behaviour is correct today — but it is the only case in the switch missing its break (FIRST_UPDATE returns at 135, SECOND_UPDATE falls through *deliberately* with a comment at 138, ACTIVE breaks at 187, PAUSE_MENU at 215, RESULTS at 238), and inserting any new case between END_MENU and `default` silently changes behaviour.

2. `case pause_menu_action::QUIT:` (lines 206-213) declares a local with a non-trivial constructor directly under a case label with no enclosing braces:

        case pause_menu_action::QUIT:
            this->_level->stop_music();
            MainMenuMidwayLoadSettings settings;   // MenuLevelSettings member -> non-trivial init
            settings.settings = MenuLevelSettings();

   This only compiles because QUIT is the last label in that switch. Adding any case after it makes MSVC reject the whole function with C2361 ("initialization of 'settings' is skipped by 'default' label"). Every other case that declares this same local wraps itself in braces (247, 257, 267, 277, 285) — this one was missed.

The wider issue is that `GameLevel::update` is a 170-line nested switch (lines 128-301) mixing frame skipping, input polling, level ticking and five different menu constructions; the missing brace and missing break are symptoms of that.
findings.suggestion: Add the `break;` and the braces. Then split the body: one small handler function per `game_level_state` (`update_active()`, `update_pause_menu()`, `update_results()`, `update_end_menu()`), each returning the next state. The FIRST_UPDATE/SECOND_UPDATE pair (a two-frame warm-up implemented as two enum values that just fall forward) should be a named `int _warmup_frames` or removed entirely once the cause of needing it is understood.

findings.title: Dead code on the end-of-match path: unreachable FINISHED branch, empty draw_end_screen, unused Level member
findings.suggestion: Delete all three. Then move the music/sound teardown into `~Level` (or a single `Level::end()` called from one place) so the seven duplicated `stop_music()` calls in `GameLevel::update` collapse to zero, which also fixes the two branches that currently forget `stop_player_sounds()`.

findings.title: All four JSON loaders overflow a 1-byte heap buffer on every read (sizeof(unique_ptr) as size)
findings.detail:
Every JSON loader in the codebase uses the identical idiom:

    std::unique_ptr<char> readBuffer = std::make_unique<char>();
    FileReadStream is(fp, readBuffer.get(), sizeof(readBuffer));

`make_unique<char>()` allocates exactly ONE byte. `sizeof(readBuffer)` is `sizeof(std::unique_ptr<char>)` = 8 on x64 (4 on Win32), not the buffer size. The vendored rapidjson does `readCount_ = std::fread(buffer_, 1, bufferSize_, fp_)` (external/rapidjson/include/rapidjson/filereadstream.h:71) and then `buffer_[readCount_] = '\0'` (line 76) — so it writes up to 8, and indexes up to buffer_[8], on a 1-byte allocation. This is a heap buffer overflow on every single refill, repeated for the whole file.

The shipped data makes the scale concrete: ArtAttack/textures/sprite_sheet_1.json is 14,165 bytes and ArtAttack/levels/king_of_the_hill.json is 21,955 bytes, so startup performs roughly 1,771 + 2,745 + (turbulence 21,493) + (close_quarters 12,730) + (sound_bank_1.json 3,166) + (save_data.json 53) / 8 overflowing freads — about 9,000 out-of-bounds writes before the main menu appears. It happens to "work" only because MSVC's heap allocates a padded block for a 1-byte request.

All four sites, identical bug:
- ArtAttack/LevelLoadedInfo.cpp:100-101 (runs 3× — one per level)
- ArtAttack/SpriteSheet.cpp:74-75
- ArtAttack/SoundBank.cpp:154-155
- ArtAttack/Save.cpp:16-17

All four also then call `readBuffer.release()` (LevelLoadedInfo.cpp:107, SpriteSheet.cpp:81, SoundBank.cpp:161, Save.cpp:23), deliberately leaking the allocation — presumably a misunderstanding of `release()` vs `reset()`. And none of the four checks `fopen` for NULL, which rapidjson only guards with `RAPIDJSON_ASSERT(fp_ != 0)` — a no-op under NDEBUG (defined in both Release configs, ArtAttack.vcxproj:138,164).
findings.suggestion: Replace the whole idiom with a shared helper that reads the file into a `std::string`/`std::vector<char>` and parses via `rapidjson::MemoryStream`/`StringStream`, or if FileReadStream is kept: `std::array<char, 65536> buf;` and pass `buf.size()`. Check `fopen` for null and throw a diagnostic naming the path. Drop the `release()` calls. Fix all four sites together.

findings.title: Every projectile flies straight through the shipped ramp in king_of_the_hill
findings.detail:
`Projectile::is_matching_collision_object_type` gates all projectile collision on:

    bool structure_collision =
        other_type == collision_object_type::STRUCTURE ||
        other_type == collision_object_type::STRUCTURE_PAINTABLE ||
        other_type == collision_object_type::STRUCTURE_JUMP_THROUGH;

`STRUCTURE_RAMP_LEFT` / `STRUCTURE_RAMP_RIGHT` are absent, even though `is_structure()` (ArtAttack/collision_object_type.h:75-82) includes them and `Player::is_matching_collision_object_type` (ArtAttack/Player.cpp:142-147) uses that helper. `Projectile::on_collision` (ArtAttack/Projectile.cpp:120-152) repeats the same three-way test, so it would not delete the projectile either. No subclass overrides it — ProjectileSpray.cpp:59, ProjectileJet.cpp:57, ProjectileBall.cpp:58, ProjectileMist.cpp:59, ProjectileRolling.cpp:51 all call the base version.

The shipped content reaches this: ArtAttack/levels/king_of_the_hill.json:257-273 declares `"name": "mountain_level_1_ramp_east"`, `"type": "StructureRamp"`, `"collision_type": "STRUCTURE_RAMP_RIGHT"` with triangle (300,6000)-(1700,6000)-(1700,5550) — a 1400×450 unit slope that is the entire approach from team A's spawn to the central mountain. ArtAttack/LevelObjectBuilder.cpp:144-177 maps that string to `collision_object_type::STRUCTURE_RAMP_RIGHT` and builds a plain `Structure` with a `TriangleRightAxisAligned` shape. Result: players collide with the ramp (Player handles it), but all five projectile types pass through it as if it were air, and are never deleted on it. It is also a plain `Structure`, not `StructurePaintable`, so it cannot be painted either.
findings.suggestion: Replace the hand-written three-way test with the existing `is_structure(other_type)` predicate in both `Projectile::is_matching_collision_object_type` and `Projectile::on_collision`, so ramps (and any future structure type) are covered by construction. Better still, delete the enum-switch dispatch entirely and put a `bool blocks_projectiles()` on the collision interface.

findings.title: Paintable-face flags are permuted: edge index map disagrees with RectangleF::get_edges() ordering
findings.detail:
`RectangleF::get_edges()` (ArtAttack/MattMath.cpp:808-818) returns edges in the order **top, bottom, left, right**:

    std::vector<Segment> edges = { get_top_edge(), get_bottom_edge(), get_left_edge(), get_right_edge() };

`StructurePaintable::generate_paint_tiles()` matches the JSON-derived `_paintable_edges` against that vector and then decodes the index as **top, right, bottom, left**:

    if (i == 0) top_edge = true;
    else if (i == 1) right_edge = true;    // edges[1] is the BOTTOM edge
    else if (i == 2) bottom_edge = true;   // edges[2] is the LEFT edge
    else if (i == 3) left_edge = true;     // edges[3] is the RIGHT edge

So three of the four faces authored in the level JSON are wired to the wrong face. Only `top` is correct. `LevelObjectBuilder.cpp:108-126` reads `paintable_faces.left/top/right/bottom` faithfully, so the data is fine; the decode is not.

I simulated this against the shipped levels. Concrete misbehaviour in ArtAttack/levels/king_of_the_hill.json:
- `castle_ceiling` (json:525-545, rect 1650×25, faces `bottom:true` at json:537-543) → produces 6 tiles down its RIGHT edge instead of 412 tiles along its bottom. The castle ceiling is effectively unpaintable.
- `castle_wall_right` (json:503-523, rect 25×750, `left:true`) → 6 tiles along its BOTTOM instead of 187 down its left face.
- `castle_wall_left` (json:459-479, `right:true`) → tiles on its LEFT face (buried inside the facade) instead of the right face that lines the castle interior.
- `castle_floor_left` (json:437-457, `top,right`) → top + LEFT instead of top + right.
- `castle_floor_right` (json:481-501, `left,top`) → top + BOTTOM (350 tiles) instead of top + left (181).
- `castle_room_floor_left`/`_right` (json:658-700, `top,bottom`) → top + RIGHT instead of top + bottom.
Same in ArtAttack/levels/close_quarters.json `lower_paint` (json:246, `top,bottom` → top+right) and ArtAttack/levels/turbulence.json `central_divider_ledge_paint` (json:297, `left,top,right` → bottom,left,top).

Because King-of-the-Hill scoring sums paint-tile areas (`StructurePaintable::get_paint_total`, lines 300-319), this silently changes the win condition: e.g. castle_floor_right contributes 350 tiles of score surface where the designer asked for 181, and castle_ceiling contributes 6 where 412 was intended. Objects that declare all four faces true are unaffected, which is why the bug survived.
findings.suggestion: Delete the index-decoding entirely — the builder already knows which faces are wanted. Pass a `PaintableFaces{left,top,right,bottom}` struct (the commented-out struct at StructurePaintable.h:17-23 and LevelObjectBuilder.cpp:101-105 is exactly this) instead of round-tripping booleans through geometric `Segment` equality. If the segment matching must stay, drive it off named accessors (`edge == rect.get_top_edge()`) rather than a positional index into `get_edges()`.

findings.title: Weapon::stop_sounds() throws for Sniper and Bucket — crashes at the end of every match
findings.suggestion: Make `stop_sounds()` virtual and override it in WeaponSniper/WeaponBucket to stop the wave (or do nothing), or better: give `WeaponDetails` an optional instance-name provider so `stop_sounds` is a no-op when the weapon has no instance. The switch-on-wep_type in `get_sound_effect_instance_name` should be data on the weapon, not a hard-coded ladder.

findings.title: A player left on 'no team' in team select spawns at team B's point and then throws during level build
findings.suggestion: Either forbid confirming on NONE in `MainMenuTeamSelect` (require `team != NONE` in `all_players_confirmed`), or drop NONE from `player_team` and model 'unassigned' as a separate menu-only state. The `if (A) … else …` in PlayerBuilder should be an explicit switch that rejects NONE rather than aliasing it to team B.

findings.title: Shipped levels generate 3,348-5,574 PaintTile objects, each updated every frame and scanned linearly per projectile hit
findings.detail:
`generate_paint_tiles()` tiles a face at `paint_tile_consts::WIDTH = HEIGHT = 4.0f` (ArtAttack/PaintTile.h:12-13). Applying that to the shipped level data gives:
- king_of_the_hill.json: 3,348 PaintTiles across 13 StructurePaintables, of which `boundary_floor` (json:229-250, 6000×1000, top face) alone is 1,500.
- turbulence.json: 5,574 PaintTiles across 9 objects.
- close_quarters.json: 1,160 across 2.

Each `PaintTile` is a `TextureObject` + `ICollisionGameObject` that also owns a `PaintTileSplash` (an `AnimationObject`, PaintTile.h:83), so level load constructs ~5,600 polymorphic objects and does ~11,000 sprite-sheet/resource-manager lookups. `StructurePaintable::update()` (lines 37-43) then calls `paint_tile.update()` on every tile unconditionally every frame — ~5,600 virtual calls per frame doing nothing for tiles that were never painted.

Worse, `StructurePaintable::on_collision` (lines 64-102) does a linear `is_colliding` scan over all of that object's tiles for *each* colliding projectile. A single spray projectile landing on `boundary_floor` costs 1,500 AABB tests, and `Level::update_level_logic` (Level.cpp:180-322) already tests each pair twice per frame in its player×object and object×object loops. With a sprayer firing at ~1 projectile/frame this is the dominant cost in the whole simulation.

There is also no per-tile visibility culling: `StructurePaintable::draw` (lines 45-52) draws every tile once the parent structure passes `is_visible_in_viewport` in Level.cpp:527. Unpainted tiles bail out early in `PaintTile::draw` (PaintTile.cpp:35-47, `default: return;`), so this is mostly wasted call overhead rather than wasted draws — but it scales with tile count, not screen area.
findings.suggestion: Store paint coverage as a flat bitmap/grid per structure (one `std::vector<uint8_t>` of team ids) rather than a vector of full game objects, index it arithmetically from the impact point instead of scanning, and drop `update()` on tiles entirely — the splash animation only needs to tick for the handful of recently-painted tiles.

findings.title: Unknown frame name silently draws a 0×0 sprite and mutates a shared map from render threads
findings.detail:
Both `SpriteSheet::draw` overloads look the frame up with `std::map::operator[]`:

    this->_sprite_frames[frame_name].get_source_rectangle()

`operator[]` default-constructs and inserts on a miss. `SpriteFrame`'s default source rect is `RECT _source_rectangle = { 0, 0, 0, 0 }` (ArtAttack/SpriteFrame.h:21), so a misspelled frame name produces a silent degenerate draw with no error — in sharp contrast to `get_animation_strip` (SpriteSheet.cpp:15-18) which uses `.at()` and throws.

The shipped data proves the failure mode is real, not hypothetical: ArtAttack/levels/unused/test_1.json:159 and ArtAttack/levels/unused/structure_test_old.json:261 both contain `"frame_name": "grsquare_white_4ass"` — a botched find-and-replace of `grass` → `square_white_4`. That frame does not exist in ArtAttack/textures/sprite_sheet_1.json, and nothing would have told the author.

Second, sharper problem: these overloads are non-const and mutate `_sprite_frames`, and they are called from the multi-threaded draw path. `Level::draw_active_level` dispatches `draw_player_view_level` (Level.cpp:491-593) as ThreadPool tasks, each recording into its own deferred context but all going through the *same* `SpriteSheet*` handed out by `ResourceManager`. A single missing frame name therefore causes a concurrent `std::map` insert while up to three other threads are reading it — undefined behaviour, and a heisenbug that only appears when content is wrong.
findings.suggestion: Make both `draw` overloads `const` and use `_sprite_frames.at(frame_name)`, or a `find()` that throws a message naming the frame and the sheet. Validate all frame/strip names once at load time against the atlas rather than at draw time.

findings.title: STRUCTURE_RAMP_LEFT is an empty TODO with no art and no data — the builder accepts it anyway
findings.suggestion: Either finish the left-ramp case or reject `"STRUCTURE_RAMP_LEFT"` in the builder with a clear 'not implemented' error, and delete the three fully commented-out StructureRamp* translation units from ArtAttack.vcxproj.

findings.title: close_quarters ships two 900-unit-tall vertical jump-through 'fences' that teleport falling players to their tops
findings.suggestion: Resolve jump-through collisions against the structure's top *edge* with a max penetration depth (reject if the overlap exceeds a few units), or introduce a distinct one-way-direction field on the collision object so a vertical fence is expressible. Either way the two close_quarters fences need re-authoring.

findings.title: The 4th team-A spawn point is embedded inside the spawn-room jump-through ceiling in all three shipped levels
findings.detail:
`spawn_locations.team_a` entries 0-2 are at y = 4870.0, but entry 3 is:

    { "x": 196.0, "y": 4800.0 }

`PlayerBuilder.cpp:38` builds the player as `RectangleF(position, DEFAULT_SIZE)` where `player_consts::DEFAULT_SIZE = {52, 120}` (ArtAttack/player_consts.h:21) and position is the top-left — so that player occupies y ∈ [4800, 4920], x ∈ [196, 248].

The same level declares `spawn_a_ceiling` (king_of_the_hill.json:163-177) as a `STRUCTURE_JUMP_THROUGH` at x 0-300, y 4855-4865. The 4th team-A spawn point therefore starts the player straddling that one-way platform, whereas the y=4870 spawns start cleanly below it (4870 > 4865). Because `Player::on_structure_jump_through_collision` requires `_prev_rectangle.get_bottom() <= other_rect.get_top()` to resolve, a player spawned already overlapping never gets pushed out and simply falls through — inconsistent with players 1-3.

The identical spawn arrays (including the 4800 outlier) are copy-pasted verbatim into ArtAttack/levels/close_quarters.json:9-49 and ArtAttack/levels/turbulence.json:9-49, and into all four ArtAttack/levels/unused/*.json. It reads as a typo for 4870 that was then propagated by copy-paste.
findings.suggestion: Change y to 4870.0 in team_a entry 3 of all three shipped levels. Separately, add a load-time validation pass that asserts no spawn rectangle intersects a collision object — this class of authoring error is otherwise invisible until playtest.

findings.title: No parse-error check on any of the four ParseStream calls; rapidjson's own guards are compiled out in Release
findings.detail:
All four loaders do `d.ParseStream(is);` and immediately dereference members, with zero error handling: LevelLoadedInfo.cpp:104, SpriteSheet.cpp:78, SoundBank.cpp:158, Save.cpp:20. Grepping the whole first-party tree for `HasParseError` / `GetParseError` returns nothing.

On a truncated or empty file the `Document` is left as `kNullType`, and the very next line (`this->_json_doc["level_name"]`, `d["resolution"]["x"].GetInt()`, `d["waves"]`, …) hits `GenericValue::operator[]`, whose only protection is `RAPIDJSON_ASSERT(IsObject())`. That macro is `assert(x)` (external/rapidjson/include/rapidjson/rapidjson.h:437), and both Release configurations define NDEBUG (ArtAttack.vcxproj:138,164) — so in a shipping build the assert vanishes and rapidjson walks `data_.o.members` on a null value. Undefined behaviour, not an exception.

This is directly reachable for the save file, which is the one JSON the *program itself* rewrites at runtime (`Save::write_save_file`, Save.cpp:58-83): an interrupted write or a hand-edited `ArtAttack/save/save_data.json` (currently 53 bytes: `{"resolution":{"x":1920,"y":1080},"fullscreen":false}`) yields a Release-mode crash with no message. It is also reachable for a fresh copy of the built exe: there is no post-build asset copy step and paths are relative (`"./save/save_data.json"`, ArtAttack/directory_consts.h:11), so if `./save/` is absent, `write_save_file`'s `fopen` returns nullptr → returns false → `load_from_json` then `fopen`s NULL → `fread(buf,1,8,NULL)`.
findings.suggestion: Check `d.HasParseError()` and `fp != nullptr` at all four sites and throw an exception naming the file and `GetParseErrorCode()`/`GetErrorOffset()`. Factor the shared open/read/parse into one function so the fix lands once. Also define `RAPIDJSON_ASSERT` to something that survives NDEBUG if you intend to rely on it.

findings.title: Global player counter indexes per-team spawn arrays with no bounds check; safe only by coincidence of the shipped data
findings.suggestion: Track separate per-team counters and use `.at()`, or better: assert at load time in `LevelLoadedInfo` that both spawn arrays have at least MAX_PLAYERS entries and fail the level load with a clear message.

findings.title: Two of the four levels/unused/*.json files cannot be loaded at all; nothing marks them as unloadable
findings.detail:
`ResourceLoader::load_level_info` (ArtAttack/ResourceLoader.cpp:38-43) currently loads only king_of_the_hill, turbulence and close_quarters, but four more level files sit in `ArtAttack/levels/unused/` and are one line away from being selected. Two of them would fail, in different ways:

- ArtAttack/levels/unused/test_1.json uses `"collision_type": "STRUCTURE_FLOOR_PAINTABLE"` (lines 94, 115) and `"STRUCTURE_WALL"` (lines 136, 150). Neither string exists in the builder's ladders (LevelObjectBuilder.cpp:24-35 accepts only STRUCTURE / STRUCTURE_JUMP_THROUGH; :71-78 only STRUCTURE_PAINTABLE), so it throws `std::exception("Invalid collision type")` — a message that names neither the file, the object, nor the offending string.
- ArtAttack/levels/unused/level_0.json is a completely different schema: its top-level keys are `level_name`, `spawn_locations`, `tile_types` — no `sound`, no `level_bounds`, no `collision_objects`, no `non_collision_objects`. Every `LevelLoadedInfo` accessor (`_json_doc["sound"]["music_name"]` at :78, `_json_doc["level_bounds"][...]` at :33-61, `_json_doc["collision_objects"]` at :66) would hit a missing member with the NDEBUG-disabled rapidjson assert described elsewhere.

Both also carry the `"grsquare_white_4ass"` frame-name typo (test_1.json:159, structure_test_old.json:261).
findings.suggestion: Delete `ArtAttack/levels/unused/` from the repo — it is dead content in an incompatible schema. If it is kept as reference, at minimum make the builder's exception messages include the file path, object `name` and the unrecognised string, so a bad level is diagnosable rather than a bare 'Invalid collision type'.

findings.title: The 'name' field on every level object is never read, and duplicate names in the data prove nobody would notice
findings.detail:
Every object in every level file carries a `"name"` field — 33 collision objects + 6 visuals in king_of_the_hill.json alone (json:84, 99, 114, 134, …). `LevelObjectBuilder::build_collision_object` and `build_non_collision_object` read only `type`, `collision_type`, `sheet_name`, `frame_name`, `colour`, and `rectangle`/`rectangle_tlbr`/`triangle`/`paintable_faces`. `json["name"]` appears nowhere in the codebase.

Evidence that this silently rots: king_of_the_hill.json:164 and king_of_the_hill.json:209 are both named `"spawn_a_ceiling"` — the second is actually team B's ceiling (x = 5700). The identical duplication exists in close_quarters.json and turbulence.json. Nothing surfaced it because nothing consumes the field.

Also unread: `"rectangle_tlbr"` is supported by the parser (LevelObjectBuilder.cpp:45-52, :88-95) but no level file on disk uses it — a whole code path with zero coverage from either data or tests.
findings.suggestion: Either use the name (store it on the object and include it in the builder's exception messages — 'Invalid collision type "STRUCTURE_WALL" for object "floor_2" in test_1.json' is worth far more than the current bare string), or drop it from the schema. Duplicate names should then be a load-time error.

findings.title: projectile_consts::DETAILS_DEFAULT names an animation strip 'test' that does not exist in the atlas
findings.suggestion: Point DETAILS_DEFAULT at `error`/`projectile_3` like the other entries, or delete it since it is unused. Prune the 15 dead atlas entries, and add a startup validation that every name constant in *_consts.h resolves in the loaded sheet — it is a dozen lines and would have caught all of this.

findings.title: Orphan plaintext save file, plus a git-tracked save file the game rewrites at runtime and a silent resolution downgrade
findings.detail:
Three separate problems around the save data, all visible from the shipped files:

1. `ArtAttack/save/save_data.txt` contains `1920x1080\nfalse` — a plaintext predecessor of the JSON format. It is tracked in git (`git ls-files ArtAttack/save` returns both files) and **no code reads it**: the only save path in the codebase is `directory_consts::SAVE_FILE_PATH = "./save/save_data.json"` (ArtAttack/directory_consts.h:11), used at Save.cpp:35, :55, :60. Dead file.

2. `ArtAttack/save/save_data.json` is tracked *and* rewritten at runtime (`fopen(SAVE_FILE_PATH.c_str(), "wb")`, Save.cpp:60) by `set_resolution_and_save` / `set_full_screen_and_save`. Changing a setting dirties the working tree. Runtime-mutable state does not belong in version control.

3. `Save::convert_ivec_to_resolution` (Save.cpp:112-135) hard-codes four resolutions and its `else` returns `S_1280_720`. A save file holding any other resolution — including one written by a future build, or hand-edited — is silently downgraded to 1280×720 with no message and without correcting the file, so the value stays wrong until the user changes it in the options menu. The counterpart `convert_resolution_to_ivec` returns `{-1,-1}` for an unknown enum (Save.cpp:150), which would then be written into the JSON.

Minor, same file: Save.cpp:90 is `std::cout << ctime_s(buffer, sizeof(buffer), &legacy_start) << " Saving...\n";` — `ctime_s` returns an `errno_t`, so this prints `0 Saving...`, never a timestamp. (And `std::cout` in a `wWinMain` GUI app with no console goes nowhere regardless.)
findings.suggestion: Delete save_data.txt; add `ArtAttack/save/save_data.json` to .gitignore and generate it on first run (the code already does this via `check_if_save_file_exists`). Replace the resolution if/else ladder with a table lookup and log/repair an unrecognised value instead of silently substituting. Fix the ctime_s line to print `buffer`.

findings.title: The unused wave_bank_1.json omits a field SoundBank::load_from_json reads unconditionally, and carries three fields nothing reads
findings.suggestion: Delete `ArtAttack/sounds/unused/`. Make `load_from_json` use `HasMember`/`FindMember` with an explicit default for `create_effect_instance_for_each_wave`, and either honour `volume`/`pitch`/`pan` or remove them from the schema.

findings.title: Device restore rebuilds SpriteBatches on the 16 deferred contexts of the destroyed device
findings.detail:
`create_deferred_contexts` is called exactly once, from `Game::initialize` (Game.cpp:52) — grep confirms no other call site. `DeviceResources::HandleDeviceLost` (DeviceResources.cpp:418-453) does `m_d3dContext.Reset(); ... m_d3dDevice.Reset(); m_dxgiFactory.Reset(); CreateDeviceResources(); CreateWindowSizeDependentResources();` and then calls `OnDeviceRestored`. `Game::OnDeviceRestored` (Game.cpp:282-287) calls `create_device_dependent_resources()`, which at Game.cpp:226-232 does `std::make_unique<SpriteBatch>(this->_device_resources->get_deferred_context(i))` for i in 0..15 — i.e. it builds brand-new SpriteBatches, and `_states = make_unique<CommonStates>(device)` at line 252 on the NEW device, on top of the OLD deferred contexts, which still belong to the removed device. `DeviceResources::_deferred_contexts` (DeviceResources.h:128) is never cleared or recreated on device loss.

Every frame after a restore, `Game::clear()` (Game.cpp:136-149) then does `deferred_context->OMSetRenderTargets(1, &renderTarget, nullptr)` with the NEW device's RTV on an OLD device's context, and `GameLevel::draw` (GameStates.cpp:328) / `MenuPage::draw_mobjects_in_viewports` (MenuPage.cpp:161) call `immediate_context->ExecuteCommandList(...)` on the new immediate context with command lists produced by the old device. Cross-device resource use is invalid in D3D11.

In Debug this trips the info-queue break installed at DeviceResources.cpp:238-239 (`SetBreakOnSeverity(D3D11_MESSAGE_SEVERITY_ERROR, true)`) — a hard debug break. In Release it is silent corruption: black or garbage frames for the rest of the session. This is reachable from the two normal device-loss paths, `Present` (DeviceResources.cpp:485-494) and `ResizeBuffers` (DeviceResources.cpp:290-304).
findings.suggestion: Move deferred-context creation into `DeviceResources::CreateDeviceResources()` (so it is redone by `HandleDeviceLost`), release the old ones first, and store them as `Microsoft::WRL::ComPtr<ID3D11DeviceContext>` so the reference is dropped when the device is torn down. Longer term, a `TryEnableDeviceLossHandling`-style test path or at least a manual `DXGIGetDebugInterface`-triggered device removal should be exercised once — this code has clearly never been run.

findings.title: OnDeviceLost/OnDeviceRestored replace every shared service, leaving all live game objects with dangling pointers
findings.detail:
`Game::OnDeviceRestored` (Game.cpp:282-287) calls `create_device_dependent_resources()`, which does not "recreate device-dependent resources" — it reconstructs the entire service graph: `_thread_pool` (Game.cpp:236), `_resource_manager` (239), `_resource_loader` (241), `_dt = std::make_unique<float>(0.f)` (244), `_viewport_manager` (247), `_states` (252), `_partitioner` (255), each republished into `GameData` (237, 240, 243, 245, 250, 253, 256). `GameData` is only a bag of raw pointers (GameData.h:49-61); every consumer copied those pointers into its own members at construction and is never notified. Confirmed consumers: `Level::_resolution_manager/_viewport_manager/_resource_manager` (Level.h:117-119), `Level::_dt` (Level.h:140), `Level::_thread_pool/_partitioner` (Level.h:146-147), `Player::_dt` (Player.h:170). After one device restore mid-match, `Level::update` dereferences six freed objects.

Worse, the crash arrives before the restore: `Game::OnDeviceLost` (Game.cpp:277-279) calls `_resource_manager->reset_all_sounds()`, which is `sound_bank.second->reset_all_instances(); sound_bank.second.reset();` (ResourceManager.cpp:119-126) — it destroys every `SoundBank`. `Player::_sound_bank` (Player.h:168) and `Level::_sound_bank` (Level.h:107) are raw pointers into those destroyed banks, and the next `play_wave` (SoundBank.cpp:16-21) is a use-after-free. Audio is not a D3D device resource at all — tearing down sound on D3D device loss is gratuitous.
findings.suggestion: Split `create_device_dependent_resources` into (a) genuinely device-dependent GPU objects (SpriteBatches, CommonStates, textures/fonts) and (b) one-time services (`_dt`, thread pool, partitioner, resource manager, viewport manager) that must survive device loss; only (a) may be re-run from `OnDeviceRestored`. Stop resetting sounds on device loss. Frame time should be a `float` passed as an argument, not a heap `float*` handed out to 26 headers.

findings.title: Backbuffer is sized from the save file, not the client rect; AdjustWindowRect and GetClientRect results are both discarded
findings.detail:
Main.cpp:146-150 builds `RECT rc = {0,0,res.x,res.y}` and calls `AdjustWindowRect(&rc, WS_OVERLAPPEDWINDOW, FALSE)` — and then never uses `rc`. `CreateWindowExW` at lines 156-158 / 162-164 is passed the *unadjusted* `res_ivec2.x, res_ivec2.y` as nWidth/nHeight, which are the OUTER window dimensions. So a saved 1920x1080 gives a client area of roughly 1904x1041 in windowed mode. Line 202 then calls `GetClientRect(hwnd, &rc)` and that result is also discarded — the following `g_game->initialize(...)` (line 207) sizes the swap chain from `get_resolution_manager()->get_resolution_ivec()` instead (Game.cpp:38-40 `_device_resources->SetWindow(window, window_size.x, window_size.y)`).

Result, every windowed run, from the first frame: a 1920x1080 backbuffer presented into a ~1904x1041 client area. The swap chain is created with `DXGI_SCALING_STRETCH` (DeviceResources.cpp:321), so DXGI rescales it non-uniformly — the whole game is slightly squashed and resampled. Silent visual corruption, no crash.

The fullscreen path is worse. `ShowWindow(hwnd, SW_SHOWMAXIMIZED)` at line 191 fires WM_SIZE synchronously, which reaches `Game::on_window_size_changed` (WndProc Main.cpp:299-302) with the true monitor client size — but `DeviceResources::WindowSizeChanged` bails immediately at DeviceResources.cpp:397-398 (`if (!m_window) return false;`) because `SetWindow` has not been called yet (that happens at Game.cpp:39, from `initialize` at Main.cpp:207). The real monitor size is thrown away, and since a maximized borderless window never gets another WM_SIZE, `m_outputSize` stays at the saved resolution forever. Saved 1920x1080 on a 2560x1440 monitor = a 1920x1080 backbuffer stretched to 2560x1440 for the entire session.
findings.suggestion: Create the window from an `AdjustWindowRect`-corrected rect, then call `GetClientRect` and drive `SetWindow`/`CreateWindowSizeDependentResources` from the actual client size. The saved resolution should be a *request*, and the actual client area the single source of truth thereafter.

findings.title: create_window_size_dependent_resources is an empty stub, so every viewport, camera and UI layout stays pinned to the saved resolution after any resize
findings.detail:
`void Game::create_window_size_dependent_resources() const { auto size = _device_resources->GetOutputSize(); }` — the local `size` is unused (also an unreported /W4 C4189, since `TreatWarningAsError` is set nowhere). This is the only hook that fires on a resize (`Game::on_window_size_changed`, Game.cpp:197-205), so nothing outside `DeviceResources` ever learns the new size.

Everything that positions pixels reads `ResolutionManager` instead, i.e. the value loaded from save_data.json: `ViewportManager::get_fullscreen_viewport` (ViewportManager.cpp:19), all three `apply_player_viewport` overloads (ViewportManager.cpp:49, 58, 66 — note line 60/69 also feed it to `SpriteBatch::SetViewport`, so the sprite projection matrix is built from it), `get_player_viewport` (:87), `get_viewport_dividers` (:126), `MenuPage::get_float_resolution` (MenuPage.cpp:190-193), and the gameplay cameras: `Level.cpp:80-84` and `196-200` feed `CameraTools::calculate_camera` a `viewport_size` from `_viewport_manager->get_player_viewport(...)`, and `Level.cpp:150-156` builds the zoom-out camera from `_resolution_manager->get_resolution_vec()`. `get_fullscreen_d3d11_viewport()` (ViewportManager.h:43), the one function that could have been backbuffer-driven, is dead — grep shows no caller.

Concrete first visible consequence of dragging a window corner: WM_EXITSIZEMOVE (Main.cpp:309-318) resizes the swapchain to, say, 800x600, `Game::clear` sets the correct 800x600 viewport (Game.cpp:143-149), and then the draw path immediately overrides it with `RSSetViewports` at 1920x1080 (ViewportManager.cpp:50/59). D3D clamps to the render target, so you see only the top-left 800x600 corner of the scene and the HUD/menu is mostly off-screen. Enlarge the window instead and the game renders into the top-left corner surrounded by the black clear colour. No crash, permanent wrong output.
findings.suggestion: Either make the render size authoritative — have `create_window_size_dependent_resources` push `GetOutputSize()` into `ResolutionManager` (renamed to something like `RenderTargetSize`) and have ViewportManager/MenuPage read that — or render to a fixed-size offscreen target at the design resolution and blit it letterboxed. Do not keep two independent notions of "the resolution".

findings.title: Fall-through in calculate_viewport makes the 3-player layout draw a 4th full-screen viewport over everything
findings.detail:
The outer `switch (layout)` has no `break` or `return` on the fall-out path of any case. `case screen_layout::TWO_PLAYER:` (line 166) contains an inner switch whose `default: break;` (line 181-182) falls straight into `case screen_layout::THREE_PLAYER:` (line 184), whose `default: break;` (205-206) falls into `case screen_layout::FOUR_PLAYER:` (208), whose `default: break;` (235-236) falls into `default: //1P screen` (238) returning a full-screen viewport.

This is not theoretical. `ViewportManager::get_all_viewports` (ViewportManager.cpp:90-104) does:

    if (player_count == 3) { result.push_back(this->get_player_viewport(4)); }

With `_layout == THREE_PLAYER` and `player_num == 4`, THREE_PLAYER's inner switch misses, falls into FOUR_PLAYER's inner switch (which only handles 0-3), misses again, and lands on the 1P default — returning `{0, 0, screen_size.x, screen_size.y}`. `MenuPage::draw_mobject_in_viewports` (MenuPage.cpp:99-115) draws each widget once per entry of `get_all_viewports()`, so in every 3-player game the pause menu, results menu and HUD get a 4th copy stretched across the whole screen on top of the three player panels. The index is also off by one: the intended empty bottom-right quadrant is FOUR_PLAYER's `player_num == 3`, not 4.
findings.suggestion: Give every case an explicit `return`/`break`, use `player_num == 3` for the filler quadrant, and replace the nested switches with a small table (layout -> array of normalised rects) so a missing entry is a compile-time or assert failure rather than a silent fall-through.

findings.title: Options apply path: dead SetWindowPos, no re-derivation of render size, and fullscreen guarantees a viewport/backbuffer mismatch
findings.detail:
`MainMenuOptions::update` (line 318) on "apply" sets `ResolutionManager`, writes the save (line 329), then calls

    SetWindowPos(get_data()->get_window(), HWND_TOP, 0, 0, res_i.x, res_i.y, SWP_NOMOVE | SWP_NOZORDER);   // lines 334-340

which is dead in both branches: `apply_fullscreen_setting(fs)` on the next line either does `SetWindowPos(..., SWP_NOMOVE|SWP_NOSIZE|SWP_NOZORDER|SWP_FRAMECHANGED)` followed by `ShowWindow(hWnd, SW_SHOWMAXIMIZED)` (lines 435-438), or another `SetWindowPos` with the same `res_i` plus SWP_FRAMECHANGED (lines 448-449). It is also missing SWP_FRAMECHANGED, so it does not even apply the style change it precedes.

No code path re-derives the render size from the new client area — see the empty `Game::create_window_size_dependent_resources` (Game.cpp:264-267). In the fullscreen branch, `ShowWindow(SW_SHOWMAXIMIZED)` synchronously produces WM_SIZE, so `DeviceResources` resizes the backbuffer to the MONITOR size while `ResolutionManager` now holds the user's chosen enum. Pick 1280x720 in fullscreen on a 1920x1080 monitor and every `RSSetViewports` is 1280x720 into a 1920x1080 target: the game renders into the top-left third and the rest is black. Pick 3840x2160 on that monitor and the viewport is clamped to the target — you see the top-left quarter of the menu.

Finally, only two of the three widget trees are rescaled: lines 347-350 rescale `_texture_container` and `_text_container`, while `_background` is left at the old resolution because its rescale is commented out at line 352 — so the background quad no longer covers the screen after an apply.
findings.suggestion: Make apply do one thing: request the size, let the WM_SIZE handler be the single place that updates both the swapchain and the layout resolution, then rebuild the current menu page from the new size. Delete the dead SetWindowPos at 334-340 and either fix or delete `_background`'s rescale.

findings.title: Borderless-fullscreen window is WS_EX_TOPMOST and never drops topmost when deactivated
findings.detail:
The fullscreen window is created with `CreateWindowExW(WS_EX_TOPMOST, ..., WS_POPUP, ...)` (Main.cpp:156) and `MainMenuOptions::apply_fullscreen_setting` re-applies `SetWindowLongPtr(hWnd, GWL_EXSTYLE, WS_EX_TOPMOST)` (MainMenu.cpp:433). Nothing ever removes it on focus loss: `Game::on_deactivated` (Game.cpp:165-169) is `this->_gamepad->Suspend();` and nothing else, and WndProc's WM_ACTIVATEAPP case (Main.cpp:329-341) does no window management.

Alt-tab away from the game and a topmost, screen-filling WS_POPUP window stays above every window you switch to. The window also has no WS_MINIMIZEBOX and is never minimised programmatically, so it cannot get out of the way. This is the single most user-visible defect in the window lifecycle.
findings.suggestion: On WM_ACTIVATEAPP with wParam == FALSE, `SetWindowPos(hwnd, HWND_NOTOPMOST, ...)` (and optionally `ShowWindow(hwnd, SW_MINIMIZE)`); restore HWND_TOPMOST on activation. Better still, drop WS_EX_TOPMOST entirely — modern borderless fullscreen does not need it.

findings.title: Game keeps simulating, presenting and playing audio while unfocused; while minimised it spins at unbounded frame rate
findings.detail:
The message loop is `if (PeekMessage(...)) {...} else { g_game->tick(); }` (Main.cpp:213-224) with no focus/minimise gate, and `Game::tick` (Game.cpp:75-84) unconditionally runs `update` then `render`.

Alt-tab out (WM_ACTIVATEAPP, Main.cpp:329-341): `on_deactivated` (Game.cpp:165-169) suspends only the gamepad. The audio engine is untouched — `_audio_engine->Suspend()` appears only in `on_suspending` (Game.cpp:175) and the destructor (line 27) — so background music keeps playing over whatever the user switched to. `_timer` is not reset and `update()` keeps running, so `Level::_timer` (Level.h:121) keeps counting down and the match can end while the player is in another app; the gamepad being suspended just means the player cannot react.

Minimise (WM_SIZE/SIZE_MINIMIZED, Main.cpp:282-291) does call `on_suspending`, which suspends gamepad and audio — but still does not stop `tick()`. `render()` runs, and `DeviceResources::Present` (DeviceResources.cpp:456-504) calls `m_swapChain->Present(1, 0)`, which on an occluded/minimised window returns DXGI_STATUS_OCCLUDED (0x087A0001). That is a SUCCESS code, so `ThrowIfFailed(hr)` at line 497 passes silently and DXGI does not block for vsync — the minimised game busy-loops the CPU and GPU at maximum rate on a clear+present cycle that is never displayed.
findings.suggestion: Track a `m_suspended`/`m_minimized` flag in `Game`, skip `render()` (and optionally `update()`) while it is set, and handle DXGI_STATUS_OCCLUDED in `Present` by switching to `Present(0, DXGI_PRESENT_TEST)` until it clears. Suspend audio on deactivation too, or at least duck it.

findings.title: Audio device loss is explicitly caught and discarded: game is permanently silent after any default-device change
findings.suggestion: Implement the standard retry: on `!Update() && IsCriticalError()` set a retry flag, and each subsequent frame attempt `_audio_engine->Reset()`; on success, re-create the sound effect instances held by `SoundBank`. This also needs to be a documented engine-level service, not a `// more about this below...` in `Game::update`.

findings.title: 16 deferred contexts are raw, never Released, and get_deferred_context is noexcept yet throws
findings.suggestion: Store `Microsoft::WRL::ComPtr<ID3D11DeviceContext>`; drop the `unique_ptr<vector<...>>` indirection; remove `noexcept` from `get_deferred_context` (or make it return nullptr / assert); and fix MenuPage to index by partition, not by object.

findings.title: Process is manifested Per-Monitor V1 DPI aware with no WM_DPICHANGED handler and no DPI query anywhere
findings.detail:
The built EXE's embedded manifest (extracted from x64/Debug/ArtAttack.exe) contains `<dpiAware ...>True/PM</dpiAware>` and no `<dpiAwareness>PerMonitorV2</dpiAwareness>`. That comes from `<EnableDpiAwareness>PerMonitorHighDPIAware</EnableDpiAwareness>`, duplicated in all four ItemDefinitionGroups (ArtAttack.vcxproj:104-106, 125-127, 151-153, 177-179). `ArtAttack/settings.manifest` itself declares only supportedOS GUIDs — nothing about DPI — so the awareness level lives in a completely different file from the manifest that appears to control it.

WndProc (Main.cpp:234-407) has cases for WM_CREATE, WM_PAINT, WM_DISPLAYCHANGE, WM_MOVE, WM_SIZE, WM_ENTERSIZEMOVE, WM_EXITSIZEMOVE, WM_GETMINMAXINFO, WM_ACTIVATEAPP, WM_POWERBROADCAST, WM_DESTROY, WM_SYSKEYDOWN (body entirely commented out, lines 368-397), WM_MENUCHAR — and no WM_DPICHANGED. Grep for `WM_DPICHANGED`, `GetDpiForWindow`, `SetProcessDpiAware*`, `AdjustWindowRectExForDpi` across ArtAttack/ returns zero hits.

Under Per-Monitor V1 the OS does none of the work for you: it sends WM_DPICHANGED with a suggested rect in lParam and expects the app to `SetWindowPos` to it, and it does not scale the non-client frame either. With no handler, `DefWindowProc` ignores it. Dragging the window from a 100% monitor to a 150% monitor leaves it at its old pixel size with frame metrics computed for the old DPI, and the game silently ignores the user's display scaling entirely — the UI, laid out in 1920x1080 design units and scaled exactly once in each page's `init()` (e.g. MainMenu.cpp:558-562 `scale_objects_to_new_resolution(DEFAULT_RESOLUTION, resolution)`), ends up physically about a third smaller than every other application on that display. Wrong-looking output rather than a crash, but it is invisible to the author because it only shows on a mixed-DPI setup. `AdjustWindowRect` at Main.cpp:150 is likewise the non-DPI-aware variant.
findings.suggestion: Either drop to `<dpiAware>true</dpiAware>` (system aware) and accept OS bitmap scaling, or commit to per-monitor and add a WM_DPICHANGED case that `SetWindowPos`es to the suggested rect from lParam and re-runs the size-dependent path. If per-monitor, prefer PerMonitorV2 via a manifest `<dpiAwareness>` entry so the non-client area scales itself, and move the DPI declaration into settings.manifest so it lives in one place instead of four vcxproj blocks.

findings.title: on_deactivated/on_suspending dereference _gamepad and _audio_engine with no null check, and WndProc routes messages to Game before initialize() runs
findings.detail:
`on_activated` (Game.cpp:157-163) guards with `if (this->_gamepad)`, but `on_deactivated` (165-169) is a bare `this->_gamepad->Suspend();`, `on_suspending` (171-176) is `this->_gamepad->Suspend(); _audio_engine->Suspend();`, and `on_resuming` (178-184) is `_timer.ResetElapsedTime(); this->_gamepad->Resume(); _audio_engine->Resume();`.

The `Game*` becomes reachable from WndProc inside `CreateWindowExW` itself: WM_CREATE stores `params->lpCreateParams` in GWLP_USERDATA (Main.cpp:246-252), and CreateWindowEx then synchronously sends WM_SIZE/WM_MOVE. So from Main.cpp:156/162 onwards every message handler is live — but `_audio_engine` is not constructed until Game.cpp:47 and `_gamepad` not until Game.cpp:59, after `create_device_dependent_resources()` (line 54) has run `_resource_loader->load_all_resources()` (line 258), i.e. after all textures, fonts and sound banks have been loaded from disk. A WM_SIZE/SIZE_MINIMIZED or a deactivation delivered during that window is a null dereference. The equivalent hazard on the size path is masked only by chance, by `if (!m_window) return false;` at DeviceResources.cpp:397-398.

These three handlers are also declared `const` (Game.h:39-45) while mutating the gamepad, the audio engine and the timer through owned pointers — const that means nothing.
findings.suggestion: Guard all four handlers uniformly (or better, add an `_initialized` flag checked once at the top of each), and drop the meaningless `const` on handlers that change engine state.

findings.title: WM_DISPLAYCHANGE only updates the colour space; nothing re-derives the render size on a monitor or mode change
findings.detail:
`Game::on_display_change` (Game.cpp:192-195) is `_device_resources->UpdateColorSpace();` and nothing else — it does not consult the new display mode, does not re-check whether the saved resolution is still meaningful, and does not touch `ResolutionManager`. `Game::on_window_moved` (186-190) calls `WindowSizeChanged(r.right, r.bottom)` using the *cached* `m_outputSize` (DeviceResources.h:50), so the compare at DeviceResources.cpp:404-410 always matches and it degenerates to `UpdateColorSpace()` — dragging the window to another monitor changes nothing about how the game renders.

So: change the desktop resolution from 1920x1080 to 1280x720 while running borderless-fullscreen, and Windows resizes the maximized window, producing a WM_SIZE that resizes the swapchain to 1280x720 — while `ResolutionManager` still says 1920x1080 and drives every viewport (ViewportManager.cpp:49, 58, 66, 87, 126). The divergence described in the `create_window_size_dependent_resources` finding becomes permanent and is not recoverable without editing the save file. There is no validation anywhere that the saved `screen_resolution` (ResolutionManager.cpp:47-63, four hardcoded 16:9 sizes) is supported by, or even smaller than, the current monitor — no `EnumDisplayModes`, no `GetSystemMetrics(SM_CXSCREEN)`, no `IDXGIOutput::GetDisplayModeList` call exists in the codebase.
findings.suggestion: Have WM_DISPLAYCHANGE (and the resize path) re-read the client rect and republish it as the layout resolution; validate the saved resolution against the current output on startup and clamp it, rather than trusting save_data.json.

findings.title: apply_player_viewport(int) sets the viewport on the immediate context from a worker thread, for a SpriteBatch owned by deferred context 0
findings.suggestion: Delete the one-argument overload; the zoom-out path should use `apply_player_viewport(0, deferred_contexts->at(0), sprite_batches->at(0))` like the rest of the draw code. Nothing on a worker thread should ever touch the immediate context, and `set_layout` should not be called from a `const` draw function.

findings.title: 1-byte rapidjson read buffer declared as 8 bytes: heap overrun on every launch (4 sites)
findings.detail:
`auto read_buffer = std::make_unique<char>(); FileReadStream is(fp, read_buffer.get(), sizeof(read_buffer));`

`make_unique<char>()` allocates exactly **1 byte**. `sizeof(read_buffer)` is `sizeof(std::unique_ptr<char>)` = **8** on x64 (4 on Win32), not the size of the buffer.

What rapidjson does with that (verified in the vendored copy, external/rapidjson/include/rapidjson/filereadstream.h:44-81):
- ctor asserts `bufferSize >= 4` — 8 passes, so the guard never fires (and asserts are off in Release anyway);
- `Read()` line 71: `readCount_ = std::fread(buffer_, 1, bufferSize_, fp_);` → **fread of 8 bytes into a 1-byte heap block**, repeated for every 8-byte chunk of the file;
- line 75-76: on the final short read, `buffer_[readCount_] = '\0'` writes at index up to 8.

So it is a **7-byte heap overrun per refill**, not a one-off. Parsing still *works* (rapidjson walks the buffer one char at a time and refills), which is exactly why the game appears to run: in Release the MSVC small-block heap has ≥16-byte granularity so the extra 7 bytes land in slack. Under the Debug CRT heap the 1-byte block gets 4-byte no-man's-land guards, so the overrun smashes the trailing guard *and* 3 bytes of the adjacent block header.

`read_buffer.release()` (line 23) then abandons the pointer without freeing — a leak, and it also means the corrupted block is never passed to `free()`, so the debug heap's damage check never runs and the corruption stays silent.

REACHABILITY: LIVE ON EVERY LAUNCH, before the window exists. wWinMain (Main.cpp:96-99) → `Save::load_save_file()` (Save.cpp:43-56) → `Save::load_from_json` (Save.cpp:12).

Identical pattern at three more sites, all on the startup path via Game::initialize → ResourceLoader::load_all_resources (Game.cpp:258):
- ArtAttack/SpriteSheet.cpp:74-81 (← ResourceLoader.cpp:122, once per sprite sheet)
- ArtAttack/SoundBank.cpp:154-161 (← ResourceLoader.cpp:164, once per sound bank)
- ArtAttack/LevelLoadedInfo.cpp:100-107 (← LevelLoadedInfo ctor, LevelLoadedInfo.cpp:10, once per level file)

All four also call `fopen` without checking for NULL (Save.cpp:14, SpriteSheet.cpp:72, SoundBank.cpp:152, LevelLoadedInfo.cpp:98); rapidjson's `RAPIDJSON_ASSERT(fp_ != 0)` is a no-op in Release, so a missing asset file is a null-deref inside fread.
findings.suggestion: Replace all four with a real buffer and RAII file handling, e.g. `char read_buffer[65536]; FILE* fp = fopen(path, "rb"); if (!fp) throw ...; FileReadStream is(fp, read_buffer, sizeof(read_buffer));` and delete the `.release()` calls. Better: factor a single `rapidjson::Document parse_json_file(const char*)` helper into one engine-level file and have Save/SpriteSheet/SoundBank/LevelLoadedInfo all call it — the same 10 lines are copy-pasted four times. Note `sizeof(x)` on a smart pointer is a bug pattern worth grepping for globally.

findings.title: Match end throws an unhandled exception if any player picked Sniper or Bucket
findings.detail:
`Weapon::stop_sounds() const` (252-257) calls `get_sound_effect_instance_name()` (258-277), whose switch only handles `SPRAYER`, `ROLLER`, `MISTER` and ends in `default: throw std::exception("Weapon::get_sound_effect_instance_name() - invalid weapon type");` (273-274).

Can Sniper/Bucket actually be equipped? Yes, three independent ways:
- `MainMenuWeaponSelect::cycle_weapons` (MainMenu.cpp:1524-1554) cycles `0..MAX_PRIM_WEP` where `MAX_PRIM_WEP = RANDOM_PRIMARY = 5` (wep_type.h:4-18), i.e. SPRAYER(0), SNIPER(1), ROLLER(2), MISTER(3), BUCKET(4), RANDOM(5). `update_weapon_select_visuals` (MainMenu.cpp:1585-1608) draws icons for all of them, so they are visibly selectable.
- `get_random_weapon()` (MainMenu.cpp:1519-1523) is `rand() % 5` → picks SNIPER or BUCKET with probability 2/5.
- `WeaponBuilder::build_weapon` (WeaponBuilder.cpp:22-25, 34-37) happily constructs `WeaponSniper` / `WeaponBucket`.

Why it does NOT throw every frame (this matters — an earlier reading implied a broader crash): both classes override the *virtual* `handle_shoot_sound` (WeaponSniper.h:22 / WeaponSniper.cpp:28-35, WeaponBucket.h:23 / WeaponBucket.cpp:28-35) and use `play_wave` directly, bypassing `get_sound_effect_instance_name()`. But `stop_sounds` is declared **non-virtual** at Weapon.h:44, so it is not overridable and always lands in the base version.

REACHABILITY: LIVE, and it fires at exactly the 'match ends' step of a normal session. Shortest chain:
Game::tick (Game.cpp:75) → Game::update → StateContext::update → GameLevel::update → Level::update (Level.cpp:126-135, `_timer <= 0` → ZOOM_OUT) → Level::stop_player_sounds (Level.cpp:323-328) → Player::stop_sounds (Player.cpp:1048-1051) → Weapon::stop_sounds (Weapon.cpp:252) → throw at Weapon.cpp:273.

There is no try/catch anywhere on that path (see the separate finding on Main.cpp:211-224), so this is `std::terminate`.
findings.suggestion: Two fixes, both needed. (1) Make the sound-name lookup total: give SNIPER and BUCKET entries, or better, put the `SoundEffectInstanceWeaponDetails` on `WeaponDetails` so it is data, not a switch — the switch at Weapon.cpp:264-275 duplicates knowledge the subclass already has. (2) `stop_sounds` must be `virtual` and overridden alongside `handle_shoot_sound` in WeaponSniper/WeaponBucket (which have no looping sound to stop, so their override is empty). The real defect is that one half of a two-method protocol was made virtual and the other half wasn't.

findings.title: No exception handler anywhere on the frame loop, while ~58 sites throw as ordinary control flow
findings.suggestion: Wrap the loop body (or `wWinMain`'s contents) in try/catch that logs `e.what()` and shows a MessageBox before exiting cleanly. Separately, `throw std::exception(const char*)` is an MSVC-only extension — use `std::runtime_error`/`std::logic_error`. And most of these 58 sites are asserting invariants that should be enforced by types (exhaustive `enum class` switches, `std::optional` returns) rather than thrown at runtime.

findings.title: get_delete_timer() returns _timer, so the projectile lifetime check is `_timer > _timer` and no projectile ever expires
findings.detail:
```
float Projectile::get_delete_timer() const
{
	return this->_timer;
}
```
`Projectile` has no `_delete_timer` member (Projectile.h:69-79); the intended value lives in `_details.delete_timer` (projectile_details.h, populated in projectile_consts.h:19/32/53/66/79/100). The check at Projectile.cpp:278-281 is therefore
```
if (this->get_timer() > this->get_delete_timer())   // _timer > _timer -> always false
    this->set_for_deletion(true);
```
and can never fire. `get_timer()` returns `_timer` (Projectile.cpp:220-222); both accessors return the same field.

REACHABILITY: LIVE, every frame, for every projectile. Level::update (Level.cpp:128) → update_level_logic (Level.cpp:183-186, `object->update()`) → e.g. ProjectileMist::update (ProjectileMist.cpp:34) / ProjectileRolling::update (ProjectileRolling.cpp:33) → Projectile::update_movement (Projectile.cpp:278).

Observable consequences over a 3-minute king_of_the_hill match:
- The only remaining removal paths are `on_collision` with a structure or an enemy player (Projectile.cpp:120-153) and the out-of-bounds check, which **throws** instead of deleting (Level.cpp:315-321).
- MIST has gravity 0 and wind_resistance 0 (projectile_consts.h:76-77) and launches at 300 u/s (weapon_consts.h:120). Designed lifetime 5 s; actual lifetime is however long it takes to cross the 6000-unit level ≈ 20 s. That is a 4× increase in live projectile count, and the collision loop in Level::update_level_logic (Level.cpp:259-293) is O(n²) over `_collision_objects` — so ~16× the pair tests.
- Worst case is ROLLING: `DETAILS_ROLLING` has `delete_timer = 0.000001f` (projectile_consts.h:66), i.e. it is designed as a one-frame hitbox. It also has `starting_vel_length = 0.0f` (weapon_consts.h:92) and `shoot_interval = 0.0001f` (:91), so the Roller spawns a **stationary** 50×50 hitbox with `player_damage = -1000` every frame the trigger is held, and `ProjectileRolling::draw` is empty and `is_visible_in_viewport` returns false (ProjectileRolling.cpp:36-47). With the timer broken, holding the Roller trigger in mid-air leaves a permanent field of invisible instant-kill hitboxes.
findings.suggestion: `return this->_details.delete_timer;` — or better, drop `get_delete_timer()` entirely and inline `if (this->_timer > this->_details.delete_timer)`. Two accessors on the same field with different names is precisely how this hid. Also add a unit test for projectile expiry; nothing in MattMathTests covers game objects because the engine is not built as a library.

findings.title: Out-of-bounds objects throw instead of being despawned, turning a routine event into a process abort
findings.suggestion: For collision objects, replace the throw with deletion (set the for-deletion flag and let the existing sweep at Level.cpp:296-305 remove it), and run the out-of-bounds pass *before* that sweep so it happens in one place. A player leaving bounds is a game rule (respawn / kill), not an engine error — it should call the respawn path, not throw. Also note the sweep at 296-305 relies on `size_t i` wrapping to SIZE_MAX on `i--` at index 0; use `std::remove_if` + `erase` instead.

findings.title: ProjectileMist registers itself as projectile_type SPRAY; PROJECTILE_MIST_* is unreachable
findings.detail:
```
DiffusingProjectile(velocity, team, player_num, team_colour,
    SPRAY, dt, resource_manager,
    DETAILS_MIST, DIFFUSION_DETAILS_MIST, ...)
```
The 5th argument is `projectile_type`; it should be `MIST`. Compare ProjectileRolling.cpp:19-22 which correctly passes `ROLLING`. Because `projectile_type` is an *unscoped* enum (Projectile.h:10-17) among otherwise scoped enums, `SPRAY` is a bare identifier in scope and the mistake compiles silently.

What actually differs at runtime (traced, not assumed):
- `Projectile::get_collision_object_type()` (Projectile.cpp:155-195) switches on `get_type()`, so a mist projectile reports `PROJECTILE_SPRAY_TEAM_A/B`. `PROJECTILE_MIST_TEAM_A` and `PROJECTILE_MIST_TEAM_B` become **unreachable enum values** — every branch handling them (Player.cpp:673-678, PaintTile.cpp:122/130, StructurePaintable.cpp:77-78, Level.cpp:674-675, Projectile.cpp:165-166/181-182) is dead code.
- Damage: `Player::on_projectile_collision` (Player.cpp:645-682) selects damage by collision type, so mist hits apply `SPRAY_DAMAGE` instead of `MIST_DAMAGE`. **Currently invisible**, because player_consts.h:65 and :69 both define the value as `0.01f`. The bug is latent until someone tunes one of them.
- Painting and team attribution are unaffected — PaintTile.cpp:118-133 and StructurePaintable.cpp:69-78 accept both spellings.
- Debug projectile count (Level.cpp:658-682) still counts it, just as the wrong category.

REACHABILITY: LIVE whenever the Mister is equipped, but with no visible symptom today.

Worth noting alongside: `Projectile::get_player_damage()` (Projectile.cpp:295-298) returning `_details.player_damage` has **zero callers**. So there are two parallel damage systems with opposite sign conventions — `projectile_consts::DETAILS_MIST.player_damage = -0.05f` (dead) versus `player_consts::MIST_DAMAGE = 0.01f` subtracted at Player.cpp:676 (live). The per-projectile damage data in projectile_consts.h is entirely inert.
findings.suggestion: Pass `MIST`. Then make `projectile_type` an `enum class` so an unqualified `SPRAY` cannot be substituted for a `MIST` at a call site. Longer term, delete the `collision_object_type` cross-product (class × team × weapon, 23 values) — `Player::on_projectile_collision` should ask the projectile for its damage via `get_player_damage()` rather than re-deriving it from an enum, which also deletes the whole if/else ladder and the dead constants.

findings.title: CONFIRMED infinite recursion in MTexture::is_visible_in_viewport, but it is DEAD CODE - it does not crash the menu
findings.detail:
```
bool MTexture::is_visible_in_viewport(const RectangleF& view) const
{
	return this->is_visible_in_viewport(view);
}
```
The claim is factually correct: unconditional self-call, guaranteed stack overflow. It was almost certainly meant to be `return this->_rectangle.intersects(view);` (cf. Visual.cpp:50-53, Structure.cpp:39-42, PaintTile.cpp:149-152, which all do exactly that).

But it is UNREACHABLE, and the prior report's implication that the main menu stack-overflows immediately is WRONG. Exhaustive call-site analysis (repo-wide grep, 40 hits, of which only 4 are calls rather than declarations/definitions/comments):
- Level.cpp:518, :527, :536 — inside `Level::draw_player_view_level`, iterating `_non_collision_objects`, `_collision_objects`, `_player_objects`. None of those ever hold an `MObject`: `LevelObjectBuilder::build_non_collision_object` (LevelObjectBuilder.cpp:182-200) only ever produces `Visual`, and `build_collision_object` only produces `Structure`/`StructurePaintable`. So no `MTexture` reaches these.
- Mh.cpp:117 — inside `MContainer::is_visible_in_viewport` itself, which has **no callers anywhere**.
- Level.cpp:424/432/440 are inside a fully commented-out function.

Menu drawing never culls: `MenuPage::draw_mobject_in_viewports` (MenuPage.cpp:89-122) goes straight to `widget->draw(sprite_batch, viewports[i])` at line 112. That is why the game runs.

The root cause is structural and worth fixing even though the bug is dormant: `MObject : public IGameObject` (Mh.h:8) forces every UI widget to implement `is_visible_in_viewport(const RectangleF& world_view)`, a level-space culling query that has no meaning for screen-space UI. The sibling implementations confirm nobody could implement it either — `MText::is_visible_in_viewport` (Mh.cpp:278-282) and `MTextDropShadow::is_visible_in_viewport` (Mh.cpp:343-347) both just `return true;` with a `// TODO: implement text bounding box` comment.
findings.suggestion: Fix the body to `return this->_rectangle.intersects(view);` so it is not a landmine, but the real fix is to stop deriving UI widgets from `IGameObject`. Split `IGameObject`'s drawable contract from its world-space/cullable contract: menus need `update()`/`draw()`, not viewport culling. That also removes the `DirectX::SpriteBatch` and `MattMath::Camera` hardwiring in IGameObject.h:11-12 from the UI layer.

findings.title: RectangleRotated(Segment, thickness) forgets to normalize its axes and throws for every segment of length != 1 - dead code, but the rejection of this finding was wrong
findings.suggestion: Add `this->_x_axis.normalize(); this->_y_axis.normalize();` (or build from `center_line.get_direction().normalized()`), and add a test for the Segment overload — it currently has zero coverage, which is why nobody noticed. Also `_hw_extents.x = length/2 + thickness` looks wrong independently: it extends the box past the segment ends by `thickness` on the long axis, which is a capsule approximation, not a rectangle around the segment. Decide which is intended and document it.

findings.title: edges_valid() validates stale _points, so it is a tautology in both constructors
findings.detail:
```
bool RectangleRotated::edges_valid() const
{
    std::vector<Segment> edges = this->get_edges();   // built from this->_points
    ...
}
```
`get_edges()` (4284-4294) reads `_points` via `get_edge_0..3` (4434-4449), which index `this->_points`. But both constructors call `is_valid()` **before** assigning `_points`:
- 4194-4199: check, then `_points = calculate_points()`
- 4209-4214: check, then `_points = calculate_points()`

At the moment `edges_valid()` runs, `_points` still holds its NSDMI value `{ZERO, ZERO, ZERO, ZERO}` (MattMath.h:1119-1120). All four edges are degenerate `(0,0)->(0,0)` segments: every `get_direction()` is `(0,0)`, every dot product is 0 (passes the perpendicularity test at 4550-4551), every length is 0 (passes the opposite-lengths test at 4558-4559). So `edges_valid()` unconditionally returns true from the constructor path and validates nothing.

In the mutators (`inflate` 4295-4305, `set_x_axis` 4359-4369, `set_y_axis`, `set_half_extents`, `set_half_x_width`, `set_half_y_width`) the same ordering means the validity check runs against the *previous* geometry, not the new one.

This is a separate defect from the missing normalize, and it is why the Segment constructor's other invariants were never caught: only `half_widths_valid` and `axes_valid` (which read the just-assigned members directly) actually do anything.

REACHABILITY: dead today (nothing constructs a RectangleRotated), but MattMathTests exercises the 4-arg ctor heavily and has been getting false confidence from these checks.
findings.suggestion: Compute the points first, then validate: `_points = calculate_points(); if (!is_valid()) throw ...;` — and do the same in every mutator. Better still, make `_points` a derived value computed on demand (or cached lazily) rather than a member that must be kept in sync by six separate setters, each of which currently repeats the same `if (!valid) throw; _points = calculate_points();` boilerplate.

findings.title: MatrixF(int,int) never sizes _elements, so every Matrix3x3F factory writes through a null vector - entirely dead code
findings.suggestion: Either fix it (`_elements.resize(static_cast<size_t>(rows) * columns, 0.0f);` and have `set_element` assert against `_elements.size()`) or, given the engine has DirectXMath available and uses `XMVECTOR`/`XMMATRIX` elsewhere, delete the hand-rolled `MatrixF`/`Matrix3x3F`/`Vector4F` hierarchy outright. A dynamically-sized matrix class carrying a heap allocation is the wrong tool for 3x3 transforms in a 2D engine. Also note `rows * columns != elements.size()` at 2487 compares `int` to `size_t` (/W4 C4018) — the whole class predates any review.

findings.title: Reference member bound to a builder local - the reference genuinely dangles, but there is NO live use-after-free
findings.detail:
`const std::vector<MattMath::Segment>& _paintable_edges;` is bound in the mem-initializer list at StructurePaintable.cpp:30 to the ctor parameter, which at the sole construction site is a function-local:
```
std::vector<Segment> paintable_edges;            // LevelObjectBuilder.cpp:107
...
return std::make_unique<StructurePaintable>(..., paintable_edges, ...);  // :140
```
`build_collision_object` returns at line 132-142 and `paintable_edges` dies. The member reference is dangling for the object's entire remaining life. CONFIRMED.

But the severity as previously filed is WRONG. I traced every read of `_paintable_edges` in the whole file: there are exactly two, both inside `generate_paint_tiles()` at StructurePaintable.cpp:191 (`this->_paintable_edges.size()`) and :193 (`this->_paintable_edges[j]`). That function is called from **the constructor body**, StructurePaintable.cpp:33, while the builder's local is still alive. After construction the member is never touched again — `update` (37-43), `draw` (45-62), `on_collision` (64-102) and `get_paint_total` (300-319) do not reference it. And `_collision_objects` holds `unique_ptr`s, so the object is never copied (Level.cpp:296-305 moves pointers, not objects).

So: real defect, zero runtime symptom today. It is a landmine, not a live bug.

Two genuine secondary issues in the same header:
- `StructurePaintable() = default;` (line 28) is **implicitly deleted** by the reference member. Declaring it is legal; it just silently isn't there. Nothing uses it, which is the only reason this compiles.
- The reference member also deletes implicit copy-assignment, which is invisible from the declaration.

Contrast with how the shape is handled correctly two arguments earlier: `&rectangle` is also a pointer to a builder local (LevelObjectBuilder.cpp:136), but `Structure`'s ctor clones it — `_collision_shape(collision_shape->clone())` (Structure.cpp:22) — so that one is safe. The edges just never got the same treatment.
findings.suggestion: Make it a value: `std::vector<MattMath::Segment> _paintable_edges;` (or drop the member entirely, since it is only consumed during construction — pass it to `generate_paint_tiles(const std::vector<Segment>&)` as a parameter and store nothing). The latter is better: the member exists only because the loop was moved into a helper. Also delete the now-meaningless `StructurePaintable() = default;`. Reference members in classes with any lifetime beyond the enclosing scope are a rule worth banning outright in this codebase.

findings.title: CONFIRMED - closest_pt_point_OBB iterates 3 axes on a 2D OBB and throws on i==2, but it has zero callers
findings.suggestion: Change the bound to 2, or better delete the function until something needs it. While in this file: EricsonMath.h is roughly 50% commented-out declarations (lines 13-73, 102-111) and EricsonMath.cpp ~233 lines of commented-out bodies. Delete them; git has them. A dead function that throws is worse than no function, because a future caller gets a runtime abort instead of a compile error.

findings.title: Level indexes the connection-compacted input vector by player ordinal - OOB read on any pad dropout
findings.detail:
`Level::update_level_logic` walks `*this->_player_objects` with a running counter and uses it as a subscript into the input vector:

```cpp
int player_index = 0;
for (const auto& object : *this->_player_objects)
{
    object->set_player_input(player_inputs[player_index]);   // Level.cpp:192
    ...
    player_index++;
}
```

`_player_objects->size()` is fixed at level build time and equals the menu's player count (`PlayerBuilder::build_players`, PlayerBuilder.cpp:27, iterates `settings.get_player_settings()`, whose size is forced to `_player_count` by `MenuLevelSettings::set_player_count`, MenuLevelSettings.cpp:9-25).

`player_inputs.size()` is NOT the player count. `PlayerInput::update_and_get_player_inputs` (PlayerInput.cpp:126-137) only `push_back`s entries for slots that reported `IsConnected()`, so its size is the number of *currently connected* pads.

Mid-match trace (2 players, pads in XInput slots 0 and 1, player 2's pad unplugged):
1. PlayerInput.cpp:124 `get_raw_input(1)` -> `pad.IsConnected()` false -> `current[1].connected` stays false (PlayerInput.h:25 default).
2. PlayerInput.cpp:129 skips the push_back, so `result.size() == 1`.
3. GameStates.cpp:141-142 hands that 1-element vector to `Level::update`, GameStates.cpp:185.
4. Level.cpp:192 with `player_index == 1` reads `player_inputs[1]` on a size-1 vector - out of bounds. `std::vector::operator[]` is unchecked in Release; in Debug MSVC's `_ITERATOR_DEBUG_LEVEL` assert fires and the process aborts.

Observable effect in Release: player 2 is fed ~48 bytes of whatever follows the vector buffer, reinterpreted as `PlayerInputData`. `x_movement` becomes a garbage float that is multiplied straight into velocity (`X_INITIAL_VELOCITY * x_input`, Player.cpp:769; `X_ACCELERATION * dt * x_input`, Player.cpp:774) - so the abandoned player teleports or accelerates unboundedly, which then trips `throw std::exception("Player out of bounds")` at Level.cpp:312. Nothing catches it; the app terminates.

The *all* pads case is worse and does not need an unplug: if the vector is empty, `player_inputs[0]` is dereferencing a null/garbage `_Myfirst` pointer.

Note `Level.h:143` declares `std::vector<PlayerInputData> _player_inputs` which is never read or written anywhere - a vestige of the design that would have avoided this.
findings.suggestion: Stop compacting. Have `PlayerInput::update_and_get_player_inputs()` return a fixed 4-element (`GamePad::MAX_PLAYER_COUNT`) array/vector where disconnected slots carry `connection_state::DISCONNECTED` and zeroed axes - the `connection` field in `PlayerInputData` already exists for exactly this and is currently dead. Then store the owning XInput slot on `Player` (it already has `_player_num`, Player.cpp:1077) and look up `player_inputs[player->get_pad_slot()]`, treating DISCONNECTED as "no input this frame" rather than as a shorter vector. As a stopgap, guard the loop with `if (player_index >= player_inputs.size()) { object->set_player_input(PlayerInputData()); }`.

findings.title: PauseMenu subscripts the menu-input vector with an unvalidated player index - guaranteed OOB if any pad drops
findings.detail:
`PauseMenuInitial::update` does:

```cpp
std::vector<ProcessedMenuInput> inputs = this->get_menu_inputs();
int player_num = this->get_pause_menu_data()->get_player_num();
...
if (inputs[player_num].action == menu_input_action::BACK ||   // PauseMenu.cpp:53
    inputs[player_num].action == menu_input_action::PAUSE)
```

There is no size check anywhere in the function - `inputs[player_num]` is subscripted at lines 53, 54, 59, 82 and 98, and again in `PauseMenuConfirmation::update` at lines 222, 229, 256 and 257.

`player_num` is not a stable pad identity: it is the *compacted index* returned by `GameLevel::check_for_pause_input` (GameStates.cpp:348-358, `return i;` where `i` indexes the already-compacted `player_inputs` vector), stored into `PauseMenuData` at GameStates.cpp:156.

This is the only unguarded menu-input subscript in the codebase - every other page loops `for (i < inputs.size())` (MainMenu.cpp:50, EndMenu.cpp:32, ResultsMenu.cpp:266) or bounds itself with `i < num_inputs && i < player_count` (MainMenu.cpp:1160, 1443, 1790).

Three concrete ways to fire it:
- Player 3 of 3 pauses (`player_num == 2`), then any one pad is unplugged: `MenuInput::update_and_get_menu_inputs` (MenuInput.cpp:139-148) returns 2 entries, `inputs[2]` is OOB.
- Every pad is unplugged (or all batteries die) while paused: `inputs` is empty and `inputs[0]` dereferences the empty vector's null data pointer.
- Alt-tab: `Game::on_deactivated` (Game.cpp:165-169) calls `GamePad::Suspend()` while the main loop (Main.cpp:213-224) keeps calling `tick()` unconditionally, so the pause menu keeps polling a suspended gamepad.

Secondary consequence even without the OOB: the pause menu is only exitable by the pad at that compacted index, so if that specific pad dies the match cannot be resumed, restarted or quit at all.
findings.suggestion: Guard every access: `if (player_num < 0 || static_cast<size_t>(player_num) >= inputs.size()) return;` at minimum. Properly, carry the XInput slot (not a compacted index) in `PauseMenuData`, index a fixed-size input array by that slot, and add an explicit "controller disconnected - reconnect or press START on any pad" state so the menu never becomes unresponsive.

findings.title: Input vectors are compacted by connection state, destroying the pad-slot to player mapping; the connection_state field that exists to prevent this is dead
findings.suggestion: Return `std::array<PlayerInputData, GamePad::MAX_PLAYER_COUNT>` indexed by XInput slot, with `connection` correctly set per slot and axes zeroed for disconnected pads. Add an explicit binding step ("press A to join") that records slot -> player, and surface a `pad_disconnected(slot)` event so gameplay can pause and prompt instead of reading garbage. For a reusable engine this belongs behind an `IInputDevice`/`InputSnapshot` abstraction, not an XInput-shaped `std::vector`.

findings.title: Zero controllers connected makes the entire application inert and unexitable from within - there is no keyboard or mouse path anywhere
findings.detail:
With no XInput pad connected the app boots normally, loads all resources, plays the menu music (`play_effect(MUSIC, ...)`, MainMenu.cpp:107) and then does nothing forever:

```cpp
void MainMenuTitle::update()
{
    const std::vector<ProcessedMenuInput> inputs = this->get_menu_inputs();
    for (int i = 0; i < inputs.size(); i++)   // MainMenu.cpp:50 - inputs is EMPTY
    { ... }
}
```

`get_menu_inputs()` returns an empty vector every frame (MenuInput.cpp:141 never fires), so the loop body never executes and the title screen can never advance. Same on every subsequent page.

There is no non-gamepad input anywhere in the project. Grepping the whole `ArtAttack/` tree for `Keyboard`, `Mouse`, `WM_KEYDOWN`, `WM_CHAR`, `WM_LBUTTONDOWN` and `GetAsyncKeyState` yields exactly two hits, both unused includes: `pch.h:67 #include "Keyboard.h"` and `pch.h:69 #include "Mouse.h"`. Neither `DirectX::Keyboard` nor `DirectX::Mouse` is ever instantiated. `WndProc`'s only keyboard case, `WM_SYSKEYDOWN` (Main.cpp:367-398), is 100% commented out - the classic Alt+Enter fullscreen toggle is dead code.

The only in-application quit is the "exit" menu item (`DestroyWindow`, MainMenu.cpp:167), which is three gamepad presses deep and therefore unreachable.
