In fullscreen mode the window is created as bare `WS_POPUP` with `WS_EX_TOPMOST` and `SW_SHOWMAXIMIZED` (Main.cpp:156-158, 191) - no caption, no system menu, no close button, and it sits above everything else.

There is also zero on-screen indication that a controller is required: grepping all .cpp for `controller|gamepad|connect|plug` returns only identifier names, never a user-visible string. A fresh clone on a machine without an XInput pad presents a silent, unresponsive window.

For the stated goal - a reusable 2D engine - this is worse than a game bug: the engine has exactly one hardcoded input backend (`DirectX::GamePad`, PlayerInput.h:38 / MenuInput.h:54), the input structs are shaped around XInput's button names (`RawPlayerInput::jump_trigger`, `secondary_shoot`, PlayerInput.h:15-26), and there is no abstraction to plug a keyboard, mouse, touch or remapping layer into. Any second game built on this engine inherits "gamepad or nothing".
findings.suggestion: Introduce an input-source abstraction that produces the same `PlayerInputData`/`ProcessedMenuInput` from any backend, and add a `DirectX::Keyboard`+`Mouse` implementation (the headers are already in the PCH and the libs are already linked). Independently, add a "No controller detected - connect a gamepad" overlay on the title screen when `GamePad::GetState(i).IsConnected()` is false for all slots, and make Escape quit.

findings.title: Team select cannot be completed when the chosen player count exceeds the number of connected pads
findings.suggestion: Query the connected pad count before offering player counts and disable/grey the unreachable options with an explanatory label; or key `_select_states` by pad slot and mark slots with no pad as auto-confirmed/absent. Longer term this disappears once the input vector is slot-indexed rather than compacted (see the PlayerInput finding).

findings.title: on_deactivated/on_suspending dereference _gamepad and _audio_engine without the null guard on_activated has
findings.suggestion: Guard all three consistently, or better, move `_gamepad`/`_audio_engine` construction into the `Game` constructor (they have no window or device dependency) so they are non-null for the entire lifetime of the object that receives window messages. Suppressing the symptom with `if (x)` in three places is the weaker fix.

findings.title: The main loop never gates on suspend/minimise, so update, render and Present keep running on a suspended app
findings.suggestion: Track suspension in `Game` (set it in `on_suspending`/`on_deactivated`, clear it in `on_resuming`/`on_activated`) and either skip `tick()` entirely or fall back to `WaitMessage()`/`GetMessage` while suspended. At minimum, make the state machine tolerate a zero-length input vector for the frames where the pad is suspended.

findings.title: Left-stick deadzone applied twice and never rescaled - horizontal movement steps discontinuously from 0 to half speed
findings.detail:
Confirmed - the prior allegation is correct. Two deadzones are stacked:

1. PlayerInput.cpp:20 requests DirectXTK's own radial deadzone: `this->_gamepad->GetState(gamepad_num, GamePad::DEAD_ZONE_CIRCULAR)`. DirectXTK's `ApplyStickDeadZone`/`ApplyLinearDeadZone` removes `XINPUT_GAMEPAD_LEFT_THUMB_DEADZONE` (7849/32767 ~= 0.24) radially and *rescales the remainder back to the full [-1,1] range*, so what comes out already starts at 0 and reaches 1 at full deflection.

2. On top of that, `calculate_player_input` applies a second, larger cut with no rescale:

```cpp
if (std::fabs(current.left_analog_stick.x) > STICK_DEADZONE)   // STICK_DEADZONE = 0.5f, PlayerInput.h:12
{
    result.x_movement = current.left_analog_stick.x;           // PlayerInput.cpp:88 - passed through raw
}
else
{
    result.x_movement = 0.0f;
}
```

Resulting response curve for `x_movement`: flat 0 for the first ~62% of physical stick travel (0.24 native + 0.5 of the remaining 0.76), then an instantaneous jump to 0.5, then linear 0.5 -> 1.0 over the last ~38%. Half the usable analogue range is thrown away and the useful range is compressed into a third of the stick's travel.

This is not cosmetic - `x_movement` is a direct velocity multiplier, so the discontinuity is felt as a lurch:

```cpp
MovingObject::set_velocity_x(X_INITIAL_VELOCITY * x_input);     // Player.cpp:769
MovingObject::alter_velocity_x(X_ACCELERATION * dt * x_input);  // Player.cpp:774, 783, 792-793, 798-799
```

A player can never walk slower than half speed; the character snaps from stationary to 0.5x the instant the threshold is crossed.

Inconsistently, the *raw* unfiltered `left_analog_stick` is also copied through at PlayerInput.cpp:113 and read directly for the drop-through-platform check (`this->_input.left_analog_stick.y > DROP_DOWN_ANALOG_THRESHOLD`, Player.cpp:762, threshold 0.8 at player_consts.h:39) - so the Y axis uses a different threshold with a different filtering path than X, in the same struct.

The right stick at PlayerInput.cpp:96-103 is defensible: it thresholds on `length()` then `normalize()`s, so the magnitude discontinuity does not matter for an aim direction. Only the left stick is broken.
findings.suggestion: Either drop the second deadzone entirely (DirectXTK's DEAD_ZONE_CIRCULAR has already done the job) or, if a larger deadzone is wanted, rescale so the response is continuous: `x = (fabs(x) - DZ) / (1.0f - DZ) * sign(x)` clamped at 0. Apply the same treatment consistently to both axes rather than leaving Y on a raw comparison in Player.cpp.

findings.title: Menu stick navigation has no hysteresis - PRESENCE and ABSENCE thresholds are both 0.8, so stick jitter repeats moves
findings.detail:
The two constants exist specifically to form a hysteresis band and are set to the same value:

```cpp
constexpr float DIGITAL_PRESENCE_THRESHOLD = 0.8f;   // MenuInput.h:11
constexpr float DIGITAL_ABSENCE_THRESHOLD  = 0.8f;   // MenuInput.h:12
```

They are then used as the two ends of an edge test that is consequently a bare threshold crossing:

```cpp
bool analog_down = previous.left_analog_stick.y > DIGITAL_PRESENCE_THRESHOLD &&
                   current.left_analog_stick.y  < DIGITAL_ABSENCE_THRESHOLD;   // MenuInput.cpp:72-75
```

With presence == absence this reduces to `prev > 0.8 && cur < 0.8`, i.e. it fires on *any* crossing of 0.8, in either direction of noise. Identical for up (76-79), left (80-83) and right (84-87).

Compounding it, `MenuInput::get_raw_input` deliberately asks for unfiltered axes: `GetState(gamepad_num, GamePad::DEAD_ZONE_NONE)` (MenuInput.cpp:19). So a worn or drifting stick parked around 0.80 produces prev>0.8 / cur<0.8 repeatedly and the menu highlight walks by itself at up to 60 moves/second, each one also firing `play_wave(DIRECTION_SOUND)` (e.g. MainMenu.cpp:172).

Separately, note the navigation is release-triggered (the move fires when the stick returns *below* threshold, not when it is pushed), which makes menus feel laggy and gives no auto-repeat when a direction is held - but that at least is a deliberate choice; the missing hysteresis is not.
findings.suggestion: Set `DIGITAL_PRESENCE_THRESHOLD` meaningfully above `DIGITAL_ABSENCE_THRESHOLD` (e.g. 0.7 / 0.4) so the edge test has a real dead band, and switch `get_raw_input` to `DEAD_ZONE_CIRCULAR` so drift is filtered before it reaches the comparison. Consider trigger-on-press with a repeat delay rather than trigger-on-release.

findings.title: `throw new std::exception` in two branches that are provably unreachable dead code
findings.suggestion: Delete both branches - they encode an invariant the code above already guarantees. If a real invariant check is wanted, use an assertion. Never `throw new`; and prefer `std::runtime_error`/`std::logic_error` with a message over MSVC's non-standard `std::exception(const char*)`.

findings.title: `get_menu_inputs() const` is a stateful edge-consuming poll disguised as a const getter
findings.suggestion: Split polling from reading: have the owning state (`GameMenu`/`GameLevel`) call `MenuInput::update()` exactly once per frame and cache the snapshot, then have `MenuPage::get_menu_inputs() const` return a `const&` to that cached snapshot. That makes the const honest and makes double-reads harmless.

findings.title: Player slot count hardcoded as literal 4 in six places instead of GamePad::MAX_PLAYER_COUNT
findings.detail:
The magic number 4 is repeated across both input pumps with no named constant:

- `RawPlayerInput _prev_inputs[4];` (PlayerInput.h:34)
- `RawPlayerInput current[4];` and the two `for (int i = 0; i < 4; i++)` loops (PlayerInput.cpp:121, 122, 127)
- `RawMenuInput _prev_inputs[4];` (MenuInput.h:50)
- `RawMenuInput current[4];` and two loops (MenuInput.cpp:133, 134, 139)

DirectXTK already publishes the right value: `GamePad::MAX_PLAYER_COUNT` (GamePad.h:76-79), which is **4 for XInput but 8 when built against GameInput or Windows.Gaming.Input**. So if the engine is ever retargeted to a backend supporting 8 pads, slots 4-7 are silently ignored with no compile error - exactly the kind of hidden platform assumption that defeats the reusable-engine goal.

Also dead in the same area: `Level.h:143` declares `std::vector<PlayerInputData> _player_inputs = std::vector<PlayerInputData>();` which is never read or written anywhere in the project - a leftover of an earlier design where `Level` cached the frame's inputs, and precisely the member that would have made the Level.cpp:192 bounds bug visible.
findings.suggestion: Replace all six literals with `DirectX::GamePad::MAX_PLAYER_COUNT` (or a single engine-level `constexpr int MAX_PLAYERS` if you want the engine to own the number), use `std::array<RawPlayerInput, MAX_PLAYERS>` instead of C arrays, and delete the dead `Level::_player_inputs` member.

findings.title: Every draw task mutates the same shared game objects: unsynchronised data race on Player/PaintTile state
findings.detail:
`Level::draw_active_level` (Level.cpp:386-397) submits one task per *partition of players*, and each task runs `draw_player_view_level`, which iterates **all** objects, not just its own partition:

```cpp
for (auto& object : *this->_non_collision_objects)  // Level.cpp:516
    if (object->is_visible_in_viewport(camera_view)) object->draw(sprite_batches->at(i), camera);
for (auto& object : *this->_collision_objects)      // Level.cpp:525
    ...
for (auto& object : *this->_player_objects)         // Level.cpp:534
    ...
```

With 4 players there are 4 concurrent tasks and every task calls `draw()` on every one of those objects. `IGameObject::draw` is declared **non-const** (IGameObject.h:11-12) and the implementations write member state:

`Player::draw` (Player.cpp:47-88):
```cpp
this->_animation_state = new_animation_state;          // :59
TextureObject::set_sprite_sheet_name(info.sprite_sheet); // :62  (std::string assignment)
TextureObject::set_element_name(info.uniform_texture);   // :63  (std::string assignment)
set_animation_strip_and_reset(...); set_frame_time(...);  // :65-72
TextureObject::set_effects(effects);                     // :83
AnimationObject::set_effects(effects);                   // :86
```

`PaintTile::draw` (PaintTile.cpp:34-53) does the same: `this->set_colour(...)`, `this->_splash.set_colour(...)`, `this->_splash.set_rectangle_center(...)` — and every `StructurePaintable` forwards `draw` to its whole tile grid (StructurePaintable.cpp:45-52), so thousands of tiles are concurrently written by 4 threads.

These are plain non-atomic member writes, including `std::string` assignment (which reallocates). Four threads writing the same `std::string` is heap corruption, not just a torn value. There is no mutex, no atomic, no per-thread copy anywhere in the codebase.

This is the root design error behind the whole parallel-draw scheme: `draw` was allowed to be a mutating operation, so it can never be run concurrently over a shared scene.
findings.suggestion: Make `IGameObject::draw` (and every override) `const`, and move all the state changes it currently performs — animation-state selection, sprite-sheet/element switching, effects flags, paint-tile colour — into `update()`, which runs single-threaded. The compiler will then enforce that a draw task cannot mutate shared scene state. Until that refactor lands, the parallel draw path is not safe and `draw_active_level` should fall back to the serial loop that is still sitting commented out at Level.cpp:402-490.

findings.title: SpriteSheet::draw calls std::map::operator[] on a shared sheet from up to 16 worker threads
findings.suggestion: Make both string-keyed overloads `const` and replace `_sprite_frames[frame_name]` with `auto it = _sprite_frames.find(frame_name); if (it == _sprite_frames.end()) throw/log;`. That removes the mutation, makes the missing-frame case loud instead of silent, and is a prerequisite for any multithreaded draw. Longer term, resolve frame names to indices/handles once at load time so the render path does no string lookups at all.

findings.title: draw_zoom_out_level_component runs on a worker thread but mutates ViewportManager and touches the IMMEDIATE device context
findings.detail:
`draw_zoom_out_level` pushes the whole zoom-out draw onto the pool:

```cpp
void Level::draw_zoom_out_level(...) const
{
    int num_threads = this->_thread_pool->get_max_num_threads();   // :599  never used (C4189 under /W4)
    this->_thread_pool->add_task([this, deferred_contexts, command_lists, sprite_batches]()
        { this->draw_zoom_out_level_component(deferred_contexts, command_lists, sprite_batches); });  // :601
    this->_thread_pool->wait_for_tasks_to_complete();               // :606
}
```

The callback body then does, **on a background thread**:

```cpp
this->_viewport_manager->set_layout(screen_layout::ONE_PLAYER);  // :619
this->_viewport_manager->apply_player_viewport(0);               // :620
```

Two separate defects:

1. `ViewportManager::set_layout` (ViewportManager.cpp:79-82) is a **non-const mutator** writing the shared `_layout` member that the main thread reads from `get_all_viewports`, `get_player_viewport`, `get_viewport_dividers`. It is reached from a `const` member function through the non-const raw pointer `ViewportManager* _viewport_manager` (Level.h:118) — the `const` on `draw_zoom_out_level` is decoration only. It is also a permanent side effect hidden inside a draw call: the layout is clobbered to ONE_PLAYER and never restored.

2. `apply_player_viewport(int)` — the one-argument overload (ViewportManager.cpp:63-70) — does:
```cpp
auto context = this->_device_resources->GetD3DDeviceContext();  // the IMMEDIATE context
context->RSSetViewports(1, &vp);
this->_sprite_batch->SetViewport(vp);                            // sprite batch #0, owned by deferred ctx 0
```
So a worker thread issues a command on the immediate context and reconfigures SpriteBatch 0 while the main thread is inside `Game::render`/`Present`. `ID3D11DeviceContext` is explicitly not thread-safe; the whole point of the 16 deferred contexts (Game.cpp:52, DeviceResources.cpp:716-730) is that workers must never touch the immediate one. The three-argument overload that takes an explicit context exists (ViewportManager.cpp:53-61) and is what the rest of the worker code correctly uses (Level.cpp:506, MenuPage.cpp:107).

Submitting exactly one task and then immediately blocking on it also means this path pays a full thread-pool round trip to gain zero parallelism.
findings.suggestion: Do not run this on the pool at all — call `draw_zoom_out_level_component` directly on the calling thread and delete the unused `num_threads`. Hoist `set_layout` out of the draw path into `Level::update` (draw must not change simulation/presentation state). Replace `apply_player_viewport(0)` with the three-arg overload `apply_player_viewport(0, deferred_contexts->at(0), sprite_batches->at(0))` so the immediate context is never touched off the main thread, and delete the one-argument overload so it cannot be reached again.

findings.title: No exception barrier in work_callback: every draw body throws, so one bad frame terminates the process and leaks the closure
findings.detail:
```cpp
void CALLBACK ThreadPool::work_callback(PTP_CALLBACK_INSTANCE instance, PVOID parameter, PTP_WORK work)
{
    std::function<void()>* task = static_cast<std::function<void()>*>(parameter);
    (*task)();      // :63  no try/catch
    delete task;    // :64  skipped if (*task)() throws
}
```

The bodies this invokes throw as a matter of routine:
- `Level::draw_player_view_level`: `throw std::exception("Deferred context not created")` (Level.cpp:500) and `throw std::exception("Failed to finish command list")` (Level.cpp:590)
- `Level::draw_zoom_out_level_component`: Level.cpp:616 and :649
- `MenuPage::draw_mobject_in_viewports`: MenuPage.cpp:96 and :120
- plus every `->at(i)` in those functions (Level.cpp:498, 503, 506, 587; MenuPage.cpp:176) can throw `std::out_of_range`
- and `DeviceResources::get_deferred_context` (MenuPage.cpp:175) throws too — see the separate `noexcept` finding.

A C++ exception unwinding out of a Win32 thread-pool callback finds no handler on the worker thread's stack; the result is an unhandled-exception process termination, not a caught error. Consequences, in order: (a) the process dies with no diagnostic tying it back to the draw code, (b) `delete task` never runs so the heap `std::function` leaks (moot at that point, but it is the same missing-cleanup bug that bites if cancellation is ever added), (c) `wait_for_tasks_to_complete` at Level.cpp:399 / :606 / MenuPage.cpp:150 is never reached, so the `PTP_WORK` handles are never closed either.

There is no `try`/`catch` anywhere on the path either — `Game::tick` (Game.cpp:75-84) and the message loop (Main.cpp:213-224) have none, so even a main-thread throw is an unhandled crash.
findings.suggestion: Wrap the invocation: `try { (*task)(); } catch (...) { /* record to an atomic failure flag or a per-batch exception_ptr */ }` and put the `delete` in a `std::unique_ptr<std::function<void()>> owner{static_cast<...>(parameter)};` so it is released on every path. Then have `wait_for_tasks_to_complete` rethrow the captured `exception_ptr` on the calling thread (the standard `std::async`/`packaged_task` contract) so failures surface where they can be handled. Separately, stop using exceptions as the reporting channel for per-frame conditions like "context is not deferred" — that is an assertion about program structure, not a runtime error.

findings.title: get_deferred_context is declared noexcept but throws — guaranteed std::terminate, called from a worker thread
findings.detail:
Declaration:
```cpp
ID3D11DeviceContext* get_deferred_context(int index) const noexcept;   // DeviceResources.h:88
```

Definition:
```cpp
ID3D11DeviceContext* DeviceResources::get_deferred_context(int index) const noexcept
{
    if (index < 0 || index >= this->_deferred_contexts->size())
    {
        throw std::out_of_range("Invalid index.");   // DeviceResources.cpp:742
    }
    return this->_deferred_contexts->at(index);      // :744  .at() can throw too
}
```

Throwing out of a `noexcept` function calls `std::terminate` immediately — no unwinding, no catch site, no chance for any handler. This is not a theoretical path: it is called from inside a thread-pool task at `MenuPage::draw_range_of_mobjects_in_viewports` (MenuPage.cpp:175) with `i` being an index into the caller's `mobjects` vector, while the guard is against the number of deferred contexts (16). Any menu page that pushes more than 16 `MObject`s into its `mobjects` vector — see the pattern at MainMenu.cpp:38-45, PauseMenu.cpp:205, ResultsMenu.cpp:204-211, all currently 2 — terminates the process from a background thread.

Secondary: `index >= this->_deferred_contexts->size()` compares `int` against `size_t` (C4018 under /W4, which is enabled but not treated as an error), and `_deferred_contexts` is dereferenced without a null check even though it is `nullptr` until `create_deferred_contexts` runs.
findings.suggestion: Drop `noexcept` from both the declaration and the definition (or, better, keep `noexcept` and change the contract: return `nullptr`, or assert on the precondition, since an out-of-range context index is a programming error not a runtime condition). Then fix the real bug behind it: `draw_range_of_mobjects_in_viewports` should index the context/command-list/sprite-batch arrays by *task* index, not by mobject index, so the number of drawable widgets is decoupled from the number of deferred contexts.

findings.title: OnDeviceRestored rebuilds ThreadPool, Partitioner, _dt, CommonStates and ResourceManager, but the live Level keeps the old raw pointers
findings.detail:
`OnDeviceRestored` simply re-runs the full construction path:

```cpp
void Game::OnDeviceRestored()
{
    create_device_dependent_resources();   // Game.cpp:284
    create_window_size_dependent_resources();
}
```

and `create_device_dependent_resources` (Game.cpp:218-261) **replaces** objects that are already published to, and cached by, live gameplay code:

```cpp
this->_thread_pool = std::make_unique<ThreadPool>(NUM_THREADS_MIN, NUM_THREADS_MAX);  // :236 destroys the old pool
this->_data->set_thread_pool(this->_thread_pool.get());                                // :237
this->_resource_manager = std::make_unique<ResourceManager>();                          // :239
this->_dt = std::make_unique<float>(0.f);                                               // :244 old float freed
this->_viewport_manager = std::make_unique<ViewportManager>(...);                       // :247
_states = std::make_unique<CommonStates>(device);                                       // :252
this->_partitioner = std::make_unique<Partitioner>();                                   // :255
```

Republishing into `GameData` is not enough, because `Level` and the objects under it snapshot those raw pointers **once**, at construction. `GameLevel::init` (GameStates.cpp:113-120) passes `get_thread_pool()`, `get_partitioner()`, `get_dt()`, `get_resource_manager()` and `get_common_states()->PointClamp()` into `LevelBuilder`, which stores them in `Level` as `ThreadPool* _thread_pool` (Level.h:146), `const Partitioner* _partitioner` (:147), `const float* _dt` (:140), `ID3D11SamplerState* _sampler_state` (:141), `ViewportManager* _viewport_manager` (:118), `ResourceManager* _resource_manager` (:119). The same `const float* _dt` is copied into ~26 other classes (Player, Weapon, AnimationObject — see `*this->_dt` at AnimationObject.cpp:88).

So the first frame after any device reset (fullscreen alt-tab, driver TDR, GPU hot-swap, `HandleDeviceLost` at DeviceResources.cpp:493), `Level::draw_active_level` calls `this->_thread_pool->get_max_num_threads()` (Level.cpp:379) on a destroyed `ThreadPool`, `Level::get_dt()` reads a freed `float`, and `_sampler_state` points at an `ID3D11SamplerState` released by `_states.reset()` (Game.cpp:276). All four are use-after-free.

Note also that nothing drains the pool before it is replaced: line 236 destroys the old `ThreadPool` while, in principle, its callbacks could still be outstanding. `~ThreadPool` blocks (see the `CloseThreadpoolCleanupGroupMembers` finding), so it would deadlock-or-crash rather than silently corrupt, but the ordering is unguarded either way.
findings.suggestion: Split `create_device_dependent_resources` into (a) genuinely device-dependent GPU objects that must be recreated — SpriteBatches, CommonStates, textures — and (b) device-independent services that must NOT be — ThreadPool, Partitioner, the frame-time value, the resource *manager* (as opposed to its GPU payloads). Only (a) should run in `OnDeviceRestored`. Then stop distributing raw snapshots: pass frame time as a `float` parameter to `update(float dt)` instead of a `const float*` member, and have long-lived objects reach services through the `GameData` accessor at point of use rather than caching the pointer at construction — or, better for the reusable-engine goal, inject an interface reference whose implementation can be swapped behind the callers' backs.

findings.title: HandleDeviceLost destroys the D3D device but never recreates the deferred contexts; SpriteBatches are then built on dead contexts
findings.detail:
`HandleDeviceLost` resets everything and recreates the device:

```cpp
m_d3dContext.Reset();  // :430
m_d3dDevice.Reset();   // :443
CreateDeviceResources();
CreateWindowSizeDependentResources();
if (m_deviceNotify) m_deviceNotify->OnDeviceRestored();   // :451
```

It never calls `create_deferred_contexts` (DeviceResources.cpp:716-730), which is invoked exactly once, from `Game::initialize` (Game.cpp:52). So `_deferred_contexts` still holds the 16 `ID3D11DeviceContext*` created from the **destroyed** device.

Then `OnDeviceRestored` → `create_device_dependent_resources` immediately builds new SpriteBatches on those dead contexts:
```cpp
this->_sprite_batches[i] = std::move(std::make_unique<SpriteBatch>(
    this->_device_resources->get_deferred_context(i)));   // Game.cpp:229
```
DirectXTK's `SpriteBatch` constructor calls `GetDevice` on that context, so this is a call through a dangling COM pointer. And every draw task dereferences the same dead pointers — `deferred_contexts->at(i)->GetType()` (Level.cpp:498), `FinishCommandList` (Level.cpp:587).

Compounding it, those contexts are raw `ID3D11DeviceContext*` in `std::unique_ptr<std::vector<ID3D11DeviceContext*>>` (DeviceResources.h:128) and are **never `Release()`d** — `~DeviceResources() = default` (DeviceResources.h:32), and `create_deferred_contexts` starts with `this->_deferred_contexts = std::make_unique<std::vector<...>>();` (:718), which drops the old vector without releasing its contents. So the 16 contexts leak at every exit, and 16 more would leak on every re-call.
findings.suggestion: Store deferred contexts as `std::vector<Microsoft::WRL::ComPtr<ID3D11DeviceContext>>` so they are released deterministically, and call `create_deferred_contexts(NUM_THREADS_MAX)` from inside `CreateDeviceResources()` (or at the top of `Game::OnDeviceRestored`, before `create_device_dependent_resources`) so the context pool is always rebuilt with the device it belongs to. Everything downstream that caches a context pointer must then be rebuilt too — which is the same stale-snapshot problem as the ThreadPool/CommonStates finding.

findings.title: Destruction order is inverted: the live State outlives every Game member, and the ThreadPool is destroyed after the SpriteBatches its tasks use
findings.detail:
`class Game final : public DX::IDeviceNotify, public StateContext` (Game.h:16) and the members are declared:

```
:59 _device_resources   :62 _states       :64 _resource_loader  :65 _resource_manager
:66 _dt                 :67 _state        :68 _gamepad          :69 _viewport_manager
:70 _data               :71 _thread_pool  :72 _sprite_batches   :73 _sprite_batches_ptrs
:74 _audio_engine       :75 _partitioner
```

C++ destroys members in reverse declaration order, then base classes. At `g_game.reset()` (Main.cpp:226) the actual sequence is therefore:

`_partitioner` → `_audio_engine` → `_sprite_batches_ptrs` → **`_sprite_batches`** → **`_thread_pool`** → `_viewport_manager` → `_dt` → `_resource_manager` → `_states` → `_device_resources` → **then the `StateContext` base, which finally destroys the live `GameMenu`/`GameLevel` and the whole `Level` under it.**

Two concrete problems:

1. **`_sprite_batches` is destroyed one step before `_thread_pool`.** `~ThreadPool` (ThreadPool.cpp:30-36) calls `CloseThreadpoolCleanupGroupMembers(_cleanup_group, FALSE, nullptr)`, and `FALSE` means *do not cancel — wait for outstanding callbacks to run to completion*. So the one place in the program that actually drains the pool runs **after** the `SpriteBatch` objects those callbacks write into (`sprite_batches->at(i)->Begin(...)`, Level.cpp:513) have already been destroyed, and after `_sprite_batches_ptrs` — the very vector `GameData` hands to the tasks — has been destroyed. Any task still outstanding is guaranteed to use freed memory on a background thread.

2. **The active `State` is destroyed dead last**, after `_device_resources`, `_resource_manager` and `_states`. `Level` and everything it owns (players, projectiles, sprite sheets holding raw `ID3D11ShaderResourceView*`, `SoundBank*` into the already-destroyed `ResourceManager`) is torn down when the D3D device, the resource manager and the sampler states are already gone. `Game::_state` at line 67 is a *third* problem: it is a dead member that never appears anywhere in Game.cpp — the real state lives in the private `StateContext::_state` (StateContext.h:16). It reads as though `Game` owns its state in member position, which is exactly the ordering guarantee it does *not* provide.

The only reason this does not crash today is that no draw ever leaves work outstanding — which is an accident of every draw calling `wait_for_tasks_to_complete` before returning, not a guarantee the design enforces.
findings.suggestion: Give `Game` an explicit teardown that runs before any member is destroyed: `Game::~Game()` should first `transition_to(nullptr)` (or add a `StateContext::clear_state()`) to drop the active State while all services are still alive, then `_thread_pool->wait_for_tasks_to_complete()` / reset the pool, then let the members go. Delete the dead `_state` member at Game.h:67. Better still, stop relying on declaration order for lifetime at all: make the pool the first thing constructed and the first thing shut down, and hold the state machine by composition (`StateContext _states;` as a member) rather than by inheritance, so its position in the destruction order is visible and controllable.

findings.title: add_task is not exception-safe and there is no RAII drain, so a mid-loop throw abandons tasks pointing at the caller's stack
findings.detail:
```cpp
void ThreadPool::add_task(std::function<void()> task)
{
    PTP_WORK work = CreateThreadpoolWork(work_callback,
        new std::function<void()>(task), &_callback_environment);   // :40-41
    if (!work)
    {
        throw std::runtime_error("Failed to create thread pool work object.");  // :44  leaks the new'd std::function
    }
    _work_items.push_back(work);   // :46  can throw bad_alloc -> `work` leaked, never closed
    SubmitThreadpoolWork(work);    // :47
}
```

(The submit/push_back ordering itself is fine — push happens first, so `wait_for_tasks_to_complete` cannot miss a submitted handle. The problem is what happens when the loop around it unwinds.)

All three call sites submit in a loop and only wait *after* the loop, with nothing between them but ordinary code:

```cpp
for (int i = 0; i < partitioned_players.size(); i++)
    this->_thread_pool->add_task([...]{...});   // Level.cpp:388
this->_thread_pool->wait_for_tasks_to_complete();  // Level.cpp:399  — NOT in a destructor
```

If `add_task` throws on iteration 2 of 4, the two tasks already submitted keep running while the stack unwinds straight past line 399. What they are pointing at is the caller's stack:

- **MenuPage.cpp:142-143** captures two locals **by reference**: `&partitioned_mobjects` (local at :134) and `&command_lists` (local at :128). It also captures `mobjects`, a pointer to the *caller's* local (e.g. `std::vector<...> mobjects;` at MainMenu.cpp:38, ResultsMenu.cpp:204, MainMenu.cpp:1775 — nine such sites).
- **Level.cpp:388-389** captures `command_lists`, a pointer to `GameLevel::draw`'s local `std::vector<ID3D11CommandList*> command_lists(...)` (GameStates.cpp:313).
- **Level.cpp:601** captures the same `command_lists` pointer.

So on the throw path, live background threads write `command_list` out-params and read the partition vector through references to frames that no longer exist. The `PTP_WORK` handles are also leaked (never `CloseThreadpoolWork`d) and `_work_items` is left holding stale entries for the next batch to trip over.

This is entirely unguarded: no `try`/`catch`, and `wait_for_tasks_to_complete` is a plain statement rather than a destructor, at all three sites (Level.cpp:399, Level.cpp:606, MenuPage.cpp:150).
findings.suggestion: Introduce a scoped batch handle — `class TaskBatch { ~TaskBatch() { pool.wait(); } }` — obtained before the submit loop, so the drain happens on every exit path including unwinding. Inside `add_task`, own the closure with `auto payload = std::make_unique<std::function<void()>>(std::move(task));` and only `payload.release()` after `CreateThreadpoolWork` succeeds *and* `push_back` succeeds; reserve the vector up front so `push_back` cannot throw. Separately, stop capturing stack locals by reference into tasks — the by-value capture used at Level.cpp:388 is the right pattern, and MenuPage should match it.

findings.title: ThreadPool has no batch identity and no documented thread affinity: one shared _work_items vector serves two unrelated subsystems
findings.suggestion: Return a handle from submission — `[[nodiscard]] TaskBatch submit(span<function<void()>>)` — and have `wait` be a member of the batch, so drains cannot cross owners. Add an assert (or a `std::thread::id` check in debug) that `add_task`/`wait_for_tasks_to_complete` are only ever called from the thread that created the pool, and say so in a comment on the class. Longer term this should be `std::async`/a `std::latch`-based parallel-for, not a hand-rolled wrapper over PTP_WORK; the Win32-specific bits are the least reusable part of the engine.

findings.title: ~ThreadPool silently blocks the main thread on all outstanding callbacks, and the cancel path (if ever used) leaks every closure
findings.suggestion: Call `wait_for_tasks_to_complete()` explicitly as the first statement of `~ThreadPool` so the drain is visible in the source rather than buried in a Win32 flag, and add a comment stating that the destructor blocks. Then remove the raw `new`/`delete` entirely: pass a `std::unique_ptr<std::function<void()>>::release()`d pointer and reclaim it with a `unique_ptr` at the top of `work_callback`, and register a cleanup-group cancel callback (the third argument at ThreadPool.cpp:27) that deletes the closure, so cancellation becomes a supported option instead of a leak.

findings.title: transition_to destroys the running State from inside that State's own update(), leaving `this` dangling for the rest of the call chain
findings.suggestion: Make the transition deferred: have `transition_to` stash the incoming state in a `_pending_state` member and have `StateContext::update()` perform the swap after `_state->update()` returns, at a point where no State frame is on the stack. That makes self-destruction structurally impossible and gives you one well-defined moment per frame at which it is safe to tear down a Level — which is also the right place to assert that the thread pool is idle.

findings.title: Two heap allocations plus a std::function copy per task, plus a full partition-vector copy per closure, every frame
findings.detail:
`add_task` takes the closure **by value** and then **copies** it again into the heap:

```cpp
void ThreadPool::add_task(std::function<void()> task)          // :38  copy #1 (caller's lambda -> std::function)
{
    PTP_WORK work = CreateThreadpoolWork(work_callback,
        new std::function<void()>(task), &_callback_environment);  // :41  copy #2, not a move
```

`task` is a by-value parameter and is never used again after line 41, so `std::move(task)` is free and correct; as written every submission does a redundant `std::function` copy, which for a non-SBO-sized closure is an extra allocation on top of the `new`.

The caller makes it worse. `Level::draw_active_level` captures the partition table **by value** into each of up to 16 closures:

```cpp
auto partitioned_players = this->_partitioner->partition(this->_player_objects->size(), num_threads);  // :382
for (int i = 0; i < partitioned_players.size(); i++)
    this->_thread_pool->add_task([this, i, partitioned_players, ...]{ ... });   // :388  full vector copy per task
```

Each copy heap-allocates a `std::vector<std::pair<int,int>>` that every task then indexes at exactly one position, `partitioned_players[i]`. Also note `Partitioner::partition` (Partitioner.cpp:4-22) returns a fresh `std::vector` by value on every call, so the table itself is reallocated every frame even though it only changes when the player count does.

Net cost on the hot path, at 60 Hz: per task, one `CreateThreadpoolWork`, one `new std::function`, one redundant `std::function` copy, and one vector copy — for a workload of at most four players. (`partitioned_players.size()` is also `size_t` compared against `int i` at line 386 — C4018 under the project's /W4.)
findings.suggestion: `std::move(task)` at line 41. Capture only what each task needs — `int start = partitioned_players[i].first, end = ...;` before the lambda, then capture the two ints by value — instead of the whole vector. Cache the partition table in `Level` and recompute it only when the player count changes. Best of all, replace the per-frame submit/drain with a persistent parallel-for that takes an index range, so no closures are allocated on the render path at all.

findings.title: Paintable-face index map is wrong for 3 of 4 faces; JSON faces paint on the wrong side of the structure
findings.detail:
`generate_paint_tiles()` maps edge indices to faces as `i==0 -> top_edge`, `i==1 -> right_edge`, `i==2 -> bottom_edge`, `i==3 -> left_edge` (lines 195-210). But `RectangleF::get_edges()` (ArtAttack/MattMath.cpp:808-818) returns `{ top, bottom, left, right }`. The correct map is 0->top, 1->bottom, 2->left, 3->right. So only `top` is right; the other three are permuted:
  JSON `bottom:true` -> matches at i==1 -> generates a RIGHT band
  JSON `left:true`   -> matches at i==2 -> generates a BOTTOM band
  JSON `right:true`  -> matches at i==3 -> generates a LEFT band
Because top/bottom bands use `num_paint_tiles_x` and left/right bands use `num_paint_tiles_y`, the permutation also changes the tile count, so the paintable surface area of the map is wrong, not just mirrored. Worked out against the shipped JSON:
  king_of_the_hill.json `castle_ceiling` (1650x25, `bottom:true`): intended 412 tiles across the 1650-wide underside (area 19,800); actually generates 6 tiles as a 12-wide strip on the right end (area 300) - a 66x loss, and the castle ceiling is effectively unpaintable.
  king_of_the_hill.json `castle_wall_right` (25x750, `left:true`): intended 187 tiles down the inner face (area 9,000); actually 6 tiles along the bottom (area 300).
  king_of_the_hill.json `castle_floor_right` (700x25, `left`+`top`): intended 181 tiles; actually 350 - the designer-disabled underside gets a full 700-wide band while the intended left face gets nothing.
  close_quarters.json `lower_paint` (3000x50, `top`+`bottom`): intended 1,500 tiles (area 72,000); actually 762 (area 36,600). The main arena platform's underside cannot be painted at all; instead a 12x50 sliver appears on its right end.
Level totals, actual vs intended: king_of_the_hill 3,348 vs 4,116; close_quarters 1,160 vs 1,898; turbulence 5,574 vs 5,230. Note `castle_wall_left` and `castle_floor_left` in king_of_the_hill happen to keep the same tile count but paint the opposite physical face.
findings.suggestion: Stop matching by index entirely - it couples StructurePaintable to the ordering of an unrelated function. Either have `LevelObjectBuilder` pass a `PaintableFaces { bool left, top, right, bottom; }` struct straight through (the struct is already written and commented out at StructurePaintable.h:17-23 and LevelObjectBuilder.cpp:101-105), or compare the matched segment against `rect.get_top_edge()/get_bottom_edge()/get_left_edge()/get_right_edge()` by value instead of by position in `get_edges()`. If index matching is kept, add a static assertion / unit test pinning `get_edges()` order.

findings.title: winning_ratio divides winner by loser (not by total): yields >100%, negative, inf and NaN percentages
findings.detail:
`winning_ratio() = winning_score() / losing_score()` (line 115) and `losing_percentage() = 100.0f - winning_percentage()` (line 127). Worked through the shipped scoring path: after `Level::get_level_end_info` (ArtAttack/Level.cpp:706-735) sums tile areas, a close_quarters match where A paints the whole 750-tile top band of `lower_paint` (36,000) and B paints the 187-tile top band of `upper_paint` (9,000) gives `winning_ratio() = 36000/9000 = 4.0`, `winning_percentage() = 400%`, `losing_percentage() = -300%`. Three further broken cases:
  - B paints nothing: `losing_score() == 0` -> `36000/0` = +inf under /fp:fast with no trap -> `winning_percentage()` = inf, `losing_percentage()` = -inf, and `std::to_string` would render "inf%".
  - Genuine draw with both non-zero (e.g. 100/100): `winning_team()` is NONE, so `winning_score()` and `losing_score()` BOTH return `team_a_area` (lines 90-93 and 107-110) -> ratio 1.0 -> 100% / 0% for a draw.
  - Draw with both zero: 0/0 -> NaN for every one of the four functions.
These four functions are currently unreferenced (grepped the whole repo: only `team_a_ratio`/`team_b_ratio` and `team_a_percentage_string`/`team_b_percentage_string` have callers, in ResultsMenu.cpp:131,142,228,241), so no player sees it today - but they are public API of the scoring type and the first caller to reach for `winning_percentage()` gets 400%.
findings.suggestion: Delete `winning_ratio`/`losing_ratio`/`winning_percentage`/`losing_percentage`, or define them over the total: `winning_ratio() = winning_score() / (team_a_area + team_b_area)` with a zero-total guard, and `losing_percentage() = 100 - winning_percentage()` then falls out correctly. Fix `losing_score()`'s NONE branch to return `team_b_area`. Add unit tests for the 0/0, x/0 and draw cases - LevelEndInfo is pure arithmetic and is one of the few things in this codebase that is trivially testable.

findings.title: Paint tiles are never viewport-culled: whole structures' tile lists are drawn per viewport, PaintTile::is_visible_in_viewport is dead code
findings.detail:
`StructurePaintable::draw` unconditionally iterates `_paint_tiles` (lines 48-51 and 57-60). `Level::draw_player_view_level` only culls at the structure level (ArtAttack/Level.cpp:525-531 `object->is_visible_in_viewport(camera_view)`), and `PaintTile::is_visible_in_viewport` (ArtAttack/PaintTile.cpp:149-152) is never called by anything - the only call sites in the codebase are Level.cpp:518/527/536 over `_non_collision_objects`/`_collision_objects`/`_player_objects`, and PaintTiles are in none of those lists.
Numbers for a 4-player split screen (ViewportManager.cpp:208-216 gives 960x540 quadrants; Camera scale is 1.0, MattMath.h:1010, and CameraTools never changes it, so a viewport shows 960x540 world units):
  - turbulence.json generates 5,574 tiles. Fully painted, that is 5,574 x 4 viewports = 22,296 PaintTile::draw calls per frame, each painted tile emitting 2 SpriteBatch::Draw (splash + tile) = 44,592 sprite submissions per frame = 2.68M/sec at 60Hz.
  - `boundary_floor` in turbulence is 6000 wide with 1,500 tiles; a 960-wide viewport can see at most 16% of it, so >=1,260 of its 1,500 tiles are processed off-screen per viewport, 5,040 off-screen tiles per frame across 4 viewports.
  - Each painted tile's draw performs 5 string-keyed `std::map` lookups (SpriteSheetObject.cpp:31-35 -> ResourceManager.cpp:46-58 for the sheet, x3 via the splash path in AnimationObject.cpp:33/141, plus `_sprite_frames[frame_name]` in SpriteSheet.cpp:126): 5,574 x 4 x 5 = 111,480 map lookups per frame.
findings.suggestion: Cull per tile against `camera_view` inside `StructurePaintable::draw` using the already-written `PaintTile::is_visible_in_viewport` (that needs the camera view passed down, so change the IGameObject draw signature to carry it, or precompute the visible index range from the band geometry - the tiles are a regular grid, so the visible span is two integer divisions, not a scan). Longer term this should not be thousands of sprite objects at all: a paintable face is a 1-D array of team ids and should be rendered as a handful of merged quads or a dynamic texture.

findings.title: Splash animation is drawn forever after it finishes, permanently doubling sprite count and leaving a 24x24 team-coloured blob on every painted tile
findings.detail:
`PaintTile::draw` draws `_splash` on every frame for any tile whose `_team != NONE` (lines 49-50, and identically at 69-70) with no check for whether the animation has completed. `splash_1` is defined in ArtAttack/textures/sprite_sheet_1.json:108-119 as 5 frames at 0.05s with `"looping": false`, so `AnimationObject::update` (ArtAttack/AnimationObject.cpp:99-103) clamps `_frame_index` to 4 and sets `_paused = true` after 0.25s - and the tile then keeps submitting frame 4 forever.
Geometry makes it visible, not just costly: `SPLASH_RECTANGLE` is `THICKNESS * 2.0f` = 24x24 (ArtAttack/PaintTile.h:20) centred on a tile that is only ~4 wide x 12 tall, so the frozen splash overhangs the structure's surface by 6 world units and overlaps its 5 nearest neighbours. A fully painted 750-tile face carries 750 permanently-drawn overlapping 24x24 quads (6x overdraw) plus a 6-unit team-coloured fringe sticking out of the geometry.
Cost: this is exactly the 2x in the 44,592-sprites-per-frame figure for turbulence - half of those draws are finished animations.
findings.suggestion: Guard the splash draw with the existing `AnimationObject::is_paused()` (or add a `has_finished()`), and skip `_splash.draw(...)` once the strip has run out. Better: don't give every tile its own animation object at all - a per-structure pool of a few dozen transient splash effects would cover every splash that is actually mid-playback.

findings.title: Adjacent face bands overlap by exactly THICKNESS^2 at each corner, double-counting area and paying ~2x score for corner hits
findings.detail:
The top band spans `x in [left, left+width] , y in [top, top+12]` (lines 223-227); the left band spans `x in [left, left+12] , y in [top, top+height]` (lines 264-268). Their intersection is exactly `THICKNESS x THICKNESS = 144` square units, and the same holds at all four corners. Within a band the tiles tile exactly (`num_tiles * tile_size == width`), so the only overlap is at corners.
Concrete: close_quarters.json `upper_paint` (750x50, all four faces enabled) generates 187 top + 187 bottom + 12 left + 12 right = 398 tiles with total tile area 19,200, but the union of the four bands is 19,200 - 4*144 = 18,624. `StructurePaintable::get_paint_total` (lines 300-318) sums `paint_tile.get_area()` with no de-duplication, so the score over-reports this structure's surface by 576 units (3.09%).
The gameplay-visible half is worse than the aggregate: a single projectile landing in a corner is matched against BOTH the ~3 top tiles and the ~3 left tiles that occupy the same 12x12 square, so it scores roughly twice what the identical shot scores mid-face (a 15x15 spray AABB mid-face claims ~4 tiles x 48 = 192; the same shot in a corner claims ~4 top tiles x 48 plus ~4 left tiles x 50 = ~392).
A second latent case: the top and bottom bands are `2 * THICKNESS = 24` thick combined, and the thinnest shipped paintable is 25 units (`castle_floor_left`, `castle_ceiling`, `central_divider_ledge_paint` are all 25 tall; `castle_wall_left/right` are 25 wide) - a 1-unit margin. Any 23-unit-thick paintable would have its two opposite bands overlap along their entire length.
findings.suggestion: Generate the tile grid from the shape's perimeter once rather than per-face, mitring the corners (start the left/right bands at `top + THICKNESS` and stop at `bottom - THICKNESS`), and assert at construction that `min(width, height) > 2 * THICKNESS`. That fixes both the double-count and the corner scoring exploit.

findings.title: Tile-count division has no zero guard and fabs is applied to the quotient instead of the divisor
findings.detail:
```
const int num_paint_tiles_x = static_cast<int>(std::fabs(get_rectangle().get_width() / WIDTH));
const float paint_tile_width = get_rectangle().get_width() / num_paint_tiles_x;
```
Two defects:
1. `num_paint_tiles_x` is zero for any structure narrower than `WIDTH` (4.0), and the very next line divides by it. Float division by an int-converted zero yields +/-inf under the default masked FP environment (and /fp:fast is on in all four ArtAttack configs), so it does not crash - the face silently produces no tiles and `paint_tile_width` is inf. Same for `num_paint_tiles_y` / `HEIGHT`.
2. The `fabs` is on the quotient, not on the divisor. A negative extent therefore gives a POSITIVE tile count and a NEGATIVE tile size: `width = -100` -> `num = 25`, `paint_tile_width = -4`. Those tiles get negative `RectangleF::get_area()` (MattMath.cpp:819-822), so they subtract from the team's score in `get_paint_total`, and `get_rectangle_i()/get_win_rect()` produce inverted RECTs for SpriteBatch.
Proof that nothing shipped triggers either today: the smallest paintable dimension across all three levels is 25 (king_of_the_hill `castle_wall_left`/`castle_wall_right` 25 wide, `castle_floor_left`/`castle_floor_right`/`castle_ceiling` 25 tall; turbulence `central_divider_ledge_paint` 25 tall), giving `num >= 6`, and every paintable uses the `"rectangle"` form with positive width/height - `grep -c rectangle_tlbr levels/*.json` returns 0 for all three. But the negative path is reachable from data: `LevelObjectBuilder.cpp:88-95` accepts `rectangle_tlbr` and `RectangleF::from_top_left_bottom_right` (MattMath.cpp:1122-1128) does not normalise, so a JSON file with `right < left` produces a negative-width paintable with no diagnostic.
findings.suggestion: Validate the rectangle where it is built (LevelObjectBuilder) - reject non-positive width/height with a message naming the object - and in `generate_paint_tiles` compute `num = std::max(1, static_cast<int>(width / WIDTH))` on an already-positive width. Better still, normalise in `RectangleF::from_top_left_bottom_right` itself.

findings.title: Every projectile hit linear-scans the structure's entire tile list; ~6,000 tile tests per frame on the shipped levels
findings.detail:
`on_collision` walks all of `_paint_tiles` calling `paint_tile.is_colliding(other)` for every tile (lines 89-91). Each of those is a virtual `get_shape()` plus `Shape::AABB_intersects` plus possibly a narrow-phase `intersects` (ArtAttack/PaintTile.cpp:84-109). The tiles are a regular grid whose index could be computed in O(1) from the projectile's AABB.
Sizing it with the shipped data: turbulence's `boundary_floor` holds 1,500 tiles, `left_lower_paint` and `right_lower_paint` 774 each. The sprayer has `shoot_interval = 0.0f` (ArtAttack/weapon_consts.h:41) and `Weapon::check_if_shooting_and_ammo_update` gates on `shoot_timer > shoot_interval` (Weapon.cpp:202), so it emits one projectile per 60Hz fixed update per player - roughly one landing per player per frame in sustained fire. With 4 players spraying the floor that is ~4 x 1,500 = 6,000 tile intersection tests per frame; a burst of 8 projectiles contacting paintables in one frame is ~12,000. Each hit also re-enters from `Level::update_level_logic`'s O(n^2) pair loop (ArtAttack/Level.cpp:277-292).
findings.suggestion: Store the tiles per face in index order with the band origin and pitch, and on a hit convert the projectile AABB to a `[first, last]` index range - a couple of divisions instead of a scan. The tile grid is uniform by construction (`num * tile_size == extent`), so this is exact.

findings.title: Score is share-of-painted, not map coverage: fill bar is always exactly full no matter how little of the level was painted
findings.detail:
`update_team_a_fill`/`update_team_b_fill` set widths to `RESULTS_MENU_TEAM_FILL_SIZE.x * team_a_ratio()` and `* team_b_ratio()` (lines 229 and 242). `team_a_ratio()` is `team_a_area / (team_a_area + team_b_area)` (ArtAttack/LevelEndInfo.cpp:18-33), so the two ratios always sum to 1 and the two bar widths always sum to `RESULTS_MENU_TEAM_FILL_SIZE.x` = 700 - 2*10 = 680 (ResultsMenu.h:17-23). Unpainted area is never computed anywhere - `Level::get_level_end_info` (Level.cpp:706-735) only accumulates painted tile area and never asks a structure for its total paintable area.
Worked example on close_quarters (55,800 units of generated tile area, post-face-bug): A paints `lower_paint`'s 750 top tiles (36,000) and B paints `upper_paint`'s 187 top tiles (9,000); 358 of 1,160 tiles are painted, 19% of the surface. The results screen shows "80.0%" / "20.0%" (LevelEndInfo.cpp:42-61 truncates `std::to_string` at one decimal, which is correct) and a completely full 680px bar - i.e. the identical display you get if the whole map is covered. For a Splatoon-like whose entire point is territory covered, the headline number is measuring the wrong thing.
Degenerate case: if nobody paints anything, `team_a_ratio`/`team_b_ratio` return the hardcoded 0.5 (lines 20-23, 28-31), so an empty map renders as a full bar split 50/50 with "50.0%" on both sides.
findings.suggestion: Have `IPaintableGameObject` also report total paintable area (it already knows - it is `sum(tile.get_area())` over all tiles regardless of team), aggregate it into `LevelEndInfo::total_area`, and express both percentages over that. The bar then reads as coverage with a genuine unpainted remainder, which is what the mechanic is.

findings.title: Every paint tile's animation is ticked every frame, and all N splashes start unpaused so the whole level animates for the first 0.25s
findings.detail:
`StructurePaintable::update` iterates all `_paint_tiles` and calls `PaintTile::update` -> `_splash.update()` (ArtAttack/PaintTile.cpp:30-33) once per fixed update for every tile in the level, painted or not. `AnimationObject::_paused` defaults to **false** (ArtAttack/AnimationObject.h:51) and nothing pauses a freshly built `PaintTileSplash`, so at level start every tile's splash is playing from frame 0. `AnimationObject::update` (AnimationObject.cpp:81-107) calls `get_animation_strip()`, which is two string-keyed `std::map` lookups (SpriteSheetObject.cpp:31-35 -> ResourceManager.cpp:46-58, then SpriteSheet.cpp:15-18).
turbulence: 5,574 tiles x 2 map lookups = 11,148 lookups per update tick for the first 15 ticks (5 frames x 0.05s), on the single game thread, right at level start where the frame budget is already spent on load. After that the splashes pause and `update` early-returns, but the 5,574-element loop still runs every tick forever.
findings.suggestion: Construct `PaintTileSplash` paused (call `stop()` in the PaintTile ctor, or default `_paused = true`), and keep an active-splash list on the structure so `update` touches only the handful of tiles actually animating instead of all 5,574. Resolving the sprite sheet once at construction into a cached pointer would remove the per-frame map lookups entirely.

findings.title: Const draw path mutates shared std::maps from 4 render threads (std::map::operator[]), reached thousands of times per frame by paint tiles
findings.detail:
`SpriteSheet::draw` is non-const and indexes with `this->_sprite_frames[frame_name]` (line 126) - `std::map::operator[]`, which default-constructs and inserts on a miss. It is called from `TextureObject::draw(...) const` (ArtAttack/TextureObject.cpp:26-33), which `PaintTile::draw` invokes at PaintTile.cpp:52/72. The sheet itself is fetched through `ResourceManager::get_sprite_sheet`, which is also `_sprite_sheets[name]` with `operator[]` (ArtAttack/ResourceManager.cpp:46-58) - and whose `catch (const std::out_of_range&)` at line 53 is dead, because `operator[]` never throws that; a typo'd sheet name silently inserts a null `unique_ptr` and the caller dereferences nullptr.
`Level::draw_active_level` dispatches these draws onto up to 4 ThreadPool tasks over the same `ResourceManager`/`SpriteSheet` instances (ArtAttack/Level.cpp:388-397), so four threads concurrently invoke non-const members on the same containers - formally a data race per [res.on.data.races], and a real one (RB-tree rebalance under concurrent readers) the moment any key is missing. Paint tiles make this the single hottest path in the renderer: 5,574 tiles x 4 viewports x 5 map lookups = 111,480 concurrent map accesses per frame on turbulence.
findings.suggestion: Make both lookups const and non-mutating: `SpriteSheet::draw(...) const` using `_sprite_frames.at(frame_name)`, and `ResourceManager::get_sprite_sheet(...) const` using `find()` with an explicit throw on miss. Then resolve `SpriteSheet*` and the `SpriteFrame*`/`AnimationStrip*` once at object construction and cache the pointers, so the render threads do pure reads of immutable data.

findings.title: StructurePaintable does not override is_colliding, so it inherits Structure's unconditional `return false` - painting works only by accident of loop order
findings.detail:
`StructurePaintable` overrides `update`, both `draw`s, `on_collision` and `get_paint_total`, but not `is_colliding`, so it uses `Structure::is_colliding` which is `return false;` (ArtAttack/Structure.cpp:43-46). In `Level::update_level_logic` the object-vs-object loop tests `object->is_colliding(object_2)` and, on a hit, calls `on_collision` on both sides (ArtAttack/Level.cpp:287-291). Paint therefore fires only in the ordering where the PROJECTILE is the outer `object` - `Projectile::is_colliding` accepts `STRUCTURE_PAINTABLE` (Projectile.cpp:98-106). In the reverse ordering the structure reports false and nothing happens.
The mechanic works today, but it depends entirely on the double-sided `on_collision` dispatch at lines 289-290 and on projectiles being in the same list as structures. Anyone who changes the loop to a single-sided `object->on_collision(object_2)`, adds an early `continue` for objects that report no collisions, or moves projectiles to their own list, silently disables the entire paint system with no compile error and no runtime error. It also means `Level.cpp:268-272` (collision-object vs player) can never fire for a paintable.
findings.suggestion: Give StructurePaintable a real `is_colliding` (type filter for offensive projectiles + AABB against the structure rect) so the object is honest about its own collisions, and stop relying on `on_collision` being invoked on both participants. The deeper fix is to have one place decide a pair collides and one place resolve it, instead of every concrete class re-implementing the same broad+narrow phase (the identical body appears in Player.cpp:148-185, PaintTile.cpp:84-109, ProjectileSpray.cpp:56-87 and the other four projectiles).

findings.title: Zoom-out/overview draw path has no visibility culling at all, and runs single-threaded exactly when the map is most painted
findings.detail:
`draw_zoom_out_level_component` iterates `_non_collision_objects`, `_collision_objects` and `_player_objects` and calls `object->draw(sprite_batch, camera)` with no `is_visible_in_viewport` check (lines 628-642), unlike the active path at 516-540. This is the state used for `ZOOM_OUT`, `OVERVIEW` and `FINISHED` (Level.cpp:365-372) - i.e. the end-of-match survey of the painted map. It is dispatched as a single ThreadPool task (lines 601-606) onto deferred context 0 with one SpriteBatch.
Worst case on turbulence, fully painted: 5,574 tiles x 2 sprites = 11,148 SpriteBatch::Draw plus ~27,870 string-keyed map lookups, all in one batch on one thread, at the exact moment tile paint coverage peaks. The active 4-way split path at least spreads its work across 4 deferred contexts.
findings.suggestion: Apply the same `is_visible_in_viewport(camera_view)` gate the active path uses, computing the view rect from `_zoom_out_camera`, and cull per tile (see the StructurePaintable::draw finding). The overview camera is zoomed out so most objects will pass, which is exactly why the per-tile merge into a few quads matters more here than anywhere else.

findings.title: Tile vector is built with push_back(const&) and no reserve: ~25k PaintTile constructions and 151 reallocations to produce 5,574 tiles
findings.detail:
`auto paint_tiles = std::vector<PaintTile>();` (line 106) is never reserved, and each band does `auto paint_tile = PaintTile(...); paint_tiles.push_back(paint_tile);` (lines 228-233, 249-254, 269-274, 289-294) - a named local copied in, not moved or emplaced. So each tile costs one construction plus one copy, on top of MSVC's 1.5x growth moves.
Measured against the shipped data (sizeof(PaintTile) ~= 376 bytes on MSVC x64 release: DrawObject 56 + two std::strings 64 = TextureObject 120, + ICollisionGameObject vptr 8 + RectangleF 24 (Shape is polymorphic, MattMath.h:68-89, so the rect carries a vptr) + player_team 4 + TeamColour 32 + const float* 8 + PaintTileSplash 176):
  king_of_the_hill 3,348 tiles = 1.20 MiB, 169 vector reallocations, 7,835 move-constructions, 14,531 PaintTile constructions total
  close_quarters   1,160 tiles = 0.42 MiB,  34 reallocations,  3,089 moves,  5,409 constructions
  turbulence       5,574 tiles = 2.00 MiB, 151 reallocations, 13,505 moves, 24,653 constructions
Each of the 5,574 real constructions also builds a `PaintTileSplash`, whose ctor does two string-keyed map lookups (AnimationObject.cpp:21) = 11,148 map lookups at load. And 128 of every tile's 376 bytes are four `std::string` members holding just two distinct literals ("sprite_sheet_1", "pixel", "sprite_sheet_1", "splash_1") - they fit SSO so there is no extra heap traffic, but that is 713 KiB of duplicated string storage on turbulence.
findings.suggestion: `paint_tiles.reserve(2 * num_paint_tiles_x + 2 * num_paint_tiles_y)` up front and `emplace_back(...)` in place. That removes every copy and every reallocation. Replacing the four per-tile `std::string`s with a shared, resolved `SpriteSheet*` + `const RECT*` would cut ~34% of the per-tile footprint and every one of the per-frame map lookups at the same time.
